<meta>This page serves as the formal title page for the 1550 first edition of Girolamo Cardano’s "De Subtilitate." It follows the modern library identification page. The page features several historical ownership marks, including a handwritten note identifying its former place in the Jesuit Roman College library and a stamp from the Vatican's censorship office.</meta>

<meta>Handwritten note at top: Entered into the Catalog of the Roman College of the Society of Jesus. Shelf mark: 12 / 26 / H / 6</meta>
<meta>Institutional stamps present on left and right sides of the page.</meta>

# GIROLAMO <note>original: "Hieronymi"</note>
## Cardano, Physician of Milan <note>original: "Cardani Medici Mediolanensis"</note>
# ON SUBTLETY <note>original: "De Subtilitate"</note>
### In <term>twenty-one books</term> <note>Latin: "Libri xxi." Cardano organized this massive encyclopedia of natural wonders into 21 distinct sections or "books."</term> Dedicated to the most illustrious Prince Ferrante Gonzaga, Governor of the province of Milan.

<margin>
<insert>
Stamp: SACRED CONGREGATION FOR THE INDEX OF BOOKS <note>original: "SACR. CONG. PRO-IND. LIBR." This stamp indicates the book was reviewed by the Catholic Church's office responsible for the Index of Prohibited Books.</note>
</insert>
</margin>

->JOHANNES PETREIUS TO THE READER,<-

In this book, honest Reader, you have more than fifteen hundred causes, powers, and properties of various things—not common, but difficult, hidden, and very beautiful—observed by the author through experiment in various places. These are not only delightful for the sake of knowledge, but also far more useful for various uses, both private and public, than the writings of many others produced until now. If those other works are of Philosophy, the reader will hardly disagree with me that they are of less importance when comparing them to these; as can be clearly seen for each item in the attached index.

---

->Printed at Nuremberg by Johannes Petreius, now first published.<-
->With Imperial and Royal Privilege for six years. <note>A "privilege" was an early form of copyright granted by a sovereign, protecting the printer from unauthorized reprints for a set period.</note><-

## The Year 1550.

<summary>This is the title page of the first edition of Girolamo Cardano’s influential work on natural science and philosophy, "On Subtlety." It establishes the author’s credentials as a Milanese physician and frames the book as a collection of 1,500 experimental observations intended for both intellectual pleasure and practical use.</summary>

-> <gloss>WHAT IS TO BE SHALL SURELY BE... TOWARDS THE BETTER... <note>original: "ΜΕΛΛΟΝ ΟΤΙ ϗ ΓΕΝΗΣΕΤΑΙ ΜΟΝ... ΕΙΣ ΤΟ ΦΕΡΤΕΡΟΝ ΟΤΙ ΕΙ..." This is Cardano’s personal motto, often truncated in his portraits; it reflects his fatalistic philosophy and his belief in the progress of knowledge.</note></gloss> <-
-> <gloss>GIROLAMO CARDANO <note>original: "HIE. CAR."</note></gloss> <-

### A POEM by Thomas Venatorius <note>Thomas Gechauff (1487–1551) was a German mathematician and theologian who worked closely with the printer Johannes Petreius.</note> in praise of Cardano.

He drank here from the fountains of Wisdom, and from the rivers of the Muses,
Things not unpleasant to Apollo, nor to learned men.
From these he mixes medicinal juices, and the bodies of kings
Are entrusted to him—his greatest concern is their Trust.
Then, the Mathematics of the <term>Syracusan citizen</term> <note>original: "Syracusij... ciuis." A reference to Archimedes of Syracuse, the greatest mathematician of antiquity, with whom Cardano was frequently compared.</note> are born again,
While all other things are known on earth and increased by the heavens.

### A POEM by Laurentius Durnhofer <note>Lorenz Durnhofer (1532–1594) was a Nuremberg scholar and poet who often contributed prefatory verses to scientific works.</note> in praise of the same.

Neither flaming fires nor wave-sounding waters, Cardano,
Shall be able to extinguish your praise.
It is vast and powerful, resounding through the whole world,
Indeed, it reaches even to the high Pole of heaven.
While you reveal hidden things, covered by a certain darkness,
You open up various wonders and teach difficult matters.
While your medicine heals human pains,
And you treat the wounds of the heart with God’s help.
While you show the stars, and the constellations of the painted sky,
And the arts which the spacious world possesses.
While you bring all disciplines into common use,
Which makes for excellent and good craftsmen.

--- Page 5 ---
<meta>This page follows the frontispiece and introductory poems. It marks the beginning of the formal dedication of the work to Ferrante Gonzaga, the Imperial Governor of Milan. Gerolamo Cardano uses this opening to establish a philosophical framework for why a scholar should dedicate their work to a powerful ruler, comparing the true honoring of a Prince to the true worship of God.</meta>

<margin>A ii <note>Signature mark indicating the second leaf of the first quire of the printed book.</note></margin>

# TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND
-> EXCELLENT FERRANTE <-
-> GONZAGA, PRINCE OF MOLFETTA, <-
-> Duke of Ariano, Lord of Guastalla, Governor of the <-
-> province of the Insubres <note>The Insubres were an ancient Celtic people of Northern Italy; in the Renaissance, this term was used by humanists to refer to the territory of Milan.</note>, and Commander of the Emperor's <note>original: "Cæsaris." Referring to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (r. 1519–1556), whom Gonzaga served as a key general and diplomat.</note> armies, <-
-> Gerolamo Cardano, <-
-> physician of Milan, <-
-> sends many greetings. <-

**NEARLY ALL PEOPLES IN OUR** time, Most Illustrious Prince, worship God: yet none do so with the best reason—which is the best thing to do—save for the wise alone. For some adore God because, by honoring Him, they hope for many good things, and by scorning Him, they fear great evils. Thus, this is not love, nor is it veneration, but rather hope or fear. And even if this fear or hope were not in vain (though they certainly are empty if they refer to mortal outcomes rather than the rewards of the soul), nevertheless, the cause of the best action would not be the best. But now (in my opinion), this way of divine worship is not only improper but even futile in those people. 

There are others who worship God out of their own custom, or that of others. And just as these are worthy of absolutely no praise, so too those who honor God solely out of fear of the laws—who are certainly wicked—ought to be less blamed. There are also those for whom it is a matter of profit to have honored God, such as the priests. Others, under this name, hunt for a certain reputation for integrity. Thus, just as the former should be called <term>mercenaries</term> <note>Cardano uses this term to describe those who treat religious devotion as a commercial transaction for personal gain.</note> if they do it for no other reason, so too the Truth itself has condemned the latter with the name of hypocrites. 

Certain others, more ambitious than the rest, adore God because they think they themselves are His special concern. Therefore, you would not praise them so much for adoring God as you would blame them for promising themselves so much based on a presumptuous opinion. Therefore, only the wise—who honor God because He is the best and most excellent, even if He bestowed no benefit upon us—worship and honor Him correctly. For by honoring the best and holding the wicked in hatred, we ourselves are made better; furthermore, it is because He is simultaneously the cause of all our goods: whether as the first author He brings all things to pass, or (as the Philosophers <note>Cardano likely refers here to the Aristotelian and Neoplatonic traditions regarding divine providence and the governance of the cosmos.</note> will have it) He governs and moderates things already existing through Himself. I believe that wise men ought to maintain a similar reasoning in honoring Princes: namely, that they should honor only those who are the best, and best [deserving] of...

<meta>catchword: three <note>original: "tria"</note></meta>

<summary>Gerolamo Cardano begins his dedication to Ferrante Gonzaga by arguing that true worship of God—and by extension, true honor given to Princes—must be based on an appreciation of excellence rather than fear, hope for reward, or habit. He distinguishes the "wise" who honor God for His own sake from "mercenaries" and "hypocrites" who seek personal gain.</summary>
<keywords>Ferrante Gonzaga, Gerolamo Cardano, dedication, piety, philosophy of religion, Milan, Charles V, virtue, wisdom</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication of Gerolamo Cardano's work to Ferrante Gonzaga. In the previous page, Cardano discussed the nature of true worship and honor. Here, he pivots to praising Gonzaga’s specific virtues, lineage, and political achievements before reflecting on the value of his own scientific and philosophical writings.</meta>

# Epistle

...deserve their three-fold reward. Therefore, since I recognize you as the best, most just, and strongest of men, and since I behold your favors toward my own homeland, I have judged you worthy of every kind of praise. Among others, the greatest things one might possess are the virtue of ancestors, great deeds, power, and fame. You, who have had as Lords of Mantua not only a father or grandfather, but great-grandfathers, great-great-grandfathers, and great-great-great-grandfathers—such that you are now the tenth in that line—yet this is not what I shall proclaim, lest perhaps you say with Ulysses:

> *Both lineage and ancestors, and those things which we ourselves have not done,*
> *I scarcely call our own. —* <note>original: "Et genus, & proauos, & quae non fecimus ipsi, Vix ea nostra uoco." A famous quote from Ovid's Metamorphoses, Book XIII, where Ulysses argues that a man should be judged by his own merit rather than his family history.</note>

But this is not your primary praise, O Prince—you who have even more abundantly adorned the glory in military matters of your family (which in that field is second to none), a glory taken up from your ancestors. For through your courage, you brought the most fortified cities of Gaul <note>Referring to the French territories during the Italian Wars.</note> under your power. Yet you are no less a master of the arts of peace than those of war: for by your virtue you so reconciled Henry, King of Britain <note>Henry VIII of England.</note>, to Charles the Emperor <note>Holy Roman Emperor Charles V.</note>, that among other examples of faith and friendship, the King, when dying, left the Emperor as the guardian for his only son and heir. Through your integrity while you ruled the Sicilians and the Insubres <note>The people of the Duchy of Milan.</note>, you renewed the Age of Saturn <note>A classical reference to the "Golden Age," a mythical period of peace and prosperity.</note>, so that both provinces, having left behind an age of iron, now enjoy an age of gold.

But shall I say only a few things out of many? Or will you feel yourself bound by a certain silent suggestion to that which the immense nobility of your soul has compelled? Far from it. Therefore, someone might say: "What, then, do you bring forward worthy of such a great Prince?" Something, I say, than which I could offer nothing greater. 

For my works on **Arithmetic** are of a most pleasant study and singular invention, yet they are things of which the more dull-witted <note>original: "obesiores," literally "fatter" or "grosser," here meaning those lacking intellectual refinement.</note> might say: "To what end is such a spectacle of human ingenuity?" So too they quibble with our **Geometry**, and even our published writings **On the Immortality of the Soul**. I have cultivated **Astronomy** with wonderful, new, and true discoveries, but it had already contracted so much infamy from the vice of the ancients that the name of the discipline subtracts more authority from the book than our name adds to it. My **Medical** works are excerpts from the writings of others; the books **On Consolation** are of an ill-omened name; those **On Wisdom** teem with errors. And in general, as they say, all these are of a certain kind that bring no profit, except for the Medical ones, of which only the smallest part has been published to this day. 

"Let him publish," these critics say, "some new and subtle invention which is useful to the human race and even for the acquiring of wealth." I say it is not now the time for these individual slanders to be discussed. One must obey even one's enemies and acquiesce to their conditions, since by these conditions—which are within our power—every handle for speaking ill is snatched away. Therefore, I shall teach those critics that it was not the strength that was lacking, but the will. Meanwhile, however, this best effort must be offered to the one who deserves best of virtue and of my homeland. I was looking about here and there, to see if I might find <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "uenirem" at the bottom of the original page indicates the word "inuenirem" (find) continues on the next leaf.</note> anything worthy...

<summary>Cardano praises Ferrante Gonzaga’s military and diplomatic achievements—notably his role in Anglo-Imperial relations—and defends his own diverse scientific publications against critics who demand more "profitable" inventions.</summary>
<keywords>Ferrante Gonzaga, Mantua, Henry VIII, Charles V, Milan, Golden Age, Arithmetic, Astronomy, scientific merit, patronage</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This page concludes the dedication of Gerolamo Cardano's work to Ferrante Gonzaga. In the preceding text, Cardano praised Gonzaga's military and diplomatic achievements. Here, he discusses his motivations for the scientific rigor of this book, comparing it to his earlier works and the classical tradition of Pliny the Elder.</meta>

# Dedication

...I should come before so distinguished a Prince, and yet no subject occurred to me of a nobler or more useful nature for the human race than this very discussion, for the reason that it embraces all things at once and clarifies them with solid proof <note>term: demonstratione. In a Renaissance context, this refers to logical or mathematical proof that moves from known causes to effects.</note>. For I was afraid that if these matters were handled without proof—as happened in my books *On the Variety of Things* <note>original: "de Rerum uarietate". One of Cardano's most famous encyclopedic works, published in 1557, covering natural history and the occult.</note>—even though the facts were true, faith in this book might be withdrawn if one or two experiments among so many failed to succeed, just as happened to Pliny.

But the authority of antiquity and the history of his own time protect Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the monumental "Natural History" in the 1st century AD. Cardano notes that while Pliny often recorded inaccuracies, his status as a classical author keeps him respected.</note>; now that his credibility is established and his style of speaking is so well-suited to the material he treats, he is defended even though he more often lies. If the reputation for truth should fail us, however, what else is there with which I might defend this book? Yet it is not possible to firmly hold a reputation for truth—even if you have been confirmed by experiment—without a knowledge of the causes. 

When I realized how great the difficulty was in this matter, I carefully balanced the obscurity found in the demonstration of causes with the simplicity and ease of my language. I did this so that I would not cause boredom for my readers, nor seem to have wished to write only for myself. 

->Therefore, most kind Prince, whatever the quality of this work,<-
->I dedicate and give it to you; and I pray for the<-
->happiness and long years of Luigi, the<-
->founder of your family. For in this way,<-
->the Emperor’s <note>original: "Cæsaris". Referring to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, whom Ferrante Gonzaga served as a general and governor.</note> affairs<-
->will be well served.<-
->Farewell.<-

<summary>Cardano concludes his dedication by explaining the need for scientific "demonstration" (causal proof) to ensure his work's credibility, contrasting his approach with Pliny the Elder. He formally presents the book to Ferrante Gonzaga, invoking the name of the Gonzaga family founder, Luigi.</summary>
<keywords>Gerolamo Cardano, Ferrante Gonzaga, Pliny the Elder, De Rerum Varietate, scientific method, Luigi Gonzaga, Charles V, Renaissance science</keywords>

<meta>This page marks the official beginning of the main text, following the table of contents and the damaged signature page A 2. The catchword from the previous section was not clearly visible due to damage, but here we begin with the title and dedication of the work.</meta>

# THE TWENTY-ONE BOOKS ON 
# SUBTLETY BY GIROLAMO 
# CARDANO, PHYSICIAN OF MILAN. DEDICATED TO THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS
## Prince Ferrante Gonzaga, Governor 
## of the Province of Milan.

### BOOK THE FIRST

### On principles, matter, form, the vacuum, 
### the resistance of bodies, 
### and natural motion.

<margin>Definition of subtlety.</margin>
<margin>The difficulty in writing the work.</margin>
**T**he purpose of our endeavor in this work is to treat of subtlety. Subtlety is a certain reason <note>In this context, "ratio" implies a logic, quality, or defining principle.</note> by which perceptible things are grasped by the senses, and intelligible things by the intellect, only with difficulty. Therefore, if individual things that consist of subtlety present a great task in themselves and are most difficult, what, I ask, must be said of this treatise, in which the whole nature of subtlety must be explained? And only that can seem clear and easy which is the most obscure part of every discipline. A greater task remains for us in the treatment of the subject than in the subject itself. For since writers labor in four categories—the obscurity of things, the doubt of uncertain matters, the discovery of causes, and their correct explanation—all of these are found more abundantly in this book. If obscurity breeds difficulty, this book selects only the most obscure matters. If to know for certain has always been laborious, what could be more laborious than this book? A work where I have those I must avoid, such as Pliny and Albert <note>Pliny the Elder and Albertus Magnus, both prolific authors of natural histories whom Cardano often critiques for inaccuracy.</note>, to whom no trust is given in this genre because they openly lie, yet I have no one to follow. And yet, if everything is not perfectly explored by me—to the very fingernail, as they say—I shall waste my effort and my oil <note>original: "operam et oleum perdam." This is a classical idiom for wasting time and resources on fruitless labor, referring to the oil burned in a scholar's lamp.</note>. What shall I say of causes? Which, untouched by all others, must be brought forth as if received from some oracle. But faith was given to oracles without demonstration; for us, if we do not add proof, none will be given. These are things entirely unattempted for so many centuries, even by the philosophers who knew the subjects themselves, which must now be explained by me alone. Since some things have either vanished or were recently discovered, they either lack names, or the names lack the things themselves. Furthermore, to find names for new things in a language that is growing old <note>Cardano refers to the challenge of using Classical Latin to describe new Renaissance scientific discoveries.</note> is most difficult. Even if I find them, to avoid the slander of those who have recently written about these matters, I am forced to add my judgment <meta>catchword: forced (cogor).</meta>

<summary>This page introduces Cardano's monumental work, defining "subtlety" as the quality of things that are difficult for the human mind to grasp. He establishes his mission to provide a rigorous, evidenced-based natural philosophy, distancing himself from the perceived inaccuracies of earlier authorities like Pliny.</summary>
<keywords>Girolamo Cardano, Ferrante Gonzaga, Subtlety, natural philosophy, scientific method, Pliny the Elder, Albertus Magnus, linguistic challenges, Renaissance science</keywords>

--- Page 40 ---
<meta>This page continues Cardano’s introduction to his massive work on "Subtlety." Following the previous page's definition of subtlety as something difficult to grasp, he here outlines the structure of the book and the physical principles he will cover.</meta>

# Book the First

...I am compelled. For the rest, not even Oedipus <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus was the famous solver of the Sphinx's riddle; Cardano suggests the text is so difficult even a master of riddles would struggle.</note> himself could satisfy the reader. And so, although we have undertaken a task of immense labor, the reward of utility and glory will not grow in proportion to the greatness of that labor for the work itself. There were also certain matters besides these that were not correctly handled by the ancients. But I do not worry over these, since there is no authority that holds weight against those who write based on experiments <note>original: "experimenta" — Cardano emphasizes empirical observation over the traditional reliance on ancient texts.</note>. Therefore, there are so many and such great proofs of difficulty in this treatise. 

But to return to the matter itself: although things are often obscure, thin, meager, and subtle, they are not all so, nor always. For those things that are obscure and tangled due to a fault of words rather than by any skill <note>original: "arte" — here meaning technical expertise or scientific method.</note>—like knots accidentally twisting back upon themselves—as well as those which seem thin in sense but not dense, these do not deserve the name of "subtlety." Such are the spindly legs of men, damaged from the beginning by poor nutrition or some other mishap.

<margin>In what things subtlety exists.</margin>
Therefore, subtlety consists in three things: substances, accidents <term>accidents: properties that are not essential to a thing's existence but characterize it, such as color or temperature</term>, and representations. There are four kinds of representations: image, species <note>original: "species" — the mental or sensory form an object takes in the mind.</note>, speech, and writing. Of substances, some are indeed joined to the body, while others are devoid of it. Some accidents depend on substances, such as light, radiance, and heat; some are the means through which substances themselves come to be, such as mixture, action, and generation; some belong to both categories, such as the qualities they call "primary," like hot and cold. There are also accidents that are the causes of other accidents, such as changes, though most of these are motions. Unless one pays close attention, he will easily confuse these and think the same thing has been said twice. 

The thinness of bodies is sometimes due to the nature of their substance, like air, and sometimes due to the logic of quantity, like dust. By mixture, some things are thin, like gold, and among those made by art, silk. 

<margin>What things are to be taught.</margin>
However, we must seek signs in these things so that we can grasp the underlying subjects—and even more so the subjects themselves. Again, the causes of all these must be sought, for we are not said to know something unless its causes are known. It is also necessary to recognize what the substances or natures of the subjects are, and the different types of subtlety itself. 

<margin>Order.</margin>
Therefore, we must speak first of substances rather than accidents, and of general principles rather than others. Representations will follow accidents; for just as substance is prior to all things by nature, so representations do not exist without accidents. Among substances, corporeal ones will come first because they are perceptible to the senses, and simple things will come before composite ones. Among accidents, those that depend solely on substances will be put first, for they are simpler and more similar to substance. The treatment of accidents which provide the cause for substances or other accidents is often closest to the works of the arts <note>Cardano refers to the "mechanic arts," or technology and applied science.</note>. Regarding representations, images will be arranged first, then speeches and writings, and finally species. 

First, therefore, we shall speak of matter, then of form, then of the vacuum, then of the soul of the universe <note>The "anima mundi," a concept where the universe is seen as a living organism.</note>, and the motion of the elements. Then of earth, water, air, and fire; afterward of the heavens, and of those things that come from the heavens and light. After this, we shall return to composite things: types of earth, juices, minerals, metals, stones, and types of water; then to plants, animals (both those born from decay and those that are perfect), and from here to the figure of man...

<summary>Cardano defines the categories of subtlety (substances, accidents, and representations) and provides a detailed table of contents for the entire work, ranging from basic elements to the complexity of human biology.</summary>
<keywords>substance, accidents, representations, primary qualities, vacuum, world soul, order of nature, Aristotelian physics, empirical observation</keywords>

--- Page 41 ---
<meta>This page continues Cardano’s systematic breakdown of "subtlety." Having defined the term on the previous page, he now categorizes the subjects he will investigate—ranging from physical properties like density to spiritual entities—and argues for the existence of "primary matter" as the foundation of all change.</meta>

# On the Principles of Things.

...shape, temperament, the senses and sensible things, powers lying hidden within, the intellect, known arts and unknown sciences, and those things known by **Spirits** <note>original: "Dæmones" — in the 16th century, these were often viewed as neutral intermediary spirits or "geniuses" of knowledge rather than purely evil beings</note>, then from there to the celestial Intelligences, the universe, and God. Certain other things among these will be of a somewhat uncertain kind, such as weight, lightness, brightness, transparency, density, rarity, roughness, smoothness, figure, hardness, and softness; these are usually present in mixed bodies, and sometimes even in simple ones. Furthermore, regarding attraction, retention, concoction, and expulsion—as well as generation, growth, and nutrition—it is appropriate to speak of these primary qualities of things and their properties when we treat substances that consist of generation; for all these are either necessary for that process or follow after it. Of representations, there are two kinds: the false and the true. The false is divided into the empty and that which is useful. Therefore, each of these must be discussed one by one.

<margin>Utility.</margin>
From such great labor, no small utility is gained, but rather as much as can be had from any other treatise, whether it refers to a single category or to many. First, it contributes to all knowledge of nature, the science of difficult things, and the discovery of obscure matters; it also assists in some part with the interpretation of all books. It teaches the powers of the arts and demonstrates certain new things that are pleasant to know, including those which bring no small momentum to the acquisition of riches and wealth. It also decides what is true regarding ancient and significant doubts, such as in **chemistry** <note>original: "chymicis" — referring here to alchemy and the study of the properties of matter</note>. It reveals the miraculous works of both nature and art. It even recalls ancient inventions to use—those which had faded away through old age or the most heavy wars. And it teaches why all things that seem admirable to the senses occur as they do. Now, let us approach the task at hand.

<margin>That primary matter exists.</margin>
The perpetual generation of things themselves shows that **Hyle** <term>Hyle: a Greek term used by Aristotle and later scholars to refer to "prime matter" or the raw, formless stuff of the universe</term> exists; for generation always occurs from something else. Indeed, grain comes from the earth and moisture, animals from seed and blood or eggs, and ash from wood. Nothing is so tiny that it is made from nothing. Nor is it enough that just "anything" be present; since much ash cannot be made from a reed or a straw, yet a small amount of ash never comes from a large oak. Therefore, something common remains in every act of generation, which we call **primary matter** <term>primary matter: "materia prima," the underlying substance that persists when a thing changes from one form to another</term> or Hyle. For when something is generated from another, if the "form" perishes—otherwise the thing would be the same as it was and yet not the same—it is necessary that something remains, and that thing is matter. Corruption shows the same thing, since nothing at all truly perishes while it is being corrupted: for an apple rots and passes into worms, and wood, while it burns, is changed into ashes, and water is changed into vapors or smoke by the heat of fire or the sun. Moreover, vapor and smoke are "something," for they can suffocate a man, and if collected, they turn back into drops of water. It is manifest, therefore, that there is something in the nature of things lurking beneath the **form** <note>In the Aristotelian tradition Cardano follows, "form" is what makes matter a specific thing (like a tree or a dog); when the form changes, the underlying matter remains.</note>, which is neither created through generation nor perishes through corruption itself. This very thing, as a certain primary thing that is subject to many forms, we are accustomed to call "primary matter": unbegotten and never to perish. It remains...

<summary>Cardano outlines the scope of his work—from physical properties to divine intelligences—and argues for the existence of "primary matter" (Hyle) by observing that in nature, nothing is created from nothing and nothing truly vanishes.</summary>
<keywords>primary matter, Hyle, generation and corruption, alchemy, utility of science, physics, Aristotelian philosophy</keywords>

--- Page 42 ---
<meta>This page continues Cardano’s exploration of the fundamental principles of nature. Having established the scope of his inquiry on the previous page, he now dives into the nature of "primary matter"—the basic "stuff" of the universe—arguing that it exists as a real entity (actuality) even when it is waiting to take on a specific shape (potentiality).</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>
<header>Book One</header>

# Book One

<margin>That primary matter exists in actuality.</margin>
Now, that which remains is; therefore, matter exists in **actuality** <note>actuality (actus) refers to a thing that is fully realized or currently existing, as opposed to something that merely could exist</note> in the way we have described: yet, when compared to **forms** <note>the "form" is the specific blueprint or essence that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "form" of a chair makes wood into a chair)</note>, it is in **potentiality**, for it is capable of receiving them. Therefore, compared to a form, matter is potential; but in itself, it exists in actuality. Just as a fetus, when it is not yet perfected, is an infant in potentiality, but it is a fetus in actuality—for it is indeed this specific, delineated mixture, appearing exactly as it is seen. However, when it is compared to the form of an infant, it is said to be in potentiality; for if it were already in actuality, it would be an infant now, not a fetus. 

Therefore, primary matter exists in actuality, albeit in a—so to speak—diminished state. Compared to forms, it is in potentiality; for if it did not have the potential for them, it would never receive them. Indeed, a human is not made from a stone, because a stone does not possess the potentiality to receive the form of a human. Once it is embraced by a form to which it is then subject, it attains a more perfect actuality—though not yet a "perfect" one, for a perfect act is one that lacks potentiality entirely. We shall say, therefore, that the matter of a fig tree, considered by itself, exists in actuality, but in a very thin sense; however, as it is compared to other forms, it is in potentiality toward them; but while it is subject to the specific form of the fig tree, it stands in actuality.

<margin>That primary matter retains a certain quantity.</margin>
But primary matter is not stripped of all things: for as I have said, a handful of straw does not become a handful of iron because the matter is too sparse, nor conversely does a handful of iron become a handful of straw because of its redundancy. It follows, therefore, that primary matter retains a certain quantity, which we call "indefinite." For it does not describe fixed limits for itself, since it hides sometimes under a form filling a larger space, and sometimes a smaller one. For if fire is made from earth, it occupies a larger place; wherefore that prior matter which was subject to a smaller quantity, by a change of form, has filled a larger space. 

Nevertheless, it has circumscribed limits of greatness and smallness, within which, like a certain **Proteus** <note>In Greek mythology, Proteus was a sea god capable of changing his shape into any form. Cardano uses him here as a metaphor for how matter shifts through various sizes and shapes</note>, it undergoes infinite boundaries of magnitude. And since this certain determination of quantity belongs to it in actuality, why is it strange that primary matter itself—for the sake of which magnitude itself was established—exists and subsists in actuality? These things have been stated somewhat obscurely by others, not only because of the subtlety of the subject itself, but because many, wishing to write about things they did not perfectly grasp, wrap the treatment itself in speech that is not only obscure but even ambiguous.

<margin>The utility derived from primary matter.</margin>
Furthermore, it follows from the knowledge—indeed, the essence—of matter, that when we block incoming forms, the prior one remains. In this way, cold water preserves a balance in those of a "bloody" temperament <note>Referring to the "Sanguine" humor in medieval medicine, characterized by an abundance of blood</note> by preventing the generation of bile. For since it is necessary for primary matter to always lie under some form, if a subsequent form is blocked by art or by chance, the prior form must remain. <margin>Where the method of preservation took its origin.</margin> From this principle, therefore, the entire method of **preservation** <note>original: "praeferuandi," likely a variant or typo for "praeservandi." In a medical context, this refers to prophylaxis or the prevention of disease</note> took its origin.

Similarly, in transformations, an equal quantity of matter must be sought: since a greater or lesser amount cannot be suitable. For that reason, like things are made more easily from like things than from unlike things. Again, the reasoning of the **rare and the dense** <note>referring to density and porosity/thinness</note> is taken from the abundance or scarcity of matter; but we shall speak of these things below.

<summary>Cardano argues that primary matter is a real, existing substance that retains an "indefinite quantity" even as it changes forms. He uses this physical principle to explain practical applications, such as medical preservation and the transformation of elements.</summary>
<keywords>primary matter, actuality vs potentiality, Aristotelian physics, indefinite quantity, Proteus, medical preservation, humoral theory, transformation of elements</keywords>

<page-num>5</page-num>
<header>On the principles of things.</header>

# On the principles of things.

<margin>That a vacuum does not exist.</margin>
Since, therefore, matter was whole from the beginning and filled this concavity of the world, and because it could not be limited, a **vacuum** <note>a space entirely devoid of matter</note> could not exist. For if a vacuum were increased, it would be necessary for matter to be removed; there were also many things which demonstrated that a vacuum cannot exist. And even if **Hero** <note>Hero of Alexandria (c. 10–70 AD), an ancient engineer and mathematician</note> in his *Pneumatics* <note>original: "Spiritualibus," referring to Hero's work on air pressure and mechanical devices</note> strives to show that it exists, it is truly not the mark of a wise man to refute every absurdity—nor is it our purpose to pursue with obscure arguments those things which can be demonstrated by evident reasons. 

That a vacuum does not exist is shown by closed **bellows**, which, if they are stretched too much and with force, they break. For a larger space having been made, since it cannot be filled with air—the bellows not admitting such thinness of air to enter—nor can a vacuum be granted, a third option remains: that the bellows themselves are burst asunder. It is because of this necessity to avoid a vacuum that water ascends while we draw it through a pipe, and it descends downward, drawing a bucket-full from a jar. These things, however, will be demonstrated below.

<margin>The miraculous lamp.</margin>
For this reason, a **miraculous lamp** was devised in the shape of a tower, closed on all sides, and containing only a hole <term>D</term> through which the oil itself is poured until the lamp is completely filled. It is made solid of tin, and when it is turned as it now lies, the oil cannot be poured out through <term>D</term>. For if that which is in <term>C</term> were poured out, it would descend toward <term>D</term> by reason of its weight and the vacuum; and what was in <term>B</term> would move to <term>C</term>, and what was in <term>A</term> to <term>B</term>; therefore a vacuum would be left in <term>A</term>. Therefore, lest a vacuum be left in <term>A</term>, the oil remains; for which reason nothing is poured out from <term>B</term>, <term>C</term>, or <term>D</term>. 

But in what way, then, while the oil is consumed by the lit wick in <term>F</term>, can it exit through the channel <term>E</term> from <term>D</term> itself? It seems necessary to return again to the reasoning of the vacuum. For whether the oil is drawn by the force of heat, or the oil descends of its own accord, it seems to make no difference as far as the reasoning of the vacuum is concerned. Nevertheless, experience teaches that the lamp does indeed burn, and thus gradually becomes empty; but the oil by no means descends of its own accord. The cause, therefore, is that the fire, by heating it, makes the oil thinner and more **rarefied** <note>rarefaction is the process of making a substance less dense, often through heat</note>; this rarefied oil swells and overflows through the hole <term>D</term>, and its lightest part meanwhile ascends to the top of the lamp, where we have written <term>A</term>. Since this part is filled with much air, it fills the space with air, and thus the air gradually increases while the oil is poured out. Wherefore it is also necessary to be carefully on guard that the channel <term>D E F</term> is not shorter than is proper, or the wick in <term>F</term> larger; for in both ways the oil swells more quickly from the excessive heat, so much so that it overflows.

<margin>Everywhere there are three things: matter, form, and soul.</margin>
Matter, therefore, is everywhere; but it cannot exist without **form** <note>the essence or structure of a thing</note>, wherefore it is necessary that form also be everywhere. But there is also a certain **soul** <note>or "animating principle"</note>, either because generation occurs everywhere, or—what pertains more to the present treatment—because in whatever body, when it is outside its own place, there appears to be a **principle of motion** <note>the internal "drive" that makes a rock fall or fire rise</note>. But whether motion is from the soul or from nature makes no difference to me, provided that (which is alone necessary for my present treatment) you admit there is a certain principle of motion. For concerning the soul, whether all nature...

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 5 regarding the impossibility of a vacuum. While the previous page used the example of bellows and pipes to show how nature "fears" empty space, this page explains how bodies move to prevent such gaps and introduces the counter-principle: that two bodies cannot occupy the same space simultaneously.</meta>

<page-num>6</page-num>
<header>Book One</header>

# Book One

<margin>
Two bodies cannot occupy the same place.
</margin>

...must be considered later. For now, let it suffice to say that since all bodies are either **mixed** or **simple**, some of these are carried upward as light things, while others are carried downward as heavy things. They are not actually pushed—for they would then return to their proper places with violence—nor are they pulled, for "place" is merely an accident <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that does not affect the essential nature of a thing.</note>, and the element itself does not pull from everywhere, as when water is pulled upward. Therefore, the drive comes from within: the element moves itself, or the mixed body is moved by the element within it. I say "mixed" because a stone is moved downward by the **earth** <note>one of the four classical elements</note> that is within it, just as water is. Indeed, mixed bodies are usually moved by the element or elements that dominate within them. 

However, when bodies are not of the same kind, they cannot be in the same place, for that **primary matter** would then have to hold two forms at once. That a single body can be "more" or "less" <note>referring to density and rarity</note> is shown by **glass eggs** <note>original: "oua uitrea"; likely glass bulbs or cupping vessels used in physics experiments</note>, which, when air is sucked out through a small hole, draw water in. This happens because the air, having been made thinner due to the suction, is then forced together again; it occupies a smaller place than before, and thus, so that a **vacuum** is not created, it draws water into itself. Therefore, air can be compressed and, in a sense, enter into itself, and by the same reasoning, it can become thinner. Just as there is a certain limit in "thinness" <note>rarity</note> that acts like a vacuum and thus causes movement, so there is another limit of "thickness" <note>density</note>. If one tries to surpass this limit, it triggers a motion called **impulse** <note>original: "impulsus"; the force resulting from compression or the resistance to being squeezed</note>. 

Let it be understood, then, that an impulse occurs either when one body enters the place of another, or when the same body becomes so thickened that it cannot endure such great density; then, seeking another larger place, it triggers the motion of impulse. Just as **attraction** arises from a vacuum or excessive thinness, so **impulsion**—which is the opposite of attraction—arises from greater density or the pressing of bodies together into one.

<margin>
That there are three natural motions from the beginning.
</margin>

Therefore, in the whole of the universe, there will be three **natural motions**. The first and most powerful arises from the "flight from a vacuum," or more truly, from the **form** of the element, since it cannot admit a greater thinness, nor can the parts of matter ever be separated. When, therefore, the opening in **bellows** is greater than that small amount of air can endure, the air is first made thinner; but since primary matter does not allow for separation, the air—unable to sustain further thinning—either draws something into itself or the bellows burst entirely. Thus, no motion actually comes "from the vacuum" itself, but rather from the forms of things—especially air—when they can no longer be stretched or separated. 

That this motion is natural is shown by the consensus of the entire universe and the obedience of all bodies. To satisfy this law, they will abandon their own proper motions: heavy things will ascend of their own accord, and light things will descend. The second motion, as I have said, is directly contrary to this. In appearance, it is like the first; just as the first arises from a vacuum, this one seems to happen so that bodies do not penetrate one another. More truly, it exists for the opposite reason: to prevent the **form** from claiming more of the primary matter than is right, just as the first motion prevents it from claiming less. We have demonstrated that this motion is natural and proceeds from **Nature** for the same reasons as the first, though for some people it is certainly less obvious. It is not entirely clear which of these motions is the more powerful, yet this much is certain: both are much stronger than any **violent motions** <note>motions caused by an outside force rather than an object's internal nature</note>, and even stronger than the natural motions of the elements themselves.

<summary>This page explains that nature prevents vacuums and the overlapping of matter through "natural motions" (attraction and impulse). It argues that bodies will even move against their own weight—heavy things rising and light things falling—to ensure that space remains filled and matter remains at its proper density.</summary>

# On the principles of things.

<margin>War machines propel according to the order of the universe.</margin>
...nor is there any need to account for this kind of impulse or attraction, nor almost any concern for whether a thing is heavy or light. And by that same principle, which we shall follow in its proper place, war engines <note>original: "tormenta bellica"; referring here to cannons or high-powered ballistae</note> discharge those iron balls with such force that no other power could achieve anything similar by mere pushing. Indeed, were it not for the risk of the machine itself shattering, nothing would prevent an object from being propelled all the way from the Germanies to India, since such movement follows the order of the universe. The third motion is that of heavy things toward the lower regions and light things toward the upper: a motion which everyone plainly admits is natural, so I shall labor little over it. Yet even if we were to grant that other motions should be called natural—provided they always happen for the reasons I have stated—it would not hinder what we proposed to declare. There was also a fourth kind of natural motion, by which certain things are moved toward others; because this is not a general rule, it will be moved to its own section, such as the discussion of the so-called <term>Herculean stone</term> <note>the lodestone or magnet</note> and iron, or <term>amber</term> <note>original: "electro"</note> and straw <note>a reference to static electricity</note>.

<margin>The Ctesibian Machine.</margin>
With these principles demonstrated, we now consider the design of the <term>Ctesibian machine</term> <note>a double-action suction pump invented by Ctesibius of Alexandria in the 3rd century BCE</note>, which is constructed in such a way that even **Juanelo Turriano of Cremona** <note>original: "Ianellus Turrianus Cremonensis"; the famed clockmaker and hydraulic engineer to Emperor Charles V</note>, a man of great genius in all things pertaining to machines, has expressed it through his own work. There is a bronze basin **A**, the top opening of which, through which water must be poured, is **B**. At its bottom are two holes, **C** and **D**, over which valves <note>original: "axes"; likely meaning wooden flaps or pivots</note> or leather seals are placed just as in bellows. These are raised from the lower part toward **A**, but if they are compressed, they block those openings and stick to the basin. From the openings **C** and **D**, two pipes, the right and the left, are extended as **E** and **F**, and are inserted into the <term>cylinders</term> <note>original: "modiolis"; literally "small buckets," used here for the pump cylinders</note> at **G** and **H**. These cylinders are hollow and submerged in water, having holes <margin>Vitruvius Book 10, Chapter 12.</margin> **K** and **L** in the middle of their bottoms. Over these are valves with leather as in the basin, which can be raised upward, but when pressed, they seal the openings perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem"; literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for precision</note>. Inside the cylinders are "male" <term>pistons</term> <note>original: "emboli masculi"</note> **M** and **N**, polished on a lathe and worked with oil so that they fill the cylinders exactly. These are then fitted with levers and rods so that, moving back and forth, when **M** rises and the vessel below is emptied, **N** descends in turn, fills the piston area, and squeezes out whatever is contained within. By this arrangement, when the male piston **M** is drawn up, the space **Q** of the cylinder is emptied; therefore the valve and leather over **K** are raised, and water rises until the cylinder is filled according to the principle of primary motion. Meanwhile, when **N** has been pressed down, it begins to be drawn from the bottom in alternating motion, and piston **M** descends. Since the water contained in space **Q** cannot flow out (as **M** seals the top of the cylinder's capacity perfectly) nor can it descend through **K** (since the valve presses on the hole, and the more it is urged by the weight and impetus of the water from above, the more exquisitely it sticks to the hole **K**), it follows that the water exits through **G**, which is the only open exit. Rising through pipe **E**, it enters the basin, lifting the lid...

<margin>Brambilla’s Machine.</margin>
Of the same design is the ship’s pump <note>original: "tuba nauium"; literally "the ship's trumpet," a common term for a nautical siphon or pump used for bailing water</note>, which sailors use to empty ships in danger from flooding. In this section, it is received by the vessel *C*, which is submerged in the water and perforated on all sides so that water can enter, while stones and sand cannot, because the bottom of the vessel *C* is solid. Thus, the tube will draw pure water from the vessel when needed, rather than the gravel or sand that would jam the machine. In the spot *M*, where the narrower part is joined to the wider, a leather seal is attached from above at *M*. Over this hangs a thin lead plate, so that when it is lifted from side *Q*, it falls back by its own weight and perfectly seals the channel *L*. The "male" <term>piston</term> <note>original: "embolus masculus"; the solid plunger that moves within the pump barrel</note> *A E* is narrower than the width of the tube, yet at the very top where *D* is, it plugs the opening of the tube precisely. The space *O P* is empty. From the bottom of the piston, three solid iron rods extend to the inner sides of the tube; you should wrap these in leather so they do not scratch the tube by contact. These rods resemble a tripod, being wider and more spread out at the bottom *F* than at the top *E*. It is clear, therefore, that the entire space near *N* is empty, containing nothing but these small rods. Consequently, a path is open from *O* and *P* into *N*, and conversely from *N* into *O* and *P*, for the entire space above *F* is empty, containing nothing besides the piston and rods. ...let it be covered with a thin plate at <term>m</term> <note>These letters refer to a diagram, likely lost or on an adjacent page, showing the pump's components.</note> as has been said, so that when it is covered, air cannot pass through, yet the leather can be lifted toward <term>n</term> with the lead weight and uncover the opening itself. Again, from the heads of those rods, three other rods should project straight out, adhering to the sides of the <term>pipe</term> <note>original: "tubae"; here referring to the main cylinder or rising main of the pump</note> on the inside. Leather surrounds these everywhere, adhering precisely to the sides of the pipe on the inside from part <term>f</term> at the top down to <term>g</term>, so that air cannot leak from <term>k</term> into <term>n</term>. Thus it will appear like an inverted <term>chamber</term> <note>original: "modiolus"; a bucket-like housing or cylinder used in hydraulic machines</note> <term>h</term>, for the bottom is <term>f</term>, and it is covered all around with leather in a rounded shape, and at <term>g</term> it is open and gaping. Once these things are so arranged, let <term>g</term> lie upon <term>m q</term> and begin to be raised; then the air contained in space <term>h</term>, having been made thinner, eventually pulls and lifts <term>q</term>. Following this, air ascends from <term>l</term> into space <term>k</term>, and in turn, water ascends from <term>b</term> into <term>l</term>. However, when the piston descends by the impulse of the air and the weight of the lead, <term>q</term> immediately descends. For this reason, the water in <term>l</term> necessarily remains; for if the water were to descend when the lid <term>m q</term> is closed, that small amount of air in the upper part of <term>l</term> above the water would be stretched thin, since it cannot draw in other air from <term>k</term> because of the lid <term>m q</term>. But the air that was contained in <term>k</term>, while <term>g</term> descends and lifts the lid <term>f</term>, escapes into space <term>o</term> and exits through the opening at <term>p</term>. Thus, by repeating the ascent and descent of <term>g</term> and the piston, the space <term>l</term> is filled with water. Afterward, when <term>g</term> is raised again—and by the logic of the first motion, so that the air in <term>k</term> is not overly stretched—the lid <term>q m</term> is lifted and water enters space <term>k</term> until it is full, and along with it space <term>h</term>, which as I said is shared with <term>k</term>, because <term>g</term> is the open mouth of the chamber and is not closed off on any side. 

Suppose it is now full and the piston descends again; the water in <term>h</term> will then lift the lid <term>f</term> and fill spaces <term>n</term> and <term>o</term>. When the piston is pulled upward, the lid at <term>f</term> prevents the water that had ascended into <term>o</term> from descending again; falling by both its own weight and the weight of the water pressing down on it, the lid blocks the opening. Thus it is established that by this machine, water always ascends and can never descend; hence, when it reaches <term>p</term>, it is poured out through the mouth of the pipe <term>p</term> into whatever place you wish. Then, with very little labor, you will draw as much water as you want from <term>b</term>, for once the pipe is full, the motion of the piston <term>a</term> becomes easier.

By the same logic, we shall call "impulse"—whether it be motion or rest—a result of density, just as we call the third motion of an element "heavy" or "light." For example, consider a lamp...

<margin>*On the clock-spring.*</margin>
<insert>The clock-spring</insert>
with a certain singular reasoning when we teach the motion of the elements. Now, however, we shall approach the motion which occurs because of density alone, an example of which is evident in <term>war engines</term> <note>original: "tormentis bellicis"; referring here to mechanical artillery like catapults.</note>, in which only the motion of impulse is visible. Of this same kind is the motion that occurs in the <term>drive-mechanisms</term> <note>original: "mola"; literally a mill, but here referring to the mainspring or winding mechanism of a clock.</note> of clocks. Just as <term>ballistae</term> <note>Large ancient engines for throwing stones.</note> function through rarefaction, so do <term>scorpions</term> <note>Smaller, arrow-firing siege engines.</note> and other engines of that sort; for when the cord is stretched too much, it moves with a sharper impulse in order to contract itself, and it drives the stone or arrow placed upon it. Therefore, this principle is reduced to the motion of rarefaction. 

By the opposite reasoning, as I have said, the drive-mechanism is twisted in a clock. For steel, having been made soft, is reduced into a very long and narrow thin plate (as you see in the figure). Then, it is gathered by force into a very tight circle and enclosed in a small case. A thin but very strong cord is wound around the case, the end of which is fastened to the wider axle of a wheel. Thus it happens that while the steel, pressed by excessive density, tries to stretch out, it turns the case, which pulls the cord. From there, the axle is gradually turned, and it drives the wheel, which in turn drives others with its interlocking teeth. The sixth example shows in what way rest can occur because of an impulse.

<margin>*Why a bucket full of water does not spill when swung around.*</margin>
There are several examples of this kind. A pitcher having a pipe full of air, while the pitcher itself is full of water: when the pipe is turned downward, the water itself seems to hang there. By a similar reasoning, stones thrown upon the water bounce off it, and a bucket full of water swung around very quickly does not pour out the water. This is because, as time is lacking for the division of the air, the water stays put so as not to be overly compressed. By the same reasoning, a 

<margin>*Why a wide lead plate cannot sink if it rests evenly on water.*</margin>
wide lead plate floats on the water; for in descending, the parts that are in the middle, having no place to flee, would be overly compressed; or if they slipped away beforehand, a vacuum would necessarily be left in the middle. Therefore, it cannot descend in any way unless it is first tilted to one side. Let these things suffice regarding these two prior motions and the state of rest that arises from them, since it is not the present purpose to speak of machines—that is done in the second book of *On the Variety of Things*, and in the tenth commentary on <term>Vitruvius</term> <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman author of "De Architectura." The author is likely referring to his own published commentary on this classic work.</note>. Let it be enough to have explained these examples so precisely, just as I have explained the modes: for six examples suffice for the six modes. Therefore, it is clear that heavy things move downward and light things move upward. But some people, not content with this, wish to add that light things tend to remain above heavy ones.

# On the Principles of Things.

...to be, from which even air existing under water, although in its own region, nevertheless strives to emerge higher: as is manifest in pitchers when they are turned over half-full, and in a bladder full of air that is submerged in water. But this motion is no different from the first, for water itself, when it is in a high place, endeavors to descend, and upon its descent, the air ascends so that it is not too greatly compressed. But in a bladder which is in a river, since the air is in the place of the water, it strives to ascend; therefore, one reason for the motion of elements to their proper place will suffice. However, that the water pushes the bladder upward and not that the air ascends [by its own power] is clear, since a bladder placed under the earth does not ascend.

<margin>
How water rises exactly as much as it is able to descend.
</margin>

But what is more worthy of inquiry is how water rises as much as it can descend while it is assisted by the <term>motion of rarefaction</term> <note>The force created by a vacuum or the thinning of a substance, which "pulls" the liquid upward.</note>; this very thing will be made clearer by an example. Let there be a vessel full of water, the top of which is **E** and the bottom **F**, in which there is a channel **A B C**. Let there be a line **C D**, equidistant from the <term>horizon</term> <note>original: "finitore"; the boundary line or level.</note> according to which a <term>level</term> <note>original: "libella"; a tool used to determine a perfectly horizontal line.</note> is drawn. Let the channel **A B C** be filled with water, and let the water be let out through **C**. I say that it will exhaust whatever water is above the line **C D**, but none of that which is below the line **C D**; instead, the channel will hang full, and the vessel will be seen to be full of water up to **C D**. Thus, an example declares this to be so. Perhaps someone might say these things ought to have been transferred to the treatment of water [specifically]: but it was not necessary, since whether the vessel be full of water, or wine, oil, or milk, it makes no difference. Therefore, the reasoning for this experiment must rather be rendered.

The water, therefore, which is above **C D**, since it is <term>precisely</term> <note>original: "ad unguem"; literally 'to the fingernail,' an idiom for perfect accuracy.</note> as much as that which ascends, is as much as that which is poured out from **C**, whether the channel be wider at **C** than at **A**, or narrower; because the entire channel is always <term>perfectly</term> full, the water which is poured out through **C** is lighter. The reason why the water in the part above **C D** is lighter than at **C** is because the water above **C D** desires to descend so that it may be lower than that which is in **C**, therefore it compresses the water and drives it into the channel. But that which is below **C D** does not desire to be in **C**, because **C** is higher than its place, and so it does not wish to ascend. But the water which flows out of **C** does not provide a cause for consideration, even though it is lower than the water contained in the vessel itself, because that <term>attraction</term> <note>The siphoning effect.</note> does not happen except by reason of <term>continuity</term> <note>The physical principle that a liquid column will not break unless air enters.</note>: continuity depends on the principle of <term>rarefaction</term> <note>Meaning a vacuum would be created if the water column broke.</note>, which cannot exist once the water is already exiting the mouth of the channel **C**.

Finally, this entire contemplation is resolved by this argument: that water which must draw other water with it must be contained in a vessel, since without it, it cannot be pulled away; but it is helped by the arriving air so that the continuous body may reach <term>equilibrium</term> <note>The balanced state of the fluid levels.</note>. Therefore, when the opening **C** is lower, the water will reach it; but when it is higher, it will not descend: because that which is directly from a lower place, as in **A**, will be forced to ascend to **C**, which is directly across from **D**. <margin>
How much weight ships carry.
</margin>
...if the weight is ten thousand <term>talents</term> <note>original: "talentorum"; an ancient unit of weight, roughly 60–70 pounds</note>, that <term>trireme</term> <note>original: "triremis"; an ancient galley with three banks of oars</note> will carry ten thousand talents in a river. But if that same ship in the sea displaces, as I said, those same thousand <term>amphorae</term> <note>original: "amphoras"; here used as a unit of volume displacement</note>, let it carry a weight of twelve thousand talents; for sea water is heavier than river water, and thus in the sea the same ship will carry twelve thousand talents of weight. And by this reasoning, it is manifest why we are accustomed to name ships by their measure—such as a ship of one thousand or five hundred amphorae. For it is the same as if you were to say it can carry one thousand or five hundred talents of weight. For such is the capacity, as I said, of a ship in relation to the water: it can carry as much as the weight of the water it displaces. It is manifest from this, therefore, that the same ship will carry different weights in different waters, since the weights of the waters themselves are different. Truly, according to this reasoning, it is clear that the magnitude of the weight is in proportion to the force of the water pushing against it. For if, to give an example, a <term>skiff</term> <note>original: "cimba"; a small boat</note> supports twenty amphorae, this is because the air enclosed within is pushed upward by twenty amphorae of water, so that the water which would have been contained in the ship may regain its place. This experiment, therefore, agrees beautifully with the reasoning stated above: namely, that a bladder full of air is pushed upward by the water because the bladder occupies the place of the water. Therefore, it will support a weight in the air equal to the size of the water the bladder could contain—that is, with the weight placed upon the bladder so that the weight itself is entirely in the air and not in the water. But the weight which is in the water (to return to the raising of a ship) is rendered lighter in proportion to how much heavier the water itself is; hence, fewer skiffs will be needed than those which would be required to carry the weight of the submerged ship.

<margin>
Ships are more easily extracted from the sea than from rivers or lakes.
</margin>
Indeed, for a double reason, ships are extracted from heavier waters more easily than from lighter ones: and therefore more easily from the sea than from rivers or lakes. One reason is that the skiffs in the sea support more weight; the other is that the sunken ship is less heavy in that water. For this reason, however, one must take care, since as it has been said, the ship becomes heavier at the surface of the water (because it is partly in the air) than at the bottom; so that as it is lifted more by the skiffs, more and larger skiffs should be attached, lest, deceived by this reasoning, the ship not only sinks again but also, with added momentum, drags all the skiffs down into the deep with it.

Hero’s Machine.
</margin>

It is arranged thus: **A** is a basin full of water; under which is vessel **B**, also full of water, joined to **A** in such a way that water cannot pass from one to the other. Under **B** is another vessel, called **C**, which is empty. Let pipe **D** be led from **B** into **C**, the top mouth of which almost reaches the basin. There is another pipe **E**, which ascends quite a bit above the basin, and being inserted into the basin, penetrates into the middle...

# Book One

...extends all the way to the bottom of the first vessel, but is not joined to the bottom itself. Another pipe **F**, whose upper opening is situated in the bottom of the basin, should have its lower mouth end in the partition between the two vessels, so that water from the basin is carried through the upper opening into vessel **C**. Then indeed we see the water which is in vessel **B** being emitted through pipe **E**: and it continues to do so until the water in the basin is finished. How this happens must be demonstrated from two combined motions. Water descending through pipe **F**, since air in **C** cannot remain there, ascends through pipe **D** into the upper vessel **B**. But since that place is full of water, the water is forced to ascend through pipe **E**, pressed by the air; and thus it is poured out. It is manifest, therefore, that here there are two motions according to the nature of the descending water from the basin into vessel **C** through pipe **F**. The second motion is of the ascending air from vessel **C** into vessel **B**, because, as was said, it is driven upward by the water. From these two natural motions, a forceful impulse is created, by which the water from vessel **B** ascends through the pipe.

<margin>On alternating motion.</margin>
Truly, when the motion of a heavy weight is repeated alternately, it moves <term>bellows</term> <note>original: "folles"; used for stoking fires or powering organs</note> or other machines in turn, which was appropriate to demonstrate in the <term>Ctesibian machine</term> <note>named after Ctesibius of Alexandria, the 3rd-century BC inventor of the water organ and the force pump</note>: so that the male <term>pistons</term> <note>original: "emboli masculi"</note> could ascend and descend in turn in the <term>pump cylinders</term> <note>original: "modiolis"</note>. This is done thus: Let a wheel with fins be positioned near the fall of descending water, as is usually done, so that by the perpetual downward flow of water over the fins, the wheel revolves. In this wheel is an axle **A**, which clearly must also be turned. I omit the description of the wheel, as it is a most well-known thing and visible in all mills. Let a beam lying over the timbers and enclosed in round holes be called **B**, so that it is movable and can revolve on hinges. Near its end **E**, a ring is fixed, to which another ring with an iron rod **F** is attached; this again ends in a ring, which receives another ring **G** attached to rod **H**. At the end of **H**, a ring is joined, which is connected by a rope to a nail at the top of axle **A**, so that it moves with the axle; but when the axle returns, the ring also returns to its former place and position. On the other part of the beam, two rings are placed opposite each other, **C** and **D**; it is also possible to place two pairs or three pairs opposite each other in this way. Therefore, if the pistons or bellows, one at **C**, are joined by a rope and the other at **D**, as the axle revolves, the beam is first pulled toward **D**, and then one of the bellows is raised from **C** while the other falls from **D**. But when the wheel has turned half the axle, the ring at the bottom of **H** returns to its place and pushes **E**, on account of the rods, and the beam is bent toward **C**, and thus, by turns, the bellows are moved. For the beam "nods" <note>the author uses "nutat" to describe the oscillating, rocking motion of the beam</note> to the right and left in turn but does not revolve. Therefore, it is possible to move many pairs of bellows by many rings placed opposite each other on the beam; but a strong force of water is needed. It is also possible to join another beam to the same axle from the left, as smiths usually do, and thus the number of bellows will be doubled.

<page-num>15</page-num>

# On the Principles of Things

No other help is needed, nor any industry other than that which has been revealed in one, but only with greater force.

Having just seen these things, and after we have finished the discourse on all general motions—the fourth example having been declared in the balancing of waters, and **Hero's machine** satisfying the composite motions of elements—it will be worthwhile to briefly collect those ten examples into one. For **rest due to rarity**, we provided the example of the lamp. For **motion from rarity**, a tube placed in a vessel, where we discussed the descent of water. For **rest due to density**, a lead plate and then skins spread over water. For **motion due to density**, the impact of war machines. For **motions of attraction due to rarity** and **impulse due to density**, the <term>Ctesibian machine</term> <note>named after Ctesibius of Alexandria, the inventor of the force pump; this machine uses air and water pressure to create motion</note>. For both motions, as well as rest due to rarity, the <term>Brambilic machine</term> <note>original: "Brambilica machina"; likely referring to a specific hydraulic device described by contemporary engineers</note>. For the **motion of a light element**, the recovery of a ship; for a **heavy simple element**, the motion of clocks. For a **heavy but frequently repeated element**, the alternating movement of bellows. For a **heavy and light element tending together toward one end**, Hero’s machine.

<margin>Demonstration that no motion comes from a vacuum.</margin>
It remains, therefore, that I say something about the magnitude of gravity. For we do not move light things, but rather they move us. First, however, we will show that **no motion is from a vacuum**, nor similarly because of a vacuum, nor because of bodies joining together. This demonstration will be general, so it will suffice to show it only regarding the vacuum, for the same logic can be transferred to the joining of bodies into one. First, indeed, a vacuum does not exist; how then can that which does not exist effect anything? Next, even if it is assumed to exist, a vacuum is not a substance, nor does it proceed from a substance, and to conclude in a single word: it is nothing; and therefore it can have no operation. Perhaps someone will say that nature, out of fear of a vacuum, or to avoid it, stirs motion? But not even that: for since air is rarer than water, it would be necessary—before attraction occurs by reason of a vacuum when it ascends with water following it—for the earlier water to be turned into air, and this again into fire, which is rarer than air. Then the fire itself would be thinned, and finally this attraction would occur. But we see that water is not turned into air but is pulled, and similarly air before it passes into fire: therefore, nature does not struggle for that attraction (which they call "from a vacuum") out of fear of a vacuum, since so many intermediate stages still remain, but out of **fear of rarity**.

<margin>The motion of attraction from rarity is not violent.</margin>
Nor should I say, with <term>Averroes</term> <note>original: "Auerroe"; the 12th-century philosopher known for his influential commentaries on Aristotle</note>, that it is <term>violent</term> <note>in Aristotelian physics, "violent" motion is that which is forced against an object's natural inclination, whereas "natural" motion follows its essence</note>: for it is entirely natural. Just like the motion of water when it is in the air and descends. For it rests by force, and therefore moves naturally. Thus, an element that pulls because of rarity suffers a violence from which it frees itself by that motion. But that a heavy thing is pulled upward by that motion happens by chance, and it is sometimes violent for that which is pulled and sometimes not—as if a light thing were pulled upward. It is enough that the motion is natural from its own principle. But against its will, or at least not helping...

<summary>The author summarizes ten examples of physical motion related to density and rarity, then argues that motion is caused by the "fear of rarity" rather than the traditional "fear of a vacuum." He critiques Averroes' classification of such motion as "violent," asserting instead that it is a natural response to environmental displacement.</summary>

## Book One

...was helped? <note>original: "uante", completing "iuuante" from the previous page</note> Indeed, what moves toward a place moves of its own accord, as an element or a composite, not merely as something heavy or light. For it forgets its own nature because it moves by the consent of another. Just as one who encourages a son toward life's danger while the city walls are being besieged by the enemy exercises piety; whereas if a common cause did not impel him, he would be considered cruel for doing so.

<margin>How weights may be easily moved.</margin>
But let us now come to the motions of heavy things. This motion, moreover, is free, or occurs by an attached weight, as in a <term>balance</term> <note>original: "libra"</note> and <term>steelyard</term> <note>original: "statera"; a weighing scale with unequal arms</note>. It is usually asked why weights are moved more by other weights: for let weight **B** be moved by handle **A** over the fork **c**. It is established that if a weight is added to the handle itself—such as lead up to a certain limit—it descends more easily from the sides to the center with the help of the weight; but on the contrary, it is moved more with difficulty from the center to the sides. Because of this, a certain limit of weight must be maintained, up to which the ease of motion increases. If you exceed this, however, the motion is rendered more difficult. For this reason, they add heavier hilts to swords so that the swords seem lighter and are handled more easily. But here too, a measure must be observed.

<margin>How water may propel itself upward.</margin>
We have added this because most instruments suitable for drawing water are driven by the strength of men or pack animals. But even if the machines are driven by the rapid force of the waters themselves, weights added to the handles again make the motion easier. It is possible, therefore, by the sole force of descending waters, to propel the waters themselves into higher places and to irrigate fields with lower waters. But this is only in those that run down and have force by falling. For let there be fitted, on one side, a <term>Ctesibian</term> <note>a force pump named after the inventor Ctesibius</note>, or <term>Brambilian</term>, or another kind of machine; for as I have said, there can be innumerable types of them, although these are more elegant. And as we have already taught, let the alternating motion of the handle be performed by a wheel driven by fins <note>paddles</note>; thus it will happen that the water spontaneously propels itself upward. For art may compel nature to act against its own inclinations. Some cities, which are located in higher places than the river, follow this example.

<margin>On the balance and its principle.</margin>
After these things, we must look at the weights that are set in a balance. Let there be, therefore, a balance whose <term>beam</term> <note>original: "trutina"</note> is suspended at **A**, and the end where the sides of the <term>scale pan</term> <note>original: "lanx"</note> are joined is **B**, and the pan is **C D**. It is manifest that **C D** moves around **B**, as if around a certain center, because **C D** cannot be separated from **B** itself, and let the angles **A B C** and **A B D** be right angles. I say that a weight placed at **c** will be heavier than if the pan were placed in any other location, such as if the pan were placed at **F**. Moreover, so that we may know that **c** is heavier in that position than in **F**, it is necessary that in an equal time it moves through a greater space toward the center. For we see that heavier things, for the same reason in other cases, are carried more swiftly toward the center. As for why this happens...
