<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of mechanical motion, specifically focusing on the geometry of the balance and the "science of weights" that was briefly introduced at the end of the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>On the Principles of Things.</header>
<sig>c</sig>
<meta>Catchword: will be [original: erit]</meta>

...reaches <note>original: "tingat", likely completing "contingat" from the previous page</note> a greater weight when the <term>balance</term> <note>original: "libra"; the weighing beam</note> is located at **C** than at **F**, which I demonstrate by two reasons. The first is that if it moves from **C** into **E** in a certain amount of time, and arc **CE** is equal to arc **FG**, it will descend more slowly from **F** into **G** than from **C** into **E**; thus, it will be lighter at **F** than at **C**. Second, assuming that it moved from **C** into **E** and from **F** into **G** in an equal span of time, it would still approach the center [of the world] more through the arc **CE** (which is equal to **FG**) than through the motion made in arc **FG**. Therefore, for this double reason, a weight will press down more when the scale pan is positioned at the <term>perpendicular</term> <note>The vertical line directly beneath the pivot point.</note> with the <term>fulcrum</term> <note>original: "trutina"; here referring to the suspension point or needle of the scale.</note> than in any other place.

The first point is thus declared: it is manifest in <term>steelyards</term> <note>original: "stateris"; a type of scale using a sliding weight on a long arm.</note> and among those who lift weights, that the further a weight is from the fulcrum, the heavier it seems. But a weight at **C** is distant from the fulcrum by the length of line **BC**, and at **F** by the length **FP**. However, **CB** is greater than **FP**, according to the 15th proposition of the third book of Euclid’s *Elements* <note>original: "15 tertij elementorum Euclidis"; a standard reference to classical geometry.</note>; therefore, when the scale pan is placed at **C**, the weight will appear heavier than at **F**, which was the first point. From this demonstration, it is also manifest that the more the balance descends from **A** toward **C**, the heavier the weight it returns, and the faster it moves; but from **C** toward **Q**, by the opposite reasoning, the weight is rendered lighter and the motion slower, as experience also teaches.

The second point is demonstrated thus: Because **CE** is equal to **FG**, let **CH** be taken as equal to **CE**. Thus **CH** will be equal to **FG**, and the straight line subtended by **CH** will be equal to the straight line subtended by **FG**. Therefore, from the 8th proposition of the first book of the *Elements*, angle **BFG** is equal to angle **BCH**. Thus, when the perpendicular lines **FL** and **HK** are drawn, angle **FGL** (which itself would be a part equal to **BFG** from the 5th proposition of the first book) is smaller than angle **KCH**. Therefore, side **CK** is greater than side **FL**, for the straight lines **FG** and **HC** were equal, and the triangles are <term>orthogonal</term> <note>Right-angled.</note> or rectangular. Therefore, **BN** is greater than **OP**, and thus **BM** is greater than **OP**. While the balance moves from **C** to **E**, the weight descends along line **BM**, or is returned closer to the center than it was at **C**; and while it moves through the space of arc **FG**, it descends through **OP**, and **BM** is greater than **OP**. Therefore, even assuming it passed from **C** to **E** and from **F** into **G** in equal time, it still descends faster from **C** than from **F**. Therefore, it is heavier at **C** than at **F**, which is the second point.

<margin>Why an empty balance returns of its own accord to a straight position, or if the weights were equal.</margin>
From this, moreover, is demonstrated what the **Philosopher** <note>Aristotle.</note> says: that if the weights in **F** and **R** are equal, the balance nonetheless returns of its own accord to the position **CD**, where the fulcrum is **AB**. Neither did **Jordanus** <note>Jordanus de Nemore, an influential medieval mathematician who wrote on the "science of weights."</note> demonstrate this, nor did he understand it. Similarly, why—when the fulcrum **QB** is positioned below the balance itself, or as happens when the balance is turned over so that you hold the fulcrum with your hand while the balance rests upon it—the weight which had already descended is drawn to **R**, where another equal weight is placed at **F**, or even if the scale pans are entirely empty, they do not only return to the position **CD** (that is, the perpendicular), but rather **R** descends toward **Q** and **F** ascends toward **A**, as is evident by experiment. This also **Jordanus** did not demonstrate. **Aristotle** says this happens when the fulcrum is above the balance, because the angle **QBF** of the <term>pointer</term> <note>original: "metæ"; likely referring to the needle or indicator of the scale.</note> is greater than the angle **QBR**. And similarly when the fulcrum is **QB**...

<page-num>38</page-num>
# Book One

Let **A B** be the <term>vertical limit</term> <note>original: "meta"; the vertical line representing the path of direct descent toward the center of the world.</note>, and then the angle **R B A** will be greater than the angle **F B A**. Since a larger angle produces a heavier weight, when the <term>fulcrum</term> <note>original: "trutina"; the pivot or needle of the scale.</note> is at the higher position **F**, the weight at **R** will be heavier; therefore, **F** will pull the balance toward **c**. Conversely, when the fulcrum is at the lower position **R**, it will be heavier than at **F**, and so it will pull the balance toward **Q**. Now, if someone should object that a weight at **F** would therefore be heavier than at **c** (the balance being hung at **A**), even though the opposite has already been demonstrated, we reply as follows: a wider angle from the vertical limit makes a weight heavier when the straight lines [the arms of the beam] are equal. However, as has been demonstrated, a weight at **c** is further from both the vertical limit and the fulcrum than it is at **F**. Therefore, the logic of the angle does not apply there. But when we compare weights at **F** and **R**, they are at an equal distance from both the fulcrum and the vertical limit; therefore, in that case, the ratio of the angle must be considered. Thus, the general rule is this: the further weights are from the vertical limit—that is, the line of descent—whether by a straight or oblique path (meaning by an angle), the heavier they are. But first, the length of the straight line must be considered: where the straight lines are equal, the larger the angle, the heavier the weight will be rendered.

<margin>Why weights move toward the middle.</margin>
But why do weights seek to move toward the middle? This is easily explained if one keeps in mind what we have said. For a weight at **F**, while it travels toward **c**, is rendered closer to the center of the world, toward which nature is carried along line **P B**. And while it moves from **c** to **Q**, it follows line **B Q**. Thus, the intent of a weight is to be carried in a straight line to the center; however, because it is prevented by its <term>tether</term> <note>original: "uinculo"; referring here to the physical arm of the scale that restricts free fall.</note>, it moves in the way that it can—namely, from the right or left toward the <term>plummet</term> <note>original: "pendiculum"; the vertical line of the scale's suspension.</note> and the middle. But you might ask, why then does the balance not move toward **Q** when **c** is empty? I reply that in that case **D** would have to move toward **A**. But as we have seen by the logic of the straight line, if **c** were placed at **Q** and **D** at **A**, as much would be lost on the side of **D** as would be gained by **c**. However, the loss on the side of **D** would be more "against nature" than the gain for **c** would be "according to nature." Therefore, the harm would be greater than the benefit. For this reason, when the weights at **c** and **D** are equal, they will not only not move from that position of their own accord, but if moved by force, they will return to it.

<margin>A method for making a scale that shows the weights of things to be greater than they actually are.</margin>
Having considered these principles, we can construct a balance that appears equal when empty of weights, but which represents the weight of objects as greater than they truly are by using "standard" marks. In this way, as Aristotle reports, those selling <term>purple cloth</term> <note>original: "purpuram"; expensive ancient dye/fabric often associated with luxury and trade trickery.</note> used to deceive their buyers. The logic is as follows: If one wishes for a balance that displays twelve ounces for only eleven, let a metal rod **A B** be taken and divided into twenty-three equal parts (for that is the sum of eleven and twelve joined together). At the end of the eleventh part and the beginning of the twelfth part, let the <term>needle</term> <note>original: "lingua libramenti"; the indicator of the scale.</note> and the <term>needle-sheath</term> <note>original: "agina"; the fork or opening in which the needle moves.</note> be fixed. It is clear then that the side **A D** is the larger part by one-eleventh. Since **D C** is slightly longer and heavier than **A D**, we shall make it lighter by filing it down or drilling holes, or we shall add a lighter scale pan to **c** than to **A**, so that while the pans of the length **A C** are empty, the fulcrum lies exactly under the sheath due to the calculated ratio of thinness, with the balance leaning to neither side.

## On the principles of things.

If, however, we add a weight of eleven ounces to side **c**, and the twelve-ounce mark is in pan **A**, the balance will show equilibrium. Therefore, since the markings on the weights are not counterfeit, nor does the scale appear faulty when the pans are empty, a fraud is clearly detected by switching the goods and the weights back and forth, so that the weights are in **c** and the goods in **A**. For side **c** will descend for a double reason: both because a greater weight is in its pan, and because the arm **c D** is itself longer than **D A**. The principle of the <term>steelyard</term> <note>original: "statera"; a type of scale where a single weight is moved along a graduated arm to balance the load.</note> is more difficult and obscure, about which I spoke in my works on Arithmetic. Now, however, since it is related to this investigation, it will be best to add as much as is necessary for this purpose. Therefore, the entire principle consists of three parts. The first of these is from <term>Archimedes</term> <note>The famous Greek mathematician (c. 287–212 BCE) who established the foundations of statics and the law of the lever.</note> in his works on parabolas; it applies when the beam
<margin>Principle of the steelyard.</margin>
of the steelyard is considered to have no weight of its own. In this case, the ratio of weights in equilibrium is the reciprocal of their distances from the <term>fulcrum</term> <note>original: "trutina"; the pivot point of the scale.</note>. For example, if weight **D** hanging at **c** balances with weight **G** hanging at **F**, and the ratio of length **FB** to **BC** is fourfold, then weight **D** will also be four times weight **G**. The second part applies when a weight is hung only on the shorter side, and the beam itself is heavy and uniform in its size and weight. When equilibrium is achieved, the ratio of the hung weight to the weight of the entire beam is as the difference between the beam's parts is to double the weight of the smaller part. For example, let weight **D** hung at **c** create equilibrium with the rod **B L** without any other weight, and let **B L** and **B C** be as I have described, and let **B K** be made equal to **B C**: then I say that the ratio of **D** to the weight of **C L** is as the weight of **L K** is to the weight of **K C**. From this we have a rule: once the weight of **C L** and **C K** is known, to find weight **D**, we multiply the length **K L** (let it be 40, for example) by itself, which makes 1600; divide this by the weight of **C K** (let it be 16), which gives 100; add the weight of **L K** (which is 40) to this, and the weight of **D** becomes 140. In this way, we can know how much weight the steelyard represents for any measurement we desire. The third part is derived from these two: if the rod is considered to have no weight, but a weight equal to the difference in length from the <term>pivot-hole</term> <note>original: "agina"; the opening or eye in the scale beam through which the pivot pin passes.</note> is spread evenly across the whole rod, it will exert the same gravity as that same weight would if it were hung at a single point distant from the balance-bar by half the length of the entire rod. Suppose the rod **C L** has no weight, and **CB** is equal to **B K**, and a weight is spread out equally—as if in the shape of a rectangle—so that it balances with **D** hung at **c**. If weight **G** is taken to be equal to that spread-out weight, and **B M** is half of the entire length **C L**, I say that **G** suspended at **M** will create equilibrium with **D**, and will weigh just as heavily as if it were spread across the whole rod.

<margin>How the centers of weights may be found.</margin>
The centers of weights in circles and rectangles are at the common intersection of the two diameters. In all equilateral figures that can be inscribed in a circle, the center of gravity is the same as the center of the circumscribing circle. It is assumed in all these cases that these heavy objects have an equal thickness everywhere, and that they are made of material that possesses an equal weight everywhere. In all triangles <term>trigonis</term> <note>From the Greek "trigonos," meaning a three-angled figure or triangle.</note>, [the center of gravity is] at the common intersection of three lines, each of which, coming from the opposite angles to the individual sides, divides them into equal parts <note>These lines are known in modern geometry as medians.</note>. It is necessary that these concur by intersecting each other in one point, even if Archimedes did not demonstrate it. We, however, have shown that generally in our *Geometric Elements*, but now it shall be declared out of necessity.

For with sides AB and AC divided equally at D and E, and CD, BD being drawn, and through the common intersection G, [the lines] AGB and DE [are drawn], which will be parallel to the third side, whence [triangles] BEC and CDB will be equal, because they are on the same base BC; and by subtracting the common triangle BCG, the remaining triangle CEG will be equal to DBG. Likewise, AGE and AGD are equal, because they are on equal bases and between parallels: wherefore AGE and AGD are equal. And since they are upon the same line AG, they will be of equal height, which height is also that of triangles FGD and FGE, which stand on the same base FG; therefore they too are equal to each other. Because BC is parallel to DE, from the 29th proposition of the first book of the *Elements* <note>Euclid's Elements of Geometry.</note> and the 15th of the same, DGE and BGC will be equiangular, and the ratio of BG to GE will be as CG to GD. From the same also BGH and GEF are similar, and likewise CGH and DGF. Wherefore the ratio of triangle BGH to EFG is as the square <note>original: "dupla" — in the context of Euclidean ratios of areas of similar figures, this refers to the duplicate ratio, or the square of the ratio of the sides.</note> of the ratio of BG to GE, and CGH to DFG as the square of the ratio of CG to GD. But as was said, CG is to GD as BG is to GE; wherefore BGH to EFG is as BCG to DFG. Since DFG and EFG are equal, BGH and CGH will be equal. And since they are between parallels, they will be on equal bases BH and HC; therefore all the triangles ABH, ACH, CDB, CDA, BEC, and BEA will be half <note>original: "medietas"</note> of triangle ABC, wherefore a triangle suspended at point G could not incline in any direction.

The center of the section of a parabola or a right-angled cone is on its diameter, at that point which is further from the summit of the cone by half than it is from the base, which is the straight line placed beneath the angle of the cone. When therefore

Given a rod $CL$ of a weight equal to 7 ounces, and the scale-hanging point at $B$, such that $KL$ is 10 and $KC$ is 4, and $G$ <note>The sliding weight or counterpoise.</note> is one pound, we shall thus construct the steelyard <term>statera</term> <note>A steelyard is a scale with unequal arms, where a single weight is moved along a graduated beam to find the weight of an object.</note>. I multiply the weight $LK$, which is 5, by itself, making 25; I divide this by weight $KC$, which is 2, making $12 \frac{1}{2}$; to this I add the 5 ounces of $LK$, making $17 \frac{1}{2}$. I shall therefore place the iron link <term>vinculum</term> $CD$ at $5 \frac{1}{2}$ ounces, and there will remain the weight $LK$ of one pound. Therefore, when we have placed $G$ at $K$, it will be equal to a pound, and it will be necessary to add another pound at $D$ because of $LK$; therefore at $K$ we shall show two pounds, and we shall mark it so. Then at $s$ 3, at $r$ 4, at $f$ 5, at $v$ 6, at $l$ 7, with equal spaces. From this it is clear that all these spaces can be distributed by ounces, except for the first, $BK$. We could, however, divide even that, so that a pound is understood at $B$, and the ounces added through equal spaces in $AB$ at $K$ will signify: the first 13, the second 14, the third 15, and so on for the others.

<margin>Why balances are generally more exact than steelyards</margin>
It is clear from these points why balances <term>librae</term> <note>The "libra" here refers to the traditional balance with two equal arms and two pans, as opposed to the sliding-weight steelyard.</note> are more exact than steelyards for three reasons. This, moreover, was our proposition from the beginning. First, because in a steelyard it is difficult to construct a rod so exact in its dimensions; and even if it is exact in size, it will not be so in weight, for we can scarcely achieve this. Second, it is most difficult to divide $LB$ into equal intervals absolutely perfectly. Third, the weight is rarely hung at the very extremity $C$, and when it is hung elsewhere, it produces confusion.

There are also many additions that spoil the steelyard, none of which exist in the balance. For this reason, precious items are not usually examined on a steelyard, but on a balance. It matters much for the exact construction of a steelyard that $G$ be light, as also $LC$, and that $LB$ be triple the length of $BC$, for thus $LK$ will be equal to $KC$, and that the links $CD$ be at the extremity of $LC$, and of equal weight with $LK$. For this type of steelyard will be closest to the balance.

<margin>How much weight skins sustain in water.</margin>
Truly, how much weight skins <term>utres</term> <note>Inflatable bladders or animal skins used as floats or pontoons.</note> sustain in water for the construction of bridges is shown by experiment. For a bladder full of air, which was capable of holding five pounds and one ounce of water, sustained a weight of fourteen and a half pounds of bricks: from which it follows that in the water of rivers, they can support nearly triple the weight of the water the skins are capable of holding.

<margin>How a man remains still and supine upon the water.</term>
One should also not omit that it arises from the ratio of density that men, when they keep themselves supine <note>lying on the back</note> in the water—so that like performers on ropes they are not bent at all in any part, remaining motionless—then they do not sink by any means.

# BOOK TWO

## On the Elements, their Motions, and Actions.

<margin>On the number of the elements.</margin>
**N**ow indeed let us treat the Elements, which consist of form and primary matter, and seem as if they were animated; the Greeks call them <term>stoicheia</term> <note>The Greek word "στοιχεῖα" means the fundamental components or "first principles" of the physical world.</note>. First, however, it is necessary to learn thoroughly how many and of what kind they are. <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose physical theories dominated European thought for centuries.</note> considers there to be four: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire. For first, there are four primary qualities <note>The four primary qualities are hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>. These alone do not constitute an element, because they would lack the power of acting and being acted upon; nor do more than two joined together, lest opposites be present at the same time. For if you take any three of the hot, cold, dry, and moist, it is inevitable that you include opposites. But neither can hot be joined with cold, nor dry with moist. Therefore, by joining two qualities that are not opposites, only four pairings <note>original: "coniugationes"</note> will be made, which constitute the four elements. Furthermore, between the lowest and highest place, it is necessary that two places lie in between—the "not-quite-lowest" and the "not-quite-highest"—and thus as many simple bodies. We also see, if probable arguments carry any weight, these four elements within mixed bodies themselves. For no one can doubt Earth, Air, and Water because of their magnitude and vast masses, such as the sea of waters, and the air and earth in the universe. But as for Fire, its increase, power, and simplicity—whose source is also believed to be in the concavity of the Moon—are noted <note>In the Aristotelian model, a "sphere of fire" was thought to exist just below the orbit of the moon.</note>. Many also think these four are seen in distillations, and the senses detect as many humors in animals <note>The four humors—blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm—were thought to correspond to the four elements.</note>. Indeed, many believe that Comets are formed for this reason: because vapors are ignited by the element of fire beneath the heavens. But certainly, there is no fire beneath the sphere of the Moon. For since the heavens are a most pure thing, it was not fitting to place the most burning and scorching thing beneath something devoid of every quality. For Nature always joins extremes by means of intermediaries. Between flesh and bone, she placed a membrane; between bone and ligaments, cartilages; between bone and brain—because the brain is softer than flesh—she placed a double membrane, with the harder one closer to the bone. Nor can the velocity of motion be either a cause or proof of heat. For those things that are solid, even if ignited by motion like stones, lead, and animals, are nonetheless dissipated; the faster they move, the colder they become, like water and air. For all strong winds are cold, and fast-flowing rivers have the coldest waters. There is also another significant argument for this matter, namely that comets

## Book Two

...or torches kindle intolerable heats in these things: what then will happen if such a vast region and the entire world were surrounded by fire? For what will prevent it from setting the air itself on fire, and then all these remaining things, especially since the heat of the stars will help. For <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), an Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> thinks that all light is hot. They also want Air to be extremely hot; but the moist quality resists least of all. How then will the Air itself resist the most violent, greatest, and sharpest of elements [Fire]? Therefore Averroes himself, seeing this, sometimes said that fire is not hot <term>in act</term> <note>original: "actu" — a scholastic term meaning "actually" or "currently functioning as," contrasted with potentiality.</note>. But if it is not hot in act, what kind of potentiality is this? We say medicines have "potential" when, after being swallowed, they provide heat: but will this fire be swallowed by some enormous animal? Then, if fire is not hot, nor water cold by equal reasoning, this would be to throw the order of the universe into confusion. 
<margin>In the first commentary on the *Canticle* [of Avicenna], 15.</margin>
What also prevents it from shining? Although they evade this as a trivial argument. If there is fire there [in the upper regions], why is it that the higher we climb, the colder everything appears, so that they assert snow abounds on the peaks of mountains even under the <term>torrid zone</term> <note>The tropics; the region of the Earth between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.</note>? This is less surprising if one considers that not only in winter is there snow, but even in the middle of summer, the coldest hailstones are generated. But they say those places are away from the reflection <note>original: "radiorum repercussu" — the bouncing of sunbeams off the earth which was thought to heat the lower atmosphere; without this reflection, the upper air was believed to remain cold.</note> of the [sun's] rays: But this can be an argument for lesser heat, but not for coldness. Finally, if [fire] were there, it would be primarily for the sake of generation: but it cannot be for this reason, since it is celestial heat that generates, even by the testimony of the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>Aristotle.</note> himself, and the lightest thing could hardly descend so far.

Perhaps someone will say that this fire is carried upwards, and from that it will be conjectured that its place is there. But first, these rhetorical arguments are unworthy of being brought into serious matters: nor is this [terrestrial] fire of the same nature as that which they say is higher up, since this one burns, shines, and corrupts, none of which they say belong to that [celestial] fire. We will say later why that happens, and we will show that it does not even always happen. Nor do those arguments prove it; rather, the opposite. For between two extremes, not two, but only one middle is usually assigned. If that were established, there would be only three elements, not four. If this does not demonstrate it, much less will it demonstrate that there are four. Nor do torches [meteors] or comets suggest to us that fire is there, since the Philosopher himself asserts that these things occur below the fire and near the earth in the air, so that these very things are not entirely in need of fire. 

But fire is not even seen in mixed bodies. For if it were present, it would be in <term>euphorbium</term> <note>A very pungent resin from a succulent plant used in early medicine.</note> and pepper—whose power is hot and dry to no small degree—rather than in the coldest stones. <term>Sublimations</term> <note>An early chemical process of heating a substance to a gas then cooling it to a solid; used here to analyze a substance's components.</note> also teach that there are only three substances: water representing water, oil in place of air, and earth which settles at the bottom. But if you say the redder part of the oil represents fire because it is the sharpest, we reply seriously that this sharpness and bitter taste proceed from a more pungent force of fire; the evidence is that no part of metallic oils is without a very sharp taste, so that if all of this...

<header>On the Elements and their actions.</header>

# On the Elements and their actions.

That which is most sharp relates to fire; there ought to be no air present at all. Therefore, we return to only three elements. There are four humors in animals, but what has this to do with the elements? What if I say, along with <term>Turisanus</term> <note>Pietro Torrigiano de' Torrigiani (d. 1313), a famous commentator on Galen's "Microtechne."</note>, the commentator on <term>Galen's medical art</term>, that there are only three? But even if sense-perception shows there are four—not at all!—for even they themselves do not admit that this fire <note>referring to the fire we use on earth</note> is the actual element. Therefore, our senses declare three to us rather than four. Nor should it be called an element just because it quickly consumes everything; for if that were the case, motion itself would be an element. Nor should it be an element because it grows quickly; for then even mice would be elements <note>The author uses a "reductio ad absurdum" here, mocking the idea that rapid growth or consumption defines a fundamental element.</note>. But neither of these qualities is found in the earth, which nonetheless everyone with one voice confesses to be an element. Therefore, all these arguments for demonstrating that there are four elements, and that fire is an element, have very little credibility. Indeed, as we proposed from the beginning, they show the opposite. There remained that greatest argument from the <term>pairings of qualities</term> <note>The Aristotelian system paired Hot/Cold with Moist/Dry to create the four elements.</note>, but they do not see that they are showing this in mixed bodies; for some things are hot and moist, others hot and dry, and so on. But in the elements, since such immoderate heat and dryness would have led everything to destruction, he substituted in place of the element a celestial heat, well-tempered, from which all things might be generated. This matter which they call fire is usually generated both by rot and by motion. Fire, therefore, is produced, but it is by no means an element.

I already know what some will say: "Who are you, so bold, who dares to think against <term>the Philosopher</term> <note>A standard title for Aristotle in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>? Especially regarding such a confirmed and ancient opinion of things." Then, [they will ask] in what way the generation of hail and snow shows that fire is not there, since even if no fire is present, it is still not right for that region to be the coldest, since it is illuminated by the rays of the stars, and nonetheless the air itself in which it is located is a very hot region. Also, when we say "fire" and "element," we understand something thoroughly hot and dry; our fire here is hottest and driest, which happens because it is unmixed; for if it were mixed, it could not be such. Therefore, this fire is an element.

These are the objections which, even if they are not currently thrown at me, I feel could be thrown. Therefore, to come to Aristotle: he was a man, and he erred in dissection and in many specific particulars. Even those after him, <term>Theophrastus</term> and <term>Galen</term>, wrote many things erroneously. Therefore, if it was permitted for Aristotle to leave <term>Plato</term> for the sake of the truth, why will it not be permitted for us to desert Aristotle for that same truth? He attempted to build up certain general propositions which experience teaches are false: such as his claim that "no animal has a pleasant smell" <note>Aristotle claimed in "History of Animals" that only the panther had a naturally good scent.</note>, or that "a heavy thing cannot protrude on both sides," and therefore that the earth does not protrude from the water on both sides—claims which are found to be false by experiment. Therefore, if we admit that he erred in two or three out of a thousand propositions, we would say he did nothing unworthy of a man, even a very wise one...

...we shall see. For he is deserted even by <term>Averroes</term> <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the influential Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> himself in a few matters, refuted in some, but in most cases he is defended by a shifting of the sense. This, however, is truly a matter of refuting him, not protecting him. Yet we do not disagree with <term>Aristotle</term> on this point: for in the concave of the Moon’s sphere, he intends there to be neither fire nor anything very hot. 
<margin>1. Meteorology, Chapter 4.</margin>
As for the region of the air, it is obvious that it is extremely cold solely because of its motions; indeed, no other plausible cause can be assigned. For what is said about vapors and the so-called <term>antiperistasis</term> <note>original: "antispasi." Antiperistasis is the Aristotelian idea that a quality is intensified when surrounded by its opposite, such as heat being compressed and strengthened by surrounding cold.</note> is more like a fable than a record of natural science. Therefore, if fire were placed in the concave of the Moon and rotated there very swiftly, it would be extremely cold. Thus, we attack that theory; we do not abandon experience. For it is clearer than daylight that the air there is extremely cold, especially that which is in the concave of the Moon, but it is 
<margin>What the Aether is and where it is.</margin>
tempered by the proximity of the stars, and most of all the Moon. And although the Moon is directly aligned with only one small part, because everything is mixed together and is of the finest substance, that air is perfectly tempered; it is also most pure, clear, and entirely unadulterated. For this reason, the ancients rightly called it <term>Aether</term>, and indeed even the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>A standard title for Aristotle in academic texts of this period.</note> himself did so at times. This matches most beautifully the location and nature of the heavens, being almost similar in its thinness and the balance of its quality. For the aether is not "tempered" because it is an equal mixture of hot and cold, but because it is devoid of both qualities. Likewise, it cannot be called dry, because it flows, nor moist, because it does not dampen; but it is pure, as I said, and clear, and most suited for generation, about which we shall speak later.

<margin>Air is tempered by nature, not hot.</margin>
That the air is "extremely hot" is something no experiment teaches and no reason compels; rather, it is tempered by its own nature, and by motion it even becomes cold. All these things agree with experience. Those chimerical fabrications of the Aristotelians—lest I seem merely to accuse him—end in inexplicable questions that are <term>still before the judge</term> <note>A Latin idiom (sub iudice) meaning the matter is undecided or still under legal/intellectual debate.</note>. Therefore, it is better to uphold the truth and the experiments themselves with a few things changed, than to know nothing about the nature of things while perpetually talking nonsense with them. For who but a madman would listen to someone arguing and affirming that air is hot at its furthest and highest point, yet then, solely because of motion or vapors without motion (as in the North), it becomes so cold that it produces ice, snow, and hail? No one complains of the air's heat except by the power of the Sun, while everyone complains of its cold; and yet they dare to attribute to air a heat almost no different from that of fire. Why is fire, though it is of a thinner substance than air, never deprived of its immense heat, nor does its nature and fervor soften, much less become cold? If they say that this air is not the air that moves or receives vapors, it is impossible—even in Aristotle's judgment—for the substance to remain the same after such a great transformation from "extremely hot" to "extremely cold." It is obvious, since all the air that surrounds us is cold, or at least

<header>On the Elements and their actions.</header>

# On the Elements and their actions.

<margin>The nature and number of the elements.</margin>
...tempered, as is the case with the region situated next to the sphere of the Moon. For the entire mass of the air, as is evident from fiery apparitions <note>Original: "igneis apparitionibus." This refers to phenomena like meteors, comets, or lightning, which were believed to occur in the upper atmosphere.</note>, is carried around by the motion of the heaven in twenty-four hours. This is admitted by <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose "four elements" theory (earth, water, air, fire) dominated science for centuries.</note> himself: that this entire engine of the air is cold or tempered. If this were not so, we would have to search for another "elemental" air elsewhere, perhaps above the heavens or in the depths of the earth. Therefore, it is sufficiently clear that all this air which is carried around is temperate by nature, the earth is dry or very cold, and the water is cold and moist; and all these are well-tempered by the heat of the Sun and all the remaining stars. There are, therefore, three elements. But to return to my purpose: I do not call something an "element" simply because it is the most dry or the most hot; for as I have said, you will hardly see any other thing besides water—which is cold, though not excessively so—that possesses such a potent quality.

<margin>That this fire is not an element.</margin>
But I now define an "element" as that which neither requires fuel <note>Original: "pabulo," literally "food" or "fodder."</note>, nor perishes of its own accord, nor wanders about, but holds a certain fixed seat, possessing a very great mass, and is prepared according to nature for <term>generation</term> <note>The process by which natural things are born, formed, or brought into existence.</note>. Since none of these characteristics suit fire, we shall by no means call it an element.

<margin>What flame is.</margin>
<margin>Why flame never rests.</margin>
<margin>How fire burns.</margin>
<margin>Flame does not remain the same.</margin>
<margin>Why flame mostly ascends.</margin>
Fire is moved, however, being unable to live without nourishment, and it scorches the nearest air; this burning is called **flame**. For flame is nothing other than ignited air. It is, moreover, perpetually in motion and never rests. Because the substance of fire is extremely thin and always burns the material placed beneath it, it is also in perpetual motion. Because of its fineness, it enters through the narrowest openings; because of its motion, it divides and cuts; and having split things apart with immense heat, it burns them and converts them into its own substance. Therefore, a flame never remains the same, but one succeeds another in a perpetual cycle of generation, and for this reason, it is necessary that it always appears to be moving. For that which has already been generated invades the nearest part of the air, feeds on its moisture, and in dying, excites another new flame. Since, therefore, the moisture that was there before is turned into flame—its volume increasing immensely from this mutation—and since it cannot push through the hard fuel beneath it, it necessarily ascends violently into the upper part and pushes against the flame that was already above it. From this, it happens that flame is usually carried upward with great force and strikes. Nevertheless, if beams located above are burning, the flame must be carried downward by the same logic. Therefore, flame is not *always* carried upward, but usually so because the fuel is located at the bottom.

<margin>Why inverted candles are extinguished.</margin>
<margin>How smoke is generated.</margin>
Yet when it is carried to the bottom, it burns so intensely that if the material being burned is moist, it suddenly liquefies and suffocates the fire; for this reason, candles are spontaneously extinguished if the flame is turned downward. Wood, however, does not do this, because its moisture cannot be liquefied in the same way. They are also extinguished for another reason: because, as I said, the upper part of the flame is always propelled by the lower part, which is closer to the nourishment; hence the highest part of the flame, extinguished by its continuous passage, is generated into **smoke**.

<margin>Twofold smoke.</margin>
...is turned into smoke. <note>The text begins mid-word, completing the sentence from the previous page.</note> For smoke is a middle state between flame and air, and is therefore twofold: one kind follows the flame, and this is thin and necessary. For every flame is turned into smoke, but because this kind is very thin, it passes quickly into the air; and for that reason, it neither suffocates nor burns the eyes, but only warms and dries. The other is the smoke that precedes the generation of flame, and this is more moist, and burns the eyes and suffocates, because it is not easily converted into air. This same kind is usually stirred up from poor coals and damper wood. Therefore, the first kind [the thin smoke] descends when candles are inverted; while it strives to ascend, it meets the flame itself and very quickly suffocates it. For we have explained that an immense quantity of this is produced, since at every moment the flame which is furthest removed from its nourishment, and near the air in its circumference, passes into smoke; it is no wonder that the fire meeting such a quantity is very quickly suffocated. Therefore, because of this very rapid movement, the flame destroys everything, and not only by reason of its immense heat. Yet this internal motion in the flame escapes our notice because it happens gradually. Nor does the whole flame perish instantly, but only that which is on the outer edge; for that which is in the middle remains until it finally comes into contact with the air; otherwise, there would be nothing in the middle of a flame.

<margin>Why flame is more lively than other fire.</margin>
Since, therefore, three things are necessary for fire to burn—fuel <note>Original: "pabulum," literally food or fodder.</note>, motion, and that which penetrates—and since in a flame the motion is greater and more manifest (and thus the entry into the fuel that follows the motion is also greater), it is not at all obscure why a flame is more lively than any other kind of fire. Therefore, as long as the flame is vigorous, candles burn until the nourishment is exhausted; when the flame ceases, they are completely extinguished, either of their own accord or in a moment.

<margin>Causes of great flames.</margin>
However, because a flame consumes much fuel, it very often lasts for a shorter time than glowing coals <note>Original: "prunis."</note>; but this is not due to its own nature, but because the fuel is finished more quickly. For these reasons, long-lasting flames are created from oily moisture, and immense flames are created from thin and dry substances. For in a thin and dry substance, flame follows flame in rapid succession, and for that reason, it grows into a massive size. But if both are joined—a dry, thin substance and an oily, abundant moisture, as in bitumen—then the greatest and longest-lasting flames are stirred up.

<margin>Why does water sometimes excite fires?</margin>
Because of this, it becomes clear why water thrown onto burning bitumen excites greater flames, which even <term>Georgius Agricola</term> <note>A famous German scholar (1494–1555) known for his work on mining and geology; the author considers him a "man worthy of memory in our time."</note> recounts. He says that on the island of <term>Iceland</term> there is a mountain named <term>Hecla</term> <note>Mount Hekla, a famous active volcano in Iceland.</note>, from which the fire sent forth is extinguished by dry things, but is actually nourished by water. Moreover, this is common to almost all stronger flames, which is why blacksmiths are accustomed to excite fires by sprinkling water; for when the fire has become hotter, it is incited by the cold and nourished by the moisture, both of which are present in water.

<margin>Why bellows kindle fire and where they are more necessary.</margin>
For that reason also, a fire kindled by bellows, since it is strong, is not extinguished by a small amount of water, but becomes more robust. For bellows kindle fires because they stir up motion; from which...

<header>On Elements and their actions.</header>

# On Elements and their actions.

Through motion, the power [of fire] penetrates and burns away; however, [bellows] are necessary for metals, because they do not melt from a small fire, but from a forceful one they do melt, though slowly; therefore they are burnt away before they can melt. But when fire is stirred by bellows, it moves and penetrates, and melts the metals. From this, there is no small advantage in a swift outcome: both that less expense is wasted, and a smaller portion of the metal is burnt. Therefore, bellows are most fit for kindling a fire and for softening and melting [metal].

And so, to return to the subject, water is accustomed to kindle forceful fires, because the very moisture it exhales is rendered fattier, nor is it consumed by the surrounding smoke, but the fire itself feeds entirely upon it; by this process, having been made purer and simultaneously gathered together by the cold, the fire rises up more eagerly. From this come those fires 
<margin>
Artificial fires which are not extinguished by water.
</margin>

Yet another [recipe] of liquid varnish, sulfur oil, juniper oil, and that which is made from linseed, and petroleum, and larch resin <note>original: "lachrimæ larignæ"</note> in equal parts of each, and three and a half parts of burning water: then as much saltpeter and dry laurel wood reduced to powder as is sufficient, so that all mixed together may take on the thickness of mud. Receive all these in a glass vessel and bury them in horse manure for three months. If, therefore, wooden balls made from these are attached [to something], they are kindled spontaneously by rain, but this does not always happen. That which always happens, however, is that once kindled, it cannot be extinguished by any water. The powder which burns most easily, and whose flame burns most vehemently, consists of gunpowder <note>original: "pyrio puluere"</note> and a third part of sulfur and Greek pitch. <header>Book Two</header>

# Book Two

<margin>Methods for extinguishing large fires.</margin>
...combustible material, or by erecting a wall of stones and throwing stones over the fire. By this method, some friends of ours saved their neighboring house from a fire. Alternatively, we use the method common when groves or crops are burning: the part toward which the fire is moving is intentionally set ablaze <note>This refers to a "controlled burn" or "back-burning," where a firebreak is created by consuming the fuel before the main fire reaches it</note>. For once that fire is extinguished—or even if not yet fully out—the majority of the fuel has been removed, and by this dangerous but useful discovery, we save the rest. Our own groves in the territory of Novara <note>A city in the Piedmont region of Italy</note> were saved by this kind of help, a method not much different from that by which the lord of the place has often freed himself from danger.

<margin>Places that burn.</margin>
There are, therefore, places abundant in bitumen or sulfur that burn spontaneously and are not extinguished by water at all. The fire of Mount Etna in Sicily is the most famous. It has two craters: the lower one is narrow, shaped like a well, surrounded by a narrow stone rim; the upper one, however, is said to be a sling-shot’s distance from the bottom and has a circumference of four stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient Greek unit of length; four stadia is roughly half a mile</note>. It spews ashes for a hundred miles in every direction, shrouding everything in the deepest darkness for two days—a fact also affirmed by Pliny <note>original: "Plinius"; refers to Pliny the Elder, the Roman natural historian</note>. But in our own times, this activity seems to have diminished. Truly, in Pozzuoli <note>original: "Puteolis"; a volcanic area near Naples</note>, shortly before we wrote these words—situated twenty miles from Naples, as I hear—a very great loss occurred due to a fire. These fires occur where sulfur or bitumen is produced, usually near the sea, because bitumen and sulfur receive their nourishment from marine impurities and heat.

<margin>Fire harmless to plants.</margin>
We shall discuss below how the prepared material is ignited; however, fire that remains hidden during the day and is only seen at night—as we saw in the Mugello region of the Apennines—is harmless to trees and even to herbs. This phenomenon is twofold: one is truly fire, but it arises from vapors that signify a loss over time as they underlie the material. The other is entirely harmless and is not truly fire at all, but like the rotting substance of wood <note>This refers to bioluminescence, often called "foxfire," caused by fungi on decaying wood</note>, it reflects a glow at night through its brilliance alone, but without heat.

<margin>The Star of Helen, which announces the sinking of a ship.</margin>
Of almost the same kind of true fire is the "Star of Helen" <note>An ancient name for a single point of St. Elmo's fire</note> seen around the mast of a ship; when it falls, it even melts bronze vessels—a certain messenger of sinking. For this occurs only in heavy storms, nor can that vapor be compressed upon a ship and burn at the same time except by the thickest spirit and a great force of winds; hence, it announces imminent destruction. Conversely, what were once called the divine powers of Castor and Pollux are now called the lights of Saints Peter and Nicholas; these are usually twin lights leaping among the ropes like birds with a certain sound, moving from one to another. They show the end of the storm and safety. For these are vapors clinging to the ropes which, as time passes and the fire moves from one to another, present the appearance of a lit candle. They indicate safety because they are small and not at all sluggish—otherwise they would have joined into one—and because each is consumed quickly. Although they create a false image of leaping, when there are several, they usually resemble two; as they follow one another, many in succession create the appearance of a single, longer-lasting light.

<margin>How the motion of bellows works.</margin>
Up to this point, we have spoken of fire and added the utility of bellows in the meantime...

<header>On the Elements and Their Actions</header>

# On the Elements and Their Actions

It seems right that we should also add an account of motion, since, as we have said, nothing remarkable is accomplished by a fire that is not assisted by bellows. These must be double—whether there be two, or four, or more—so that the work is never interrupted. Their motion varies in alternating turns, and is clearly a mixture of the <term>violent motion</term> <note>In Aristotelian physics, "violent motion" is movement forced upon an object by an external power, while "natural motion" is the object's inherent tendency to move toward its proper place</note> by which they are opened and draw in air, and the <term>natural motion</term> by which they spontaneously descend and press out the air they have captured. It is evident, moreover, that the more quickly they press it out, the more fiercely they drive the fire. For this reason, they weigh them down with weights. But because heavy things are not easily or quickly raised, the machine for them must be turned by large wheels and a great force of water.

<margin>Why fire causes more harm through heat than ice does through cold</margin>
For these reasons, it is clear that ice, even if it be extremely cold, cannot cause as much harm through coldness as fire does through heat. For while fire penetrates everything by its motion, and through its entry dissipates things before it even burns them, ice consists of a certain stillness and a thick substance, which makes it impossible for it to penetrate anything at all. That ice is no less cold than fire is hot is shown by an experiment: for if you place as much ice upon a burning piece of wood or brick, the ice will not be dissolved any faster than the fire is entirely extinguished. Since fire, through its motion and thinness, penetrates more—and more easily corrupts and consumes than ice—it serves as proof that the entry and <term>subtlety</term> <note>Original: "subtilitatem"; here meaning the fineness or lack of density that allows a substance to pass through pores</note> of these elements are the causes of these wonderful effects. This is why things that cannot be penetrated, such as gold and diamonds, are not consumed or burned by fire, nor can they truly be called "fiery" at all; likewise, ice resists more through its density and stillness, and lasts longer. For while fire is always in flux, ice remains the same and sometimes lasts for many years in the frozen mountains <term>under the Bear</term> <note>original: "sub ursa"; a reference to the constellations Ursa Major and Minor, signifying the far North or Arctic regions</note>, and the same is true of snow.

<margin>Fire and ice are complete opposites.</margin>
Therefore, ice and fire are complete opposites.

<margin>What fire is.</margin>
For fire is the hottest, thinnest, of the swiftest motion, and one that easily invades all things and remains only for a moment; but ice is the coldest, densest, entirely still, of slow progress, and extremely long-lasting.

Therefore, the solution to a great question now emerges from these points: namely, whether this fire of ours is a <term>substance</term> or an <term>accident</term> <note>In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, a "substance" is a thing that exists in itself (like iron), while an "accident" is a quality that exists only within a substance (like heat or color)</note>. For if it were a substance, it seemed difficult to explain how two substances—the fiery and the metallic—could be mutually interpenetrating at the same time in glowing iron. Then, indeed, if one were dissolved (such as the metallic substance) while it conceives fire, a "corruption" would occur, and when the fire is extinguished, a "generation" would be said to happen, which is quite absurd. If, however, you say that only the air inside a burning brick is what glows, the substance of the wood would not be dissolved into ashes, nor would iron turn out so much the worse for it; therefore, the internal moisture of the iron burns while the iron brick is heated. But if fire is entirely an accident, how does it change the substance of wood into ash, and consume iron and almost everything else? And so, as I have said, this fire is nothing other than the highest heat joined with dryness. Nor can it be called a substance, unless in the same way as ice; if ice is understood as a thing congealed by frost, so fire is the thing itself which...

It concludes by defining fire not as a unique material substance, but as the quality of extreme heat and dryness acting upon an object.</summary>

<margin>Fire can be hotter than other fire.</margin>
...which burns. Fire, therefore, is entirely an <term>accident</term> <note>In the philosophy of the time, an "accident" is a quality or attribute that exists within a substance but is not the substance itself—like the color of an apple or the heat in a piece of iron.</note>, and extreme heat combined with dryness; it inheres in a substance always just like other accidents, and therefore it cannot be an element, as we also demonstrated above. For the "principle of nature" would then consist of a mere chance occurrence and would have to be carried around by uncertain fuel; indeed, by that same reasoning, ice would be a different element. But if fire were a distinct element, since it is equally hot as this fire or more so, then it too would require fuel, because it would need to be fed: from where, then, would the fuel for such a massive volume come? If, however, it is less hot, the reason for which it was established as an element ceases to apply. For if fire was categorized as an element, it was because it was thought to be a certain substance of the highest heat and dryness, possessing both these qualities, or at least one of them, in a perfect state; yet it will not possess them, since it is now established that this fire <note>original: "hunc ignem"</note> is far hotter, drier, more burning, and more penetrating than that supposed elemental fire.

<margin>Fire becomes more powerful in six ways.</margin>
<margin>A method of cooking with a small fire.</margin>
<margin>Why lime is ignited by water.</margin>
<margin>Why lightning possesses such great power.</margin>
But a clear solution to another doubt also emerges: can one fire be hotter than another fire? It is well established that fire does not become hotter solely because of its fuel—as the fire in iron is hotter than that in straw, or that in oak wood hotter than that in willow—but just as in ice, some is barely frozen, some is hard, and some is very hard, so some fire is barely fire, such as when iron begins to glow; some is whiter, and some is most brilliant. For since it is an accident, it can be increased or diminished. Therefore, fire becomes more powerful than other fire in six ways. By **Nature**, as we said, for a more burning fire consumes more and faster. By **Matter**, such as the fire that resides in iron compared to that in stalks. By **Motion**, for it becomes more penetrating. By **Magnitude**, whether by its own size or by the duration of time; this can be obscure to no one. Finally, by the **obstruction of respiration** <note>In this context, "respiration" refers to the "breathing" or ventilation of the fire—how air reaches it.</note>: sailors are not ignorant of this, who, by placing a pot over a tiny hearth, force all the pots to boil, which is a consideration for the poor. But it is necessary, as I said, that the little fire not be extinguished by its own smoke, and that it be allowed to breathe a little. Because of this, those who are mindful of expense construct small furnaces of bronze in the shape of a pot, with narrow iron gratings at the bottom so that the ash can fall out. The last way is when fire is **compressed**, and because of this, <term>lime</term> <note>Quicklime (calcium oxide) produces intense heat when mixed with water, a chemical reaction the author interprets as "trapped" fire being released.</note> is ignited by water: for the heat acquired and hidden in the furnace, since (as I said) it is of the genus of fire, is shut inside by the cold of a little water; then by both motion and the compression itself, it breaks out into fire. How heat is left behind in those things which burn, and how it is turned into fire by motion and compression, we shall show below. Truly, motion not only forces it to penetrate more, but also ignites the heat itself, and as I said, makes one fire hotter than another. It is no wonder, then, that there is such great force in lightning, and that this fire, as if foreign to the nature of other fires, performs certain miracles. For on account of its swift motion, it not only penetrates more, but that fire exists as much hotter than all other fire. Therefore, it kills all animals except man by a mere touch, but a man can hardly ever escape it. Nevertheless, **John** escaped...

# On the Elements and Their Actions

<margin>How lightning melts coins while the purse remains unharmed.</margin>
<margin>Why lightning rarely strikes columns, and why?</margin>
<margin>Precaution against lightning.</margin>
Iohannes Maria Cardanus <note>Giovanni Maria Cardano (1443–1505), the father of the famous polymath Girolamo Cardano</note> survived a lightning strike by a rare miracle. But what other fire is there that kills by touch alone? This, therefore, is its unique property: that it is the hottest of all things hot, and, if one may say so, the *fire of fires*. Therefore, it matters greatly whether it comes from afar and from high above, or from nearby. Thus, it sometimes melts money while the purse remains unharmed; this is neither a fable nor a miracle. For while that which causes damage usually destroys by its bulk or by lingering, this fire—being extremely subtle—does not tear the purse; and because it moves with extreme speed, it does not stay, and for that reason, it is harmless to the purse. Air demonstrates how things can pass through without sticking due to subtlety; air itself enters and fills an empty, open purse, which could not happen unless it entered through <term>hidden passages</term> <note>original: "abditos meatus." This refers to the Renaissance belief that seemingly solid materials like leather or stone contained microscopic pores</note>, since the mouth of the purse might be tightly closed. Therefore, a spark of fire and a part of lightning, being far thinner than air itself, is fixed into the metal once it has entered, and by that excellent force and momentum, it suddenly melts it. Some shamefully call this extraordinary power of heat and immoderate dryness a "property," as if it were rare and hidden due to its rarity, when it is clearly immoderate heat, and, as I said, the *fire of fires*. But why does it not strike columns or hulls? It rarely strikes these, though not never; for in Florence, in the great cathedral—or rather in the precinct of the cathedral—we saw a column struck and damaged by lightning. Yet it does not strike them frequently, nor does it shatter them much, because the blow slides off due to their roundness. It does not strike hulls for the same reason, except rarely; for it is said that lightning cannot descend more than five <term>cubits</term> <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of measure, roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters</note> under the earth. Now, the hull of a ship is low, but the mast is tall, and lightning frequently touches the mast. Therefore, it is certain that the best protection against lightning is to hide oneself in deep caves; for this is safer than being crowned with <term>laurel</term> <note>In antiquity, laurel was famously believed to be immune to lightning, a belief attributed to the Emperor Tiberius among others</note>, or covered with the skin of a seal or an eagle, or carrying a <term>hyacinth stone</term> <note>likely zircon or a similar gemstone believed to have protective properties</note>. For they say these are not touched by lightning. But I heard that even a laurel tree was wounded by lightning in Rome a few years ago, and we shall discuss the hyacinth stone below, for the authors who affirm this are not of light authority.

<margin>The force of fire-machines.</margin>
<margin>Method of making fire-machines.</margin>
The power of lightning was once wondered at, but it has ceased to be so because of the effects and abundance of modern <term>war engines</term> <note>original: "bellicorum tormentorum," referring here to gunpowder artillery or cannons</note>, for they seem to differ little from the violence of lightning. We do not know where lightning comes from, or how far, or how much weight it carries with it; there are even those who affirm it is only fire with momentum, and no stone. This alone we know for certain: that entire towers are sometimes shattered by a single blow. From a single tower of the Cardani <note>The Cardano family home</note>—the only one that remains, though it is ancient—lightning struck out and scattered more than 12,000 bricks with a single blow. Yet these modern machines often carry 60 pounds of iron for five thousand paces—certainly a marvelous thing to say, if experience did not provide faith in the saying. These same machines batter walls; they shake and shatter walled cities, and no force can resist such an evil. The lightest are made of <term>Cyprian bronze</term> <note>original: "aes cyprium," the Latin origin of the word "copper"</note> in the manner of a trumpet-like channel, and they should not be narrower or wider at the bottom; indeed, if they are wider, they are not sealed exactly by the ball...

Furthermore, if they are made narrower without being made longer, they receive far less powder than is necessary. If they are made longer at the base but turn out shorter at the top, they lose much of their power because of it. If the iron ball does not descend as far as it ought, leaving a vacuum, they produce a weaker strike, shake the engine, and sometimes even break it. And yet, to the great misfortune of Princes, craftsmen devise certain narrower measurements so that their most obvious methods do not appear too common; some make them narrower at the bottom, others wider, doing so erroneously, when there is but one true method: that they be equal in all parts, which is the best and safest.

The ratio of the weight of the engine to the weight of the ball is one hundredfold: so that if the ball which it must fire weighs 20 pounds, the engine will weigh 2,000 pounds. The thickness at the base, where the place for the <term>gunpowder</term> <note>original: "pulveris pyrii," literally "fire-powder"</note> is located, should be three-quarters of the diameter of the ball. At the muzzle, the thickness of the engine’s lip should be no less than one-third of the diameter of the ball. The diameter of the bore, as I have said, should be equal to the diameter of the ball, and the weight of the gunpowder should equal the weight of the ball itself. In smaller pieces of artillery, however, it is fitting for the weight and thickness of the engine to have a greater proportion relative to the ball for the sake of safety, and by the same reasoning, the weight of the powder should be a little less than that of the ball. 

From this, the ratio of how much space the base ought to take up is clear: for it must be enough to contain the powder that equals the weight of the ball. The vent where the fire is ignited should also occupy part of the base, for the engine is not driven backward as much when the fire is only moved forward; because of this, one may aim the shot more correctly and with less danger. # On the Elements and Their Actions

[...large] engines are placed on mobile carriages in such a way that they are parallel to the ground and the horizon; thus, when they have caught fire, they are driven straight backward and forward without danger.

<margin>Two new kinds of war machines.</margin>
There is also another new kind of fire-engine, a cubit and a half in length, weighing between 70 and 80 pounds. The barrel <note>original: "canalis"</note> holds a sphere the size of a small ball. It is supported by an iron rod when discharged and held by a tail-piece—the machine and its load being a burden for only one man. Furthermore, on account of its thickness, it is wonderfully strong and no less safe. There is another type in which there is a wide cavity near the opening; various <term>chambers</term> <note>original: "modioli," literally small measures or hubs; here referring to interchangeable breech-blocks</note> are placed into the cavity, all of the same size, whose bores correspond directly to the bores of the machine. This is so that by changing the chambers, the machine does not overheat. We saw these at Pavia, the inventions of the Prince of Saxony. They are made, as I said, of **Cyprian copper** <note>a common term for bronze or brass alloys</note> for the larger ones, but the safest are made of **iron**. For this reason, all the smaller ones are now made of iron, though it is laborious to make the larger ones from iron.
<margin>From what material war machines are made.</margin>
Because of this, most are made of Cyprian copper. The smaller ones are made with a lathe; the larger ones by the work of molding molten metal, and thereafter finished with a lathe. Usually, the molds for casting the machines are made of three pieces, because it would be too difficult to mold them from one, as they are heavy enough as it is. One part is the barrel, the second is the <term>plunger</term> <note>original: "embolus masculus"</note>, and the third is the base. The machine itself, however, usually consists of one piece. I have also seen one consisting of two, with one bound to the other from the bottom by a turned screw. The material, as I said, is artificial Cyprian copper, consisting of the copper itself and about a seventh part of black or white lead, or <term>brass</term> <note>original: "aurichalco," or orichalcum</note>. But the reason for such great force lies in the **gunpowder**. <margin>Composition of gunpowder.</margin> This consists of three parts <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "halinitri"</note>, two parts willow charcoal, and one part sulfur; this is suitable for large engines. But for medium ones: ten parts saltpeter, three of willow charcoal, and two of sulfur. For small ones, however: ten parts saltpeter, and one part each of sulfur and charcoal from knot-free hazelwood. These should be crushed with a wooden mallet, having first been moistened with well water so that they do not catch fire while being pounded. There are those who add vinegar or <term>spirits</term> <note>original: "ardentem aquam," literally "burning water," referring to distilled alcohol</note> and dry it in the sun, but they do not pound it then, for it could easily catch fire. Indeed, the greatest care is taken that all things are so purged of earthy parts—especially the saltpeter—that it burns completely and nothing remains. Next, it must be reduced to the finest particles, for thus the parts will best cling to one another; this happens if it is frequently pounded, moistened, and dried. Thirdly, when it is finished, it should be dried in the sun. For to place it near a fire is most dangerous.

<margin>Why gunpowder sends a ball from the engine with such great force.</margin>
Therefore, let the cause of such a great effect now be sought: when this powder is placed in the machine and the ball is shut in, and fire is applied from the outside at the bottom of the machine, almost the whole mass is instantly ignited. It strives to occupy a space more than a hundred times greater [than its original size]. Experiment shows that a tiny amount of powder in the palm of the hand occupies no less than a hundred times the space, since a grain of millet—that is, a quantity of this powder the size of a millet seed—once ignited, fills the space of a nut with fire.

# On the Elements and their Actions

...[large] engines are positioned on mobile carriages in such a way that they are parallel to the ground and the horizon <note>original: "finitori," the boundary of sight</note>, and thus when they have caught fire, they are driven straight back without danger.

<margin>Two new types of war machines:</margin>
There is also another new type of fiery engine <note>a hand-cannon or early arquebus</note> a cubit and a half in length <note>approximately 27 inches</note>, weighing between 70 and 80 pounds. We saw these inventions of the Prince of Saxony at Pavia. They are made, as I said, of Cyprian bronze <note>original: "cyprio ære," likely a bronze or copper alloy</note> in the larger sizes, but the safest are made of iron. Wherefore, 
<margin>From what material war machines are made.</margin>
now all the smaller ones are made of iron, though it is laborious to make the larger ones from iron; for that reason, most are made of Cyprian bronze. The smaller ones are made with a lathe, the larger ones by the work of molding with molten metal, and thereafter finished with a lathe. The molds for casting the machines are usually made of three pieces, since it would be too difficult to cast from one, seeing as it is heavy even this way. One part is the barrel <note>original: "canalis"</note>, the second is the male plunger <note>the core of the mold</note>, and the third is the base. The machine itself, however, usually consists of a single piece. I have also seen one consisting of two pieces, with one bound to the other from the bottom by a turned screw. The material, as I said, is artificial Cyprian bronze; it consists of the copper itself and approximately a seventh part of lead (either black or white) or brass <note>original: "aurichalco"</note>. But the 
<margin>The composition of gunpowder.</margin>
reason for such a great force lies in the <term>gunpowder</term> <note>original: "pyrio puluere," literally 'fiery powder'</note>. This consists of three parts saltpeter <note>original: "halinitri"</note>, two parts willow charcoal, and one part sulfur; this is suitable for large machines. But for medium ones, ten parts saltpeter, three of willow charcoal, and two of sulfur. For small ones, however, ten parts saltpeter, and one part each of charcoal from hazelnut wood without knots and sulfur. These should be pounded with a wooden hammer, having first been moistened with well water, lest they catch fire while being pounded. There are those who add vinegar, or "burning water" <note>original: "ardentem aquam," likely alcohol or aqua vitae</note> and dry it in the sun, but they do not pound it then, for it could easily catch fire. Indeed, the whole care is that all things be so purged of earthy parts—especially the saltpeter—that it burns entirely and nothing remains. Next, it must be reduced to the finest particles, for thus the parts will best adhere to one another; this happens if it is pounded, moistened, and dried repeatedly. Thirdly, when it is finished, it should be dried in the sun. For to place it near a fire is most dangerous. Therefore, 
<margin>Why gunpowder sends the small ball from the engine with such great force.</margin>
let the cause of such a great effect now be sought: when this powder is placed in the machine and the small ball is shut in, with fire applied from the outside at the bottom of the machine, almost the whole is instantly ignited and strives to occupy more than a hundredfold space. For experiment shows that a tiny amount of powder in the palm of the hand occupies no less than a hundred times the space, since a grain of millet—that is, as much as a grain of millet—fills the space of a nut with fire when ignited.

# Book Two

<margin>
The cause of the loud noise made by engines when they are discharged.
</margin>
Reason also shows this, for fire is a thin and rare substance contained within narrow limits, whereas earth and powder are solid and dense. Thus, when the powder is ignited while in a confined space, it violently strikes the engine in every direction. Finding no easier exit than where the ball was forcibly enclosed, it thrusts the ball out with great effort—first through the length of the <term>bore</term> <note>original: "canalis"</note>, and then, maintaining that same violence, it expels it outside. With its momentum continued from that point, it covers great distances of land and overturns or destroys whatever stands in its path. It is also natural that these things happen with a great roar, since that fire exits in abundance and with such force that it suddenly strikes the air. The ball itself also makes a certain whistling sound as it swiftly cuts through the air. Furthermore, <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "halinitrum," a primary ingredient in gunpowder</note> and every kind of salt, even when placed on an open fire, creates a significant crackling. For these three reasons—but especially the first—such a great crash is produced when the engine is discharged, not unlike thunder. 

However, if the powder does not burn all at once, either because it is sluggish, impure, poorly processed, or contains too little saltpeter, it discharges slowly and weakly with little sound. But if it is more refined than is proper, the whole mass ignites at once and shatters the engine. It is evident, therefore, that since the speed of the transition into fire depends on the proportion of heat to the resistance of the powder—and since resistance is diminished when the powder is finely ground—this refinement of the powder can proceed infinitely, to the point that it ignites entirely in an instant. Then, because it cannot find an exit suddenly (as all motion requires time), it will break the engine. Therefore, it is possible not only to make powder that will shatter all engines, but if a finer powder is put into larger engines, they will be destroyed; conversely, with a coarser powder, small and thin engines will scarcely be able to eject the ball. This principle is therefore set within certain narrow limits, which are tied to the danger of those handling the engines. He alone will handle them safely and with the greatest force, and direct his shots accurately, who prepares and administers the correct powder according to the requirements of the engines.

<margin>
The principle of the fiery tunnels which they call mines.
</margin>
Furthermore, the principle of <term>mines</term> <note>original: "cuniculorum," literally "rabbit-holes," referring to subterranean siege tunnels</note> is the same as that of the engines, but even more miraculous. The author of this terrifying invention was Francesco di Giorgio of Siena <note>Francesco di Giorgio Martini (1439–1502), a celebrated Sienese architect and military engineer</note>. He taught the Spaniards how to overthrow the Lucullian Citadel near Naples—which the French were defending and is now called the "Egg" <note>Castel dell'Ovo in Naples</note>. By his sacred work, the mountain, along with the French who were inside, was moved even into the sea. Therefore, since the citadel sits mostly upon a mountain and appears impregnable due to its location, they dig an oblique tunnel, four cubits high and two wide. The slant does not matter much while you are far off, but when you reach the place you intend to undermine, the cave must be oblique—as at point A <note>referring to the accompanying diagram</note>. There, the solid substance of the mountain is required so that the force of the enclosed fire does not dissipate through the looseness of the ground; then that place is almost entirely filled with <term>gunpowder</term> <note>original: "puluere pyrio"</note>, and that of the finest sort. A fuse is then led down from point A as far as...
