# On the Elements and their actions.

From A to the mouth of the cave B—here next to A, where the powder is, it is thick and wide like a flake of wool. The entire rope <note>Referring to a fuse</note> is boiled in vinegar, sulfur, and saltpeter <note>original: "halinitro"</note>; then, once coated in gunpowder <note>original: "pyrio puluere"</note>, it is dried in the sun. Once dried again, it is sprinkled with the finest gunpowder and encased in a reed from A to B. Then, the opening at C is closed with wedges and stones, and likewise up to D, so diligently that only space for the reed is left. Therefore, when the beginning of the rope at B is lit, the fire reaches A very quickly because of the gunpowder and ignites the whole mass. Since the place is obstructed by wedges and stones, and no exit is open even if they were pushed out—because E is not in a direct line with A, nor D in a direct line with C, nor B in a direct line with E and D—it is necessary that the mountain be disrupted, overturning whatever is above it and shaking the entire mass of the mountain. For this reason, the path from B to A must not be short, nor should the location of A be in any thin part of the mountain, lest the fire break through where the obstacle is weak and leave the upper part unharmed. 

Perhaps someone will object that it does not pertain to a physician to teach things that lead to the destruction of men, such as these, just as one should not teach about poisons. But we do not teach these things; rather, we demonstrate the causes of things already commonly known and widespread, whose causes remain hidden. Nor have I ever written anything that could bring about some new form of destruction. Truly, now that these things which originate from the secrets of nature are known, my purpose is to show their causes so that, through firm demonstration, they may be as clear as the <term>elements of Geometry</term> <note>Referring to fundamental, self-evident mathematical principles</note>. Thus, the <term>obliquity</term> <note>The indirect, zigzagging path of the tunnels (A, B, C, D, E) described earlier</note> is the cause of such a great miracle that even mountains are overturned.

<margin>Why fire is preserved under ashes.</margin>
But leaving these things aside, let us return again to the power of fire, from which no small doubts arise. For since we have said that fire is preserved by motion, someone might ask why a burning coal <note>original: "pruna"</note> is better preserved under ashes than when exposed, since ashes prevent all motion? This is an easy doubt to resolve and hardly pertains to this book, in which the intention is only to pursue great, difficult, and beautiful matters. For this reason, I shall abstain from such questions in the future. Thus, it is enough to answer him that fire always has some motion, but in burning coals it is quite thin, remaining even under the ashes. Therefore, when the coals are exposed, the surrounding air destroys that fire; for the air would rather destroy than be destroyed, and such a thin motion cannot preserve the fire. But when covered by ash, it is safe from the assault of the air. Thus, fire is preserved in three ways: either when it excites motion from itself, as in wax candles and generally where a flame protects itself by its own motion; or when it is fostered by motion from elsewhere, as when the wind blows or with bellows, which is why almost all great fires have occurred while strong winds were blowing. Third, when it is safe from the air, yet in such a way that it can breathe, as under ashes; and it does not matter whether the ashes are from another source or whether, as happens with certain woods, it prepares them for itself all around.

<margin>Why we say fire is more of a substance than ice.</margin>
There is also another doubt: why we are more accustomed to calling fire a <term>substance</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "substance" refers to something that exists in itself rather than as a quality of something else</note> than ice; for no one calls ice a substance...

<page-num>38</page-num>
<header>Book Two</header>

...called it a substance, but most did not just say it, but truly believed it: although both are accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a quality or property that can change (like temperature) without the thing itself (the "subject") ceasing to exist.</note>. The cause is obvious. We usually call "accidents" those things that are present while the subject remains undamaged; ice seems to be of this sort. For when frozen—water, oil, milk, and wine—they are seen to be the same once the frost has melted. But most things are destroyed by fire; and those that remain, like stones and metals, seem violently damaged—except for gold, silver, and a few gems. For this reason, they thought fire was something greater than heat; however, we taught the cause of this difference above.

<margin>Whether there is any fire that does not shine.</margin>
There was another point worthy of doubt, since fire seemed to be something separate from any other heat; for although it changes color, it easily produces something similar to itself. But not all fire shines: for fiery iron ignites and burns sulfur, from which it is clear that it has already taken on the form of fire, yet it does not shine.

<margin>Burning water burns while leaving the cloth it soaks unharmed.</margin>
By a different reasoning, the fire which burning water <note>original: "ardens aqua" — a term often used for distilled alcohol or ethanol.</note> emits is different, not only because of the thinness of its substance, but because it is less hot. For this reason, even if it is consumed and shines, I would hardly say that it should be called "fire," since it does not burn the linen it clings to and which was soaked by the water itself. 

<margin>How a hand may burn without the person feeling it.</margin>
By the same logic, if it is distilled longer and thinned out more, by a great miracle a hand will burn and not feel it. Therefore, if one looks at it correctly, after heat has reached a certain limit, it deserves the name of fire; however, this limit is not just one thing, but occurs when it can overcome the air. When it has reached that point, it acquires as much splendor, light, and strength as the heat itself, and the fire itself is increased. 

<margin>The nature of fire consists no less of dryness than of heat.</margin>
Therefore, as I said from the beginning, fire is nothing other than very great heat joined with dryness; for without dryness, fire cannot exist. Otherwise, boiling water could be fire. Therefore, the essence of fire depends no less on dryness itself than on heat.

<margin>How torches may be made from any wood.</margin>
For this reason, we have been taught to make torches from any wood. But if they are made from denser and more solid wood, they last longer. You shall divide an oak branch <note>original: "stolonem querneum"</note>, a cubit thick, from top to bottom into many pieces—perhaps twelve or sixteen, or more—yet in such a way that the bottom remains whole. Then let it be dried in a furnace for two or three days; thus, once the watery moisture is excluded and only what is fatty remains, it burns like a pine torch. And if it equals a man's height, a lively flame lasts for the space of an hour and a half with a most brilliant light. Fire is extinguished by cold things as much as it is overwhelmed by moist things: by moist things for two reasons—both as opposites, and because they prevent it from breathing and moving—but by cold things only as opposites. Therefore, it is extinguished by water for a triple reason.

<margin>Fire is extinguished by water for three reasons.</margin>
<margin>Modes by which fire is generated.</margin>
Now at last it remains for us to show the causes of its generation, which possess no small amount of obscurity. Therefore, let us first consider in how many ways it occurs. It happens by propagation, opposition <note>original: "antipasi" — likely referring to antiperistasis, the intensification of a quality when surrounded by its opposite.</note>, percussion, friction, rot, and gathering <note>original: "coitione" — the concentrating of light or heat.</note>. For that which is generated either by concave mirrors or by transparent spheres clearly pertains to gathering. But the logic of gathering is not obscure; for if you distribute ten coins to ten men, each will have one coin...

# On the Elements and their Actions

...minimum, but if into five, two each. If therefore heat, which is dispersed through a large space, is contracted into one, whatever was in that large quantity is also present in that small one; for which reason a great heat contained in a small space will produce great effects, and for that reason it will deserve to be called "great," and thus "fire." This has been so clearly explained that it is not necessary to repeat it. But that which happens by counter-pull <term>antispasis: a technical term from Greek medicine and physics meaning a "drawing back" or "diversion." Here, the author uses it to describe the movement of heat into a concentrated point</term> is reduced to a coming together. For counter-pull ignites for no other reason than that it forces [heat] into one place; therefore, the cause of this is also known. Furthermore, we have shown by "propagation" how it is generated above. For everything that is stable by nature or mortal is fit to generate something like itself; thus it is no wonder that fire is kindled from fire. However, friction and striking take their beginning from motion; rot <note>original: "putredo" — often used in natural philosophy to describe chemical breakdown or fermentation</note> by itself is not sufficient to kindle fire, but it is strengthened either by other heat, or by motion, or by counter-pull and concentration.

<margin>How motion generates heat and fire.</margin>
Therefore, if we teach how fire is kindled by motion, we will demonstrate at the same time all the ways in which fire can be kindled: and that there are truly only three—concentration, propagation, and motion—although they seem to be far more numerous. To show how fire is generated from motion is nothing other than to demonstrate how motion is the cause of heat, for if motion is the cause of heat, it will also be the cause of its increase. Fire, as we have said, is nothing other than heat increased beyond measure. Therefore, the Aristotelians <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy, who dominated medieval and early modern science.</note> inquire in what way motion may produce heat, and they talk much nonsense; at last, they return to the point that heat is an "effect" of motion, which is as if they were saying, "we do not know." For to show the same thing by the same thing is a certain sign of a trifling and unskilled argument.

<margin>Averroes in the Paraphrase of Metaphysics, treatise 2, column 7.</margin>
Finally, some have said—obscurely and in their usual manner—that this heat is already in the air, but through motion it is led to that form [of fire], and that this heat is that which has come from the stars <note>original: "syderibus"</note>. O distinguished man! They do not believe the stars are hot, yet they want that heat of the stars to be fire. But even if it were granted that the stars, though not being hot themselves, produce heat: the doubt emerges again as to how motion increases that heat. For it is certain that the heat conceived from the stars beforehand, without motion, is not yet fiery.

<margin>How fire is struck from stones.</margin>
Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle.</note> rightly perceives that fire is not "struck out" from stones, but the air contained there is turned into fire by the sudden friction. But if this is so, why is it not struck out from the most solid stones, such as porphyry <term>porphyrite: a very hard, purple-red igneous rock prized in antiquity</term> and the hardest stones, more than from softer ones, such as crystal and chalcedony <term>chalcedonio: a translucent variety of quartz</term>? Again, why does fire come from crystal and steel more than from two stones of the same kind, such as two crystals? Then—and this is the most important point—if only the air is ignited, why do those sparks for the most part appear large and descend as if heavy in a slow process? For pure fire either does not descend, or if it is forced by an impulse, it descends quickly. Since, therefore, certain things descend slowly, they do not consist of air alone. Therefore, Alexander correctly said that fire is not "contained" within the stone. For the fire would burn the stone, and again...

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the origins of fire, specifically challenging the idea that fire is physically stored inside stones or created solely from compressed air. It follows the previous page's introduction of friction and motion as primary causes of combustion.</meta>

<page-num>40</page-num>
<header>Book Two</header>

## Book Two

...otherwise, the stone would burn the hand of the person touching it, and it would be easily set on fire, and it would require fuel, and it would be easily struck out by two stones knocked together—such as two **chalcedonies**—for the friction alone would be enough to strike out the fire. Since none of these things are true, it is clearly established that fire is not contained within the stone. But neither is it generated from the air, as I have said; for stones, being harder, require a more forceful strike for fire to be produced. Therefore, if it were enough for the air alone to be suddenly struck by a blow—such as the kind by which fire is struck from steel and crystal—fire could be generated from two pieces of steel, but this is not the case. Rather, as I said, harder materials require more violent blows, and they create a more solid and lively fire, so much so that its spark sometimes lasts for a considerable time. Indeed, there are even some stones that are glassy and soft which produce fire with the lightest strikes, or even by being merely touched, though this fire is not at all long-lived. 

It is, however, certain evidence that fire is generated from the substance of the stone itself because it is never struck out without the stone being worn down by friction; furthermore, as we have said, air turns into a flame, not into sparks. Moreover, millstones being turned emit fire even when they are covered with water rather than air; also, the stones themselves only emit fire from their corners <note>The author observes that fire sparks from the sharp edges/angles of stones during impact, suggesting the material is being sheared off</note>. Therefore, fire does not lie hidden away inside stones, nor is it generated from the air when air is struck. 

But there is also no certain evidence that fire exists in them potentially; for stones are hardly set on fire even when thrown into a furnace, nor are they ever ignited by cold, and if ground up and drunk <note>original: "epoti" — This refers to the historical medicinal practice of consuming powdered minerals or "stone waters" to cool the body</note>, they act as powerful cooling agents. Therefore, it is manifest that fire is generated from the friction of the stone when its substance is reduced to the tiniest particles, and that the matter of one stone may be more suitable for this than another. For those that are purer, quite hard, and made of a fine substance, such as chalcedonies, crystals, and the like, are the most suitable. Conversely, those that are fragile, or excessively hard, or made of a coarse substance, are the least suitable.

But I must return to the point from which I digressed regarding motion kindling heat, for almost everything seems to depend on this. Therefore, we never see fire kindled from water; and from air it occurs only by spreading <note>original: "propagatione" — the movement of an existing fire through the air</note> rather than by motion; and if any liquid is kindled, such as oil or wine, it is inflamed by an existing fire, not by motion. Therefore, that which is kindled by motion must be dry, not wet; whereas that which is kindled by another fire can also be wet. 

That which is dry and rubbed violently is already half-fire. For as I have said, fire is intense heat and dryness; therefore, that which is dry needs only to be heated to such an extent [to become fire]; indeed, the logic is the same for the part as it is for the whole. For if it grows warm through violent motion, it will eventually grow intensely hot. When, therefore, a dry thing is struck by motion, it must necessarily become thin and rare; and a thin, dry substance is fiery by its very nature. For every kind of matter, when reduced to a certain tiny quantity, seizes its corresponding form <term>form: in Aristotelian philosophy, the "form" is the essential nature of a thing. Here, the author argues that when matter is ground fine enough, it loses the "form" of a stone and adopts the "form" of fire</term> for itself. 

This alone is therefore well said: that the heat which is present from the influence of the stars <note>original: "syderibus" — referring to the "innate heat" or celestial influence believed to reside in all earthly matter</note>, when joined to dry matter and excessively thinned out by motion—with no moisture resisting it, since we have already assumed the material to be dry—and with the previous form (such as that of a stone) being so weakened by this thinning...

The author explains that the "form" of fire is naturally adopted by any dry substance that becomes sufficiently thinned out through violent motion.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of fire and heat, moving from the physical friction of stones to a theoretical explanation of the four qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness—and how matter changes state through thinning (attenuation) or gathering.</meta>

# On the Elements and Their Actions

...lest the qualities of the stone be present while the substance is absent, they take on the form of fire through the action of heat. Therefore, this mode is almost the opposite of gathering; in that case, the matter remains constant while the heat is compressed, but here, under the same heat, the matter itself is thinned out <note>The author uses "attenuation" to describe matter becoming less dense, a process he believes turns solids into fire or liquids into air.</note>. Evidence that this is the cause can be seen in the way water is turned into air by motion, as anyone can see where water falls with great force. For once the substance is thinned out and joined with moisture, it takes on the form of air.

<margin>
*Cold is nothing in actuality, but only the privation of heat.*
</margin>
Truly, you might wonder why heat arises in cold air and in matter where cold already prevails, such as in a stone, since cold is more powerful? I respond that if cold is understood as an "act," it is nothing except a tiny amount of heat; if it is not even that, it has no operations of its own. Because of this, cold does not "rise up" or act, since it is only a certain <term>privation</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, a "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be there, like blindness is the privation of sight.</note>, but heat does, which is nevertheless great when compared to the smallness of the underlying matter. Evidence that cold is nothing at all besides the privation of heat is the shivering of <term>tertian fevers</term> <note>A type of malaria where fever and chills recur every three days; the author notes that patients feel intense cold even when no "cold substance" has entered the body.</note>, in which there is no cold matter, but only the flight of heat, yet a significant cold is felt. Where a small amount of heat exists in a little matter, it is preserved.

<margin>
*Dryness is nothing but the privation of moisture.*
</margin>
By the same reasoning, dryness is nothing else than the privation of moisture. For this reason, it is impossible for dry things to be moistened <note>The author is likely speaking of the "state" of dryness as a lack; one cannot simply "turn back" a privation without adding new material.</note>, since there is no return to a state of being from a privation; rather, it is more difficult to moisten them because moisture is a principle from the element, whereas heat comes from the heavens, which always diffuse it. Things are restored, therefore, by the addition of solid materials; otherwise, it is more easily granted that things become cold or dry, since these changes occur through an impediment. Justly did the ancients set down <term>aether</term> <note>The "upper air" or fiery element of the heavens.</note> and water as the principles of natural things, because heat abounds in one and moisture in the other. More justly air, if it were both hot and moist. No one chose Earth, for it is cold and dry. But things that are hot beyond their nature are only cooled with difficulty, for motion preserves [heat]. Therefore, it is more difficult to cool things that are naturally such, for their motion is perpetual. Truly, in cold air, a spark of fire is extinguished immediately if help is not brought. But air cannot prevent the generation [of fire] that occurs within, as it only surrounds it.

But again you will say, if cold is nothing in act but only the privation of heat, how do cold things cool just as hot things heat? Cold is always associated with much matter, for it is impossible for something very thin to be cold; much matter acts as a barrier, so that heat can neither penetrate nor move. Why then does it cool in this way? Therefore, what heats does so of itself, but what cools does so only <term>by accident</term> <note>A philosophical term meaning a secondary or non-essential effect; the object cools not because it "attacks" with cold, but because its density blocks or absorbs heat.</note>. You might perhaps object, since we feel ourselves being cooled by cold things no differently than we suddenly feel heated by hot ones, so that a certain "species" of cold seems to be produced. Indeed, as I said, a cold thing is nothing other than the privation of heat; and things that move and do not stand still are cooled, like water and the air of strong winds. Furthermore, when something is cooled by contact, only the surface is cooled, while the heat clearly flees inside; for this reason, it is not possible for anything to be cooled suddenly, but over a period of time, even the innermost parts are cooled.

<summary>This page argues that cold and dryness are not active forces, but rather the absence (privation) of heat and moisture. It explains that cooling occurs "by accident" when dense matter blocks the movement of heat, rather than through an active "cold" quality.</summary>

## Book Two

And these are the true foundations of natural things, in which there is nothing contradictory. However, those who imagine these qualities to be fixed to substances, and who believe that <term>coldness</term> <note>The author argues against the contemporary view that "cold" is a physical thing in itself; he views it merely as the absence or blockage of heat.</note> is a primary principle of nature, fall into the most difficult questions. They cannot explain the causes of things as they appear, and they are forced to shroud everything in silence and obscure words, relying on ambiguous arguments. Therefore, heat itself is the characteristic quality of the heavenly bodies, which, by agitating them and aided by motion, creates fire. If this heat is overwhelmed or hindered by matter, it produces cold. Furthermore, whatever things do not remain the same through motion become colder, such as water and air; however, the temperature of the air is created by the multitude of the sun's rays and the stars it receives, which warm it. Earth, truly, cannot be as cold as water, because it does not move.

<margin>
Types of <term>fineness</term> in substance. <note>The original term "subtilitas" refers to how "thin" or "fine" a material is—ranging from coarse solids to invisible spirits.</note>
</margin>

With these principles established—through which we shall reveal not a few secrets of nature that have long remained hidden—let us return again to the history of fire. But first, it is necessary to set forth a few things regarding the fineness of substances. Some things are said to be "thin" or "fine" by their very nature, such as air; some by their quantity, such as hairs; some because they flow, such as blood; and some because they can be divided into the tiniest parts, such as gold. Others are fine because they possess several of these traits, such as the <term>spirits</term> <note>In early medicine, "spirits" were subtle fluids believed to flow through the nerves and arteries to power the body’s functions.</note> which are the instruments of our bodily operations. Many fine things are also produced by human art, but art itself neither mixes nor thins the substance; it only reduces the quantity.

<margin>
How fineness from art, nature, and fire differ.
</margin>

If fire thins matter, it does so by separating it; or, if it mixes matter, it does not thin it. For by separating those parts which are thick, it gives the appearance of thinning. Nature alone can simultaneously mix and thin a substance. For as I have said, when I speak of "fine" things that can be drawn out, these must be ductile or moist.

<margin>
How fire thins matter.
</margin>

Since fire actually dries things out, it cannot thin them unless it separates them. Therefore, it thins matter either by crushing dry things (as when it reduces sand to powder), or by melting them (as with metals), or by separating the thin parts (as in distillations). Truly, while it burns, as it crushes dry things and melts moist ones, it also thins them.

<margin>
The uses and types of distillation.
</margin>

It happens, however, in <term>distillations</term> <note>The process of heating a liquid to create vapor and then condensing it back into liquid to purify it.</note> that something is thinned and mixed with another when the process is driven by warm moisture rather than by direct fire. For heat mixes, and together with moisture, it thins. This is done by placing vessels into boiling water, which they call the **Bain-Marie** <note>original: "Mariae balneum." A "Mary’s Bath" or water bath, used for gentle, even heating.</note>. The next best kind of distillation is performed in horse dung; after that, through ashes; and the most excellent is in the remains of olives after the oil has been extracted. For since that substance is warm and moist, it can preserve heat for many months—and for a longer span of time than grape seeds, because the substance of olives is denser and fattier. Yet none of these can melt metals; for those, fire is required. But just as the most intense distillation is done by fires, it is unsuitable for true mixing and thinning, much like the distillation done through ashes. For if you mix the results of fire-distillation with their own dregs, the whole will become heavier than before in proportion to its mass, and also drier.

<margin>
Fire does not truly thin matter.
</margin>

Therefore, fire does not truly thin a substance, but nature itself does, which "cooks" and mixes the entire substance.

### On the Elements and their Actions

...grows. Whence, because of their <term>fineness</term> <note>original: "subtilitatem"; referring to the quality of being thin, pure, or refined rather than coarse</note> all things come together into one, and the mixture becomes denser, yet it is composed of the finest parts. Therefore, in <term>natural concoction</term> <note>The process by which nature or art refines a substance, often compared to digestion</note>, so that those things which are hardest to melt may also obtain the power of fire—and the softness of a mild bath in thinning them—the coarser parts are broken down, which cannot be achieved by fire alone.

<margin>
Whether distilled waters have medicinal powers
</margin>

But from these things, no slight doubt arises; for if fire heats and dries all things, then all waters obtained by <term>distillation</term> <note>The process of vaporizing and then condensing a liquid to purify it or extract its "essence"</note> ought to be hot and dry. Nor does the substance itself resist this on the grounds that it is "watery," for such water, when it is <term>burning</term> <note>original: "ardens"; likely referring to distilled alcohol or "aqua vitae"</note>, even catches fire and wonderfully heats and dries human bodies. On the other hand, all waters are naturally cold and moist because that substance prevails in them. But neither of these is always true; rather, some of these waters are more similar to the plants from which they are extracted, such as rose water, in its scent, taste, and medicinal powers. A jar of plantain water can stop blood flowing from anywhere. The water of lettuce does not do the same, even if it is colder. Recently, someone while striving to increase his memory, infused <term>lemon balm</term> <note>original: "melissa"</note> in white wine for three days; then, having lightly pressed the wine, he collected the water by distilling it, and by drinking it he seemed to recover his memory. But since he had a <term>hot liver</term> <note>In the medical theory of the time, a "hot liver" was a constitutional imbalance; adding "hot" remedies like distilled wine could be dangerous</note>, it almost completely overturned his good health. And this practice of extracting the essence of a thing is called by Philosophers "fixing the stars in the sky."

It is therefore usually asked whether these waters retain their own specific powers? We said once, while speaking about the method of medical use, that there are no powers in them because they are destitute of scent and taste. For the water of <term>wormwood</term> <note>original: "absinthium"</note> neither smells of wormwood, nor is it bitter; rather, which is strange, it is somewhat sweet. Yet "burning" water <note>alcohol</note>—to pass over rose water—gives proof that a specific power exists in distilled waters. For if you say such a power is only due to the fire used, why is it that no other waters are like it? For this "burning" water wonderfully heats, dries, penetrates, smells sharp, and burns. Thus it is now certain that powers are present in waters, but neither in all of them, nor in equal measure. For whatever things have a "thin" substance joined with a cold nature, emit a water not unlike themselves, such as the rose. But those that have a thin and hot substance emit something similar but "burning," such as wine and certain metallic substances. Those which have a thick and hot substance emit something dissimilar and base, like wormwood. Those which have a thick and cold substance emit something dissimilar but not base, such as gourds. According to this reasoning, you will easily learn the powers of waters which are extracted by a light fire. For those which require a powerful fire all dry strongly, and for the most part, even heat the body.

<margin>
Whether it is possible to make a water which might prolong life for many centuries.
</margin>

Therefore, here again another doubt arises: whether it is permitted to make a "tempered" water, which they call the <term>Fifth Essence</term> <note>original: "Quinta essentia"; the "Quintessence," a fifth element beyond the four earthly ones, believed to be incorruptible</note>? This, as I shall teach, will be the <term>Aether</term> <note>The pure air of the heavens</note>, that is, a most thin, mobile substance, and one which by its motion retains a tempered heat, and a great deal of it. This, therefore, can preserve all powers and prolong life. For since it is most thin, it mixes itself with the primary moisture of the body, penetrating solids, and separates the waste which is contained therein. Because it truly has a great deal of heat, it ejects whatever is impure, and on that account the natural heat...

# Book Two

...restores the matter. For old age is nothing other than the diminution of <term>natural heat</term> <note>The innate warmth believed in pre-modern medicine to be the vital force of life</note>: it is diminished because motion is hindered, as I have said concerning fire, for the reasoning regarding this is similar to that. Indeed, motion is hindered because of the abundance of earthy substance. Since earth alone contains the most matter and lacks motion entirely. Therefore, that water—since it is of a tempered heat—will neither vex the heart nor be harmful to the liver. Thus, this alone is able to provide those things we have mentioned. They report that on the island of **Bonicca** <note>Likely referring to Bimini or a similar island in the Bahamas, often associated in early accounts with the Fountain of Youth</note>, which is 1,200 miles distant from Hispaniola in the New World, there is a spring at the summit of a mountain that restores the elderly; however, it does not change gray hair, nor does it remove wrinkles already contracted. Of this matter, besides the persistent rumor, there is the rich testimony of **Peter Martyr d'Anghiera** of Milan <note>A historian of the Spanish Age of Discovery</note>, formerly of the Secrets of the King of Spain, in his *Decades of the Newly Discovered World*.

Therefore, to return to the matter so that it need not be sought so far afield: when <term>burning water</term> <note>original: "ardens aqua"; high-proof distilled alcohol</note>, through the long motion of <term>circulation</term> <note>The alchemical process of continuous distillation and condensation in a closed vessel</note>, retains its fineness but casts off its heat and the sharpness of its taste and smell, it becomes **ether**. And yet, at first, it is fragrant. For a fragrant odor is nothing other than a sharp one when it has become moderated. The evidence for this is that pepper is not fragrant, nor is ginger, because they are immoderately sharp; yet a small quantity smells good. But those things which smell good for the opposite reason—cinnamon, amomum, saffron, cloves, lilies, and musk—are moderately sharp. And if you place a great deal of these under the nostrils, like pepper, they strike the brain and do not seem to smell good. Garlic and onions, because they possess a moisture not devoid of putrefaction, and even if they are sharp, yet also because they are not moderated, they stink. Therefore, it is necessary that burning water, if it returns to a tempered state while retaining its fineness, becomes fragrant: and if it becomes fragrant, it must in turn be converted into ether.

There is also a water made to restore youth with the <term>flesh of a viper</term> <note>original: "tyri carne"; vipers were a key ingredient in "Theriac," a famous panacea</note>, and one made with hellebore, such as I saw at my father’s house; but these distress the bodies and buy back a painted image of youth, they do not provide true youth. But ether provides true youth, since it retains for a long time that which it possesses, and adorns it.

<margin>
Whether fire is finer than ether.
</margin>

But is not ether finer than fire, which is the hottest? Certainly so, for it is contiguous to the heavens and therefore the lightest; for it moderates the heat impressed by the stars through circulation while retaining its fineness. In the same way, this water, having been reduced to the highest fineness by the heat of fire, is cooled by that very motion and acquires a tempered state. Thus, both this water and the ether are a kind of medium between things mortal and immortal. For since it possesses both a location and a tempered state, as well as a substance very close to the heavens, it cannot be corrupted. However, while it is driven downward, it is cooled, and thus after many centuries, it is corrupted. Therefore, it is a medium, as it were, of the mortal and the immortal, of which kind the **Stoics** <note>Ancient Greek philosophers who believed the soul was a physical, though highly refined, substance</note> believe the human soul to be.

<margin>
On the difference between lime and ash.
</margin>

But because here ether is elaborated from burning water, since it is thinned by heat and not compressed by motion, it emerges not a little finer. Thus, by a similar reasoning, both are produced. In this way, indeed, whatever things are transformed by the heat of fire, their evident calidity...

Once carefully dried and purified by fire, they are distilled in glass vessels. That which flows out first is collected separately. Finally, when the face of the vessel appears saffron-colored, the fires are increased and another substance follows, which is usually received by the first. Even if you receive it in spring water, it is still so sharp that it nonetheless dissolves silver and separates it from gold. It is separated thus: take a small portion of the extracted water, in which you place the weight of an <term>obol</term> <note>original: "oboli"; an ancient weight, here defined as 12 grains</note> (that is, 12 grains) of the purest silver, and once placed, leave it in the [warm] ashes until the silver is dissolved. It will cast down these dregs, similar to thin lime, to the bottom of the vessel. Once these are removed, you shall add what remains of the clearer water to all the water from which you had previously taken it. By a similar process, this water itself will also cast down similar dregs to the bottom. Once these are removed, you will have the entire water at its purest and more effective for dissolving silver and other metals, except for gold. But since it easily evaporates, it is kept in a glass vessel carefully sealed. If one estimates how much strength it has—seeing as that which is received (as I said) in well water reduces silver into water within twenty-four hours even without fire, and with a moderate heat of ashes in two or three hours—there is no one who would not attribute a marvelous, indeed incredible, power to those final vapors and the water into which they are turned.

This water, made by the same art, does not even spare stones. If, however, you add some <term>emery stone</term> <note>original: "oſtracitis lapidis Smiridis"; a hard mineral used for polishing gems</note>, which they use to polish gems, you will have a more abundant and better water, because it does not burn up. Therefore, having accepted these experiments, let us see why this water becomes so powerful: for manifest experiment teaches us that the drier part, thinned by the force of fire, receives a fiery and eroding power.

<margin>A comparison between "burning water" and "separating water."</margin> But why does <term>water of separation</term> <note>original: "aqua ſeparationis"; nitric acid</note> not burn like <term>burning water</term> <note>original: "aqua ardens"; distilled alcohol</note>? Because burning water is hotter, thinner, and less dry; therefore it is able to burn and to heat excellently, yet not to erode. The other, however, can erode but not burn, and it provides little heat. By a similar reasoning, the oil which is extracted from vitriol by the force of fire is extremely sharp and strikes the tongue like fire, since it turns the driest part into a liquid.

<margin>Water which can break a bladder stone.</margin> It is established, therefore, by this reasoning, that a water can be made which, when introduced through a <term>catheter</term>, will immediately shatter a stone in the bladder. For since two things are necessary—that which wears down the stone and that which is harmless to the bladder—the method and the material will provide the first. ## Book Two

For in this way, a water will be made that may even crush <term>porphyry</term> <note>original: "porphyritem"; a very hard, reddish-purple igneous rock used in ancient monuments</note>. Furthermore, it ensures safety if the material from which the water is extracted is entirely free of saltiness. Therefore, one should not extract the water from any kind of salt, or from <term>alum</term>, or <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: "calchanto"; copper or iron sulfate</note>, or wine dregs, but from one of those substances we have recently mentioned. 

There is always a need for diligent experience in confirming subtle reasoning, so that those things which we have explored so precisely can be brought into use for mankind once they are securely confirmed through practice. Indeed, I know that <term>pigeon dung</term> and <term>pellitory</term> <note>original: "paritariam"; the plant Parietaria officinalis, long used in folk medicine</note>, when reduced into a water by this art, are able to break the hardest stones of the bladder. However, which specific substance will do this without causing harm must be declared by experience. For even <term>goat’s blood</term>, hare skin, and glass are much approved by reason; yet perhaps none of these work separately, but only when some of them are joined together in a certain measure. Certainly, such a thing must be metallic in nature, or changed into the nature of metal. I once heard that a certain <term>Genoese man</term> <note>original: "Ianuense"; a resident of Genoa, Italy</note> discovered this, but it was lost again upon his death, as he wished to make the secret known to no one. It is surely certain that this can be found, and that this is the art of it.

<margin>How the effects of fire appear without fire</margin>
But to return to the matter: a doubt arises. If a great heat produces these waters—consider <term>aqua fortis</term> <note>original: "ardentem... separationis"; literally "burning water of separation," usually nitric acid</note>—why are they cold to the touch? Or, if they have already been cooled, why do they melt metals? Or, if some heat remains, why is it not entirely extinguished when at rest? And if it is aided by some motion, why does it not ignite material that is so ready to burn? Experience teaches none of these things. 

The same logic applies to natural mixtures. For <term>sulfur</term> is very easily ignited, yet it is cold of itself. <term>Pepper</term> burns the tongue and vehemently heats the body if eaten, yet it is cold to the touch and hardly catches fire when brought near a flame. It would befit the <term>Philosophers</term> <note>likely referring to the Scholastic or Aristotelian academics of the time</note> to seek these things which are evident to the senses and which we handle daily—which, when discovered, bring great utility—rather than abandoning what we have "in our hands" (as the saying goes) to devise new questions with new names. In those academic questions, you remain as uncertain about what is being asked as you are about how the answer should be determined. Furthermore, even if the question were resolved correctly a thousand times—which hardly ever happens—it would bring no benefit to the human race.

<margin>Only three things are truly in mixtures: earth and water as the matter, and celestial heat as the agent. See Aristotle, *On the Parts of Animals*, Book 2, Chapter 1, at the beginning.</margin>
A manifest sign of this is that in so many centuries, these "eminent men" have discovered nothing for the use of life, because they lean upon false principles, and it suffices for them only to talk nonsense and make a noise. Therefore, lest I become like them by criticizing them, it is now time to resolve this very necessary question. First, we must suppose that which we see with our eyes: that earth and water alone are the materials of mixtures—which the <term>Philosopher</term> <note>Aristotle</note> also said as if by divine inspiration—and that heat itself is what cooks these things by mixing them. If, therefore, there is a great deal of earth and heat, a fiery thing is produced...

<header>On the Elements and their actions.</header>

# On the Elements and their actions.

...as in the waters already mentioned. If moderate heat exists with a great deal of earth, the substance is called **earthy**. An example of the first is **pepper** <note>original: "piper"; here the author views pepper as a combination of intense heat and earthy matter</note>; of the second, **stones**. If water exceeds and there is little earth, but the heat is great, it becomes **airy**, which includes anything fatty and which burns easily: such as all oils, fats, sulfur, and bitumen. If there is little heat, it becomes **watery**, as are most vegetables. Why then does pepper not catch fire easily? Because while it has a refined part, it contains much earthy matter. Moreover, we have taught that the earthy quality, because it contains much material and prevents movement, resists the generation of fire. But you will say that pepper is light: I respond that this is because it is hollow, but the substance itself is heavy, and if it is ground thoroughly, it is not light at all. **Sulfur**, however, since it is moist, does not burn the tongue, yet it burns with fire because it is vehemently hot.

Taking these things as first principles, let us proceed to the resolution of the question. In these mixtures, only three things appear: **earth**, **water**, and the **heat** that mixes them. For it is clear that earth and water mix spontaneously; air shuns the mixture, nor can you ever mix it with these, nor if there were anything else thinner than it. Regarding **fire**, however, there is no doubt: since it is neither an element, nor does it generate anything. Therefore, *it is demonstrated that fire does not*
*generate; if mixtures consisted of these, they would be mixed by force. Moreover, it is demonstrated that fire does* 
<margin>It is demonstrated that fire does not generate.</margin>
*not generate.*
Fire also dries, and those things which are generated require moisture, which acts like a glue to make the parts cohere into one. Again, fire separates and divides, but the generation of a solid body requires more than just mixing. Fire also brings qualities to their extreme, but those qualities that are suitable for generation and which are mixed together break or temper one another. Finally, it is the proper task of **celestial heat** <note>original: "coelestis caloris"; the life-giving warmth of the sun or "vital heat," distinguished here from the destructive heat of a common fire</note> to generate, but not that of fiery heat; for the power of fire is not life.
<margin>The powers of fire in mixing.</margin>
Fire does mix bodies, but in doing so, it divides and separates the substances themselves. For this reason, **bread** is prepared by fire, but **meat** is corrupted by it; however, because custom does not allow us to eat raw meat, we cook it with fire. Yet, if it were the custom to eat raw meat and eggs, it would contribute not a little to the length of life. 
<margin>Raw things are more useful for the constitution of the body's life.</margin>
But because it is hardly permitted to eat these things for health, those which *can* be eaten raw—milk, honey, oil, butter, sugar, and most vegetables of a thinner substance—will be more useful for both life and health if they are eaten that way. For even if, as I said, fire mixes bodies and creates **cinnabar** <note>original: "cinnabarim"; a bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide, used as a pigment</note> from sulfur and quicksilver, it nevertheless separates the substances of foods: and by severing the thin from the thick, it renders them worse. Therefore, if distaste did not stand in the way, it would be better to eat eggs, oysters, and long shellfish raw rather than cooked. And universally, if strengths were vigorous and distaste did not trouble men, there would be almost no necessity or utility for fire in regard to food. But men have preferred to live elegantly and briefly, rather than for a long time in the manner of wild beasts or rustics. Nevertheless, I think the eating of raw foods contributed not a little to the length of life for those who have lived in the <term>desert</term> <note>original: "ἐρήμῳ" (erēmō); referring to the desert fathers or hermits who were famous for their longevity and simple, uncooked diets</note>. For raw things, when they are digested, are better than cooked ones, which are not free from the fault of the fire. But one must become accustomed to this from a young age.

<header>Book Two</header>

## The Four Kinds of Heat

<margin>Fourfold heat, and the resolution of the question.</margin>Heat, therefore, is of four kinds: one exists in the primary agent, that is, in the **rays of the stars**; the second is also active, but joined to **dryness**; the third is joined to **moisture**; and the fourth is a **trace of heat** rather than heat itself. We are accustomed to call the first kind "celestial," and it is the origin and source of the others; as such, it warms, yet it does not yet generate life because it is not yet joined to matter. The <term>Aristotelians</term><note>Followers of Aristotle’s natural philosophy, who dominated scientific thought in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note>, who boldly argue in matters where they cannot be proven wrong, would say this is not heat at all. They claim no star is actually hot, because the heavens are supposedly free of all physical qualities.

The second kind is called **fiery heat**; it generates nothing. When joined to dryness, it is an instrument of corruption and separation rather than of <term>mixture</term><note>original: "mixtionis aut crasis"; "crasis" refers to a balanced temperament or blending of elements.</note>, without which no generation of life can occur. Not only fire, but every heat of that category destroys and resists generation. For this reason, eggs placed in ashes do not produce chicks <note>The author distinguishes between the harsh, dry heat of fire/ash and the gentle, moist heat required for incubation.</note>. 

The third kind is named **natural heat**, which itself requires movement; for all heat existing in act requires motion and feeds upon the underlying matter. This heat is twofold: one has a visible motion and release, as is most evident in "perfect" animals and especially those with blood; the other has an "obscure" or hidden motion, such as in plants, and even more so in their seeds and in metals. In these, the motion is hidden, yet it still dissolves moisture. The proof is that stored seeds dry out, even if they are oiled for a year or two; they age just like men, contracting with wrinkles, and they become lighter and even infertile. 

**Potential heat** occurs when the power of heat, as in **pepper**, is derived from the whole plant into the seed, or from the whole mountain into the metal. If a great deal of heat acts upon the earthy part, it becomes fiery; if there is little, it becomes stone. If a great deal of heat acts on a watery substance, it becomes fatty; if there is little, it remains watery.

You might ask, perhaps, does the heat remain "in act" <note>Meaning "currently active" or "manifest."</note>? It does indeed remain, but since it is natural heat, it is founded in a moist substance (such as that of pepper), which is why it cannot burn away—especially since, once the seed is plucked from the tree, very little heat is left behind. Therefore, pepper cannot be hot because of active natural heat (since that is very thin), nor because of a burnt substance, since that retains only a **trace of heat**, not heat itself. Similarly, **burning water** <note>original: "aqua ardens"; a common term for distilled alcohol or spirits.</note> retains a trace of heat but not heat itself, as does cooled ash. **Lime** <note>original: "calx"; specifically quicklime, which reacts violently with water.</note>, however, retains heat for some time, and does so in a dry state; thus it is hot to the touch, especially on the inside, for the outside is chilled by the air. Thus, if a little water is sprinkled on it, it usually catches fire. 

But you will say: does fiery heat not seem to exist in moisture, as when a candle burns? It does not; for it is nourished *by* the moisture, but it is not *in* the moisture. Just as a man is not made of "apple-substance" simply because he eats apples, but remains "flesh-substance," so <margin>How fish may be fried in paper as if in a frying pan:</margin>fire is nourished by thin things, both moist and dry, but it is founded only in the dry, and the thinnest part of that. For that reason, a method has been discovered by which fish may be cooked in **paper** no differently than in a frying pan. Choose paper which...

# On the Elements & their actions.

Take that which we call **paper** <note>original: "papyrum"; likely referring to early modern rag paper rather than ancient Egyptian papyrus</note>, fold it with simple, upright edges in the manner of a lamp, and pour oil into it from all sides. Before the oil seeps through, place it upon clean, glowing coals without a flame. The paper will neither be penetrated by the fire—which it retreats from—nor will it burn, because it cannot be dried out while the oil resists it. Fire, truly, cannot ignite without extreme dryness, and neither flame nor motion can thin the material enough for it to catch fire. Nevertheless, it grows hot as the coals are gradually changed, and it even boils—which seems a marvel—to such an extent that fish placed within it may be cooked. <margin>A thread wrapped around an egg does not burn in fire.</margin> But why does a thread wrapped around an egg not burn, not only on coals but even in a flame? It is because fire cannot exist unless the heat is brought to its highest point; yet the heat is always prevented by the egg from reaching that peak, because an egg cannot be consumed by fire. Moreover, that which is not burned always, in some way, cools that which is extremely hot. 

But if heat generates life within moisture, why is there no generation of life in boiling water? It is because that heat is either not within the substance of the water itself, or it resides in something else that is dry. The evidence for this is that boiling water burns just as fire does. That the heat is not truly within the water's substance is indicated by the fact that once the fire is removed, the water cools down of its own accord. 

However, if heat is present in moisture, it does generate life: as when meat is exposed to the sun, little worms are created; and worms are born in dung; and in Egypt, eggs covered in dung produce chicks. <margin>Historical Note: Pliny the Elder records this story of Livia, the wife of Augustus, using a warm bosom to incubate an egg as an omen for her pregnancy.</margin> It is even said that long ago, **Livia Augusta**, having warmed an egg in her bosom—and with her handmaidens taking turns to keep it warm—hatched a crested rooster. 

**Putrid heat** <note>In ancient medicine, "putrid heat" was the type of heat associated with decomposition and certain types of fevers</note> is of the fiery kind because it is dry, yet it is similar to natural heat because it is associated with the generation of life. It differs from fiery heat because it has no manifest motion, whereas fiery heat does; therefore, there is a transition from one to the other. For moderate fiery heat causes putrefaction, while increased putrid heat burns, glows, and ignites. This is why **putrid fevers** are accompanied by such intense heat. <margin>The mutual transmutations of heats.</margin> 

The reasons why fiery heat cannot be transmuted into natural heat are manifest. For fiery heat is dry, and it cannot become moister through heat, which is the nature of natural heat. Furthermore, fiery heat draws out and separates substances, while natural heat draws them inward and mixes them. Indeed, every moist heat creates a **mixture** <term>mixture</term><note>original: "miscet"; in this context, the alchemical or physical blending of elements to form a new substance</note>. Yet natural heat can transition into putrid and fiery heat, because moisture is dried out by heat. <margin>Why fire whitens some things and blackens others.</margin> For this reason, fire usually blackens moist things, because it draws out the external moisture and expels the air; yet it whitens dry things, because it consumes whatever moisture was left within.

Furthermore, you may wonder: if fire acts upon water, it generates air <note>meaning steam or vapor</note>; why then does it not generate a fatty moisture? I respond that fatness is the result of a mixture, whereas fire separates. It separates for the sake of its own utility, because it drives away the watery part which cannot be burned, as seen in green wood which sweats water when ignited. However, it feeds upon the fatty moisture, in which a hollow heat was once established while the plant lived. Therefore, whatever burns must necessarily be very thin and very dry: such as straw, **burning water** <note>original: "aqua ardens"; an early term for distilled alcohol or "water of life"</note>, and **gunpowder** <note>original: "pyrius puluis"</note>. But in this last one, there is something earthy because of the **saltpeter** <note>original: "halinitrum"; a key ingredient in gunpowder that provides the oxygen for the explosion</note>, and therefore it emits a loud noise. Because of this, some have attempted to compose a powder without saltpeter, which might launch a small sphere without a sound. This can be done if it is done slowly and without great force. And so...

<margin>
Various powers of fire depending on application.

Regarding <term>gunpowder</term> <note>original: "Puluis pyrius"; literally "fire powder"</note>, Brasavola <note>Antonio Musa Brassavola (1500–1555), a famous Italian physician and scholar from Ferrara</note> records that the Duke of Ferrara discovered a type that could eject a shot without force, reaching only about twelve paces. However, as I have said, to do this with great force is entirely impossible. Even if the <term>saltpeter</term> <note>original: "halinitro"; the oxidizing component of gunpowder</note> is removed, gunpowder can still be so refined that it emits a small ball without a bang. But in general, however much you take away from the noise, you will take away an equal amount from the force. Therefore, the nature of fire and its strength usually vary according to the fuel used; fire from coals or solid woods like oak, or from stones or fixed in metals, harms the eyes significantly, whereas fire from willow wood or straw is almost harmless. By the same logic—which is quite remarkable—metals melted by fire from soft woods are rendered more tenacious and softer, while those from stronger woods become hard and brittle; such is the power of the variety of the fuel. Fire also takes on different qualities from its own nature and the way it is applied. It is weakest when placed underneath, as when we cook meat; it is applied beneath so that it may act more vehemently, for as we have said, the nature of fire is to tend upward. Next to this is what they call **reflected fire**; this occurs when it is applied both above and below, or from opposite sides, with the sides reflecting the force of the fire. By this method, soft metals are extracted from the stones to which they are joined, and silver is separated from copper. The third kind is **ambient fire**, when the object we intend to burn or melt is surrounded by fire on all sides without the use of bellows. The final method, than which none is more violent, is used when we wish to melt the most difficult materials contained within the hardest stones.

<margin>
Metallic sleeves.
</margin>
It is done in this manner. Vessels are made from black flint speckled with white spots, four or at least three cubits <note>A cubit is roughly the length of a forearm, about 18 inches</note> in length, nine inches wide, and three inches thick. They are curved at the bottom and formed almost into the shape of an elbow, without a base. In the middle of its length is a hole, and in it a pipe is precisely placed through which the breath of the **bellows** may be carried inside; at the bottom is another hole through which the melted material may descend. The lowest part of the vessel is blocked—except for the opening I mentioned—with a mixture of clay and crushed charcoal, pounded together and reduced to the form of a tenacious cement. These arrangements are called **Metallic Sleeves** <note>original: "Manicæ metallicæ"; likely referring to a sleeve-like furnace or crucible</note> because of their resemblance to them. They are filled inside with the material intended for melting and with charcoal alternately; this enclosed fire possesses the greatest power, and everything within must either melt or be consumed.

<margin>
The utility of bellows in liquid metals.
</margin>
The "breath" <note>original: "spiritus"</note> sent inside through the pipe from the bellows is of no small utility. First, as is obvious, it kindles the fire, stirs the flame, and forces the fire itself to penetrate more vehemently. Second, since it is cold, it compresses the heat conceived by the metal and drives it inward, thus dissolving the matter in which it resides. Third, if something has already melted, it prevents it from being "burnt" <note>likely referring to oxidation or the loss of volatile components</note> and moderates the heat.

How the elements exist in a mixture.

# On the Elements and their actions.

Or, given hot and moist matter, what prevents us from proposing that air is also present in mixtures? For just as cold and dry matter is there—not pure earth—and cold and moist matter—though not water—so too the hot and moist matter existing there could be called air, and the hot and dry called fire. Thus, this matter would once again return to the opinion of the *Aristotelians* <note>Followers of Aristotle, who believed all physical matter was composed of four elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>. But the difference is not small. First, because there is no actual air there; for air is produced by an igneous heat that is not natural, and even if it is produced, it is expelled. This is evident: men who possess a strong <term>natural heat</term> <note>original: "calorem naturalem"; the vital heat believed to sustain life and digestion in living beings</note> are free from <term>flatulence</term> <note>original: "flatus"; intestinal gas or "wind"</note>; whereas those who abound in bile and are hot by nature, yet have only a small amount of natural heat, abound in flatulence. Furthermore, it is one thing to say that at the beginning of generation the four elements are mixed, and another to say that in mixtures, after they have been mixed, parts are found that are similar to these elements. It follows that the part which seems similar to fire is similar to our common fire, which is well known to be no element at all. Finally, and more importantly, when the parts of earth and water are separated, they resemble earth and water not only in quality but also in their substances; however, the igneous and aerial parts do so not in substance, but only in quality. Therefore, as was said before, earth, water, and heat in a moist environment generate all things; from these, however, four substances seem to be created according to a similarity of qualities, though in truth, only cold stands firm according to this opinion. Another question, more difficult than this one, follows: if heat is <term>putrid</term> <note>original: "putridus"; heat associated with decay or rotting</note> in a dry environment, how does it generate? For we have established that it is of an igneous nature, and yet it is clear that it generates animals. But if it is in a moist environment, how does it cause corruption? Truly, putrefying heat itself generates nothing living; rather, by separating the matter, it leaves behind a terrestrial fatness which, when stirred by the heat of the *Sun*, conceives the seeds of life.

<margin>How putrid heat generates animals and other things.</margin>
We are deceived, however, by the proximity of these operations: because a corpse seems to rot and a worm seems to be generated at the same time. But if you wish to see that worms are not generated by putrid heat—leaving aside the reason that the same thing cannot produce opposites, and that putrefaction acts by separating while generation proceeds by mixing—consider that animals of the same species and likeness are generated in different places and from different matter. This does not proceed unto infinity; therefore, it is necessary that they be created by one general heat, namely that of the *Sun*. Neither would flies in *Persia* <note>modern-day Iran</note> and those from dung in *Italy* be similar if they were generated by putrid heat; they are therefore created by natural heat situated in moisture. Fire generates nothing by the process of corruption, because its violence prohibits the action of natural heat and induces an excessive dryness that is repugnant to all generation of living things. In dung, therefore, there are two heats: the putrid, through which it is corrupted, and the natural, through which plants and animals are generated. If putrid heat were the cause of generation, these things would be generated most when the rot was at its strongest. But they are not generated at that time, but rather while the putrid heat languishes; and when it ends, then life flourishes most. For this reason, when dung is steaming, life appears not in the middle but on the sides where...

# Book Two

...where it has cooled, worms and herbs are born <note>The author refers to "spontaneous generation," an ancient belief that life forms like insects or plants could arise directly from decaying matter once it reached a certain temperature</note>. Therefore, this discourse is truly demonstrative, for it holds everything that is evident to the eyes as consistent, and it dissolves all doubts. Accordingly, if medicinal ingredients are buried in dung once their decay is finished, they conceive a certain natural heat, and are thus mixed; in this way, oil and wine buried beneath the earth unite into the form of <term>opobalsamum</term> <note>original: "opobalsami"; a rare and precious aromatic resin or balm, often associated with the biblical "Balm of Gilead"</note>. But again, I say, if natural heat does not corrupt, why do <term>hypenemia</term> <note>original: "hypenemia"; wind-eggs, or infertile eggs produced without mating</note> eggs rot when a hen warms them? We shall say that in those things which have no principle of generation, after the heat has acted with too much effort, it becomes sharpened and causes rot. For even the flesh of a calf bound over the eyes rots, because there is no principle of natural heat within it. For every external heat is "unnatural" to that which it is outside of; moreover, it is external when there is no natural heat within. For we have said that movement comes from the innermost heat: therefore, for heat to be called "natural," it must be internal and fixed in moisture. By a similar reasoning, it is clear why the heat of a viper, even if it is natural to the snake, kills a man rather than helps him; for even if it is situated in moisture, it does not suit the moisture of a man: for it is overwhelmed by one thing and dissipated by another. Thus, in turn, a small amount of natural heat compels the moisture, while another kind burns it away. Therefore, just as all fiery heat burns, not everything that burns away a certain moisture is fiery, but it is fiery only to that specific thing.

<margin>The composition of the Elixir.</margin>
It remains, therefore, for us to teach that nothing is closer to the Sacred Liquor—of which we spoke above—than the <term>Elixir</term> <note>In alchemy, the Elixir was a prepared substance capable of prolonging life or transforming metals</note> which my father constructed. Many fragrant woods and herbs are caught in "burning water" <note>original: "ardente aqua"; likely *aqua ardens*, an early term for distilled alcohol or brandy</note>, and when buried in dung, they partially decay; from this, as has been said, the thinner part is separated from the earthy part. Then, by <term>distillation</term> <note>The process of heating a liquid to create vapor and then condensing it back into a liquid to purify it</note>, we draw off whatever is best, leaving only the dregs behind. This elixir strengthens the teeth, delays gray hair, and aids digestion, memory, and the senses; yet it is far inferior to the Sacred Liquor, even though it leads many into a great old age.

<margin>The difference between putrid and igneous heat.</margin>
But you will say: if putrid heat corrupts, why does igneous heat <note>Fiery heat or fire itself</note> not also do so, since it is of the same kind? This is because igneous heat is external, while putrid heat is internal; because of this, igneous heat, since it draws to itself by both drying and pulling, dries out the interior parts and prevents rot. Putrid heat, although it dries, because it is internal and draws to itself—for all heat draws to itself—it moistens and rots the interior. Therefore, putrid heat agrees with igneous heat in that it also dries; and it agrees with natural heat in that it lies in the innermost parts. Because of this, putrid heat is rightly called "middle" heat by some, between the igneous and the natural. For its substance is similar to the igneous, but its position, in comparison to nourishment, is natural; for igneous heat is always placed outside the nourishment. But you will say, why is putrid heat the author of poison, while igneous heat resists all poisons? For wounds resulting from poisonous animals, if they are cauterized with a glowing iron, become free of poison, and <margin>Fire resists all poison.</margin> any medicines, when they are burned and reduced to ash, cease to be poison. However, <term>sublimated</term> <note>original: "sublimata"; substances purified or altered through sublimation, a process where a solid is turned into gas and back into solid</note> things—for that is what those things are now called which in ancient times were called "cooked"—the more often they are cooked, the more destructive and more present they become—

# Concerning the Elements and Their Actions

<margin>Treatment of the plague with sublimated silver <note>original: "argento sublimato"; here referring to mercury</note>.</margin>
...instantaneous to death. The reasoning is the same in the case of rot and in things that are sublimated <note>Sublimation is a process where a substance is heated until it turns to vapor and then cools back into a solid, often used by alchemists to "purify" materials</note>; for where heat is increased and the moisture is not used up—as in things being cooked or rotting—the power of the poison is made worse. However, where things are burned, since every moist part perishes and the heat ends at the same time (as in ash), it is necessary for the entire power of the poison to depart. Therefore, it was not absurd that a certain man used to treat the plague with sublimated quicksilver <note>original: "argento vivo"; mercury</note>, for every poison is ended by the power of fire. Thus it is rightly said in the works of Ausonius <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius was a 4th-century Roman poet</note>:

> *An unfaithful wife gave poisons to her jealous husband,*
> *Yet she did not believe enough had been given to cause death,*
> *She mixed in the lethal weight of quicksilver,*
> *So that the doubled force might compel a swift end.*
> *Therefore, while the noxious drafts fought amongst themselves,*
> *The lethal harm yielded to the life-giving one.*

->Then, after a few lines, he adds:<-

For as I said, sublimated quicksilver has the nature of fire. Nevertheless, he who treated the plague in this way killed more people with the medicine than he cured. If, therefore, a harmless and fiery medicine were prepared, it would be able to cure. Yet that medicine, of whatever kind it might be, should be used just as warm linens applied to the skin weaken the natural heat. But by a contrary reasoning, a young boy or a fat puppy <margin>Strengthening the innate heat of the stomach.</margin> applied to the belly greatly assists digestion and increases the natural heat, even though that heat is not the same; indeed, it differs even in species from the heat of a puppy. It is manifest, therefore, that natural heat—when it is not offended by another natural heat—is strengthened by movement, just as one fiery thing is strengthened by another.

<margin>Why air was made.</margin>
With these things explained, let us return to the history of the elements, which we have taught are three: Air, Water, and Earth. It was not necessary for air to be mixed in the process of generation <note>The creation or birth of things</note>, since heat is very little suited to being acted upon; the elements concur as matter, and therefore earth and water were sufficient. But nor was it needed for the purpose of heating, since another heat was necessary—heavenly in origin—and that was sufficient for the work; if there had been two heats, like two rulers, matters would have proceeded worse, nor would the cold elements have obeyed a foreign heat and a contrary element. Rather, this would have been a kind of battle, not generation. Perhaps someone will wonder why I felt differently in my books of contradictions. But there, the purpose was to follow the opinions of the ancients; here, however, it is to teach the truth. For what cause, then, was the element of air made? It was made so that it might be subjected to the rays of the stars and receive their powers; and indeed, it receives them so much that in sudden <margin>Why suddenly cooled air brings so much harm.</margin> changes it kills not only animals but even plants. For example, in this year 1549, in the space of three days, it dried up all the citrus trees <note>original: "citrangula"</note> of Liguria <note>A coastal region in Northwest Italy</note>—no small omen. The cause is that when the cold comes upon the heat, it finds the bodies of both plants and animals open, and it extinguishes the heat that is within; a cold that creeps in gradually does not do such lasting damage, even if it were far greater. This indeed could not happen if air were, as they say, naturally very hot of its own accord; and for that reason...

<margin>
Why do we warm things by breathing with open lips, but cool them with narrowed lips?
</margin>
Indeed, a point that confirms this view and solves a difficult question is the fact that when people exhale with their whole mouth, they heat the air; yet if they blow with narrowed lips, they cool it. It is clear that the cause is no other than this: since air is naturally cold, when it is driven out with force, it is compelled to leave the warm vapors behind, and by the very power of its momentum, it enters the 
<term>pores of the skin<note>original: "cutis oscula", literally "the kisses of the skin." Renaissance anatomists often used poetic terms for pores.</note></term>. Because of these two factors, it cools intensely. Neither of these happens if you exhale slowly with the whole mouth open. However, if you blow either quickly with an open mouth, or with it narrowed but with your hand held very close, you will warm it slightly, or hardly cool it at all. 
<margin>
How a grotto is made colder.
</margin>
Therefore, if the plan is to cool a 
<term>cryptoporticus<note>A covered gallery or sunshade, often partially underground, used in Roman and Renaissance architecture to provide a cool walkway.</note></term>, you should direct several narrow and long porticos into it. 

Air is also extremely thin, so that it might receive all impacts. For in the earth, because of its solidity, movements do not occur except obscurely; in water, they are even slow; but air alone is most fit for receiving impacts, seemingly because of its very thinness. 
<margin>
The seven simple motions.
</margin>
There are, moreover, four other simple motions besides the three mentioned above. First is the Celestial motion, which is the most natural; then another natural motion which arises from a certain "obedience" of things, such as that of the water due to the 
<term>Moon<note>A reference to the tides.</note></term>, and of iron toward the 
<term>Herculean stone<note>The lodestone or magnet.</note></term>; third is voluntary motion, which belongs to animals; the fourth of these is 
<term>violent motion<note>In Aristotelian physics, "violent motion" is any movement imposed on an object by an external force that goes against its natural tendency (like a stone being thrown upward).</note></term>, which is the subject we now propose to discuss—for we shall speak of the others in their proper place. In total, therefore, there are seven simple motions, and composite motions are formed from these. 

<margin>
Concerning how violent motion occurs.
</margin>
Therefore, since this proposition was accepted from the 
<term>Philosopher<note>Almost always refers to Aristotle in this period.</note></term>—that nothing is moved without a mover, and that a thing moved by violent motion does not have the principle of movement within itself (because its motion is purely "violent" or forced), it follows that the principle is outside. Thus, things moved violently are moved by something outside the moved object. This mover can be nothing other than the air; therefore, things moved violently are moved by the air. 

Yet the same doubt fell upon the air because of one proposition which is true: that every body that moves something is itself in motion. Therefore, if the air moves a thrown stone, the air is moving; thus, the air is moved by something else, and so we are stuck with the same problem we had with the stone.

They say that since air is light, it is moved by its own form. According to this view, four opinions have arisen, none of which the commentators understood—especially the opinion of 
<term>Aristotle<note>Aristotle (384–322 BCE), whose theories of physics dominated European thought for centuries.</note></term>, of whom they boast so much. 

The **first** opinion is that a moved object, such as a stone (marked A), is moved by a force acquired from the thrower. Just as something heated by a fire continues to heat other things afterward because of the acquired heat, and the object itself remains hot for a long time, so the moved object receives that force from the mover, by which it is carried until it comes to rest. This is a sensible opinion, yet it was rejected by the ancients using an argument brought forward by Aristotle. But it can also be a sign that an object is moved by the air that a
