<page-num>55</page-num>
<header>On the Elements and their actions.</header>

# On the Elements and their actions.

...meanwhile, that which was in the place of the moving object, that is in **<term>A</term>**, fills the space between **<term>A</term>** and **<term>B</term>**, and so it touches the moving object **<term>A</term>** with motion. In this way, it always fills the place which the moving object **<term>A</term>** leaves behind with the same impulse with which **<term>A</term>** is already moved; for this is necessary because of the thinness of motion, or so that a **<term>vacuum<note>In classical physics, many philosophers believed "nature abhors a vacuum" and that space must always be filled with matter like air or water.</note></term>** is not created. Thus, **<term>Plato</term>** is able to argue: when moved by any impulse, the air follows behind, filling the place with that same impulse, and it touches the moved object **<term>A</term>**. Therefore, the air itself will move **<term>A</term>** with the same impulse as before, creating a continuous motion. He calls this method **<term>antiperistasis<note>original: "antiperistasin." A Greek term meaning "circular displacement." This was a theory used to explain how a stone keeps flying after it leaves the thrower's hand: the air it displaces rushes around to the back to push it forward.</note></term>**, that is, a succession of places through change. **<term>Aristotle</term>** says that motion does not happen in this way: because even if antiperistasis occurs, the moving object cannot be propelled by it. His reasoning is as follows: those things that move by antiperistasis are themselves moved; therefore, while they are not being moved, they do not move other things. But when the air existing in **<term>A</term>** has moved into **<term>B</term>**, it is then moved by nothing, for it has occupied the place it was meant to fill; therefore, existing in **<term>B</term>**, it cannot move **<term>A</term>** from its place. It is clear, because a body does not move another body unless the mover itself is moved. This demonstration was not understood by the commentators, and yet it clearly shows **<term>Plato's</term>** opinion to be false.

The third opinion was that of certain ancients: that the air preceding the moving object—suppose in **<term>C</term>** while the moving object is in **<term>B</term>**—is moved toward **<term>D</term>**, and in succession (so that no vacuum is created), **<term>B</term>** is transferred into **<term>C</term>** to the place of the moved air. Thus the same air is moved from **<term>D</term>** into **<term>E</term>**, and the moving object follows with the same impulse. It is just as if an ox held the place or played the part of the preceding air, and a wagon the part of the weight or moving object; the bond by which the ox pulls the wagon is the "thinness" or the necessity of avoiding a vacuum. Thus, however much the ox is moved and with whatever velocity, the wagon will be moved just as much and as fast. In the same way, with whatever velocity the air before the moving object **<term>A</term>** is moved, the moving object **<term>A</term>** will follow, and thus continuous motion is achieved. This was the opinion of certain ancients which some have falsely believed to be the Philosopher’s <note>In the Renaissance, "The Philosopher" almost always refers to Aristotle.</note>, though it is actually rejected by him, as the same reasoning used against the first opinion militates against this one. 

Namely, if the air at **<term>C</term>** is transferred to **<term>D</term>**, it is asked: by what? If by the moving object, then they will move each other in turn, which is impossible; for the moving object would propel the air from **<term>C</term>** to **<term>D</term>**, and it is already assumed that the air transferred from **<term>C</term>** to **<term>D</term>** pulls the moving object from **<term>C</term>** to **<term>D</term>**. Therefore, the same thing would be both cause and effect relative to the same result. If you say that the air transfers itself, he asks: why then can the moving object not also do this? And we return to the first opinion. If you say that the air can do this because it possesses a "principle of motion," it follows that this motion will be perpetual, because that air will always remain the same and is moved by its own form; therefore, it would always move at an equal velocity, but this is contrary to **<term>experience<note>original: "experimentum." In this context, it refers to observable physical reality rather than a modern laboratory experiment.</note></term>**. Also, it would never stop, which is also against experience. For in that case, a stone thrown by a hand would travel through the whole world with equal force, because it is clear that its preceding air would always be moved with equal force, and no one could show a reason why that impulse ought to be weakened. 

The fourth opinion is that of **<term>Aristotle</term>**, that the air...

<page-num>56</page-num>
<header>Book Two</header>

## Book Two

The air which is in **<term>B</term>**, set in motion by the person who throws the stone, is moved before the mobile object is, and it propels the air which is in **<term>C</term>**; that which is in **<term>C</term>** propels the air in **<term>D</term>**, and that in **<term>D</term>** propels the air in **<term>E</term>**, and so on until it reaches **<term>G</term>**, which cannot move **<term>H</term>** because it is too weak. Then, since **<term>H</term>** is not moved, it will not pull the weight, and so the motion comes to rest in **<term>G</term>**. He speaks in this way: **<term>violent motion<note>original: "motus uiolentus." In the physics of this period, "violent" motion is any movement forced upon an object that goes against its natural tendency—such as throwing a stone upward when its nature is to fall.</note></term>** becomes weaker because **<term>F</term>** is moved by **<term>E</term>**, and therefore with less impulse than **<term>E</term>**, and **<term>E</term>** with less than **<term>D</term>**. Thus, violent motion is always weakening, as is also apparent through experience. Here, too, there is no motion without a **<term>mover<note>original: "motore." A core principle of Aristotelian physics was that nothing moves unless something else is currently pushing or pulling it.</note></term>**, because every part is moved by the one preceding it, just as **<term>F</term>** is moved by **<term>E</term>**, and **<term>E</term>** by **<term>C</term>** itself.

Thirdly, the reason for this saying is clear: any part of the air stops *being moved* before it stops *moving* the next part. For when **<term>D</term>** is moved by **<term>C</term>**, it moves **<term>E</term>** because it was moved by **<term>C</term>**; therefore, while **<term>D</term>** is already coming to rest in the place of **<term>E</term>**, it moves **<term>E</term>** out of its place. Thus, it stops being moved before it stops moving another, because **<term>D</term>** stops being moved while **<term>D</term>** is in **<term>E</term>**, for then **<term>C</term>** (which was moving **<term>D</term>**) is in the position of **<term>D</term>**. Therefore, when **<term>E</term>** is in **<term>D</term>**, **<term>D</term>** rests in **<term>E</term>**, and then **<term>C</term>** is moved toward **<term>F</term>**, and it is not moved except by something, and that something is **<term>D</term>**. Thus, **<term>D</term>** stops being moved before it stops moving another, because while **<term>D</term>** is in **<term>C</term>** it is not moved but rests, and yet it still moves **<term>E</term>** toward **<term>F</term>**.

And if you object that a body does not move another unless it is itself being moved, I say that this is true; however, the end of the first motion (that of the mover) is joined to the start of the second motion. They are not the same, but the mover stops its own motion before the object it moves does; and this is because, at least by nature, the mover is moved before it moves something else. Therefore, the fourth point is clear: the motion of a thrown object is composed of infinite motions succeeding one another, and it is **<term>continuous by accident<note>original: "continuus per accidens." This means the motion appears to be one single, smooth action, but is actually a chain of many separate events triggered one after the other.</note></term>**. For it happens by air at **<term>B</term>** being transferred into **<term>C</term>**, and air at **<term>C</term>** meanwhile into **<term>D</term>**, and that which was in **<term>D</term>** into **<term>E</term>**, and so on with the others. And for this reason, such motion is also fast, because the ends of one are so closely joined to the beginnings of the next that they seem as if they ought to be transferred at the same time—though it is not so.

But let us imagine ten oxen, one in front of the other and all in front of a wagon, and let each have a goad on its forehead with which it touches the back leg of the ox in front of it. Then, when the first ox moves, the wagon will follow; that same ox will move the second, and the second the third. You see that every ox is moved by another before it moves the next, and yet the last ox will move almost at the same time as the first. This is because such a succession is composed of only ten parts (there being only ten oxen); but the succession of air is composed of infinite parts. Therefore, there is a perceivable amount of time from the beginning of the stone's motion until the end. But to remove the problem of infinity, the **<term>condensation of air<note>original: "condẽsatio aeris."</note></term>** helps, as **<term>Averroes<note>A 12th-century philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were the standard textbooks for science in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note></term>** rightly said; this condensation is the cause for the motion stopping more quickly, making it unnecessary to assume infinite motions, but only "innumerable" ones.

And this is the opinion of **<term>Aristotle</term>**, which until this day has been understood by none, regarding the motion of things moved by force. But we have more need of the first opinion, which is the simplest and also does not suffer from such great difficulties: when it is assumed that everything which is moved is moved by something, it is a most certain truth.

<header>On the Elements & their actions.</header>

# On the Elements & their actions.

What moves the object is an acquired **<term>impetus<note>original: "impetus acquisitus." In early physics, this was the idea that a moving object "carries" a force given to it by the thrower, similar to how hot water "carries" heat from the fire even after being moved away.</note></term>**, just like heat in water, which is there contrary to its nature because it was introduced by fire. Yet, even when the fire is removed, it still burns the hand of someone touching it; and thus, an **<term>accident<note>original: "accidens." In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality or property (like heat or speed) that is not essential to what a thing is, but can be added to it.</note></term>** adhering by force retains its power. Let us therefore first state the things that are manifest: there are four causes of a **<term>violent motion<note>original: "motus uiolentus." This refers to any movement forced upon an object that goes against its natural tendency, such as throwing a stone upward.</note></term>** that is long-lasting and fast.

<margin>Four causes for the speed and duration of violent motion.</margin>
The first cause is that the moving force moves it quickly from the beginning. The second is that it moves through a great distance; for this reason, the longer the **<term>war engines<note>original: "machinae bellicae." Likely referring to catapults, ballistae, or early cannons.</note></term>** are, the further they hurl their projectiles. The same is true of flexible bows: the more the bow is stretched, for both reasons <note>speed and distance</note>, the further it sends the arrow. For if it is stretched only to **B**, the arrow will move with the string only from **B** to **D**; but if it is stretched to **C**, it will move from **C** to **D**. Therefore, if it is stretched to **C**, it will be launched much further, according to the proportion of distance **CD** to **BD**. Likewise, a string pulled back to **C** will return to **D** with greater force than from **B** to **D**. Therefore, the arrow will be moved faster by the string, and consequently, it will also move faster after it has been released. It is not necessary to add that the power moving it must be "strong," for it is enough for us that it moves "quickly"; if it can move something quickly, the cause that moves it is strong. For even if a cause were strong, if it moved slowly, it could not launch an object far.

<margin>Nothing can be sent far if moved slowly:</margin>
Indeed, nothing can move something slowly and still have it go a great distance. For what is moved slowly consumes much time in its motion, during which its force must necessarily be weakened, since it is striving against nature. The third cause is the thinness of the **<term>medium<note>original: "medij." The substance through which an object travels, such as air or water.</note></term>** through which it is moved. For an object moves swiftly in air, slowly in water, and in earth it is hardly possible to propel anything.

<margin>Ship captains take care that war engines do not submerge the balls under water, which they fire into an enemy fleet.</margin>
And because of this, those who attack enemy ships with engines take great care that the blow does not strike the part of the ship lying under water—even though that would be more **<gloss>destructive</gloss>** <note>original: "pnitiofior," likely a shorthand for "perniciosior."</note>—because the force of the ball's strike is weakened by the resistance of the water. They prefer to strike the ship above the water, but still at the lowest point they can. The fourth cause of a fast and long-lasting strike is the sharpness of the projectile, which is less hindered because it encounters a smaller quantity of air in its path. From this, it seems that the first opinion is truer than that of **<term>Aristotle<note>Aristotle believed that a projectile is kept in motion by the air itself pushing from behind. The author here is critiquing that idea, favoring the theory of internal impetus.</note></term>** regarding the cause of violent motion. For it is not clearly apparent in his theory why objects moved by force are carried faster and for a longer distance when they are sharper. Furthermore, if any objects are very close to a bowstring but not actually touching it, even though the air is moved just as much as the air preceding an arrow, those nearby objects are not moved at all, let alone carried over a long distance. Moreover, since air is soft, it can neither be moved so violently nor compressed into one mass so as to move an iron ball. Nor would an object propelled by force move any less in water than in air—even though it actually moves not just slower, but far slower, in water than in air. And even in the air itself, heavy things ought not to be carried slower than light things if they followed the logic of a vacuum. But these reasons do not show that sharp things are carried faster because the first air is moved with greater force, from which the remaining parts [are moved] according to the same...

<page-num>58</page-num>
->## Book Two<-

They are driven by the same cause. The other reasons, besides the last one, demonstrate against Plato's opinion concerning **<term>antiperistasis<note>original: "antiperistasi"; the theory that a projectile is pushed forward by air rushing from the front to the back to prevent a vacuum.</note></term>**, but not concerning the preceding air. The last reason, however, has evident experience against it; for even in motion through **<term>rarefaction<note>original: "raritate"; a medium that has become thin or less dense.</note></term>**, the ascent of a heavy object is more difficult than that of a light one, and therefore also slower.

<margin>
Demonstrative reasoning in favor of Aristotle. *On the Heavens*, book 2, text chapter 45; and in the division of Simplicius, text chapter 20.
</margin>

But what gives credit to Aristotle's opinion is what he said: that **natural motion** becomes stronger at the end, **violent motion** becomes stronger at the beginning, and the motion of **projectiles** becomes strongest in the middle. **<term>Averroes<note>A 12th-century Islamic philosopher known as "The Commentator" for his influential work on Aristotle.</note></term>**, following **<term>Simplicius<note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle's physics.</note></term>**, and having a corrupted version of the text, read "projected animals" instead of projectiles. Simplicius, although he had the correct text, did not understand Aristotle well and interpreted it as "projected animals"—suggesting they moved sideways like thrown objects—a most absurd comparison and interpretation. This moved him because he had already said that violent motions move more vehemently at the start and natural ones at the end; projectiles ought to have belonged to one of these types. But he did not understand the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note>. For since projectiles are moved by the motion of the preceding air, and the air itself is made movable by the motion of the projectiles, it consists in a way of both the natural and the violent. Natural motion increases at the end, while violent motion increases at the beginning; therefore, the mixture of these two, which is the motion of projectiles, is strongest in the middle. This reasoning is consistent and teaches the solution to this doubt most beautifully.

<margin>
Why the strike of Scorpions, engines, and missiles is stronger at a certain distance than when too close.
</margin>

For we see that **<term>engines<note>original: "machinas"; likely referring to catapults or trebuchets.</note></term>**, **<term>scorpions<note>original: "scorpiones"; a Roman-style torsion engine that fired heavy bolts or arrows.</note></term>**, and even missiles thrown by hand deliver more vehement blows at a certain distance than when they are too close, or so to speak, right under the missiles, scorpions, or engines themselves. The cause is one that no one else can provide except he who thinks the motion is caused by this principle proposed by Aristotle. For at the start of the motion, that air helps the movement only a little; as time passes, the natural motion of the air as it is moved becomes stronger, but as it moves the object, it "opens up" <note>original: "dehiscit"; perhaps meaning the air offers less resistance or creates a flow</note> a little; wherefore it is necessary for the speed of the motion to increase until it begins to move less than it is naturally inclined to be moved.

<margin>
The reasoning for the motion of heavy things when they are moved violently.
</margin>

Therefore, having understood the reason for violent motion, let us show how those things which are not moved of their own accord are carried. Let us take this beginning: that heavy things moved by some blow, and not according to their nature, have three components from which the motion is composed: their own **gravity**, by which they are carried downward; the **natural force of the medium** as it is moved; and the **acquired force** by which it moves another part of the air. Now, let **AB** be a line parallel to the **<term>horizon<note>original: "finitori"; the boundary line between earth and sky.</note></term>** which the line **CD** cuts at a right angle, so that **CA** is equal to **BC**, and let **AC** be divided equally at **E**. That which must be moved is at **F**, and it is manifest by itself that it will be struck out toward **D** with a very strong blow, because it will be carried toward **D** by the impetus of the thrower and by nature at the same time. But it was likely that the weakest blow would be the one contrary to it, that is, toward **C**, and the strongest toward the upper parts, neither of which is established by experience.

<header>Of the Elements and their actions. 59</header>

...stands: but the strongest is the upper F E, the medium is F C, and the weakest is F A; why so? Indeed, because air is carried more in a straight line than to the sides, therefore the impact from F to A is weakest. According to this reasoning, the strongest impact ought to have been from F to C, but because the entire weight of the mass stands in the way, it follows that where the air is moved most and the weight has the least gravitational resistance, which is in line F E, there the ball is launched most powerfully. 
<margin>The way in which heavy objects descend after impact.</margin>
It remains, therefore, that it is carried at a medium strength from F to C, that is, straight upwards. Do not, however, be mistaken regarding arrows, which because of their length and wings are sometimes carried faster from F to A than in C, but never more than in E. For this reason, those who shake walls <note>Referring to siege engineers using artillery like catapults or early cannons.</note> place their machines at a **<term>semi-orthon<note>A technical term from Greek meaning "half-upright," referring to an angle of 45 degrees, which was historically believed to provide the greatest range.</note>**, that is, at the **<term>level<note>original: "libellam"; a sighting line or a level used for aiming.</note>** F E: for the impact is increased by nearly a third part. When the ball has reached its highest point straight up, it does not descend again immediately in a circle, nor straight down, but in a middle line which nearly imitates a **<term>parabola<note>The curved path of a projectile. The author is noting that the trajectory is neither a perfect circle nor a straight line.</note>** surrounding the line such as B C is, and finally from C to D it moves by the motion of a heavy object straight as a hair <note>original: "ad unguem"; literally "to the fingernail," meaning perfectly or precisely.</note>.

Those things which are projected consist of three motions: first, the violent; last, the purely natural; and the middle, mixed from both. Because the calculation of such motion is so complex, it is clearly impossible to measure it perfectly, yet one may reach it through conjecture. 
<margin>Why hardly anyone is struck by lead pellets which are sent upward in great numbers.</margin>
The motions from B to C are clearly the weakest, whence lead balls dissipated by heat also cause less harm; for this reason, among so many thousands of shots, you will hardly see one or two people wounded or seriously struck by impacts intended for the heights, even though balls heavier than half an ounce are frequently sent up for the sake of birds or for clearing a machine. 
<margin>Concerning the motion of a ring.</margin>
But since heavy objects are moved with such difficulty along a line parallel to the horizon, why is it that suspended things are pushed so easily, so that a ring hung on a thread seems to move of its own accord, and for this reason even presents the appearance of an incantation? The cause is that the entire force is left whole to the one pushing: for he who throws a weight does two things—he supports it and he pushes it. But with a hung weight, since it is already supported by something else, whatever strength is applied remains whole for the impulse. Furthermore, when it is pushed, it returns to the middle with almost as much force as it was pushed away with; therefore, since it has been pushed from the middle by a certain force—for example, through the space of a cubit—it will necessarily depart by the same amount in the opposite direction, and so it comes to rest very slowly through continuous and alternating return. When, therefore, this motion in a ring is helped a little even by the hidden motion of breaths <note>original: "spirituum"; referring here to physical air currents or the "spirit" of the air rather than ghosts.</note>, it increases so much of its own accord that you would believe there was power in the words [of a spell]. For this reason, when the motion of the ring is a little more excited—the ring now moving itself, as I said—it seems as if a **<term>Demon<note>A supernatural entity. The author is explaining that what looks like magic or demonic intervention is actually just the physics of a pendulum.</note>** is inside the ring moving it. Moreover, this motion is even easier on a longer thread, by evident demonstration. <header>Book Two</header>

# Book Two

And let L be the center of the earth: it is established, therefore, that while a body is at F, it will be moved against its natural motion through F G, and while it is at H, through H K. But H K is shorter than F G, as we demonstrated in the first book concerning circles. Therefore, since the moving power is the same and the object being moved is the same, and it traverses a greater space at F than at H—that is, moving further from the center or ascending more—it will traverse that space in a longer time. Therefore, if they must be moved in an equal time, H requires less impetus than F; and for this reason, the higher an object is suspended, the more easily the mobile body is moved and with less labor. Thus, when the string is long, it will take the beginning of its motion either from the careless movement of the hands, or from the air, or from the **<term>spirits<note>original: "spiritibus"; in Renaissance physics, these were subtle fluids or "vital breaths" thought to transmit force or life through matter.</note>** themselves, whose force even descends through the string. Since its motion is so easy, and with so many causes moving it, it is no wonder that the ring is moved even when the fingers and the top of the string remain still; and once moved, it can hardly find a beginning of rest, since a heavy hanging object (as I said) moves itself so persistently. In this way, it appears to be moved by **<term>incantation<note>original: "præcantatione"; the author is providing a natural physical explanation for phenomena that might look like magic or dowsing.</note>**.**

But after these things are clear, someone will wonder why thin bodies <note>Substances with low density, like air or fire.</note> not only admit swift motion—which is consistent with reason—but also produce it, which seems inconsistent. For the impact of water is less violent than that of air, and that of air less than that of fire. Evidence for this was 
<margin>A machine that strikes without fire.</margin>
an instrument which, as I hear (for I have not seen it), a German man brought: it was twenty **<term>ells<note>original: "ulnas"; a measurement of length roughly equal to a man's arm.</note>** long, made of cypress, whose bore was so narrow that it would not have admitted a chickpea even if it were perfectly round. Its thickness was less than an ell. It propelled a very tiny lead ball, yet one that fit the bore, with such force that it pierced through a board. It was a safe thing, without noise or the expense of powder, having these three advantages; but it had just as many disadvantages: weight, great size, and a weakness relative to its size. But if we employ the impact of fire, we will require a much shorter and smaller instrument; therefore, fire impels more than air, and air more than water. The cause is twofold: first, because in an impact it is necessary not only to move but also to be moved; but we have demonstrated that rarer things are moved most easily, and because of this, they produce a great blow. The other cause is that things which are rare can be compressed the most, because they are far distant from extreme density; water, however, since it approaches the density of earth, can be compressed further very little. Therefore, every machine is either necessarily large or it produces a weak blow, or it acts with a great noise; for those that act with fire make a noise for the stated reason, while those that act with air are either large, like **Catapults** and **Ballistae**, or they produce small blows. But they are accustomed to [launch] arrows from **<term>scorpions<note>original: "scorpioni-"; a "scorpion" was a smaller type of Roman torsion siege engine.</note>**—

A marvelous instrument for sifting flour.

But since these things might be called **<term>minor works<note>original: "parerga"; a Greek-derived term for secondary works or digressions from the main subject.</note>**,** I have nonetheless decided to describe a very beautiful instrument for sifting flour, invented within the last three years, to demonstrate the ingenious invention of men which took its origin from the nature of the air. This is so that men may understand how easily wealth may be acquired through simple things, provided they are clever. For now, since all bakers possess it for its utility—and indeed the inventor obtained a **<term>privilege<note>original: "priuilegium"; a 16th-century equivalent of a patent, granted by the Emperor (Caesar) to protect an invention.</note>** from the Emperor so that no one may have it without his consent—he makes his living from this industry and has built a house for himself in a very short time. For it is not only bakers, but also colleges of priests, and virgins consecrated to God, and whatever nobles maintain a large household, who possess it for its outstanding utility, if not its necessity. Many others, too, whom the wonder of the thing itself incited rather than its utility, have taken care to have one made. This is its structure:

There is a small wheel **B**, on the outer circumference of which is a handle **A** by which it can be turned; these two extend outside the machine. In the middle of the wheel is a small rod **C**, which is turned by the motion of the wheel. On this rod **C** are two small wooden teeth placed opposite each other, and two others nearby, also 

->[A technical diagram of a flour-sifting machine showing a crank, wheel, gears, and vibrating sieve mechanism labeled with letters A through P.]<-

placed opposite each other, but in a position intermediate to the first ones. Thus, when the wheel is turned once, it touches the broad wood—or rather, the small board **D E** suspended from both sides of the box—four times. As the wheel turns, the board is perpetually agitated with a trembling motion while it is touched by the teeth. Furthermore, the rod **C** and a small part of the board are enclosed by the box. Above the wood or board **D E** stands the **<term>bolting sieve<note>original: "cribrũ polinariũ"; a fine sieve used to separate the finest flour (pollen) from the bran.</note>** **F G**, hanging at an angle and suspended from **G** into **H** so that it does not fall out. This is made everywhere of thin boards—or rather, very thin and light ones—except at the bottom where the flour is shaken out through the sieve: for that part, as is customary, consists of a linen cloth. All these things are contained and enclosed on all sides by this box, at the top of which is a small hopper...

# Book Two

**K** is positioned, and upon it is a very light, square wooden tray in which the flour lies; this is suspended in such a way that it can be easily shaken. It is shaken, moreover, by a small cord attached to it and to a wheel on the right side next to **B** on the other end of the same cord. You should also remember that the sieve **F G** is open at both ends: at the top so that it may receive the flour from the tray, and at the bottom so that it may eject the **<term>bran<note>original: "furfur"; the outer skins of the grain separated during sifting.</note>** from **G**. The entire box is divided into three sections, **L**, **M**, and **N**, with upright partitions made of thin, sturdy boards that are completely immovable; it can also be divided into four sections if one prefers.

Once this is set up, when the wheel **B** is turned, the cord shakes the small tray, and the little teeth shake the board. The tray shakes the flour into the sieve **F G**, and the board shakes the sieve. From this, it happens that the **<term>finest flour<note>original: "flos farinae," literally "the flower of the flour"; the highest quality, most finely ground flour.</note>** is shaken out first and falls into the **N M** part of the casing. As it descends, however, being shaken more vigorously, another, less pure part is shaken out into **L M**. Finally, from there, the entire bran descends through the lower mouth of the sieve **G** into **L O**. Thus, three things are collected separately: the finest flour in **M N**, the coarse flour in **M L**, and the bran in **L O**. Whatever flour flies around inside is necessarily returned to its place so that absolutely nothing is lost, since the casing is nowhere open to the air.

You must also ensure—as you can easily perceive by logic—that the sieve **F G** is not too steeply inclined; otherwise, the flour would reach **G** too quickly and be ejected along with the bran. For this reason, if you move the partition **L** all the way to the mouth of the sieve, or add another partition as at **P**, and at the same time curve the mouth **G** slightly upward as you see, you will not suffer the loss of even a **<term>single penny<note>original: "oboli iacturam"; an obol was a small coin, used here to mean "the smallest possible amount."</note>** of flour.

Now understand how many advantages follow from this instrument. First, by the labor of just one man—who turns the wheel, puts the flour in the tray, and collects the sifted flour and bran when the spaces are full—he fulfills the roles of three sifters. Second, because this work is neither so laborious nor harmful, anyone is sufficient for it; even common porters can be used, who are hired for a much lower price than professional sifters. Third, the entire flour is collected and nothing is lost, whereas with manual sifters, it is inevitable that a significant portion is lost due to the movement of hands and arms. Furthermore, since the linen sieve only vibrates, it does not wear out as much; indeed, it lasts much longer than when flour is sifted by men, for it is necessary for them to shake the sieve violently, as is their custom. It also contributes to profit because the flour is extracted more exquisitely, so that the bran is entirely pure. All these things are achieved without the messiness of the house, and without the waste and inconvenience to the men. Furthermore, the nature of the instrument distinguishes two or three grades of flour, which cannot be done by manual sifters except by uncertain guesswork at first, and then inconsistently.

<margin>Why the air is not felt.</margin>
But let us now return to the treatment of the air, now that the narration of all violent motions is finished. And so, we have already taught that the air extends all the way to heaven, and that the purer part of it is called the **<term>ether<note>original: "aethera"; in ancient and Renaissance science, this was the "fifth element" or the rarest, purest form of air in the upper heavens.</note>**; but neither the ether nor the air can be felt because of the purity of their substance. This was done for the sake of living creatures;

# On the Elements and their actions.

For if air possessed colors, the things that are seen through it would appear to be of that same color. Just as everything appears green to someone looking through green **<term>spectacles<note>original: "conspicilia"; an early term for eyeglasses or lenses.</note>**; so too, if the air shared in a color, all things would be seen as being of that same color. Similarly, if it had a scent, all things would seem infected with that same odor. Likewise, if it put forward a sharp or sweet taste, all things would seem sweet or sharp. In the same way, if the air should ever become hot, as in summer, it causes all things to appear hot. For that reason, night reveals even the lightest sounds and noises, because during the day the air is not entirely devoid of sound. Therefore, so that it might be able to receive all things—tastes, smells, sounds, colors, and heat and cold—and represent them properly to the senses, it was made devoid of the nature of all of them. Since it is subject to the **<term>primary qualities<note>The four basic qualities in Aristotelian physics: hot, cold, wet, and dry.</note>**, it flees from the opposite quality; and this is proof of what we have already said: that the qualities themselves act through themselves.

<margin>Why air in winter is forced into a round shape.</margin>
For in winter, the air that is breathed out, since it is warm, is forced into a round shape; this is indeed by the heat itself, not by the nature of the air. For cold air is not compressed, nor is warm air when breathed into a warm place. But why into a round shape? Because that shape, while being the most spacious, is also the strongest, and also because it exposes itself to the cause of injury at only a single point. For this reason, those about to fight, or to receive a blow, or to undergo a weight, gather themselves entirely into a rounded shape.

<margin>The contrary powers of air.</margin>
When air is trapped, it destroys living things but preserves things lacking a soul <note>original: "anima carentia"; referring to inanimate objects like wood or stone.</note>. However, when it is free, it destroys things lacking a soul but preserves those that are living. For air wears away inanimate things by its motion; therefore, in a place where the wind blows through, it destroys them, but it purifies and cools the heat of animals. Yet, when shut away and not moving, it preserves uninjured those things that are free from rot, because lacking motion, it does not wear them away. But it destroys, kills, and putrefies animals and things capable of rotting when it remains motionless and, therefore, becomes stagnant.

<margin>A plague from a small opened chest.</margin>
Indeed, trapped and motionless air becomes so corrupted that when the soldiers of the Emperor **<term>Marcus Antoninus<note>Commonly known as Marcus Aurelius (reigned 161–180 AD).</note>** under **<term>Avidius Cassius<note>A Roman general who led the campaign against the Parthian Empire.</note>** opened a small chest found in the temple of Apollo in **<term>Seleucia<note>A major Mesopotamian city on the Tigris river.</note>** in Babylonia, hoping to find gold, the air coming out was so foul that it infected the entire region with plague. Carried from there by the winds into Greece, and from there even to Rome, it stirred up that pestilence which consumed nearly a third part of the entire human race.

<margin>Causes of the rot of air and plague.</margin>
By a similar reasoning, grain shut up under the earth spoils the air, and in turn, the grain is spoiled by it. Corruptions of the air also happen because of earthquakes. For when the earth is opened, air that had been hidden for many centuries usually brings a great plague when it emerges; for this reason, severe pestilences usually follow great earthquakes. They also occur because of rot, such as after great slaughters <note>referring to battlefields with unburied corpses</note>, after floods, and the death of locusts. These indeed are the pestilences from the air.

<margin>A wondrous plague.</margin>
But those that happen after a famine are of a different kind. Yet there is a wonderful variety of plagues; for authors worthy of trust report that in Constantinople, which once...

<margin>Why the plague does not exceed three years.</margin>
...it was once said of Byzantium <note>The ancient name for Constantinople, modern-day Istanbul.</note> that a plague arose of such a kind that those who were suffering, or those whom the disease threatened, seemed to be struck by another man; and, thrown into confusion by this terror, they died. It is certainly established that there are almost as many modes of plague as there are seasons. Yet no plague rages beyond a three-year period. The cause is manifold: first, because if it were to rage for so long, it would eventually have almost no one left to rage against. Furthermore, the air itself, being of the thinnest substance as has been said, cannot undergo further **putrefaction**. For it was shown above that things which have thoroughly rotted are no longer capable of rotting. To this is added the fact that it can hardly happen that, in such a long time, the air is not moved and the winds do not carry away that which is corrupted; it also seems that a certain limit has been imposed upon all the worst things by the benefit of God. For neither do serpents seem to multiply beyond a certain boundary, nor do acute diseases persist beyond the fourteenth day, nor can any violent evil be long-lasting. In the case of a long-lasting and slow kind of plague, however, no fixed limit can be found, as in the **<term>French disease<note>original: "Gallica lue"; a historical name for syphilis, which began its first major recorded European epidemic in 1494/1495.</note>**, which it is well known has now exceeded its fiftieth year since its origin.

<margin>The threefold nature of poisons.</margin>
The types of plague originating from the air have the nature of a poison. For there are certain poisons by nature, such as those which are born <note>i.e., naturally occurring</note>, and the worst of the snakes; others by **putrefaction**, among which number is the plague itself; and others which are fashioned by art, once called "cooked" but now called **<term>sublimated<note>original: "sublimata"; in early chemistry/alchemy, this refers to substances purified or altered by heating them into vapor and collecting the deposit, such as "corrosive sublimate" (mercuric chloride).</note>**. The sharpest and most instantaneous poisons are made by nature, as she surpasses art in every way; but these are nevertheless rare, while those made by art are most frequent. Since the human race is far more wretched than nature when it comes to devising evils, nature does not consider it a disgrace to be surpassed by men in these matters (though this is a rare example), provided that the prize for the sheer magnitude of the thing remains with her.

<margin>That there are poisons which kill by touch alone.</margin>
Indeed, there are some among these that kill by touch alone; for if the foam of a **rabid dog** falls upon a place that is in any way wounded, or from which only the cuticle <note>The outermost layer of skin.</note> has been removed, it is accustomed to kill. Also, **<term>squill<note>original: "scylla"; likely referring to the sea squill (Drimia maritima), a plant known to cause skin irritation and used in ancient medicine/poisoning.</note>** smeared on the skin torments the flesh, and **<term>cantharides<note>original: "cantharides"; also known as "Spanish fly," these beetles contain a toxic blistering agent called cantharidin.</note>** held in the hand provoke the passing of blood in the urine. What wonder is it, therefore, if there is a poison that kills by contact alone, especially when we see that the plague can kill a man who sits upon a saddle or a plank because the contagion adhered to them? Why few people perish in this way is due to several causes. First, few people wish for this; for Princes hold those things in hatred which others could also use against them. Even fewer are those who know these things; the wise do not wish to set a very bad example, and the unskilled are not capable of it. Add to this that any sane person would hardly handle such a violent beast willingly; furthermore, these things cannot cause harm unless they are administered in great quantity and everything sticks, and against such things the caution of Princes is greatest. There also looms a danger so great for traitors if they are discovered—not only from those against whom they plot, but also from those for whose sake they plot, lest they have a witness to the crime after it is performed. Finally, those who are well-instructed either by nature or by art wish to be without this knowledge, which exists only for the destruction of men. I, since I have been quite curious about all things which [belong] to mortals...

# On the Elements and Their Actions

...to know such things, I have considered this ignorance alone to be in place of the best knowledge. I neither sought it, nor if someone had offered it of their own accord would I have wished to have it. Rather, if anything had to be devised, I turned it toward help and precaution. <margin>Precaution against poisons.</margin> The help, therefore, is not to linger in any one place until the hand warms up; frequent washing of the parts with lukewarm water; and also the anointing of oil of rue—not the common kind, but that which is made in the same way as <term>spikenard oil<note>original: "spicatum"</note></term> and <term>clove oil<note>original: "gariophylatum"</note></term> are usually made by the apothecaries. But if anyone fears they have already been caught [by poison], I believe that oil distilled from <term>orpiment<note>original: "auripigmento"; a deep orange-yellow arsenic sulfide mineral.</note></term> or <term>Misy<note>original: "Myſi"; an ancient term for a mineral related to copperas or iron sulfates, often found in mines.</note></term>, rubbed upon the arteries and the region of the heart, can save a person from death. I have also said that fire applied to the area extinguishes every poison; and there is no one who does not know how much drinking **Theriac** <note>A famous ancient and medieval "universal" antidote made of many ingredients, including viper flesh.</note> contributes, if it is properly prepared.

<margin>Oil which, when rubbed on, drives away poisons.</margin> But since we have fallen into these discussions, I think it is not beside the point to ask: in what way can an oil be prepared which, when rubbed on the arteries, forces the poison to be expelled by vomiting, purging, sweat, or urine? It is certain it must be metallic, which ought to be very powerful; I have occasionally seen such a thing, and from its weight alone I guessed without doubt that it was metallic. It must also be of the nature of the poison, for by immoderate heat, as has been said, it destroys the previously conceived evil power; and by similarity, it draws out from the exterior what is harmful, and by contrariety, it repels it. It must also have no small power of dispersal within it, and again a certain contrariety against the poisons themselves—two qualities that suit the juice of <term>laser<note>original: "laſeris ſucco"; likely silphium or asafoetida, highly prized in antiquity for medicinal use.</note></term>. Therefore, those things which are to drive out poison ought to be metallic poisons—yet not the most harsh or hottest—dispersing agents, and in some way contrary to the poisons. The material for these can consist of: **Misy**, **orpiment**, **laser juice**, **gentian**, the fat of poisonous serpents, and **aconite** <note>Monkshood, a highly toxic plant.</note>. If more of these are in some earth, the oil drawn out by the power of fire will be the most excellent of all, the safest, and that which ejects by vomiting; but when the poison has already been delayed [in the body] for some time, it is not sufficient. <margin>Explanation of a difficult sentence in line 5 concerning similar medicines, chapter 18.</margin> Moreover, that which purges the poison ought to be a poison like a substance—just as rhubarb, when it does not purge bile, is turned into it; for this is to be such a substance that can be converted into that [poison].

But indeed, someone will wonder: in what way is it possible to expel poison solely by anointing the arteries? And is this the most excellent method? By Hercules! I would not call this the most excellent in the sense that—even if besides this you give **Theriac** in a drink, or milk, or the juice of the <term>vomic nut<note>original: "vomicæ nucis"; the seed of the Strychnos nux-vomica tree, which contains strychnine.</note></term> extracted by fire (which imitates water in color but not in smell or taste), or something else better if you have it (such as what some traveling doctor was perhaps selling as an antidote against poisons while I was emending these things)—it would not be even more effective. <margin>How things rubbed on the arteries eliminate poisons, the itch, and such things.</margin> [I would not say] that anointing the arteries and things applied externally are better and more powerful than those which are drunk—with this one exception: when the poison is still in the stomach...

## Book Two

...[so that the poison does not] remain in the stomach. For in the case of those things which provoke powerful vomiting, milk, lye, oil, and the water of <term>nux vomica<note>original: "aqua nucis uomicae"; the seed of the Strychnine tree, used historically in small doses as a stimulant or emetic, though highly toxic.</note></term>, which we just called juice, are most excellent. Therefore, in poisonous diseases, in the stings of venomous creatures, in poisonous ointments, and in the drinking of poison—which has thus penetrated to the heart—remedies applied externally are more powerful. And so, some are accustomed to place themselves inside the bodies of living mules that have been disemboweled. <note>A radical historical treatment where a patient was placed inside a warm animal carcass to "draw out" toxins through heat and sympathy.</note> For that heat draws the poison outward and breaks its malice. 

Poison also kills by its force penetrating to the heart; but those things which are smeared over the heart arrive with almost their full powers and most quickly. In contrast, those things which are drunk, besides the fact that they penetrate late and involve a long delay—first in the stomach, then in the veins leading to the liver, then in the liver itself, and finally in the right chamber of the heart—are so weakened in their strength that hardly a trace remains at the time when they ought to be strongest. 

<margin>Book 4, chapter 1.</margin>
Therefore, as with **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento uiuo"; mercury.</note>, concerning which we dealt in the treatise on the **French disease** <note>original: "Gallica lue"; a common early modern term for Syphilis.</note>, where scabies, psoriasis, and the French disease are expelled because it penetrates by its subtlety, thins by its heat, and expels by its corrupt and harmful quality; by the same reasoning, poisons smeared on are carried through the arteries promptly into the left ventricle of the heart. That they can change the whole body even in this way, and move, change, and eject all <term>humors<note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to govern health in ancient and medieval medicine.</note></term>, is shown by experience with the French disease, where it even affects the bones if necessary. But you will say, perhaps too late, that this is because it is not reduced to the form of a thin oil, but the substance of quicksilver itself is used, nor do we apply it to the heart as we do with poisons.

The continuity of my discourse has carried us too far from the intended purpose. Since we were attempting to show that air is always moving in those places where it is free, and thus in the upper region, by the fact that stagnant air putrefies—and from this we slipped into a narration of the plague, and not being called back, we fell rather from that into the history of poisons—though not useless, we have nonetheless wandered far, as I said, from the purpose. Therefore, the pen must be recalled to the movement and stillness of the air.

<margin>The highest mountains in the whole world.</margin>
**Solinus** <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Latin grammarian and compiler.</note> reports that **Mount Olympus** in Thessaly is carried so high into the air that when the annual sacrifices are finished, the ashes remain undisturbed until the following year's sacrifice; this is because throughout the whole year, the peak of the mountain is free of winds due to its height. 

<margin>Aristotle, Meteorology, Book 1, Chapter 13.</margin>
But if this is the cause, why does the same not happen to **Mount Caucasus**, which separates the Albani and Colchis from Sarmatia? **Aristotle** reports that it is of such great height that it can be seen from the mouth of the **Maeotian marsh** <note>The Sea of Azov.</note>, and it shows the sun at its peak with rays illuminating it until the third part of the night. Although the logic of the sphere <note>The geometric curvature of the Earth.</note> does not allow this, I would nonetheless not deny that this is a very high mountain, and by the same reasoning applied to Olympus, it ought to share the same property. The same will happen to the mountain on **Tenerife**. This is one of the seven islands that **Ptolemy** calls the <term>Fortunate Isles<note>The Canary Islands.</note></term>, beyond the Pillars of Hercules; for if it is right to believe it, he affirms it rises to sixty thousand paces, with its peak even in the shape [of a diamond...]

# On the Elements and their actions.

...mass, in Beregua <note>likely Veragua, in modern-day Panama</note> even for fifty thousand paces <note>approximately 46 miles</note>, and in Gaira the mountain peaks are covered in snow, even though it is only ten degrees distant from the equator. Both provinces are located next to Paria <note>a region in modern-day Venezuela visited by Columbus</note>. Therefore, I know for certain that the air is moved there for the reasons stated. But if it does not even disturb ashes, it may be because the air is extremely thin, and for that reason very healthy; this matches the accounts given of Mount Athos—if any credit can be given to Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman grammarian and geographer</note>—who narrates the same thing. But if you consider those stories fabulous, then you have nothing to use against us. Thus he wrote that Mount Athos in Macedonia, which ought to be numbered among the four highest mountains in the world (though it is not clear in what order it should be ranked among them), has the citadel of **Acroathon** on its summit. Its inhabitants live half as long again as other mortals, and there, ashes are neither washed away by water nor blown away by winds. 

<margin>Book 2, chapter 1.</margin>
Pomponius Mela <note>a Roman geographer, c. 43 AD</note> subscribes to this same opinion regarding the longevity of life. He also affirms the same regarding the ashes; therefore, it is not that the air is unmoved, but if this is true, it must be that the air is moved very gently and is pure and extremely thin. For it is well established that when air is stagnant it rots, just as the earth is worn down when it is shaken.

<margin>Differences between earthquakes.</margin>
The earth is shaken in three ways: by *inclination* <note>tilting or leaning</note>, by *succussion* <note>a violent upward jolting or shaking</note>, and by *vibration*. Vibration is free from danger; succussion never is, and it rarely happens without total ruin. Inclination, however, is the companion of ruin, though I have seen inclination occur without a total collapse.

<margin>Causes of earthquakes.</margin>
This happens when matter that is prone to burning is ignited: **sulfur**, **saltpeter** <term>Halinitrum<note>original: "Halinitrum"; a historical term for nitre or saltpeter, the primary oxidizing ingredient in gunpowder.</note></term>, or **bitumen** <note>a naturally occurring petroleum or tar</note>. For when these are set on fire and find no exit, as in mines or siege engines, they move and shake the earth. The worst shaking is caused by saltpeter, a moderate amount by bitumen, and a slight amount by sulfur.

<margin>Why saltpeter makes a louder noise than sulfur.</margin>
From this, a question arises again: why does saltpeter, although it burns with more difficulty and more slowly than sulfur, nevertheless shake and shatter siege engines more violently and make a louder noise? The cause is that saltpeter is drier; therefore, when it is pure, it burns more swiftly, and it only burns slowly if it is impure. But while it is pure, being dry, it burns in an instant. This is not so for sulfur, which, being "fatty" <note>oily or resinous</note>, requires time to ignite. Another cause is that because it is "earthy" <note>dense or mineral-heavy</note>, it occupies a greater space when it is converted into flame. Thus, for two reasons—both because it burns faster and because it is earthy and dense, and therefore occupies more space—it creates a greater force than sulfur. For sulfur, as we shall show below, is fatty and airy, and not at all earthy.

<margin>The purification of saltpeter.</margin>
It is established that saltpeter consists of a dense and very thin substance. It is purified in this way, as Vannoccio Biringuccio <note>author of "Pirotechnia" (1540), the first printed book on metallurgy</note> teaches. Take three parts of ashes, bones, and olives <note>likely olive husks or pits</note>, one part of **quicklime**, half and a quarter part <note>three-quarters</note> of liquid alum, and 120 parts of water; let them boil and be cooked until the volume decreases by nearly half. Afterwards, two or four pounds of this strained water are added to the saltpeter while the water is boiling and thickening, at the time when the foam is seen to leap out of the pot from the intense heat. There is another more noble way, but it is more costly...

# Book Second.

...is refined. Saltpeter <term>Halinitrum: A naturally occurring mineral, often called saltpeter, which was a critical ingredient in the production of gunpowder and chemical experiments</term> is received in an iron vessel and also covered with an iron lid. With coals moved close, it is roasted until it liquefies. If it is not perfectly melted—which is discovered once the cover is removed—let it be pressed by fires for as long as needed until it liquefies perfectly. Afterward, sprinkle it with the finest powder of sulfur; if this does not ignite on its own, let it be lit. Then, whatever is "fatty" <note>original: *pingue*; in early chemistry, this referred to oily or combustible impurities</note> should be allowed to burn away, for this floats on the surface. Once removed from the fire, with the earthy dregs left at the bottom, the whole mass hardens into the appearance of white marble. It is therefore clear that whatever is fatty resists quick burning; bitumen contains some salt, and for that reason, it vibrates more than pure sulfur.

<margin>The effect of a vibrating motion.</margin>
Every shaking motion has something greater in it than a simple blow, which is why things struck with a trembling <note>or "vibrating"</note> blow are broken more easily.

First, experiments teach us this: for if you fix a sword into a peach and suspend it by hand, then strike the sword with a stick, you will divide not only the peach but also the pit with a light blow; I have experienced this quite often. Furthermore, they say that if a cow's leg (meaning the bone) is placed upon a heap of straw, and an ax is placed upon the bone, and then the ax is struck, the bone itself is shattered by the bundle of straw. Even if this seems wondrous, it is established that a most powerful force resides in a trembling blow. We must therefore ask for what reason. The explanation, as it seems to me, is one of two things, or perhaps both. First, if what is being struck stands upon a solid board, the board's resistance makes the object and the part receiving the blow denser; thus it yields very little to the strike, for the denser a thing is, the more difficult it is to divide. But if it rests upon a soft layer like a bed, or straw, or nothing at all, it cannot be made denser, but rather it gapes and falls apart. Because of this, dry things are divided more easily in this way. The other cause is that in a trembling blow, the object being struck returns before the first vibration has finished; therefore, if it must return while the second vibration remains, the object must necessarily be divided entirely. For this reason, if a sword is long,

<margin>The construction of a sword that splits armor.</margin>
it is struck back more violently and the blow will be doubled; thus it will divide more easily. But if the sword is skillfully shaped to be wider at the end, and the strike is at that end, it will be struck back vehemently because it catches much air, and therefore it will divide even the hardest things. By another method, Barbarians <note>A common term for non-European cultures; here likely referring to Middle Eastern or Central Asian smiths</note> fashion curved swords with a cavity in the back, into which they place quicksilver <term>Quicksilver: The liquid metal mercury</term>. While it sits near the hilt, it makes the sword very light, but when it descends, it increases the blow by its weight and speed to such an extent that if the edge is firm, it splits armor. If there is strength in the mind and the steel <note>original: *chalybs*</note> is hard and tough, nothing more violent than this type of sword can be devised for human use.

<margin>Signs of an earthquake.</margin>
But now I return to the signs of earthquakes, since I remember that I have already explained the causes and types. When the water of wells [smells of] metallic sulfur or something else...

# On the Elements and Their Actions

...if [wells] smell of anything, or if they wobble, or are clouded, or grow warm, or are dried up beyond reason, they foretell that an earthquake is imminent. Thus it is said that Anaximander <note>Anaximander of Miletus (c. 610–546 BC), a Greek philosopher often credited with being the first to attempt a scientific explanation for earthquakes.</note> and Pherecydes <note>Pherecydes of Syros (c. 6th century BC), who famously predicted an earthquake after tasting well water.</note> each predicted an earthquake coming in their own times. This is not without reason, for the vapors of the earth can infect the waters much more easily—and therefore more quickly—than they can shake such an immense weight as the earth itself. Yet you should not think the entire earth is shaken, for they report that Egypt has never trembled. For neither solid lands—because they do not contain air—nor muddy lands such as Egypt—because they lack cracks—nor sandy lands—because they "breathe" <note>meaning they allow gasses to escape easily</note>, are shaken by an earthquake. 

<margin>Places that are never infested by earthquakes.</margin>
Yet some of these are shaken because the depths of the earth are not always similar to the surface. Mountains are sometimes created by earthquakes: for their origin is threefold. Either the earth swells, agitated by frequent tremors, and gives birth to mountains like blisters <note>original: *vesicis*; the author compares the geological uplift to a skin blister or boil</note> rising from a body—such as the mountain named **Modernus** <note>This refers to Monte Nuovo ("New Mountain") near Naples, which formed during a volcanic eruption in 1538, making it "modern" to the author.</note> in Campania near Lake Avernus—or from soil heaped up by the winds, as often happens in Africa, 

<margin>How mountains arise.</margin>
or (which is the most characteristic and frequent cause) mountains form from running water or even the sea demolishing the earth and leaving stones behind. For the water of a river descends into a valley, and the stony mountain itself rises above the valley; therefore, almost all mountains are made of stone. 

<margin>Why mountains consist of stones.</margin>
Their height above the rest of the ground exists because fields are eaten away daily by rains and the earth itself crumbles, but stones, besides the fact that they do not crumble, also frequently grow, as we shall show below. In truth, valleys are hollowed out by waters and torrents, and thus they are lower even than fields and plains.

In the sea, however, rocks <term>scopuli: specifically refers to jagged, protruding sea rocks or reefs</term> are formed by the same logic; and from islands, earth eaten away by the waves gives rise to them; 

<margin>How rocks are formed.</margin>
these same rocks, as earth is added or as they swell, turn into islands. For this reason, most islands abound with mountains: because if the sea were dried up, the rocks would turn into mountains. 

<margin>The origin of islands.</margin>
For this reason, it is no surprise that parts of ships, oysters, and shells are found in mountains near the sea. For what else is this than evidence that those mountains were once rocks in the sea, or that some heavy flood occurred at some time? And although mountains often resist the damage of water, they sometimes fall when water hollows out their roots, but this is rare and happens only to small mountains; 

<margin>By what things mountains are destroyed.</margin>
yet they collapse from earthquakes and, with the earth gaping open, they descend into the depths due to their weight; others are gradually seized by the sea. They are also broken by strong winds and cold, so that it is not safe to be near or under cliffs. Human diligence also sometimes levels hills. They say that Hannibal broke through the ridges of the Alps with hot vinegar and thus crossed them. <note>A famous historical anecdote from Livy, claiming Hannibal used heat and vinegar to crack mountain rocks blocking his path.</note> But this was a very small thing if we look at mountains, though a great thing for convenience. Caves are opposed, as it were, to mountains. They are formed when an earthquake occurs in a dry place and the earth gapes open, or likewise by waters flowing through the hidden parts of mountains, whence in some...

<margin>The cause of caves.</margin>

## Book Two

<margin>The power of caves.</margin>
...there are rivers. They are also formed from fiery exhalations, which at times burn, at times eat away, and at times expel stones. This is why many caves exhale a deadly breath, such as the <note>original: "Plutonium os"; literally "Pluto's Mouth," a name for a shrine or opening to the underworld.</note> **Plutonium Mouth**, which is located near **Hierapolis** in **Phrygia** in a certain mountainous part of the territory. Its opening is situated on a certain hill that equals a <term>jugerum</term> <note>A Roman unit of land area, roughly five-eighths of an acre.</note> in size and is surrounded by square fences. These are shrouded in such a foul darkness that they can scarcely be seen. The mouth itself is large enough to hold a man; if a bull is sent into it and immediately pulled back out, it is found dead. When **Strabo** <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer and historian who described this site in his "Geographica."</note> sent in little sparrows, he pulled them out dead at once. For the priests of the **Great Mother** <note>original: "Solis magnae matris"; referring to the goddess Cybele.</note>, the cave is harmless, perhaps due to a remedy known only to them; they do not breathe the air while they are looking in. Some believed the priests could endure it because they had been <note>original: "execti"; castrated. Ancient writers often speculated that the physical alteration of Cybele's priests, the Galli, rendered them immune to the toxic vapors.</note> castrated. 

But nowhere are more such caves found than in **Italy**. One lies between **Naples** and **Pozzuoli**, where the road turns toward the **Agnano Marsh**. These vapors especially harm the head, both because it is weaker than the heart and because it lacks a "fence" to ward off the foul vapors; for the air that enters the heart is forced to pass through the substance of the lungs. The nature of the illness shows this as well: those who are sent in first tremble, then lose sense and motion, and finally die in a dazed state. Even those who escape become swollen, as do those who die. 

Yet caves are not only pestilential; some are even healing. If one uses them correctly, a path to a cure for even the most desperate diseases can sometimes be found, such as the <note>original: "Salvetatae sudarium"; a sudarium is a "sweat-room" or steam bath used for medicinal purposes.</note> **Sweat-bath of Salvetata** in the mountains of **Baiae** and **Cumae**, in the mountain that the common people call **Tritulus**. There are also those that inspire prophecy, as we remember writing previously regarding the opinion of the philosophers concerning **Delphi**. 

<margin>Identifying caves.</margin>
In general, the power of caves is usually hostile to the human race and acts like a poison. For if that breath could eat away at stones and the hardest rocks, what power will it hold over mortals themselves? However, a sign of safety is the flow of sweet and healthy waters through them, and the lush growth of familiar herbs and trees at the <margin>What lies beneath the earth.</margin> entrance. But these are also the dwellings of wild beasts and serpents. Someone might wish to know what lies beneath harmless and deep caves. They say that **King Philip** once ordered a diligent search for precious metals that had ceased to be produced; when men were sent in through the mountain entrance with food and lights, they reported finding rivers there and lakes of standing water, which were not weighed down by earth but by dark and gloomy air.

<margin>Properties of the Earth as a whole.</margin>
But why do I now scrutinize the depths and hidden things? A place will be given in which it will be appropriate to treat these matters; now let us consider the properties of the Earth as a whole. The entire Earth is stable, round, and in the middle of the universe; these things are demonstrated by the mathematicians. For the whole Earth can no more be moved from its place than the heavens can be at rest, nor do the mountains diminish the Earth’s roundness in any way. For no mountain—even if writers tell many fables—is even a <note>The text ends mid-word: "millefi[sima]" or "one-thousandth."</note> thousandth part of the Earth's total diameter.

# On the Elements and Their Actions

<margin>The circumference of the entire Earth.</margin>
...occupies a thousandth part of the sphere by its height. This is how mathematicians discovered the circumference and the diameter of the entire Earth. They recognized the distance in hours on the same equinoctial circle through the timing of lunar eclipses; once they had this, they determined the difference between locations by traveling on the ground. By multiplying that distance by the twenty-four hours of a single day, and dividing by the hours of distance from the lunar eclipse, they found the circumference of that circle. From there, through a geometric demonstration, they calculated the circumference of the equinoctial circle—the greatest circle—and of the whole Earth. By multiplying this by seven and dividing by twenty-two <note>This is a calculation using the approximation of Pi as 22/7, which was standard in the Renaissance.</note>, they achieved a quite accurate calculation of the Earth's diameter. Alternatively, by traveling straight from the south to the north, they increased the altitude of the celestial pole by one degree. Measuring the road, they found it to be eighty-seven and a half Italian <term>miles</term> <note>original: "M. passuum"; literally "thousands of paces," the Roman mile.</note>. It is by these units that we now measure the distances between places, rather than the paces of **Ptolemy** <note>Claudius Ptolemy (c. 100–170 AD), the Greco-Egyptian geographer whose measurements were often smaller than reality.</note>. Therefore, if we multiply 87,500 miles by the 360 parts of the heavens—for it is divided into that many—we will have 31,500,000 miles. If we multiply this circumference of the whole Earth by seven and divide by twenty-two, the diameter of the Earth will be 10,022 miles. However, to seek a perfectly precise measurement in these matters is foolish. Let us say then, by subtracting the twenty-two, that the diameter of the earth is ten thousand miles. But those who sail, driven by many errors and following a winding rather than a straight path (sometimes by choice, and at other times deceived by the uncertain and varying force of the winds), have recorded a much larger circumference for the Earth. But this calculation is as true as it is most certainly confirmed by experience. It greatly helped the **Spanish**, who, when they understood that such a long and lasting journey was incompatible with the Earth's size, <margin>How much knowing the truth benefits us.</margin> corrected the error with careful reasoning and contracted the voyage by nearly a third, both in terms of distance and time.

<margin>Types of Earth.</margin>
And these are the benefits of such precision. Indeed, the earth itself does not appear to be of just one kind; for this reason, **Aristotle** correctly divided it into two: first, <note>original Greek: "ὀρυκτὰ καὶ μεταλλευτά"</note> **mined and mineral** <note>Or "fossil and transmutable."</note>. The "mined" earth remains the same and is truly earth. The "mineral" earth changes in appearance and sight, for it passes into metals or "juices" <note>original: "succos"; refers to substances like bitumen, salt, or sulfur.</note> and other things of that sort; we shall speak of this in its proper place. There are two species of true earth: one is pure, which is of a dark color, or close to it; the other is not pure, yet contains nothing metallic, and is of another color. For every earth that is endowed with a foreign color has been transformed by an exhalation, according to the opinion of **Aristotle**. <margin>Causes of the variety of earth colors.</margin> But **Theophrastus** <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC), a successor to Aristotle known for his work on stones and minerals.</note> thinks it is due to a variety of heat. Yet both are true: for sometimes metallic substances are found beneath it and the earth is tinted by their exhalation; at other times nothing is found, and it is tinted by heat alone. Indeed, that which is tinted by exhalation has a sort of shine; that which is tinted by heat alone does not shine, and has a dull, iron-like, or black color. For there are as many colors of the earth as there are types of colors, <note>original Greek: "ὥσπερ"</note> **just as** with that which is white; others are yellow, like a certain kind of clay...

# Book Two

<margin>colors of the earth.</margin>
There is a certain type called **Ochre** <note>original: "Sil"</note> by the Romans; it can be green like **gold-glue** <note>original: "chrysocolla," likely malachite used as a solder for gold</note>, red like **sandarac** <note>original: "sandaracha," a red-orange mineral pigment</note>, blue like **deep-blue stone** <note>original: "κύανος" (cyanos)</note>, or black like **black clay** <note>original: "pnigitis"</note>. Although these contain no metal, and others are identified by the example of metallic ores, we do not categorize them as metals because these earths are found pure and perfectly reflect these colors. There are also saffron-yellow earths, as I have said, and dark-brown ones, and those that can be dyed, such as the earth from Eretria which becomes violet when rubbed against copper. **Strato of Lampsacus** <note>A Greek Peripatetic philosopher known as "the Physicist."</note> believed that white earth was evidence of silver ash. There are some who attribute to **Aristotle** the view that earth fundamentally possesses no color. Here, we present the teaching confirmed by the evidence of the senses, caring nothing for such trifles. We call earth "dark-brown" because pure soil is often that color, and that which is such is usually also the best.

<margin>The best soil.</margin>
The best soil, therefore, is not always of a single color. Although, as I said, it is often dark-brown, some black soil is also excellent—it is clay-like and uncorrupted by any defects. Defects include soil that is: parched, rough, pitted, whitening, spongy like pumice, or full of holes. Soil is sterile if it grows only long, sharp thorns, or **broom** <note>original: "genistae"</note>, or if pests like **locust-grubs** <note>original: "bruchumúe"</note> are born there; these are certain signs of a poor soil. It is not just these, but also when a single type of weed is frequent—one you do not see in meadows, but only in uncultivated and parched places. The earth that is finest, clay-like, soft, best at absorbing water, and yielding colors—that which lacks faults and which, when dried and then sprinkled with rain, emits a very sweet scent—that will be the best for trees and crops.

<margin>Why the best soil smells good when sprinkled with rain.</margin>
But why does this earth smell good when moistened by a light rain after long droughts? This happens precisely because, during dry spells, the small amount of moisture contained in the earth is refined by a moderate and natural heat. When the rain arrives, it mixes with this moisture and evaporates, and thus it smells wonderful because it has been perfectly "cooked" <note>The author uses "concoctio," the Aristotelian idea that heat matures or refines substances.</note>. Therefore, the sweetness of the scent is a sign of tempered heat and, consequently, of the greatest fertility. One can also easily judge by the results: for when weeds and trees flourish in it, especially those that require rich soil, you have a certain proof of the ground's goodness.

<margin>Species of earth by substance.</margin>
Regarding substance, there are three types of earth: coarse, which is called **sand** <note>original: "arena"</note>; fine, which is **clay-like** <note>original: "argillaceum"</note>; and medium, which is a common mixture. Here you see the excellence of "fineness" even in the earths themselves; for just as sand is sterile, it is also unsuitable for almost any potter's work.

<margin>Signs for recognizing soil.</margin>
In contrast, clay is both fertile for plants and most suitable for potters. Any clay-like soil that bears **clover** <note>original: "trifolium"</note> is excellent; that which bears grass is best for pastures. That which bears **goat's rue** <note>original: "rutha capraria"</note> is fruitful; that which nourishes the vine well is best for all trees, even though the olive tree may shy away from the vine. Since one earth is best for crops, another for pastures, and another for trees, you will recognize each type by its own signs. Indeed, in places where **alfalfa** <note>original: "medica"</note> grows, there is no more certain sign for pastures than the abundance of that herb. From the clay-like genus was also that white earth which...
