<header>On the Elements and their actions.</header>
<sig>k</sig>

# On the Elements and their actions.

<margin>Walls made of earth.</margin>
In the past, people in Spain used a substance they called **Tasconium** <note>original: "Tasconium," a hard, sandy clay described by Pliny the Elder</note>, from which they built watchtowers on the ridges of mountains. Even now, as the distinguished physician **Georgius Agricola** <note>A famous German scholar known as the "Father of Mineralogy" (1494–1555).</note> reports, there is a tower at Colditz <note>original: "Coruerium," likely referring to Colditz or a similar town in Saxony</note> in Saxony made of it. This material is safer against fire, wind, and rain than structures built of mortar and stone: it is safe from wind because of its weight, it grows harder when exposed to fire, and it is safe from water because it does not absorb it. It must therefore be oily, very fine, and dense, yet for that reason also light. Some earth is made finer by the cold, such as that from **Goslar** <note>original: "Gosselaria," a historic mining town in Germany</note>, which, when it is in chunks, is broken down into tiny particles by the frost. 

<margin>Types of sand.</margin> 
There are truly three types of sand: river sand, sea sand, and pit sand <note>original: "fossicia," sand dug from the earth</note>. Even in these, the fineness makes a significant difference; for the finest sand makes mortar fit for the eternal foundations of walls. Provided it is pure, such slight fineness either adds many centuries of life to structures or causes them to fail. River sand is better, however, if no extra processing is used, because it lacks saltiness, while pit sand is purer. 

<margin>Species of earth categorized by use.</margin> 
There are also distinctions among earths based on their uses: such as **common earth**, which is approved by farmers; **clay** <note>original: "argilla"</note> for potters; **red ochre** <note>original: "rubrica"</note> for carpenters; **Cimolian earth** <note>original: "cimolia," a white clay used by "fullers" to clean and thicken cloth</note> for fullers; **blue pigment** <note>original: "caerulea"</note> for painters; **Lemnian earth** <note>original: "lemnia," a medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos</note> for physicians; and **silvery earth** for silversmiths. All these are varied and perfected by water and heat. Thus, nothing is better than having well-watered lands, for they flourish with every kind of fruit, tree, and herb.

<margin>How the earth stands above the waters: seven opinions.</margin>
But how the earth can stand above the waters has been rightly debated. Some have said it is because it pleased God. These people are more to be blamed for being unable to find a reason than they are to be praised for believing God could do it without reason. Those who say this was done for the sake of living creatures explain the *purpose* for why it was done, but to achieve that purpose, other physical causes are needed, which they fail to teach. 

There are those who say the earth is held up by the stars; first, this would be a forced or violent arrangement. Second, it would require the stars to be fixed and motionless. Furthermore—and this is a greater point—the stars would have to be in the opposite region; for instance, some under the Arctic would support Europe, while others in the south would support **Brazil** <note>A very early reference to the South American continent in a scientific context.</note>, which is opposite to Europe. 

If you were to establish two centers, one for the water and another for the earth, then one of them would be different from the center of the universe. Two centers of gravity could not allow parts of the earth to protrude from opposite regions—yet they do protrude, as seen with Brazil and Europe. Nor would there be any **Antipodes** <note>People living on the opposite side of the globe.</note>. 

Those who claim the earth is supported by air trapped in caves also propose something forced: both that the earth is held up by thin air and that the air is violently held in the caves. The caves would have to be vast to support Asia, Africa, Europe, Brazil, and so many islands; and if they consider it correctly, the entire earth would be one single cave. It would be a miracle if such a massive weight did not collapse into even the smallest opening, and if the air were pushed out, the entire mass of the waters would descend into it. 

**Aristotle**, in his *Meteorology*, believes that because of the pole, where the earth is higher, it does not admit the water. But if this were so, the earth would not be round, nor would there be land under the equator <note>original: "aequinoctiali"</note>, nor would that height be comparable to the difference in placement between land and water. Imagine...

# Book Two

...for it cannot be true that the earth is a million <note>original: "M.millibus passuum." A Roman pace (passus) is approximately five feet; a thousand paces make a Roman mile. Here he is calculating a distance of a million paces, or a thousand miles.</note> paces higher, even if the place of the water were around the earth. If the water were two thousand times a thousand <note>i.e., two million</note> paces higher than the earth in proportion to its size, even right under the arctic pole itself, the earth would be beneath a million paces of water, and even more so in all other places. It shames me that he <note>The author is likely refuting a specific ancient or medieval authority, possibly a commentator on Aristotle, who argued for a massive sphere of water surrounding the earth.</note> said these things more on account of a man's authority than the truth; I say this so that everyone may understand that I am drawn by the love of truth to criticize him. Therefore, it is not true that the water is so vast, nor is it a noteworthy part of the whole earth’s mass. Because of the earth’s density, only a small amount of water remains on top, filling whatever is low and uneven on the earth’s surface. By this reasoning, while it forms so many seas, the vast ocean, and so many rivers, the earth is still judged to be the larger element. If we look only at the circumference, perhaps the claim could be true; but when compared by depth, there is no comparison at all. The evidence is that nowhere, except in deep abysses <note>original: "gurgitibus," referring to deep trenches, whirlpools, or oceanic "bottomless" pits.</note>, does the sea water have a depth worth mentioning. Elsewhere it is 1,000, or 500, or 200, or 300 paces deep. If anyone compares this depth to the size of the earth, it is like **a man covered in sweat**. In the abysses, the water is somewhat deeper, as it is fitting that such a place be filled with water rather than the very light air. Therefore, the earth underneath is solid, and in those parts a modest amount of water is poured into the hollows; in other places, a little air—not much—is contained for a few years, but not forever. If water were an element and as large as they say, it would be necessary that even on land the greatest part of the sea would lack a bottom. For it is certain that if it occupied a million paces for every thousand paces, or double this—which would be its size if it were as large as they think—no trace of a bottom would appear to mortals. Since the bottom appears everywhere except in the deep abysses as I said (and those abysses are narrow things), it is manifest that water is scarcely a thousandth part—and perhaps much less—of the whole earth.

<margin>The size of the elements.</margin>
Thus there are three elements, of which the lightest and largest is air, and the next in size is earth. Both of these are necessary in themselves: air is on high and earth is at the bottom. The smallest and almost unnecessary element is water, placed between them. For if men could live without food, like stones for example, water would not be necessary. But because it was necessary not only to live, but to be nourished, generated, and grow, water was created. Since the space available for water is more capacious than the element of water itself (for it fills whatever is low on the earth), the earth bulges out everywhere with continents and islands, and provides a dwelling place for men and other animals.

<margin>The cause of floods.</margin>
Therefore, from this it is manifest how easily those inundations occur which are commonly called floods. Since water is small by nature and situated on the surface of the earth, if it increases even a little, it overwhelms the low places, but is soon withdrawn again, because it remains small even when increased. But if it were as great as...

## **On the Elements and their actions.**

...if the water were as large as was thought, it would require a massive increase to cause floods. For this reason, floods would never have happened, and if they had happened, they could scarcely ever have been reversed unless the human race were entirely extinguished, <margin>In the *Timaeus*.</margin> and the land would have remained hidden under the water for many years, not just months. But as Plato relates, <note>In his dialogue *Timaeus*, Plato discusses cataclysmic floods that periodically cleanse the earth, though the most famous account of Atlantis appears there as well.</note> these floods occurred not once but many times, and they subsided again within a few months. <margin>The cause of the smallness of the water.</margin> Therefore, the amount of water was made small so that a place would be left for habitation, so that it might temper life with its coldness rather than destroy it, and since this generation of "mixed things" <note>In Aristotelian physics, "mixed things" refer to compounds like minerals, plants, and animals formed from the four elements.</note> was necessary only on the surface of the earth, it was made small and situated on the earth's surface for that reason—to occupy the surface alone, in which metals, plants, animals, and fish must be nourished and generated.

<margin>The cause of the movement of waters toward the south.</margin> But because there was a significant danger that the water might be overly consumed by the air and the rays of the Sun, a perpetual motion was joined to it. For this reason, waters that do not move, as I have said, quickly rot and are greatly diminished. Provision was also made for its generation beneath the poles and in the mountains; and since the earth beneath the <term>Torrid Zone<note>The region of the Earth between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn, traditionally thought to be scorched by the sun's direct heat.</note></term> was excessively scorched, nature saw to it that this place should be the lowest, and because of this, all waters flow toward the south. Thus the Nile, although it arises near the <term>Circle of Capricorn<note>The Tropic of Capricorn; the author is discussing the source of the Nile in the Southern Hemisphere.</note></term> according to the movements of the Moon, nevertheless, having crossed the equinoctial circle <note>The Equator.</note>, it penetrates the entire torrid zone, carried by the same impetus into our sea near Alexandria. It was necessary, therefore, for the greatest part of the cold and moist element <note>Water.</note> to settle there, where the need for it was greatest due to the heat of the Sun.

At the same time, provision was made for the safety of the intermediate places; for as water always flows toward the same part, those regions could not be submerged. This is the same precaution taken by those who clear fields of flooding and those who drain marshes: for if there were no downward slope for the waters, the entire earth would now be a swamp. Indeed, the heat of the Sun—which consumes and erodes—made the land lower toward the south, while the cold near the poles—which preserves—kept the mountains very high. For we have already taught that heat consumes and eats away, while cold preserves. For these reasons, the region near the poles is, was, and always <margin>Why the Sun does not approach the poles.</margin> will be the highest, and the middle region the lowest. Therefore, it was not appropriate for the Sun to be carried around everywhere, nor to the poles; for if it were carried across the entire globe in every part, the earth would necessarily become flat, and for that reason, it would either be entirely dried up or entirely overwhelmed by waters. 

But since this was not enough for the free course of rivers—as higher places frequently occur in their path, which would have caused floods, stagnation, and corruption—<margin>Why water rises as much as it falls.</margin> wise nature gave water the power to ascend as much as it descends, <note>This refers to the principle of "communicating vessels" or hydrostatic pressure, allowing water to travel through siphons or pressurized underground channels to cross hills.</note> so that, having overcome mountains and hills, it is finally carried into the sea. <margin>On the cause and sign of the size of the elements.</margin> Therefore, the water is small and situated on the surface of the earth. If it were as large as is claimed, and lay hidden beneath the earth, it would either cause a perpetual motion of the earth if it moved, or it would rot if it stayed still. Since we see neither of these things, it is impossible for the water to maintain such a great size in comparison to the earth as is said...

->## **Book Two**<-

...great [quantity of water], and that it lies hidden in the depths of the earth, but we have shown that our senses teach us there would not be much of it on the surface: therefore the water is quite small indeed. Truly, since the earth was the seat of animals, and the center of the world about which the stars move, and the foundation of all things, it has attained a sufficiently suitable magnitude, although compared to the circuit of the heavens it holds the place of a point. <margin>On the origin of rivers.</margin> In my judgment, we have explained the causes and the manner of the downward flow of rivers quite correctly, but it has often been doubted where they originate, given such a perennial and manifold downward flow of waters. Therefore, the Philosopher <note>original: "Philosophus"; this almost always refers to Aristotle in Renaissance texts.</note> thinks they are generated; Solomon <note>Referring to Ecclesiastes 1:7: "All the rivers run into the sea... unto the place from whence the rivers come, thither they return again."</note> that they are derived from the sea through a circuit; others that they are accumulated from rains and snows; others that they emerge from springs existing under the earth. 

It is clear that all water is not generated in the mountains, nor from the air: since the Tanais <note>The Tanais is the ancient name for the Don River in modern-day Russia.</note> bubbles up in the plains of Muscovy. Truly, since water does not ascend unless it descends from higher mountains, it must be derived from there. Nor can it ascend from the sea itself to such a height as the peak of mountains, and before it reaches the mountains, there is no reason why it would not break out everywhere; nor would rivers ever be diminished, and the sea itself would not suffice for so many rivers, but would eventually be dried up, since the greatest part of the waters vanishes by the heat of the Sun. Also, that motion under the earth would shake the land, as I have said. Nor is there a reason why it would flow from one mountain and not another. That it should also be rendered so pure of all saltiness and bitterness is hardly likely. Nor does it come from snows alone: since water also flows from mountains when they are covered with no snows and are moistened by no rains. Truly, it is entirely incredible that such a mass of water, and one so perennial, should be generated [out of nothing]. 

What then should be said? That it happens from all these causes, but the greatest origin is because air turns into water; <note>This reflects the Aristotelian view that elements can transform into one another; here, air condensing into liquid within the cool Earth.</note> afterwards, continuous snow and rains contribute not a little to this. Herodotus also thinks this is the cause of that inundation which the Nile makes in Egypt.

<margin>Book 2. The cause of the Nile's flooding.</margin> Indeed, his opinion is such that the Nile begins to swell at the summer solstice, and increases until the hundred days following, and floods Egypt, and decreases for nearly the same number of days. The cause, in my opinion, is that the Sun in the springtime, while it is in the middle of the sky—that is, under the equinoctial—makes cold winds and draws much moisture to itself, which it later lets down onto the lands when it comes to the summer solstice, with the south and southwest winds blowing. Since winter then begins near the sources of the Nile, which are placed toward the Circle of Capricorn, <note>The author correctly identifies that the Nile's headwaters are in the Southern Hemisphere, where the seasons are reversed.</note> it then draws up rains and waters from the earth and rivers again when the Sun has proceeded to the autumnal equinox, but it does not let them down at the sources of the Nile because the Sun is going there and making summer, drying the air and the lands, at which time it is necessary for the Nile to be most greatly diminished. 

In ancient times, namely that of Herodotus, an increase to fourteen cubits brought the greatest fertility, and to eight, sterility; later, in the times of Strabo, <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer.</note> it increased less, and an increase of eight cubits did not occur. I have recently explained the poorly translated and worse-understood opinion of Herodotus regarding the increase of the Nile, which <margin>Book 17 of the *Geography*, chapter 15.</margin> Strabo confirms. For what is surprising, since the Nile has its origin where the Sun, being present, makes winter for us in our summer, which for them is the beginning of winter, snows and rains...

...and that these [rains] provide the increase for the river and from that the occasion for a flood; but now the flood has become much smaller over time: for in the times of **Strabo** <note>Strabo (c. 64 BC – 24 AD) was a Greek geographer whose work was rediscovered in the Renaissance.</note>, the fields were already drying up within sixty days. The cause of a flood is the magnitude of the river. For as **Arrian** <note>Arrian of Nicomedia (c. 86 – 160 AD) wrote extensively on the geography of India following Alexander the Great’s campaigns.</note> writes, the **Ganges** is the greatest of rivers, after which comes the **Indus**, and then the **Nile**. Therefore, the Ganges will be counted first, the Indus second, the Nile third, and the **Hister** <note>The Hister is the ancient Latin name for the lower part of the Danube River in Europe.</note> fourth. Into the Nile, no other river flows at all. Arrian is the authority that the **Acesines** <note>Now known as the Chenab River in modern Pakistan and India.</note>, which flows into the Indus, has a width of nearly four miles. But where the Ganges is narrowest, it spans twelve miles, and five hundred [paces] besides; where it spreads wide, it seems to have no boundaries. If the Spaniards report truly, they have discovered other rivers of incredible vastness in **Brazil**, which discharge into the sea with a mouth sixty miles wide. There is also the **Maragnonus** <note>The Marañón River, a major tributary of the Amazon; early explorers often used this name for the Amazon itself.</note>, which, where it is carried into the sea, has a width of ninety miles, and another one hundred and twenty. Both of these are on the Northern shore near **Paria** <note>A region in modern-day Venezuela visited by Christopher Columbus.</note>. But the calculation of their size changes over time. For there is a certain rhythm of change for all mortal things: for inflowing rivers are accustomed to dry out not only other rivers into which they flow, but even the seas. **Herodotus** <note>Known as the "Father of History," Herodotus (5th century BC) often wrote about the physical geography of Egypt and Greece.</note> relates that the **Achelous** <note>The largest river in Greece.</note>, flowing into the sea, brought so much silt <note>original: "arenarū" (sands or silt)</note>—for it is in this way that they dry the seas—that it has already added half of the **Echinades** islands to the mainland. **Polybius** <note>A Greek historian of the Hellenistic period.</note> is the authority that the **Tanais** <note>The Don River in modern Russia.</note> and other rivers so fill the **Euxine Sea** <note>The ancient name for the Black Sea.</note> and the **Maeotian Swamp** <note>The Sea of Azov.</note> in his own time, that it now has a water depth of no more than seven cubits <note>original: "ulnas", an ancient unit of measurement based on the length of the forearm.</note>, and it has been made fresh instead of salty. Strabo reports that some of the Echinades are now joined to the mainland, and others are joined day by day, since the one furthest away is only fifteen stadia <note>A stadium was an ancient unit of distance, roughly 600 feet.</note> from the mouth of the Achelous river.

<margin>
Why the Nile lacks a breeze.
Why no river is salty.
</margin>
But since we have fallen into a narration of rivers, it will not be beside the point to consider why the **Nile** alone lacks a breeze—or at least did lack one. For Herodotus asserts this constantly; it ought to be our greatest concern to find the cause of things, so that if things happen over the course of time in some places that have ceased in others, we do not later remain stuck in perplexity. Therefore, a breeze <note>original: "aura"</note> mostly occurs where water has conceived warmth from the Sun; the evidence for this is that it arises around rivers in summer at sunrise and sunset, not at midday. For when the Sun rises but does not yet draw [vapor] to the upper regions, the air is driven by the movement of the water, which, having been cooled by the water, produces a sweet breeze, which we are accustomed to feel near rivers at sunrise and sunset in summer. But because the beginning of the Nile is undoubtedly beyond the winter circle <note>The "winter circle" or *circulum brumale* refers to the Tropic of Capricorn.</note> and it is carried entirely through the torrid region, it can never conceive a breeze: for even if one is created, it is immediately consumed by the immoderate heat of the Sun. Indeed, by the same course by which the river cools the air, it is purged of all earthly filth: therefore **no river is salty**, although it could happen where salty material flows into it from a nearby place; yet even if it could happen, you would not easily find an example of this for the reason stated. Thus the Nile, since it comes from the most distant regions and is scorched by the heat of the Sun, carries down the most healthy waters. But all seas are salty and also bitter, the reason for which I shall explain [before]...

# Book Two

I shall now set forth the question previously proposed. We very often see among us how water from rain is able to increase rivers, when after rains, rivers that were previously thin grow so much that they flood the fields. Indeed, there are certain torrents whose beds remained as mere ditches full of pebbles, yet for many days they flow with such copious water—more than they received from rains alone or from melted snows—that they take on the role and appearance of a great river. Nor does a torrent differ from a river, except that it is not perennial; for the cause of the latter is not of that kind. Therefore, if you visit the mountains in the morning, you will find them damp <note>original: "hudos" — meaning moist or soaked with water</note>. Thus, gradually, both inside and outside the mountains, the collected water flows out into rivulets; and many of these, coming together into one, create a river. Unless this is aided by rains or the melting of snow, you will see it always thinned. At such a time, a small amount of water suffices, not only because its channel contains little water, but because while it flows slowly, that same water satisfies many places. Truly, because of this cause, no doubt remains 
<margin>Why rivers swell most in the morning.</margin> 
as to why rivers are accustomed to swell in the morning, and then especially near their source in that part where they are closest. Specifically, much dew falls at night in summer, and much mist in winter, which results in the river beginning to grow significantly at the following sunrise; this happens especially in the middle seasons of Autumn and Spring, when the falling frost is dissolved by the sun. Therefore, the water which is created inside the mountain by the coldness of the stones, and that which is created outside with the help of the night, gradually glides inward. A part is also collected into rivulets on the outside, and from many rivulets a small river is often created, and from several small ones a large one, such as the <term>Po</term> <note>original: "Padus"</note>, the <term>Danube</term> <note>original: "Hister"</note>, the <term>Indus</term>, and the <term>Euphrates</term>. And this is the cause of the permanence of rivers, just as rains and snows are the cause of their increase. 

But the <term>Don</term> <note>original: "Tanais"</note> and all springs that gush forth from flat places are not created there but in the mountains; they are carried to that place by the principle we recently mentioned: that when water is pressed from higher places, it rises as much as it had descended, and thus they emerge from the earth. The sea, however, does not send forth springs unless they are salty <note>original: "falsos" — likely meaning brackish or "untrue" fresh water</note>, for some are born nearby, but they are salty. I would not deny, however—though it is most difficult because of the sea's heat—that by the waters of the sea running under the earth with great force and for a long distance, a spring of fresh water could gush forth. The evidence for this is that the saltiness is diminished by the length of the distance, as dug wells are less salty the further they are from the sea. Yet perhaps this happens not so much by the separation of salt through distance, as by the mixing of other fresh waters. Nevertheless, one must consider that the water of the wells which the <term>people of Milan</term> <note>original: "Mediolanenses"</note> call <term>Hausum</term> <note>Likely a local term for "drawn water" or "well-water."</note> is derived from the sea. Thus, the sea provides a very great convenience. Regarding the origin of rivers, <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BC) whose "Meteorology" was the foundation for these theories.</note> seems to have perceived correctly: where they flow into a hollow and wide place, they create lakes. Thus, we have stated the cause of rivers, springs, torrents, and lakes.

<margin>Why the sea is salty.</margin>
It remains for us to teach what the cause is why the sea is salty. According to the opinion of <term>Aristotle</term>, which has been understood by few, it is the constant falling of rains into it, persisting now from eternity. Although this [does not]...

# On the Elements and their actions.

...the sea becomes eternal in the place where it now lies; nevertheless, since the sea is formed from the sea, it is necessary that it is and has been eternal through the continuity of the waters. The proof is that all are derived from one: the Mediterranean, the Red, the Euxine <note>original: "Euxinum" — the Black Sea</note>, the Caspian, the Magallanic <note>Likely referring to the southern waters near the Strait of Magellan</note>, the Hyperborean <note>The far northern Arctic waters</note>, the Germanic, the Herculean <note>The Strait of Gibraltar</note>, the Cantabrian, the British, the Sarmatian, the Indian, the African, the Baltic, the Glacial, as well as the gulfs: such as the Barbaric, the Atlantic, the Great, the Arabian, the Persian, and the Maeotian marsh <note>The Sea of Azov</note>, are parts or offshoots of the ocean. Nor am I unaware that Ptolemy feels differently about the origin of the Caspian Sea, separating it from the Ocean: but this is not according to the opinion of Pliny, nor Strabo, nor Solinus, or Priscian. But this matters little, for it does not contradict [the point], and even if it were not [connected], it would still be a sea that does not agree with others: such as the Dead Sea and the Sea of Galilee, which, although they agree with each other, are nonetheless not members of the Ocean. Yet both are salty, and what is more wonderful, the Dead Sea is even bitter—which gave cause to history—and yet it is further from the Syrian Sea (which is part of the Mediterranean) than is the Galilee. Therefore, that nothing besides this and the Dead Sea (which was once called Lake Asphaltites <note>original: "Asphaltis lacus"</note>) is separated from the ocean is clear enough; nor does anything prevent these from communicating with it through subterranean caves. And for this reason, one may call every sea eternal—not because the water stays in the same place, but because of its continuous state and its constant saltiness. 

Three things seem to suffice for preserving the saltiness: the heat of the Sun, by which the earth is scorched and the waters stagnate <note>original: "putrescunt" — literally "rot" or "decay," referring here to the lack of movement compared to fresh rivers</note>, because it does not flow like rivers, and it receives rains. For all rain-bearing water is somewhat salty because it is parched by the Sun and stagnates over time. But lakes are truly born [from another source], since the rivers from which they are made had a beginning. For this reason, even if they receive rains, they cannot acquire a salty flavor. Nor can there be salty lakes, unless the earth itself where they are located offers salt; for this reason, they are not even large. A proof can be Lake Acronus, which they now call Constance <note>original: "Constantiensem"</note>, which although it seems almost equal in size to some sea, is yet full of sweet waters, not salty ones, because its beginning was from the Rhine river. Yet the immense vastness of the sea aids its saltiness, in which, as in a vast space of earth, it is necessary that not a few mountains of salt are contained. Therefore, when the salt is dissolved, especially with the help of

<header>Book Two</header>

# Book Two

However, the preservation of the waters and the air was not enough to prevent them from rotting. For if the water of the sea is not moved, it rots in vessels, as **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher whose works formed the basis of medieval and Renaissance science.</note> testifies. Yet the water in the Mediterranean is more agitated by being enclosed by the winds, and for that reason it does not rot. In what manner it is moved by the stars and the Moon, we have taught in our works on **Astronomy**. All the seas that have the character of the whole—such as the **Ocean**—move from east to west, because the element is essentially one, and it is driven by the stars. Therefore, all those seas that lie directly open to the ocean are themselves moved by that same motion; however, those on the side are not moved at all, such as the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, which are on the Northern side. For in places so situated, the force of the waters running from east to west must necessarily be broken. And although the Mediterranean may seem to be positioned toward the east, since the ocean is to the west, it only enters the Mediterranean during the reflux <note>the ebb or outward flow of the tide</note>, when it is no longer driven by the stars but urged by its own gravity, which is why it cannot maintain the motion. Another piece of evidence for this matter is that in the Mediterranean itself, on the coast of Africa near **Zygris** <note>A town in ancient Marmarica, modern-day Libya</note>, because that shore extends directly from east to west, a tide occurs due to the position of the shore aiding the slight power of the Moon. But the **North Sea** <note>original: "Norticum" — referring here to the Atlantic/Caribbean waters near the equator</note>, which is near the equinoctial circle <note>the Equator</note> by **Paria** <note>A region in modern-day Venezuela visited by Columbus</note>, is carried very swiftly from east to west because the Sun is more powerful there and drives the waters. But in the **South Sea** <note>original: "Australi Sureno" — the Pacific Ocean</note> in the region of **Beragua** <note>Veragua, a province in modern-day Panama</note>, a most powerful tide occurs; whereas where the North Sea lies on the Northern side, there is almost none. Therefore, the magnitude of the tides at the full and new moons, and their smallness at the quadratures <note>the quarter moons</note>, shows that the waters are moved in their tide by the Moon; as does their rising and falling with the Moon until it reaches the middle of the sky, and their swelling directly under the star, and the time of their revolution, which is roughly twenty-five hours, in which space of time the Moon returns from the east to the east. Since, however, the sea seems to follow the star in this way and travel around the earth every day, why is it that ships are barely driven six thousand paces <note>approximately 6 miles</note> in an hour when urged by the winds? 

<margin>Why ships do not move very swiftly in the tide of the sea.</margin>
The reason is that the whole body of water does not follow the Moon, nor does one single part, but the nearest parts are transferred into the next; just as if someone, by pressing on flesh, were to raise a swelling, the flesh itself would move very little from its place, yet the swelling would be transferred very quickly across the whole leg. But in the North Sea where we said there is almost no tide, it is necessary for ships to move swiftly as if in a river, due to a long-lasting course of three months, because the same part of the water is always moving forward.

<margin>The reasoning of the Philosopher showing that the world is eternal.</margin>
But since we have fallen into these discussions, I will not remain silent on the **Philosopher's** <note>Referring again to Aristotle</note> reasoning, by which he proves the world is eternal from the saltiness of the sea. It is this: if the sea had a beginning, it was either sweet or salty from the start. It was not salty, since so much salt could not have been mixed in as to corrupt the water—for one must believe that all things were made pure <note>original: "syncera"</note>. For things that are born, such as lakes and rivers, lack flavor. But if it lacked flavor from the beginning, and was made salty only by the passage of time, then that saltiness would have ages <note>stages of development or increasing intensity</note>; but it does not have them; for neither...

<margin>Rivers beneath the earth and bursting out from it.</margin>
Furthermore, there are also collections of water beneath the earth in the form of lakes, from which the **Don** in **Muscovy** <note>The Tanais river in Russia.</note>, the **Lycus** in **Asia**, and the **Tigris** in **Mesopotamia** burst forth in a perpetual flow. They also report that the **Timavo** <note>A river near Trieste famous for its underground course.</note> rises in the territory of **Aquileia**, and a spring of uncertain name rises in **Atina**. 

<margin>Caverns beneath the earth.</margin>
Since there are caverns beneath the earth—and not very deep ones, as in the territory of **Gabii** at the first mile-marker from **Rome**, where the ground used to tremble when chariots and horses passed over—it is no wonder that they either fill with water, or the earth gaps open of its own accord, or the air becomes corrupted in these openings. Even if this depth is small compared to the size of the earth, it can still undermine cities, swallow lakes, or leave mountains standing over uneven hollows, since the earth does not always give way in a straight line. But since the waters of wells are a kind of spring, they are usually hidden at a depth of four feet or a little more; for if the water were continuous <note>meaning a solid sheet of water under the whole surface</note>, the earth would crack open, and every well would have the same depth. 

<margin>Why well waters are warm in winter.</margin>
Their water is no warmer in winter than in summer, but it seems so because the air is cold in winter and hot in summer. By comparison, the same water appears warmer in winter than in summer; for all things are judged by comparison to our bodies, which are surrounded by the environment. Thus, it happens that while we are hot, we judge the things we touch to be cold, and while cold, we judge them to be hot. The water also warms up a little bit due to heat being drawn into the innermost parts because it cannot escape or spread out on the earth's surface. For this reason, snow—which does not usually last long—always tends to bring fertility, and sometimes even long-lasting snow does so. Additionally, the entire earth in that part where water can reach is bituminous <note>containing bitumen, a naturally occurring petroleum</note>, or salty, or even metallic, which causes trapped vapors to heat the water. And for this reason it also happens—though it is rare—that some springs are warmer in winter than in summer, appearing as a kind of miracle. These waters are scented or foul-smelling because of this, and have a distinct taste, which is easy to recognize when they bubble up, allowing one to either avoid or use them. 

<margin>How we may investigate whether water lies beneath in arid places, and what kind it is.</margin>
But if they are hidden and it is uncertain whether they lie beneath in a dry place, and of what sort they are, they are detected by this art: A lead vessel—or a new clay pot if that is not available—should be coated inside with oil. Dry white wool, containing a small stone in its center, should be attached to the bottom of the vessel with wax. Bury it four paces <note>original: "quatuor passus." In this context, likely a measure of depth or distance from a marker.</note> deep at sunset, with the mouth of the vessel turned downward, taking care that the wool does not fall out, and gradually cover it with the dug-up earth. At the following dawn, dig up the vessel and inspect the wool: if it is not far off, the coldness of the stone and the night, combined with the moist oil, will turn the trapped vapors of the earth into droplets of water. Collect what is squeezed out; if there is little, judge that the water is still far away; if much, it is near. You will easily understand what kind it is by smell and taste. For there are some of these—as well as those existing on the surface—which do not only smell of salt or bitumen, but even boil, such as the **Aponian** springs <note>The hot springs of Abano Terme, near Padua.</note> near **Padua**; and these are so frequent that no...

# Book Two

<margin>The cause of hot springs.</margin>
While some provinces may lack them, hot springs burst forth in many locations across numerous regions. **Gaul** <note>Modern-day France</note> abounds in them, **Germany** much more so, and **Italy**, the parent of all good things, far more than all others. The cause of this phenomenon must necessarily be fire, decay <note>The author refers to "putrefaction," an Aristotelian concept where heat is generated by decomposing organic matter, similar to a compost pile.</note>, or heat that is either natural or celestial. Celestial heat cannot be so great, especially in winter or at night, that it could cause waters to boil. Natural heat <note>Here meaning "innate" biological heat.</note> only exists in living animals because they possess a soul and sensation. Heat from decay cannot be so great, nor is it likely that matter could be generated and decay at the exact same time. Indeed, the long duration of this miracle <note>The permanent nature of hot springs.</note> demonstrates that the matter itself must be continually generated. 

It remains, therefore, that the cause lies rather in fire; for unless heat reaches its peak, its movement is slight and it is easily extinguished on its own. But there are two types of fire: **glowing coals** <note>original: "pruna"; refers to solid, smoldering fuel.</note> and **flame**. It is not reasonable to believe a flame exists there, for a flame requires obvious "breathing" <note>Air circulation/oxygen.</note> and consumes a vast amount of material, such that entire mountains of <term>bitumen</term> <note>A naturally occurring petroleum-based substance like asphalt or tar, then thought to be the primary fuel for subterranean fires.</note> would burn up in a single month. Frequent earthquakes would also follow due to the release of vapors, the water would be much hotter than it is, and fire would occasionally be seen or burst out at intervals in these places—yet it is never seen. This indicates that a flame cannot be perpetual beneath the earth, because where it does break out, it never happens except at intervals. 

It is certain, then, that **glowing coals** lie beneath. But how is it fed? From where does its movement and breathing come? It was demonstrated above that fire requires these three things. "Breathing" is provided by dry and porous stone that fosters the fire, in exactly the same way that hot ash protects a spark. Movement is provided by new matter that is perpetually ignited; thus, the fire moves by changing its location. We see this in soot: as long as there is fuel, a "creeping fire" is preserved. It does not burst into flame because that bitumen is impure and mixed with earth. Therefore, the matter burning beneath the earth is very similar to soot; thus, there is no doubt that soot is a form of bitumen. 

There are two reasons why it does not break out into a flame: first, because the bitumen is impure; second, because it cannot breathe. Thus, it happens that occasionally a thinner part of it catches fire and emits a flame, and it is then that earthquakes and Great noises are heard. But the fire does not spread because the matter is mixed with rock and cannot "sigh" <note>Venting gas or air.</note> well. 

But by what means is it not extinguished, or why does it not change its seat as it consumes the matter? There are two reasons it is not extinguished: the bitumen itself and the coldness of the water, by which the heat is driven inward. This is not unlike how water ignites fire in <term>lime</term> <note>Quicklime (calcium oxide) produces intense heat when mixed with water, a process called slaking.</note>. That same cold keeps the fire in the same place because it is always under water. Over a long distance, the water boils; in a narrow space, it bursts forth. 

Truly, there are four reasons why a small fire suffices for such great heat:
1.  **First**, because it does not breathe out, as in steam-baths.
2.  **Second**, the nature of the stone, which is <term>tufa</term> <note>A porous volcanic rock.</note>; it is hot by its very nature, absorbing much heat and releasing it steadily and abundantly.
3.  **Third**, the ash, which is left behind hot and in great quantities, and is by its nature quite dry. Thus, when water is poured on it, even our own fire—which is far weaker—makes it...

...it heats them up. Finally, it must be added that this water is divided into small channels, and because of this, it easily absorbs and retains heat; whereas if it were gathered into a single mass, it could scarcely be heated even by the fire of an entire mountain, and once heated, it would return very quickly to its own natural state. For this reason, no sea, no lake, and no river can boil because of the sheer abundance of water. Springs, however—and the smaller they are, the more intensely they do so—boil from the sun. But why is the greater part of the <term>bitumen</term> <note>A naturally occurring petroleum substance, like tar or asphalt, believed to be the fuel for volcanic heat.</note> not ignited? Because only that which is stripped of its watery moisture can be set on fire. Since this bitumen is entirely overflowing with such moisture—and it is by this very quality that it differs from <term>sulphur</term>—it must necessarily be dried out before it can be ignited. Because of this, it resists even a nearby fire for a long time. Thus, it happens that the fire consumes the material joined to it very slowly. Since the fire can neither grow greatly nor be completely extinguished for the reasons mentioned, and since there is much material prepared for it, and only a little heat is sufficient to maintain the boiling, it is inevitable that this heat should persist for many centuries.

<margin>Excellent waters.</margin>
It is clear, therefore, that all waters that boil are naturally light and endowed with medicinal power. But such water is not suitable for the use of maintaining health. The best water lacks color, smell, and taste; it is transparent, and when drunk, it does not linger in the stomach. Such is the water of the **Eulaeus** river <note>The modern Karkheh River in Iran.</note> which flows through **Susiana** <note>The region around Susa, an ancient capital of the Persian Empire.</note> from Mount **Zagros**; for the Kings of the **Persians** used to carry it with them on their expeditions. Even when they were in **Persepolis**, although it was five hundred thousand paces away from the Eulaeus, they still used it.

<margin>Extremely cold waters.</margin>
Next to this in quality is the water of the **Nile**, and after that, the **Tiber** in **Italy**. There are others famous for their coldness: one formerly flowing from the summit of a mountain in the territory of **Corinth** was colder than snow. **Georgius Agricola** <note>A 16th-century German scholar often called the "father of mineralogy."</note> reports a spring within the first milestone from **Culma** called the "Insane Spring," which, though it appears to boil, is actually freezing cold.

<margin>Waters making the greatest noise.</margin>
In **Bohemia**, again, near the river **Eger**, there is a spring called the "Furious," which is notable because it boils with bubbles not from heat, but rather by producing a sound like thunder. It strikes the ears with such a noise as it falls. In a similar way, after the **Rhine** leaves **Lake Constance** near **Schaffhausen**, it is cast down from such high rocks that it can be heard many miles away; up close, the crash seems like thunder.

<margin>The cause of the noise of waters.</margin>
<margin>The cause of the coldness of waters.</margin>
For the cause of the noise of waters is a fall from a height, or an exit with force from narrow places. Likewise, the causes of cold are snow, marble, metals, the freezing sky, and rapid motion.

<margin>The tastes of waters.</margin>
They also report that in **Elbogen** <note>A town in the Czech Republic, now known as Loket.</note> the water makes no small noise and has an acidic taste. **Aristotle** mentions that there was once water in the **Sicanian** territory of **Sicily** which the inhabitants used instead of vinegar. Similarly, they report that in **Cardia**, near **Lake Dascylus** in a place called the "White Field," the water is sweeter than milk; there is another such spring near the bridge on the way to **Waldburg**. There are also waters that resemble wine, as was once the case on the island of **Naxos**, one of the **Cyclades** in the **Aegean Sea**; regarding this, **Propertius** writes in the third book of his *Elegies*:

> From which the Naxian crowd drinks your wine.

<margin>Mead turns into wine with age.</margin>
Is it any wonder when Pliny and Dioscorides report that <term>Hydromel</term> <note>original: "Hydromel"; a beverage made of honey and water, essentially mead.</note> turns into wine as it ages? Aristotle attributed the cause of water’s flavors to heat.

<margin>The cause of the taste of waters.</margin>
<margin>Springs dripping with oil.</margin>
<margin>Why springs drip with oil.</margin>
For the earth, when "cooked" by heat, changes and provides flavor to the water. In this way, certain springs even appear to be drenched in oil, such as in Saxony near the noble town of Brunswick, and in Swabia near the monastery named after Lake Tegernsee; and again in the valley of the Jura mountains. The cause is a very fatty <term>bitumen</term> <note>A naturally occurring petroleum substance. Early scientists believed oil springs were caused by water washing through underground deposits of this "fatty" earth.</note>, for there is no doubt that bitumen contains oil. Thus, when it is washed out by water, it provides a spring of oil to the water floating upon it. However, it should not be believed that the whole spring consists of oil. Why should it be surprising, then, that a spring of oil gushed out near the tent of Alexander the Great, as Arrian—the most truthful of all historians—reports? Or that the same occurred in Rome during the time of Augustus? Whether it actually happened or not, I do not argue; it matters little here, since we have shown that it *can* happen, and how. For these things happen rarely and in few places, which is why they are considered omens when they occur. Others attribute such things to God. There are also "sharp" or acidic waters, which are the opposites of the fatty ones, such as those of Gelnica.

<margin>The colors of waters.</margin>
<margin>Causes for the colors of water.</margin>
The reasoning for colors is the same: for instance, the water is white at the second milestone from the town of Glauchau in Meissen; red in the Röder river of Meissen near Radeburg; green in the Carpathian mountains near Banská Bystrica; blue like the Piave between Feltre and Treviso; and black as ink in the Aller river of Saxony where it empties into the Weser. The causes are the colors of the clay, specifically the finer particles; for thick clay does not cling to the water and therefore does not tint it.

<margin>Where water is lightest.</margin>
<margin>At the end of book 15.</margin>
Some waters even change color, such as the Nile when it dries up during droughts, according to Theophrastus. Some remain untainted, like the Tiber. Strabo reports that the Persians ordered water to be brought from the Eulaeus river in the province of Susiana; the Eulaeus is no less than five hundred miles from Persepolis, the royal seat of Persia. As Strabo himself reports, the water of the Eulaeus was lighter than others by a drachma <note>A unit of weight; here used to show that a specific volume of this water weighed less than others, which was a historical test for purity.</note>, that is, by the measure of an Attic bowl; according to Pliny's teaching, that is about a fifteenth part. They were so diligent in protecting life, for water is the substance closest to air in sustaining life. It is no wonder that Artaxerxes the Long-handed lived so long. For they were wonderfully and carefully selective about the healthfulness of the air and the water.

# On the Elements and their actions.

<margin>The reason why some things turn to stone.</margin>
Drops from the Gothic spring <note>original: "Gottici fontis"; likely referring to the Gottleuba spring in Saxony, known for its mineral properties.</note>—for this is the name given to it by the common people—turn to stone when they are scattered. In the Cepusian region of Dacia <note>Szepes (Spiš) in modern-day Slovakia, formerly part of the Kingdom of Hungary and associated with the Roman province of Dacia.</note>, water poured into jugs likewise turns to stone. However, the explanation for all these is not the same. For those waters that change into stones because of heat can be safely drunk, since porous stones are formed around all hot springs. But the springs that harden because of the cold are gypseous <note>Containing gypsum or lime.</note> and are not free from poison, for cold hardens all things and forces them into stones. For this reason, in the beds of rivers—and because of the perpetual motion which carries away the earth—there is almost always an abundance of stones, unless the rivers flow with a slow motion.

<margin>In what ways Ether and water agree and disagree.</margin>
Motion and transparency are common to water, air, ether, and the heavens. Belonging specifically to the ether are lightness, purity, thinness, very rapid motion, and the fact that it is devoid of qualities—though no more so than the heavens themselves. As for water, because there are so many species of it, it can have almost nothing in common across all types.
<margin>The difference in waters based on location.</margin>
For there are waters of the sea, lakes, rivers, marshes, ponds, torrents, springs, wells, those from rain clouds, storms, snow, ice, hot springs, and those collected in cisterns, as well as "puddle-waters," if I may call them that.
<margin>The nature and powers of waters.</margin>
The best are those from springs. Glacial water weakens the stomach and the joints, as do snowy and stormy waters, for they descend from a high and cold place; however, glacial water is less harmful than snowy water, and just like glacial water, sea water is suitable for medicine. The water of torrents, rapid rivers, and lakes—though to a lesser extent—creates a type of dropsy <note>A condition of swelling caused by excess fluid.</note> which is called <term>ascites</term> <note>A specific form of dropsy where fluid collects in the abdominal cavity.</note>. The waters of soft-flowing rivers, such as the Nile, the Po, and the Tiber, are very close to spring waters. Marsh water is bad; pond water is worse; and puddle water is the worst of all. For in addition to dropsy, it produces a hernia of the throat, creates a poor condition of the body, and causes <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: "morbum regium," literally "the royal disease," an old term for jaundice.</note>, fevers, and a short life. Hot waters do not have just one power, but these have been discussed in medical treatises, as have those collected in cisterns. Storm waters, as I have said, contain a salty and half-putrid quality.

<margin>Why the lightest waters rot slowly.</margin>
The lightest waters in every category are safer and rot more slowly. For they are less humid and more "cooked" by the celestial heat. Because of this, the drier they are, the less they chill the body; they are closer to the substance of air, and therefore they are lighter, rot with more difficulty, and are consequently much more healthful.

# BOOK THREE
## On the Heavens.

<margin>The substance of the heavens is unequal and varied.</margin>
**E**nough has been said about the Elements; now we must treat the heavens. Whether they are eternal, as Aristotle thinks, or created, as Plato believes, or "made" according to the Theologians, they appear to have a varied substance. First of all, Amerigo Vespucci <note>original: "Albericus Vesputius"; the Italian explorer for whom the Americas are named.</note> in his third voyage to the Indies <note>Referring to the 1501-1502 expedition to the coast of South America.</note> diligently handed down these observations concerning the magnitude of the stars: namely, that there are three "Canopi" <note>Vespucci used the name "Canopus" to refer to several bright southern stars or nebulae (possibly including the Magellanic Clouds) rather than just the single star Canopus.</note> which are large but not bright. The first is nine and a half degrees from the South Pole, the second is twelve, and the third—which is thirty-two degrees from the same pole—is the largest but is somewhat dark. The Conciliator <note>original: "Conciliator"; the nickname for Pietro d'Abano (c. 1257–1315), a physician and astrologer who wrote the "Conciliator of the Differences of Philosophers and Especially Physicians."</note> also reports, though relying on the accounts of others, that there are certain large stars there that are not very brilliant, such as those we mentioned above. Ptolemy <note>The 2nd-century Greco-Egyptian astronomer who formulated the geocentric model.</note> also mentions Canopus as a famous star, but he does not describe its size; however, I believe this is the last of those described by Vespucci. <margin>Near the Southern pole the stars are very large.</margin> Gonzalo Fernández <note>original: "Gonzalus Ferdinandus"; likely referring to Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo (1478–1557), a Spanish chronicler of the New World.</note> reports that four stars are seen at a latitude of 20 degrees from the South Pole which resemble the shape of a cross <note>The Southern Cross constellation (Crux).</note>. Furthermore, the different colors of the stars, their sizes and brightness, and the spots on the Moon show that the substance of the heavens is varied, and that in the southern region the stars are far larger, with some of the fixed stars being no less bright than those here. For the "Greater Dog" <note>Sirius, the brightest star in the sky.</note> is beyond the equatorial circle, and everyone can see how brightly it shines. It is well established that Canopus is large and is less than 38 degrees from the Antarctic pole. Indeed, in Alexandria, the entire heaven is visible except for only 41 degrees. For far more is known about the heavens than the earth, <margin>How much of the heavens is known.</margin> because the heavens are placed on high and are perpetually in motion. Because of these two reasons, almost the whole of it is known; for only 31 degrees around the South Pole were unknown to Ptolemy. <margin>Book 1 of On the Sphere and Cylinder, propositions 40 and 41, or Book 2, proposition 3.</margin> Therefore, according to the demonstration of Archimedes <note>The famous Greek mathematician and engineer (c. 287–212 BC).</note>, nearly one part out of thirteen—or a little less than a thirteenth—is unknown compared to what is known; thus, only a fourteenth part of the entire heavens was unknown to Ptolemy.

Someone might ask about the Moon, why it has spots. I will not explain this now, because enough was said about the substance of the Moon and the motion of the heavens, as well as about hail, snow, frost, winds, chasms, and the dew of the heavens, in the book on "Supernal Things" <note>original: "libro de supernis"; likely referring to a commentary on Aristotle's *Meteorologica* or the author's own previous work on atmospheric phenomena.</note>, so I did not think it necessary to speak of them here. But I will narrate here only the general matters pertaining to the history of the heavens, <margin>Whether all stars have their own light.</margin> beginning with the Moon because it is closest to us. Its light, as some believe, does not depend entirely on the Sun, and much less does the light of the remaining stars. For it is established...

# On the Heavens.

...for in the greatest eclipses <note>original: "deliquijs"; refers to lunar eclipses.</note> it glows red like a kind of burning coal, and this is its own light; but since at night nothing seems more obscure than fire at a distance, and a flame appears red, yet the Moon appears from so far away during eclipses, it is manifest that the Moon has a clearer light of its own than any flame or candle. Imagine, therefore, the Moon to be very similar to a most great and bright flame, spontaneous and unaided by any rays of the Sun; then consider how much brighter the Moon is when aided by the light of the Sun, as in a full moon, than when it is in an eclipse. You will easily understand that the Moon, illustrated here by the rays of the Sun, is more splendid and clear than the Sun itself <note>The author is likely referring to the apparent brightness or the intensity of reflected light compared to the darkened state.</note>, so that even the eye of an eagle—which they say can look securely at the Sun—would not dare to gaze upon it. Furthermore, if you make a comparison of this to the radiance of the Sun, it is undoubtedly established that the saying of the Prophet <note>Isaiah 30:26: "the light of the moon shall be as the light of the sun, and the light of the sun shall be sevenfold."</note> is not false: that the Sun, Moon, and stars will have a sevenfold light on that day. For now, they possess a light in the heavens far greater than sevenfold compared to what is seen here, being both clear and fruitful. Therefore, everything above the ether <note>term: "ether"; the classical "fifth element" believed to fill the space of the universe above the terrestrial sphere.</note> shines and flashes so much that if we were to look at the Moon from there, even during an eclipse, we would be blinded by the splendor, just as if we had fixed our eyes upon countless most splendid lit wax candles. 

<margin>Why the stars appear to twinkle.</margin>
But why do the stars appear to twinkle? <note>original: "scintillare"; to sparkle or twinkle.</note> Since the substance of the heavens is extremely rare, the rays coming to us are refracted <note>original: "franguntur"; literally "broken," the term used for optical refraction.</note> frequently, yet always toward the perpendicular; because of this, as the air moves—just as pebbles at the bottom of water seem to tremble because of the movement of the flowing water—so those stars seem to waver. In the case of lights, this is called "scintillating." However, the wandering stars <note>term: "Stellæ errantes"; the planets.</note> and the Moon do not twinkle because their rays reach us with robust strength. For they are far closer to us than the fixed stars. 

<margin>A sign of future wind.</margin>
Evidence that this is so is that when they twinkle more, and even the planets (which usually do not twinkle) begin to do so, they predict a coming wind. For the middle air, which is high up, when it is more violently agitated, causes them to appear to twinkle more frequently and intensely. 

<margin>Stars appear much smaller and higher than they are.</margin>
Mars, however, since it is somewhat dark and red, also twinkles, especially to those who see weakly. For this is consistent with reason, that those who see more weakly persuade themselves that the stars twinkle more. By the same reason, the stars that are beyond the equinoctial line <note>The celestial equator.</note> twinkle more, for they are more remote. Hence also the Greater Dog <note>The star Sirius in the constellation Canis Major.</note>, which ought to twinkle less because of its splendor, actually twinkles more because of its size, for it is very far away. And you will see stars twinkle more in one part of the heaven and less in another: very little at the zenith <note>original: "uertice".</note>, and those that shine greatly and are large, and those near the poles, for there the air moves less, and where there are no winds.

<margin>
Where the thing being seen always appears.

...things appear larger than they actually are, and all water appears shallower and is judged less deep when viewed from the side. Consequently, some people, not noticing this and being deceived, have run the risk of drowning <note>original: "submersionis"; the author is warning that water always looks shallower than it truly is due to refraction.</note>.
Therefore, let us show the cause of this and other things that must be discussed: where the thing being seen is, and in what place it appears to be. Thus, every object seen appears to be in the place where there is an intersection of the **perpendicular line** <note>original: "cathetus"; a line dropped at a right angle from the object to the surface of the medium.</note> of the thing seen (drawn from it to the medium which is the cause of seeing) and the line through which the thing is seen, which always extends from the object to the eye. Suppose first that the eye is at **A** and the object at **B** in the same medium; then **B** will be seen in its own place, because the perpendicular line is the same as the line coming to the eye. Suppose again that the eye **A** is in the air and the object **B** is in the water; let the perpendicular to the air be **BE**. Let the straight line **BDF** be bent <note>original: "inflectatur"; this refers to refraction, where light "breaks" or bends as it moves from water to air.</note> from the perpendicular to the eye from **D**, so that it becomes **BDA**. Let **AD** be extended to **C**, and **B** will be seen at **C**; therefore, the depth of the water will appear to be only **CG**. The ray which proceeds directly is **BFC**; when it reaches the denser medium at **F**—that is, the air—it is bent toward the <term>cathetus</term> <note>term: "cathetus"; the geometric normal or perpendicular line used as a reference point to measure the angle of light.</note>, so that **BFA** is the path through which the eye **A** sees the star **B**. Therefore, let **AF** be extended directly, and **B** will be seen at **D**, namely where the cathetus **BE** from the object to the medium and the line **BFA** (when directed from the part that reaches the eye, that is, the part **AF** touching the eye) meet.

For even a <term>cubit</term> <note>term: "ulna"; a traditional unit of length based on the forearm.</note> on a tower is judged larger by an eye that perceives the distance, even though the cubit itself makes a smaller angle in the eye. Therefore, the stars seem close because there is no intermediate body between them and the eye whose length the eye can detect; and for that reason, the eye considers them to be less far away than the ratio of the medium would show them to be. But the fact that stars appear larger in the east and west is also caused by the density of the air—not the air we are in, but that which is far from us. The proof of this is that in foggy weather, the stars also appear much larger. This could not happen if it occurred solely because of distance.

Three things that are necessary to understand the logic of sight.

The same logic shows the location of the object seen in columnar and conical mirrors. Now, therefore, there are three things necessary for sight: the location of the object seen, and that the object is not smaller than the minimum size that can be seen at that distance—for it is necessary to find that minimum at any distance—and that any object smaller than that minimum is as if it did not exist. In this way, it is not difficult to know the cause of why the stars, though they appear flat, are nevertheless round. Therefore, they will all appear to rise from the same plane; thus B D C will appear flat. Consequently, all round things will appear flat from a distance.

### Book Three

...is equal <note>The text begins mid-sentence; "lis" is the end of "equalis" (equal).</note> to F B, opposite the right angle; therefore B D is equal to F H, and M C is equal to K G by the same reasoning. Thus, since C D is greater than F G, as is evident from the fourth proposition of the sixth book of Euclid’s *Elements*, it follows that B C can be increased so much that B D and M C—which always remain equal—are smaller than the given minimum quantity in comparison to the distance. Therefore, according to the third hidden assumption, the difference between F B and G C will be treated as if they were parallel <note>original: "æquidistantes"</note>. Vitello <note>Vitello (Witelo) was a 13th-century Polish friar and philosopher whose work on optics was the standard textbook for centuries.</note> attempted to show this, but he did not clarify it; after many errors, he finally tried to show something that is false: namely, that B L was smaller than F H. This, however, is false; for as I have demonstrated, it is equal. From this equality, B L has a smaller ratio to B C than F H has to F G, and this is sufficient to demonstrate the proposition. Therefore, when the Sun or Moon or another star casts a shadow on the Earth nearly equal to the object seen, or to a piece of wood placed against its rays—whether the rays proceed from a single point or from the whole body—it is established by this rearranged demonstration that the proportion of the height to F G is beyond comparison. Since this also happens with the tallest towers and mountains, it is necessary that the lines F B and G C be parallel; therefore the height A of the star is very great, and the star itself must be very large to be seen at such a distance under the magnitude we observe. By a calculation deduced from the Earth's shadow during solar eclipses <note>original: "deliquijs Solis"</note>, the diameter is eleven parts to the two parts of the Earth’s diameter. Therefore, since the Earth’s diameter is ten thousand miles <note>original: "bis quinque M. passuum"; literally "twice five thousand paces." In Roman measurement, 1,000 paces (mille passus) equals one mile.</note>, the Sun's diameter will be fifty-five thousand miles: that is, one thousand times fifty-five thousand paces.

<margin>
Comparison of the sizes of the Sun, Moon, and Earth.
</margin>

The ratio of the Sun’s body to the Earth is one hundred sixty-six and three-eighths to one. The circumference of its greater circle is 174,250 miles. Furthermore, the ratio of the Earth's diameter to the Moon's diameter is 17 to 5. Thus, the body <note>volume</note> of the Earth contains the body of the Moon nearly thirty-nine times and two-thirds over. The Moon’s diameter is 2,441 miles, and the circumference of its greater circle is 9,264 miles. But why does this one alone take on various shapes, while all the other stars are perpetually round?

<margin>
Why only the Moon changes its shape.
</margin>

The Moon changes its shape because it is opaque, and the light it possesses of its own is so much weaker <note>original: "imbecillius"</note> than the light of the Sun that the part not illuminated by the Sun remains hidden, and that part appears to be missing. Therefore, if all the other stars are round, it happens either because their own light is so bright—though still weaker than the Sun's—or because they are translucent in every part.

<margin>
Why the stars appear small.
</margin>

Therefore, as I have said, the stars are at a vast distance from us according to this calculated reason, but because that distance is hidden from our senses, they are thought to be small for that reason. But because the distance of towers is perceived, and we also retain their size in our memory—and since the angle they form is larger than that of the stars—towers [appear] larger than stars...

<page-num>63</page-num>
<header>On the Heavens.</header>
<sig>m ij</sig>

# On the Heavens.

<margin>Whether the heavens can move in different directions, higher and lower, if the touching surface is one?</margin>
...we judge [the higher parts] to be <note>The text begins mid-word, continuing from the previous page's discussion on perspective.</note>; for this reason, towers appear wider if we view them from the bottom than if we were able to inspect only the uppermost part, because while we see the base, we also see the distance. But how are these heavens joined? For if there is one concave surface of the superior heaven and one convex surface of the inferior, how can the upper and lower heaven be moved in different directions? 

If there are two [surfaces] of the touching spheres, the indivisible is touched by the indivisible. But it is necessary that there be two, yet they do not constitute a quantity; this, however, suffices for Aristotle <note>The author refers to Aristotle's physics regarding the "continuum," arguing that surfaces can touch without merging into a single object.</note>, so that a continuum is not composed of non-continua. 

Now indeed, that which is most marvelous regarding the stars—which are so far away—is how the seas and lands lying before our eyes become known to them <note>The author personifies the stars as "knowing" the Earth they shine upon.</note>; I omit that the ancients, with the stars as guides, plowed the seas. That which is more worthy of wonder is that those driven by a storm into unknown parts of the sea or land are able to recognize where they are by the help of the stars. <margin>How ships in unknown and scattered regions, driven by storms, may be able to discern where they are.</margin> John Baptist of Ponte Vigo requested this [explanation] of us. 

The reasoning is as follows: Once the sky has become clear, take the altitude of the Sun by day, or of another planet by night, with a planisphere <note>A flat representation of the celestial sphere, such as an astrolabe.</note> or armillary spheres <note>A model of the objects in the sky, consisting of a spherical framework of rings representing the principal celestial circles.</note> while the star is at the meridian. From this, subtract the declination <note>original: "declarationem," likely a variant or error for "declinationem"</note> of the Sun's position if the Sun is between the beginning of Aries and the beginning of Libra; add the declination of the Sun's position if it is from the beginning of Libra to the beginning of Aries. Subtract the result from 90, and you will have the latitude of the place, which even those who recently inhabit the Indies <note>The author refers to the explorers and colonists in the Americas or the East Indies during the Age of Discovery.</note> know how to find. 

But for longitude: having obtained the latitude, you will find the hour of the day by means of a planisphere using the altitude of the Sun or another known star. Then, using the armillary spheres and the latitude of the place, you will seek the position of the Moon as it appears; to this you will add or subtract the difference arising from the <term>parallax|The difference in the apparent position of an object viewed along two different lines of sight.</term> <note>original: "aspectus diuersitate"</note>, and you will have the true position of the Moon at that hour. According to this, you will find the position and motion of the Moon for each current day from the Alfonsine Tables <note>The *Tabulae Alphonsinae* were the most famous astronomical tables of the Middle Ages and early Renaissance, used to calculate the positions of celestial bodies.</note>. 

Therefore, consider the difference between the Moon’s positions found by the instrument and those found by the tables; divide the daily motion by this difference, and the result will be the hours and minutes of the difference. Therefore, for each hour take 15 degrees, and for each minute take a quarter of one degree. You will add these to the distance from the Fortunate Islands <note>The *Insulae Fortunatae* (Canary Islands) were used by ancient and Renaissance geographers as the Prime Meridian, or the zero-point for measuring longitude.</note> of the place listed in the Alfonsine Tables, if the Moon's position found by the instrument is later—that is, further from the beginning of Aries—than the position found by the tables. Or, you will subtract them if the position from the tables has more degrees and minutes than that found by the instrument. What remains or is gathered is the longitude from the Fortunate Islands of the unknown place, which you will seek on a globe of regions <note>original: "sphaera regionum"</note> along with the latitude. Thus you will know where in the world you are, and by which winds you may return to your homeland. Because those who write the history of Indian affairs are ignorant of this, they provide the latitude but omit the longitudes of places. 

Now truly, whether there is one world or many? Or infinite? Or one infinite world? And whether there is anything outside it? And whether it is eternal or created? This has been discussed in the books on the *Secrets of Eternity*. Now, however, we shall speak of the light and radiance that flow forth from the stars.
