<header>BOOK FOUR: On Light and Radiance.</header>

# BOOK FOUR
## On Light and Radiance.

<margin>All stars have light and shadow.</margin>
**A**ll stars possess their own light, motion, and magnitude; and just as a smaller light is obscured by a greater one, so does shadow lie hidden beneath shadow. The Moon creates no shadow during the day, but does so at night. If the Moon is shining, you will not see the shadows of the other stars; yet when she is hidden, you will sometimes see the shadows of certain stars so distinctly that I once mistook the light of Venus entering through a window for that of the Moon.

<margin>The cause of the Milky Way.</margin>
Therefore, every single star has its own <term>lumen</term> <note>original: "lumen". In Renaissance physics, "lumen" usually refers to light as it travels through a medium, whereas "lux" is the light at its source.</note> since it has its own <term>radiance</term> <note>original: "lux"</note>. It follows that from the many stars mingling their light, the eye perceives a "milky circle." This is aided by the dense substance of the heavens and the thinness of the stars, as seen in comets, which have a tail or "hair"; for since it never changes, it is established that the comet is in the heavens themselves, not below them <note>The author is arguing against the Aristotelian view that comets were atmospheric phenomena, placing them instead in the celestial spheres.</note>.

<margin>Why reflected rays are visible and increase heat.</margin>
But how is it that rays passing through the void appear refracted, since the Sun's rays in the air are not visible to our sight? This is the same reason why rays are also reflected on the earth, such that in valleys the heat is far greater; for if a ray simply penetrates, it is only one, but when it is reflected, there are two; when reflected again, three rays are in the same place. Thus, great heat is generated here. In the Milky Way, however, the rays are reflected not twice or thrice, but a thousand times—partly due to the proximity of the stars and partly due to the density of the medium. Since there are so many of them, it must necessarily result in a whiteness like milk in the center. I have seen this beautifully imitated by chance using many candles, so that experiment confirms what reason suggests.

<margin>Why fire is kindled by concave mirrors, but not on white material.</margin>
By the same reasoning, fire is kindled in concave mirrors because many rays converge into a small space. However, this does not happen on white material, because it removes the condition by which they can ignite. They can ignite because they converge, but a white surface dissipates and separates them. Because of this, white cloth is easily burned by a direct fire or even a spark, but it is not burned by the solar rays focused by a concave mirror <note>The author observes that white surfaces reflect light rather than absorbing it, preventing the concentration of heat needed for ignition.</note>.

<margin>Why fire is kindled by crystal spheres placed in the sun.</margin>
The reasoning is exactly the same for a small crystal sphere or a round glass jar full of water. But whereas in these objects the rays converge on the opposite side, in concave mirrors they converge in front. Truly, the principle of burning or not burning is the same in both. For when you place a white object beneath them, that cone of light is visibly dilated, and therefore it cannot burn. That it dilates can even be detected by the naked eye.

<margin>How the Sun produces heat.</margin>
But why does concentrated light, especially that of the Sun, heat these lower regions so intensely, since the Sun itself is not considered to be "hot" <note>In traditional Scholastic philosophy, the heavens were made of a fifth element (aether) and were not "hot" in the way terrestrial fire is; their heat was considered a secondary effect of motion or light.</note>? Truly, I would not fear to assert that the Sun is hot, as I consider nothing else to be hot with that specific kind of heat; for this was shown above. For putrid or fiery heat does not generate life but corrupts it, whereas the heat of the Sun and stars generates life. However, the heat of things that lack life is not active heat...

But if you wish to defend the opinions of Aristotle, you will say that while air and water strive to receive that light, they are moved and scattered by a certain natural faculty—by which heavy things descend and light things ascend. Also, the heat which was already in them in potential is awakened and brought into <term>actuality</term> <note>original: "ad actum". A core Aristotelian concept where a latent quality becomes active.</note>. Indeed, water is heated by the air, because it does not have heat of itself; for this reason, either only the topmost surface is hot, or it is hottest there. Rarity follows this motion, and heat follows rarity; for it has been shown above how this happens. 
<margin>Subtlety, heat, and motion are causes of one another in turn.</margin>
For heat, motion, and thinness are causes of each other in a certain mutual circle; for subtlety is the cause of heat; heat, while it consumes, is the cause of motion; but motion itself is again the cause of subtlety, for motion thins parts by colliding them. A thin substance, because it receives a great force of the ray, becomes hot; but a hot thing, by attracting and dispersing, stirs up motion, which <term>vicissitude</term> <note>The constant alternating change between states</note> provides life in animals and is most manifest. For we taught above that cold is nothing other than that which lacks heat and does not receive it; therefore, it is impossible for something very rare to be cold. It seems, therefore, that the ray itself or radiance is the substance of heat, and this would suffice for us, who follow the reasons of things only insofar as they help in achieving the truth of experiments. Whether, therefore, you say the rays of the Sun and stars are hot in themselves, or that they are not hot but cause heating, we shall be equally satisfied. To me, however, it seems that heat is the substance of a star’s ray, yet this heat is not a quality that can be destroyed, since it is inseparable from light. For the heat received in the elements or mixed bodies is not celestial, but only a celestial image; therefore, just as light is proper to the stars, so is heat, to which no cold is
<margin>What source-light and radiance are.</margin>

Because of this, the brightest stars are also the hottest, such as the Sun, both Dogs <note>The stars Sirius (the Greater Dog) and Procyon (the Lesser Dog), historically associated with the "dog days" of summer heat.</note>, and Jupiter; therefore radiance, clarity, and heat are not three things, but one, taking on different names and even a different image and representation by the comparison of different things. # Book Four

The strong colors are: black, green, white, red, and <term>cyan</term> <note>original: "cyaneus"; here referring to a deep sky-blue or lapis lazuli color</note> or celestial blue. Fire can do this even more distinctly, and do far greater things, such as representing images of serpents. However, it is necessary that such a power exists and is aided by its own smoke to represent the images of things. <note>The author is likely describing early optical experiments or "magic lantern" effects where light projected through colored glass or smoke creates shapes.</note> But we shall speak of colors in their proper place; now the treatment is of light and its representations.

<margin>Are the stars solid?</margin>
However, there is no small doubt as to how light is reflected by the stars. For if light is reflected from a star, the star must be solid; but if it is solid, why is it not broken by its own motion, and why does it not tire the one by whom it is moved? In the bodies of animals, it is necessary for the soul to move spontaneously and with alacrity; yet in us, that alacrity fails because the force is only transmitted from the heart where the soul dwells. But in the heavens, since the soul is everywhere, there is an eternal alacrity. For this reason, the soul is not fatigued by its will, because it requires no bodily aid—nor is the heart fatigued, because the soul is within it—yet it has the appearance of fatigue. The heavens, however, since they never rest and have the soul present everywhere, can never be fatigued.

<margin>How the ether is moved.</margin>
But regarding the circle of the Moon, there is a question that is not so clear: whether it drags the <term>ether</term> <note>The "fifth element" believed to fill the space of the universe above the terrestrial sphere.</note> along with it. For it ought to be fatigued. Truly, it is better to say that this belongs to the whole ether spontaneously: that every single part is carried around from east to west, and when individual parts are pushed from their place, they return to it spontaneously. This question is in our favor, for we have judged in our books on the <term>secrets of eternity</term> <note>original: "de aeternitatis archanis"; likely a reference to a previous work by the author discussing the origin and end of the universe.</note> that the world will have an end and had a beginning. Or perhaps we shall say that just as water moves according to the motion of the Moon <note>A reference to the tides.</note>, so the ether is carried around the first heaven spontaneously—not by the nature of an element, but out of obedience to higher things. Or, that for preserving motion, this is sufficient without any effort, though the beginning would not have happened without labor. But since this motion is eternal, it lacked a beginning.

<margin>The reason for twilights.</margin>
But enough of these things; let us return to the history of light and radiance. Here, perhaps, one might rightly ask why the air shines and is brighter before the Sun rises and after it sets? This time is called <term>twilight</term> <note>original: "crepusculum"</note>. But while the evening has kept the name of twilight, the morning has passed into the name of <term>dawn</term> <note>original: "aurora"</note>. Virgil mentions this with twelve clear <term>proofs</term> <note>original: "experimentis"; here used as poetic observations or examples.</note>; it is enough to recount the first:

->*Now Dawn, shining with her saffron veil, had left the Ocean,*<-
->*and, carried by her pair of horses, was turning red:*<-
->*the bright orb flooded the pole with glittering light,*<-
->*and the clear radiance flashed as the Sun arose.*<-

Therefore, all that is contained under the heaven ABF, and above by...

<margin>
The altitude of the Sun and the Moon and the Earth's shadow.
</margin>
...is illuminated by the light of the Sun, except for the triangle **C D E**, and yet the parts **F** and **G** do not appear bright because the Sun’s rays penetrate them but are not reflected. Nor can the Sun, by its sheer size, cause <term>crepusculum</term> <note>twilight; the period of partial darkness between day and night</note>: both because the rays would be visible and we would see the Sun itself, and because, as we have demonstrated by its maximum altitude, lines **C E** and **D E** are rendered almost parallel. For as is gathered from *Ptolemy's* <note>Claudius Ptolemy, a 2nd-century astronomer whose model of the universe was standard for over a millennium</note> demonstration, the altitude of the Sun is 5,005,000 <term>paces</term> <note>original: "passuum"; a Roman unit of distance. Here used as a general term for miles in early scientific contexts</note> from the center of the earth; that of the Moon, however, is 323,833 paces; while the point **E**, which is the cone of the shadow, is 1,340,000 paces. Therefore, by subtracting 5,000 paces <note>the assumed radius of the Earth used in these calculations</note> from each of these, you will have their altitudes from the surface of the earth. Therefore, twilight occurs because the part that is above the earth, contained beneath point **E**—that is, within the Earth’s shadow—being condensed by <term>vapors</term> <note>in early science, "vapors" referred to moisture or particles in the air that make up the atmosphere</note>, catches the Sun's rays and reflects them to us.
<margin>
*Book 5, Chapter 15.*
</margin>

<margin>
A demonstration showing to what height vapors can ascend from the earth.
</margin>
Let us observe, then, the Sun when it is at the equinoctial circle, which begins twilight 19 degrees before rising—that is, almost an hour and a quarter before the Sun's own ascent. It is clear that then, for the first time, the Sun’s ray which illuminates the air touches the earth; for if it did not touch it, the ray would reach a lower place than before, having been drawn as a tangent to the earth from the highest point of the vapors, and thus twilight would begin earlier than has been stated. This being established, let a circle be drawn representing the earth, whose center is **C**, the tangent line **A D**, the highest part of the vapors **E**, the location of the Sun’s ray **F**, and where it intersects **A D**, let **G** be placed. Because the Sun’s distance is immense compared to the Earth, the angle **F G D** is as if it were at the center **C** of the earth; wherefore it is 19 degrees, and thus also **E G A**, as if at the center of the circle. But **A** and **B** are right angles; therefore, since **E** is common to the two triangles **C B E** and **A E G**, they will be similar, and thus the ratio of the sides is known. Now, **B C** is 5,000 paces, as was said; therefore **A E** is 288,000 paces, and to such an altitude do the vapors ascend.

Behold, you see how far the subtlety of human ingenuity reaches! I am well aware that *Vitello* <note>Witelo, a 13th-century friar and physicist famous for his work on optics</note> was deceived, for he recorded that they ascend only to 52,000 paces, when they actually ascend five and a half times more than he said. Truly, although he contracts the circumference of the earth and thereby makes the paces somewhat larger, he still cannot bring it even to a fourth part of the proper altitude. But if twilight were to be brought to its maximum, occurring two hours before daybreak, the angle **C** on the circumference would be 60 degrees (equal to **G**), and **E** would be 120; wherefore line **A E**, which is the height of the vapors, would be 5,272,000 paces—and this is the maximum.
<margin>
*Vitello's* error.
*Book 10, Chapter 60.*
</margin>

# Book Four

The maximum distance to which vapors can rise from the earth is the limit for where <term>Rainbows</term> <note>original: "Irides"</note>, <term>Rods</term> <note>original: "Virgae"; these are light phenomena like sun dogs or atmospheric streaks</note>, celestial fires, and <term>openings in the sky</term> <note>original: "hiatus coeli"; likely referring to gaps in cloud cover or auroral displays</note> can occur. Similarly, triple Suns <note>parhelia or sun dogs</note>, double Moons <note>paraselenae</note>, and much less so rain, hail, snow, frost, and whatever else takes its origin from vapors, cannot form higher than this. However, one must consider that this height varies in different places, though it never exceeds the prescribed number of <term>paces</term> <note>original: "passuum"; a unit of measurement used here to calculate atmospheric depth</note>. Let us assume, therefore, for us who are distant from the <term>Tropic of Capricorn</term> <note>original: "circulo Capricorni"; the winter circle</note> by approximately 68 degrees, that the eye is at point **B**, in Milan; and the point which is seen under the circle of Capricorn is **E**. It is therefore established that the ratio of **CE** to **CB** is almost as 8 to 3. Since it is equal to **CB**, the ratio of **CE** to **CA** will also be as 8 to 3. Therefore, **AC** is to **AE** as 5 is to 3. Thus, **AE** is 8,332 paces—the small remainder of which I do not care about. It is clear enough that the place which must be seen by an inhabitant of Milan under the winter circle is distant from the earth by more than ten times the height reached by vapors.

<margin>That a Comet is not formed in the region of the elements.</margin>
But comets are seen by us there; therefore, they are not made of vapors. Yet they are not made further up in the <term>aether</term> <note>the "fifth element" or the substance of the higher heavens</note> either, since there is no material there that can be set on fire. But you might say that moisture is snatched up and drawn that far by the power of the stars, even though that place is higher than this common region of vapors. First, the objection stands that most comets last longer than two months, and some do not even end in the third; the entire mechanism of the earth would not suffice for such a conflagration. For it was shown above that fire is never in the same material but perpetually requires new fuel. This star, moreover, usually has a tail and is in the aether, which means it is no smaller than the Moon. It is entirely impossible for so much matter to burn and last for three months. Add to this that some would be lower, which would be hidden before sunset or be immobile, neither of which has yet been seen. There are many other things that show the absurdity of this opinion, which I shall refrain from mentioning—such as that idea of <term>Albumasar</term> <note>Abu Ma'shar, a famous 9th-century Persian astronomer</note> that a comet is above Venus. Venus, however, is much higher than the Moon. But it is quite easy to detect whether a comet is in the region of the <term>elements</term> <note>the terrestrial sphere of earth, water, air, and fire</note> or occurs in the heavens. For if it has a greater <term>diversity</term> <note>original: "diuerfitatem"; refers to parallax, the difference in apparent position when viewed from different points</note> than the Moon, it must be in the region of the elements. But if it has less, it occurs in the heavens without a doubt. I have written about this in the book on "Higher Things," since measurements were necessary. You see by what slight devices human subtlety proceeds to uncover the secrets of the heavens.

<margin>Three things which are common to all Comets.</margin>
It is common to all comets that they are moved by a triple motion: one from East to West, just like all the other stars in 24 hours; the second from West to East, by a little more or less than one degree of the sky, almost in the likeness of Venus. For the comet of the year 1532, when it had risen on the 22nd day of September and had set on the 3rd of December, in 71 days it proceeded from the 5th part of Virgo into the 8th of Scorpio. By this fact, it proceeded only 63 degrees of the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferi"</note> in longitude over 71 days—which is, of course, less than one degree per day...

<margin>How long a Comet lasts.</margin>
<note>Pliny the Elder was a Roman author and naturalist whose "Natural History" was a standard reference in the Renaissance.</note> Pliny thinks that a Comet does not appear for more than eighty days, and is not hidden sooner than seven. By similar reasoning, <note>Girolamo Fracastoro (1478–1553) was an influential Italian physician and astronomer.</note> Girolamo Fracastoro, the author of the previous example, reports in his book *On Homocentric Orbs* that on the eighth day of September, in the year 1531, a Comet was a little more to the east than the Sun—that is, near the 23rd part of <term>Virgo</term>—but near the beginning of October, when Jupiter was in the third part of <term>Scorpio</term>, the comet had moved near to it.
<margin>Section 3, chapter 23.</margin>

It is read in his own book in the twelfth part, which cannot be possible: that on the 17th day, and much less before then, Jupiter arrived at the 13th part of Scorpio. Therefore, in one month—for he was rather negligent in his explanation—the Comet covered about 40 parts in longitude; that is, progressing from the 22nd of Virgo to the second or third of Scorpio, a movement which is not much unlike the movement of Venus or Mercury. The third movement is the greatest according to latitude, so that (unless he is mistaken) it is carried with incredible speed, now one toward the North, now another toward the South; these processes occur when Comets are near the poles, for then a small variation in position compared to the <term>zodiac</term> <note>original: "signiferum"; the belt of the heavens containing the paths of the sun and planets</note> changes the latitude considerably. Another thing common to Comets is that the tail always looks precisely toward the part opposite the Sun; thus, when the Sun sets, the Comet has its tail pointing exactly toward the east, just as we are permitted to see every day on the dark part of the Moon.

<margin>What a Comet is.</margin>
A third point is that a comet usually accompanies the Sun in longitude, appearing only during twilight, though not always. From this it becomes clearly evident that a Comet is a globe situated in the heavens, which is seen because it is illuminated by the Sun; and while the rays pass through it, they form the likeness of a <term>beard</term> <note>original: "barbae"; a term for a comet's coma or shorter tail</note> or a tail. Therefore, if "generation" <note>the creation of new matter</note> occurs there, it can happen in the heavens; but if that is not admitted, it is necessary to say—which is more true—that the heaven is full of many stars that are not very dense, which subject themselves to our eyes when the air has dried and thinned, or even for other reasons. For even Venus is sometimes seen at midday, and it is well established that she was not newly "generated."

<margin>The omens of Comets.</margin>
From this it happens that as the air dries, the seas are greatly agitated by storms, and very great blasts of wind often follow. Also, nobles and Princes—who are dried out by cares, sleepless nights, spiced foods, and potent wines—suffer death. For this same cause, there occur a decrease in waters, the death of fish, sterilities, changes in laws, and seditions; and even the subversions of kingdoms for that reason. All these things, as I have said, happen because of the immoderate thinness and dryness of the air, so that a Comet can indeed be a *sign* of these things, but not the *cause*.

<margin>How the colors of the Rainbow are made.</margin>
Concerning the <term>Rainbow</term> <note>original: "Iride"</note>, however, because it is more frequent and because it is obvious that it occurs in the region of vapors, there is less doubt. For just as a drop of water, when it is toward the Sun...

## Book Four

<margin>Why shadows appear black.</margin>
When the Sun is observed, it reflects many and all brilliant colors; likewise, from a dense, dewy cloud dripping with droplets, the <term>Iris</term> <note>the rainbow</note> is formed. For everything dark is as if it were black: shadows are proof of this, for they all appear black for that reason. But when a dark thing is illuminated, and if it is smooth, it passes into colors according to the quantity of light. Since a cloud is dark and the water droplets are smooth, they reflect colors according to the variety of the light. <margin>The reason for the order of colors in the rainbow.</margin> Since the inner circle is closer to the darkness, it appears <term>cerulean</term> <note>blue</note>; the middle, which is more luminous, is green; and the outer and largest, being illuminated by more ample light, is <term>saffron</term> <note>yellow-orange</note>. Purple and <term>xanthus</term> <note>original: "xanthus"; a golden-yellow color</note> are not primary colors, but rather arise when a transition occurs from one color to another due to the variation of light; where the boundaries meet, it is necessary for other subtle colors to appear in the middle, just as in paintings. Moreover, the center of the Sun, the eye, and the Rainbow are all in one line. <margin>Why the rainbow is round in shape.</margin> For in this way, perpendicular rays are reflected from the hollow mist; and even though the mist itself might not be round, only those rays of the sun that are reflected from the round part—because only they are perpendicular—reflect the image of the Sun. Because this image is weak and weakly reflected, it presents the appearance of colors. For when light is rendered weak, it passes into a brilliant color; if it is weakened further, it changes into colors closer to black; then, if it reaches colors without light, it finally turns to black where there is the least light; and lastly, when light fails entirely, it passes into darkness. Therefore, since rays are reflected to the center only from the round and hollow part—even if the cloud is not hollow, and many droplets are in front—the rest of the entire cloud is indeed seen, but the perpendicular reflection occurs from the hollow and round part. This represents the rainbow (that is, the Sun), not otherwise than how you might see various and brilliant colors in drops of water. <margin>Why the rainbow appears in the shape of a semicircle while the Sun is on the horizon.</margin> Thus, when the Sun is on the <term>horizon</term> <note>original: "finitore"; the boundary circle of the observer's vision</note>, and the eye (as I said) is in a straight line with the center of the rainbow, the center of the rainbow will necessarily be on the horizon. Therefore, at that moment, the rainbow will appear exactly in the form of a semicircle: for the other half is necessarily entirely below the horizon if the Sun is upon it. <margin>Why the rainbow appears smaller when the Sun is higher.</margin> But when the Sun stands higher, it is manifest that a line drawn from the center of the Sun through the eye will fall below the horizon; therefore, the center of the rainbow will then be below the horizon. The higher the Sun stands, the lower the line drawn from the Sun through the eye will be, and consequently, so will the center of the rainbow which lies on this line. Thus, the further the center of the rainbow is below the horizon, the larger the part of the upper semicircle that is hidden from our eyes. Therefore, the higher the Sun is, the smaller the portion of a circle the rainbow must be. It is clear from this both that the middle part of the rainbow is without mist, and that since it lies hidden beneath the earth, the rainbow is nothing [there]: for the rays are not reflected from the center of the mist, but the center exists only in the imagination. <margin>Why only two rainbows can be seen at the same time.</margin> That only one can usually be seen is beyond doubt. For since the eye is on the line that proceeds from the Sun to the center of the mist, no other rainbow can be seen unless it shares that same center. But neither [can another appear] under the same center, since a reflection from the Sun cannot occur,

<header>On Light and Luminance.</header>

# ## On Light and Luminance.

<margin>
The order of colors in the secondary rainbow.
</margin>
For the eye holds the character of the center of a cavity—not because it is the exact center, but because from two points on the same line that comes from the center, two lines cannot be reflected to the same points at equal angles. It remains, therefore, that one is reflected from the first; for this reason, the second must be larger than the first, and much weaker, so that it is impossible for a third to arise from the second. Therefore, because the second arises from the first reflection, it is necessary that the inner lines or rays of the prior circle of the <term>Iris</term> <note>rainbow</note>, since they make a larger angle, bounce back further, while the outer ones bounce closer. For this reason, the inner circle of the secondary rainbow will be <term>cerulean</term> <note>blue</note> and the middle will be green, just as the outer circle of the first was <term>saffron</term> <note>yellow-orange</note>; the reasoning is exactly the inverse of the first.

<margin>
Why the rainbow does not appear at noon.
</term>
I believe it is also clear from these facts that when the Sun is at its midday point near the summer solstice, it has the greatest altitude in its half-circle. Because of this, the center of the rainbow's entire circular diameter is below the <term>horizon</term> <note>original: "finitore uisus"; the "finisher of sight"</note>; therefore, the rainbow will not be seen. But it will be seen near the autumnal equinox, throughout the winter, and after the vernal equinox, though it will appear smaller as it approaches the summer solstice and midday, as has been said.

<margin>
Why the smaller the portion of the circle the rainbow represents, the larger that circle's part seems to be.
</margin>
But why, when the rainbow is small and rises only slightly above the horizon, does it seem to be part of a much larger circle? The reason is that the eye judges the rainbow to be more distant the lower it is, because it perceives distance in the same way we described regarding the stars. When the eye judges the peak of the rainbow to be further away, it also estimates it to be wider—just as I mentioned regarding the rising Sun and Moon. But the larger angle of the circle shows that it is indeed larger, which anyone can easily understand by inscribing a smaller circle into a larger one so that they touch; for it appears that the larger one is wider in its surrounding line. For that reason, a smaller portion of the rainbow appears to be part of a larger circle.

<margin>
Rainbows from oars, lamps, and droplets.
</margin>
But rainbows are formed not only from clouds, but also from oars while they are moved in the sea by the reflection of light from water droplets. In winter, when the south wind blows, they are seen around lamps, especially by those who have "moist" eyes. They also appear from droplets sprayed on a wall while illuminated by the Sun, provided the eye is looking from a dark place directly toward them. There is one single cause for all these things, as Aristotle rightly reports.

<margin>
On the crown, sundogs, and rods.
</margin>
But <term>Parhelia</term> <note>sundogs</note>, <term>Virgae</term> <note>luminous "rods" or streaks</note>, and the <term>Corona</term> <note>halo</note> which we see around the Sun (they call it a <term>Halo</term>) have the same cause for their color as we have described. However, the Parhelia themselves are formed solely by reflection to the eye, with no actual image existing in the clouds; and thus the cloud at that time consists of small droplets.

<margin>
What the rainbow and sundogs signify.
</margin>
Therefore, the rainbow and sundogs usually announce gentle rains, because the droplets are made of water and are divided, and the Sun's ray penetrates them. The <term>Corona</term>, however, has substance: for it is made by the reflection of the Sun, or the Moon, or another star, as if from a center, out of a dense cloud in a surrounding circuit in a round shape. Thus, the eye does not "create" them as it does the rainbow and sundogs, but they are actually formed and exist within the clouds.

<margin>
How the true colors of the rainbow are made by crystal and glass.
</margin>
Similarly, if you expose a triangular crystal (a prism) or a hexagonal one to the Sun, you will see the colors of the rainbow—not false ones, but true ones—on the opposite wall. You may see the same thing if a glass vessel full of water is exposed to the Sun or even to a bright light. But they will be "false" <note>optical illusions</note> if you look directly into the crystal itself.

# Book Four

or glass; for the kind of rainbows you see, and where you see them while the Sun is present, a companion will not see at all—or they will see them differently, or not in the same place. This is because they are not real objects, but proceed only from the perspective of the eye's vision.
<margin>How the rainbow makes trees smell sweet.</margin>
Because of this, I wonder at those who affirm that wherever a rainbow has rested, it makes those plants fragrant, especially if they are already of such a nature: such as laurel, juniper, or myrtle. I believe rather that the cause is what I have previously stated: why the best earth smells sweet after a drought when a rain shower follows.
<margin>Aristotle, Problems, Book 12, Problem 3.</margin>
For who has ever seen a rainbow actually resting upon a tree, since, as I said, it exists only in the imagination of sight? Therefore, what ought to be said—following <term>Aristotle</term> <note>Referring to the Greek philosopher's "Meteorology" and "Problems"</note>—is that when a rainbow appears with droplets, there is a low-lying cloud which, coming upon trees already naturally fragrant after long droughts, immediately "cooks" the thin moisture of the droplets, which then vanishes into wonderfully fragrant vapors. Indeed, I saw this myself once on a summer morning upon a rose bush that was already withering; for such a fragrance wafted from the dew even without a rainbow that I would hardly dare compare anything else to it. For this reason, those who have seen the rainbow and are ignorant of its nature attribute the cause of the scent to the rainbow itself.
<margin>What the halo and "rods" foretell.</margin>
In contrast, the <term>halo</term> <note>original: "corona"; a circle of light around the sun or moon</note> and <term>rods</term> <note>original: "uirge"; likely light pillars or parhelic streaks</note> either remain undisturbed for a long time and predict rainstorms (for the cloud is dense if it remains unmoved so long and is not consumed or dissipated by the rays of the star), or, if part remains and part is suddenly dissipated—or all is dissipated at once—it foretells winds. These winds come from the direction that looms directly over the dissipated part, as if the wind were the string of the remaining arc of the Halo, or parallel to the topmost part or the side of the dissipated "rod." But if they fade away gradually, it is a sign of the thinness of the vapors and therefore a sign of clear weather.
<margin>How "rods" and sun-dogs differ; also the rainbow and halo.</margin>
However, <term>sun-dogs</term> <note>original: "pareliæ"; bright spots of light appearing on either side of the sun</note> and "rods" differ from each other, even though both are straight. (For the difference between the rainbow and the halo is not obscure, since the halo is a complete circle). "Rods" are oblong and distinguished by the colors of the rainbow—sometimes with one, often with two or more colors. Sometimes they appear at the top of the clouds as if looming over one's head; sometimes they appear as if descending according to the position of the clouds. They are not very wide but narrow, which is how they took their name. But sun-dogs are roundish or slightly oblong, showing a doubled Sun or Moon. Sometimes there is one on each side of the Sun, so that they occasionally reflect three Suns. I saw this once myself, and I could not distinguish well enough with my eye which was the true one; so brightly did those on the sides shimmer with rays. There was also at that time one rainbow and even a halo in the middle of the sky—a wonder to say, since no Sun was there, but all were in the

However, it is impossible for an image of the Sun to escape everyone’s notice, since so many mortals are out under the sky. They say that in Germany—where it is seen more frequently due to the height of the pole and the density of the clouds—this has been seen only twice in one lifetime. It is much whiter than the solar rainbow: so that instead of blue there is a dark green, instead of green a saffron yellow, and instead of saffron an almost white color is substituted. By these reasons it is clear—since the Sun or <margin>A rainbow in the south cannot be seen by us.</margin> Moon are never behind our heads toward the north <note>The author is writing from a Northern Hemisphere perspective.</note>—and because the center of the rainbow is on a line from the Sun through the eye, that a rainbow can only be observed in the east, the west, and the north: never in the south. This is true except for how much the difference between the Sun and the horizon allows in summer, when the walls toward the north are illuminated by its first rays in the morning. For when the Sun rises in summer where the circle of Cancer <margin>In summer, morning and evening shadows are as if southerly.</margin> cuts the horizon, the logic of the sphere teaches us that, for those of us looking south, it stretches out shadows so obliquely that they seem to tend toward the south. The same logic holds when it sets; for since the axis of the vertex descends to the center of the earth, but the Sun is carried in the circle of Cancer above the center of the earth, it is necessary that the closer the Sun is to the horizon, the more northerly it appears to us, since the line tending toward our vertex is truly northerly in comparison to the lowest part.

Since, as has been explained, vapors rise very little, and clouds far less—as **Albertus Magnus** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on natural philosophy.</note> estimates, no more than **15** stadia <term>stadia</term><note>An ancient Greek unit of distance; 15 stadia is approximately 1.7 miles or 2.7 kilometers.</note>—it is therefore as if angle **H C M** were at the center of the earth. Consequently, the ratio of **F L** to **L E** is known, and since **L E** to **L C** was already known from triangle **E L C**, the ratio of **F L** to **L C** is established. Therefore, by squaring **C F** and **F G**, the square root of their sum is the line **C G**, which is the distance from the location of the rainbow to where it touches the earth.

<margin>
How the largest possible rainbow can be seen.
</margin>
It is clear, however, that if someone were to climb a very high mountain, they would see a rainbow larger than a semicircle; and the higher the mountain stands, the larger the rainbow will appear, because the empty space before one's eyes allows for this proportion.

<margin>
How high the rainbow can be raised above the horizon.
</margin>
Nor is it right to be ignorant of the fact that the largest rainbow is raised no more than 42 degrees above the horizon <note>original: "finitorem"</note> in our regions. A rainbow becomes largest when the **Sun** is at its setting or its rising, and the line **C F** is at its longest. It follows, therefore, that it is also possible to know how great the maximum distance of the rainbow is from us, assuming its size is known; or indeed to find its size from the distance itself, as has been defined: by comparing line **F G** to the now known line **C G**.

<margin>
A star in the water due to a mirror.
</margin>
Now indeed, it is established from reflection that if a mirror <note>original: "speculum"</note> is placed under water, an image of the **Sun** will be reflected by the water which represents the **Sun** itself. Another image, however—which is narrowed at the surface of the water because of the density of the medium—will be reflected from the mirror and represents the image of a tiny star. People think there is some star near the **Sun** that is revealed by this trick, whereas it is well established that it is an image of the **Sun**, but refracted by the water into the mirror. People usually see this in the mirror when they are eager to observe a solar eclipse <term>eclipse</term><note>original: "deliquijs" (failures or fadings of light).</note>.

We have already demonstrated this in the figure above; and even more so because rays proceed from the entire Sun, not from a single point. The other reason is that as the shape increases the further it travels, the eye actually leaves behind that part of the object which is weaker than the smallest part of a thing it can see, as we have already assumed from the beginning. It is necessary that in eclipses <note>original: "deliquijs"</note>, the forms that are traced onto flat surfaces by rays passing <term>p</term> <note>original abbreviation for "per" (through)</note> through angular openings are neither angular nor round, but lunar, or shaped like a little boat. However, as I have said, it is clear that rays proceed from the entire Sun as if from a fire in every direction, because at the time of an eclipse <note>original: "deliquij," referring to a solar eclipse</note>, the part which is opposite the center is occupied by the Moon, and yet the air and walls are still illuminated.

<margin>How a concave mirror collects all rays into one.</margin>
There is also the logic of the concave mirror <term>concave mirror|a mirror curved inward like a bowl, which focuses light</term> showing this, because all rays could not come together into a single point unless they proceeded from the whole Sun. Imagine that the mirror was illuminated only from the center of the Sun; surely only one single ray would return to the center of the mirror. This is why a fire is always kindled in the center of a concave mirror: because all the rays from the Sun converge there. Indeed, Euclid rightly demonstrated this in his *Catoptrics* <note>original: "specularibus," referring to Euclid's work on the geometry of mirrors</note>. For from points A, B, C, D, and E, all rays are reflected into the center at F; therefore, a fire is kindled at F.

<margin>Why perpendicular rays alone are strong.</margin>
But you will rightly wonder, first, why the rays that are reflected back onto themselves—and these are only the perpendicular <term>perpendicular|rays hitting the surface at a direct 90-degree angle</term> ones—are strong. The cause is manifest: that which is reflected from the perpendicular returns onto itself, as from E into F and back from K; therefore, the entire ray is doubled along its length. However, a ray that reflects from another point into K merely intersects the other and passes away; and that which intersects at a point, intersects only at a point, and therefore offers no force. For since a point lacks quantity, it also lacks power; therefore, even if infinite rays are reflected through the same point, they are no more robust. For that which is nothing, no matter how much you redouble it, produces nothing. Therefore, in the case of rays that are not reflected from the perpendicular, there is no force at all where they intersect. Nevertheless, the closer they are to the perpendicular, the greater their force, because ray is near to ray; not because they intersect at a point—for the intersection matters nothing since, as I said, it occurs in an indivisible space—but because of their proximity. For if a ray clings to another ray along its length for a long time and over a great distance, the force of both joins into one and is, as it were, doubled. I say "as it were," because only the ray from the perpendicular, since it returns onto itself, exquisitely doubles its own power.

<margin>Final arrangement.</margin>
<margin>Why rays near the perpendicular are strong.</margin>
<margin>The larger the concave mirror, the more easily it ignites.</margin>
The second doubt was: if the mirror is large on the side of K and G, why do the reflected rays not illuminate the surrounding parts around F, so that at least some brightness is returned? In truth, all these rays are reflected below F. For if a ray is drawn from E to G, the angle E G K will be greater than the right angle in angle F G E; therefore, it will be reflected below F G through the angle F G E. Therefore, the larger the mirror is, and the larger the portion of its sphere, the more greatly and more quickly it kindles fire. However, a mirror of this kind cannot kindle a fire far away, since the rays are always forced into the center.

<margin>Why concave mirrors, although they reflect rays everywhere, do not provide an image everywhere.</margin>
There remains a third doubt of no small weight: since the rays which are on the side of E and C are reflected from point K—just as a ray proceeding from point D toward H will be reflected—they should at least illuminate the parts near F; yet experience shows the opposite. It is evident that this is more...

# On Light and Radiance.

...more so in the rays drawn from B and C into K. The cause of this is that they are scattered, and none is a perpendicular <term>perpendicular|a ray hitting a surface at a direct 90-degree angle</term> ray; moreover, the massive light in F obscures the nearby parts. A ray reflected from a concave mirror is even weaker than one from a plane mirror, because it slips away if it is not perpendicular. <margin>Causes of the strength of rays essentially and incidentally.</margin> Therefore, the causes of the strength of rays *per se* <note>essentially/by their own nature</note> are their convergence from the perpendicular, as in concave mirrors. Next to this is reflection from the perpendicular without convergence, as in plane mirrors directly exposed to the Sun. Third follows reflection not from the perpendicular, but nonetheless at equal angles, as from a plane mirror not directly exposed to the Sun; for the eye cannot endure this either. The fourth type returns an image but can be endured, when the rays are reflected at an equal angle but are scattered, as in concave mirrors outside of either pyramid <note>original: "pyramidem," here referring to a cone of light</note>—both the one from the center of the mirror to the mirror, and the one from the center of the mirror to the object seen—such as outside the pyramid F K L and F A C. The fifth is when rays are reflected from an unpolished body; these are useless for sight but not for heat, for these reflected perpendiculars, as I said, redouble the heat because of their convergence, but they do not return an image. However, the "accidental" causes of the strength of rays are said to be the size and proximity of the light source, and that the ray proceeds from the center of the light; then also the purity of the medium <note>the substance through which light travels, like air or water</note> and of the rays themselves. Due to these causes, it happens that one light turns out stronger than another; hence, because of the distance, we can tolerate the reflection of solar rays from the Moon and the stars (though they are purer), yet we cannot bear the light from crystal and water with our eyes.

<margin>In how many ways burning mirrors are made.</margin> Indeed, since there are seen to be three ways of kindling fire from a mirror: The first is so that all incident perpendicular rays are collected into one point through reflection; this happens, as has been said, with a spherical concave mirror. The second is so that all rays proceeding from the center of the Sun are reflected almost into a point, and this happens by means of a parabola, because due to the distance such rays converge as if into one, and take the place of only a single ray. This also happens from a plane mirror, but it does not kindle fire, nor is it permitted to place anything in between. The third way is so that all parallel rays which proceed from the Sun are collected into one point; this also happens by a parabola. I find in the works of Conrad Gessner <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss scholar and bibliographer</note> that Francesco Maurolico of Messina <note>An influential mathematician and astronomer (1494–1575)</note> wrote that the books of Archimedes exist concerning this, where he teaches that burning mirrors consist of a parabola. The matter stands thus: When a surface cuts a cone, and the diameter of the surface is parallel to the side of a triangle inscribed in the surface of the cone cutting through the vertex, and the first surface itself (which does not pass through the vertex) cuts its own base while being perpendicular to the line which stands at right angles to the axis and diameter of the former, the first surface is called a parabola, which is formed as A B C. Its straight line from the vertex B, dividing the underlying straight line A C with equal sides and the curves B A and B C, shall be called the diameter B D. One must then find a single line, say B F, which will always have such a proportion to any perpendicular...

# Book Four

...from the side meeting the diameter, just as its own perpendicular is to the part of the diameter intercepted between the vertex and the perpendicular. Just as that line E F is formed, so E F will have the same proportion to H K as H K has to K B; and similarly, E F will have the same proportion to A D as A D has to D B, and so on for the others. It is therefore established that it is necessary for that line E F (of which E G is half) to be double B C; E F will then be called the <term>latus rectum|literally 'the straight side'; in geometry, this is the chord through the focus of a conic section perpendicular to the major axis</term>, and all lines parallel to B D, or the rays, will be reflected into G. Or more briefly, since it comes to the same thing: if that line is set as A D, then A D is equal to D B, and B G is a fourth part of B D. For it does not matter whether the side is extended from side to side, or from the side to the diameter, provided you know that the point of convergence is distant from point B by a fourth part of the *latus rectum*.

<margin>
On the mirror that burns ships approaching from afar.
See Galen, *On Temperaments*, book 3, chapter 2.
</margin>

But if the intention is to make a mirror that burns from a distance, such as Galen <note>Galen (129–c. 216 AD) was a Greek physician and philosopher; here the author refers to his account of Archimedes' inventions.</note> relates that Archimedes made (who burned the enemies' triremes <note>Ancient warships with three banks of oars.</note>): it is manifest that the mirrors, whether they are derived from a <term>parabola|a symmetrical open plane curve formed by the intersection of a cone with a plane parallel to its side</term>, or from a circle and a sphere, must be very large—that is, portions of the largest spheres or the largest cones, but not the largest part of the parabolas. For example, if one wishes to project fire to a distance of 1,000 paces, we will describe a circle whose diameter is 2,000 paces. We will take such a portion of this that the roundness is not hidden, namely a sixtieth part, to which we will add the diameter for the height at one end; and with the diameter fixed, we will rotate the part of the circle, which will describe for us a portion of a sphere. When we have polished this and exposed it to the Sun, it will ignite a very powerful fire far off at 1,000 paces. Nowadays, however, it is not so useful because of military engines <note>likely referring to the advent of gunpowder and cannons</note>; but in the past, it was a most secure defense. The burning that proceeds from a parabola is more violent, but more laborious to construct.

<margin>
A mirror that reveals hidden things.
</margin>

Truly, since I have begun to relate marvelous things about mirrors, I have proposed to teach the construction of a mirror by which we may see hidden things. Take two flat mirrors made of artificial crystal, such as those made in Venice <note>Venice, specifically the island of Murano, was the world leader in high-quality glass and mirror production during the Renaissance.</note> (because they do not deteriorate as much as steel ones), and join them exactly at the edges: so that the length of one adheres perfectly to the length of the other, and so that it can be rotated around an axis like a hinge. In this way, the surface of one may sometimes form a single plane with the surface of the other, and sometimes a solid, right, obtuse, or acute angle, as desired. Then, you shall suspend a fixed mirror high up, directly facing the hidden place, so that the face of the mirror hangs perpendicular to your floor. The face of the movable mirror should have its length opposite the place you desire; then, whatever is done in that room, provided light is present, you will observe everything by rotating the movable mirror until it makes an equal angle—which your eye will reveal to you when you see what you are looking for.

<page-num>107</page-num>
<header>On Light and Brightness.</header>

# On Light and Brightness.

If the place you wish to see is higher than where you are, hang the mirror in a more elevated position.

By the same logic, if you want to see something far away—say, five miles <note>original: "v M. passuum," literally five thousand paces, the Roman mile.</note> off—and there are walls in between, or it is in a hostile city, hang a mirror as large as possible in a high place, positioned either perfectly vertical or parallel to the horizon. Then, holding another mirror in your hand so that its face looks toward the mirror you placed above (neither completely flat nor perfectly upright), gradually move yourself away from the direct line of the first mirror. Turn slightly left and right until you can clearly see the location in your own mirror. Then, keeping it steady, you will see whatever is being done there. As I said, this device serves no other purpose than to hinder the fire-throwing machines of the enemy.

<margin>
A method for viewing hidden places in their natural colors.
</margin>
If you would like to see what is happening in the street, place a glass sphere <note>A solid glass ball or thick lens used to focus light.</note> in the window while the Sun is shining. Then, closing the window, you will see images transmitted through the hole onto the opposite surface—though the colors will be dim. Place a very white sheet of paper where you see the images, and you will achieve your aim with wonderful results. A concave mirror will show double faces, four eyes, or three; it can make you look one-eyed or show your image reversed, along with countless other wonders. This is true not only of spherical mirrors but also of conical and cylindrical ones. <margin>Mirrors representing various things.</margin> This last type [the cylindrical] will represent even stranger things: four faces, or an image that is long and extremely narrow, or very short and wide. And what then? It shows almost everything except the truth—much like the people of this age, who know how to do everything better than doing good or telling the truth.

<margin>
Mirrors that represent images in the air in a wonderful way.
</margin>
There are also mirrors that show many faces, being made of many flat surfaces; others that start fires, being made of many circles; and finally, there are infinite monstrous composite shapes which would be pointless to list. Let us now show those that project images into the air. We spoke of concave mirrors above; there are also convex spherical ones, but the most exquisite are convex cylindrical ones. Set a slit in a window directly across from some painted board <note>A "tabula picta" refers to a painted panel or sign.</note>, so that it can be seen from somewhere in the room through the slit. In that spot, place a convex cylindrical mirror on a tripod, perpendicular to the floor. Position your eye so that you can see the board outside through the mirror; you will then see that image hanging in the air between the mirror and the window slit.

<margin>
A mirror that represents flying men.
</margin>
If you wish to see flying men in a mirror, so that they appear to fly, four things are necessary: they must move, and they must wave their arms. The person you wish to see flying (whether it be yourself or others) will provide these two. You could also simulate movement by moving the mirror, though that is quite difficult. The third requirement is that they hang high up, so as not to seem stuck to the ground...

### Book Four

...it may seem to be: the fourth is that the feet, as if in flying birds, are equidistant from the floor along with the head and arms; these two things the mirror will provide most beautifully. Therefore, you shall compose two equal beams joined at a right angle, so that the right angle is at the top, and smooth them in the manner of a <term>gnomon</term> <note>A gnomon is usually the shadow-casting part of a sundial, but here refers to an L-shaped carpenter's square or frame.</note>. Next to the inner angle, set up two large flat mirrors facing each other at an equal height, which you understand well enough must be hanging. When you move away from these just enough so that in one you can see your heel perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem," literally 'to the fingernail,' a Latin idiom for perfection.</note>, by moving in a straight line and swinging your arms, you will appear to be watching yourself flying.

<margin>How to see your image approaching and receding at the same time.</margin>
By the same reasoning we have mentioned, if you place two mirrors touching each other and existing on one flat surface, arranged so that as one approaches you, the other recedes—which happens if they are placed straight and vertically upon a beam, and a cord wound around them is gradually unwound—you will see your image approaching in one mirror, and in the other, moving away.

<margin>How you may view your back.</margin>
If you wish to see your back, you can easily achieve this with two flat mirrors; the larger they are, the better. First, place one behind you in a position halfway between lying flat and standing upright. Place the other in a higher spot than you are, between tilted forward and upright, before your eyes: you will be able to see whatever you have on your back perfectly.

<margin>What occurs with two mirrors.</margin>
Remember also if, for example, you place a ring opposite a mirror, and the ring itself is a mirror—perhaps with an enclosed Sapphire—you will see the image of the ring in the mirror, and in the gemstone of that ring, your own image will appear. This happens due to multiple reflection. The same will happen with two mirrors, and with an even greater miracle in three.

<margin>How we see the womb and the throat.</margin>
But if the goal is to see deep and dark places like the womb <note>Here, "uterum" likely refers generally to internal cavities or the abdomen in a medical context.</note>, the throat, or a dark room, place a large glass jar full of water directly in front of the spot. Place a light behind the jar so that the jar is in the middle of a straight line between the light and the place you wish to see. Then, having removed all other light, position your eye where you do not block the light from the jar but can still look into the spot; you will see everything as if in bright light.

<margin>Wonders of the crystal prism.</margin>
A crystal <term>prism</term> <note>A solid triangular glass or crystal used to refract light.</note> truly possesses many of the powers of mirrors, such as reflecting many shapes; it even captures them upside down with heads at the bottom and feet at the top, like concave mirrors. It can make people look one-eyed or four-eyed. In it, the most beautiful and inimitable colors appear, especially when it is placed lengthwise facing the Sun. When applied to the eyes—especially where there are trees and meadows—it reflects a celestial beauty: crowns, rainbows, and carpets scattered everywhere, with the most brilliant colors—rosy, white, green, scarlet, blue, golden, and all of them mixed—offering a most pleasing sight. It shows another image of things high up and reversed, as if the plains were rising into mountains. It even fashions the <term>horizon</term> <note>original: "finitorem," the 'finisher' or boundary of sight.</note> and distant regions with a very great distance and a joyful view, such as does not weaken the eye but refreshes it:

## On Light and Luminosity.

...created: however, it is necessary that the <term>prism</term><note>A transparent optical element with flat, polished surfaces that refract light; in the 16th century, these were often made of high-quality glass or rock crystal.</note> be large and the crystal of the purest quality.

But truly, having now left behind mirrors and crystals, it seems time that I should report some false images of direct sight—namely, how one thing can be seen as two. This happens because sight normally functions correctly when the rays fall upon the <term>pupil</term> orthogonally—or you might say perpendicularly—and are carried as if in a straight line to the junction of the nerves <note>A reference to the optic chiasm, where the optic nerves from both eyes meet.</note>. Therefore, when the eyes are tilted so that the nerves are strained upward or downward, one thing will appear as two. And generally, whatever things are perceived as distinct in place, shape, size, or color will appear as two, even if they are actually one. This happens whether one of the eyes is moved from its place, or if we see through different media—such as if a lens is placed before one eye while the other sees through pure air, or if an object is partly in water and partly in air. In such cases, things are judged to be broken or double. Likewise, if an object is placed between the eyes that prevents a single thing from being seen—which, if it is not placed correctly relative to the position of the eyes (as if equidistant) or shows various colors—then two things will be more firmly thought to be one.

<margin>The variety of things hindering sight.</margin>
For certain things near the eye do not hinder vision at all because they are smaller than the distance between the eyes; yet at a distance, they cover the object being viewed. Conversely, other things close to the eyes do hinder sight but do so very little at a distance, because the angle formed by them is narrowed near the eye due to the distance. By this same logic, things that are painted on a flat surface appear to be solid.

<margin>The method of painting a solid on a flat surface.</margin>
This illusion occurs chiefly for two reasons. The first is **shadow**, from which the eye derives its judgment: if there is shadow, the eye assumes a shadowed and solid body. Indeed, the senses have become so accustomed to this judgment through long-standing habit that they act instinctively—much as it is reported that in the recently discovered and previously uninhabited islands, birds that do not flee are caught by hand <note>This is a common Renaissance metaphor; the author suggests that our sensory perception of depth is a "learned instinct" so powerful it functions like a natural reflex.</note>. The second reason is that you must consider which part of the body is visible, such as the top, front, right, or left of a **cube**; the remaining surfaces are hidden. From there, you will position the shadow relative to the light (which you imagine to be before you) at a height of half a right angle <note>original: "dimidij recti," referring to a 45-degree angle, a standard for consistent lighting in perspective drawing.</note>, and the body according to the lines extending from the eye to the cube on the plane. You can also establish the view from a corner and the light from the side. Again, the method for a panel hanging on a wall is one thing, and the method for a panel lying beneath the eyes and hands, parallel to the **horizon**, is another. Truly, in all these cases, the common rule is that you must position the object in the same place and represent the same angles and points on the flat surface—toward the eyes and toward the light—as the boundaries of the thing seen. For when the angles are equal and assisted by colors and shadows, they must necessarily represent the same bodies. For the same thing represents the same, and the like represents the like.

<margin>The method of measurements in painting.</margin>
Remember, however, to observe a level point of sight; this is located at the head of a human figure when a person is painted in the scene. For whatever things are seen below that level will appear low, and whatever is above it will appear high, just as the eye would judge if they were truly in such a position. Therefore, to represent solids, there are these four...

<header>Book Four</header>

## Book Four

<margin>Painting is the imitation of the appearances <note>original: "affectuum"; here referring to the physical qualities or dispositions of an object as perceived by the eye.</note> found in bodies in relation to light.</margin>
...to be completed: the form of a thing is derived from the rays of the eyes, the shadow from the rays of light, and the color should be none other than that of the body itself when placed under that specific light and in that specific position. Finally, the placement on the panel must be established in relation to the person being depicted, whose crown should be level with your eyes. For what else is painting but an imitation of the physical qualities found in bodies in relation to light, rendered upon a single plane? For even if it is possible to guess the dispositions of the soul from a painting, it is only insofar as they are expressed through physical appearances. I said "in relation to light" because the face of a living person will appear one way in the rays of the Sun, another in the obscurity of night, another in the light of the Moon, and another by the light of a candle; for this reason, it is fitting to experiment by bringing a lamp near.

<margin>Certain things are seen better from a distance than from nearby.</margin>
Why do you wonder at light? Since some things are visible from a distance that are hidden up close—as on my steel purse, a pattern marked with square black lines is visible from afar but otherwise unseen. So too the stars are seen at night which are hidden by day; for this reason, they <note>likely referring to artists or observers</note> also assist their work with a <term>reticulum</term> <note>A grid or "little net" used by artists to help maintain correct proportions and perspective.</note>. <margin>An aid for painting correctly.</margin> For in a small space, even the smallest error cannot remain hidden, and it directs the hand of the artist toward correctness.

<margin>On the mirror for testing paintings.</margin>
For almost the same reason, paintings should be tested with a mirror. For since a mirror shows things in reverse, it reveals many things that were previously hidden. Just as arrangement hides many things—which is why <term>jewelers</term> <note>original: "gemmarij"</note> arrange pearls in a certain order, placing flawed ones in the middle and the most beautiful at the outer edges, gradually descending from the beautiful to the baser ones so that the base ones are not recognized by comparison—sometimes placing those that retain charm despite a change in flaws next to each other—so, by the opposite logic, the mirror detects faults by reversing the previous order that made the painting pleasing. Thus, because a mirror shows everything in a contrary and backward order, we can correctly read letters written in reverse when the mirror represents them.

<margin>The order of colors that harmonize with one another.</margin>
Furthermore, to return to painting, colors should not be arranged haphazardly: but if dark colors have a place among light ones, and light among dark, they bring beauty and ornament to the painting. Therefore, red should be placed between blue and green, <margin>White color is a poison to paintings.</margin> and white should be interposed between ash-gray and saffron-yellow. But one must be careful not to use much white in paintings: for it is like a poison to them. For by its brightness, it first takes away the charm and a certain dignity from the work of art, obscures the remaining colors, and spoils the shadows of things.

But colors must be discussed again in their proper place. For now, we have begun a discourse on light, luminosity, and the shadow that follows these. <margin>Why, although the Sun is larger than the Earth, it does not send straight rays and shadows everywhere.</margin> Therefore, since we have said that rays proceed from the whole Sun, and that the Sun itself is far larger than the Earth, many are filled with wonder as to why shadows are not straight for everyone, and why it is not summer everywhere always? But the cause of this is that, although perpendicular rays are carried down to the Earth as if it were flat—for this is accom-

<page-num>333</page-num>

# On Light and Luminescence.

<note>original: "De Luce & Lumine"</note>

...[necessary], yet these rays of the sun are not directed toward the center of the earth. Since the earth is round and not flat, the rays reaching us cannot be perpendicular based on the position of things resting on the earth. Consequently, the sun touches only the peak <note>original: "uerticem"; the highest point relative to the observer</note> as if from a single point from a northern direction; therefore, it cannot produce southern shadows. You can easily illustrate this with a figure if you draw two circles, one smaller and one larger. In the smaller one, if you draw lines from the center and extend them slightly outside the circle, consider whatever is outside to be people, plants, towers, and mountains. You will see how small a space is occupied by those who can receive rays from the larger circle from both sides. Therefore, only those who are directly beneath the sun for a distance of half [of that space]—that is, for 1,044 miles <note>original: "paffuum M.xliiij."; Roman paces or miles</note>—will have straight shadows.

<margin>Why it is not summer everywhere.</margin>
While this is easy to understand, it is more difficult to give a reason why it is not summer everywhere all the time, since solar rays fall perpendicularly onto the plane of the earth everywhere. But you will say they are not perpendicular, for they do not tend toward the center of the earth. Yet that does not seem sufficient, since the logic of reflection (as we have shown) gains its strength from the ray returning upon itself; but the size of the earth causes this; for even flat mirrors reflect at a perpendicular if they are placed flat on the ground. 

<margin>How flat mirrors should be placed in the Sun to produce a perpendicular ray.</margin>
But this is not so: on the contrary, reflected rays tend toward the opposite side of the sun. How then will a <term>perpendicular: a line meeting another at a 90-degree angle</term> reflection occur from flat mirrors? This happens when it is exposed to the sun in such a way that its surface, if understood to be extended as far as I wish, will always be equidistant to the flat surface touching the sun at a point through which a line produced from the center of the sun passes straight to the surface of the mirror. Imagine, therefore, lines coming from the center of the earth to its surface meeting planes at right angles <note>original: "orthogonias"</note>. You will understand that these planes do nothing to ensure that the rays from the sun—even though the sun is far larger than the earth—are at right angles <note>original: "orthogonij"</note> to those planes. Since, therefore, the rays of the sun come to us and our flat land, they are not perpendicular in relation to the center of the earth (since they do not tend toward the earth’s center), nor are they like rays on an upright mirror surface (since the plane of the earth is that upon which the perpendicular from the earth's center falls). Nor can this plane be equidistant to the plane of the sun into which the perpendicular from the sun's center comes straight. In neither way will they come to us as perpendiculars; therefore, summer will not be everywhere. 

<margin>Buildings which can greatly heat the air.</margin>
It is clear from these points that buildings can be constructed which will heat the air significantly even in winter. These buildings should not be erected perpendicular to the center of the earth; rather, they should be built so that they receive the winter sun at a right angle. To provide an example, let our dwelling be at A, on the plane AF; let the perpendicular to the center of the earth be AB, which is known to be 44 and a half degrees distant from the equinoctial circle. It will therefore be 68 degrees distant from the winter circle. Let there be a quarter of a circle BCF, and let bc be 22 parts out of the 90 parts that make up BF; point C will therefore be 90 degrees distant from the winter <insert>sun</insert>...

## Book Four

...the winter tropic <note>original: "hyemali tropico"; the Tropic of Capricorn, the sun's lowest point in the sky for the northern hemisphere</note>: therefore, when the Sun is there, if a flat or hollow cylindrical surface A C is erected, it will receive perpendicular rays at midday. If an arc C E of 47 degrees <note>The 47-degree arc represents the total distance between the summer and winter solstices (approx. 23.5 degrees each way from the equator).</note> is also made, and markings are drawn according to the Sun's declination for each day, and the mass A C is moved back accordingly; in this way, it will receive perpendicular rays throughout the entire year. This allows you to have vegetables and fruits before their natural season, and it makes for a pleasant dwelling.

<margin>Only a sphere does not change its shadow by its orientation.</margin>
<margin>The calculation of the size of shadows.</margin>
Now, for these reasons, you understand not only the dual nature of perpendicular rays but also the differences in shadows. These shadows change in all bodies based on the body’s orientation—except for the sphere. For a sphere, while remaining in the same place and with the light source staying still, produces the same shadow regardless of its rotation. This is not so for other bodies. For instance, if rods <note>original: "uirgæ"; thin sticks or measuring poles</note> are extended along the length of the Sun's rays, they produce almost no shadow at all, except for the thickness of the rod itself. However, if a rod is positioned so that its shadow falls perpendicularly upon the shadow of another upright rod on a flat surface, then this shadow will be a "middle shadow," exactly equal to the length of the rod—except for what might be lost due to the <margin>The end of shadows for all bodies in the Sun.</margin> distance from the ground because of the Sun's immense size, though that loss is very small. Indeed, it is so small that every body exposed to the Sun terminates its shadow at a distance equal to one hundred and nine times the <term>diameter<note>The width of a circular or spherical object passing through its center.</note></term> of that body. Such is the nearly exact proportion of the Sun's distance from the Earth to the Sun's own diameter. From this, a clear method is revealed for <margin>A method for knowing the proportion of any celestial body to its height.</margin> knowing the proportion of the height of any star <note>original: "syderis"; in this context, it refers to any celestial body, including the sun or planets.</note> to its size. For if you place a sphere of a known diameter on a mountaintop, you will see at what distance its shadow ends; from that, you can conclude that the ratio of the height to the star's diameter is the same as the ratio of the straight distance to the shadow's end to the diameter of the sphere. Therefore, when you place another rod perpendicularly over a rod parallel to the ground (which creates a "middle shadow"), so that the solar ray itself falls perpendicularly upon it, then the largest possible shadow will be created that can come from such a size and such a solar position. This shadow will be not a little larger than the length of the rod itself; this happens because of the inclination of the Earth's surface relative to the position of the surface upon which the perpendicular ray from the center of the Sun falls. All other shadows are formed between these extremes, and the causes of their size or smallness are mixed according to how much they approach or recede from these simple positions.

However, to return to the height of the Sun and the other stars, it is a matter of wonder <margin>Why the stars follow us as we travel while riverbanks recede.</margin> why all the stars seem to follow us as we travel, while the riverbanks seem to recede from us and move backward when we are carried past in a boat. The reason is not obscure: since the distance of the stars has a vast proportion to the entire size of the Earth, our forward movement cannot change the perceived location of the star. For what the eye does not perceive is as if it were not there at all.
