## On Light and Illumination.

...as we have already taught. When, therefore, a star—for the sake of example—is ahead of us by the width of a cubit <note>original: "cubiti magnitudine"; a cubit was an ancient unit of measure, here used to describe the perceived angular distance in the sky</note>, even when we have traveled three thousand paces, the star must still appear to be a cubit ahead of us. This is because three thousand paces, when compared to the vast height of the star, create no perceptible angle. Therefore, as we move forward, because the star always seems to stay a cubit ahead, it necessarily appears to move along with us; by the same logic, the stars behind our backs necessarily seem to follow us. 

However, if you watch someone else walking while you yourself remain still, those stars will not seem to move. In that case, the stars will not maintain the same position relative to your eye because of the difference in perspective; for some stars will appear to have been left behind your back which were previously in front of you. Since this change in perspective does not happen when we ourselves are the ones moving—but rather we see the stars always in the same position relative to our location as they were before—it is necessary for this reason that they seem to travel with us and accompany us perpetually. 

But in a ship, since we seem to ourselves to be at rest while the ship is moving, the things that were in front are left behind our backs. Therefore, since the eye perceives motion but the mind thinks we are still (because we are at rest within the ship), it necessarily judges the banks and trees to be moving toward us and then passing behind us; this is the opposite of how we perceive the motion of the stars.

<margin>Why the Sun and its rays appear to be at rest, even though they circle the Earth in 24 hours.</margin>
For the same reason, a doubt arises—though in the opposite way—as to why the rays of the Sun and the Sun itself do not appear to move, even though they travel around the entire circumference of the Earth, and the Sun across the heavens. Neither the Sun in the sky nor its rays on the earth seem to move, even though the rays themselves travel thousands of thousands of paces <note>original: "millies millena passuum"; millions of miles</note> every single hour, if not even more. 

Regarding the Sun, the reason is that the circle in which it is carried does not appear large to the eye; therefore, the motion is seen, but the Sun itself does not seem to be "moving" <note>The author distinguishes between knowing the Sun has changed position over time and actually seeing the motion happen in real-time.</note> because it advances so gradually. The space it is perceived to cross is minimal; to put it more clearly, the angle it creates at every moment due to its motion is imperceptible. Therefore, according to our principles which we taught earlier, the Sun will not appear to move, nor will any other star for the same reason. 

However, there is a different reason regarding the rays. Indeed, by their motion, they create a perceptible angle in the eye, and therefore they ought to appear to move. The reason they do not seem to move is this: imagine the Earth, whose center is <term>A</term>, and its plane (as I said) which is represented by point <term>D</term>, though to us, because of its size, it appears as the line <term>B C</term>. Imagine a tower which is perpendicular to the plane <term>D E</term>, and the edge of the Sun at <term>F</term>. When the Sun produces a ray <term>F E H</term>, it creates a shadow <term>H D</term>. When the Sun has moved to position <term>G</term>, producing the ray <term>G E K</term>, it leaves the shadow <term>K D</term>. Therefore, since the rays <term>F H</term> and <term>G K</term> are judged as one by the eye, the Sun only appears to have moved from <term>H</term> to <term>K</term> while the actual Sun moves from <term>F</term> to <term>G</term>. But the space <term>H K</term> is small when compared to the height of the tower <term>D E</term>, which is...

# Book Four

...[continually], therefore, since it moves gradually and traverses only the space *H K*—say, in a quarter of an hour—at any single moment it traverses no space that would form an angle perceptible to the eye. Therefore, based on that frequently repeated premise, the ray *F H* will appear to remain at rest while it is actually moving.

But you will say: I clearly see the reason why it appears to be at rest, but I do not see how it can traverse thousands of miles <note>original: "passuum millena"; Roman miles, each consisting of a thousand paces</note> in one hour if it only moves from *H* to *K*. The reason for this is that the ray *F E H* is not the same as *G E K*, but changes for every moment. For since the Sun moves in the circle of its own orbit, the point which illuminates *E*, which is *F*, always moves higher; because of this change, the Sun's light on the earth appears to shimmer perpetually. Since one ray after another follows perpetually and this change happens extremely quickly, it creates the appearance of a shimmering object. Another reason, which is greater and more relevant to the matter, is that this motion is very unequal in comparison to the tower *D E*. For even if in an hour it traverses a space of only two cubits—for instance, when the Sun is at midday—in another hour it travels an infinite distance, such as in the final hour of the day. In that hour, a shadow of (for example) a thousand cubits becomes infinite; for when the Sun's altitude from the line *B C* (extended to the heavens of the Sun) is as great as the height of *D E*, then it is clear that the shadow of the tower will be infinite.

<margin>Why the Sun’s illumination on the earth always seems to shimmer.</margin>
<margin>How the altitude of any celestial body from the earth may be obtained at any hour.</margin>
Once these things are understood, human ingenuity has progressed so far that it is able to find the altitude of any celestial body <note>original: "syderis"; the author uses this to refer to stars, planets, or the sun</note> at any hour from the center of the earth. Therefore, let there be a celestial body *F*—whether at its center or the part where it can be seen, I do not mind—and a rod *D E*, which is of a known length and perpendicular to the plane *B C* in the previous figure, and let its shadow *D H* be known. I take the altitude of the body *F* using a planisphere <note>a portable astronomical instrument used to map the stars and calculate their positions</note>, which, when subtracted from 90 <note>original: "lxxxx"; the degrees in a right angle</note>, gives me the angle *F A E*. But because the angle *D* of the triangle *H D C* is a right angle, and the proportion of the shadow *H D* to the measure *D C* is known, then from a table of chords and arcs <note>an early form of trigonometric tables used before the modern sine and cosine system</note>, the angle *D E H* will be known, and therefore the remaining angle *A E F*. Consequently, the final angle *A F E* is also known, since we have already shown that *A* is the angle of the difference of the altitude from 90 degrees. Therefore, all the angles of the triangle *A F E* are known, as is the proportion of the sides from the same table. Since *A C* is the diameter of the earth (for the rod *D E* is not significant in size relative to it), the proportion of *A F* to *A D* will be known. But *A D* is, as we have said, five thousand miles; therefore, it is known how many thousands of miles *A F* is.

<margin>The construction of the rod by which the altitude of celestial bodies is obtained.</margin>
If you seek the angle *F A E* not from a planisphere but from the location of the celestial body itself, you will act more correctly. However, you must have a rod *D E* with a steel circle at the bottom upon which a square <note>original: "orthogonia"; an instrument for ensuring a 90-degree right angle</note> rests, and the plane must be perfectly smooth on the lower part of the circle so that when it is applied to a surface, you can tell if that surface is truly flat. It should also have lead plumb lines <note>original: "plumbea pependicula"; weights hung on strings to determine a perfect vertical line</note> hanging from the four sides at the top, and it should be of a known size from the very top down to the lowest surface of the steel circle. When the rod is fixed as far as that circle and adheres to the plane on all sides, and the plumb lines also hang flush with the rod, then that plane is truly flat, and it is such that a line drawn into it from the center of the earth...

<margin>How we may find the magnitude of any celestial body.</margin>
If you should later wish to know the magnitude <note>size or diameter</note> of a celestial body <note>original: "syderis"; refers to stars, planets, or the sun/moon</note> as well, you can find it from the end of the shadow, as I said above, once you already know the altitude. However, because determining this end of the shadow is laborious and not at all easy—especially with celestial bodies other than the Sun and Moon—you may achieve this very easily by another way. Take the diameter of the celestial body on a planisphere <note>original: "planisphærio"; a device used to map the stars onto a flat surface</note>, double it, and add a nineteenth part to it; then always divide seven thousand two hundred by this sum. The resulting number is the ratio of the altitude to the diameter of the celestial body. Since you already have the known altitude of the body and the ratio of that altitude to its diameter, it is clear that the diameter is also known. For example, let us suppose the diameter of a celestial body is nine and a half minutes <note>arcminutes, a unit of angular measurement</note>. I will double this, making nineteen minutes, to which I always add a nineteenth part (on account of the size of the diameter on the table), making twenty minutes. I divide seven thousand two hundred by this, and the result is three hundred sixty. Therefore, it is manifest from this that the diameter of that celestial body is a three-hundred-and-sixtieth part of its altitude. Thus, it is clear from all these things how much utility the study of rays provides, and how subtle a contemplation it is.

# BOOK FIVE
## On mixture, and im-
## perfect mixtures, or
## metallic things.

<margin>Observations of the Moon for the preservation of flour and beer.</margin>
**H**itherto, nearly five parts of the entire work have been completed: first, on the more hidden principles—matter, form, vacuum, and the union of bodies; second, on the elements, since the principles would now be complete, absolute, and manifest; third, on the heavens; fourth, on light and illumination. We have not fully completed the fifth part, which concerns things that appear, since much is missing that pertains to the ears and other senses, as well as the mind and even the eyes. Now, therefore, we must deal with mixtures. For mixtures require those first principles, as well as the elements, the heavens, and light; for that reason, we treated those first. That these mixtures themselves require the heavens, and how much the constitution of the heavens can influence these lower things, can be perceived by manifest proofs. For flour that is made from grain by a mill in the month of August is usually kept uncorrupted among us for the whole year. And beer <note>original: "zythum"; an ancient Greek term for beer, originally associated with Egyptian fermented drinks</note> which is made during the March Moon is said to last the whole year, whereas in summer it remains unspoiled for twenty days, and in winter for two months. The cause may be that in the month of March, the seeds of the willow-wolf <note>original: "lupi salictarij"; the plant we now call hops (*Humulus lupulus*), which was believed to "strangle" willows like a wolf among sheep</note> are still alive, while the moisture is then clearly consumed—for that time is furthest from when that seed was collected—because of this, it can produce an effective and minimally damp Beer or ale <note>original: "Birram seu ceruisiam"; the author notes that Germans gave these names to the "zythum" described by the ancient physician Dioscorides</note>. The seed is effective then because it is accustomed to sprout at that time.

<margin>The wonder of the Pleiades herbs. Pliny, book 18, chapter 27.</margin>
There are infinite experiments on this matter: for the Pleiades herbs <note>original: "Vergiliae herbae"; referring to plants whose life cycles were thought to be linked to the rising and setting of the Pleiades constellation, known in Latin as the Vergiliae</note> rise and set with the stars of the same name. But I am compelled to repeat only this: that all these mixtures, with the sole exception of man, consist of earth, water, and celestial heat. Part of these lie hidden under the earth, others in the waves, and others truly above the earth; now, however, it is my purpose to speak of those which nature keeps hidden.

<margin>It is demonstrated that there are four kinds of all those things which lie hidden under the earth.</margin>
Therefore, whatever mixtures are under the earth or the waters and are devoid of motion are divided into four kinds: Earths, juices <note>original: "succos"; in early modern science, this referred to "congealed juices" or minerals that could be dissolved, such as salts, vitriols, or bitumens</note>, stones, and metals. It is shown by this argument that there cannot be more kinds: for they either melt and, upon returning to their own form, remain hard—and these are called metals. For a metal is nothing other than that which can melt and remains hard when it returns to a solid state. By "hard," I mean two things: that which does not easily yield, and is not easily broken.

# On Mixtures and Metallic Substances.

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's discussion on the properties of matter.</note> Therefore, it is manifest that every substance which can be "led" <note>original: "duci"; referring to ductility, or the ability of a material to be hammered thin or drawn into wire</note> is of such a sort; for example, **bitumen** <note>a naturally occurring petroleum product like asphalt or tar</note> can be led and does not resist. **Crystal** resists, as does **antimony** <note>original: "stibium"; a brittle, silvery-white metalloid</note> even more so, but they cannot be led; for this reason, they are easily shattered when struck. That which melts, yet is not hard when it returns to a solid state, is called a **juice** <note>original: "succus"; in early mineralogy, this referred to "solidified juices" like salts, vitriols, or bitumens that could be dissolved or melted</note>. That which does not melt at all is either called **stone**, if it is hard, or **earth**, if it is soft and very easily crumbles into the smallest pieces.

<margin>There are eleven types of composite bodies.</margin>
Besides these four, however, there are many other types of bodies mixed from them. If one knows how to count correctly, he will find there are eleven, and no more. These are: juice, stone, juice-earth, juice-metal, metal-stone, metal-earth, earth-stone, then juice-earth-stone, juice-earth-metal, juice-stone-metal, earth-stone-metal, and finally juice-stone-earth-metal. Examples of the "simple" forms are **sulfur** for juices, **crystal** for stone, **Lemnian earth** <note>a medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos</note> for earth, and **silver** for metal. I shall provide examples of the composite forms in their proper place, lest I be forced to repeat many things uselessly. These examples of simple substances were necessary because I will not treat all of them at once: for I call those that remain solid and "perfect" **metals and stones**, about which I shall speak later. The softer things I call "imperfect," including both the mixtures, the juices, and the earths; I shall name all of these **metallic things**, to distinguish them from stones and metals proper. Therefore, I shall now begin to learn about these metallic things, taking my start from the types of earths.

<margin>On the distinctions of earths.</margin>
The types of earths are distinguished by their colors, their scent, or their use. We have spoken generally above regarding those distinguished by use; the discussion concerning the other distinctions of color is also complete. It remains for us to speak of the use of certain ones, and also of their scent.

<margin>Sweet-smelling earth.</margin>
Scented earths are rare, while those that smell foul are common. For all that have a scent are mixed with metallic parts. **Agricola** <note>referring to Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "Father of Mineralogy"</note> reports that in Mariaberg in **Saxony**, while silver was being dug out of the mine of Saints Sebastian and Fabian in the presence of Henry, Prince of the Saxons, such a fragrant odor burst forth that the Prince exclaimed that **Calicut** <note>a city in India famous at the time for the spice trade</note> was present; for that is the city of India which sends forth all scented things.

<margin>Foul-smelling earth.</margin>
But examples of a bad odor are more frequent, and indeed these foul scents are so potent that they can be savage. For in **Annaberg**, in a silver mine named the "Rosy Crown," as the same author reports, twelve men were suddenly suffocated. Because of this, the mine was abandoned out of a great fear that evil demons inhabited it. People were persuaded of this, although the deaths occurred because of the scent of the earths or stones; for once drawn into the brain, it immediately kills. It is no wonder that many foul things lie beneath the bowels of the earth, just like the dung of animals.

<margin>What is beneath the earth.</margin>
<margin>British earth.</margin>
But not only foul things, but materials of every kind for various uses are found beneath it. For example, in **Britain**, a white earth <note>likely marl or chalk used for soil conditioning</note> used to be dug out of pits no less than a hundred paces deep. After you had removed the silver from it, the fields where it was sprinkled were rendered so fertile that once...

# Book Five

## Book Five

<margin>Time reveals many things and hides others.</margin>
...it would be enough to have scattered them into life. Thus, all the earth that lies hidden, much like the internal organs <note>original: "viscera"; the author uses an anatomical metaphor to describe the earth's interior</note> of a human being, is of some use. But we remain ignorant of their uses partly because they are hidden, and partly because our own negligence discourages us from digging them out. There are everywhere—and I mean even in cities, let alone the countryside—various stones beneath the ground and various types of useful earths of different colors, most of them containing metals, yet we seek them only in the mountains. The evidence that this is so can be seen in the fact that lands once considered barren, such as **Germany**, are now most fertile in silver. Other lands have ceased to be productive after once being fertile. The reason for this is that while metals, stones, and juices <note>referring to "solidified juices" like salts or vitriols</note> are everywhere, they are revealed as the earth erodes over time, or hidden as the earth accumulates. Thus, **Anaxagoras** <note>a Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who argued that "everything is in everything"</note> seems to have spoken rightly. In the mountains, however, besides the abundance of materials, there is this practical advantage: if any water is encountered, it can easily be drained away to lower ground.

<margin>On water beneath the earth.</margin>
<margin>Tunnels beneath water.</margin>
In the fields, however, when the water that flows beneath the earth is scarce, we will first dry the area by draining it; then we will block and obstruct the places from which it flows using walls or stones. In this way, men dig **tunnels** <note>original: "cuniculos"; used here in the sense of military or mining saps</note> to overthrew fortified towns even beneath water, and they overcome the trenches themselves by digging beneath them. In another way, by leading water through circuitous routes—as **Cyrus** was taught by **Croesus** in the writings of **Herodotus** <note>referring to the historical account of the Persian King Cyrus diverting the Euphrates to capture Babylon</note>—we exhaust rivers, leading them back into their original channel further downstream. In the same way, it will be possible to divert streams flowing beneath the earth to another place and then lead them back again, so that we may dig below the water level. There are also lower-lying places into which we sometimes divert the water without bringing it back, a defense which is most permitted in the mountains due to the height of the location.

<margin>On water which is found everywhere beneath the earth.</margin>
For the water that is found everywhere beneath the earth is neither extremely deep, nor level, nor continuous. That it is not deep is shown by the foundations of walls and houses, which frequently reach the earth that lies beneath the water. That it is not of a uniform depth is declared by the varying depths of wells. That it is not continuous, but derived from frequent small streams, is easy to understand: for the waters of two wells separated by scarcely six paces may differ greatly in flavor and healthfulness.

<margin>Why the streams of water are winding.</margin>
Furthermore, these streams are not led in a straight path but are usually winding, either because they encounter other water, or because of stones positioned in the middle of their path, or because they have found some cavity into which the waters more conveniently flow together. Therefore, if one wishes to dig beneath it, it is possible in the three ways I have described, allowing one to find different kinds of earths, stones, metals, juices, and other things of this sort.

<margin>The best pottery vessels.</margin>
But I return again to the use of earths: In **Waldenburg** <note>original: "Valdeburgia"; a town in Saxony, Germany, famous for its medieval and Renaissance pottery</note> in Germany, there is a type of clay <note>original: "argilla"</note> that is dense and "fat," and of the finest substance; it is neither damaged by fire, nor does it absorb or leak liquids. Indeed, these five qualities are seen as the merits of pottery vessels: that they be very light, that they do not absorb, that they do not leak, that they are not easily broken, and that they resist fire. It is a marvel how a small difference in the clay ensures that their vessels are not broken by the heat. The **Florentines** achieve great convenience in the seasoning of food, while the people of **Milan** <note>original: "Mediolanenses"</note> do not; therefore, it is necessary for the clay to be fine...

<page-num>119</page-num>
<header>On Mixed Bodies and Metals.</header>

# On Mixed Bodies and Metals.

The clay must be of the finest quality, even extremely thin, and by nature light and fatty. If this kind of clay is worked well and for a long time, it produces vessels very close to Myrrhine <note>original: "Myrrhinis"; likely referring to "Murrhine" ware, a luxury material in ancient Rome, possibly made of fluorite or a type of ancient porcelain</note>. 
<margin>Myrrhine vessels or Porcelain. Natural History, Book 37, Chapter 2.</margin>
Indeed, those Myrrhine vessels are what we today call Porcelain, as Pliny describes. The East sends Myrrhine to us; for it is found there in several places, though not prominent ones, mostly in the Parthian kingdom, but especially in Carmania <note>an ancient province of the Persian Empire, now Kerman in modern Iran</note>. They believe it to be a fluid <note>original: "Humorem"</note> thickened by heat beneath the earth. In size, they never exceed small sideboards; in thickness, they are rarely as large as what is considered necessary for a drinking vessel. Their brilliance is without intensity, more a luster than a true shine. But their value lies in the variety of colors, with spots shifting between purple and white, and a third color arising from both, glowing as if by a transition of color, with the purple turning reddish or the white becoming milky. Some people especially praise the edges of these vessels and certain reflections of color, like those seen in a rainbow. Thick spots are pleasing in these items. For them to be translucent or pale is considered a defect. Likewise, salt-like grains or warts are undesirable, unless they are flush with the body of the vessel. There is also some praise for their scent. 

Therefore, who does not see that these are made of clay, and are of that kind which, as I said, we usually call Porcelain today? For these also consist of a certain juice <note>or fluid substance</note> thickened beneath the earth and are brought from the East. Yet our modern versions are paler, lack a scent, and those that are more translucent are more highly prized; they are also decorated with leaves and images. There is no trace of the purple color, all of which seems to differ from the ancient Myrrhine. However, the variety of times and craftsmen, as well as usage, have brought this about. For the high price led to plenty, as they sought to increase the quantity; but when the more noble material was lacking, they substituted another. Thus, painting was devised for the sake of covering up its cheapness, and so the honor and purity of the vessel declined. Either the material is cheaper, or not the same, or entirely more impure, or not so well-crafted, or the vessels themselves are dug out before their time due to a greed for profit by those impatient with delay. Whatever the case may be regarding the price, location, material, and the way they are made, it teaches us that these are the same as Myrrhine. Yet it is no less grand to dine from these than from gilded or silver vessels. 

And these also have a greater nobility than other types of earth or clay, much like Lemnian earth. 
<margin>Lemnian earth.</margin>
Lemnos is an island in our sea <note>the Mediterranean</note>. The mountain that produces it has neither stone nor tree. It is useful for bloody fluxes and ulcers, but even more so against poisons. For this reason, it does not nourish trees because it is extremely dry, nor does it harden into stone because it is of such a thin substance that it does not take in water, but is rather taken in by water. It also has a certain oiliness by which it resists poisons. It is clear from this that we can produce such a substance by art: if we pound common clay for a long time and sprinkle it with water in which water-germander <term>Scordion: a medicinal herb known for its garlicky smell, used as an antidote to poison</term> and juniper seeds have been boiled, and form it into mounds, pounding it again, sprinkling it, shaping it into mounds, and drying it. A loss of time will certainly bring an advantage and make up for the effort. For the price of Lemnian sealed earth <note>original: "Lemniæ sphragidis"; a famous medicinal clay stamped with a seal to prove its authenticity</note> is equal to its weight in gold.

# Book Five

...by weight, thus a most vile thing grew immensely in value once it ceased to be common due to rarity; for, being intercepted by the ambition of the royal physicians who attend the King of the East, it began to be held as more noble. Yet it does not smell, for this <note>pleasant scent</note> is rare in all lands and waters. For them to smell well, there is a need for thin moisture and a well-concocted <note>original: "concocto"; in early science, this refers to a substance being "ripened" or refined by natural heat</note> substance. The moisture of water cannot be well-concocted because it contains too much earth that is not thin; therefore, as I said, the odor is not sweet. However, when certain things are mixed in, it happens that the earth or water smells good. For this reason, it is manifest that earth and water, even if they smell good, lose their odor in a short time, as happens with rose water, and even more so with violet water. Therefore, the greatest part of earth and water lacks odor; a large part also smells foul, and the smallest part smells good.

<margin>Why earth rarely smells good.</margin>
<margin>Why waters quickly lose their good odor.</margin>

<margin>Armenian earth. 74.</margin>
<margin>Why gems are useful in the plague.</margin>
Next to Lemnian earth <note>a famous medicinal clay from the island of Lemnos</note> is **Armenian earth**, which is red and dries exceptionally well. Because of this, it is healthy for pestilential diseases and for consumption <note>original: "tabi"; a wasting disease</note> that arises from an ulcer of the lung. For the same reason, **Carbuncles** <note>red gemstones like garnets or rubies</note>, **Emeralds**, **Sapphires**, **Hyacinths**, **Pearls**, and **Corals** are useful in the plague, specifically because they dry vehemently. But while they do this less than the Armenian clay, these stones are more useful for repairing the **vital spirit**. Armenian clay is therefore extremely dry, moderately cold, and not at all sharp; yet it is very thin. Because of this, it is also healthy against corrosive poisons, such as "Spanish flies" <note>original: "cantharidibus"; blister beetles used in medicine but toxic in high doses</note>, and likewise against putrefying substances like the sea hare <note>original: "marino lepori"; a toxic marine mollusk used in ancient pharmacology</note>.

There is also a red clay from **Apulia** <note>a region in Southern Italy</note>, not unlike the Armenian in its powers, though far weaker. Yet what prevents it from being made even better than the Armenian? Therefore, wash the Apulian clay: purge it of sand; then, having dried it diligently, take it up with very sharp vinegar and a sixth part of oil, so that it is reduced to the form of a paste. You shall bury it in a damp place for many years. Thus, by this reasoning, you will create medicines against poisons and worms: using the purest clay-like earth, oil, vinegar, scordium <note>water germander</note>, juniper seed, gentian, and dittany, by pounding them for a long time and then burying them for many years.

<margin>A method for making an artificial Armenian clay superior to the natural kind.</margin>

<margin>Why metallic things are generated in mountains.</margin>
One might ask, perhaps, how such a long burial helps toward life? It is surely the same cause that leads to the generation of metallic things in the mountains. But it is more "vivid" in the mountains for several reasons. For mountains have a certain appearance of life, since they consist of rocks. We shall teach that **rocks are alive**, and where there is life, there all natural generation is more prompt. Add to this that the powers of mountains are not exhausted by hoes, rakes, or the plow; nor are they forced to "breathe out" in any way by the industry of men. The substance of mountains is also more solid, whence that heat is better contained, which in the fields is blown away due to the softness of the earth. Moreover, we have already taught that this heat is **celestial**, both because one part is fiery and only slightly putrid, while the rest is useful for generation, and also because we see that in the East and the South, nobler gems and the most perfect gold are more frequently generated. Indeed, if one were to compare gems of the same kind in the East and the South...

<header>On Mixtures and Metallic Substances.</header>

# On Mixtures and Metallic Substances.

<margin>
The reason why gold and gems are generated more in the east and south.
</margin>
...born in the south <note>The text begins mid-word with "-die", likely completing "meridie" (south)</note>, such as carbuncles <note>red gemstones like rubies or garnets</note> and amethysts, he will notice that they differ in a wonderful way in both hardness and brilliance from those which Germany sends; indeed, they differ so vehemently that one might not think they are of the same kind. The reason is that the East is hotter, more humid, and richer <note>original: "pinguior"; literally "fatter," referring to a fertile, oily quality of moisture believed to form minerals</note>. Therefore, if these were generated from seeds, there would be either that fiery heat or a putrid one; and since on the island of Iceland in the north the mountains burn with fire, what would prevent the most perfect gems from being generated there, and for it also to abound in gold?

There are also snows and lasting ice in the mountains, which store up heat in the depths and make all things flourish for that reason, whereas in the fields, the heat is dissipated by the external heat of the air. This brings me back to the matter of mountains: mountains are better prepared for the generation <note>the natural process of "birthing" or forming minerals within the earth</note> of metals. Nor is their strength drained by trees or herbs: for mountains are more sterile than fields, even if the fields are very fertile. Water and moisture also flow down more from the mountains because of the sloping terrain; if they were present in abundance on the surface of the fields, the generation of metals would be hindered.

But you will say: just now you listed the consumption of moisture among the reasons why fields do not produce metallic substances, yet now you judge that an abundance of moisture in them stands in the way of the generation of metals. And by Hercules, both are true: for <margin>Rich moisture is suitable for generation; watery moisture is useless.</margin> the more rich moisture <note>original: "humidum pingue"</note> abounds, the more fertile the soil is rendered, not only for metals but also for plants; however, watery moisture <note>original: "aqueum"</note> hinders it. The cause of this is that moisture fit for generation must also be warm. Watery moisture, however, is cold and resistant to concoction <note>original: "concoctioni"; in early science, this refers to the natural "ripening" or refining of substances by the earth's internal heat</note>. Therefore, hot regions, when they abound in waters, are all most fertile, because the watery moisture quickly passes into a rich state through the heat of the Sun. In cold places, however, much water produces sterility and chills the fields.

And the reason is nearly the same regarding the seasons. For meadows enjoy waters in summer, but in winter constant irrigation makes the herbs sprout more slowly. Thus it is established that fields, if compared to mountains, have more watery moisture and less of the rich kind. Therefore, you will see that mountains fertile in trees and vines hardly abound in metallic substances, except in the deep, because the rich moisture is consumed by the plants. But where there are very large and solid stones, the moisture held for a long time within the rocks and distilling very thinly hardens into noble gems. And for that reason, the more brilliant gems are mostly found among the hardest and largest rocks. To these many advantages of mountains for the generation of metals, it is added that where you have dug two hundred or three hundred paces <note>a "passus" or pace was roughly five feet</note> into the mountains, you can still say you are above the earth, and from there you can more easily divert and move the waters and the excavated earth from the side. On level ground, this labor is entirely doubled; you cannot open a place for debris as you can in the mountains, nor can you easily divine where the metallic substances lie, nor follow them once found as you can in a high place, since you cannot be aided by any signs from the sides.

### Book Five

<margin>
Whether another water is formed beneath the first water that is under the earth.
</margin>
For these many and such great reasons, few people bestow their labor upon the plains, even if <term>metallic substances</term><note>original: "metallica"; referring to ores and minerals</note> exist everywhere; instead, most men apply themselves to excavating the mountains. For it is one labor to have found the location and the type of metal, but another, far greater task is to understand the <term>trunk of the mine</term><note>original: "truncum fodinae"; likely referring to the main vein or mother lode of the ore</note>. However, to have learned this from a more elevated place alone is most laborious. Indeed, to trace the matter back more deeply: since everywhere beneath the earth, as I have said, streams of water flow, and again beneath the water lies earth in which metallic substances mostly lie in the plains. Again, many believe there is water even beneath that earth, just as some have believed there are fresh waters even beneath the bottom of the sea—though this is an experiment difficult to perform. I hear it was attempted in vain elsewhere in **Venice**, where it is not yet established whether another water exists beneath the first water. An argument for this matter seems to me to be that even in the lowest part of the human body there are veins; and they report that the river **Arethusa**, coming from **Elis** <note>A region in Greece</note> under the name of the **Alpheus**, emerges in **Sicily** near **Syracuse** after passing through the sea. There are those who call Arethusa a spring rather than a river; even the fresh waters found on islands can persuade one of this. Finally, since we see water emerge both on the ridges of mountains and also in the lowest depths, what else can we conjecture about the earth: whether the mountain or the land is buried or stands out, it must have the same rationale. This argument demonstrates that evidence. However, I do not sufficiently know what might have prevented them from finding fresh water in Venice.

<margin>
*Meteorology*, Book 2, Chapter 3. How fresh water may be obtained in the sea.
</margin>
But there are those who even draw a small amount of fresh water from the sea on the authority of **Aristotle**, and not by a false experiment. For a wax vessel, sufficiently thick and closed on all sides, is lowered; when it has remained in the sea for a long time, it lets in water but does not let in salt. From this, fresh water, suitable for drinking, is extracted: for while the water is thin it enters, but the salt, because it is <term>earthy</term><note>original: "terrestre"; in the Aristotelian sense, salt was considered an "earthy" or dry element mixed into the water</note>, is blocked by the wax.

<margin>
A fourfold kind of mixture.
</margin>
Therefore, to return to the proposed matter, beneath the first water a <term>mixture</term><note>original: "mixtio"</note> occurs in the earth, and as I said, especially in the mountains, along with the generation of diverse mixed things. Now, "mixture" is properly defined here. For since it may happen in four ways: one is of dissimilar things that change their form, which is called **generation** <note>The creation of a new substance entirely</note>, about which we shall speak here. Another is of those things which are dissimilar but do not all change their form; if this occurs with liquids it is called **crasis** <note>A blending of liquids where properties might mingle, but the substances remain</note>, such as when water and wine are mixed. If, however, it is of dry things, it is called **mixture**: as when millet, wheat, and oats are joined together. And if they are similar things, it shall be called a **heap** <note>original: "aceruus"</note>; and this is the fourth kind of mixture, as when grain is gathered together into a pile.

<margin>
How *crasis* occurs.
</margin>
Before I speak of perfect mixture, I shall have a discussion about *crasis*, as it is more manifest to the senses. We said that wine mixed with water is mixed through *crasis*: for since neither substance perishes, the form of the wine also remains. Therefore, lest a mutual entry of bodies be granted, or a division into the smallest parts—so that bodies would consist of indivisible parts <note>A reference to the "atomist" theory, which the author is here questioning or refining</note>—it was necessary that...

<header>On Mixed Bodies and Metals.</header>

# On Mixed Bodies and Metals.

Aristotle correctly judges concerning <term>growth</term><note>original: "augmento"; in Aristotelian physics, this refers to the increase in size of a living thing</note> that the **form** increases, but not the **matter**. For when something is added to the smallest part, it is impossible for the whole to be truly mixed. Indeed, if matter were mixed with matter, bodies would penetrate one another <note>A reference to the physical principle that two solid objects cannot occupy the same space at the same time</note>. But just as in wine mixed with water, the **form** of the wine is seen everywhere, even if the matter of the wine is not everywhere—but rather the places are filled with the matter of water—so it happens in a true mixture. For as I have said, water is not truly mixed with wine. For it is necessary that the forms of those things which are truly mixed perish, at least in part. But the form of wine
<margin>How water may be separated from wine.</margin>
by no means perishes. Experiment shows that water is not perfectly mixed with wine. For if a linen cloth is placed into wine mixed with water, and it hangs out
outside the jar, all the water ascends from the vessel through the linen, and leaves the pure wine in the cup. By this experiment, the diluted is separated from the pure, which could not happen if the wine and water were truly mixed. Furthermore, the water seeks the bottom of the cup, and for that reason the drink at the bottom is tasteless; it is also far better to pour wine over water than
<margin>In what way wine is to be mixed.</margin>
water over wine. For if you place wine upon water, it will float on top, not only for the reason stated, but because if you first place a small crust of bread upon the water and then slowly pour the wine over the crust, you will see
<margin>How water floats upon wine in the cup.</margin>
quite clearly, even when the crust is removed, that the wine floats upon the water, with no mixture having taken place at all. Therefore, one may look at these three separately in a cup: wine under oil, and water under wine.

Wherefore it is right to ask: which of these is thinnest? For the sake of position, if the oil stays above the wine because it is lighter, and the wine is lighter than water, this is also suggested by the fact that oil burns readily, water never, and wine behaves in a middle fashion.
<margin>The booklet on weights.</margin>
Add to this that wine is heavier than oil by a ninth part, according to the testimony of Galen <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire</note>; for when you have filled a vessel that holds nine pounds of oil with wine, the wine
<margin>Oil, wine, and water: which of these is thinnest.</margin>
will equal a weight of ten pounds. Therefore, nothing is more excellent for the length of life than oil: because it is the thinnest, the fattest, and free from <term>waste products</term><note>original: "excrementorum"; in Renaissance medicine, this refers to any metabolic byproduct the body needs to expel, including sweat and urine</note>, which results in it greatly kindling natural heat due to its richness and thinness. Moreover, because of its purity, it tires that heat the least
<margin>Oil is most conducive to prolonging life.</margin>
and does not obstruct the passages. These two obstacles contribute much to the shortness of life; let honey-wine with oil therefore prevail as much as is permitted. For it is best to produce no waste products at all; the next best thing is to have immediately ejected those that are produced. For retaining waste products brings so much harm that retained urine is accustomed to produce a **stone**; for this reason, those accustomed to play, reading, and writing
<margin>Why bladder stones are generated.</margin>
easily fall prey to that kind of disease <note>The author suggests that a sedentary lifestyle (like that of a scholar) leads to kidney or bladder stones</note>. Indeed, not expelling superfluities sometimes even brings instant death; therefore oil benefits life in so many ways. A fourth argument for the thinness of oil is that it penetrates easily: for this reason it is applied to locks so that keys may be turned easily. By a contrary reasoning, <term>saltpeter</term><note>original: "halinitrum"; likely referring to niter or a similar mineral salt</note> mixed with melted wax prevents leather boots from
<margin>How boots are made immune from water.</margin>
transmitting water at all: if they are thoroughly and diligently soaked with it by a fire; however, the saltpeter must be very finely ground. But if you mix something fatty with the wax, it will be even better.

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the physical properties of fluids, specifically focusing on the comparative density and "thinness" of water, oil, and wine. It follows previous discussions on the nature of mixtures and whether substances truly blend or merely sit alongside one another.</meta>

<page-num>324</page-num>
-># Book Five<-

But I return to the proposed discussion: for there are three things that show water is thinner than both oil and light wine. First, if water and oil are mixed and placed in a vessel over a fire, the water is entirely consumed before almost a single drop of oil, even though water’s coldness resists the heat more, and, being positioned at the bottom, it receives less heat (since the cauldron is cool there). Furthermore, it can hardly evaporate while being weighed down by the oil, even if it is being turned into air. Second, if someone drinks water in the summer, it immediately passes out through sweat, which is not the case for oil or wine. Third, water is more transparent than both. However, the reason for this transparency is that it lacks color; the reason for its quick resolution is that it is not at all "fatty"; and the reason for the sweating is that it does not provide nourishment, and because of its coldness, it pushes out the moisture already dissolved by heat. It does not exit the body itself, but only expels the boiling, watery part of the humors.

<margin>Aristotle’s *On Sense and the Sensible*.</margin>
But you will say that Aristotle feels that water is thinner than oil; however, by "thin," he understood something rare and not at all viscous, or even something not compressed. Perhaps he would argue that wine is thinner than water because it floats on top; yet that proves nothing. For "fatty" substances also stay on top of water because they are compressed; they do not descend because they are tenacious, just like a thin sheet of lead. For fatty things do not sink even if they were heavier, not only because they contain air, but also because they would be forced to descend all at once. Therefore, since such things are barely able to be mixed, they will never achieve a <term>mixture</term><note>original: "crasim"; a technical term referring to a perfect blending or "tempering" of different substances into a single new consistency.</note>.

<margin>How spoiled wine may be corrected.</margin>
For the same reason, milk does not mix with wine. It is common practice to transfer spoiled wine into a clean vessel and gradually add a tenth part of milk. Then, after eight days, the vessel is opened and the wine is sold in small quantities. Although it appears clear and good, if it stays in the cup or vessel for a longer time, it spoils again. It also leaves a buttery "fatness" on the rim of the cup when poured out, which is how the fraud is detected. Nevertheless, it is a profitable deception. However, if the goal is to prevent the wine from putrefying before it becomes disturbed, a tenth part of <term>burning water</term><note>original: "ardentis aquæ"; a historical term for distilled alcohol or brandy.</note> mixed in will do it. Sulfur is far better, but its smell gives away the trick—I remember drinking such wine. Alum can do the same, but both are harmful and severely damage one's health. It is also easy to distinguish all wines adulterated with metals.

<margin>How adulterated wine may be recognized.</margin>
For if left in a cup for twenty-four hours, the metal seeks the bottom due to its weight, while the wine is left with the color of <term>flat wine</term><note>original: "uappæ"; refers to wine that has lost its vigor, becoming flat or vinegar-like.</note>. Why then does milk "improve" wine? Because a sort of mixture is made where the fat of the milk sinks to the bottom, dragging the cloudy impurities with it; the watery part of the milk is left in the wine, which hides the wine’s defects. Thus, small portions of wine reveal the defects because, due to their weakness, they are more quickly corrupted again by the air.

<margin>How wine may be made fragrant.</margin>
Furthermore, a foul odor can even be changed into a pleasant one by using <term>cloves</term><note>original: "gariophili"</note> stuck all over a <term>citron</term><note>original: "citrangulo"; likely a bitter orange or citron fruit.</note>, which is suspended in the vessel so that it does not touch the wine. Therefore, things that are not similar in nature do not create a true mixture, such as wine with water (unless it is a weak blend), much less wine with milk, and even less so—indeed not at all—do these liquids mix with oil. But <term>pomace wine</term><note>original: "lora"; a thin, cheap wine made by soaking the pressed skins of grapes in water.</note> is more truly a mixture.

# On Mixtures and Metals.

<margin>Elements are actually present in all mixtures.</margin>
...it is because it has boiled over, yet they are not fully mixed, since mixing is a work of nature and not of art <note>The author distinguishes between "art" (human craft/chemistry) and "nature."</note>, nor even of fire. Whatever things are truly mixed, therefore, show only one form of an element, and not even that in its pure state; of the remaining elements, they show only their powers. For if the elements were not present everywhere in the mixture, the resulting mixture would be a mere heap <note>original: *acervus*; a collection of parts rather than a unified whole</note> and not a "generated thing." If they are everywhere, then according to their substance, the bodies would mutually penetrate one another. This has been shown, however, in the books of medicine.

<margin>2. Contradictions, tract 1, conclusion 1.</margin>
<margin>How mixing differs from growth and nutrition.</margin>
The form of a mixture is therefore an imperfect version of the "victorious" <note>The "victorious" or dominant element is the one that gives the mixture its primary character (e.g., earthiness in a stone).</note> element. Thus, all mixtures are either earthy, such as stones and plants; or watery, such as milk and oil; or fully mixed, such as the bodies of animals. Mixing, therefore, does not happen in the same way as <term>nutrition</term> <note>The process by which a living thing takes in food and turns it into its own substance.</note> or <term>growth</term> <note>The increase in size of a living body.</note>. For in mixing, one thing is added to another; but in those processes, that which is <term>potential</term> <note>Matter that has the capacity to become something else.</note> is added to that which is <term>actual</term> <note>The completed, living form.</note>, and growth occurs according to every part of the form, but not according to the matter, since matter can be divided without end. The same applies to nutrition. Therefore, growth and nutrition truly happen according to the form; but according to the matter, it is a simple addition, since something is placed next to it on all sides. Thus, when nourishment is added, the smallest part of the flesh is increased entirely according to its form, but not according to its matter, except on its outer edges. But not even in this way is it strictly addition; rather, as I said, the logic of growth and nutrition is almost the same—even that of generation. For these things are performed by the <term>soul</term> <note>original: *anima*; the animating principle of life, not necessarily the modern religious concept.</note>; for it is the work of the soul alone to be able to thin, then unite, and then transmute matter in such a way. Indeed, if anything else lacking life could do this, fire would be most capable of it, for it is the strongest of all things that do not live; yet it cannot. For as we have already taught, that which is added to fire is simply placed next to what is being burned; it does not enter into the prior substance. Thus, it is necessary that all mixtures either live or have lived.

<margin>Eight reasons are shown for why all mixtures are alive.</margin>
Let the reasoning be taken this way: because they are nourished, and nourishment does not happen except by the soul; and whatever has a soul lives. Even if you deny they are nourished, you will at least concede they are generated; yet nothing is generated except by the soul, because, as I said, she alone performs the mixing.

We see also that all mixtures gradually diverge from the heavier elements—beginning with stones, then the less metallic earths, then juices, then metals, then plants, and imperfect animals, and then gradually more perfect ones until we reach man. Man’s composition seems to be so far removed from the nature and substance of the elements that one would in no way believe he consists of them. Therefore, if man, animals, and plants live, since there is one and the same <term>celestial heat</term> <note>A vitalizing heat believed to descend from the stars and sun, acting as the bridge between spirit and matter.</note> which mixes all these—though it mixes those things less and these things more, as we shall show in its proper place—it is manifest that Hippocrates spoke rightly when he said the soul is nothing other than that celestial heat. This also adheres to Aristotle's opinion, where he maintains that the heat of the spirit <margin>Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals*, book 2, chapter 3.</margin> has a certain proportion to the element of the stars. For whether the soul is heat,

# Book Five

...or if it is its primary instrument where heat resides, it is clear that the soul itself must also be present, and therefore life as well; for life is nothing other than the work of the soul. <margin>What life is.</margin>

<margin>Lead increases in weight while it is being turned into white lead.</margin> This same point becomes clearer through an experiment: for when lead is turned into <term>ceruse</term> <note>White lead (lead carbonate), historically used as a pigment and cosmetic.</note> and is burned, it increases in weight by a thirteenth part. This happens because that celestial heat vanishes; for it is certain that nothing is added, yet the weight grows. Since a similar reasoning seems to apply to animals, which become heavier at death because, as the soul breathes out, the heat also vanishes with it, along with whatever was produced by that heat: it is manifest that metallic bodies and even stones themselves are alive.

<margin>Why the bodies of the dead are heavier than the bodies of the living.</margin> But you will say: how can that which is left behind become heavier when the lighter part—namely heat—is removed from animals or metals? It is clear that this happens just as it does with glass eggs <note>Hollow glass spheres used in physics demonstrations.</note> that float on water; indeed, even steel or lead ones will float if the air contained inside supports them. But once broken, they immediately sink. In our case, it is not air that does this; rather, just as air acts within the water in those spheres, so in animals and metals, the fiery part within the air <note>The "vital spirit" or innate heat that provides buoyancy to living things.</note> takes away weight.

<margin>How elements exist in a mixture in two ways.</margin> For indeed, as I have said, some substances of the elements are present in mixtures, but they are "broken" <note>Meaning they are no longer in their pure, simple state but have been transformed to fit the mixture.</note>; the qualities of others are also present. For example, in milk there is a watery substance, but the air, earth, and the ethereal or fiery part have been processed by heat according to their quality. Elements exist in mixtures in two ways: one is by generation, and in this way only earth and water are present as substances; in the other, the substance of the remaining elements does not appear. However, as celestial heat has acted upon them, the four forms of the elements are seen to differ in substance and nature, and not only in quality.

<margin>Why some dense things are light, and some rare things are heavy.</margin> Thus it happens that some dense things can be light, and some <term>rare</term> <note>In this context, "rare" means porous or low-density, the opposite of "dense."</note> things can be heavy. For when a small quantity of earth is heated so that it is transmuted into the substance of air, yet air does not actually enter it, the object becomes light—that is, it is both light and dense, as is the case with all fats and with <term>aloeswood</term> <note>A dense, resinous wood that, despite its density, contains volatile oils.</note>. Conversely, if the earth is poorly processed, but a large part of air is inside and visible everywhere in tiny parts, it will be called "rare," and yet it will be significantly heavy. However, we easily understand that "heavy" usually implies density, and "light" implies rarity.

<margin>Whether any mixture is heavier than earth.</margin> From this, the solution to a significant question becomes clear: why lead is heavier than earth. In lead, there is almost no rarity <note>porosity</note>, whereas earth, since it does not cling together, admits air; for that reason, earth seems lighter than lead because it holds air in its gaps. This earth, as I said, is also not "pure" earth, but has a metallic substance mixed into it.

<margin>Four causes why a vessel full of ash accepts as much water as an empty one could contain.</margin> This is also why they testify concerning ashes that a vessel full of them "drinks up" just as much water as if the vessel were empty, without the ash being displaced. It is clear that a large amount of air must be present in the dry ash; when water is added, the thinner part of the ash exhales, while the rest of the ash thickens and is compressed, and part of the water is absorbed by the excessive dryness.

## On Mixtures and Metals.

<margin>Why there are many metallic things under the earth and few animals.</margin>
<margin>That metallic things are almost innumerable in species.</margin>
<margin>That metallic substances are the fruits, leaves, roots, and exhalations of metals.</margin>
...is discovered by observation <note>The Latin 'mento' is likely the end of 'experimento' (by experiment or observation) continued from the previous page.</note>, for in the mountains they are born no differently than plants, indeed with spreading branches, roots, trunks, and even as if with flowers and fruits. Thus, a metal or metallic substance is nothing other than a buried plant, born entirely under the earth. It could not grow above the ground because it was either too brittle, such as <term>vitriol</term> <note>original: 'calchantum'; historically referring to copperas or hydrated sulfate minerals.</note>, or too heavy, like lead—just as we see the mole among animals, as well as worms and toads, being born under the earth. 

However, it was not suitable for as many animals to be produced under the earth as plants; for while life and nutrition—the only things metals require—can be achieved and perfected underground, respiration (which perfected animals require) is quite difficult there. For this reason, nature has produced types of metallic things under the earth in far greater variety than one might think, so much so that I would dare to say they cannot be numbered. For if nature adorns the world with more than five hundred species of herbs and has introduced animals upon these, it is probable that she has "played" <note>A reference to 'lusus naturae' or the "games of nature," a common Renaissance concept where nature creates diverse forms for its own sake.</note> in no fewer ways beneath the earth—indeed, in far more—but many remain hidden in the depths. Others, however, we classify into the nearest categories due to a similarity of color or substance. Some are rare, so that even if they were above ground they would be hard to find, just as in our own times there are many types of plants which <term>Dioscorides</term> <note>A Greek physician and botanist (c. 40–90 AD) whose work 'De Materia Medica' was the standard botanical text for centuries.</note> mentions but are now scarce. Others began to be disregarded after they were first found because their use was unknown; thus it happens that out of a vast number of metallic things, we recognize very few. Even of those we do recognize, the "genera" are fewer than we think, since some are merely the fruits, leaves, exhalations, or roots of others, and these are parts that are never truly separated from the whole. We shall discuss what these are and their locations in their proper places; for now, let us pursue the question at hand.

We have said that metallic substances, metals, and even stones are alive. For those things which possess maturity, ripeness, and old age also possess life. Indeed, certain stones are found "immature," with a dilute color and a substance not yet "concocted" <note>In ancient chemistry, 'concoction' was a process of ripening or perfecting a substance through internal heat, similar to digestion or the ripening of fruit.</note>. Furthermore, one part of a stone is often seen to be purer than the rest, just as one finds in the fruits of the same tree. There are, moreover, veins and instruments of nutrition, and channels—not wider, but softer—as can be seen in stones. By these we can easily be persuaded that stones are nourished no differently than plants, or as bones are nourished in animals; for if they grew only by external accumulation and addition, they would have no need for such internal structures. 

Stones that harden solely by heat, which we call <term>tufa</term> <note>original: 'tophos'; a porous rock formed by the accumulation of volcanic ash or calcium carbonate.</note>, and those formed solely by cold, do not have veins or an organized substance like true stones that possess life; for tufa lacks life. There is also death in them, and where there is death, there must be life. For the <term>Herculean stone</term> <note>The lodestone or natural magnet.</note> in my possession has often "died" within a few years; for while it once drew iron eagerly, after a passage of time it ceased to do so. For what else is life but the operation of the soul? Moreover, it has been shown in medical treatises that only living things possess "operation" <note>The term 'operatio' here refers to a specific functional power or activity inherent to a being's nature.</note>. Even the elements live in some fashion, as has been said, since they move toward their own proper regions of their own accord; likewise mixtures...

<margin>*A reasoning demonstrating against Simplicius, that the bone of the kite-fish does not attract gold.*</margin>
...but all these things are far better: for nature always intends something better than the material from which a thing is constituted. On this account, I would hardly believe Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> when he says: just as iron is drawn by the Herculean stone <note>original: "Herculeo lapide"; a common Renaissance term for the lodestone or magnet.</note>, so it is thought that gold is drawn by the bone of the kite-fish <note>original: "piscis milui"; likely referring to a species of ray or the tub gurnard, which ancient lore sometimes endowed with magical properties.</note>. For what he wrote in his physical expositions contradicts reason: since that bone is not alive. Moreover, it has been shown that every operation belongs to a living thing, and occurs as it lives. For even if the elements themselves are alive, this work cannot be the work of the elements; rather, the attraction of a specific thing belongs to the life of a living being which makes use of at least some nourishment. But the bone of the fish is not alive once you have removed it from the animal, at least not with that kind of life that uses nourishment. For once the soul is removed, the sensing part is clearly gone, yet the nutritive part is the same. Therefore, I trust in this demonstration so much that, although I have not tested it myself, I would dare to say it is impossible for the bone of the kite-fish to draw gold just as the Herculean stone draws iron. However, this could undoubtedly be done by some other living thing, such as a stone, an animal, or a tree, as long as it remains alive.

<margin>*In what way metallic substances lie in the mountains.*</margin>
<margin>*Why metallic substances usually lack flowers and fruit.*</margin>
Therefore, metallic substances lie in the mountains no differently than trees: with their roots, trunk, branches, many leaves, and certain thin parts, and sometimes even with flowers and fruits. For they mostly lack fruits and flowers, just as we see happens even to plants that grow in wells, in the shade, or in an excessively dry place—such as <term>maidenhair fern</term> <note>original: "adiantho"</note>, <term>hart's-tongue fern</term> <note>original: "scolopendro"</note>, lichen, and many wild figs <note>original: "caprificis"</note> when they grow on walls. For it is clear that fruit and flowers are the signs of a luxuriant and fertile tree. Fertility comes both from moisture and from the heat of the Sun. For this reason, it is no wonder that flowers and fruit are mostly missing from metallic things, since the Sun is always absent, and copious moisture is also usually lacking.

<margin>*How we may discover metallic substances to be abundant in mountains by 15 signs.*</margin>
<margin>*Why the south abounds more in gems, and the north more in metals.*</margin>
But if you wish to discover where metallic substances abound, you need certain and numerous conjectures. First, a productive province shows it, as Germany is now fertile in silver. In Italy, by contrast, it is scarcely possible to dig for silver, and in no way for gold. Therefore, just as there are more fertile fields in a fertile region, so in a province productive of metals, most mountains bear metals even beyond expectation. Also, the highest mountains, while they are more difficult to excavate, are more liberal in what they bestow; for this material is rarely found in abundance in lower hills. Usually, the peaks of mountains that stretch toward the south, with their roots looking toward the north <note>original: "boreas"</note>, provide evidence of metal—and especially of silver, whose more productive mines tend to stretch in a straight line from east to west. Mountains in hot regions are also more abundant in gems: because in the south, moisture is more dried out and thinned; for this reason, stones are generated by dryness, and gems by thinning, but metals are formed from much thick moisture. This moisture flourishes in the North <note>original: "Septentriones"</note>.

Mountains that are entirely sterile are also metallic, for two reasons: for the moisture...

<page-num>129</page-num>
<header>On Mixed Bodies and Metals.</header>

# On Mixed Bodies and Metals.

The internal moisture is consumed, for which reason plants cannot be produced there, and foul vapors kill even those plants that have already sprouted. Furthermore, the color of mountains, stones, and earth teaches us not only that metals are present, but also what kind they are: a green color is produced by copper <note>original: "ære"; in this context, copper or its alloys</note>, black from silver and gold, purple from pyrite, a leaden-blue from lead and iron, a sallow yellow from chalcantite <note>original: "calchanto"; copper sulfate or "blue vitriol," often appearing as yellow or greenish crusts in mines</note> and similar juices, and an ashen or dark color from sulfur. Odor also reveals them; for when you rub two stones from the same mountain together, if metal lies beneath the mountain, they smell strongly of sulfur. Because of this, it has been falsely believed that metals consist of sulfur, when in fact this odor is a metallic excrement and an indication of an over-abundance of coction <term>coction: the "cooking" or natural refinement process that ancients believed occurred underground to turn base matter into metal</term>. Also, if stones or earth are heavier than their size would suggest, it is a certain proof of metallic material. If they also shine too much in some part, or, being solid, lack all luster, you may know for certain that the material of metal lies beneath. Finally, if you melt it with fire, you will discover at once that it is metal, as well as its type and quantity. Even the flowing waters offer a slight hint for this conjecture; if they exhibit a strange smell or color, you will undoubtedly declare that metal is in the mountain. You should also diligently explore the bottom of the stream bed, for you will find a portion of metal; it is hardly possible, through the long passage of time and the daily accumulation of sediment, that a trace of metal would not appear from the descent of the heavier part. Even a mountain full of cracks occurs because of the sharp vapors of the metallic deposits.

<margin>A comparison of metallic plants.</margin>
There are also plants that delight in the company of metals: and as those that delight in metals are rarer, they provide a more evident testimony of them if they are present. Generally, these are types that bear no fruit, or very little, such as the dwarf juniper, ivy, the wild fig, the wild pine also, and many of the thorny plants. Also, the leaves of trees are either pale or falling, the trunks are meager, and everything wilts. Is it any wonder, when a pregnant nurse is provided for a nursing child? For metals and plants share the same nourishment; therefore, the nature of the place can hardly satisfy both. But metals drink up more than the trees: for the offspring of metals is far greater than that of trees, just as the beasts of the sea are far larger than the terrestrial animals themselves.

<margin>The wondrous size of a silver mine.</margin>
I find in the works of Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "Father of Mineralogy," author of *De Re Metallica*</note> that a silver mine—even though silver is a less fertile metal—was thirty feet in length, nine inches <note>original: "dodrantis"; a measure of about 9 inches or 3/4 of a foot</note> in width, and sixty feet in depth. From this, it is manifest that it was similar to a tree: for a tree's height is its greatest dimension, next its length or the spreading of its branches, and its smallest is its thickness, which is taken as the width in mines.

Therefore, if silver is so great, what of copper, what of lead, and iron, and sulfur? Finally, how great is it in the stones themselves? Yet it is not for the same reason that sea beasts surpass land animals in size—namely, an abundance of moisture—but because weight in metallic things and stones brings no danger since they do not "hang," whereas it does in trees. For trees, because they hang <note>referring to their upright growth being vulnerable to gravity and wind</note>, are easily uprooted by the winds, and that diligence of nature is frustrated.

<header>Book Five</header>

# Book Five

<margin>Necessary parts of metallic bodies.</margin>
Regarding the similarity I mentioned, both trees and metals rejoice in a northern aspect. They possess four nearly indispensable parts: the root, the bark, the substance, and the veins. For a stone, the root is another stone or earth, as we shall teach in the proper place; for a metal, it is metal, metallic material, or earth. The bark, however, clearly differs from the rest of the substance in its position and hardness, while the veins appear manifest within the substance. What else, then, is a mine <note>original: "fodina"</note> but a plant buried by earth and stones? These substances are, as I said, either the metallic earth I mentioned, or a "nobler juice," or a metal, or a stone. It is common to all metallic bodies that they render things harder and colder. Indeed, Eretrian earth <note>A type of medicinal clay found on the Greek island of Euboea, highly valued in antiquity for its cooling properties.</note>, metals, stones, and most metallic things are cold. Yet some, even if they are dry, have a softening effect due to an abundance of oiliness, such as Asphalt and Jet <note>original: "Gagates lapis"; a hard, black form of lignite coal used in jewelry and believed to have protective qualities.</note>. These are dry because they are earthy. Fire, or rather heat, can warm them, but it cannot moisten them.

<margin>Two reasons why almost all metallic things have a bad taste or none at all, yet may have a pleasant odor.</margin>
It is also necessary that almost all metallic things have a bad taste or none at all. Pure stones and pure earth have no taste; the rest have a bad one. The reason is that they are scarcely freed from adustion <term>adustion: a state of being "scorched" or "burnt" by the intense internal heat of the earth during their formation</term>, and they are dry, as we have said, whereas sweet things are moist. Even if some moisture is present and the flavor is pleasant, when it is mixed with something foul, the pleasantness does not overcome the foulness but is corrupted by it. For if you mix a little gentian with much milk, you will have an unpleasant taste. It is not so with odors, for a stronger scent usually obscures a lesser one. Copper is bitter and of a most foul taste, while iron is somewhat bitter; then there is white lead, which we call tin <note>original: "plumbum album, quod stannum vocamus"</note>, which is astringent with bitterness. Alum and chalcantite <note>original: "calchantum"; a sulfate mineral, often blue vitriol.</note> are also bitter, but even more so are the others like sulfur and bitumen <note>A naturally occurring oily or tar-like petroleum product.</note>. Silver, however, offers a pleasant and somewhat sweet taste, and gold has a far better one, though it does not excel it. These tastes are known if a liquid is collected and kept in such vessels, or if a part of the metal is dissolved in wine, broth, or water and left there for a long time.

<margin>All metallic things are dissolved in three ways.</margin>
Furthermore, all metallic things—if they consist of moisture congealed by cold—are dissolved by fire, such as sulfur and metals. Some, having congealed with heat, are dissolved by cold and water, such as alum, salt, ink-stone, and nitre. Some are only softened by water, such as many stones. Agricola <note>Referring to Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "Father of Mineralogy," whose work *De Re Metallica* revolutionized mining science.</note> reports that he saw a piece of marble made soft by water after it had lain in it for a long time; these must be earthy materials that never perfectly liquefy. Therefore, those that liquefy perfectly are aqueous, even if from moisture; those that cannot liquefy perfectly are earthy. The "juices" <note>In this period, "juices" (*succi*) referred to any mineral substance that could be dissolved in water or melted, considered the "sap" of the earth.</note> therefore consist of an aqueous substance, such as alum, bitumen, sulfur, salt, nitre, chalcantite, and many of that kind. I would, however, call salt an earth with juice rather than a pure juice, but it is not my present purpose to treat each one individually, but only those of clearer example and utility.

<margin>A sharp and potent juice.</margin>
For there are indeed certain rarer juices, such as that found at Annaberg <note>A famous silver mining town in Saxony, Germany.</note> in the tunnel of the mine of Emperor Otto, which was hard and white, and so sharp...
