# On Mixed and Metallic Substances.

...so that it might kill mice by corroding them. But now our discourse will concern better-known things: among
<margin>Rock alum and its powers.</margin>
which is liquid alum, called **Rock Alum**, which possesses such an astringent power that if
you boil two or three ounces of it in water until they are dissolved, our paper
immersed in that water and then dried, retains ink excellently, and does not allow it to be 
wrongly diffused or spread: even if the paper were of the worst quality, it is a sign that the alum
has soaked through because it shines. By the same reasoning, it makes goose quills 
better, and also hides; and it prevents wines from becoming turbid in their vessels. The alum which they call
<margin>Scaiola alum.</margin>
**Scaiola** <note>Likely a reference to scagliola, a type of plaster of Paris, or a specific local mineral variant.</note> is the "Samian Star" of the ancients, and it is not of the genus of juices.
<margin>Feather alum.</margin>
Just as **Feather Alum** <note>original: "Alumen plumae"; historically used to refer to fibrous minerals like asbestos or halotrichite.</note> is not, which consists of earthy parts; and therefore if it is 
ground thinly and sprinkled on a bed, it provokes a constant itching, for it has 
sharp and stinging parts. But if lamp-wicks are made from it, they do not burn away,
<margin>Wicks which are not consumed, and cloths from fire.</margin>
but the oil is perpetually consumed while the wicks themselves remain. This is common 
to almost every kind of "crusted stone." For even in Eisleben <note>A famous mining town in Saxony, Germany.</note>, from pyrite and 
another fissile stone placed on a fire, a green liquid flows out, which, when it is 
thickened after the fire is extinguished, no longer feels the heat of fire. Thus also from the stone **Asbestos** <note>original: "Amianto lapide"</note>
there are napkins in Rome, and **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy."</note> affirms there are tablecloths in Verebergo in Bohemia, 
which are cleaned not by water but by fire. And from **Magnesia**, a scaly stone
of silvery and leaden color in Boldecrana, tables are made which are 
purified by fire and not damaged; and from the thinner part, wicks are made for lamps.

These things will seem incredible to some to speak of, yet they are not only 
true but also necessary and easy to find. For since almost all 
stones resist fire (especially if not for a long time), the scaly ones can often be spun 
because of their fibers. If, therefore, you spin a material that is stubborn against fire, it will be possible to make napkins, tablecloths, 
and wicks that are not subject to fire. Truly, in feather alum 
there is not enough "juice" <note>In this context, "juice" refers to the binding resinous or fluid quality required for processing.</note> that you might be able to spin it. Therefore, it should not 
be considered a miracle that a wooden tower remained uncorrupted when fires were set against it, 
having been sprinkled with this kind of alum.

<margin>Types of Bitumen and the nobler ones.</margin>
But bitumen has no less power than alum, though there is more than one kind of 
it: there is what is properly called **Asphalt**, and **Pissasphalt** <note>A natural mixture of pitch and asphalt.</note>, and **Naphtha**, 
**Jet**, **Ampelites** <note>A bituminuous earth or "cannel coal."</note>, **Maltha** <note>A mineral wax or thick petroleum.</note>, **Thracian stone**, **Mineral coal**,
<margin>What Camphor is, and its powers.</margin>
**Amber**, **Ambra**, **Petroleum**, and **Camphor**. And there is enough agreement about all of them, 
except for camphor; there are those who call it *Caphura*—I yield my hand, let it be his right, 
I do not challenge it; the doubt is about the thing itself; I leave the name to be fashioned by you, 
whoever you are who is so fastidious. Since they find wood in it, they believe it to be 
the "tear" <note>A botanical resin.</note> of a tree, not a bitumen. Nevertheless, if amber burns—which 
is undoubtedly a bitumen—and the smoke is caught by a cloth moistened with water, 
it smells of camphor. But it does not matter much to a physician to know this, but rather that it is 
excessively dry, so much so that if carried in the bodices of virgins, it renders 
young men impotent to love; it likewise dries and whitens ulcers: for it is of a very thin 
<margin>Jet.</margin>
substance, and for these reasons it also keeps sleep away. The common people call Jet...

# Book Five

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, describing gagates, or jet.</note>...black <insert>jet</insert>. Beads for prayer-ropes are made from it; it is shiny and bright, so much so that many count it among the precious stones. It is black in color and attracts straw. Travelers bring images <note>Likely small carved icons or figurines.</note> made of it to us from Spain. It burns, for this is common to every kind of bitumen. It seems to excite those with the "comitial disease" <note>term: comitial disease; a historical name for epilepsy, so called because the comitia (Roman assemblies) were dismissed if someone had a seizure.</note>, just like amber. But the ancients also wrote that it provokes the disease; it is possible it does both. The common cause for both is a moderate heat, thinness, and dryness. Furthermore, because it is fatty, it is also fragrant.

<margin>Amber.</margin>
There has been great dispute regarding **amber** <note>original: "succinum"</note> until this day; nevertheless, it is a bitumen and a certain "fatness" of the earth. There are several kinds. The **white** is the most precious, sweet to the taste, and smelling best—so much so that when used for fumigation in rooms against the plague (for it helps), it makes the room smell good for up to three days. It is clear, therefore, that this confers much when mixed into medicines. It is mixed either for its scent, or for the sake of drying, or—what is more evident—as an aid in "attraction." For it attracts all light things: straw, stalks, thin metal filings, and basil leaves, despite the erroneous contradiction of **Theophrastus** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and student of Aristotle, known as the father of botany and author of a work on stones.</note>.

<margin>Why amber attracts straws.</margin>
The cause of this is that it contains a fatty and sticky moisture; when this is emitted, the dry object—desiring to "drink it in"—is moved toward the source, that is, the amber itself. For every dry thing, after it has begun to drink in moisture, is also carried toward it, just as fire is toward its fuel. Hence, if it is rubbed more vigorously, it attracts even more because of the heat. Nor is the reason for attraction the same for the **lodestone** <note>original: "lapidis Magnetis"</note> and amber: for amber attracts every light thing, while the magnet attracts only iron. Amber does not move straw if a body is placed between them; the magnet moves iron <note>The author notes that magnetism can pass through solid barriers, whereas the static electricity of amber is easily blocked.</note>. Amber is not in turn attracted by straw; the magnet is also attracted by iron. Straw is not directed in any specific direction by amber; iron tends now to the north, now to the south by contact with the magnet. Finally, the attraction of amber is much aided by heat and friction; that of the magnet only by the fact that the purer part of the stone is restored. In short, the attraction of amber is undoubtedly similar to that which occurs from a **cupping glass** <note>term: cucurbitula; a glass vessel used in medical bloodletting, which uses heat to create suction.</note> by fire and other hot things, due to that innate fatty heat, which also, sticking to walls as I said, makes rooms smell good even into the third day. For there is in every bitumen a fatty, hot moisture, because of which it also burns easily. But in the power of attracting, amber is the best among bitumens; and among the kinds of amber, the **ashen** kind, which is dug up on this side of the mouth of the Vistula at Puck <note>original: "Pucecam"; a town on the Baltic coast in Poland.</note> on the seashore. For this kind, as **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), a famous German scholar often called the "father of mineralogy."</note> reports, while being rubbed with iron, attracted leaves from the ground into the air to a height of two feet. This type is therefore most suitable for ointments. The **white** kind is taken from the German Sea <note>The Baltic or North Sea.</note>, from which gaming dice are also usually made. There is also a **honey-colored**, a **wine-colored**, and a **golden** kind, which is usually found in a spring in Swabia, near the monastery whose name is **Lake Tegern** <note>original: "Degeræ lacus"; Tegernsee in Bavaria.</note>. In amber, all kinds of small things shine through: flies, ants, small fish, leaves, scraps. For, being caught in the sticky moisture of the amber, they cannot escape; then, as the moisture flows abundantly, they are encased, and they are dried, and because...

# On Mixed Substances & Metals.

...they are unable to rot, and they shine in an eternal tomb, in a mausoleum more noble than that which **Artemisia** <note>Artemisia II of Caria, who built the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, for her husband Mausolus.</note> constructed. Amber naturally smells very little, but when it is burned, it sends forth the sweet scent of myrrh.

<margin>Ambergris.</margin>
**Ambergris** <note>original: "Ambra"; though related in name to amber (succinum), ambergris is a substance produced by sperm whales, often found washed up on beaches and used in perfumery.</note> is more fragrant than amber, such that it is compared with the most precious wares. It is born near Sichrim, a small town in **Arabia Felix** <note>The ancient name for the southern Arabian Peninsula (modern Yemen), known to the Romans as "Fertile Arabia" due to its spice trade.</note>. Its power for the brain is marvelous; many find it smells heavy because of the greatness of the scent; it has thin parts mixed with thick ones. <margin>Petroleum.</margin> **Petroleum**, moreover, is an oil that flows spontaneously from bitumen by the force of heat; it is very thin and hot, with a heavy smell. The common folk call it **Oil of Rock** <note>original: "oleum de Saxo"; this is the literal etymology of the word petroleum (petra = rock, oleum = oil).</note>. It is a present help for "cold" pains, even long-lasting ones. <margin>Asphalt.</margin> **Asphalt**, properly so called, smells less badly—to me it seems to smell good. It is similar to pitch, but harder, more brilliant, and less foul-smelling, even to those who usually dislike the scent. <margin>Coals.</margin> **Coals** <note>original: "Carbones"; referring here to mineral coal or lignite.</note> consist of a fatty, light, black earth; they are dug up throughout **Meissen** <note>A region in Saxony, Germany.</note> in the mountain near the city of **Zwickau** located on the **Mulde** river. They are used by blacksmiths; their power is less than that of asphalt, but they are of the same kind. Amber is sometimes faked with honey-colored saffron and egg white, which is why people are surprised when such pieces do not attract straw. <margin>Sulfur and its uses.</margin> Truly, just as amber and bitumen usually smell good, **sulfur** always smells bad. It is common to both that they burn easily. But while sulfur burns more easily, asphalt burns longer. But beware lest for "Asphaltum" bitumen you read **"Aspalathum"** by changing a letter; that is a fragrant tree, which our people, I believe, call **Sandalwood**. <margin>Sandalwood is Aspalathum.</margin> The use of sulfur is excellent and manifold: for from it first **gunpowder** <note>original: "pyrius puluis"; literally "fire powder."</note> is made, nor can it be made without it; for it is a material fit for every fire, as we demonstrated above. It even resists water, so that things immersed in it remain for many centuries. One is safer from an enemy—which is now the case for many—by water than from a "friendly" fire. Also, when melted, it reproduces engraved figures on gems to a hair's breadth <note>original: "ad amussim"; meaning with perfect precision.</note> better than anything else. And when applied as an ointment or used as incense, it kills, prohibits, and puts to flight serpents, ants, and gnats. Applied and drunk, it removes scabs, leprosies, and the **French disease** <note>term: French disease; a common historical name for syphilis.</note>. But its oil has a more vehement power. How it is made, we have taught in the books on the French disease.

<margin>Salt contains oil.</margin>
**Salt** of the earth partakes more of sulfur; hence it can be called a "juice" combined with earth. It contains oil within itself if it is mixed with bitumen. For this reason **Arrian** <note>A Greek historian and philosopher of the Roman period.</note> reports in his *Indica* <note>A work describing the customs and geography of India.</note> that among the **Fish-eaters** <note>term: Ichthyophagi; ancient name for coastal peoples whose diet consisted primarily of fish.</note>, they extract oil from salt. It is also an indication of this that olive trees delight in the seashore, for salty soil is also notably fatty. But as I said, all things contain oil in such a way that it can be drawn out by the force of fire. However, it cannot contain much unless it has bitumen mixed in. <margin>Kinds of salt.</margin> There is a kind of mined salt, such as what we call **Saltpeter** <note>original: "Sal petrae"; potassium nitrate, essential for gunpowder.</note> and **Ammoniac**. This is the bitterest of all, as it is dug out from under burning sand. For when salt is boiled further, as **Galen** <note>The most influential physician of the Roman Empire, whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> testifies, it turns bitter. Therefore, Sal Ammoniac can also be made by art, though many have labored in this in vain. **Rock salt** <note>original: "Sal gemma"; literally "gem salt," referring to clear, crystalline halite.</note> shines in the manner of crystal and is sharper than man-made salt.

### Book Five.

<margin>Niter.</margin>
<margin>Aphronitrum.</margin>
In all things produced and refined by art without complex mixing, nature achieves a similar effect; thus, sulfur that occurs naturally is far more expensive—as well as more useful—than the rest, and the same is true for copperas <note>original: "calchanto"; copperas or vitriol, a sulfate mineral used in dyes and medicine.</note> and other substances. Among the types of salt, **halinitrum** <note>literally "salt-niter"; historically referring to saltpeter (potassium nitrate) found as an efflorescence on walls.</note> is the finest, occupying a middle ground between common salt and niter <note>original: "nitrum"; in this period, "nitrum" could refer to either natron (sodium carbonate) or saltpeter (potassium nitrate).</note>. Niter is found especially in the sands of the Nile. **Albertus Magnus** <note>a 13th-century Dominican friar and philosopher famous for his works on natural science.</note>, by his surname, relates that in Goslar <note>a famous mining town in Germany.</note>, water collected at the foot of a mountain rich in copper ore was found to turn into niter when condensed. A certain whiter and more porous part of this hangs in caves like icicles, and sometimes even sweats out from the soil; it is called **Aphronitrum** <note>literally "foam of niter."</note>. It is falsely believed in our time that both of these substances have disappeared, which has caused the composition of the **Diaspolitic** <note>a medical preparation originally from Diospolis in Egypt, often used for digestive issues.</note> remedy to be thrown into confusion.

<margin>Halinitrum.</margin>
<margin>Halinitrum generates.</margin>
Niter is more bitter than salt and less salty, with *halinitrum* being in the middle, as I said. It consists of thin and very dry parts because it coalesces through a kind of decay; hence it arises in old mortar <note>original: "cementis"; referring to the lime-based mortar in old walls where saltpeter often blooms.</note> and where the excrement of beasts has rotted in the earth. It is a marvel that once the *halinitrum* is removed from the earth, if that earth is piled back up, it yields a more copious "interest" <note>original: "foenus"; the author uses a financial metaphor, suggesting the mineral "grows" back like interest on a loan.</note> after five or six years. Nor should it be called absurd to say that salt "bears fruit." For as I have said, whether the mounds of earth from which it was taken are kept under sheds, or *halinitrum* dissolved in water is sprinkled back onto the mounds of earth, it is just as if wheat had been sown: after five years, a more abundant fruit is returned. For there are powers in all things so that they may return in **actuality** something that was previously held in **potential** <note>The author is using Aristotelian terminology: "potentiality" (the capacity to become something) and "actuality" (the realization of that capacity).</note>. That which is in potentiality also reaches actuality through the power of the Sun; thus, worms and flies in the places where they dwell leave behind that by which the capacity for the generation of others of their kind and the multiplication of their species is supplied.

<margin>Why salt crackles in the fire.</margin>
Therefore, to return to the nature of *halinitrum*: there is a thin part within it, as there is in salt, mixed with water and earth. When it burns, it forces the earthy parts to be scattered, and for that reason salt and *halinitrum* jump and crackle when placed in the fire. Once, when my father-in-law was standing by the fire, a fragment of a very old tile was thrown in; it suddenly crackled, and the fragments flew out with great force in different directions, though, miraculously, no one standing there was hurt. The cause of this, I believe, was a small portion of *halinitrum* trapped within it (because the tile was old).

<margin>Candles that are consumed very slowly.</margin>
<margin>Alkali salt or potash.</margin>
For the same reason, candles made of salted tallow or wax crackle, but they certainly last much longer than others. Among the types of salt, **alkali salt** <note>original: "sal chali"; derived from the Arabic "al-qali."</note> or **potash** <note>original: "alumen catina"; a salt derived from plant ashes used in glassmaking.</note> is usually classified; it is not only a medicine for niter—in that it makes it ductile—but also its raw material. It is brought from the East, but **Brasavola of Ferrara** <note>Antonio Musa Brassavola, a famous Italian physician and botanist (1500–1555).</note> affirms that an excellent version can be made from a herb that grows near Como on the banks of salty waters. If we believe him, and the story is true, propagating this herb would yield no small financial gain, and this art would be quite lucrative. It is well enough established that this kind of salt is made from the **Usnen** <note>likely referring to a species of soda-rich plant or lichen.</note> herb, which grows to the size of a tree and has a salty taste; some think this is the **Anthyllis** plant <note>a plant mentioned by ancient botanists, possibly "kidney vetch" or a similar coastal plant.</note>.

It also introduces industrial salts like alkali, used in medicine and glassmaking, noting their potential for commercial profit.</summary>

-># On Mixed Substances & Metallic Minerals.<-

<margin>Copperas.</margin>
<margin>Why copperas blackens so much.</margin>
<margin>Misy.</margin>
<margin>In every type of mineral, there is something that shines.</margin>
<margin>Copperas (Couperose).</margin>
<margin>Oil of vitriol.</margin>
The first kind is **phyllitis** <note>a leaf-like mineral or stone</note>. The substance of salt is thinner than the material of copperas <note>original: "calchanti"; also known as vitriol or iron sulfate</note>, the species of which are so varied that it is no light task to explain them. The common people call copperas "vitriol." It blackens things so thoroughly that it is used to make the ink with which we write. This powder is ash-colored after it is ground, but if it is put into wine or water, it immediately makes them jet black. The reason for this is that it is a "juice" <note>original: "succus"; a term used in early mineralogy for substances that could be dissolved or melted</note> and is quite dense, yet it consists of thin and scorched parts. Because it is a juice, it dissolves into a moist substance and can cling to surfaces without clogging the pen—which would not happen if it were purely earthy, even if it were ground into the finest powder. However, because it has been "burnt" by nature, it blocks light and creates a black color; and because it consists of very fine parts, it does not make the writing ink sticky. From these things, it is easy to infer its properties. More elegant than this is **Misy** <note>a yellow variety of vitriol</note>, which they call "Roman vitriol." Its smoke is so heavy that it even kills trees and disfigures forests. Sometimes Misy shines and sparkles with what look like golden droplets. Indeed, in every kind of mineral <note>original: "fossilium"; in the 16th century, this referred to anything dug out of the ground</note> there is something that sparkles: among the juices there is Misy, among the metals there is gold, among the stones there are gems and marbles, and among the earths there is silver-earth <note>original: "argentaria"; a white earth used by silversmiths</note>. For brilliance occurs when dense matter is polished by art or nature, and in every class of mineral, something dense must necessarily be found. The part of copperas or Misy that is extracted like a foam and is not further processed is called **Cuperosa** <note>couperose</note>, though Galen and other ancient writers called it **chalcitis**. It is white, very close to the nature of copperas, not at all shiny, and is remarkably effective at inducing vomiting. When copperas or Misy is burnt by the force of fire in glass vessels, **oil of vitriol** <note>original: "oleum uitrioli"; concentrated sulfuric acid</note> is drawn out. This is extremely sharp and hot; if one touches warts that have already been lanced with it, they will fall away. To the taste, it strikes the tongue no differently than a red-hot iron. Nevertheless, it is used to dry out severe internal ulcers where there is not much corruption, as occurs in some people suffering from consumption <note>original: "phthoe"</note> without pain. It is also useful for cutting away cancers and rotted limbs when applied with a piece of olive wood dipped in it.

<margin>Marcasite.</margin>
<margin>Why metallic minerals melt when lead is added, even if they are dry on their own.</margin>
Next, as I have said, are the remaining metallic substances mixed with juices, such as **Pyrite**, which the common people call **Marcasite**. This is composed of stone and juice. It has almost as many varieties as there are metals to be found. It is called "pyrite" because it gives off fire <note>from the Greek "pyr" for fire</note> when struck, owing to its hardness. It is mostly silvery in color, shining, and very heavy. If it is ignited and sprinkled with sharp vinegar, it dissolves a hardened spleen <note>original: "lienem"; the organ, which was thought to become "hardened" by certain humors</note> better than anything else. The cause is the thinness and heat of its parts, which enter through the skin and the peritoneum <note>the lining of the abdominal cavity</note> to thin the blockage. On its own, it hardly melts, but with the addition of lead it dissolves, which is the case for all the drier metallic minerals. For when there is little moisture or wateriness, if it is put into the fire without lead, it is consumed by the heat before it can melt. When lead is added, it is not consumed; since it was solidified by cold, it must be liquefied by fire. For this reason, when gold or silver is contained in stone, if they are melted with lead added, they do not perish...

->## Book Five<-

<margin>Pyrite sometimes contains silver, but more often copper.</margin>
<margin>Cifum.</margin>
<margin>Blue vitriol.</margin>
<margin>Alum is contained in shoemaker's ink.</margin>
<margin>Cobalt.</margin>
The expense of processing would be lost, for if these substances are committed to the fires on their own, something is always lost. This loss is rarely so small that it does not exceed the cost of the lead used. Of this **pyrite** <note>literally "fire-stone," a sulfide mineral that creates sparks</note>, one type is "sterile" <note>meaning it contains no extractable metal</note>, and another contains metal—usually copper, but occasionally silver. It was once believed that the sterile kind was merely a vapor rather than metallic matter, but it is established that it belongs to the class of metals; for when mixed with lead, it produces the small rods used as type for printing. To this class belongs **Cifum**, a substance midway between pyrite and **Galena** <note>lead ore</note>. From pyrite there sometimes "blooms" **fory**, **melanteria**, and **chalcitis**, and from these, **Misy** <note>these are various forms of iron and copper sulfates or vitriols</note>. **Melanteria** is a type of ink <note>original: "Atramentum"</note>, belonging to the vitriol family as has been said, but the variety that is blue shines with a wonderful brilliance. It is quite clear that alum is contained in shoemaker's ink <note>original: "atramento sutorio"; iron sulfate used for blackening leather</note>. For if its sludge is diluted with water, alum thickens within it, and the "oil of vitriol" <note>sulfuric acid</note> breathes forth the scent of alum. From pyrite and silver comes a certain kind of **cadmia** <note>zinc-bearing ore or furnace deposits</note> called **Cobalt** <note>original: "Cobaltum"; here referring to arsenical ores that were troublesome to miners</note>. This substance is so corrosive that it burns the feet of the miners; the cause is a heat that is not small, but moderate. If, however, the heat were great, the substance would be cast out spontaneously rather than having to be dug out.

<margin>Antimony.</margin>
But there is also a warmth in fossils <note>original: "fossilibus"; at this time, "fossil" referred to anything dug out of the earth</note>, such as those dug in the valley called **Joachim** <note>Joachimsthal, a famous silver mining town in Bohemia</note>. Although by nature such things are cold, they seem warm when first unearthed, due to bitumen, or sulfur, or some sharp "juice" <note>original: "succus"; a mineral solution</note> in their nature, or lime. Furthermore, the form of pyrite is sometimes like small gaming-stones—indeed, even like cubes or dice—such that you would say nature had competed with art. There is also a tawny kind which they call "golden." Closest to it is **stibium** <note>antimony ore</note>, which is leaden in color, with a splendid luster and a scaly texture. A red oil is drawn from it, which is extremely sharp and smells of sulfur, and the oil itself retains the power of the **Antimony** <note>original: "Antimonium"</note>; for that is what they now call stibium, though because of its thick substance, it is useful for few things. And just as stibium partakes of the nature of lead, so pyrite seems to partake of copper. For this reason, pyrite also thins the spleen, as I have mentioned. Indeed, pyrite seems to be an immature substance of copper, not a mere vapor. For in the Ocra mountains near Trieste, the mine of pyrite extends so far and wide that if it were a vapor, the whole mountain would have to be made of copper.

<margin>Cadmia.</margin>
<margin>Silver is sometimes found in antimony.</margin>
<margin>Chrysocolla.</margin>
But I return to **Cadmia** <note>zinc ore or oxide</note>; there is a type which, when roasted, smells of garlic and stinks as badly as the kind dug up at **Annaberg** <note>a mining town in Saxony known for silver and tin</note>. Cadmia itself is usually saffron-colored, and for that reason, it is most suitable for making **brass** <note>original: "aurichalco"; an alloy of copper and zinc</note>. Metals also exist within other metallic ores, just as silver is sometimes found in stibium, though it can only be separated by fire. When stibium is melted in a vessel, it turns into a certain kind of lead, which could be called a "fourth type." The reason is that Antimony is the raw material of lead, just as pyrite is of copper. Likewise, **chrysocolla** <note>literally "gold-glue"; refers to malachite or mineral solders</note> is a type of "juice" containing gold, from which it takes its name. By the erosion of "sharp waters" <note>mineral acids</note>, the chrysocolla of gold and the blue mineral <note>azurite</note> are created; they are born together, with one sometimes overtaking the other, though usually the blue prevails, as Theophrastus testifies. Copperas <note>original: "Calchantum"</note> is made from copper and Stygian water <note>original: "aquæ stygiae"; likely a reference to a strong acid like nitric acid</note>...

<header>On Mixtures and Metallic Substances.</header>

# On Mixtures and Metallic Substances.

...Stygian waters <note>original: "stygiæ"; likely a reference to a highly corrosive acid or poisonous liquid</note> from orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide, a yellow mineral</note>. Therefore, some things are produced from the raw material of metals, while others come from the metals themselves: we have already said that **pyrite** and **antimony** <note>original: "stibium"</note> come from the material of metals; whereas from corroded metals come **vitriol** <note>original: "calchantum"</note>, **chalcitis** <note>a copper-iron sulfate</note>, **chrysocolla**, and **Stygian water**, along with **Misy**, **sory**, and similar substances. Those things which cause corrosion are partly sharp, or salty, or acidic: for one may observe this same principle in the mechanical arts, though the raw material to be corroded is itself sufficient. For it is more accurate to say that vitriol and chalcitis are made from the "matter" of copper rather than from copper itself: for, as we shall show, **verdigris** <note>original: "aerugo"</note> is what is more properly made from copper metal.

<margin>Orpiment.</margin>
<margin>Arsenic.</margin>
<margin>Realgar.</margin>
**Orpiment** <note>original: "Auripigmentum"</note> itself appears to contain a portion of gold, but the cost of extracting it exceeds the profit. There are three kinds: the white, which is called **Arsenic** <note>white arsenic or arsenic trioxide</note>. There are some, however, who cook it. Then there is the saffron-colored kind, which has retained the name [orpiment], and the lurid kind, which they call **Realgar** <note>original: "Rosagallum"</note>. All of these are instant poisons; however, the saffron-colored kind, which keeps the ancient name, is the mildest of them. These are not only poisonous to humans, but also to plants and animals.

<margin>A way of killing mice and wolves.</margin>
Plants perish if they are fumigated [with these], and not only mice, but even wolves, if they eat of it and are unable to drink water, will not only die, but are driven into such a fierce madness that they attack animals of their own kind; and whatever they bite falls into that same madness, so that the entire species may perish in a short time. I have occasionally performed experiments on this matter. Nevertheless, it is dangerous, lest you also destroy domesticated and harmless animals, or find yourself frustrated by the discovery of water <note>implying that if the animal finds water, the poison's specific "madness" effect might be neutralized or altered</note>. Truly, with a small amount, if it goes well, you can clear a house full of mice. In the case of wolves, it is more difficult, as they find water more quickly.

<margin>Dry metallic substances are poison to gold and silver if melted with them.</margin>
But these are not only poisonous to living things; orpiment and other "dry" substances, such as antimony, verdigris, and **Sulfur**, are poison to gold and silver. This works by a principle opposite to that of lead, which is beneficial to them; for these substances consume the "moisture" <note>an alchemical term for the fluid, metallic essence that allows metals to melt and remain malleable</note> of the metals so that they cannot be properly melted. Instead, under the action of fire, since there is nothing to resist their dryness, the very substance of the metal is burned and turns into smoke. Thus, they consume copper more quickly than gold and silver, but even these precious metals are forced to vanish when mixed with their "greasiness." For since they contain a fatty part that burns within the mixed metals, they drive the metal’s own moisture into smoke; once this is consumed, the metal itself vanishes, for it cannot exist without that moisture. Just as large knots in trees do not burn by themselves, but burn when joined in company with other wood, so the moisture of gold and silver—which is not fit to be burned on its own—burns and is consumed when orpiment, sulfur, and such things are added.

<margin>Currency can be peeled.</margin>
From this class of substances, therefore, comes that which "peels" <note>original: "decorticat"</note> a coin, just as a snake is accustomed to shed its skin, while the image [on the coin] remains.

<margin>How chrysocolla is made.</margin>
I return to **Chrysocolla**, which they now call **Borax**; there is a synthetic kind which is usually made from split alum and **sal ammoniac** <note>ammonium chloride</note>. Galen believes it can also be made from the urine of a boy, stirred constantly in a copper mortar during the rising of the Dog Star <note>the star Sirius; this period, the "dog days," was thought to have specific alchemical properties</note>. The color of the synthetic kind is a shining saffron; goldsmiths use it for joining pieces of gold, which is where its name originated <note>from the Greek *chrysos* (gold) and *kolla* (glue)</note>.

<margin>Lapis lazuli.</margin>
But the azure or blue stone, which our people call **Lazuli**, is most beautiful, with the color of the sky flickering between...

<page-num>358</page-num>
<header>Book Five</header>

# Book Five

...with golden spots. From this, a wonderful opportunity is given to the artist by the nature of the material while it is being engraved: the gold adorns the garments or represents the stars. One must choose material that is suitable and well-defined, and engrave the figure similar to a sculpture, not hollow.

<margin>Realgar.</margin>
**Sandaracha** <note>original: "Sandaracha"; known today as realgar, a red arsenic sulfide mineral</note> is what the common people call red orpiment. But it is not orpiment; it has a sulfurous smell, and is saffron-colored on the outside, not shining, but red and brilliant on the inside. The smell is not altogether unpleasant. Because of the similarity of the outer color, they sell it mixed with saffron-colored orpiment.

<margin>Star-stone.</margin>
**Syderea** <note>literally "star-stone"</note>, which the Italians call **Manganese** <note>original: "Manganensem"</note>, is an earth most suitable for purifying soda <note>original: "nitro"; likely referring to its use as a decoloring agent in glassmaking</note>, tinting it with a blue color.

<margin>Blue pigment.</margin>
There is also another substance that tints glass <note>original: "uitium," likely a typo for "vitrum" (glass)</note> a blue color, which some call **Zaffre** <note>original: "Zapheram"; a cobalt-based pigment used in glass and ceramics</note>.

<margin>Green Earth.</margin>
There is also a green earth of a metallic kind, which the Italians call **Green Azure** <note>original: "Azzurrum uiride"; likely malachite or chrysocolla</note>, and we call **chlorogea** <note>literally "green earth"</note>. It is born in mines rich in copper and silver, from which it is likely formed by the "breath" <note>vapors or efflorescence</note> of the copper and silver. It shines, and because of this, it is very similar to the blue stone <note>lapis lazuli or azurite</note>.

<margin>Color from lapis lazuli is resistant to fire, water, and age.</margin>
Color from **lapis lazuli** <note>original: "lazulo"; the source of ultramarine blue</note> is not quite as useful for [all] works. For the color of the blue stone is spoiled neither by fire nor water, nor hardly by any age. Hence its honor and price. The reason is that it is very dense and of extremely fine substance. Thus, a small quantity suffices for a large panel, just as we shall say concerning gold and silver. The cause of its fineness and density is a long "cooking" <note>referring to the geological formation or the rigorous purification process</note> and the separation of useless parts.

<margin>False blue.</margin>
For this reason, **false blue** <note>original: "pseudocæruleæ"; likely a reference to azurite or an inferior copper-based blue</note> has almost no honor. This is brought from the Spanish lands, but it is far inferior to the blue stone, because it is not as fine nor as dense; therefore, more is required in the work, nor does it have equal power to withstand age, fire, or water. Truly, **chlorogea** still holds honor, since it does not act as a substitute but performs a principal role.

<margin>Galena.</margin>
There are also earths mixed with metals, such as **Galena**, which the Italians call **Ochre** <note>original: "Ocria"; though Galena is lead ore, the author notes the common name</note>. It consists of lead and earth. It is undoubtedly the material of imperfect lead, and therefore most suitable for smelting metals, especially when they must be extracted from the matrix.

<margin>The Mother-stone.</margin>
The **matrix** <note>original: "Matrix"</note> is the stone joined with the metal. For most of the nobler metals lie in a stony material, which we may call the matrix.

<margin>How quicksilver is found.</margin>
Truly, among metallic substances, none more excellent than **quicksilver** <note>original: "argento uiuo"; mercury</note> can be found. Men of clever industry detect where it arises. In the months of April and May, at dawn under a clear sky, they watch the rising vapors in the mountains, appearing like a cloud, not lifting itself high, but very low and almost clinging to the earth. By this means, the seekers of quicksilver find its location.

<margin>Gold alone sinks in quicksilver.</margin>
It is very heavy and very fine, two qualities which it shares with gold, so that some hoped one could be made from the other. Indeed, not only among metals, but among all things as far as I know, only gold sinks and descends into it, while all other things float on the surface.

<margin>Quicksilver passes through deer skin.</margin>
This same quicksilver, when it has "drunk" <note>absorbed/amalgamated</note> the gold or even by itself, penetrates **deer skin** <note>original: "corium ceruinum"</note>, which is very thick. For in this way they select the gold: they heat the quicksilver and place upon it fragments of gilded clothing or other things containing gold...

<page-num>139</page-num>
<header>On Mixtures and Metallic Substances</header>

<margin>A method for collecting gold that is in fragments.</margin>
...they contain, and as I have said, the gold itself is quickly absorbed by the mercury <note>original: "argento uiuo," literally "living silver"</note>; then the mercury is squeezed out through a piece of leather, while the gold remains at the bottom. Once melted with a small fire, it solidifies. There are also other ways of collecting gold, but not without "sharp waters" <note>original: "acutis aquis"; likely nitric acid or aqua regia</note>, or sulfur, and a great deal of labor. Oil does not pass through leather as quickly, which suggests that mercury is even thinner than oil.

<margin>Mercury pierces all metallic vessels.</margin>
It corrodes all metallic vessels; it pierces through brass, silver, and lead. For this reason, it is more safely stored in small wooden vessels than in metallic ones. It is an incredible thing to say, but nonetheless, anyone can experience it for themselves, as I have done. Hieronymus the Jeweler <note>original: "Hieronymus Gemmarius," likely a known contemporary craftsman</note>, called "of the eyes" <note>original: "ab oculis dictus"; perhaps a nickname referring to his keen sight or a specific family name</note>, told me this, but I could not give it credit without an experiment.

<margin>Gold smeared with mercury breaks by itself.</margin>
The fact of the matter is this: gold smeared with mercury becomes more fragile than an eggshell. It even develops cracks on its own, and is rendered not unlike the softest cement. Indeed, when I tested this on a golden crown <note>original: "aureo coronato"; a gold coin stamped with a crown</note>, I broke the whole thing into many pieces. For this reason, those who wear gold rings should take diligent care that they are not contaminated by mercury. For even the "shadow" <note>referring here to the vapors or mere presence</note> of it makes metals vulnerable, though gold far more so than silver. The cause of this must be that it penetrates the interior by its own fineness, and its coldness constricts the metal, whereby it is rendered brittle. The coldness of water shows this in steel <note>original: "chalybe"</note>; for when steel is frequently quenched in water, it is rendered so fragile—especially if the water is very cold—that it breaks of its own accord.

<margin>How the Moors achieve cooling.</margin>
That mercury is extremely cold, the touch itself demonstrates. For this reason, the Moors <note>original: "Mauri"; referring to the peoples of North Africa</note> and those who live in Africa, seeking relief from those extreme heats, fill a stone or wooden vessel with mercury, place a piece of leather over it, and lie upon the leather. If an experiment were made with iron, it would also be tempered in the same way.

<margin>Why mercury comes together of its own accord.</margin>
<margin>A comparison of mercury and water, and a fourfold similarity.</margin>
To return to the matter, mercury comes together into one mass because of its weight; for it seeks the bottom, and since the bottom is usually a single point, it gathers there. It also gathers for another reason: it is moist and oily, and as it moves, it leaves a trail behind it, making the passage easier and more inclined, by which it is carried into one mass and one location. Because it is heavy and round, it must necessarily be carried very quickly for whatever reason, which is why it hardly ever rests; hence the name "living silver" <note>quicksilver</note> was given to it. Mercury is, therefore, like a metal that has not solidified. Just as a metal is to mercury, so ice is to water; and just as ice does not vanish until it is dissolved, so metals do not vanish <note>evaporate</note> until they are liquefied. But since mercury is very swift, it vanishes spontaneously as liquid water does. However, just as water, when it vanishes (as in distillations), thickens again by cold, so mercury, after it has vanished by fire, clings to roofs and paneled ceilings. And just as mercury and metals require less cold to solidify than water and ice—for it is enough for a metal not to be hindered by excessive heat for it to solidify, whereas water requires the excessive cold of frost—so water requires less heat to vanish than mercury does.

<page-num>140</page-num>
<header>Book Five</header>
<sig>e 2</sig>

# Book Five

<margin>What quicksilver is.</margin>
Quicksilver <note>original: "argentum uiuum"; literally "living silver," the common Renaissance term for mercury</note>, therefore, is a certain kind of thickened water. It is not thickened by heat, for it is not curdled by it, nor by cold, for then it would be a stone or a metal; rather, it is thickened by a very fine and very pure earthy portion. This results in it being extremely heavy, extremely cold, shining, and liquid. It is a mixture rather than a solid mass, since, as I have said, it is liquid.

<margin>The reason why water and quicksilver become round when on a dry surface.</margin>
<margin>Quicksilver is extremely tenacious.</margin>
Quicksilver is similar to water in four ways: both are extremely cold, and when they have evaporated due to heat, they return to their original state through cold. Both flow toward lower paths, and both gather into a round shape when they recoil from something dry. Now, the reason why quicksilver and water turn round in dust or even on a dry surface is because they flee contact with the dry. Since a body can touch another body at no part smaller than a point, quicksilver and water strive to touch the dry surface only at a single point. This clearly happens if they become round; for a sphere touches a plane at only one point. Thus, when portions of water and quicksilver are scattered over a dusty table, they become round. But since large masses do not do this—nor do they form into a downward-leaning cone—it is a sign that this roundness (in which the outer edges hang from the sides and the weight is supported beyond normal expectation) is held together by a tenacious moisture <note>The author is describing what we now call surface tension</note>. And for this reason, since quicksilver gathers into larger spheres than water, even though it is heavier, it must be extremely tenacious. Furthermore, if it is scattered, its parts cling together even more than thin oil, which is proof of its tenacity. Therefore, its hatred of the dry causes quicksilver to gather into a circle, while its tenacity allows it to remain so. For this reason, parts of water maintain that roundness far less, because water is also far less tenacious than quicksilver.

<margin>Places where quicksilver abounds are lush and full of water.</margin>
<margin>Quicksilver fouls gold.</margin>
<margin>Quicksilver can be solidified in three ways.</margin>
<margin>By what things quicksilver is stopped.</margin>
<margin>How quicksilver is extinguished by saliva.</margin>
Since water and quicksilver differ very little and are of a similar nature, the mountains in which it originates are beautifully green and gush with springs. On account of its tenacity, it fouls <note>original: "fœdat"; the author uses a strong word suggesting contamination, reflecting how mercury ruins the appearance and structure of other metals</note> gold and other metals; or at least, if one prefers a milder name, it "whitens" them. It is also solidified by all those things that consume its moisture. For if it flows because it is moist and thin, it will be made firm by all those things that dry out that thin moisture. It will therefore be solidified by astringents, and also by earthy substances, provided they penetrate within it. It is not "stopped" <note>original: "sistitur"; referring to stopping its movement by turning it into a solid</note> with difficulty because it would transform into silver if it were stopped, but because it is difficult to find a substance so thin that it can be mixed through the whole of it. Therefore, it is curdled by sulfur, for sulfur burns away its thinnest moisture. It is also curdled by the substance of metals when it has "drunk" them in, and by smoke; for it is thickened by some, and by others it is restrained by their tenacity. Thus, it is no wonder if it is made firm by the juices of herbs. But it will turn out no better for it. By almost the same reasoning, it is prevented from flowing by saliva <note>original: "saliua"; this refers to "killing" mercury by spitting on it and stirring, a common trick to break its surface tension and stop it from rolling</note> because of its tenacity. For since, as we said, it is tenacious on its own, what wonder is it if it is restrained by another tenacious thing? But it is one thing to be solidified, and another to be restrained from motion. For whatever is solidified is restrained from motion, but not everything restrained from motion is immediately solidified. I say "to be solidified" when it becomes hard; and this hardly happens without the mixture of sulfur or another body. But it is easily restrained, since, as I said, that can be done by saliva alone. Therefore, on account of...

<page-num>141</page-num>
<header>On Mixtures and Metals.</header>

# On Mixtures and Metals.

<margin>Quicksilver put into trees kills them.</margin>
<margin>Quicksilver kills all insects.</margin>
Its immense coldness, weight, and corrosive power kills trees: it acts slowly and uncertainly if it does not reach the pith <note>the soft, central sponge-like tissue in a tree trunk</note>, but very quickly and surely once it has arrived there. Likewise, it destroys flies, fleas, bedbugs, and all insects, especially when mixed with black soap. There are those who deny that it and Minium <note>original: "Minium"; in this context, the author refers to red lead or a mercury-sulfide ore, often confused in early mineralogy</note> were once discovered in the East. A vein of minium was found at Scombach in Elbogen, Bohemia. But the value and authority it once held has diminished, as artificial cinnabar <note>mercury sulfide used as a pigment</note> now supplies the requirement.

<margin>Minium.</margin>
There is also another kind of Cinnabar that occurs naturally, which there is no need to mention now. But Minium is very similar to Sandaraca <note>original: "Sandaracha"; usually referring to realgar, a bright red arsenic sulfide mineral</note>, and does not differ from it except that it releases quicksilver both spontaneously and even more so when heated by fire; even if the quicksilver is not separated, the minium drinks it back in again, whereas Sandaraca does not yield quicksilver. But we have spoken above of what kind of thing Sandaraca is.

<margin>Heated quicksilver breaks vessels.</margin>
I would also like to remind you regarding quicksilver that if it is enclosed in a glass or stone vessel and cannot "breathe" [vent], it shatters the vessel if exposed to a stronger fire, for the same reason and in no different a manner than gunpowder does. However, it is set in motion even by a gentle heat. Thus, when placed in a boiling vessel, it is moved by a "spirituous" motion, which causes wonder in those who do not know the cause.

Thus far, then, we have dealt with the more noble metallic substances that nature brings forth; now, however, let us see how much power Art <note>the term "Art" refers to human technology, specifically alchemy or early chemical processing</note> has in imitating nature. For Art also has its own metallic substances, and even metals, as well as stones like the murrhine vessels which have already been discussed. Therefore, the artificial metallic substances are: Cinnabar, sublimated mercury, precipitate, psoricum <note>a medicinal mineral compound used for itchy skin</note>, smalt <note>a blue glass pigment</note>, slag [recrementum], stone, diphryges <note>a byproduct of smelting copper</note>, cadmia <note>here likely referring to zinc oxide or cobalt ore deposits</note>, pompholyx <note>often called "white nothing," a zinc oxide byproduct of smelting</note>, spodos <note>metallic ash</note>, flower of copper, then scale, verdigris [aerugo], vermicularis, stommona <note>a term for hardened iron or steel</note>, rust [ferrugo], blue pigment [caeruleum], ceruse [white lead], sandix <note>a red pigment made from lead or madder</note>, ochre, plumbago <note>lead ore or graphite</note>, froth of silver [litharge], purpurina, and nitre.

<margin>Cinnabar.</margin>
Cinnabar or vermilion: put sulfur into a pot, melt it, and add double the amount of quicksilver; mix continuously over a fire until no appearance of quicksilver remains; then allow it to cool. Then cook it again, slowly, until it stops hissing; then it is useful to cook it with increased fire until a red smoke emerges. It serves for writing and painting in a red color, and it emulates natural cinnabar.

<margin>Sublimated Mercury.</margin>
Mercury is sublimated in this way—I am speaking of "living silver," and I am not ashamed to use the barbarian name <note>the author likely considers the chemical term "sublimatum" to be "barbarian" or non-classical Latin</note>, but if one wishes to speak in Latin, though not as clearly, it may be called "thoroughly-cooked silver." Put quicksilver and shoemaker’s black <note>original: "sutorium atramentum"; likely ferrous sulfate or vitriol used for blackening leather</note> in equal weight into a mortar, and mix with the sharpest white vinegar until the quicksilver ceases to be seen; then cook it in a glass vessel smeared with clay <note>a process called "luting" to seal the vessel</note> until it hardens. If any escapes or does not combine, grind it again in the mortar with added vinegar and cook it once more.

<margin>Precipitate.</margin>
Red "cooked silver" is made thus; they call it precipitate. Take equal portions of alum and chalcantum <note>original: "calchantum"; vitriol or copper sulfate</note>, to which add half as much salt again as one of them; distill all of this in glass vessels. Put one pound of this "water" [distilled acid] and three of quicksilver into a glass vessel, then distill it; continue with increased fire until the smoke and the vessel turn red, and no water remains; finally...

<header>Book Five</header>

Finally, once the vessel is broken, collect the <term>quicksilver</term><note>original: "argentum uiuum"; mercury</note>, which you will now see has come together in the likeness of a stone. Grind this very finely upon a <term>porphyry table</term><note>a flat slab of hard igneous rock used by apothecaries and artists for grinding pigments and medicines</note>, and cook and distill it again until it is dried out in the glass vessel. Once the vessel is broken again, collect the material that remains and once more grind it most subtly upon the same table. Afterward, place it in a bronze vessel and, with a strong fire placed beneath, mix and stir it with a bronze rod for the space of two hours, until it acquires a near-brilliance and a reddish hue. Then, take it out and keep it in glass vessels.

Truly, among all things that erode flesh without causing pain and dry out rotting ulcers, this is the most excellent if it has been rightly made. Nor is it of any other use that I know of, though such processed mercury is used as <term>rouge</term><note>original: "fucum"; face paint or cosmetics</note>, for it whitens and adds brilliance to the faces of women. But it also knocks out the teeth and produces a foul stench of the mouth. Otherwise, it is conducive to many things regarding the use of silver and the art of goldsmiths.

<margin>Cooked orpiment.</margin>
Most metallic substances change their color by fire alone, such as <term>orpiment</term><note>original: "auripigmentum"; an arsenic sulfide mineral used as a yellow pigment</note> which is of a yellowish color; when cooked in a glass vessel until it adheres to the glass, it turns red and takes on the powers of <term>precipitate</term><note>mercuric oxide, often used as a caustic in medicine</note>, and it is not so much inferior as it is more useful due to the ease of its preparation.

<margin>Psoricum.</margin>
<term>Psoricum</term><note>a medicinal preparation used by ancient and Renaissance doctors for itchy skin diseases or eye ailments</note> consists of two parts <term>chalcitis</term><note>a copper-bearing mineral, likely a sulfate</note> and one part <term>cadmia</term><note>zinc oxide or furnace calamine</note>, or of silver dross. These are mixed and ground with the addition of sharp white vinegar, then buried during the <term>Dog Days</term><note>original: "caniculæ tempore"; the hottest weeks of summer (July-August) when the star Sirius rises with the sun</note> in horse dung for forty days. Once dug up, it is roasted in a new earthen pot over coals until it turns red.

<margin>Smalt.</margin>
<term>Smalt</term><note>original: "Smaltum"; a blue glass used in pigments and enameling</note> is a type of glass with which gold cavities are filled, varied in color and of extraordinary beauty. It receives colors of every kind and shines best; that which is without equal is made from alum, <term>chalcanthum</term><note>original: "calchanto"; blue vitriol or copper sulfate</note>, and stony salt; others mix the colors with glass.

<margin>Dross.</margin>
<term>Dross</term><note>original: "Recrementum"; slag or the impurities skimmed off during smelting</note> is that which is drawn away from the metal while it is being smelted; the common people call it "scum." It retains the powers and the matter of the metal from which it came; for this reason, silver and gold dross is usually smelted again, so that nothing is lost to the greed of men.

<margin>Stone.</margin>
That which does not melt when the metal is liquefied is <term>stone</term><note>often referred to as gangue; the commercially worthless mineral matter surrounding the ore</note>. This too retains something of the metal and its powers, but in the case of the more noble metals, the stone is carefully crushed and smelted again.

<margin>Diphryges.</margin>
<term>Diphryges</term><note>literally "twice-roasted"; a metallurgical byproduct mentioned by Dioscorides and Pliny</note> is formed while the stone that was joined with the copper is burned. It has a metallic taste, as is to be expected; it acquires a blue color if sprinkled with copper-water, but if it is not sprinkled, it is purple or blackish.

<margin>Cadmia.</margin>
We have said that <term>cadmia</term><note>here referring to furnace calamine, a zinc oxide buildup</note> is found naturally, but it also forms while metal is being smelted, clinging to the furnace like a cluster of grapes. The best is made from blue pyrites; while it is in pieces it is white, and when it is ground it is very white, because it is formed from silver or even from gold.

<margin>Pompholyx or tutty.</margin>
<term>Pompholyx</term><note>a fine white zinc oxide "soot"</note> adheres like a bubble while the metal is being smelted, very much like tufts of wool. Although it may cling to the walls, it is secondary to cadmia; it is white, especially when ground. It is called <term>Tutty</term><note>original: "Tutia"</note> by the common people. But by the name of Tutty they also understand <term>Spodon</term><note>a grittier, heavier metallic ash or oxide</note>, since there is not much difference between Spodon and Pompholyx, as Spodon is almost a species of Pompholyx, or may serve in its place; for Spodon is more common <insert>and more base...</insert>

<header>On Mixed and Metallic Substances.</header>

# On Mixed and Metallic Substances.

...more common is **Pompholyx**<note>original: "Pompholyx"; a form of zinc oxide produced in smelting furnaces, often called "white nothing" or "philosopher's wool"</note>, and both are useful for eye medicines. 
<margin>ash</margin>
**Ash**<note>original: "Spodos"; the soot or slag found on the walls of smelting furnaces</note> is that which sticks to the walls of the secondary furnaces in which metals are separated. It thickens from the smoke of gold, silver, and lead mixed with earth, which makes it more impure and weaker than Pompholyx. For it does not thicken from the smoke and the primary material of metals (which is itself metallic), as **Cadmia**<note>zinc ore or furnace deposits</note> or Pompholyx do, but from smoke and dust alone that does not partake of the metal. Hence, Cadmia and Pompholyx are found only in the furnaces near mines, whereas Ash is for the most part found in cities.
<margin>Flower of copper</margin>
The **flower of copper**<note>original: "Flos aeris"; small metallic grains of copper</note> is made by pouring water over copper while it is being drawn, glowing hot, from the first furnace. For as it contracts, it spits out certain small granules very similar to copper, yet such that they may be very easily reduced to powder when ground.
<margin>Copper scale</margin>
Truly, **copper scale** is struck off from copper when it is beaten with hammers.
<margin>Iron scale</margin>
That which falls from iron in the same manner is called **Stommonia**, that is, iron scale.
<margin>Verdigris</margin>
A little **verdigris**<note>original: "Aerugo"; the green pigment or crust formed on copper/bronze</note> is made by chance, but the most is made as follows: take a wiped-clean bronze vessel and place it over another vessel like a lid; in the lower vessel—which can be of stone, wood, or iron—put the sharpest vinegar. Within ten days, you will scrape the finest verdigris from the bottom of the bronze vessel that you placed there as a lid. Much is collected from many larger vessels by repeating the work; and just as verdigris comes from copper, so
<margin>Iron rust</margin>
**iron rust**<note>original: "Ferrugo"</note> is collected from iron. And just as verdigris is not only astringent but also corrosive, so iron rust is more intensely astringent and drying than verdigris, but it is free from corrosion. For in verdigris the parts are thin and sharp due to the heat, while in iron rust there is nothing either hot or thin. For this reason, it also lacks a graceful color.

<margin>Metallic things formed by fire do not retain color except for black.</margin>
It is therefore manifest in these metallic substances which are formed by fire, that color resides in the subtler substance if it is not black. Since a thin substance cannot be mixed into a thick one except by the benefit of nature (as has been demonstrated), every color except black is deciduous<note>liable to fall away or change easily</note>. But black can remain stable, since it is a privation of light which resides in earthy matter.
<margin>worm-like</margin>
Next after verdigris is **worm-like verdigris**<note>original: "uermicularis"; a high-quality verdigris prepared in a specific shape</note>. For when you take one part white vinegar and two parts old urine, and mix them in a vessel of Cyprian copper, you must stir it with a pestle until they take on a certain thicker substance. Then add a twenty-fourth part each of salt and alum. Leave it in the sun for forty days, while the **Dog Star**<note>original: "caniculæ ſydus"; Sirius, associated with the hottest part of summer (the "dog days")</note> scorches the earth, mixing and stirring it constantly. You will have "worm-like" verdigris, having the thickness of honey from the start, but the color of verdigris, though far more brilliant. Once taken from the vessel, placed on a board, and formed into the likeness of little worms (from which it took its name), it will acquire the substance of verdigris.
<margin>Azure</margin>
**Azure**<note>original: "Ceruleum"; a blue pigment</note> is made thus: pour three pounds of the sharpest vinegar into an oak vessel, but first dissolve in it a quarter ounce of any kind of **sal ammoniac**<note>ammonium chloride</note>. Then take thin plates of silver, perforated everywhere with small holes and smeared with **quicksilver**<note>mercury</note>...

...bind those [sheets] smeared [with the mixture] to a rod, and hang the rod itself over a vessel in such a way that it is not far from the vinegar, yet does not touch it: then cover everything with quite warm horse manure <note>Horse manure was a standard source of gentle, steady heat in early chemistry and alchemy</note>. After 20 days, you will scrape the **blue pigment**<note>original: "caeruleum"</note> from the silver; then replace it again, and if necessary smear the silver sheets [again], and after another 20 days scrape away whatever blue has been collected; repeat this more often. Finally, throw whatever blue has been collected into a vessel with the **dross of silver**<note>original: "argenti spuma"</note> which they call **litharge**<note>original: "lithargyrium"; a lead oxide mineral formed during the separation of silver from lead ore</note>, and roast it a little; then, once cooled, wash it with spring water so that the dust comes away, and dry it in the Sun.

<margin>Ceruse.</margin>
**Ceruse**<note>original: "Cerussa"; white lead pigment, highly valued but toxic</note> is made by pouring sharp vinegar into a vessel; then place twigs therein, and upon the twigs place thin sheets of lead weighing one pound. Bury it in horse manure. After 25 days you will collect the ceruse; or if you wish to be a more diligent guardian, scrape it after the first 10 days, and replace it again, repeating this three times. Another kind, most suitable for juice <note>likely referring to liquid mediums or inks</note> and of the brightest white, is brought from Spain. Place thin sheets of **white lead**<note>original: "plumbo candido"; in this context, it refers to tin</note>—which we, however, call **tin**<note>original: "stannum"</note>—into urine, and distill the whole of the urine; meanwhile, the lead transforms into ceruse, which is then dried, ground, and sifted.

<margin>Sandix.</margin>
From ceruse, **sandix**<note>a bright orange-red pigment, often a mixture of red lead and iron oxide</note> is made, of a most lovely reddish color. Therefore, place the ceruse in an iron pan and stir it over the fire for so long until it becomes red and shines: it is evident, therefore, that the best sandix must be made from the best ceruse. <margin>Ochre.</margin> **Ochre**—that is, the pale kind—is born naturally just as Sandix is, whence **Virgil**<note>The Roman poet Virgil, Eclogues 4.45</note> says:

> Of its own accord, the **sandix** shall clothe the grazing lambs.

But we are teaching that which is made by art. Therefore, boil down **black lead**<note>likely metallic lead or galena</note> in a vessel for so long until it has taken on the color of ochre. The color of natural ochre, however, is flame-colored. Ochre is also made from **red earth**<note>original: "rubrica"</note> while it is roasted in a vessel smeared with manure. <margin>Litharge.</margin> The **dross of silver**, which we call **litharge**, is made while lead is separated from silver; it is impure lead, and as it comes from both, it transitions into one or the other in turn. It retains, however, a certain power of the silver; and that which is yellow in color is for that reason called **golden**. <margin>Plumbago.</margin> **Plumbago**<note>here referring to a lead byproduct or lead-glance, not modern graphite</note> is itself also made from lead: for when lead is tormented by fires, it transforms into these two things, especially when joined with silver: the dross of silver and plumbago. Plumbago shines somewhat; otherwise it is similar on the outside to the dross of silver, with an ashen color at the bottom part and a mixed color in the middle: when it is reduced to powder, it turns out as if reddish-yellow. <margin>Purpurina.</margin> **Purpurina**<note>original: "Purpurina"; also known as Mosaic Gold or stannic sulfide, used as a gold substitute in illuminations</note> is of a tawny color and imitates gold if it is of the best quality: it differs in this alone, that it does not withstand the injuries of the weather, nor is it very long-lasting. It consists of equal portions of **tin**<note>original: "plumbi albi"</note> and **quicksilver**<note>mercury</note>; and again of equal portions of **ammonia salt** and **sulfur** between themselves, but let these be sixth or fourth parts of the former [ingredients]. The salt and sulfur are ground finely, and the tin and quicksilver are mixed—for the tin must be reduced into the thinnest leaves. All are mixed in a glass vessel <margin>Three uses of metallic things established by art.</margin> and distilled; and that which remains at the bottom is called purpurina.

Every metallic matter which is established by art is composed of two parts,

...is placed; one part is indeed thin and fiery, which usually burns and is of an excellent color: the other part is earthy, which dries excessively. However, the whole as it is composed is useful for changing <note>In an alchemical context, "changing" or "mutandis" often refers to the transmutation or purification of metals</note> metals. Therefore, **artificial metallic substances**<note>original: "metallica factitia"</note> are prepared for three uses: for healing the human body, for painting, and for adulterating metals or gems. A fourth can be added, which is beyond our current purpose: namely, for poisons.

<margin>Glass.</margin>
**Glass**<note>original: "Vitrum"</note> succeeds all these with a greater miracle. It is a work of art such that it rivals the gems of nature; and for this reason, it has this wonder: it possesses all those colors individually—white, blue, black, purple, and green—with a pleasing brilliance, and it can be engraved and shaped on a lathe. I have seen various kinds of this genre; one that was engraved imitated **Agate**<note>original: "Achatem"</note> with wonderful skill; another is now distinguished with white so subtly and orderly that you might say wax could not be worked more easily or subtly. 

This is a unique example of **human fragility**<note>original: "fragilitatis humanae"</note>, which Princes, among others, should perpetually contemplate not only with their eyes but with their minds. Yet human life is far more fragile than glass—by as much as a thing that breaks of its own accord is more fragile than that which breaks only by an outside force. From glass are made what are called organs, **musical instruments**<note>original: "instrumenta musicae"</note> with a very sweet voice, which show off the pride in the beauty of a human kingdom. From this come pleasant colors, a sweet-sounding voice, and a pleasing splendor—all perishing in a moment from a slight mishap. 

<margin>The composition of glass.</margin>
Glass consists of three clear stones, or sand, **alkali salt**<note>original: "sale chali"; likely referring to soda ash or potash derived from plants</note>, and **manganese**<note>original: "syderea"; likely 'magnesia vitriariorum', a mineral used to clarify glass</note>; I remember recounting the nature of these above. All these, having been ground, are committed to a great fire in vessels, and are forced by the power of the fire into glass. Once extracted, it is again cooked and worked in smaller vessels in the furnace. But now, leaving these things which either consist of art or are imperfect, let us pass on to more perfect things.

# BOOK SIX
## On Metals.

<margin>What the metals are.</margin>
**I** speak now of perfect bodies, such as metals and stones, but first we must deal with metals. The natural metals are gold, silver, electrum <term>electrum: a natural alloy of gold and silver, often considered a distinct metal in antiquity</term>, bronze, copper <note>original: "aes cyprium," literally "Cyprus metal," from which the English word "copper" is derived</note>, lead, and iron. The artificial ones, however, are steel, tin, and brass <term>aurichalcum: a golden-hued alloy of copper and zinc</term>, as well as another type of copper. There are seven natural metals, and four produced against nature by the power of art. To show why there are exactly this many and no more is a task of the greatest subtlety; nevertheless, I shall show it. But first, it must be noted that gold and all the most perfect things are found in the East, whereas iron is found in the West.

<margin>Four reasons why the East is hotter and more humid than the West.</margin>
That this occurs because the East is hotter and more humid has been abundantly declared above. However, it was necessary to demonstrate this—that the East is hotter and more humid than the West—because once shown, it is clear that better "concoction" <term>concoction: the process by which natural heat ripens or matures a substance</term> and generation take place there. From this come what the Greeks call Spices <note>original: "Aromata"</note>, and scents, and gems, and gold, and silver, and all the delights of the human race. This happens because the vapor of the sea is carried from the East over the lands and is ripened by the motion of the Sun. In the West, however, it is carried toward the ocean; even if it were driven toward the lands by the winds, it would quickly return to the ocean by the Sun's motion, or it could not be ripened without the Sun's presence. Added to this is the fact that the motion of the Sun imprints a certain similar power upon the earth from its eternal revolution: so that the beginnings of things are in the East. These things are better and more pleasing, which is why we also rejoice much more in the morning rays of the Sun than in those of the evening. Furthermore, if there are mountains in the West, the Sun’s rays—full of moisture—fill the lands along with the stars and the Moon; no benefit is to be hoped for from the western rays which burn excessively when the air is already scorched. On the contrary, in the West, mountains on that same side block the Sun, but on the opposite side they burn, and are worse than a plain. Also, the Sun illuminates the lands of the East much earlier than those of the West, because there are no mountains in the sea, but many upon the land.

<margin>It is demonstrated that there are seven metals.</margin>
But let us now return to the number of metals. A metal is anything that, as we have said, is ductile <term>ductile: able to be hammered thin or drawn out without breaking</term> and hard. For wax and mud can be drawn out, but they are not hard; conversely, stones and pyrites are hard, but they cannot be drawn out at all. Some will believe that there are seven of these metals according to the number of the planets: so that the Sun receives gold, the Moon silver, Mercury electrum, Mars iron, Saturn lead, Venus bronze, and Jupiter copper. But it is better that we distinguish them thus: every metal is either perfect, soft, and pure, and such is gold; or pure but hard, and such is silver; or hard and impure, and such
<meta>The text continues on the next page following the catchword "est" (is).</meta>

<summary>This page defines the seven natural and four artificial metals, arguing that the most perfect materials (like gold) form in the East due to superior solar "concoction." It also establishes the traditional correspondence between the seven metals and the seven planetary bodies.</summary>
