# On Metals.

<margin>A wonderful story concerning iron which is transmuted into copper.</margin>
...is iron, either soft and impure, and thus it is lead. But electrum <term>electrum: a natural alloy of gold and silver</term> consists of gold and silver. Cyprian copper <note>original: "Aes cyprium," from which the word copper is derived</note> is made from copper and iron, from which it becomes harder than either, just as that which is composed of copper and lead, for that too is harder than both, and [just as] mules are more robust than donkeys and horses. Bronze <term>Aes: though often translated as bronze, here it refers to a refined state of base metal</term> itself is iron that has been better "concocted" <term>concoction: the ripening of a substance through natural heat</term> and with stronger heat; for this reason, it smells more of sulfur. Evidence for this is iron passing into copper. For in the Carpathian mountains of Pannonia, in the town of Smolník <note>original: "Smolinitio," referring to the mining town of Smolník in modern-day Slovakia</note>, Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy"</note> reports—and I have heard it from others as well, who brought copper with them as a wonder and showed it to me—that there is a well from which water is drawn and poured into three channels, and iron placed in them is turned into copper. But if they are thin fragments, they turn into a mud, which, when smelted in fires, turns into the purest copper. The cause is that the matter of iron and copper is the same. Hence, when it is smelted more thoroughly and dyed, iron passes into copper. A mountain lies adjacent to the well, rich in "stony vitriol" <term>calchantum: blue vitriol or copper sulfate, used historically in metallurgy and alchemy</term>; it is clear that this power resides in the vitriol, as we have also seen.

<margin>A most desired question, solved below: whether metals can be transmuted into one another.</margin>
Therefore, that so-famous doubt has arisen: can metals be transmuted into one another by the benefit of art? But before this is defined, it is necessary to demonstrate the excellence of gold. Gold is born in many ways: first, mixed with sand, as in Bohemia, and near Bohemia in Legnica <note>original: "Ligis," likely referring to the Duchy of Liegnitz in Silesia</note>, in the streams near Goldberg <note>original: "Goldeburgum," modern Złotoryja</note> and Riesengrund <note>original: "Risegrundum," meaning "Giant's Ground"</note>, which in Latin is called the Valley of the Giants <note>original: "Vallis gigantum," referring to the Karkonosze mountains</note>, <margin>How gold is found.</margin> and on the banks of the Ticino and the Adda in Italy; then truly also in stones rich in silver, such as in the hill of Montisregius <note>original: "Montisregij," likely referring to a "King's Mountain" mining site</note>, for when the silver is melted, gold flows out, of which at least half an ounce of gold lies hidden in a pound of silver. Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval polymath who wrote extensively on minerals</note> relates that gold is found in very solid stones lying amidst scorched earth. He also writes that gold has sometimes been found among the upper teeth of a human skull in the form of a very fine dust, from which it is certain to be judged that gold lies hidden in human hair. I would believe, which is more likely, that gold is generated among stones; from there, it is carried by the force of running waters when it has hardened into small pieces and is found among the sands. And by the same reasoning, it was found among the teeth of a human skull after a flood occurred, for it stuck in the cracks due to the obstruction of the bone and their density. This opinion is supported by what the Spaniard Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo <note>Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo (1478–1557), a historian of the Spanish colonization of the Americas</note> recounts: in a part of the Indies called Peru, gold found at the foot of mountains is imperfect, and the closer to the mountain, the more impure it is. Nor is it found deep in the earth, but near its surface; therefore, if it were born in the fields or sand, it would lie hidden at the bottom of the earth. And just as coal which is formed on the highest peaks of mountains is found under the earth at the root, so also is gold. For this reason, it is also usually found in riverbeds among the rocks. Therefore, since the most useful metals are hidden in the depths of the earth and are for the most part impure, the nature of gold—liberal and as if extravagant—has placed that pure substance, shining with its own color and needing no fires or art, <margin>How gold is generated.</margin> upon the very surface. It is generated on the highest summits of the mountains.

<summary>This page discusses the natural transmutation of iron into copper via vitriol-rich waters in Slovakia and explores the geological origins of gold. The author cites several authorities to argue that gold is formed on mountain peaks and washed into rivers, rather than growing within the sand itself.</summary>

# Book Six

<margin>Metals are mostly mixed.</margin>
...[found in the mountain] roots, often mixed with a small amount of copper; for even those who have written the history of the gold that is usually found in India <note>In this period, "India" frequently refers to the West Indies or the Americas.</note> acknowledge this. Truly, it is often brought down to the plains while immature by the swelling of waters, and because it is of a solid and strong substance, it is **concocted** <term>concoction: a process of ripening or perfecting a substance through natural heat</term>, matured, and perfected. At the same time, through the rubbing of sand and stones, or earth, the copper itself and whatever is useless is consumed. Then, it is washed by the flow of the waters; and in that way, it shines among the sands, and for that reason, it is usually collected. Nor does its scarcity allow for mountains to be dug up in uncertain places and at overly interrupted intervals, as it would be necessary to dig up an entire mountain for a few pounds of gold—which even fire would consume while we were striving to extract it from the stones. The Adda <note>original: "Abdua," a river in North Italy</note> rises from Lake Como <note>original: "Lario lacu"</note>, just as the Ticino <note>original: "Ticinus"</note> rises from Lake Maggiore <note>original: "Verbano"</note>. Both rivers receive sands from the mountains that surround their lakes, and with these, stones and gold, which are concocted, perfected, and purified at the bottom of the lakes. Thus, in the high places of the mountains, pure gold is generated by the power of the **Sun**. It is also generated mixed with other metals, especially among fragments of silver, as I have said. For metals are mixed together: gold in silver, copper in gold, and silver is very often found with lead. But the gold that is dug up with other metals requires fire and no small amount of skill to become pure. Gold is also found, or rather extracted, from those things to which it has been attached by art: as from gilded vessels, and also from clothes, as we taught above. So 
<margin>Gold is obtained in three ways.</margin>
it is also dug up when buried, and they fish for it when it is submerged in waters. Thus, it is possible to collect gold in three ways: either by restoring what already existed to light and into a mass, or by separating it from the metals among which it lies hidden, or by collecting it in its pure state. Italy does not collect pure gold in this age, except for that small amount I recently said is found among the sands of the Ticino and the Adda. Sometime pure gold will also be dug up in Italy, when the cycle has turned, as I said: for those things which are at the bottom come to the surface.

<margin>The wonderful depth of the mines.</margin>
Whence in Germany they dig silver in certain places with wells nearly five hundred **orgiae** <term>orgia: a fathom, approximately six feet</term> or paces deep. The size of pure gold in our regions and in Germany approaches the size of a hazelnut, as has occasionally 
<margin>The incredible size of refined gold.</margin>
been found in the fields of the Carpathians at Oldenburg <note>original: "Aldeburgi," likely Stará Voda</note> and the town of Złoty Stok <note>original: "Slota," a famous gold-mining town in Lower Silesia</note>. But if credit is to be given to Gonzalo <note>Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo (1478–1557), a Spanish chronicler of the New World</note>, in the part of India [the Americas] we recently mentioned, a piece of refined gold <term>obrizi: "aurum obrizum," gold refined to the highest purity</term> was dug up that weighed forty-two and three-quarters pounds. It is common to find pieces that weigh four pounds, and sometimes it even approaches seven; such is the generosity of nature in those places, and the strength and kindness of the location. But as they abound in gold, as I said, so they lack other metals, especially iron. Gold shines most 
<margin>The brilliance of metals and its cause.</margin>
among all metals, then silver, after that copper, then white lead <note>tin</note>; electrum <term>electrum: a natural alloy of gold and silver</term> shines less than gold but more than silver. Cyprian copper <note>copper</note> and iron shine only a very little, then black lead <note>lead</note>, and the rest of this kind. For brilliance comes from a pure, shiny, and solid moisture in which light is gathered...

<header>On Metals.</header>

# On Metals.

<margin>
Metallic substances that are transparent and strongly colored.
</margin>
...[it appears] that in mirrors no metal is translucent except for raw silver <note>original: "rude argentum"; likely referring to ruby silver ore (pyrargyrite) which can be red and translucent.</note> of a red color, though not always. For sometimes, in its transparency, color, and luster, this is not unlike a carbuncle <note>A red gemstone, usually a garnet or ruby.</note>; and from it they produce something similar to red lead <term>minium: a bright red pigment, historically associated with cinnabar or lead tetroxide</term>.

<margin>
Nothing strongly colored is transparent.
</margin>
Now it must be demonstrated how this alone among metals is transparent, and why pure metals cannot be transparent. Something becomes transparent when light and brightness can pass through it; the things through which light and brightness can pass are air and water. It is clear that earth is not transparent, and where it is mixed in, it hinders transparency. When moisture is dried out, because it becomes earthy, it also loses transparency. Therefore, oil, though it is transparent when placed in a lamp, is rendered opaque because of the soot that is mixed with it due to the fire.

<margin>
All metals are of a watery and thin substance.
</margin>
All perfected metallic things are of a watery and thin substance; for they solidify through cold, as was said when we discussed ice, and they become liquid through fire. However, among the elements, being liquid is a property belonging only to water. Let this be the proof of their thinness <term>tenuitas: the "subtlety" or fineness of a substance's particles</term> above all others: that they are consumed by fires, and that earthy part vanishes along with the watery part. It is so thin, moreover, because we can make a proof of the whole from one part of a mixed lump. For if there were one ounce of silver in a hundred pounds of lead, and if it were permitted to take a proof from a tiny amount <term>scrupulus: a scrupule, a very small weight unit used by apothecaries and metallurgists</term> of the mass, as craftsmen do, it is necessary that the ounce of silver be mixed everywhere throughout the hundred pounds of lead; therefore, even the twelve-hundredth part of the scrupule will be equally mixed. This, moreover, is the fiftieth part of a single grain <note>original: "grani"; a very small unit of weight.</note>; therefore, it cannot be otherwise than that metal is of an extremely thin substance.

<margin>
Testing metals from a very small part, as is usually done, is deceptive.
</margin>
Yet it is not entirely safe to trust this trial when the mass is large, though if the error is moderate, it may cause no loss. Nor is it safe to test precious materials unless in a larger weight.

There is also a third proof of the thinness of metals: that two grains of iron or copper mixed with gold—so that they are a little more than a fortieth part—so change its color and hardness that you would say it was almost something else. For pure gold shines quite a lot, is of a tawny color, and is soft and highly workable; but when barely a fortieth part of iron is mixed in, it becomes stubborn, blackish, and of a dull luster. Therefore, if all metals are watery and thin, they must either be burnt out or mixed with earth since they are not translucent. Density cannot be the obstacle, since diamond and crystal are dense and yet transparent. If, therefore, you mix a tiny part of black and completely opaque dregs <term>amurca: the bitter, dark, watery sediment of olive oil</term> with much water, it will turn red and remain transparent, though not as much as it was before. Therefore, since silver is black by itself—which appears from the stain it leaves on those who handle it, for it seems white only because of its solidity—just as mirrors whose material is black, if it is mixed with a watery humor, it will turn red and transparent just like the dregs of oil in water, and then it shines because of the brightness of the silver. We call this mixture a carbuncle because of the resemblance, and just as when a large amount of dregs...

### Book Six

...it is not proper for it to be mixed with water, for at the same time the water would be rendered opaque and black; thus the part of silver is smaller, while the watery humor is greatest. It is clear, therefore, that this type of raw silver is largely transparent. But if it should be somewhat blackish, or more abundant than the watery portion, or impure, it will not be transparent. Why it must be red, which is transparent, and of what things it consists, has been sufficiently discussed; nor does it prevent other metallic substances made from lead or copper from being transparent. However, this happens more rarely because of their impurity, for silver is purer than copper and lead. Therefore, by this reasoning, it is also possible to forge counterfeit gemstones. But let us pursue what we had proposed from the beginning.

<margin>Why no earth is transparent.</margin>
Among stones, then, those that are translucent include magnesia <note>original: "magnesia"; in this context, likely a reference to "glassmaker's soap" or manganese used to clear glass, or a specific transparent mineral</note>, *armatura*, the specular stone <note>original: "specularis lapis"; typically mica or selenite used for windows</note>, and the flower of gypsum, which Agricola <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "father of mineralogy"</note> considers to be different from the specular stone. Among the types of marble, there is some [transparency] in each, yet *phengites* <note>A highly translucent marble or selenite used in ancient times for windows</note> alone is generally and entirely permeable to light. Gemstones are also mostly of this kind; indeed, the category of gems is so large that many believe things which are not translucent should hardly be called gems. All glassy substances made from four juices are also transparent: salt, alum, nitre <term>nitrum: naturally occurring sodium carbonate or saltpeter</term>, and shoemaker’s black <term>futorium atramentum: vitriol or iron sulfate, used for dyeing leather</term>. No type of earth is transparent, for if much water were mixed with it, it would cease to be earth; and if it were solidified from moisture, it would be turned into stone and would no longer be earth. Furthermore, earth cannot be translucent because of its fineness; for even nitre and gems, however transparent, cease to be transparent when reduced to powder. Since, therefore, earth does not cling together but is composed of the finest particles, it cannot be transparent.

<margin>The smell of gold and metallic things.</margin>
But I return to the history of gold: among metals, it alone breathes out a faint, good odor; silver follows it, and copper is the worst. The cause is the magnitude of the burning heat. In gold, because its substance is generated by a sweet heat, no bad odor is left behind; for this reason, the generation of gold requires the space of many years, while all other things are finished in a shorter time. From moderate heat, however, it is necessary that little hardness is produced; because of this, gold is soft, and whatever things smell good will be soft, such as amber.

<margin>The Misnian Geode smells good.</margin>
If the Misnian Geode <note>A stone from the Meissen region in Germany</note>—which they falsely call an *Aetite* <note>An "eagle-stone," traditionally believed to be found in eagles' nests</note> because another stone rattles inside it—should smell of violets, and if fragments of the Aldenberg stone and the Berninger stone seem to smell good, this comes to them from the moss that surrounds them. For it is scarcely possible for the substance of those stones, or other hard things, to smell good, just as we taught above.

<margin>The wonderful thinness of gold and silver in wire.</margin>
Silver follows gold in being most thin, which is also caught by experiment. A *denarius* or scruple <note>A small unit of weight</note> of twenty-four grains of silver is drawn out into a wire of 134 feet, which are nearly one hundred "arms" <note>original: "brachia"; a traditional unit of length roughly equal to a cubit or a person's reach</note> by our measurement. This entire length—incredible to say, but known to all craftsmen of this art—is surrounded on all sides by a portion of gold weighing only one-third of a grain; for two ounces of gold are distributed over twelve and a half pounds of silver. One ounce of silver [is drawn] into 4,200 feet, or 2,400 of our "arms," which are covered on every side by six grains of gold.

It concludes with a technical description of the incredible malleability of silver and gold when drawn into gold-plated wire.</summary>

# On Metals

<margin>The thinness of gold leaf.</margin>
And these things regarding ductility have been said; but the thinness granted to gold when it is extended by a hammer over silver plates is worthy of no less admiration. For one ounce of gold covers eight pounds of silver. However, when they have been beaten into leaves, you could not distinguish which is thinner, the gold or the silver; therefore, it is necessary that the gold be a hundred times thinner than the already incomprehensible thinness of silver. Thus, it happens that an ounce of gold can cover more than ten <term>jugera</term> <note>A Roman unit of land area, roughly equivalent to five-eighths of an acre; the author is emphasizing gold's incredible surface-area coverage when beaten thin.</note> of earth. This occurs because of the purity of its substance and its long "cooking" <note>original: "coctionem"; in alchemy and early metallurgy, this refers to the natural or artificial refinement of a metal through heat over time.</note>. For this reason, craftsmen adorn the engravings of iron and steel with gold at little expense, for there is more value in the labor than in the gold itself. This method is manifold, but I will explain three of the easier modes.

<margin>Methods of gilding.</margin>
Gold, having been reduced into sheets, is mixed with <term>quicksilver</term> <note>Mercury</note>; then, when it has been heated with fire, it is poured into water. Afterwards, if the vessel is made of silver, the mercury is smeared upon it; then the vessel is heated and "combed" <note>original: "pectitur"; likely meaning smoothed or brushed to ensure even distribution.</note> until it adheres everywhere. Then, once the mercury has been consumed by the fire <note>The mercury evaporates when heated, leaving the gold behind.</note>, the gold remains adhering to the silver. But if gold must be joined to copper or iron, it is done in this way: You shall first wash the vessel with wine in which <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>Ammonium chloride, used as a flux in soldering and gilding.</note> and <term>aerugo</term> <note>Verdigris or copper rust.</note> have been dissolved in equal parts with double the amount of wine dregs; then you will smear it with quicksilver as before, after they have been dried. Another mode involves "water of separation" <note>original: "aqua separationis"; usually refers to nitric acid, used to separate gold from silver.</note>, the history of which I remember writing above. A third method is to place gold leaves over glowing iron, and then rub them with <term>Spanish Hematite</term>.

<margin>Spanish Hematite and its use.</margin>
This stone's color is blood-red on the outside (from which it took its name) and iron-like on the inside, with such hardness that it scarcely feels the file. This is not that soft "German" type. From this, it is clear that the Spanish variety is the one that stops blood, for due to its hardness it can be reduced to a very fine powder and possesses exceptional drying and astringent power. Doctors, however, use the German variety with wasted effort, as it has no utility at all; therefore, it is necessary to reduce that [Spanish] stone into a fine dust if one intends to heal <term>hemoptysis</term> <note>original: "Hemoptoicos"; the condition of coughing up blood.</note> with the best aid. In matters so manifest, the doctors of our age are so blind that I have never noticed even one who used it correctly, as they are deceived by the similarity of color and substance.

Leaving aside these things which are outside our proposal, let us return to the matter itself. What they do with Hematite can also be performed with the smoothest <term>Ophyte</term> <note>Serpentine or a similar hard, decorative stone used for burnishing.</note>. Therefore, the cause of all these things is the maximum thinness of gold, which is its special privilege. Another privilege is that it yields least to fires, unless it is joined with "poisons" <note>Refers to corrosive substances or impurities that might cause gold to degrade or react.</note>. 

<margin>Gold yields very little to fire, and silver only a little.</margin>
For if it remains by itself, or even if melted with lead in a fire for twenty days, it is not diminished by any part that is manifest to the senses; indeed, I would not dare to say it is diminished at all. Therefore, one ought to learn the cause of these things before all else. 

<margin>All the privileges of gold.</margin>
At the same time, we must ask why gold does not stain. For these three things are peculiar to gold: not to be consumed by fire, not to stain, and to be extremely thin. Indeed, "fatness" <note>original: "pinguedo"; in early chemistry, this refers to a combustible, sulfurous principle that causes substances to burn or tarnish.</note> defiles and burns, and forces those things with which it is mixed to be burned; gold alone, therefore, lacks this fatness. Those things which are "watery" vanish when exposed to fires, but gold vanishes in no fires; thus it either does not consist of a watery substance, or it is protected by some...

# Book Six

...is contained in something. Moreover, we have shown that every metal consists of an **aqueous substance** <note>In the Aristotelian physics of the time, metals were believed to be composed of "Water" (for fluidity/fusibility) and "Earth" (for solidity/weight).</note>, and for that reason, it has an earthy substance mixed in that is so thin and pure that it is contained within it. If such a substance were burnt, it would smell foul and burn easily; therefore, since it neither burns easily nor smells foul, that earthy part is pure and free from burning. Thus, it is characteristic of gold to smell good, not to stain, not to be consumed by fires, and to be extremely thin, very heavy, and indeed most tenacious.

<margin>Gold more perfect than gold.</margin>
There is also gold that is more perfect than other gold, which occurs in every kind, not only of mortal things but of immortal ones; I do not say "purer," but "more perfect." For the purest gold which is brought from India is better than the purest gold which might be found elsewhere. And thus, even in our common gold, a distinction lies hidden due to the excellence of any particular gold. 

<margin>The method of separating gold from other metals.</margin>
Gold is separated from silver by **parting water** <term>aqua separationis</term> <note>Likely nitric acid, which dissolves silver and other base metals but leaves gold untouched.</note>, for that liquid melts the remaining metals, while the grains of gold sink to the bottom of the vessel; having been collected from there, they are liquefied. There is another way: a mass of gold and silver is melted, and after it has been liquefied, **antimony** <term>stibium</term> or sulfur is added, along with a twenty-fourth part of copper. Then, once the sulfur is consumed, the small vessel is shaken three or four times; the gold sinks to the bottom because of its weight, though it is not yet fully liquefied, and after the silver is poured off, you will collect the gold. Silver, however, melts more easily because it is less dense, for it is much lighter than gold.

<margin>The method of purifying gold.</margin>
Gold is also purified from filth by this method: it is crushed and reduced into broad, thin leaves, then it is submerged in urine or vinegar in which **sal ammoniac** <term>sal Ammoniacum</term> <note>Ammonium chloride, used as a flux in metallurgy.</note> has been dissolved. Afterward, a very fine powder made of three parts brick dust and one part salt is placed in a vessel; a leaf of gold is placed on top, then powder over the gold again, and so on alternately until the vessel is filled. Then, with fire placed beneath for twenty-four hours, all [impurities] are consumed; the gold is liquefied, and the silver, if any is present, is preserved among the ashes. When I said the fire is placed "beneath," I mean that it should also be placed "around" it, for if it is only placed beneath the vessel, it will be dissolved with difficulty, or hardly at all.

<margin>Gold and silver are contained in all metallic things.</margin>
Gold is the perfection and the "striving" <note>The author suggests that nature "intends" or "strives" to make gold, but sometimes stops short at other metals.</note> of metals. Silver is nearest to it; therefore, both are accustomed to lie hidden in every metal. I say there is silver in lead and gold in copper, but there is also gold in silver, for the best part of silver is the gold itself. Thus, gold is a highly refined thing, a most pure aqueous substance, thin and dense, mixed with the most sincere earthy part, congealed by cold and without "fatness" <note>original: "pinguedine"; in alchemy, "fatness" or "oiliness" often referred to the combustible principle (sulfur) that caused metals to tarnish or burn.</note>, which is why it melts but is not consumed by fire.

Whether it is therefore permitted to make gold from **quicksilver** <note>Mercury</note> or another metal—which was doubted from the beginning—must now be attempted to be demonstrated. But first, we must see from what things metals are composed. Many have thought, on account of their odor and substance, that they consist of sulfur and quicksilver.

<margin>What metals consist of.</margin>
For when they are burnt, they smell of sulfur, especially copper; and their matter is very similar to quicksilver, for in color it rivals lead and silver, and in weight it rivals black lead and gold. But from two things already existing in actuality, a third cannot be made; therefore, metals do not consist of sulfur and quicksilver...

...consist. Also, in the places where metals are found, neither **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>Literally "living silver," the standard Latin term for mercury.</note> nor sulfur is present; and where there is sulfur, the mountains are barren and desolate, but where there is silver, they are green and lush, so that both do not arise in the same place.

# On Metals.

However, it has seemed to many that metals can be transmuted <note>original: "permutari," referring to the alchemical process of changing one metal into another.</note> because of the experiment with copper already mentioned above. They also seem to change color and weight due to fire, wherefore it is probable that they can also change their substance. It is even believed that certain people have performed this, such as at the court of the most Illustrious Prince of the Venetians a few years ago, in the presence of the wise men of the city, performed by a certain apothecary from Treviso; traces of this event still remain. And since certain species of herbs are changed into one another in turn, it should not seem strange that metals can be transmuted. Truly, however, the matter is not so, for either none or not all can be changed into one another. For since iron and copper are both similar in weight and thinness, and neither of them resists fire, if they should change color and hardness, they can be transformed from one into the other—either truly, or at least without an obvious difference. 

None of the remaining metals can be changed into gold or silver; the only doubt is whether silver can be changed into gold. I think this can happen: for silver to become gold, it lacks density (which would make it heavier) and color, but these can be added to the metal. If silver is made denser, its **oiliness** <term>pinguedo</term> <note>In alchemy, "pinguedo" or "fatness" refers to the combustible, sulfurous element within a metal that causes it to tarnish or burn.</note> will be destroyed, it will resist fire better, and, as I said, it will gain weight.

As for the other metals, they cannot be transmuted into gold or silver, for those metals are already "burnt out"; and what is burnt out cannot return to its original purity. Added to this is that true generation is the work of nature, not **art** <note>In this context, "art" refers to human technology or alchemical intervention.</note>; fire, however, generates nothing, as we have demonstrated, and therefore it does not generate gold; indeed, it rather hinders all generation. Furthermore, there is no change among perfect things that differ in species and nature; yet gold is perfect and differs in species from other metals, since it resists fire entirely, whereas no other metal, as I have said, is not corrupted by fire, except for silver. Again, gold is extremely subtle <note>original: "tenuissimum," referring to the fine, dense consistency of the metal's particles.</note> and far more subtle than all other metals (I set silver aside for now); but fire either condenses things by not separating them, or thins them by separating them, neither of which leads to the generation of gold.

Also, as I said, gold is not subject to fire because it lacks oiliness; but to separate oiliness when it is in every part of the metal is not a task for fire, for it is consumed by fire, and with it the whole substance of the metal. 
<margin>
All metals are oily except gold.
</margin>
For every metal is "oily" except gold alone: we have already said this above in other words and more obscurely, for every metal except gold also stains those who handle it and is consumed by fires.

Metals, however, are made from the same material as sulfur and **quicksilver** <gloss>living silver</gloss>

<summary>The author debates the possibility of alchemical transmutation, arguing that while silver might be turned into gold by increasing its density, most base metals are too "burnt" or "oily" to be perfected.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical discussion of how metals are formed from sulfur and quicksilver, and addresses the specific claims made by alchemists regarding the transmutation of these elements.</meta>

-># Book Six<-

...living: but sulfur is formed from the thinner part and is burnt away; **quicksilver** <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>Literally "living silver," the standard name for mercury.</note> is formed from the thickest and least-processed part; and the metals are formed from a mixture and by a more tempered heat. Even if a man, a woman, and a mole <note>original: "mola," a term used in this period to describe a "mooncalf" or a shapeless mass in the womb, illustrating that sharing a source—the womb—does not mean one can become the other.</note> are created from the same blood and in the same place, it is still not necessary, nor even possible, for one to be generated from the other. For once things have been generated from the same materials, it is not necessary that they be able to be changed into one another. Therefore, even if all metals—along with quicksilver and sulfur—are generated from the same substances, it is not necessary or possible for one to become the other, unless perhaps they do not differ in kind, but only in their accidental properties <note>In the philosophy of the time, "accidents" were external qualities like color or weight that did not change the essential nature of a substance.</note>, as was said regarding copper and iron.

<margin>What chemists can do.</margin>
Therefore, **chemists** <note>original: "chymistae," referring to alchemists or early chemical practitioners.</note> can change color and weight, but they cannot change the thinness <note>original: "subtilitatem," referring to the refinement or purity of the substance's texture.</note> and firmness. Since, therefore, testing for this refinement is laborious and uncertain, they have preferred to test gold by fire; and this is a certain proof in this matter. Indeed, it is clear that if silver is to be converted into gold, it must first be converted from a liquid into an effective mud <note>original: "lutum," likely referring to a chemical paste or the "philosopher's clay" used in alchemical processes.</note>; only then can the applied mud pass over into gold.

<margin>Quicksilver is closer to gold than to silver.</margin>
But quicksilver seems to be closer to gold than to silver: for it is similar to gold in weight and thinness, but to silver in color alone. It differs from both because it flows and vanishes in fire. For this reason, for it to turn into silver, four things will be required: that it be made firm, that it resist fire, that it become lighter, and that it be of a thicker substance. But for quicksilver to be transmuted into gold, it is only necessary that it be made firm, resist fire, and be dyed <note>original: "tingatur," the alchemical process of "tincture" to change a metal's color.</note>. Since these tasks are far easier than those required for transmutation into silver, it follows that many have had higher hopes for the transformation of quicksilver—which the Greeks call <term>hydrargyrum</term> <note>original: "Hydrargyrian," from the Greek for "water-silver."</note>—into gold rather than silver. 

<margin>A marvelous experiment.</margin>
This seems to have been achieved by that apothecary from Treviso, who changed quicksilver into gold in the presence of the Prince and the wise men of the Venetian Republic. But however that event occurred, it is certain that quicksilver cannot be changed into gold, and much less into silver. 

<margin>The nature of silver.</margin>
As for silver, even though copper is closer to gold in color and lead is closer in weight, silver is so similar to gold in the thinness of its substance, its purity, and its firmness, that the best silver is essentially gold that is imperfect in substance and lacking in color. 

<margin>Transmutation of metals.</margin>
Because of this, over long periods of time, if the silver is pure, it is partially changed into gold; just as, with age, "black lead" <note>Common lead.</note> turns into silver. Yet if the "seeds" of silver are most carefully removed from copper or lead, silver will not be generated in any age, nor will gold be generated from silver.

<margin>The friendship of metals.</margin>
From this also comes the "friendship" <note>Refers to the chemical affinity or the way certain metals naturally alloy or bond with others.</note> of metals; for gold and silver "love" lead, and when they are melted, they mix with lead. Copper, however, shuns lead, and both gold and silver "hate" white lead <term>plumbum album</term>—or, if you prefer, you may call it **tin** <term>stannum</term>—provided that the physical reality is presented to the eyes, [regardless of] the names...

He discusses the specific properties of mercury and silver, and the chemical affinities (described as "friendships" and "hatreds") between gold, silver, lead, and tin.</summary>

### On Metals ###

...to use as one wishes. Thus, when **tin** <term>plumbum album</term> <note>Literally "white lead," the standard Latin term for tin.</note> is melted, it floats above the lead and silver with a rippling wave in the furnaces, and is usually extracted with iron rods.

<margin>Lead floats on silver even though it is heavier.</margin>
What is more surprising is that **lead** <term>plumbum nigrum</term> <note>Literally "black lead," the standard Latin term for lead.</note> floats upon silver while it is molten, even though it is heavier [in solid form]. For that reason, they pour off the floating lead and collect the silver remaining at the bottom of the vessel. The cause of this is that although lead is heavier than silver when solid, it becomes thinner <note>less dense</note> when melted, as it is ready to turn into smoke and continually vanishes. Silver, however, is neither consumed by fire nor thinned; for if it were thinned, it would necessarily be consumed entirely. Therefore, since the substance of lead is intermediate between its own solid state and smoke, while that of silver remains the same as before melting, it is no wonder that molten lead floats on molten silver. Furthermore, tin will also float for two reasons: it is consumed by fire, and it is lighter than lead, which is why tin stays above not only silver but also lead.

<margin>The separation of metals.</margin>
From this, the separation of metals was discovered: the lead is poured out after the tin has first been removed. The lead carries copper and iron with it; however, it is not poured out with extreme precision, lest the silver slip away with it. Whatever lead remains after the largest part has been poured off is consumed by the fires. Thus the silver remains, along with any gold that might be mixed in with the silver, which is then separated from the silver by "parting water" <term>aqua separationis</term> <note>Nitric acid, used in a process called "parting" to separate gold from silver.</note> or by the other methods proposed above. The lead that was poured off is then checked again to ensure it contains no silver, so that the craftsman does not lose that much profit.

<margin>Book 3, chapter 5.</margin>
**Copper** <term>æs</term>, however, is separated from lead—as **Vannoccio Biringuccio** <note>Vannoccio Biringuccio (1480–1539) was an Italian master metallurgist. His work *Pirotechnia* is the first printed book on metallurgy.</note> of Siena rightly teaches in his *Pirotechnia*—by placing the mass upon an iron grate and surrounding it with fire. For lead melts easily and takes with it any gold and silver that might be clinging to the lead, while the copper is left among the ashes as if burnt. Therefore, by moving these to stronger fires and purging the metal of impurities, once it has been melted into a mass, you will have the purest copper.

<margin>How metallic substances are turned into water.</margin>
Furthermore, most metals can also be turned into "water" <note>This refers to creating liquid solutions or "oils" of metals, a common alchemical goal.</note> by art, for it is necessary to burn <note>calcine</note> them. They are burned more quickly and conveniently if **orpiment** <term>auripigmentum</term> <note>A yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used to facilitate chemical reactions.</note> is added. Once burned and reduced to the appearance of lime, they are dried diligently; then, they are either enclosed tightly in a glass vessel and buried for a month three paces deep in damp earth, or they are suspended over a vessel full of boiling water for twenty-four hours so that it boils continuously, keeping it only two or three fingers' width from the water. It is fitting that what was generated from water should return to water; but gold and silver hardly pass into water on account of the solidity of their substance, as has been said.

<margin>The fourfold origin of silver.</margin>
Silver, indeed, arises in four ways: either in earth which, when forced by fire, yields it; or mixed with lead and copper; or in stones, which...

<header>Book Six</header>

# Book Six

...similarly, when troubled by fire, they emit it; or it is found in stones in a pure state, appearing almost like a certain herb with little branches rising from the stone, such as I have in my possession. I have seen what is a frequent occurrence: trees, or rather shrubs, made of that raw silver which is brought from Germany. It is found there, and in Bohemia at Abertamy, and in Meissen 

<margin>The wonderful size of raw silver.</margin>
at Annaberg and Schneeberg, so purified that when brought to a test of purity <note>original: "examen synceritatis"</note>, it decreases by only a tenth of its weight. Georgius Agricola <note>A famous 16th-century German scholar known as the "Father of Mineralogy."</note> reports that a piece of silver was found in Bohemia weighing two talents. This weight is equal to one hundred and forty pounds.

<margin>The wonderful shape of raw silver.</margin>
When it is dug out pure, it reflects various shapes: hoes, hammers, and rakes. The same author reports seeing at Schneeberg something that resembled a statue of a man carrying an infant. Silver is also fashioned by art and is created from copper, so much so that it deceives both the eyes and the Lydian stone <term>touchstone</term> <note>A dark stone used to test the purity of precious metals by the color of the streak they leave behind.</note> in many ways; but in this sordid matter, it suffices to narrate two methods.

<margin>How the change of copper into silver is not true.</margin>
Take equal weights of white orpiment <note>arsenic trisulfide</note> or common arsenic and saltpeter <term>halinitrum</term>, place them in a sealed glass vessel, and leave them over glowing coals for an hour so the whole is reduced to a powder. Of this powder, take one ounce; take the same amount of quicksilver <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>mercury</note>, and half an ounce of dried wine dregs <note>tartar</note> reduced to powder by the force of fire. From this, you then have two powders: the first consists of orpiment and saltpeter; the second is composed of that plus the quicksilver and wine dregs. Therefore, when the copper is melted, for every pound of it, add between half an ounce and an ounce of the first powder until it is purified by mixing. Then, after it has been purified, throw in a quarter-ounce of the second powder, mix it, and immediately pour it into honey. There is also a shorter way using sublimated silver <note>likely mercury sublimate</note> and tin <term>plumbum album</term> <note>literally "white lead," the standard Latin term for tin.</note>. There are those, like Pomponius Gauricus <note>A Renaissance humanist and art theorist.</note>, who mix three ounces each of saltpeter and arsenic into two pounds of copper and boil it thoroughly. This business has brought profit to some and punishment to others, as it is the foundation of counterfeit money.

<margin>The method of silver plating.</margin>
But the method of silver plating <term>inargentandi</term> is an art, approved by authors and permitted by all honest men. Smear a pot with silver dross <note>litharge or scum from refining</note>, then grind thin silver leaves with alum, salt, and dry wine dregs on a whetstone; place them in a vessel. All these are melted together by fire and poured into water. Whatever you wish to silver-plate, first wash it carefully with vinegar in which sal ammoniac <note>ammonium chloride salt</note> has been boiled; then, having smeared it with quicksilver or tin, add what you had already poured into the water. Finally, use fire to make the quicksilver or tin evaporate.

Others smear the inside of copper vessels with tin so they appear silver-plated; this custom is frequent among us, for they do not produce a bitter taste nor are they so unhealthy, and they are more pleasant to the sight. They smear the vessel itself with black pitch, then touch the tin with a glowing iron; some of it sticks, which they immediately place on the pitch. By the heat of the fire, the pitch is consumed, and the tin sticks.

# On Metals.

<margin>Concerning electrum.</margin>
<margin>Electrum reveals poisons.</margin>
The nature of electrum lies halfway between gold and silver. There are those who call amber "electrum" <note>In antiquity, the Greek word 'elektron' referred to both the gold-silver alloy and amber, as both share a similar golden-yellow luster.</note>, but our discussion here concerns the metal. One type is made by art, and another occurs naturally; however, the beauty and power of the natural kind consist of gold and a fifth part of silver. If it contains more silver than this, it cannot withstand the anvil. It is fashioned into vessels for the sake of beauty and utility, for that which arises spontaneously <note>natural electrum ore</note> reveals poisons in two ways: it makes a creaking sound and emits rainbow-like arcs. Is this a wonder, when tin and "white lead," and most especially brass <term>orichalcum</term>, take on a strange color and suddenly lose their luster at the mere contact of poisons? Therefore, the subtle moisture of the electrum, as it is consumed <note>reacting with the substance</note>, produces a creaking sound, and as the color changes, the stain appears to imitate a rainbow because of the metal's remarkable brilliance. Therefore, just as the wealthy have electrum, so the poor have their own brass <term>orichalcum</term> to guard against poisons, which reveals their treachery. But the wealthy have lost the use of mined electrum; for although it is still found today, through the pursuit of greed and ignorance of its powers, it ceases to be electrum when they separate the gold from the silver. Nor is it such a great thing that electrum is changed by poisons, since even silver is corrupted, or that a hard substance suffers from an external poison, since, as I have said, gold becomes extremely fragile at the mere contact of quicksilver <term>argentum vivum</term> <note>mercury</note>.

<margin>Four species of lead.</margin>
<margin>From Galen, On Simple Medicines, Book 9. White lead hates other metals.</margin>
<margin>Artificial tin.</margin>
<margin>Native tin.</margin>
As I have said, lead is similar to silver. There are four types of it: the black kind <note>standard lead</note>, which is common and of lower price; the white kind, which the common people usually call tin <term>stannum</term>; bismuth <term>bisemutum</term>, which was unknown until now and is a sort of middle ground between black and white lead; and a fourth kind made from antimony <term>stibium</term>. Bismuth is not commonly known even in our age, as it is found only in the Sudetes mountains of Bohemia. It is said that all lead grows spontaneously, and thus it causes roofs to collapse by its own weight. Galen <note>A famous Greek physician and philosopher in the Roman Empire whose works dominated Western medical science for centuries.</note> reports that when buried in damp places underground, it increases in size and weight. "White lead" <note>likely cassiterite or pure tin</note> differs from tin <note>here referring to an alloy</note> because white lead arises by itself, while tin is always found with silver; tin is like lead whitened by silver. White lead "hates" all other metals: if even a hundredth part is added to gold or silver, it makes them brittle. Tin is also made by art, and the more noble variety takes one pound of black lead for every twenty-five pounds of natural tin or white lead. If, however, one pound of black lead is mixed with nine pounds of white lead, it becomes hard and is excellent for making vessels. It is also praised when black lead is added up to an eighth part, but if more is added, it becomes of poor quality; the Milanese call this pewter <term>peltrum</term>. In olden times, tin was also made by mixing copper and lead. Tin "cries" <note>The "tin cry" is a distinct crackling sound caused by the shearing of crystals when the metal is bent.</note> when it flows from silver; white lead also creaks, as does tin made by art. Hardness increases in tin because the black lead becomes harder due to the white, while the white becomes less liable to cracks and fractures due to the softness and substance of the black lead which fills it.

<margin>A wonderful experiment with molten lead.</margin>
While we were writing these things, a certain man in Milan publicly washed his hands and face with molten lead, but he first washed those parts with a certain water <note>likely a protective chemical solution or a "trick" involving the Leidenfrost effect</note>.

# Book Six

However, one must consider this: for he used two protections in his performance, speed and water. In the water, there had to be an extraordinary coldness and a significant, thick power to ward off the heat of the <term>lead</term> and prevent it from sticking to the body. Some say this is achieved with the juice of mallows or "mercurialis" <note>likely *Mercurialis annua*, known as French mercury, used in folk medicine</note> because of their sliminess. For my part, since I observed him using the water so sparingly—to the point that he sometimes allowed his face to be injured in some part—I suspect it was rather a metallic solution, such as <term>antimony</term> <note>original: "stibij"</note>. Indeed, his profit was abundant, and for each turn he collected no less than a gold coin; if the solution had been gathered from such cheap herbs, he would not have needed to use it so sparingly.

<margin>BRONZE.</margin>
<margin>Why bronze is eternal in construction.</margin>
After <term>lead</term> comes <term>bronze</term> <note>original: "æs", a term used for both bronze and copper alloys</note>. Its use in ancient times was profitable not only for the armor that covers men and for shields, but also for spears. Thus, Homer spoke of Menelaus pursuing Paris "with a bronze spear" <note>original: "ἔγχεϊ χαλκείῳ"</note>. It possesses an eternal endurance in building projects because it is not touched by rust like <term>iron</term> or <term>steel</term>. For since there are three elements that emit moisture—Earth, Water, and Air—and metals are corrupted and produce rust from moisture, that which is safe from the harm of moisture is safe whether it is under the open sky, submerged in water, or buried in the earth. Now, we demonstrated above that any matter which has been "burnt out" <note>refined or smelted</note> more than is necessary is safe from the harm of moisture, as is the case with <term>bronze</term>. Since its very scent betrays its "burning," it is necessary that <term>bronze</term> itself be eternal in constructions. For this reason, I believe it was more highly valued in ancient times than <term>iron</term>, as it was not worn down by age or use. Now, since greed is the priority, they use <term>iron</term> less profitably.

<margin>The various imitations of musical organs.</margin>
The pipes of musical organs are also made of <term>bronze</term>; some are made of "white lead" <note>tin</note>, others of wood. Thus, in the same organ, you will hear trumpets, horns, flutes, pipes, drums, the lyre, the lute, and the cithara in wonderful variety, as well as other voices sounding in alternating modes. Only the human voice was missing, which is all the more difficult to imitate as it is sweeter than the rest. <term>Bronze</term> is specifically suited for trumpets, so that it may stir up Doric music with a brisk and very great clamor, and thereby inflame men for battle.

<margin>Natural Cyprian bronze.</margin>
<margin>How Cyprian bronze is made.</margin>
<term>Cyprian bronze</term> <note>copper</note> is harder than our bronze. This is of two kinds: the natural, with shining golden spots, as I have seen; they report a piece was found in Hispaniola, an island of the New World, weighing two hundred pounds, so greatly does it grow into a large mass. It is also made by art and is called <term>copper</term> <note>original: "cuprum"</note> because of the similarity of the name. The nobler kind has four pounds of "white lead"—which we call <term>tin</term>—for every pound of bronze; mixing "white lead" up to an eighth part of the bronze makes the <term>copper</term> noble. But if <term>brass</term> <note>original: "aurichalcum"</note> is substituted for the "white lead," it will be of less value. If "black lead" <note>common lead</note> is mixed with the bronze instead of the "white lead"—as is often done to avoid expense—it becomes very cheap. The use of <term>copper</term> is for large fire machines, for bells, and for cauldrons. In this, it is far superior to bronze because even without <term>tin</term> plating, it does not infect food with any taste or smell.

# On Metals.

<margin>Brass and its composition.</margin>
**Brass** <note>original: "Aurichalcum", literally "mountain copper," referring to a golden-colored alloy of copper and zinc</note> is itself a product of art and is ancient. Apollonius, in his *Argonautica*, says:
> [He wore] shining [greaves] of bright orichalcum upon his legs,
> as he turned back toward the oxen. <note>original Greek: Λαμπρὴν δ’ ἐπὶ βουσὶν ὀρειχάλκοιο φαεινοῦ, πάλιν ὁπιδνοῦσα καλαβρόπει.</note>
He refers to the times of the Argonauts and calls it **Orichalcum**, while Plautus calls it **Aurichalcum**. Caelius <note>likely the scholar Ludovico Ricchieri, also known as Caelius Rhodiginus</note> mentions that Aristotle stated in his secret works—a book I have not yet seen—that brass is never found by digging <note>meaning it is a man-made alloy, not a raw ore</note>.

<margin>How iron may be softened.</margin>
**Iron**, however, is dug out of the earth by the opposite method and is not man-made: it is the cheapest of metals yet the most noble, serving good and evil uses alike. It softens with the juice of bean husks or mallows, provided it is not quenched in water after being treated with these. To ensure it becomes workable <note>ductile</note> when it is first mined, the lump of ore is roasted and exposed to the open air: the rain softens the earthy parts, the sun melts away the moisture, and the fire consumes the harsher parts and what might be called its "poison." Thus, by being roasted repeatedly and exposed to the elements, it becomes soft and as manageable as one could wish. Even iron wires, if allowed to cool down on their own after being heated, become so flexible that you could use them like linen thread for binding. However, it is better to choose a wire that is naturally soft and tenacious from the start. They say such iron is found among the Swedes, a people of Germany <note>The author uses "Germany" broadly to refer to Northern European/Germanic territories</note>, which they call **Osmund** <note>original: "Osemutum", a high-quality Swedish iron produced in small lumps</note>.

<margin>How iron may be engraved.</margin>
Soft iron is engraved in this manner: the design you wish to shape is painted onto the iron, a lead block is placed underneath, and then the part you wish to compress is struck with a small hammer. The part that should remain raised does not sink because it is supported by the lead. In this way, they produce delicate images of animals and plants, which you would swear were pressed in wax or crafted with sharp chisels. However, if iron is quenched in cold water while it is glowing hot, it must necessarily become hard, non-ductile, and brittle. For the coldness of the water traps the fire inside and quickly consumes the iron's natural moisture; since it was that moisture that made it workable, its removal makes the metal brittle and hard. From this, it is clear that nothing can be both very tough and very hard at the same time.

<margin>How iron may be divided by a thread.</margin>
Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo <note>a famous 16th-century Spanish historian of the Americas</note> reports in the seventh book of his *History of the Indies of the New World* (a distinguished author and, in my judgment, truthful and learned—so much so that I consider him the only historian of our age worthy of being ranked among the ancients, whose book
<margin>
Francisco
Duarte, 
Imperial
Treasurer.
</margin>
was given to me by the illustrious Francisco Duarte, a Spaniard and the Emperor’s Treasurer in Italy, a nobleman of singular humanity, justice, and prudence, and wonderfully well-disposed toward learned men) that captive Indians cut through iron shackles using a thread made of **Cabuya** herb <note>a fiber from the *Agave* plant family</note> and sand, and thus they manage to escape; he says this is a common occurrence on that island of Hispaniola. If this is true, that Cabuya thread must be very stubborn so that it can be pulled frequently and drawn quickly, and it must be wide and flat so that the sand does not bounce off. The sand itself must be fine, sharp, and hard, like that of the **emery stone** <note>original: "Smirij lapidis"</note>, for iron cannot be cut otherwise. He even reports that anchors have been divided this way. Indeed, if harder stones are divided by long, steady, and rapid pulling, why should we wonder at iron? This method is superior to a file because it cannot be heard; hence they call them "silent files," which are thin and cut slowly but without sound.

<margin>How man-made steel is produced.</margin>
But more noble than iron is **steel** <note>original: "chalybs"</note>, which is of two types: natural and man-made. Both are extremely hard and, for the reason I mentioned, more brittle than iron. Man-made steel is produced from the hardest iron...

<margin>How to recognize the best steel.</margin>
<margin>Steel that can cut iron.</margin>
[Steel] consists of purified [iron] and marble <note>likely referring to a flux or carbon source used in the smelting process</note>. The best steel is that which shines with the tiniest, glittering grains, has no rust or cracks, and is lighter than iron. Once it is perfectly refined and glowing white-hot, if it is quenched in a mixture of radish juice and the water of earthworms in equal measure three or four times, it will cut iron as easily as lead. For **Albertus** <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century philosopher and scientist</note> reports that he has tested this himself. This result is achieved (and the experiment still stands today) if the steel—rendered excessively dry, hard, and thin—is treated with that medicine. Anything treated in such a way can cut iron like wood.

<margin>A breastplate resistant to firearms.</margin>
Much more useful is what my friend **Galeazzo Rosso** <note>original: "Galeaz Rubeus"</note> discovered: a way for an iron breastplate to withstand a firearm <note>original: "igneum tormentum", literally "fire engine," a common Renaissance term for guns or cannons</note>. Skill is so powerful that once you understand the logic behind it, you will cease to marvel. Hardness is the same where the material is the same, but it is sometimes stronger where it has been compressed, folded over, and multiplied many times—just as a bundle of sticks is harder to break—this makes the iron extremely resilient. Therefore, through long hammer strokes and the power of water-driven mills, the iron is made dense even if it is thin, because the fire consumes the earthy and watery impurities. It follows that the iron itself is made invincible against almost any blow, and certainly always against small engines <note>meaning smaller firearms like pistols or arquebuses</note>.

<margin>The most noble kinds of steel and iron.</margin>
There are most noble kinds of steel and iron which exceed gold in price for an equal weight: **Agiambine**, **Azimine**, **Carmanian**, and **Damascus** steel. All of these take their names from the regions as they are now called in our mother tongue. It convinces me that the region itself adds something to the metal beyond the skill of the craftsman; for although in **Virgil's** time steel was found everywhere in Italy, Germany, and Spain, he nevertheless wrote: *"But the naked Chalybes [offer] iron,"* <note>original: "At chalybes nudi ferrum" from Virgil’s Georgics. The Chalybes were an ancient people of Asia Minor famous for smithing.</note> which leads me to suspect they are included among the aforementioned peoples.

<margin>The best mirrors made of silver.</margin>
But besides these, there are artificial types of metals, some less common, such as one consisting of two parts silver and one part lead, which is the best for manufacturing mirrors. 
<margin>The method for foils placed under gemstones.</margin>
And foils <note>term: bracteae, thin sheets of metal used to enhance a gem's color</note> that are placed under gemstones are made of gold, silver, and copper. They are placed over glowing coals—suspended so they do not touch the heat directly—and from the different proportions of the metals, they take on the splendor of various colors. Those that support the carbuncle <note>a deep red gem like a ruby or garnet</note> consist of copper and a twenty-fourth part gold, which makes them quite durable. 
<margin>The most noble brass.</margin>
A most noble brass <note>term: aurichalcum</note> is also made, equal to gold in beauty. It uses calamine stone or magnesia, silver, and Cyprian copper—or common copper with glass added in its place. Glass is added so the magnesia does not evaporate, and you will not be satisfied with adding the glass and magnesia only once. Here we substitute silver for white lead <note>likely referring to tin</note>, magnesia for cadmia <note>zinc ore</note>, and Cyprian copper for common copper, and we repeat the magnesia and glass.

<margin>How metal vessels may be kept unharmed for a long time.</margin>
Vessels of great utility are made from these, and indeed from all metals, though they last little if they are not cared for. They are damaged in three ways: fire melts them; mercury <note>original: "argentum vivum", literally "living silver"</note> pierces them and makes them brittle; and they are bent by being struck or pressed by weight. Once bent, they develop cracks or break. To prevent them from bending while being washed, care should be taken to wash three or four together; once the first is cleaned, the last is moved to the front. In this way, by changing their order so all sustain the pressure equally, they all remain without the defect of bending. If they should happen to bend, it should be corrected immediately by gentle taps with a small hammer. Thus they remain as if eternal.

<header>BOOK SEVEN</header>

# BOOK SEVEN
## On Stones.

<margin>Five general types of stones.</margin>
<margin>What is called a gem and what truly is one.</margin>
**H**aving completed the account of metals, it remains for us to speak of stones. There are five general types of them in total: the Gem, Marble, the Whetstone <term>Cos: a gritty stone used for sharpening tools</term>, Flint, and Rock. Besides these, there are artificial stones, which we shall discuss after finishing our discourse on natural ones. Following common custom, we now call a "gem" any shining stone that is naturally rare and small. By the requirement of rarity, all common pebbles of the shore are excluded; by the requirement of smallness, we exclude marbles, which shine and some types of which are rare to find, yet they are not gems because they are by no means small—indeed, in every variety, some pieces of extraordinary size are found. We also mentioned that they must shine; for the Snail-stone <note>original: "Limacius", a stone traditionally said to be found in the heads of snails</note> and Borax-stone <note>original: "Borax", likely referring to toadstone or similar nodules found in animals</note> are small and rare stones, yet they are not gems, for they do not shine, or if they do, they shine very little. Therefore, in this category, we also include Pearls, Corals, Turquoises, and all stones not born in the East—such as the Carbuncle <note>a red gemstone, usually garnet or ruby</note> and the German Chrysolite, as well as the Oriental Topaz and the sky-blue stone (though we spoke of this above), and also the Emerald and Crystal—though these latter stones are scarcely affected by a file. But "true gems" are said to be those that do not feel the file <note>meaning they are so hard that a metal file cannot scratch or shape them</note>; for that reason, it would not be strictly correct to call all those we just listed "true gems." Let these, then, be called gems by resemblance; those that truly shine and do not feel the file are true gems, while those that do feel the file and shine, yet are not small, are classified as marbles. If they consist of scales, let them be called flints; if of grains, whetstones; and if they do not shine, let them be called rocks.

<margin>Types of gems.</margin>
<margin>The reason why gems reflect an image.</margin>
<margin>The origin of gems.</margin>
<margin>On a stone found in the liver of a rooster.</margin>
There are three types of gems: transparent, such as the Diamond; opaque, as the Onyx usually is; and mixed, such as the Sardonyx and Jasper, parts of which are transparent and parts opaque. Some also reflect an image, like the Sapphire that I own, and the Emerald, as well as that Carbuncle found in Orchomenus in Arcadia. The reason why gems reflect an image is, first, their luster; second, their hardness; third, their opacity; and fourth, a diluted color. For it is difficult for an image to be reflected when the color is perfectly saturated <note>deep, dark colors absorb light rather than reflecting it back like a mirror</note>. Gems are generally produced among rocks from a juice dripping from the stones into cavities, just as an infant is nourished by maternal blood <note>a common Renaissance belief that minerals "grew" in the earth like living organisms</note>. Others, however, are produced within animals, as they say of the Cock-stone <term>Alectorius: a stone believed to be found in the gizzards of old roosters, thought to bring luck or quench thirst</term>. It is certain that stones are at least born in animals, as will be explained in its proper place. **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola, the "Father of Mineralogy," who published "De Natura Fossilium" in 1546</note> reports that a stone was found in the liver of a capon that was white-brownish; the upper part, which was narrower and bulged to the right, was dark, while the lower part, which was wider, was cavernous; otherwise, considering its location, it was of incredible size: an inch long, an inch and a half high, and a finger's breadth wide.

<header>Book Seven</header>

## Book Seven

<margin>The matrices of gems.</margin>
Furthermore, gems are not generated everywhere among stones; rather, each individual gem has its own **matrix** <note>The "mother stone" or host rock in which a crystal forms.</note>. The **Emerald** is born in **Prase** <note>original: "Prassio", a leek-green variety of quartz</note>, and **Jasper** sometimes in **Flint**. They say the **Carbuncle** <note>A term for red gems, usually garnets or rubies</note> is found in the **Balas** <note>The Balas ruby, actually a spinel</note>, **Crystal** in **Marble**, and **Sarda** <note>Carnelian</note> in **Onyx**. I possess such a specimen myself, where you may see Onyx expressed at the bottom and Sarda at the top.

<margin>The specific signs of gems.</margin>
Gems are recognized by touch, sight, the file, and their substance. By **touch**, because they are heavier and colder than glass. By **sight**, because their splendor is more brilliant, more consistent, and fills the eyes more completely; nor is it dulled by the light of a lamp as glass is.

<margin>How gems are discovered.</margin>
Their **substance** is more lively and smooth; by the **file**, because, as I have said, they are not worn away by it. From this, it happens that many gems are uncovered during the day in the places where they usually grow by the brilliance of the Sun, or at night by the Moon or stars. Others are sought and found by chance, or by digging in specific places based on certain evidence.

<margin>The flaws of gems.</margin>
The flaws of gems are many. Some concern color, such as **smoke**, **shadow**, or a **little cloud**. Others concern the body, such as **roughness**, a **hair** <note>a fine crack</note>, **salt**, a **point**, **dust**, **leadenness**, **iron-rust**, **red-rust**, or a **pustule** <note>original: "vomica", an internal cavity or deep-seated flaw</note>. "Smoke" is darker, a "little cloud" is whiter, and "shadow" is thinner and blacker. A "hair" appears on the surface as if eaten away, so that the stone looks as if it has been touched by a file. "Salt" is an internal obscurity, which they call **ice**. "Roughness" is a certain harshness that nevertheless takes its origin from deep within. A "point" is like a small bubble in the body of the gem. "Dust" is like scattered fragments. By "leadenness," a dull splendor is rendered, and by "iron-rust," it is rendered with a dark color. A "pustule" appears as a deep, dense blister. "Red-rust" differs little from iron-rust, yet it is redder. Gems are flawed no more than animals or plants—indeed less so—but nonetheless, flawless gems seem to be rarer than flawless animals or plants. This is because, in gems, flaws are more conspicuous and noteworthy due to their brilliance and small size.

<margin>Why wise men seem more prone to vices.</margin>
For this reason, we consider many learned men to be more subject to serious vices because our senses deceive us. For it is not actually so; rather, because of the brilliance of their name and their "smallness" <note>referring to the rarity of such individuals</note>, flaws are more conspicuous in them and are more noticed. In contrast, obscurity covers common people; they do not have the eyes of so many men turned toward them as the wise do. In the case of Princes, their sheer "magnitude" ensures that a flaw is not noticed, just as a tiny stain is not seen on a grand garment.

<margin>Why wise men have often brought ruin to their country.</margin>
From this, an opportunity was provided for the common people to speak ill of the wise. Yet, in turn, once those wise men were provoked, a significant envy was stirred up against the fatherland, from which destruction and great calamities sometimes followed. How much did it hurt—even setting aside Divine judgment—the Jews that they killed Christ and James? Or the Athenians that they killed Socrates? Or the Romans that they forced Scipio Africanus into a voluntary exile?

<margin>The cause of transparency in gems.</margin>
Thus, brilliance and transparency in gems are the reasons why flaws become more manifest. The cause of **transparency** in gems—since we dealt with metals above—is that they lack color and possess an aqueous substance. The experiment with **Chalcedony** (which is a species of Onyx) demonstrates this: when thrown into water, it is transparent and of a watery color; when dried, it is white and not at all transparent. For it is of a rare <note>porous</note> substance, and therefore it drinks up the water; by the mixture of water, its opacity is removed. For a white color can never be perfectly transparent, since it scatters the rays...

...distorts and changes from its own nature, so that they either cannot penetrate, or if they do penetrate, they cannot show the image of the thing because the color is disturbed. For these reasons, a watery color—as is found in the transparency of water, glass, crystal, and diamond—is more suitable than all other colors for clarity.

<margin>Precious gems.</margin>
The chief among gems are the green **Emerald** <note>original: "Smaragdus"</note>, the red **Carbuncle** <note>original: "Carbunculus"; typically refers to rubies or garnets</note>, the white **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"</note>, the milky **Pearl** <note>original: "Margarita"</note>, the blue **Sapphire** <note>original: "Sapphyrus"</note>, the golden **Chrysolite** <note>original: "Chrysolitus"; in this period, often referring to peridot or yellow topaz</note>, and the many-colored **Opal** <note>original: "Opalus"</note>. Their values among us currently follow that order, except that the Opal follows the Emerald. To these may be added the **Hyacinth** <note>original: "Hyacinthus"; likely a blue sapphire or a zircon</note> and the **Prase-stone** <note>original: "Pranium"; usually a leek-green quartz, though the author describes a black variety here</note>, the former being of a purple color and the latter black, although there is a great difference in their price.

<margin>That disease, old age, and death come to stones.</margin>
We have demonstrated above that all things which are compound bodies are alive, and this applies most especially to stones. Not only do they live, but they also suffer from diseases, old age, and eventually death. For when a **Herculean stone** <note>original: "herculeus lapis"; the lodestone or natural magnet</note> is worn out by old age, it does not attract iron; it is also weakened by filth and grime, just like a living animal. For they do not perform their actions merely by physical quality, but by life: for **pepper** <note>The author compares the stone to spice to show that while a spice's "heat" is a chemical quality that lasts, a stone's "power" is a vital force that can die.</note> ceases to be pepper before it ceases to warm a person who consumes it, even if it is very old; yet stones, even those not yet decayed in any part, can be stripped of their own specific powers. All these things are more obscure in stones than in plants, just as life is less present in them and the works of life are less manifest. But if you pay close attention, you will see them grow pale, become dull, be deprived of their own powers, and suffer decay. <margin>Why stones grow again when cut out.</margin> Stones also grow for this reason: because they are alive. For the parts of plants, the claws of crabs, and the tails of lizards are repaired once they are torn away.

<margin>Why stones have greater powers than animals and plants.</margin>
Someone might rightly wonder why stones themselves seem to have greater powers than animals or plants, since animals and plants live a more distinct life. There are several reasons for this: first, because while it was necessary to prepare an animal or plant for many different functions, it was not possible to temper their mixture so specifically as to achieve those miraculous powers found in minerals. The evidence for this is that among animals, the most lowly are endowed with the most distinct virtues, such as the **Salamander** <note>fabled to live in fire</note>, the **Silkworm** <note>original: "Bombix"</note>, the **Glow-worm** <note>original: "Cicendula"</note>, and the **Chameleon**. And among stones, it is not the beautiful gems that attract iron or point to the poles, but the dark Herculean stone, which lacks all beauty. Another reason is that soft matter could not sustain such great force, just as hard matter cannot easily take on a variety of shapes; because of this, stones lack leaves, flowers, or fruit, nor do they have legs or eyes, just as animals and plants lack such powerful or miraculous mineral virtues. Furthermore, the generation of stones happens over a long time, whereas that of plants and animals is brief; thus, nature can be strengthened by the length of time. Animals also have many powers which we do not marvel at because we think they proceed from the choice of their will, or they remain hidden from us because of their "imprisonment" in the body. Therefore, we can judge the powers of stones openly, while we might not even recognize the others.

<margin>The Hyacinth and its powers.</margin>
Men worthy of authority attribute many praises to the **Hyacinth**: among whom...
