...whom Serapio <note>likely Serapio the Younger, a 12th-century Arabic medical author</note>—whom we have shown in the commentary on the *Art of Medicine* to be John of Damascus—says that it makes those wearing it safe from lightning; indeed, so safe that even wax placed under its engraving would ward off lightning if carried. He says this has been tested in those regions where many perish by lightning, yet no one who carries a **Hyacinth** <note>original: "hyacinthus"; in this period, the term could refer to blue sapphires or, as described here, reddish-orange zircons</note> is struck by it. By a similar miracle, it frees those wearing it from the danger of the plague, even those living in pestilential air. The third property is that it induces sleep, and **Albertus Magnus** <note>a famous 13th-century philosopher and theologian known for his work on minerals</note> confesses he has experienced this himself. I myself am accustomed to wearing a very large one, and it seems to contribute something, though not much, to sleep; however, mine is not of that reddish-purple kind, which is the best sort, but golden, and deviates much from the best. 

<margin>Kinds of Hyacinths.</margin> For the best is the reddish-purple <note>original: "puniceus"</note> one, which rarely exceeds the size of a lentil. When this is near fire—that is, placed over glowing coals—it becomes darker and more reddish; removed from the fire, it shines brightly. Truly, this kind differs little in nobility from the **Carbuncle** <note>original: "carbunculus"; usually a ruby or garnet</note>, though as I said, those of medium size are very rare. They attribute all powers clearly to this kind, obscurely to the golden, and in no way to the watery kind, for this latter is cheap and of exhausted strength. Furthermore, they believe it increases riches and authority, strengthens the heart significantly, and produces no small amount of joy. Let us therefore state the cause of these things, not as if they were certain truths, but as possibilities. It is of a cold temperament—and this is common to almost all gems—and it is beneficial to the human **spirit** <term>spiritus: the subtle, invisible substance believed to circulate in the blood and mediate between the soul and the body</term>, whether by similarity of substance, or by clarity, or some other cause, whereby repairing and strengthening it, it makes one cheerful. For sadness is nothing else than either a contraction of the spirit, or its scarcity, or its obscurity. 

Therefore, by the same reasoning, as some have reported from experience, if something else strengthens the heart, it also wards off the plague, which occurs most of all because of fear and weakness of the heart—two things which the Hyacinth abolishes. For this reason, children, women, and the timid are seized by the plague most quickly; the young and the bold are not, unless it is raging violently. Therefore, it will help much in warding off the plague. But also, because of the pleasantness of the spirit, it makes one pleasing, gentle, and of good counsel; hence it will increase authority, and with its growth, riches are usually also increased.

<margin>How the Hyacinth can protect a man from lightning.</margin> This one thing remains: that it makes people safe from lightning. Let us explain in how many ways this could happen: either it prevents the lightning from coming at all, or it directs the wearer’s judgment, or perhaps it only occurs to those to wear a Hyacinth who are not about to be struck by lightning, or it prevents the one wearing the Hyacinth from being harmed even if struck by lightning—I do not see that more ways can be devised. To be struck by lightning and not harmed is hardly probable; nor did those who wrote about it say they were not harmed, but rather that they were not struck. Again, to prevent the lightning from even coming would be a greater miracle than this, for actions of such conspicuous and great power usually occur through contact. But to say it is ordained by fate seems close to a fable; therefore, it is better to say that the cheered spirit of the heart achieves this benefit as well: that it directs the person to where they are entirely safe from lightning. However, to say that even if one is struck, they are not harmed, is a middle ground and more natural, although it is closer to an evident miracle.

We have spoken on these matters following the custom of the **Philosopher** <note>referring to Aristotle</note>, who thinks it sufficient in such difficult questions if we avoid the more absurd conclusions. And that stones might protect us...

# On Stones.

<margin>Turquoise.</margin>
Regarding the stone called **Turquoise** <note>original: "Turchesia"</note>, whether named by chance or after Eranus, they report that when worn in a ring, if a man should fall from his horse, it is believed to absorb the entire impact, even breaking into pieces while keeping the man safe. This has a cause that is less difficult to explain, though still arduous. They add that it must be received as a gift to work. This stone is conspicuous for its sky-blue color and it shines; however, it is neither transparent nor a true gem, for it can be worked with a file. Furthermore, its color blooms when brought near fires, and it wilts and fades from the mere moisture of the hands. Because of this, it is uncertain whether the common gossip of the jewelers has invented such great power so that a stone of great price, modest beauty, and fragile nature might find buyers. Even those among whom it is found do not think it has any powers other than against sorcery and those driven mad <note>original: "lymphaticos"; ancient medical term for those thought to be driven insane by water nymphs</note>. Therefore, if it prevents the harm of falling, this would happen because the man is less pressed down—for this same reason, we are not in danger when falling from cheaper or scrawny horses. But to believe the stone itself absorbs the blow is beyond belief; perhaps it is so soft that it is damaged more quickly than the falling rider himself. It is a lesser miracle that they claim the **Hyena-stone** <note>original: "Hyena"; a legendary stone supposedly found in the eye of a hyena</note>
<margin>Emerald.</margin>
and the **Emerald** <note>original: "Smaragdus"</note> can foreknow the future—if indeed they do. For now, I do not wish to argue about the 
<margin>How gems are able to perform divination.</margin>
fact of the matter, but rather how and why it could happen. For a gem worn in a ring, or hung from the neck (which is more powerful), or even held under the tongue (which can achieve the most at that time), confirms an opinion of a future event or deletes a non-event from the mind. If you wish to know how it does this, you might say the mind divines in no other way than through a dream. Indeed, how it happens that one divines through a dream we have taught in our little book *On the Immortality of the Soul*. Stones held under the tongue can also perform divination by increasing judgment and prudence; the divination of these is greatest, as we have demonstrated in the books *On Wisdom*. They say it has been found by experience that the **Emerald** sometimes breaks during **intercourse** <note>original: "coitus"</note>. However 
<margin>Why the Emerald sometimes breaks during intercourse.</margin>
the matter stands, the Emerald is the most fragile of all gems. When a thin and abundant moisture is added to its refinement, it is disrupted when agitated by heat; for the heated moisture turns into air and occupies a greater space, thereby breaking it, as was demonstrated above. That the body heats up greatly during sexual union is shown by the frequency of breath and the onset of sweat; this heat makes a deeper impression because it is not dissolved gradually as it is in exercise. This gem, when drunk, resists poisons most effectively. Because its nature is overcome by softness more than any other gem, its transparency refreshes the substance of the spirits, and the abundance of refined moisture 
<margin>Why the Emerald especially resists poisons.</margin>
benefits human nature and blunts the nature of poison, because the stone retains stable powers. Indeed, among those things which are pleasing to the sight, there is almost nothing that is not useful to man. I speak of gems, gold, silver, silk, and purple—provided that art does not deceive the eye. Thus, while the **Emerald** is the most excellent of gems for its beauty, just as the **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"</note> is for hardness and solidity, the **Sapphire** <note>original: "Saphyrus"</note> for grace, the 
<margin>The specific praises of noble gems.</margin>
**Carbuncle** <note>original: "Carbunculus"; likely a ruby</note> for vitality, the **Opal** <note>original: "Opalus"</note> for splendor and variety, the **Chrysolite** <note>original: "Chrysolitus"</note> for brilliance, and the **Agate** <note>original: "Achates"</note> for diversity: so also the Emerald confers more to a man's health. But as it is the softest, so it is most liable to all accidents; it is spoiled by fire and heat, by contact with harder gems (especially the diamond), by steel, brass, common bronze, and copper, by blows and rubbing—in short, this gem is vulnerable to every kind of injury. For this reason, it is on few men's fingers, due to its great price.

<margin>How gems show images in dreams.
A marvelous gem of an uncertain type.</margin>
Now, it is well established that for stones to stir dreams and images is far less miraculous than for them to provide divination <note>Predicting the future or discovering hidden knowledge</note>. For instance, I have a certain stone that stirs constant images in dreams; it reduces sleep but increases the memory. It is clear that it does this through the extreme dryness it possesses. It is the size of a large pea—not a medium one, but a large one—and is a rusty-iron color at the top with blood-red spots. It is harder than an agate and has a shine to it. At the bottom, it looks like the cloudy white of an egg; those blood-red spots resemble the shell of a snail, and where the stone is whiter, a part like the inner membrane of an egg can be seen inside.

For a similar reason, they report that the **Amethyst** stirs dreams; hence it is called *Chalam* <note>original: "Chalam" (חלם)</note> in Hebrew, which means "to dream," according to the testimony of Rabbi **Aben Ezra** <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Sephardic scholar, astronomer, and biblical commentator</note>. Certain other stones stir dreams through a different kind of change, such as the **Onyx**, commonly called the *Nicolus* <note>A variety of onyx with a dark base and a thin, bluish-white top layer, often used for cameos</note>, for it alters and agitates the "spirit" <note>In Renaissance medicine, "spirit" referred to the subtle fluid that carried sensory information through the nerves</note>. Others do this through their beauty, such as carbuncles <note>A term used for red gemstones like rubies or garnets</note>, opals, and agates. Others still do so by their inherent property. It is evident, therefore, that dreams are excited by stones in four ways. Indeed, if dreams are excited by causes other than stones, they are easily reduced to these four categories: for wakefulness (when light sleep follows) moves images due to dryness; or onions, cabbages, and mustard move them due to their vapors; or fear, joy, gardens, and love move them because they affect the mind; and some move of their own accord, about which we spoke in the first book on dreams. Truly, it is far easier to provide boldness, readiness, or even cowardice than it is to stir dreams. Moreover, that a stone should stop blood or strengthen the stomach—as we see **Jasper** do—should be almost entirely free of wonder, since these can be attributed to primary or at least secondary physical qualities. And these are the powers they have within us.

<margin>Stones are more precious as they are harder; metals as they are more ductile.
The Diamond.</margin>
Furthermore, the substance of stones is hard, and the harder it is, the more precious the stone—just as among metals, the more ductile <note>Capable of being hammered thin or drawn into wire</note> a metal is, the more it is valued. Thus, among metals, gold has the highest price. For the same reason of substance, the **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"</note> is most precious, though in color it yields to the Carbuncle, the Opal, and the Emerald. A unique feature of the diamond is that even its fragments are precious; for a "scruple" <note>A unit of weight, roughly 1.3 grams</note> is sold for six gold crowns. Because of its hardness, it cuts all other gems; it is not only convenient for engraving but necessary. Because of this hardness, a diamond is worn down and polished by almost nothing other than its own dust.

<margin>A weapon point smeared with diamond dust easily pierces all armor.</margin>
For this same reason, they report—and it is not without a logical basis—that a point smeared with diamond dust (whether it be a spear, a pike, a sword, or an arrow) can easily pierce through all armor, such as breastplates and helmets. For the iron or steel grows hot from the blow, and the diamond penetrates the iron it meets. Let this, then, be the proof of both the extreme fineness and the hardness of the diamond.

<margin>Gems that resist fire.</margin>
Another point is that it shines most greatly among gems when polished. Third, it resists fire for up to nine days, suffering absolutely no damage; it remains unharmed even after many days. After the diamond, the carbuncle and the garnet endure up to the fifth day without trouble—though not all of them, and not always. Therefore, after the diamond, these are the least vulnerable to fire and consist of the most subtle parts. For unless they were made of the finest parts, they would...

...they might send out pores, through which the entering fire (as has been demonstrated) would easily dissipate them. Their very coldness also aids their thinness and solidity, so that these stones resist fires most effectively. This is why the <term>Sapphire</term> <note>A blue variety of the mineral corundum, prized for its hardness</note> does not easily yield to fire and is harder than the <term>Carbuncle</term> <note>A general term for red gemstones, usually rubies or garnets</note>, yet it is placed third in the order of those stones least liable to damage from fire.

<margin>The difference between Diamond and Crystal.</margin>
<margin>The powers of the Diamond.</margin>
Therefore, if anyone asks in what ways the <term>Diamond</term> <note>original: "Adamas"</note> differs from <term>Crystal</term>, since both are shiny and of a bright—or rather watery—hue: we shall say that the brilliance of the diamond is lively and robust, so that it not only shines and gleams, but glows and sparkles. Furthermore, it is unchangeable by iron, water, fire, age, or use, none of which applies to crystal, which ages very quickly. The diamond also attracts straws if it is warmed, not unlike <term>amber</term> <note>original: "electrum"; the author is noting the diamond's electrostatic properties</note>, though quite faintly due to its small size. Likewise, if worn on the left arm so that it touches the flesh, it restrains nocturnal terrors, as I have often <unclear>experienced</unclear>. It is believed in vain that the diamond cannot be broken by a blow, since a small hammer can reduce it to powder; for it is only slightly harder than crystal regarding impacts. Nor does it prevent a magnet from attracting iron. These two attributes—falsely attributed to it and so often repeated and spread even by modern writers—show nothing other than the great laziness and boldness of authors. For it is the height of boldness to write absurd things that you have not proven, and even greater folly not to test what you so easily could.

<margin>All green gems are susceptible to fire, and why.</margin>
Truly, green gems—not only the <term>Emerald</term> <note>original: "Smaragdus"</note> but all others, such as the <term>Prase</term> <note>A leek-green variety of chalcedony or quartz</note> and the <term>Topaz</term> <note>In this period, "topazius" often referred to yellowish-green stones like peridot, which are more heat-sensitive than modern topaz</note>—are susceptible to fire, more so than all others. The cause is an abundance of "half-cooked moisture" <note>An Aristotelian concept suggesting the stone has not fully "ripened" or hardened through heat during its formation</note>. To trace the matter more deeply, I must discuss the variety and cause of colors, not only for an understanding of the generation of stones but also for all plants and animals, even though I had intended to postpone this matter further.

<margin>All colors consist of three things.</margin>
All colors, therefore, consist of three things: first, the underlying matter; second, the light that is mixed into it; and third, the medium. For things seen through green glass or through green air appear green even if they are not. Furthermore, the appearance of a thing seen through water or crystal is different than when seen through air. Light mixed into the thing itself also changes the colors, as seen on the neck of a pigeon; yet the underlying object also retains a color from its own particular mixture.

<margin>Colors which necessarily possess much light.</margin>
Now, all colors exist with light and brightness, but certain ones necessarily receive a large quantity of light. These are: green, scarlet, purple, wine-colored, bright white, silver, and gold—all of which are seen almost entirely in the rainbow. Therefore, if you wish to know which colors are not made without the greatest light, expose a crystal or a glass jar full of water to the Sun, and you will understand which colors are generated only with great light.

<margin>Silver color. Bright white. Scarlet. Purple. Wine-colored.</margin>
Silver is also made from ash-gray mixed with much light, just as bright white <note>original: "candidus"</note> comes from white <note>original: "albo"</note> mixed with much brightness. Thus, "bright white" is like snow, while "white" is like white lead. Scarlet <note>original: "puniceus"</note> comes from black mixed with a powerful light, as seen in a glowing coal. Purple occurs when a shaded white receives refracted rays of the Sun, as at dawn. Likewise, wine-colored <note>original: "vinosus"</note> comes from a pure, undiluted black mixed with an airy splendor, as in the <term>Amethyst</term> and in clusters of grapes. This is among the brilliant colors...

# Book Seven

<margin>
Golden.
Green.
</margin>
The following colors retain less light. **Golden** consists of yellow and a great deal of pure, refulgent light. **Green** is formed in two ways: either when moisture is gradually cooked <note>original: "excoquitur"; in Aristotelian physics, this refers to *pepsis*, the maturation of matter through heat</note> and receives light, as seen in the leaves of trees; or when black moisture is cooked further, such as the black earth found under rain gutters or on the surface of standing water after it has already turned black. The remaining colors either never receive much light at all—such as dusky, rust-colored, and jet-black—or they exist sometimes with much light and sometimes without, such as black and blue. <margin>White.</margin> **White** things are produced when moistures decay without being cooked by heat, or even without decay occurring; this is why the leaves of plants lying on the ground and most roots are white, because heat has acted very little upon their moisture. They also become white due to a lack of nourishment; this is the cause of gray hair in the elderly, and why children [sometimes] have white hair because they are not sufficiently nourished. Furthermore, hairs that turn white do so first at the tip rather than at the root; and weak animals turn white in their fur, just as within the same species, white cows and goats are weaker than those that are black, rust-colored, or red. <margin>Black.</margin> **Black** color is produced when airy or watery moisture is burned up: hence the blackest soot, the smoke of oil from which ink for printing is made, charcoal, and places soaked by rainwater. Blackness is also formed by excessive heat catching fire, yet still acting upon moisture; therefore, blackness occurs when intense heat acts upon fatty moisture by burning it.

<margin>
Why some animals are born black which, with the passage of age, cease to be black.
</margin>
As for why the hair of certain animals is darker at birth than it is as they age, the reason is that the internal heat of the womb had a greater effect while it was enclosed, and the moisture of the fetus was fattier than it is after birth. The proof of this is that you will see no animal produce black hairs after birth that later, with the passage of time, turn reddish or yellow. <margin>Why no animals have green hair.</margin> But why does no animal have green hair, nor is any human hair purple or wine-colored? It is because hair is a dense and thick substance, hardly capable of receiving light; and these colors, as we have shown, do not exist without a great deal of light. For this reason, the color of hair is usually white, black, or rust-colored; however, it is occasionally golden, as I mentioned, because if yellow light is received by a slightly denser substance, it transitions into gold.

<margin>
On the generation of stones and the cause of their colors. [See] the end of the 3rd [book] of the *Meteorology*.
</margin>
We shall demonstrate in the proper place that there are seven types of colors, but here it is enough to have recounted their causes and the names of the principal ones. **White, saffron, crimson <note>original: "puniceus"</note>, purple, green, blue, and black**; closest to black is **tawny** <note>original: "fuscus"</note>, just as yellow is closest to white. Therefore, as the **Philosopher** <note>A common medieval and Renaissance reference to Aristotle</note> says, metals are generated from moist exhalations, while stones are generated from dry ones; they are nourished, however, as we have said, by a clear logic since they grow. For that which grows—not merely by accumulation like <term>tufa</term> <note>original: "tophus"; a porous rock formed by mineral deposits</note>—must be nourished. As <margin>From the last book on the *Exposition of the Names of Physicians*.</margin> **Galen** <note>The influential 2nd-century Greek physician and philosopher</note> says: just as they are generated from different exhalations, so they take on color and substance. Tawny stones, therefore, arise from burnt earth; white ones from pure air or water; green ones from abundant moisture; red ones from intense heat acting on matter that is not very moist; blue ones from a red substance when it is "cooked" more than is proper; and variegated ones from various combinations. The proof is that even what is [governed] by nature is nourished...

# On Stones

[They] maintain the primary quality of their color throughout, just as plants do. However, if there were a continuous addition of matter <note>original: "accessio"; the author is distinguishing between the way living things grow by adding material and how minerals are formed</note>, their substance would always be varied; yet it is only varied due to veins (as also seen in trees) or because of the nature of the stone itself, as in **Agate**.

<margin>No gemstone is without some remarkable power.</margin>
But this variety is also evident in plants, such as the olive tree; yet there is no doubt that the olive tree is nourished, whereas a stone does not grow by the addition of matter. Therefore, this "exhalation" <note>The author refers to the Aristotelian theory that minerals are formed by dry or moist vapors (exhalations) trapped within the earth</note> is not accidental, but the stone, like a tree, draws toward itself that which most suits its nature. They become transparent when the watery parts have been purged of earth, and those parts that remain are thin and perfectly mixed with a watery moisture. For this reason, it happens that no stone of the highest brilliance is heavy, nor is any among them devoid of some exceptional power. Thus, some gems favor longevity, others safety, some wisdom, some riches, others love, some divination, others strength, and some good fortune; there are even some that are unlucky, making people lazy, or timid, or happy, or sad.

But you might say: if brilliant stones consist of thin moisture and very little earth, how is it that they are heavier than glass? For this is a sign used to distinguish false gems from true ones. The reason is that the substance of glass would be heavier—indeed, it is thicker than **Diamond**—but because the substance of **Diamond** is not at all porous, while glass is thin and full of pores, it follows that **Diamond** is heavier than glass. Nevertheless, no noble gemstone can be excessively heavy, as weight always adds a sense of commonness.

<margin>Why many large gems are thin and pale in color, while those of the best color are rare.</margin>
Someone might perhaps wonder why so many gems of pale or faulty color, and even spotted ones, are found in large sizes, while many elegant and flawless ones are small, and very large ones are quite rare. One cause may be that in every category, there has always been a greater abundance of common material than perfect material. Another is that there are more immature gems than those that have reached full maturity. A third reason, which is very significant, is that a small thing can be better crafted by nature and brought to completion; for this reason, large gems can hardly ever be brought to exact maturity. Furthermore, the kings themselves, in whose lands these gems are born, keep for themselves whatever they see excel in size and beauty; they only allow the small, the pale, or the faulty ones to be brought to us.

<margin>The Carbuncle.</margin>
Ludovico Varthema, <note>Ludovico di Varthema (c. 1470–1517) was an Italian traveler whose writings provided some of the first European accounts of South and Southeast Asia</note> a Roman, reports that the King of Pegu—this is a city in India <note>referring to the historic Kingdom of Pegu in modern-day Myanmar</note>—possesses **Pyropes** <term>Pyropus: a variety of deep red garnet or ruby, named from the Greek for "fire-eyed"</term> of such size and brilliance that if anyone were to see the King in the darkness, they would see him shining with a clear light as if he were illuminated by the rays of the Sun. They are accustomed to calling the more noble kind of **Carbuncle** <note>A general historical term for red gemstones, usually rubies or garnets</note> a **Pyropus**. Indeed, there are three types of that...

# Book Seven

<margin>Properties of the Carbuncle.</margin>
...[there are different types]: first, that which shines in the darkness, which Albertus <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar famous for his writings on minerals and alchemy.</note> testifies to having seen; they call this the **Pyropus** <note>original: "Pyropum"; from the Greek for "fire-eyed," likely a high-quality ruby or garnet.</note>. Next to it is the type which, when placed in a polished black vessel with water poured over it, shines in the dark. The third is of lower value, its light being visible only by external illumination, namely daylight or a candle. It is a property of the **Carbuncle** <note>A general historical term for any glowing red gemstone, usually rubies or garnets.</note> to rouse the spirit and make one cheerful, for its colors aid the vital spirits. However, its usefulness remains hidden if the stone is flawed, too small, or if the wearer is inconsistent (such as a child) or bound by excessive and heavy cares (as Princes and wise men often are).

<margin>Soft gems.</margin>
There are also **Chalcedonian Carbuncles**, such as those Germany produces; they are beautiful but soft, and for that reason, they are of almost no use. They are categorized among the "fluors" <note>The author uses this term to describe stones that are soft or "flow-like" in their structure, rather than hard crystals.</note> due to their tenderness. Theophrastus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle, known for his work "On Stones."</note> believes they are formed <term>from a flow</term> <note>original: "ἐκ ρύσεως" (ek ryseos); meaning formed by the conflux of liquids.</note>, some being water-colored, some amethyst-purple, others hyacinth-blue, and others red; some call these Carbuncles. It is a trait of all Carbuncles that, when used as seals, they pull the wax away with them; for this reason, it is considered a sin to engrave them, especially since they are then deprived of that cheerful brilliance.

<margin>The wonderful beauty of the Opal. Book 37, Ch. 6.</margin>
The **Opal** is more beautiful than the Carbuncle; truly, I have never seen one, yet I shall add a description of so remarkable a thing so that, if you happen to find one, you will not be ignorant of how highly it should be valued. In the words of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the Roman "Natural History."</note>, he says: "The Opal has a fire subtler than the Carbuncle, the glowing purple of the Amethyst, the green sea-hue of the Emerald, and all of them shine together in an incredible mixture." Some, as a testament to its supreme brightness, have compared its colors to the pigments of painters, others to the burning flame of sulfur, or even to a fire fueled by oil. Its size is that of a hazelnut. Because of this stone, Pliny recounts that the Senator Nonius was proscribed by Mark Antony. Thus, nothing among gems can be more beautiful. The **pseudo-opal** falls far short of this.

<margin>The wonderful nature of the degenerate Opal.</margin>
This degenerate stone is white and shining, but not transparent; they call it the **eye of the cat** or feline. In the one I possess, this marvel is seen: from one side it appears entirely white and milky, but from the other side it appears completely dusky—so dusky that it even seems dark. This does not happen because of a change in light, for whether you turn it toward the light or toward the shadows, it is always white on the side where it is usually seen as white, and dusky on the other. Thus, the same surface, seen from opposite sides by a mere change of perspective, shows two almost entirely contrary colors. Some of these stones are softer, others hard, like the one I have. It is necessary to explain the cause of such a miraculous property. It is because the stone is "crisped" <note>likely referring to an internal fibrous or layered structure that causes chatoyancy.</note>, and in some parts it is permeable to light while in others it is not. On the side that is not permeable, it does not receive the light but reflects it, and thus it shines white and brilliant like snow; when turned the other way, it receives the light but does not reflect it, and for that reason, the stone appears dark and dusky. This is proof that its substance, as I said, is not at all uniform. But you might ask: why does it not receive the light if the gem is permeable? Better...

Therefore, we must say that it is entirely transparent on the surface; yet, on one side it is rough and therefore black, while on the other it is polished, and for that reason, it is bright and white.

<margin>Sapphire.</margin>
<margin>The powers of Sapphire.</margin>
Next to the **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamanti"</note> and fifth in the order of noble gemstones is the **Sapphire**. It possesses the greatest hardness and a sky-blue color; if it is not faded or flawed, it is quite pleasant to the eyes. For this reason, nothing refreshes the sight more than the **Emerald** <note>original: "Smaragdo"</note> and the **Sapphire**. It also restores the person: when drunk, it helps against <term>black bile</term> <note>original: "bili nigræ"; one of the four humors in ancient medicine, associated with melancholy.</note>, melancholic conditions, and the stings of scorpions. Albertus Magnus <note>A famous 13th-century polymath and theologian who wrote extensively on minerals.</note> reports having twice experienced that the Sapphire cures <term>carbuncles</term> <note>original: "anthraces"; here referring to painful, inflamed skin sores or pustules rather than the red gemstone.</note> by touch alone. It must be a high-quality, large stone, and it must remain pressed against the flesh for a long time. This works because it possesses an <term>alexipharmic</term> <note>A substance used to ward off or treat poison or infection.</note> power. Just as the bite of the <term>dipsas</term> <note>A legendary snake whose venom was said to cause unquenchable thirst.</note> induces thirst, and the hand becomes numb by the touch of the <term>remora</term> <note>The "suckerfish," which ancient writers believed could stop ships in their tracks or affect the human body through touch.</note>, so too is the poison of a carbuncle extinguished by long contact with a Sapphire.

<margin>Heliotrope and its powers.</margin>
**Heliotrope** <note>Literally "Sun-turner," commonly known today as bloodstone.</note> is a green gemstone not unlike **Jasper**, but whereas Jasper has blood-colored spots or drops clinging to it, Heliotrope is streaked with blood-red veins. When exposed to the Sun under water, because of its vivid redness and greenness, it scatters a saffron color so that it seems to cloud the air and show an eclipse of the Sun. To this day, it has not been possible to see this, just as I have not seen a true **Astrites**.
<margin>Astrites.</margin>
This stone is hard; while it is turned around, it shows a light shining inside like the Sun.
<margin>Pseudo-astrites.</margin>
However, gem-cutters imitate it using **Chalcedony Onyx**, which soon loses its luster and its powers, especially if it is spoiled by heat or sweat. A better imitation is made from the brighter **Sard**, which they call **Cornelian**; the best is made from that stone or other harder, hollow stones, for the light is gathered in the cavity. Nevertheless, only the true Astrites retains its beauty and grace.

<margin>Astroites and its wonderful power.</margin>
The **Astroites** <note>Likely a fossilized coral or "star-stone," distinct from the crystalline Astrites.</note> differs little in name but greatly in power and substance from the **Astrites**; for it is neither a gemstone nor transparent, but is entirely marked with spots of an ash-gray color, from which it takes its name. It moves of its own accord in vinegar and even in wine, imitating the gait of animals—proceeding first to the side, and then moving backward. Rabbi AbenEzra <note>Abraham ibn Ezra (c. 1089–1167), a celebrated Jewish scholar, astronomer, and philosopher.</note> once knew this stone and its powers. It is common among us and of low price. When I had frequently considered its movement, I understood that the stone consists of a thin moisture, and that by the power of the vinegar or wine, this moisture could be converted into vapor. Seeking an exit and finding none, the vapor easily pushes the stone—which is otherwise light—here and there. Indeed, it is a sign of the thinness of the vapor that it does not release bubbles. For this reason, one should not believe the stone has large pores. There are those who believe that wearing it hung from the neck makes men victors. I have set out to write here only those things I have experienced, but I did not mind adding this so that anyone might test it: for as I said, I have frequently performed the experiment of its motion in wine and vinegar.

**Jasper** is similar to Heliotrope; if it is green and placed directly over the stomach...

### Book Seven

-> Y <-

Galen <note>A Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a thousand years.</note> wrote that it strengthens the stomach significantly; we have also seen it stop blood flowing from any part of the body, but especially from the nose. This is not surprising, since it possesses a very great <term>astringent</term> <note>A substance that causes the contraction of body tissues, often used to stop bleeding.</note> power. The best specimens are chosen from the East—not particularly small, shining, green, and sprinkled with many little blood-red droplets that vividly resemble living blood. <note>The author is describing the "Heliotrope" or Bloodstone, a variety of jasper.</note>

<margin>Agate and its wonderful variety.</margin>
Among all gems, however, one stone is set apart: the **Agate**. It is truly numbered among the gemstones, yet it is of such varied types that you would hardly believe it to be a single kind of stone. It can be white, red, saffron-yellow, ash-grey, green, black, variegated, or blue. Why should I linger on this? The colors of all other gems combined do not satisfy the range of this one stone. Through the "play of nature," it represents groves, meadows, animals, rivers, flowers, and trees. The most famous in history is the **Agate of King Pyrrhus** <note>Pyrrhus was a king of Epirus (3rd century BCE) famous for his military campaigns against Rome.</note>, which depicted the nine Muses with Apollo in the center striking his lyre <note>original: "cytharam"</note>. Each figure was shown with its own proper ornaments, so that it seemed as if nature had then competed with a painter; indeed, this ought to be called a miracle rather than a gem. We possess two Agates ourselves: in one of them, nature has painted the hemisphere of the heavens with distinct spheres, and in the center, the round earth appearing to rise above the waters. In the other, a fissure in the earth seems to emit smoke that clouds the air.

<margin>How stones are born from two types, just as animals are.</margin>
Furthermore, it is a thing worthy of wonder that the color of the smoke is distinct from the color of the air which is darkened by it: the smoke is white and dense, while the air is reddish and moderately transparent. Other Agates represent the eyes of birds—and we have such a specimen—while others represent the eyes of fish. The **Pontic Agate**, which is dappled with blood-red or black spots, represents images of mountains and valleys. Some are called **White-eyes** <note>original: "Leucophtalmi"</note> for their resemblance to human eyes; some **Wolf-eyes** <note>original: "Lycophtalmi"</note>; and some **Goat-eyes** <note>original: "Ægophtalmi"</note>. I have also seen a transparent green stone beautifully marked by two white lines, which I would believe to be of a "doubtful nature," somewhere between an Agate and a **Prasius** <note>original: "Prasium"; a leek-green variety of quartz.</note>. For just as among animals we have mules born from a donkey and a mare, or a <term>lycisca</term> <note>A fabled hybrid between a wolf and a dog.</note> from a wolf and a dog, so too are stones sometimes mixed from different kinds when their matter and the causes that produce them are combined.

<margin>The method of making a marvelous Agate.</margin>
However, as far as the Agate of King Pyrrhus is concerned, I think it is quite ridiculous to believe that it was decorated and distinguished so perfectly by mere chance. Rather, it happened in this way: a painter painted some stone of the marble variety with strong colors, depicting the nine Muses marvelling at Apollo playing in their midst. Then, whether by chance or by design, that stone lay buried for many years in a place where Agate stones are normally formed. It happened, therefore, that a transparent and watery Agate grew all around it. When it was later found, it displayed the Muses and Apollo as if they had been fashioned by the industry of nature, since the Agate had by then become a gemstone. For if ears of grain and moss cling to trees...

# On Stones.

...[stems] which, over the course of time, turn into **Agate**. I once possessed an Agate containing five ears of grain which you would have said had just fallen from a stalk of wheat, yet they were stone—indeed, a gemstone. Furthermore, a significant portion of moss was present in it. If nature can do this, how much more easily could a "painted stone," if it were soft, turn into an Agate?

Therefore, if someone were to observe the places where Agates are formed—and especially where the transparent varieties are produced, for this is necessary—they might bury a painting made with permanent colors (such as blue and gold) derived from metals. This would be most effective if the work were coated with Punic wax <note>A refined and bleached form of beeswax used in antiquity as a binder for pigments and a protective coating.</note> tempered with a little oil, or some other permanent yet transparent ointment, such as what we call **liquid varnish** <note>original: "vernix liquida"</note>, which is usually applied to more precious finished paintings. In this way, an Agate would be "born" already painted.

But you will say: "If such a thing could be prepared with so little skill, this kind of painted Agate would be common." However, you do not consider that first, it must be buried exactly where Agates are naturally generated; second, the surrounding Agate must be bright and transparent; and third, it must transition into a gemstone within a few years before the painting perishes. Furthermore, it must not be washed away by any external moisture before the image is set; and finally, it must happen to be dug up once finished. Just as there are many fish that no one ever catches, wild beasts in the woods, and birds that no one ever captures—all of which die in their own places—so you should believe there are many gemstones lying hidden in the places where they were born. They never come to light, but return to their "first mother," the earth, just as they had grown together in their old age. Although the Agate is noble for its variety, it rarely commands a high price among gems because it possesses little brilliance.

<margin>The Topaz, which is truly Chrysolite.</margin>
The **Chrysolite** <note>In the Renaissance, names for yellow and green stones were often interchanged; what they called Chrysolite is often what we call Peridot or yellow Topaz today.</note> is held in much higher esteem than the Agate. Our people call this the **Topaz**, just as they call the true Topaz a Chrysolite. For **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and naturalist whose "Natural History" was the primary source for mineralogy in this period.</note> says that Chrysolite is a gem "glittering with a golden color" <note>original: "aurei coloris micans"</note>, and these very words are true of our common Topaz. It is true that the German Topaz, like most other softer gems found in the cold <term>zones</term> <note>The "frigid zone" refers to the northern latitudes in the ancient system of geographical climates.</note>, is less durable; 
<margin>Why northern gems are often soft enough to be filed.</margin>
this is because the heat in those regions cannot sufficiently thin that "juice" <note>The author refers to the "succus lapidificus" or stone-making fluid, a common theory of how minerals formed from liquid.</note> and thus harden the stone. For as I have said, the cause of hardness is a perfect <term>concretion</term> <note>The process of mineral matter hardening into a solid mass.</note>, which occurs when the tiniest parts are mixed together. However, Pliny is not speaking of that northern Chrysolite, but of the Oriental one, which is clearly extremely hard—so hard, in fact, that it yields little or nothing to the **Sapphire**.

For this reason, I ordered my own likeness to be carved into a Chrysolite, along with the first letters of my name and surname. 
<margin>The reason why carving a profile is far easier than a full face.</margin>
I ordered a **profile** <note>original: "faciem mediam," literally "half-face."</note> to be carved, because it is extremely difficult to represent a whole face for many reasons. First, the labor of a whole face is double compared to a half-profile; moreover, he who carves a full face is forced to fashion both sides identically.

Added to this is the fact that anyone carving a full face must maintain the symmetry of the parts—

# Book Seven

Indeed, by comparing the right side to the left—the positions, the wrinkles, the cavities, the sizes, the marks, the shapes, and countless other things—if they do not maintain a thorough likeness, they reveal the foulness of the work to the fingernail <note>An idiom meaning "to perfection" or "under close scrutiny."</note>. Those who carve an entire face into stone must express the matter exactly as it is; however, those who depict a face turned halfway are helped not a little by the likeness of the aspect. For when a person is viewed from an angle, and that tilt itself achieves no small degree of variation, it happens that the face seen in this way reflects now one image, now another. Thus, while a profile representation may be established within a certain range of latitude, a true image of the whole must be expressed at a specific point. It is easier to achieve a significant quantity than a thing which consists almost entirely of thought and lacks division, such as the true likeness of a human being, which consists in the representation of the entire countenance.

<margin>A precept for engraving and painting</margin>
Those who engrave, mold, or paint ought to conceive the form in the mind, and thus first fashion a model <note>original: "typum"</note>, and then, with that present, delineate it more subtly. For there lies hidden a certain symmetry of the parts to one another, which if you have not conceived in the mind, but instead attempt to perfect relying solely on the protection of the eyes, you will have labored in vain. Nor is it permitted to mold only a half-view from the side, for no one looks at a person in that way, but rather with the head slightly turned between both positions.

<margin>Engraving is far more difficult than sculpting.</margin>
It is also far easier to sculpt <note>term: "sculpere" (sculpting), used here to mean carving in relief where the image stands out.</note> than to engrave <note>term: "cælare" (engraving), used here for intaglio, where the image is hollowed out.</note>. I say "engrave" now when we make a hollow likeness, such as is usually made by carving in gems for seals; "sculpting," however, is when we imitate statues and make the image project outward, as on coins that are stamped with the images of Princes. For since the image always consists in both, in that which projects above the flat surface, it is gradually removed by sculpting, and if it should bulge too much, there is always room left to take more away. But in engraving <note>intaglio</note>, since it is necessary to see the true image in wax, if a cavity in the gem is increased and becomes larger or deeper than is proper, it is rendered in a way that cannot be corrected unless the whole work is overturned. While in the other, as I said, it is very easily corrected by removing material, here it would be necessary to fill the cavity, which can be done by no art whatsoever. Furthermore, those who sculpt do and see the same thing, but those who engrave do not do what they see; rather, while they are working, they do not see, and while they see, they are not working <note>A reference to the fact that intaglio carvers must take wax impressions to see their progress, as the hollowed-out stone is difficult to read visually while carving.</note>. This is also most difficult in the art of engraving: that it is necessary to render the right as left and the left as right, whereas when you sculpt, the right remains right and the left remains left. For all these

<margin>To engrave a whole face is a thing of singular example.</margin>
reasons, to correctly engrave the entire face of any man is a thing of entirely singular example <note>Meaning it is an exceptionally rare and difficult feat.</note>. For this reason, I allowed only a half-face to be engraved in a **Chrysolite** <note>A golden-green gemstone, likely peridot in this context.</note> as I said, with the first letters of my name and surname. I chose this stone because it is very hard, and for that reason, it holds an everlasting work and shines not a little.

<margin>Sard.</margin>

When it has <margin>Carnelian.</margin> Onyx at its base, it is called *Sardonyx*, such as the one I possess, in the bottom of which *Onyx* is seen, and in the top, *Sard*. For as we have said, *Sard* often grows from *Onyx*. The *Sard*, *Carnelian*, and *Sardonyx* are most suitable for seals <margin>Why Carnelian is used for seals.</margin> for three reasons: First, because they do not seize the wax; Second, because they are easily engraved, for the material is tenacious and of moderate hardness; Third, because they are not easily dulled by moisture.

<margin>Onyx and its kinds.</margin>

<margin>The origin of figures in stones.</margin>
Truly, one might rightly wonder where these figures in gems and stones come from? For it is not to be believed that every figure happens by chance, since—as we shall say below—many stones of the same kind retain the same figures. Therefore, in my judgment, it should be said that there are two kinds of figures and images: one which always appears in the same stones; and this comes from nature, which, no differently than in plants, maintains the number and order of leaves and fruits. This kind of figure has power and signifies something.

<margin>The story of the stone near which serpents gathered.</margin>
Such a kind of figure was found in a black stone, shaped like a cone whose top had been cut off; this had a serpent most beautifully expressed on the upper part, as if it were painted. <margin>Stones marked with the seal of Solomon.</margin>

<margin>Various figures in stones.</margin>

<margin>Why crystal has six surfaces.</margin>
But as for why **Rock Crystal** <note>original: "Crystallus," referring to clear quartz</note> has six surfaces—for it rarely has more or fewer—this must now be explained. The cause is that just as the cells of bees are surrounded by others, and are therefore hexagonal themselves, so too are pieces of crystal surrounded by other pieces. But why are those surrounded by others hexagonal in form, when a sphere is surrounded by fourteen similar spheres, but not by six? It will be better, therefore, to attribute this power to the nature of the body; for every body bounded by straight-lined surfaces is distinguished by length, width, and height. Since this consists of six opposing surfaces, this is why **Rock Crystal** and other gems of this type, like **Beryl**, have six surfaces.

<margin>Round stones.</margin>
<margin>Crystal is not ice.</margin>
<margin>Raw silver is formed in Crystal.</margin>
<margin>Water in Crystal.</margin>
<margin>How the hardness of gems is known.</margin>
Furthermore, nature established this, as I said, for the sake of generation, as we shall discuss regarding plants. For on the island of **Cuba**, in the other world <note>Referring to the New World or the Americas</note>, perfectly spherical stones abound by the benefit of nature alone; though their use is quite obscure or less certain. But **Rock Crystal** consists of a watery substance, and therefore it melts very easily in fire and passes immediately into glass. For a similar reason, it must be said that it is not formed from ice, but from a moisture of its own kind: for ice that hangs from the mountains, when it falls and is warmed by fire, melts, but **Rock Crystal** does not, unless it is surrounded by fires and constantly pressed by wind and flame. That it stands out from the highest peaks of mountains does not happen because it was born there or because it was once ice, but because the earth and softer stones are liquefied and washed away by rains, winds, and snow, and the rock is laid bare; for this reason, **Rock Crystal** which was generated among stones and beneath the earth seems to hang there however it is attached.

In the point <note>original: "mucrone," the pyramidal tip of the crystal</note> more rarely, but frequently in the body of the **Rock Crystal**, <term>raw silver</term> <note>original: "argentum rude," likely native silver inclusions</note> is formed: this is not counted among its flaws, but among its exceptional praises, for it is considered more beautiful and a gem of rarer example. I have also seen water born within **Rock Crystal**, and in the water a thin black body which was moved to the opposite side by the motion of the water, because it was lighter than it; thus, while the **Rock Crystal** settled, it ascended of its own accord. Playing around, we used to say—and some were even convinced—that a demon was enclosed in the **Rock Crystal**. But why does it not shine much? Because it is soft. No soft gem shines. But why does a soft thing not shine? Because it does not reflect all or most of the rays. Therefore, that which shines the most cannot be so transparent; thus **Rock Crystal** is more transparent than **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamante"</note>, because **Diamond** shines much more.

There is also another cause: that where the surface is exactly smooth, the rays are reflected at exactly the same angle, and thus they become stronger. If, however, it is not hard, the surface will not be perfectly flat, for which reason the rays [are reflected] at different angles...

<margin>Prannium</margin>
Just as **Crystal** is a white gem, so **Prannium** <note>A rare, dark, and transparent variety of quartz, possibly morion</note> is black and transparent, which is rare. Its root seems to be of the same kind as Crystal, and it is found in Saxony. Sometimes, however, it happens that when the root is nearly black, other gems grow upon it, just as the **Sard** <note>original: "Sarda," a reddish-brown variety of chalcedony</note> in Cyprus arises from a translucent stone that is not quite black, and the **Hyacinth** <note>original: "Hyacintus," a term used in the Renaissance for various yellow, orange, or blue stones like zircon or sapphire</note> in Volchestein, Meissen, arises in the same way. They also arise, as we have said, in red, green, blue, and amethyst colors.

<margin>Garatronium</margin>
**Nebrites** <note>A stone mentioned by Pliny, named for its resemblance to a fawn's skin</note> is not a gemstone, but nonetheless a rare stone; it is opaque and matches the color of a deer's skin perfectly <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," meaning with exact precision</note>. Our jewelers call it **Garatronium**. It is believed that the wearer is entirely protected from being wounded.

<margin>Amethyst</margin>
**Amethyst** has the color and charm of wine; it is a gem of low price even if it is an "Oriental" <note>A term often used to denote higher quality gems from the East, particularly India or Sri Lanka</note> variety. It is believed that if tied to the navel, it prevents drunkenness, and as we also mentioned above, it stirs up dreams.

<margin>Coral</margin>
**Coral**, however, is not truly a gemstone. Its types are white, red, and black, all of which may be seen on the same plant. Because of this, they do not differ in age or species, but like other stones, they are tinted by the vapors of the sea. It is soft and grows like a strawberry tree <note>original: "arbuti instar," referring to the Arbutus tree</note> at the bottom of the sea among stones and rocks.

<margin>The Powers of Coral</margin>
The most noble is the red kind, especially that which glows like purple, emitting a certain fiery splendor. If suspended directly over the stomach, it strengthens it greatly—an effect which **Albertus** <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a prominent medieval philosopher and scientist</note> tries to attribute to **Galen** and **Avicenna** <note>Two of the most influential figures in ancient and medieval medicine</note>. It is of a delicate substance, indeed the most delicate among those things that harden in the sea; therefore, it strengthens the limbs and tempers the spirits. Because it possesses the qualities we described above, it strengthens the heart and brain, cheers the mind, and resists the **falling sickness** <note>original: "morbo comitiali," an old term for epilepsy</note>. But while its production is very frequent, the best quality is certainly very rare. For things that are abundant are easily brought to completion, and those that are easily completed cannot be perfect.

<margin>Why the best things are rare</margin>
Therefore, it is necessary that all the best things be rare. It hardens and becomes durable in the air after being pulled from the sea, because the air dries its thin moisture, and the cold also binds its parts. However, it is cooled by the air even in the middle of summer, because the part that penetrates inside becomes cold. For it has been shown that air is cooled when it is scattered.

<margin>For diagnosing future illnesses</margin>
A property of the red, pure, and shining kind, like the **Carbuncle** <note>A general name for red gems like garnets or rubies, often thought to glow in the dark</note>, is that if it is tied around the neck so that it touches the skin, when a person is ill, or about to become ill shortly, or if they have swallowed poison they do not yet feel, the stone grows pale and loses its luster—so much so that you would be amazed. I have observed this more than once. The cause is that the vapor, which cannot yet cause distress to the man, afflicts the more delicate substance of the coral in a wonderful experiment.

If I displease them, I am not so much ashamed or regretful as I am glad to be held in hatred by men of such character. Therefore, that infamous man would take a tablet of true stone—such as a **Carbuncle** <note>original: "Carbunculo," a term for deep-red gems like garnets or rubies</note> made from a carbuncle, or an **Emerald** <note>original: "Smaragdo"</note> from an emerald—that was bright but cheap because it was thin and pale in color, of which there was (and always will be) a great abundance. To this, he would add a matching, thick piece of **Crystal**, joining them as thinly as possible with glue. He would place the appropriate color between them—such as a brilliant red for a Carbuncle, green for an Emerald, or blue for a **Sapphire**—and to hide the seam, he would enclose it in gold. This also removed any suspicion of trickery, for in the more noble cities, it is forbidden to set a counterfeit gem in gold. In this fraud, nothing is lacking except the seller's authority. The seam remains hidden, buried in gold, and because of the thinness of the genuine stone, the color makes it look illustrious; the top surface, being of the true species, gives off the proper luster of a real gem. In this way, this marvelous craftsman deceived even the jewelers themselves. Finally, when the fraud was recognized, he looked to his own safety by fleeing; he was condemned to exile from all the more noble cities, and thus, for a very small amount of gold, he prostituted the honor of our city everywhere. Yet, it was no contemptible robbery: a gem worth three **gold crowns** <note>original: "aureorum coronatorum," a common gold coin of the period</note> was often sold for three hundred, or even far more. Therefore, once the fraud was discovered and his method of immoderate and effortless profit failed, he turned his hand to that notorious invention of counterfeit money, and for that, he paid the penalty.

<margin>
How a **Sapphire** is turned into a **Diamond**.
</margin>
The third method of altering gems is far more noble and less condemned, with art struggling against nature. One gem is changed into another by the help of fire. A bright Sapphire, but otherwise of a pale color, is joined with gold; fire is applied gradually until it liquefies. The gold boils for three or four hours; then the gem is removed and allowed to cool gradually, and you will find a **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamantem." The author describes a heat-treatment process to remove color from pale sapphires to simulate diamonds</note>. For the gem remains, and it cannot be touched by a file <note>A test for hardness; diamonds and sapphires are harder than steel files</note>, but whatever blue color there was perishes. For this reason, we seek out the palest Sapphires: they are cheaper, and they pass more quickly and are changed more perfectly into Diamonds. The man who first discovered this was greatly enriched in a short time. Even after the matter was revealed, profit still remains for the craft, as it shines brilliantly due to the hardness of the Sapphire. There are those who make beautiful Diamonds from "sea-water" gems <note>likely **Aquamarine**</note> that are cheaper and softer. There are also those who do not cook the Sapphire in gold, but in chalk...

<vocab>Zocolinus (proper name), jewelers (gemmarij), Carbuncle (Carbunculo), Emerald (Smaragdo), Sapphire (Sapphyro), Diamond (Adamantem), fraud (fraus), method of counterfeiting (adulterandi modus), stones (lapidibus)</vocab>

## Book Seven

...wrapped in the material in the fire alone, and the process succeeds in the same way. It must be observed, however, that the fire should be applied gradually to the cold gems, and likewise, when the work is finished, they should be allowed to cool as the fire dies out. For removing them from the heat is not safe; it is a defect if any trace of a bluish color remains.

<margin>How an emerald is made.</margin>
An **Emerald** <note>original: "Smaragdus"</note> is created with greater effort. **Crystal** is ground very finely, then **marciacocta** <note>A technical term likely referring to a lead-based flux or glaze; the name suggests "cooked marcasite," but the author defines it below as a mixture of salts, sand, and lead</note> and a most brilliant **verdigris** <note>original: "aerugo," a green pigment made from copper</note> (or "worm-like" verdigris) are added. A raw brick is hollowed out, these three things are placed inside, and it is baked in a furnace among other bricks with a mark added to identify it. From there, a mass similar to an Emerald is extracted, cut, and polished. It is, however, **glass** <note>original: "uitrum"</note>, but it is so elegant that the fraud might still be hidden today—to the incredible profit of its creators—had those who first discovered it (for this is a new invention from the last ten years) not tried to get rich too quickly with overly large pieces. By producing such large quantities and sizes, they cast suspicion. Nevertheless, they were not without profit; I have seen some so beautiful that, when set in gold, they surpassed natural stones in brilliance. This succeeds best if they are entirely free of bubbles, for bubbles reveal it to be glass and make the stone look foul.

<margin>Every gem turns into glass by the "odor" of lead.</margin>
However, it can be tested with a file, for it is glass. Indeed, every gem turns into glass by the **"odor" of lead** <note>original: "odore plumbi"; in early alchemy and chemistry, "odor" often referred to the fumes, vapors, or the influential presence of a substance</note>, especially when it has been reduced to a fine powder.

<margin>The composition of Marciacocta.</margin>
Furthermore, it is clear that lead is contained in **Marciacocta**. For Marciacocta consists of **alkali salt** <note>original: "sale chali," likely soda or potash</note>, alum, and sand, along with black or white lead reduced to **ash** <note>original: "calcem," or calx, the powdery oxide produced by roasting metal</note>. Pottery vessels are dipped in this, and when placed in furnaces, they take on the luster of glass as well as solidity, so that they neither absorb nor leak the liquid held within.

<margin>A most useful transformation not yet discovered.</margin>
This succeeds best in certain potteries of **Germany**, which are superior to others due to the local clay alone. Thus, through **marciacocta** and the "odor" of lead, gems turn into glass and then receive color. By fire alone, gems do not cease to be gems, but they lose their color rather than receiving it. Therefore, if some middle ground could be found—where the gem might receive color and soften, but not so much that it turns into glass—then the greatest profit would follow. It would be necessary to make it less soft than lead does, but more so than fire alone. In this way, a **Sapphire** <note>original: "Sapphyrus"</note> could be changed into a **Carbuncle** <note>original: "Carbunculum," a red gem like a garnet or ruby</note>, since it is harder than a Carbuncle; or, if it becomes softer, it could turn into an **Emerald** with the addition of green color. Likewise, a Carbuncle could become an Emerald, for it is much harder than one, even if it is quite a bit softer than a Sapphire. There are many things of this kind that could undoubtedly make an inventor wealthy, yet they remain hidden; for where there are extremes, there must also be a middle ground. Furthermore, among the types of glass made with **marciacocta** and crystal: if a red color is added, it becomes a **Carbuncle**; if blue, a **Sapphire**. But all these are cheaper than an **Emerald**, because they differ more from the nature of those gems than the glass that imitates an Emerald does. For no gem is not harder than an Emerald, as we said above; for that reason, they only attempt to imitate the Emerald, because only glass can be made to resemble an Emerald due to the great softness of the Emerald itself. They are made...

<summary>This page describes the technical process of creating high-quality imitation emeralds using ground crystal, copper verdigris, and a lead-based flux called marciacocta. The author also speculates on an undiscovered chemical "middle ground" that would allow real gemstones to be permanently re-colored without turning them into glass.</summary>

# On Stones.

...are produced, <note>The Latin text begins with the suffix "tur," likely completing a word like "finguntur" (are shaped) from the previous page.</note> however, even those on the side of the kiln, just like the imitation **emerald** <note>original: "Smaragdus"</note>.

<margin>A raw brick increases in weight while it is being baked.</margin>
But it is a wonder that some say baked bricks are heavier than they were before being placed in the furnace. The cause may be that when they are made, they are dried in the Sun and take in a significant amount of air; this air, lurking within, renders the stone much lighter than when it has been consumed by fire. Thus, as the brick is compressed by the heat, it becomes heavier, even though its moisture has been driven off. Bricks that are baked longer than is proper begin to mimic the color of iron; thus the cause of their weight and color may be the same: a smallness relative to the amount of matter. This smallness itself is caused by the earth being forcibly compressed and melting, retaining something metallic within it. For this reason, bricks baked more than is proper are almost always bent and warped.

<margin>Imitation whetstones that wear down gems.</margin>
<margin>Mosaic work.</margin>
Returning to my original purpose: art does not only manufacture imitation gems, but also stones and even whetstones <note>original: "cotes"</note>. First, whetstones are made from **emery** <note>original: "Smiri"</note> to wear down gems; others are made of **geodes** <note>A "stone within a stone," often iron-rich</note> to mimic geodes, and from other whetstones to make their own kind. Each of these is finely ground as one desires to make such a thing, and they are bound together with egg white, linseed oil, and "juniper tears" <note>original: "iuniperi lachryma," likely sandarac resin</note>, then dried under sand. **Mosaic work** <note>original: "Lithostroton," literally "stone-layering"</note> is also made, by which the floors of temples are decorated with various figures of men, wild beasts, and trees—as seen in the Church of Holy Wisdom <note>Hagia Sophia</note> in Constantinople, St. Mark's in Venice, and St. John the Baptist in Florence. It is also used for walls, such as in the Church of St. Lawrence in Milan, made from fragments of stones of different colors—white, red, blue, green, and black—joined together with a tenacious glue so that the images reflect not only the shape but the color as well.

<margin>Everlasting cement.</margin>
An everlasting **cement** <note>original: "Maltha," a term for various water-resistant mortars or mastics</note> is made for this work from lime and pig fat, or pitch, or egg white. This especially resists water, which is why channels for conducting water are joined with it.

<margin>From what materials water conduits are made.</margin>
Another excellent mixture for the same purpose consists of lime, egg white, oil, iron filings, and sea-snails <note>original: "marinis umbilicis," literally "sea navels," likely referring to ground shells or opercula</note>. The channels themselves are made of wood from fir, alder, pitch-pine, or wild pine; for these woods possess a very greasy and warm moisture, which allows them to best resist the damage caused by water. They are also made of lead, but the best and most eternal are made of bronze <note>original: "ære"</note>.

<margin>Every material upon which fire has acted more than is proper perpetually resists the damage of water.</margin>
Indeed, it can be held as a rule that all things which fire has burned more than usual—such as charcoal, bronze, and sulfur—are never corrupted by water, even if they were to remain in it for thousands of years.

<margin>Cement for marble.</margin>
But for joining stones or fragments of marble, a cement made of marble dust and egg white, or pitch, is sufficient. It is clear, then, why some things remain uncorrupted in water and which ones they are; others, however, are minimally subject to the damage of water due to their density, though their outer crust may still be corrupted.

<margin>Why true gems are very rare in animals.</margin>
Leaving these things aside, I return to the history of gems. Since enough has been said of those which grow under the earth, in waters, or among stones, I must now speak of those born within animals. And although true gems can be found in animals—as they say of the **Cock-stone** <note>original: "Alectorio," a stone supposedly found in the gizzards of roosters</note> in the stomach of a rooster—nevertheless, no true gem from the body...

<page-num>182</page-num>
<header>Book Seven</header>

<margin>By what reasons it is shown that all stones solidify by cold.</margin>
...[a stone] taken from some animal I have seen to this day. And those must be rare altogether, because they solidify by cold. Evidence that gemstones solidify from cold: first, they arise among stones and in the coldest places. Next, they are preserved by cold and weakened or damaged by heat. Even watery substances only shine when solidified by frost, as in ice; yet all gems shine, and most are even transparent. They also soften in fires so much that they can be pierced, like the **Diamond** <note>original: "Adamas"</note>; others even more so, and some even melt. The **Hyacinth** <note>original: "Hyacintus"; in this period, this often referred to sapphire or blue zircon</note> softens and melts with great difficulty, while **Crystal** <note>original: "Crystallus"; rock crystal or quartz</note> does so easily. There is also an indubitable proof of the coldness of all stones, even if others were lacking: their very touch. Therefore, if stones solidify by cold, and gems—being harder—by a greater degree of it, it is no wonder that gems are not generated in animals, where nothing can be extremely cold. <note>The author is following the Aristotelian theory that stones are formed by "concretion" or "concrescence" caused by cold, which contrasts with the internal heat of living animals.</note>

<margin>The Pearl.</margin>
Yet the most precious of these, as far as I know, is the **Pearl** <note>original: "Margarita"</note>, which consists of certain round layers. The nobler ones are born from round shells, though they are less round themselves; other "ignoble" round ones come from oblong shells, as if by a contrary logic. Both types of shells are striated and dwell in the depths of the sea. It is therefore a fable that they conceive from the dew of the heavens. <note>A common ancient belief, found in Pliny, held that oysters rose to the surface to catch dew, which then hardened into pearls.</note> The ignoble kind of pearls is born from **Nacres** <note>original: "Nacaronibus"; mother-of-pearl shells</note>—for so they call the long oysters, or rather I should say shells, because they are striated. The pearl ages very quickly, and in this, it is not like other stones. The northern Indian Sea yields them near the island of **Cubagua**, and the southern near **Terarequi** <note>Cubagua (Venezuela) and Terarequi (Isla del Rey, Panama) were famous pearl fisheries in the 16th century.</note>; they are also born in many other places. Their greatest merit lies in their whiteness, brilliance, and roundness. They are found in shells or oysters near **Britain**, but are more frequent in the Indian Sea. Many pearls are found in a single shell, especially very small ones, which is why there is an unbelievable abundance of them. Large ones are rare; those that are both large and without flaw are the rarest of all. They purify the blood and have a thin substance. But their color is like that of the **pseudo-opal** <note>Likely referring to a stone with a milky or shifting play of light, such as moonstone or a lesser opal.</note>, namely one that changes depending on how it is viewed. The cause has already been stated: pearls consist of layers which are polished on one surface and rough on the other. Take an experiment with several mirrors joined together in the same order, so that the shining surface covers the rough side of another. Then, if you imagine them small and so thin that they create a body that is only rough and not divided or varied, you will finally understand why the manner of viewing it changes the color and brilliance. Yet the color of the pearl is usually white, shining, or slightly dusky; they borrow this from their shells. Not unlike this...

<margin>The Indian Conch.</margin>
...is the **Indian conch** <note>original: "cochleis"; literally "snails" or "shells"</note>, which they say India sends. Regarding the color, shape, and substance, I can speak because I have seen them quite often; as to where they come from, I cannot say enough. Its shape, then, is like a **trireme** <note>An ancient Mediterranean galley with three banks of oars; here used to describe the elongated, tiered shape of the shell.</note> with a high poop-deck, in which there is another vessel; you would call it a cup designed by nature, for the size of the one I saw was large enough to hold a **cotyla** <note>An ancient Greek unit of volume, roughly equal to half a pint.</note>. It is truly a thing of most elegant use and beautiful form. This is the shell of a snail, then, similar to the shells of pearls...
