# On Stones.

...[more noble] <note>This continues from the previous page, likely describing the pearl (margarita) or a similar specimen</note>: indeed, it is so much more noble than our snail shells, just as the Indian air, and earth, and water are more excellent than our own elements; for in the course of many centuries, things turn out better in such climates.

<margin>Borax</margin>
**Borax** <note>In this historical context, "Borax" refers to the "Toadstone" rather than the modern chemical compound</note> is a name used by some for the **Chelonite** <note>original: "Cheloniten"; from the Greek 'chelone' for turtle or tortoise, though here associated with toads</note> stone. It is found, so they say, in the head of a large, old toad. **Brassavola** <note>Antonio Musa Brassavola (1500–1555), a famous Italian physician and botanist</note> reports that he found it in the head of that animal, and that it is a bone rather than a stone. It is twofold: one kind is hollow and very similar to bone, with a pale brown color; the other contains a stone within the bone itself. However, as Brassavola reports, it is actually the bone of the head which hardens with age because it is nourished by the earth. I am not certain of its powers, though some believe it to be effective against **the stone** <note>original: "calculum"; referring to kidney or bladder stones</note>. I am unsure if it truly prevents the generation of stones; it certainly cannot prevent them entirely, though whether it might delay them is a matter worthy of doubt.

<margin>Snail-stone</margin>
The **Snail-stone** <note>original: "Limacius lapis"</note> is usually generated in the head of a snail that is not covered by a shell <note>i.e., a slug</note>. As I can demonstrate, this stone ought to be white in color with a rough surface, because it is condensed from a watery substance by cold. It is small for the reason that it is found in a small animal. It is thought that when tied to the body, it brings no small benefit to those suffering from **quartan fever** <note>a form of malaria where fever recurs every four days</note>. <margin>Perch-stone</margin> It is also thought that in the **Perch** <note>original: "Perca"</note>, which is a small fish with a large head, two white, oblong, flat stones are found. They are almost toothed on one side and are believed to help with **stone disease** <note>original: "lithiasi"</note>.

<margin>How stones are generated in animals</margin>
Stones arise in animals in two ways: one by cold, as in the snail, the perch, crabs, the toad, and as they say, Indian turtles. The other way is by heat, as is often seen in the gallbladders of bulls, and sometimes even in humans. Indeed, a few years ago, a stone was found in the gallbladder of a man suffering from the type of scabies called leprosy. They are also born in the bladder and kidneys to the great misfortune of the sufferer. I even have in my possession a stone generated in the lung of an ox; it is smooth and ash-colored. All stones born in crabs, snails, and fish—such as the **drum-fish** <note>original: "coruo"</note>, the **manatee** <note>original: "manati"</note>, and many others—prevent the generation of stones in the kidneys and dissolve those already formed. Because these stones harden in these animals due to excessive cold, when they are drunk <note>as a ground powder mixed with liquid</note>, they cool the kidneys. In humans, however, stones are generated by excessive heat. Such stony matter is inherently very cold; therefore, it is appropriate that it brings relief to the excess of urine caused by either the heat or the dryness of the kidneys. It is also said that the **Cock-stone** <note>original: "Alectorium"</note> is generated in the belly of a rooster. However, these are often faked using **Sard** or **Agate** in which a flame-like spot appears; I have found nothing certain regarding a true Cock-stone.

There are also stones included in the number of gems, though they are far from being so, such as the **Geodes**. The Geodes is falsely called the **Eagle-stone** <note>original: "Ætitem"</note> because it appears "pregnant" <note>referring to the rattling sound of a smaller stone trapped inside a larger one</note>. A rusty-colored variety is brought from Gaul, and a pale one from Cani in Italy. <margin>Stone-breaker</margin> The **Stone-breaker** <note>original: "Tecolithos"</note> is of two kinds: the Indian variety, and that which **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the "Father of Mineralogy"</note> calls the "sponge stone."

<margin>Kinds of Marbles</margin>
Next to gems in glory, beauty, and grace is **Marble**. Its kinds...

<header>Book Seven</header>

<margin>
Signs of marbles.
</margin>
...[more] noble ones <note>original: "nobilius"; completing a comparison from the previous page</note> are Phengitic, Parian, Zeblican, Porphyry, and Ophite. All are judged or criticized by their color, luster, hardness, and transparency.

<margin>
Phengitic.
</margin>
**Phengitic marble** <note>original: "phengiticum"; likely a translucent selenite or a very lustrous white marble</note> shines the most and reflects images. For this reason, Nero completed the Temple of Fortune (originally begun by Servius Tullius, which he called the Temple of Seia) within his "Golden House"; he built it internally with this kind of marble so that even with the doors closed on all sides, it captured the light in such a way that the brightness of day seemed to be preserved inside.

<margin>
Zeblican.
</margin>
**Zeblican marble** <note>original: "Zeblicum"; a type of serpentinite found in Zöblitz, Saxony</note> is found in the Meissen region. It was believed to be effective against poisons; whether it truly helps, I do not know, but it is certain that it *could* help, given that it is quite soft. For if we drink or eat from vessels made of deer horn, the strength of poisons—though not all of them—will for the most part be dulled by being held in them for a short time.

<margin>
Parian and its types.
</margin>
There are many types of **Parian marble** <note>original: "Parij marmoris"; historically a fine-grained, white marble from the Greek island of Paros, though here the author uses the term more broadly for various high-quality marbles</note>, categorized by their different colors. The whitest is seen everywhere in Italy; an ash-gray variety is found in the Hildesheim district in Germany; a green variety is seen in the Church of St. John the Baptist in Florence. There is an iron-colored variety upon which the castle of Stolpen—the fortress of the Bishop of Meissen—is founded; this is of such hardness that **Agricola** <note>Georgius Agricola (1494–1555), the famous scholar of mining and mineralogy</note> reports that blacksmiths in Meissen make anvils out of it. It is clear that it must be tough, and of a finer and denser substance, and thus it is also heavy. There is also a splendid, shining black marble, which makes up the tomb of **Cardinal Caracciolo** <note>Marino Ascanio Caracciolo (1468–1538), an Italian cardinal and diplomat whose tomb is in the Cathedral of Milan</note>—a man of singular integrity and the prelate of our province—located in our great cathedral to the right of the altar. There is also a variegated type of many sorts, which is often fragile and breaks spontaneously because some parts in it are "raw" and others are "over-burned" <note>An early geological theory suggesting that stones were "cooked" by the earth's internal heat</note>. There is also a reddish marble. Why should I delay? There is no color that is not granted to marble. In Siena, seven types of Parian marble are seen together above the altar: white, ash-gray, reddish, green, black, porphyry, and ophite.

**Porphyry** <note>original: "porphyrites"</note> is a marble distinguished by red and seemingly white spots, or rather it is red with spots gleaming through it. There are two notable columns of it in Milan in the Church of St. Ambrose before the altar, as well as the tomb of **St. Dionysius** <note>The first Bishop of Milan</note>, which was transferred to the great cathedral of our city; it is the size of a human body and of considerable thickness. **Ophite** <note>original: "ophites"; from the Greek word for "snake," referring to its mottled, serpentine appearance</note> is truly green, usually with white spots throughout, though it is sometimes distinguished by other colors. I have frequently seen columns and tables made of it, just as there is a table of another variegated color at the home of **Andrea Alciati** <note>The famous legal scholar and author of the Book of Emblems</note>, which is of no small beauty.

<margin>
Natural images in marble.
</margin>
Sometimes striking forms are found in Parian marble due to the variety and meeting of the veins, which represent an image no less than a painting. For besides others, in the Church of Holy Wisdom [Hagia Sophia] in Constantinople, an image of **St. John the Baptist** covered in camel skin is seen; it is perfectly complete in all aspects, except that it does not express one of the feet as well as a painting could. I have already stated that the cause of these images is accidental rather than an inherent property of the stone.

<header>Concerning Stones.</header>

# Concerning Stones.

<margin>Alabaster.</margin>
Among the types of marble is **Alabaster**, which is translucent and usually white. From it, jars are made for fragrant ointments; it is sturdier than glass and purer than metals. It excels over earthenware because it absorbs or releases less of the ointment, making its use necessary. The reason it gains transparency when immersed in water—though it then absorbs and releases juices more—is something we discussed previously.

<margin>The whetstone and its kinds.</margin>
Next to marble are **whetstones** <note>original: "cotes"</note>. The most noble among these are the Lydian and the Damascus. The Lydian is of a very thin, black substance, shining, and with marvelous subtlety it reflects the colors of metals. By its aid, goldsmiths understand the purity of gold and silver; due to its fineness, they cause no loss <note>of the metal being tested</note>, allowing for a thousand trials without the loss of a single grain. By its blackness, it reveals the color of the metal, for the blackness gathers the luster and color. It is the nature of a whetstone to consume everything quickly and gradually without being consumed itself. <margin>How whetstones are tested.</margin> For this reason, the Damascus stones are the most excellent. For when they rub against steel, no matter how hard, they consume it very quickly, yet they themselves are worn down very little. However, over time and through long and frequent friction, they too perish and are consumed. Inferior stones are soft, decayed, veined, knotty, or too rough. From the category of whetstones comes a soft stone from which vessels for cooking food are made <note>likely "potstone" or steatite, which can be easily carved and withstands heat</note>. This stone is tender enough to be carved, yet consists of a slow moisture; as a result, it resists fire for a long time. It is ash-gray and somewhat dark in color. It is characteristic of all whetstones, but especially the Lydian, that they are best on their upper side because they are perfected by the Sun; they are worst on their lower side, where they lie against the earth and moisture.

<margin>The cutting stone.</margin>
The mention of the whetstone brings me to the memory of the razor. There is a stone among the Indians of a yellow color, transparent, which cuts like a razor. It is equal to glass or crystal and, because of its thinness, surpasses a steel razor. But what they add is marvelous: it is sharpened not by a whetstone or a millstone or any other stone, but by water itself.

<margin>Flint and its differences.</margin>
Next to marble and whetstones, though of a thicker substance, is **Flint** <note>original: "Silex"</note>. It too is of various kinds: tender, hard, tough, brittle, heavy, light, impervious to fire, and that which quickly turns to ash; some are rough, some red, and of various colors. There is a scaly flint that withstands rain and cold; it usually melts and is finally turned to ash, whereas other stones for the most part turn into lime. That extracted from the mine at Nuremberg hardens, while its other varieties are more likely to break. <margin>Cuttable marble.</margin> There is also a stone similar in nature to marble, specifically because it is "cuttable" <note>original: "sectile"</note>, but it is of an ashen color and of incredible softness, so that it is cut with a saw just like wood for various works. There is an abundance of it in the Venetian region. But because of its dull color, and because it does not take a polish, it can be categorized with flint. For it is characteristic of all flint to be scaly and not perfectly smooth (lacking the luster of marble) and to be able to be cut. This stone, however, lacks one part of each category: it does not shine, so it is not marble; and it lacks scales, so it is not flint.

# Book Seven

<margin>Rocks of six kinds.</margin>
Let the single name for the rest of the stones be "rock," but there are six kinds: one named from its property, such as **Magnetite**; one from its powers, like **Calamochus**; one from its color, like **Amo-chrysos**; one from its pattern, like **Alabandicus**; one from its shape, like **Trochites**; and one for its noble resistance to fire or water, like **Magnesia**. Therefore, we shall begin with the first kind.

<margin>Kinds of Magnetite.</margin>
<margin>What powers the iron-colored Magnetite possesses.</margin>
**Magnetite**, or the "Herculean stone" <note>original: "lapis Herculeus"</note>, appears to be of two or three kinds: for there is an iron-colored variety, a white one, and one that is white but distinguished by light and thin iron-colored veins, though it is smooth nearly everywhere. Magnetite of the iron-colored kind has two primary powers, unknown to almost no age: for it attracts iron, and iron rubbed with Magnetite attracts other iron, so much so that it has sometimes happened that the Magnetite attracts five or even more rings in a continuous succession. After that most ancient age, in the time of Aristotle—if any credit is to be given to Albert <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a medieval scholar who wrote extensively on minerals.</note>—it became known that there are two kinds of Magnetite: one that directs iron toward the north, and the other toward the south. This is how the matter stands: a thin piece of iron is rubbed at its tip, then it is suspended in balance; the iron then turns of its own accord so that the tip faces north or south.

<margin>Book 2, Concerning Metals, Treatise 3, Chapter 6.</margin>
Now, these four things were already known in ancient times. But it was also discovered in Albert's time that there is a kind of Magnetite called <term>Theamedes</term> <note>A legendary stone, the opposite of a magnet, said to repel iron. It was first mentioned by Pliny the Elder.</note>, found growing alongside the Magnetite itself, which drives iron away. Furthermore, it is known that Magnetite is even attracted by iron, and that its power penetrates bodies so that even if a board is placed in between, it still draws the iron to itself. Additionally, on Albert’s testimony, Aristotle was said to have known the use of the <term>nautical compass</term> <note>original: "pyxidis nauticæ," literally "nautical box."</note>. Thus, as is customary, many things have long been known which quite a few in our own time have thought were [new] inventions; for they attribute the theory of the nautical compass to a certain Flavio <note>Likely Flavio Gioia, to whom the invention of the compass was traditionally but incorrectly attributed.</note>, which is well established to have been known at least before the time of Albertus Magnus. Therefore, this error took its origin from the unreliability of Albertus Magnus. Because he mixed several falsehoods with certain truths, it happened that even the truths were held to be unworthy of belief. Yet I would not believe these things were known to Aristotle—neither regarding the compass nor that it directs iron to the north—since Galen and Alexander of Aphrodisias, who overlooked no wonder of nature however slight, made no mention of these matters, which are so wonderful and useful. It is also certain that these things were unknown in the time of the Romans, given the many shipwrecks they suffered for this reason; hence more than once their strength was worn down by shipwreck while fighting against the Carthaginians, and Octavian’s fleet was scattered while facing Sextus Pompey.

<margin>Reasons for nine experiments with iron-colored Magnetite.</margin>
Therefore, let us now approach the powers of iron-colored Magnetite once more, and then explain the reasons, beginning from an experiment performed. Magnetite, then, attracts iron; it also attracts <term>Steel</term> <note>original: "Chalybem"</note>. Girolamo Fracastoro <note>A 16th-century Italian physician and scholar.</note> also reports having seen it attract silver, though generally it does not attract silver at all. The reason why it attracts iron is because iron is its food—for as I have said, stones are alive—and for this reason, it is also best preserved in iron filings. What wonder is it, then, that steel, in which the greatest part is iron, is attracted? But also, if iron is touched by Magnetite...

<header>Concerning Stones.</header>

# Concerning Stones.

If it is touched first, it is more easily attracted. However, whether the silver contained some iron, or whether it was another kind of Magnet <note>original: "Magnetis"</note>, I have decided not to speak on it, as it is a matter unknown to me. Nevertheless, this satisfies our principles: that silver and other metals can be attracted by a strong stone if they contain any iron. Nor does the Magnet attract from every side, but where the "bark" <note>The outer layer or surface of the stone.</note> is thin, and more from one part than another; it also attracts polished iron more readily than that covered in rust. Indeed, iron that has been rubbed with the stone is not only attracted more quickly by the Magnet, but it also attracts other iron to itself more easily than the stone itself does. For it seems that the power of the Magnet is strengthened by the iron, because the finer parts of the stone adhering to the surface of the iron draw other iron toward it. Furthermore, a large piece of iron will, in turn, attract a small piece of Magnet, and even more so if the iron has been touched by the Magnet and the Magnet by the iron. This happens because the Magnet desires iron as its nourishment <note>Natural philosophers of this era often used biological metaphors, like "hunger" or "nourishment," to explain physical attractions.</note>; since it cannot pull the heavy iron to itself, the stone is instead carried toward the iron. This stone has two parts placed opposite each other: one that lies toward the south, the other toward the north. When it is dug out of the earth, it keeps this same power, just as animals instinctively return to their own natural habitat. However, since the stone cannot move itself due to its weight, when iron is rubbed by it and placed in a state of balance, the iron moves easily. This is also because of a certain natural principle: that nothing moves itself. Therefore, since there are two parts, the iron which is touched by the northern part of the stone directs its point toward the north; but if it touches the southern part, it is driven toward the south and not the north. It is false, therefore—as can be seen more clearly than light in our own stones—to say that the **Herculean stone** <note>original: "lapis Herculeus," another name for Magnetite</note> always directs iron toward the north, since there is a significant part in every piece that directs iron to the south no less than that well-known part directs it to the north. Thus, it seems men were late to notice its full powers. Neither do these parts point exactly <note>original: "ad unguem," literally "to the fingernail," meaning with perfect precision.</note> to the north or south, but each points to a place five degrees distant from the poles of the heavens.

<margin>Why in sundials the line of the compass and the meridian are not the same.</margin>
Because of this, in **Sundials** <note>original: "Horologijs"</note> the line upon which the iron needle must rest in the **compass box** <note>original: "pyxide"</note> is not the same as the meridian line where the shadows indicate the hours. For the line of the compass, if the dial is perfect, turns a little to the east from the meridian line; there is no other cause for this than the orientation of the stone. The stone receives its power from that direction because it looks toward the rising of the star in the tail of the **Little Bear** <note>The constellation Ursa Minor; the star is likely Polaris.</note>, which is five degrees further east than the pole of the world. By the same logic, the part of the Magnet that faces south acquires its power not from southern stars, but from that same tail of the Bear or its rising. Thus, it happens that this stone appears to have contrary powers. It is no wonder, then, that the suspicion of **Theamedes** <note>A legendary stone mentioned by Pliny the Elder that was said to repel iron, acting as the opposite of a magnet.</note> arose—that it repels iron while being a Magnet. The matter, however, is as follows: one part of the Magnet drives the iron toward the north, the other toward the south, as has been said. But if the part that is directed toward the south by the iron...

<header>Book Seven</header>

If iron that seeks the northern part <note>original: "partem borealem"</note> is applied to that same side of the stone, an innate enmity drives it away with greater force than the iron tending toward the south is attracted. And conversely, the part of the Magnet which looks toward the north, when applied to iron at the point where it touched the Magnet tending toward the south, repels it. Similar iron, tending toward the same part, is drawn to it; iron that lacks the Magnet’s influence is drawn only moderately. The cause of this is clearer than light itself: for unlike things are repelled, while like things are attracted. Therefore, iron is no longer driven away by any Herculean stone <note>A traditional name for the Magnet or lodestone, referencing its "strong" power.</note>, but acts as a participant in a contrary quality, or because the tip of the other side was touched by a similar Magnet, whence while one side is attracted, the rest is put to flight. Therefore, if both tips of the iron are touched by the northern part, both will be repelled by the southern part, as if the stone were pushing the whole piece of iron away.

There are those who affirm that there is a part in this stone which drives iron toward the east, and another which drives it toward the west, concerning which I can offer nothing certain. Truly, by the same logic that iron is either attracted or driven by a Magnet, by that same logic another piece of iron is attracted or driven by iron to which a Magnet has been joined by contact. I say that if the tip of a piece of iron is smeared with the southern part of the Magnet, it will drive away another tip (if the iron is fixed) which, being placed in equilibrium, has touched the northern part of the Magnet. And by the same reasoning, fragments of a Magnet are attracted by a Magnet when the Magnet or its fragments have absorbed the strength of the iron. Thus, it is not the Magnet that attracts the Magnet, but the iron adhering secretly to the Magnet.

<margin>A statue which is seen to be moved anywhere.</margin>
Added to these many remarkable gifts is the fact that a Magnet placed under a table very swiftly rotates iron placed in equilibrium on top of the table, even though the table is in between—not without some slight wonder from those standing by. For this reason, a wooden basin full of water is placed upon a table, and in it is located a little boat, joined together by very thin boards without iron but with glue only. In the prow is a beautiful little female figure, bent over and driving the boat with a branch <note>Likely acting as an oar.</note>, so that by the motion of that little boat the oar is moved, and with it the image of the woman. Under the woman's rear foot is a small nail with a wide head—the wider part of which is called a "cap"—which projects from the board and is fixed so that it is hidden under the prow, yet does not touch the water. Finally, a fragment of the best Magnet is inserted into the head of a wooden rod made of fir or horn, by which the stone itself is moved around under the table. Thus, with the Magnet placed underneath, the ship will be led by the motion of the stone in whatever direction you wish by means of the head of the nail. To those who cannot see the rod, that image will seem as if animated, turning and leading the ship wherever you wish, appearing exactly like someone listening and rowing. Therefore, it is not the matter itself that passes through [the table], but something similar to a spirit <note>The author is struggling to explain magnetic fields; he notes that physical bodies cannot pass through the solid table, but the magnetic force (the "spirit") can.</note>, for the table would otherwise hinder the motion, since bodies cannot penetrate one another.

<margin>A flesh-colored Magnet.</margin>
After the iron-colored Magnet comes the white and "flesh-drawing" <note>original: "creagus," from the Greek for flesh-hook.</note> Magnet, so called as if it were attracting flesh. The test for it is that it sticks to smooth lips. It is marked with certain veins and is rare; however, it is still found today, as nature has wished to hide nothing from us...

# Of Stones
<note>original: "De Lapidibus"</note>

...nature is hidden. Perhaps the dry is drawn by the moist, and it sticks to the lips, for no other reason than that by which straws are accustomed to stick to amber.

<margin>Another "fleshy" Magnet of wondrous power.</margin>
Another Magnet seems not unlike this one, of which I saw the following experiment. Laurentius Guascus of Cherasco <note>A town in the Piedmont region of Italy.</note>, an empirical doctor <note>An "empiricus" was a medical practitioner who relied on practical experience and observation rather than formal academic theory.</note> of the province of Tours, brought this stone in these days. He promised that if it touched either a stylus or a needle, it could penetrate the whole flesh without any pain. Since this seemed ridiculous to us, as is only natural, he confirmed the matter by experiment upon my companions. Finally, so that I might make a trial of such an incredible thing myself, I inserted the needle—having first been rubbed against the stone—into the skin of my upper arm. At first, I felt the very lightest sensation of a prick; afterwards, as it penetrated right through the whole muscle, I felt the needle indeed penetrating into the depths through which it traveled, but I felt absolutely no pain. Then I believed my associates regarding what I had experienced in myself. 

Indeed, I left it there for a long time, bending my arm in every direction, and I felt nothing troublesome; nor when it was drawn out did any blood flow out, nor was any hole left behind. Occasionally a half-drop of light serum <note>original: "cruoris" — often used to distinguish clotted or gore-like blood from flowing "sanguis".</note>, but not flowing blood, comes out, by which the trace of the wound is detected. Nor did the man who was the author of this matter require that the locations of nerves or veins be observed, so that we might clearly understand that the power resided in the stone. 

The stone was smaller than a small bean, white—or rather the color of boxwood than white—distinguished by rusty veins, very smooth and light, so that its whole weight fulfilled thirteen grains of wheat <note>A traditional unit of weight based on the mass of a single grain of wheat.</note>. Truly the needle itself, which I had offered to him to be rubbed, although it was as hard as before, nevertheless appeared so smooth and light that it no longer seemed to retain the nature of iron. Therefore, when I considered this, three thoughts occurred to me: 

First, that the needle did not actually enter, but by a deceptive substitution he had offered another one which retracted into itself—a trick not difficult to perform. But this was blocked by the fact that we felt the needle penetrating deep within, and when it was extracted, great effort was needed. 

Second, that since there is fat under the skin, between the skin and the fleshy membrane, if the needle were introduced between the membrane and the skin through that very fat, the entry would thus be without pain. But indeed, one could support this reasoning by the fact that he had bent the needle slightly at the tip, either while rubbing it on the stone or while forcing it into the muscle.

However, this reasoning is hardly satisfying for many reasons: First, because we perceived by sensation that it had penetrated all the way to the bone. Second, because the tip which protruded outside the flesh formed almost a right angle, such that mathematical logic would not allow it—if the whole needle remained straight except at the tip, and even there only slightly bent—to have a position almost equidistant to the skin itself. Added to this is the fact that the needle shone through under the skin near the hole and took the form of a black line. But if it had adhered entirely to the skin, that black line would have been almost equal to the length of the needle.

# Book Seven

<margin>How flesh and skin may be pierced without pain, and the cause of this.</margin>
Finally, it should be added that such a curvature <note>likely referring to the bending of the arm during the experiment mentioned on the previous page</note> could hardly have penetrated without damaging the skin or the fleshy membrane, especially since he <note>Laurentius Guascus, the doctor mentioned previously</note> entrusted this operation to whomever he pleased. Therefore, I turned to a third invention, which boys are accustomed to use: namely, when they pierce the skin of the arm with a needle after gripping it with their fingers without pain; and the fleshy lobe <note>original: "prominentiam"</note> of the ear after first rubbing it with their fingers. Through this very rubbing, four advantages seem to be gained for relieving pain: the thinning <note>original: "raritas"</note> of the part through which the needle passes without pain; the warmth, which does not allow the pain to be felt—for which reason all warm things are "acopa" <term>acopa: remedies or topical applications that relieve weariness or pain</term>; and because the pain which is stirred up by rubbing relieves the pain of the puncture. For it is written: **Of two pains which occur in the same part, the greater obscures the lesser.** <note>A famous medical aphorism from Hippocrates.</note> But this happens not only then, but also that a lesser pain obscures a greater when they are not of the same kind. Finally, from that part which feels more and contains a nerve, the spirit <term>spiritus: in Renaissance medicine, the vital force or "breath" believed to transmit sensation through the nerves</term> is excluded by rubbing, and thus that part can lose its sense of feeling. 

However, in the previous experiment, the skin itself was not rubbed; rather, it retained a tiny bit of the sensation of pain, and the needle did not stick in the surface, but passed through the muscle. Why then must the reasoning be led elsewhere? Experiment teaches that a needle smeared with tallow <note>original: "sepo"</note> excites no pain or very little when penetrating. Or perhaps there was a more oily power in that stone, or one so cold that it prevented all sensation and the flow of blood? Or is this entirely peculiar to this stone, just as it is to the "iron-stone" <note>the loadstone or magnet</note>, that iron—as I have said—is directed toward those parts which are near the poles? Or perhaps there is a place for an incantation? <note>The author wonders if the effect is magical or psychological rather than purely physical.</note>

This has been discussed, just as the causes of the Herculean stone <note>original: "lapidis Herculei" — a common name for the Magnet</note> were, by which iron directs iron to the north or to the south. One may leave some doubts for posterity. Now let the discourse return to the "iron-like" Magnet. It is found in Spain and also the island of Elba <note>original: "Ilua"</note>, which lies between Corsica <note>original: "Cyrnum"</note> and Italy, and in many other regions. But I have cited those closer to home so that those who think iron is directed by the very regions where it originates might be proven clearly wrong. For the regions where this stone originates do not face those shores towards which iron smeared with Magnet turns; nor is there only one region that produces it. It is also a substance similar to iron in both material and weight, so that it might be called "male," so to speak. Furthermore, in things endowed with sense, the male is moved toward the female, for he is drawn by sense; in things lacking sense, the female is drawn by the male. For this reason, then, iron is drawn and seized by the Magnet. Yet, as I said, they are moved mutually, one toward the other. But why is no other metal drawn by any other stone? Because no metal is as cold as iron—nor perhaps can it ever be—so that other metals might be drawn by other stones.

<margin>The Sarcophagus.</margin>
Certain stones are celebrated for their powers: the **Sarcophagus**, the **Calamochus**, **Alcyonium**, **Pumice**, **Emery**, and **Tripoli**. The **Sarcophagus** <term>Sarcophagus: literally "flesh-eater"; a type of limestone from Assos in Troas used for coffins because it was believed to consume the body</term> is, as it were, "flesh-eating"; it is light, white, somewhat ash-colored, and brittle, on the top surface of which rests a certain light powder like flour.

# On Stones.

it resides, but at the bottom and inside it appears like yellow veins. From this stone the ancients used to make coffins <note>original: "sepulchra"</note>, because within forty days the bodies themselves, except for the teeth, would be consumed.

<margin>A caustic treatment without pain.</margin>
By the same reasoning, indeed, quicklime <term>quicklime: calcium oxide, a caustic alkaline substance produced by heating limestone</term> cast into vaulted crypts with water poured over it is accustomed to eat away corpses if they are buried therein; and likewise by *cadmia* <term>cadmia: a mineral containing zinc oxide, often found as a residue in furnace chimneys</term> mixed with earth. For everything that is thin, dry, and capable of burning consumes excessively, taking away not only the flesh of the dead but also the bones—and not only of the dead, but also of the living. From this comes a caustic treatment <term>escharoticum: a substance used to produce a scab or "eschar" to heal or remove tissue</term> without pain, which easily breaks through the skin within twenty-four hours. If the skin is healthy, the substance is applied alone, bound in leather; but if there is corrupted matter <note>original: "sanies," referring to thin, blood-stained pus</note>, as occurs in abscesses, the area is washed with the sharpest vinegar. The medicine consists of soft soap and quicklime mixed very finely, so that it passes into the form of a soft ointment.

<margin>For the pains of gout sufferers.</margin>
Therefore, by the same reasoning, the Sarcophagus stone <note>The "stone of Assos," literally meaning "flesh-eater."</note> is beneficial, if anything is, for the pains of gout sufferers by thinning the humors. But also true vinegar, the sharper it is, the more it deprives one of sense and pain; for these things draw out what is inside, thinning and dissolving it, and therefore they dry it out vigorously.

<margin>Calamochus.</margin>
*Calamochus* <note>original: "Calamochus harundinũ spuma"</note> is the foam of reeds; the Arabs call it *Adarce*. it grows in damp and marshy places around reeds and dry brushwood. In dry conditions it has a somewhat salty taste, and its powers are not unlike those of the Sarcophagus stone. The color of the stone of Assos <note>original: "Asij lapidis"</note>, full of holes, is very hot and sharp.

<margin>Halcyonium.</margin>
Similar to this in power and almost in form is what is called *Halcyonium*, that is, "sea foam" <note>Halcyonium: a substance formerly thought to be the nest of the halcyon bird, but actually a type of sea-growth or sponge</note>; it is abundant and in common use.

<margin>Pumice.</margin>
It is established that Pumice is a type of softer stone, burned by sulfurous fire and carried through the air. It is said to prevent must <note>unfermented grape juice</note> from boiling over, and if taken beforehand, it is said to prevent drunkenness—though not without a heavy price <note>likely referring to its harsh effect on the stomach</note>.

<margin>Emery.</margin>
Emery <note>original: "Smiris"</note> is from the class of shell-bearing stones <term>Ostracophoros: stones that appear to contain shells or are associated with marine fossils</term>. Used with a bronze wheel, it wears down most gems and cleans the teeth by rubbing. In ancient times, they used to engrave gems with porous stone and fragments of Obsidian. If Emery is not a porous stone, it must have been unknown to the ancients. Emery consists of fine and dense parts and a solid substance. <margin>Tripoli.</margin> Tripoli, however, is a saffron-colored stone—or rather a clod or earth—softer than Emery, which they use to polish gems.

<margin>Tartar.</margin>
Tartar is also made from the dregs of wine, which has no equal in cleansing; for this reason, it purges foul spots and those born in hard places, as well as fleshy excrescences, and reveals the living flesh.

<margin>Gypsum.</margin>
Gypsum is a white, tenacious, and light earth, suitable for molding works and for bonding ulcers. Its "flower" is called Talc by many. <margin>Talc.</margin> There are those who wish the stone Talc to be different from *lapis specularis* <term>lapis specularis: transparent stone such as mica or selenite used for windows before glass became common</term>. Whatever Talc may be, it is similar to glass, scaly and transparent, and almost like a mirror. A weight of Talc equal to a hazelnut, when drunk, is wonderfully beneficial for difficulties of the intestines.

From the same genus, there seems to be a crusty stone, black in color, with golden di- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely "diverse" or "distinguished."</note>

<header>Book Seven</header>

# Book Seven

...distinguishable by its veins, from which tablets are made that are brought from Nuremberg. There are notable stones of innumerable forms. The cause of this variety is the same as that which will be said of herbs and trees <note>The author is suggesting that stones "grow" in the earth via similar formative forces that govern plants</note>.

<margin>Trochites. Entrochos.</margin>
<term>Trochites: a fossilized crinoid segment</term> is striated on a flat surface; in the middle of that plane is a point from which the grooves spread, but that plane is surrounded by a smooth, drum-like edge. Placed in vinegar, it moves spontaneously no differently than the <term>Astroites: "star-stone," often fossil coral</term>. <term>Entrochos: a column of several trochites</term> is indeed composed of many Trochites: and its power is the same as the parts from which it consists.

<margin>Pentacrinos. Encrinos. Belenites.</margin>
<term>Pentacrinos: a star-shaped crinoid fossil</term> resembles five lilies and is a striated stone. <term>Encrinos: a composite lily-stone</term> consists of several Pentacrini; it is a red stone growing upon a black one. Likewise, the <term>Belenites: "arrow-stone" or belemnite</term> is in the shape of an arrow, having a slit inside along its length, and it contains another stone which is joined to it by a golden armor <note>original: "aurea armatura"; likely referring to pyritization, where iron pyrite replaces organic material, giving it a metallic gold appearance</note>. Since some of these attract straws <note>likely referring to static electricity or confusing them with amber</note>, it was wrongly believed they were <term>Lyncurios: mythical "lynx stones" believed to be formed from lynx urine</term>, since they are born in places where lynxes are far away.

<margin>Conchites. Ostracis. Onychites. Ctenites. Strombites.</margin>
<term>Conchites: shell-stone</term> has the likeness of a shell with curved ridges and is decorated with golden armor. <term>Ostracis: oyster-stone</term> indeed resembles oysters and is dug out like <term>specularis: mirror-stone or mica</term>. Likewise <term>Onychites: claw-stone</term> is not unlike the shape of "fragrant nails" <note>original: "odoratis unguibus"; likely referring to the opercula of certain sea snails used in ancient perfumes</note>. And <term>Ctenites: comb-stone</term> is striated in the likeness of a comb. <term>Strombites: snail-stone</term> is indeed spiraled in the form of a snail shell, tending toward a sharp point.

<margin>Porphyroides. Myites. Rhombites.</margin>
<term>Porphyroides: purple-like stone</term> is of an ash-grey color, swarming with purple prickles like the studs on armor. <term>Myites: mussel-stone</term> is like a mussel, with thinner ends and swelling in the middle. But <term>Rhombites: diamond or flatfish stone</term> is of two kinds: one consists of scales having the likeness of a *Rhombus* <note>original: "Rhombi"; refers to the turbot, a flat, diamond-shaped fish</note>, from which it took its name, and this one is white; the other has the shape of a compressed cylinder, but is striated above and below so that they resemble the figure of a rhombus.

<margin>Pentagonus. Exagonus.</margin>
<term>Pentagonus: five-sided stone</term> and <term>Exagonus: six-sided stone</term> have a margin and a flat surface in the middle like a dice-box <note>original: "fritillus"</note>, in which there is a point from which rays are carried out to the edges as in the trochites. The territory of Hildesheim in Saxony provides all of these; and <term>Valerius Cordus</term> <note>A famous German physician and botanist (1515–1544)</note>, a man most knowledgeable in herbs, brought them to <term>Georgius Agricola</term> <note>The "father of mineralogy" and author of De Re Metallica</note>. Cordus was living in Rome out of a zeal for learning various things, but since he was a German, an untimely death took him, to the grief of all learned and good men.
<margin>Valerius Cordus, most skilled in herbs.</margin>

<margin>Glossopetra. Selenites. Hysterapetra, a wondrous stone.</margin>
This same man also brought other stones of singular and wonderful form: such as <term>Glossopetra: "tongue-stone"</term> <note>fossil shark teeth</note> similar to the tongue of a woodpecker, found in the aluminous mines of Lüneburg; and <term>Selenites: moon-stone</term> in the shape of the moon regrowing its horns; this is covered now with golden, now with silver, or even diamond-like armor, and is found in Marburg. Just as in the territory of Trier is the <term>Hysterapetra: womb-stone</term> <note>internal molds of certain brachiopods that resemble human anatomy</note>, which represents the form of the female genitals; and this is a black and very hard stone. And near Saalfeld in Thuringia, in a pit twenty fathoms <note>original: "orgijs"; a measurement of about 6 feet</note> deep, a stone was excavated which perfectly represented the form of an entire human chest with the distinctions of the ribs; yet it was a little narrower than a human chest.

## On Stones.

<margin>Armor-stone.</margin>
<margin>Hawk-stone.</margin>

...strap-like, scaly, from which a gold-colored sand is made, suitable for drying the ink on letters <note>This refers to "pounce" or blotting sand used before the invention of blotting paper</note>: I have found through experience that if it is kept in a fire for an entire day, it yields a more abundant, better, and more beautiful supply of sand. So too the **Armor-stone** <note>original: "Armaturam"</note>; this stone is also scaly, but of a silvery color, suitable for the same use, or at least for others. The **Hawk-stone** <note>original: "Hieracites"</note> also mimics the feathers of a hawk or partridge with its streaks and color. And the **Fire-glow stone** <note>original: "Pyraustus"</note>, which is reddish in color, distinguished by a golden armor, hollow and shining: from which, no differently than a concave mirror, it ignites a fire when exposed to the Sun; in the region of Hildesheim, this was also discovered by that man.

<margin>Alabandine stone.</margin>
<margin>If stones were not alive, gems could be made by artifice.</margin>
Furthermore, regarding the **Alabandine stone** <note>A type of dark red garnet or silicate</note>, it is enough to know that it reflects various painted figures. We have spoken also of **Onyx**, and of the stones found in the territory of **Verona**, for even in marble, the figure of a king's head with a diadem has sometimes been seen: and these things, as I said, happen sometimes by chance and sometimes due to the nature of the stone. We also spoke of crust-like stones that resist fire, and of **Flint** <note>original: "Silice"</note>, which even resists water but is melted by fire, and how the peaks of mountains crumble into fragments of stone due to winds and cold. And that it is necessary for a soul to be within stones has been demonstrated abundantly above. And would that life did not dwell in stones! For then nothing would prevent a great gem from being procreated from the powder of many **Emeralds** buried under the earth with the addition of a clear fluid.

We can understand from what has been said that stones grow in two ways: either that material is constantly added through veins and the stone is nourished no differently than a human; or that which exists potentially—as in the generation of a chick from an egg—becomes such in actuality, for in the succession of days the whole chick is completed. The parts, however, take their beginning in the matter at the same time as almost their entire magnitude, so that what was first white becomes red, then grows together into nerves, bones, membranes, and such. Nor do stones deserve to be called earthy simply because they sink in water; for any part of earth, however small, is enough to cause a descent in a congealed liquid. However, all transparent stones are of a watery substance, or congealed by cold, which is why they are dissolved by fire. **Flint**, however, is not transparent because it is earthy; yet it is dissolved because it congealed through cold. But opaque stones, such as most are, and those which turn into lime, neither congealed entirely by cold nor are they of a watery substance—or if they did congeal by cold, since they seem to be cold, they contain much earth but little water. It is manifest, therefore, that **Crystal**, because it is a transparent stone and melts easily, consists of a pure watery substance congealed by cold.

But if the surface **A B** is placed over a foil <note>original: "ungui"; refers to the "foil back" setting where a thin sheet of metal is placed behind a stone to enhance its color</note>, the color will not be seen in the angles, but will be paler; for the powerful rays in a true gem are refracted from the flat surface of the foil.

<margin>The counterfeiting of pearls.</margin>
There is also another apothecary’s trade <term>seplasia<gloss>Originally a street in Capua famous for perfumes; here used to mean the trade of preparing artificial or luxury goods</gloss></term> of no small profit, when very beautiful pearls <term>uniones<gloss>Large, singular pearls of high quality, so named because each is unique or "one of a kind"</gloss></term> are fashioned from pearl-shells. Indeed, this fraud succeeds so well that they are not even distinguished by jewelers: the color, luster, substance, and weight correspond. There are those who even fashion pearls from two pieces joined together because of the thinness of the shell.

While I was writing these things, a lawsuit was underway concerning a pearl bought from a jeweler for sixty-eight gold pieces, which had been made from a shell, though its estimated value was two hundred gold pieces. They hoped to deceive the Germans or the French, because they believe them to be less capable in wit and art. For they consider these people barbarians. Yet, we are more truly the barbarians, if indeed it is more barbarian to deceive than to be deceived. But enough has been dealt with regarding metallic matters <note>In the Renaissance, "metallic matters" often included all mined substances, including gemstones</note>; now, however, let us

# BOOK EIGHT
## On Plants.

<margin>The hatred and friendship of plants.</margin>
**P**LANTS are nobler than metals, and in them a certain image of sensation shines forth. For I think it is clear enough that plants both hate and love, and possess members suitable for their functions. For they say the olive tree and the vine hate cabbage; the cucumber flees the olive tree, and the vine loves the elm. So the Myrtle, planted near the pomegranate <note>original: "punicam malum"</note>, makes it more fruitful, while becoming more fragrant itself; both thrive and flourish in a marvelous way. Yet there is one general cause why certain plants are harmful to others nearby: for since they flourish by the heat of the Sun and the moisture of the earth, it is necessary that every shady tree be harmful to others, as well as those with many-branched roots. For by a many-branched root, the vital moisture is drained away, which ought to nourish a neighboring and weaker plant. Truly, both the plants and the soil are cooled by shade, so that the trees or herbs lying beneath the shade seem to waste away because of it. Thus the walnut is harmful for both faults: for when planted, it has thick foliage and a complex root; and the fig likewise has very large ones. I noticed while writing these things that wheat growing next to a hedge in a field was low, dry, sparse, and not at all bushy. Even though the hedge was low and thin, and did not block the rising or setting sun for long, or entirely. Therefore, these are general matters; others, as we said, are specific.

<margin>The kinds of plants.</margin>
There are four kinds of plants: trees, shrubs, undershrubs, and herbs. A tree is that whose trunk grows green again and reaches an extraordinary size, like the pear tree <note>original: "pirus"</note>. A shrub <term>frutex<gloss>A woody plant smaller than a tree, usually with several stems</gloss></term> is that whose trunk remains, but does not grow to a full size, like the rose and the myrtle. An undershrub <term>suffrutex<gloss>A plant that is woody at the base but has herbaceous stems</gloss></term> is one which also has a persistent trunk, but does not exceed the size of herbs, such as butcher’s broom <note>original: "bruscus"</note>. An herb is that which lacks a woody stem, like the <term>aizoum<gloss>from the Greek "aeizoon", meaning "always living"</gloss></term>—that is, the houseleek <note>original: "semperuiua"</note>—and sage, or it changes its stem every year, like fennel. A fifth kind can also be added, halfway between an herb and a shrub, such as rue <note>original: "rutha"</note>; for this sometimes becomes tree-like, and sometimes remains an herb. <margin>Differences among plants.</margin> Moreover, the differences among all plants are almost without number; nor is it our purpose to treat them at length, as we did with metals. For we have intended to touch only upon more obscure things, not those which are plain to the eyes; for this reason, the history of plants and animals will be very brief. Some plants, then, are cultivated <note>original: "urbanae"; literally "of the city," here meaning domestic or garden plants</note>, others are wild, some are in the sea, others in rivers, others on the bank, some in marshes, others among rocks, others in ordinary soil, and some, though rare, are born among the sands. There are also...

<header>Book Eight</header>

## Book Eight

...those which grow in wells like lichen, those in groves, and those in sunny spots. And again, some are fruit-bearing, others sterile; some lack a root, others lack leaves; some have branches, while others have flowers. There are also those that are sweet-smelling, those that are foul-smelling, and those with no scent at all. Likewise, there are those that are evergreen and those that lose their leaves; some are sparse, while others are dense like the cypress; some are spreading like the lotus tree <note>The "lotos" here likely refers to the Mediterranean nettle tree (Celtis australis), not the water lily</note> and the beech. There are tall plants and low ones, those without knots and those full of knots like the reed. Some are solid, such as "holy Indian wood" <note>original: "Indicum sanctum"; likely referring to Guaiacum, known for its extreme density</note>; some are entirely hollow like the reed-stalk, and some are intermediate like the elder.

<margin>Ways in which plants originate.</margin>
Some plants have a main trunk, others a stalk, others a shoot, and some have only leaves. There are those that grow spontaneously, those that are sown, and those that grow from grafting or buried cuttings, such as the willow and the vine; or even from the seed of another plant. Many are incomplete in form, such as mushrooms, truffles, and the maidenhair fern <note>original: "politricus"</note>. Some cling to others like ivy, some grow upon others like mistletoe, some creep like ground-ivy <note>original: "camecissos"</note>, and others grow upon the earth, like moss and lichen. However, moss also clings to trees and grows in water. There are healthy plants, harmless ones, and lethal ones, such as the yew, the nut tree, and the fig, whose shade is harmful. In some, one can see a distinction of sex, as in the oak, the hard-oak, and the holm-oak; in others, not at all, such as olives and vines. Some have a certain unique substance of their own, like the palm. Some have fruits clinging to the branches, some in a pod, some enclosed in another covering like chestnuts, and some attached by a little stalk like cherries. Some are found only in certain regions, while others are found everywhere.

<margin>Bramble and fern indicate a harsh winter.</margin>
For the bramble and the fern only grow in a cold climate and where winter is fierce—I speak of the bramble that bears blackberries—therefore they are evidence of a cold province, just as wheat indicates a temperate one, and those things that are intensely fragrant, which the Greeks call <term>aromatics <note>original: "aromata"</note></term>, indicate a hot one.

<margin>Why aromatics are found only in the hottest regions.</margin>
For seeds of an intensely hot nature cannot grow to maturity in cold air, since they are of an extremely refined <note>original: "tenuissimæ"; referring to the "thin" or "subtle" quality of the plant's essence</note> substance. Nor can nature, without the help of the air, sufficiently "cook" <note>The author uses the Aristotelian concept of "concoction," where heat matures and refines biological matter</note>, dry, and refine the substance of fruits; yet it can achieve this in the roots.

<margin>Parts of plants.</margin>
Furthermore, the parts of plants are the root, trunk, branches, leaves, fruit, stalks, umbels, berries, seeds, flowers, down, wood, bark, fiber <note>original: "neruus"</note>, membrane, vein, matrix or pith, humor, "tears" <note>Resins or gums secreted by the plant</note>, knots, and many other things; for these and other reasons, trees and herbs differ from one another.

<margin>The reason for thinness in trees. * From "On the Causes of Plants," book 11.</margin>
Therefore, trees are thinner <note>Meaning more refined or less dense in their vital spirit</note>: first, those that are surrounded by perpetual foliage, as they are hotter and drier, according to the testimony of Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note>, such as the palm, olive, cedar, and myrtle. However, this reasoning does not hold for herbs, since the houseleek <note>original: "semperuiuuum"</note> is of a thicker substance and yet retains its leaves in winter. In both groups, however, the wild versions are thinner than the domestic ones, and the fragrant ones are thinner than those that smell foul or have no scent at all. Similarly, those that grow in the mountains are thinner, which is why all of these are preferred by physicians.

<margin>Why roots are frequently fragrant.</margin>
But why are roots more frequently fragrant than other parts, except for flowers? As seen in the *fanamunda* <note>likely the Wood Avens (Geum urbanum), known for its clove-scented root</note>. The reason is that a better "concoction" is perfected in the roots.

<header>On Plants.</header>

# On Plants.

<margin>Why almost all flowers smell sweet.</margin>
They smell sweet, however, as many as have a well-refined <term>moisture</term> <note>original: "humidum"; in the science of the time, this referred to the internal fluids or "humors" of a living thing</note>; for such a substance is at once very thin and very dense. For this reason, almost all flowers smell sweet, because the moisture contained in them is very thin and quite scant, and thus it is very easily <term>refined</term> <note>original: "concoquitur"; literally "cooked" or "digested" by internal heat, a process thought to produce fragrance and ripeness</note>. But just as it is easily refined, so for the same reason it perishes more easily; it remains in roots and trunks as in the *aspalathus*—which we call **Sandalwood**—for that refined substance of the moisture adheres firmly to the earthy substance.

<margin>The breath of children and youths can smell sweet, but not that of the elderly or the immoderate.</margin>
Thus, it is believed—not without reason—that the breath of certain children and even young men can sometimes smell sweet, whereas it is wrongly expected of the elderly or the immoderate. In children, the moisture is thin, and in young men, it is moderate and can be perfectly refined by great internal heat. In the elderly, a lack of heat stands in the way, and in the immoderate, the poor quality of their moisture prevents a perfect refinement from being completed.

<margin>That Alexander's breath smelled sweet.</margin>
For that reason, some report that **Alexander [the Great]** once had sweet breath, because his body was drier and his heat most intense. For the same reason, his corpse was preserved for many days amidst the highest heat without a foul odor; although I would not deny that it may have been preserved by art, or by the power of the very poison by which he is also believed to have been killed.

<margin>Parts of plants and animals are similar to each other.</margin>
But to return to the parts of plants, each corresponds to animals and their parts. **Roots** correspond to the <term>mouth</term> <note>The author disagrees with Theophrastus here, who compared roots to the belly</note>, although we liken them to the mouth rather than the belly, as **Theophrastus** thinks; the lowest part of the stem and trunk corresponds to the **belly**; **leaves** to hair; **bark** to the hide and skin; **wood** to bones; **veins** to veins; and the **fibers** of trees and herbs to those truly found in animals. In some, the **pith** <note>original: "matrix"</note> is like the internal organs of animals, for they cannot live without it; in others, however, such as the willow—whose life resides in the bark—the bark, not the pith, serves this role; indeed, in willows, the pith should be considered in place of fat. **Eggs** are like flowers, **seed** like animal seed, the **extremities** of animals like branches, and the **fruit** itself reflects the menstrual blood, in which the seed is usually enclosed.

<margin>Which plants are fragrant in their entirety.</margin>
Nor should it be believed that fragrant plants always produce scentless flowers: for some smell in every part, such as the **sea-lavender** <note>original: "limunium"</note>, the **orange** <note>original: "citrangulum"</note>, **nard**, and the **median apple** <note>the citron</note>, in which the leaves, flowers, and fruit especially smell best, nor are the remaining parts devoid of scent.

<margin>Which plants are most fragrant.</margin>
The most fragrant of plants, as far as I know (for a new day can always bring new discoveries), are **Aloeswood** <note>original: "Agallochum seu Xiloaloes"</note>, **Cinnamon**, **Aspalathus**, **Nard**, <margin>Trees are generally of a more refined substance than herbs.</margin> **Asafoetida** <note>original: "Laser"</note>, and **Saffron**. **Pepper** and **Ginger**, although they are very hot, nevertheless have little scent. Trees are of a more refined substance than herbs, but also denser, for the length of time aids the power of the Sun, whereby refined things are rendered thinner and denser; for trees live a long time, while herbs perish quickly. Even those herbs that smell sweet cannot retain their scent for long except in their roots due to their thinness; and those that do retain it, like nard, ought to be classified as shrubs rather than herbs.

<margin>Siliquastrum.</margin>
However, the **Siliquastrum** (also called **pepperwort** or **Indian pepper**) is of extraordinary thinness. It is an herb with a long, reddish stalk, frequent joints, leaves like the laurel, white flowers, a single whitish root fibrous with small hairs, and large, long, red pods...

...just like purple, with no small brilliance, such that they suggest something venomous, with a soft yellow seed inside, so sharp that it far exceeds pepper; wherefore it must consist of the highest degree of heat and dryness as well as thinness. It is even sharper while the pod is immature, as is the rind of the pod itself; although it has come into use, having been added to our world from the island of **Hispaniola** <note>Hispaniola is the island today divided into Haiti and the Dominican Republic; this is a very early reference to New World chili peppers</note> in the other world in the year **1494**, it is not entirely free of poison. <margin>Which plants are poisonous?</margin> For plants often retain poison, either by nature or by accident, but nature is the more powerful force in these. Those which have a very heavy odor or a taste that cannot be endured are ruinous by their very nature, such as we said of this <term>siliquastrum</term> <note>original: "siliquastro"; here referring to the pepper plant, named for its pod-like shape</note>. The same is true of those which do not emit green sap, like all types of <term>spurges</term> <note>original: "Tithymalorum"; a genus of plants known for their milky, irritating sap</note>; but even the fig tree sends out a biting milk, as does lettuce when it has become excessively cold due to old age. There are also those that are brilliant, like all species of small branches, and especially **Aconite** <note>original: "Aconitũ"; also known as wolfsbane or monkshood, a highly toxic flower</note>, which is most deadly, for that brilliance arises from immoderate dryness. But plants are born poisonous by accident when they grow in metal mines, or near the chambers of serpents, or those that have grown up near bronze or iron covered in rust, or in marshes, stagnant pools, sewers, and tombs. Fungi near olive trees are also suspect. All species of **nightshade** <note>original: "solani"</note> smell bad and heavy. <margin>The thorny apple.</margin> I do not know whether I should count <term>stramonia</term> <note>original: "stramoniam"; Datura stramonium, or Jimson weed</note> or the **thorny apple** among the varieties of nightshade; certainly the leaves smell like the juice of the black poppy, but the fruits themselves, if eaten cooked, excite a present insanity and a kind of ridiculousness. It is a herb with a many-branched, rusty-colored root, a stalk the width of a finger and even much thicker, somewhat round; the leaf is large, darkish on the underside, and a yellowish green on the side facing the home; it is oblong, soft, and thin, almost like a vine. The white flowers come out of sheaths like a basket, smelling sweetly of lilies. But there is no more certain sign than the fruits, which equal <term>quinces</term> <note>original: "chrysomila"; literally "golden apples," usually referring to quinces or apricots</note> in size and shape, though they are green and thorny; inside they are filled with rusty-colored seeds the size of <term>vetch</term> <note>original: "erui"; a type of legume or pulse</note>.

<margin>Laser from which Benzoin comes.</margin> <margin>3. On the deeds of Alexander.</margin> But leaving these behind, let us return to the fragrant plants, and those which are for use rather than for loss. Therefore, first, there is such delight in **Laser** <note>original: "Laseri"; a resinous sap, historically confused with Silphium or Asafoetida</note> and its flowers that, according to the testimony of **Arrian** <note>Arrian of Nicomedia, a Greek historian who wrote the "Anabasis of Alexander"</note>, the inhabitants are forced to keep their cattle away lest they burst <note>i.e., from overeating the delicious plant</note>. Anyone might easily believe this who considers how pleasant the scent of its juice is. When hardened among us, it is also cheap in price due to its abundance, and it is called **Benzoin** <note>original: "Belzoi"; a fragrant resin used in perfumes and incense</note>. We have explained its history in our little book on the evil use of medicine, as well as its utility. It grows on Mount **Paropanisus** <note>The Hindu Kush mountains</note>, although the Macedonians boasted that they had seen it in the Caucasus. It is most fragrant and far more excellent—according to the report of **Ludovico Varthomano** <note>Ludovico di Varthema, an Italian traveler whose 1510 book described the East Indies</note>—that which is found on the island of **Sumatra** in India, so much so that it seems to be of an entirely different kind; but it is not brought to us because it is held at no small price even there. It has a stalk like giant fennel, leaves like celery, a broad, almost leafy seed, and a black root. <margin>Agarwood.</margin> They say by a nearly similar distinction that there is a wood called **Aloe** <note>original: "Aloen"; here referring to Xylaloes or Agarwood, not the succulent aloe vera</note>, far more fragrant than this of ours which is brought to us...

## On Plants.

<margin>Which woods sink in water.</margin>
...but for the same reason, it is not transported to us at all. The form of this tree has not yet been described: this much is certain, which we learned from **Desiderius Erasmus** <note>The famous Dutch humanist scholar (1466–1536), who apparently shared botanical observations with the author</note>, that it sinks in water, which we have experienced quite often; and although **Ebony** and **Boxwood**, and the **Indian wood** <note>original: "Indicum lignum"; likely Guaiacum, a dense wood from the Americas used to treat "the French pox" or syphilis</note> which cures the French pox, sink in water, this is nonetheless less surprising regarding them since they are very heavy. However, **Agalloch** <note>original: "Agallochum"; also known as aloeswood or oud, prized for its fragrance</note> is extremely light, yet it sinks immediately in water. The reason is that it contains no empty space in which air might be trapped. For woods float on water for no other reason than that they contain air within themselves due to their porousness. Because of this, oak floats, while agalloch, though much lighter than oak, sinks.

<margin>Why woods remain prone to the surface of the water and not upright.</margin>
But why do woods in water not remain standing upright <term>perpendicularly</term> <note>at a 90-degree angle to the surface</note>, but lie prone and parallel to the surface of the water, even when they are dropped from high places and descend through the air with one end first and straight? The reason is that it usually falls from one end, whereby in the air, because of the shortness of time and the momentum, it cannot turn itself; but in water, since it descends slowly due to the water's thickness, the other end of the wood also seeks the bottom, whence in the water the whole piece of wood remains in equilibrium. By this reasoning ships are secured: an anchor <term>A B C</term> tied to the ship by a rope <term>f</term> is cast into the sea, so that its bottom <term>B</term> touches the seabed; then, when pulled, so that the fixed crossbeam <term>D E</term> does not lie upright and perpendicular to the water's surface from the bottom—for <term>D E</term> lies perpendicular to the surface <term>A C</term>, so that if it were at <term>B</term> it would form a cross with the hooks. Therefore, since <term>A C</term> lies perpendicular to the surface of <term>D E</term>, and <term>D E</term> is parallel to the seabed, it will be (from the converse of the fourteenth proposition of the eleventh book of the <term>Elements</term> <note>referring to Euclid's "Elements," the standard textbook of geometry</note>) that <term>A C</term> necessarily lies perpendicular to the seabed, wherefore one of the hooks, either <term>A</term> or <term>C</term>, will be fixed into the bottom due to the weight of the sea, and the ship will be held. Therefore, if the crossbeam <term>D E</term> were not present, by the proposed reasoning <term>A C</term> would always fall parallel to the seabed, whereby it could never be fixed, nor hold the ship. For that reason anchors are also made with four hooks set in a cross, but they are trusted less safely than those which have two hooks with a transverse beam, because even if they hold, they are far weaker.

<margin>Cinnamon.</margin>
But I return to the history of plants. **Cinnamon** is not unlike the laurel tree: the leaves are like its leaves, the trunk like its trunk, and the berries like its berries, except that the berries of Cinnamon are smaller and whitish. From which one may conjecture that they are the same tree, distinguished only by region. For the heat of India is best able to ripen the moisture of the bark, which Europe cannot; moreover, Cinnamon is the <term>liber</term> <note>the inner bark or phloem of the plant</note> stripped from the shoots, for they do not harm the trunk lest the tree perish; once dried—for within a month's space—that sweetness of scent is perfected after it has been debarked. There are those who say the Cinnamon tree is like the pomegranate tree: it is full of shoots, delighting in dryness. <margin>Nutmeg</margin> **Nutmeg** indeed grows on the island of **Banda** <note>original: "Bandan"; the Banda Islands in modern-day Indonesia were the only source of nutmeg in the world at this time</note> as Cinnamon does on another island named **Ceylon** <note>original: "Zailon"; modern-day Sri Lanka</note>; both are of India. Furthermore, the tree is entirely similar to the peach tree in its trunk, branches, and leaf, except that the tree...

# Book Eight

The tree is larger, and the leaves are a little narrower. The **nutmegs** <note>original: "Myristicæ nuces"</note> themselves are surrounded by a certain flower, as if by a husk, and then by another layer, just like walnuts.
<margin>Mace.</margin>
Furthermore, the inner husk, which is even thinner and webbed <term>reticulated</term> <note>having a net-like pattern</note> beneath the nut-covering, is usually called **Mace** <note>original: "Macer"</note>; it has a pleasant scent and is in frequent use among us, for it is an astringent and does not heat the body excessively.

<margin>Cloves.</margin>
Next to **Banda** is the island of **Monoc**, which produces **Cloves** <note>original: "Gariophylum"</note>. The tree has a trunk like boxwood, with leaves a little rounder than those of a laurel. It grows among rocks or in red earth, and the trees are so dense that they form a grove. From the tips of the small branches, the clove grows—what they call the **"great nail"** <note>original: "maius quod uocant clauum"; the English word "clove" comes from the Latin "clavus," meaning nail, due to the spice's shape</note>. First, however, there is a flower on it very similar to the blossoms of the **bitter orange** <note>original: "citranguli"</note>. The tip of the clove fruit sits on the stalk, but the wider part stands out from the plant. It is red at first, then soon turns black. These three islands and the **Maluku Islands** <note>original: "Moluchiæ"</note>, which are under the equator or not far from it, produce these. They also produce **Ginger**, which grows everywhere there and elsewhere, delighting in red earth.

<margin>Ginger.</margin>
It is a herb having multiple and very large roots like a lily, so much so that some weigh twelve ounces; one is left behind for propagation. The stalk equals a medium-sized pear-tree <note>original: "pirum"; likely referring to the height of a young sapling</note>, the leaves are like grass, and it creeps along the ground like grass.

<margin>Pepper.</margin>
But **pepper** is not unlike ivy—a low shrub that cannot stand by itself but clings to other trees. It puts out many branches two or three palms in length. From each node hang six clusters no larger than a palm, not unlike the grapes from which raisins are usually made, but with more frequent and crowded grains. These they harvest while still green in the months of October and November, and by exposing them to the sun for three days, they turn them black. Moreover, the leaf of the tree is almost like a **plantain** leaf, which clings to the shoot with a very short stem. But where the leaf joins the stem it is round, while at the very tip it is pointed, much like the leaves of the **citron** <note>original: "medica mala"</note> which end in a point. On the back of the leaf there are seven veins as in plantain, but those from the sides do not originate from the one in the middle; rather, they stretch at intervals from the bottom to the top of the leaf, hedging the middle, arranged as if obliquely, neither evenly nor with that thickness found in the citron leaf. It is well established that just as we taught that the cinnamon tree is a species of laurel, so pepper is a type of ivy, perfected and cultivated by the climate of the region—for it grows in **Calicut** <note>original: "Calechuto"</note> in India, and even in the suburban fields. The proof of what we have said is that if this tree is transported to us, within a few generations it will turn back into ivy.

I will not overlook the fact that I know this contradicts **Dioscorides** <note>The ancient Greek physician (c. 40–90 AD) whose "De Materia Medica" was the primary botanical authority for centuries</note>; but the ancients wrote what they heard, being bold in their desire for glory and with a certain security that their errors would never be discovered because of the distance of the regions. But from the clove fruit, a certain flower among us took its name due to the sweetness of its scent <note>The author is referring to the "Gariophylus flos," or the Clove-pink/Carnation, which smells like the spice</note>. One is white, another red...
