# On Plants.

...reddish, another mixed from two colors, a low-growing herb with leaves like a leek but narrower; it is cultivated in pots with the greatest care, and is no less pleasant in appearance than in scent. <note>The text here likely describes a pink or carnation, often grown in pots during the Renaissance for their fragrance.</note>

<margin>Frankincense.</margin>
There is also the **Frankincense** <note>original: "Thuris"</note> plant, whose "tears" <term>resin</term> are used to incense temples, because it produces a most pleasant odor while burning. This is a small **fir tree** <note>original: "abies... pusilla"</note> which, among the **Sabaeans** <note>People of the Kingdom of Saba, or Sheba, in modern-day Yemen, famous in antiquity for the spice trade.</note>, releases this tear due to the dryness of the climate. Whence the **Mantuan poet** <note>The Roman poet Virgil, born near Mantua.</note> wrote:
> *The soft Sabaeans send their own frankincense.*

<margin>The fir is the only tree that grows straight of its own accord.</margin>
The resin that flows spontaneously is stronger, while that from a wounded tree is weaker—a fact worthy of observation in all liquid resins. But among us, the **fir tree** has a unique honor: it rises more straightly than any other tree. For this reason, it is preferred over all other woods in **sculpting models** <note>original: "plastices proplasmatis"</note> and in all manner of carpentry; for what you could hardly achieve through art in other woods—and even then not safely—nature provides perfectly in the trunk of this tree.

<margin>Libanotis.</margin>
But I return to the history of **frankincense** <note>original: "thuris"</note>. Just as the **Savin** is close to the **Cypress**, so **Libanotis** <note>Likely Rosemary (*Rosmarinus officinalis*), often called "frankincense-herb" in early botany.</note> is very close to the **Fir**. Since the **strawberry tree** <note>original: "arbutus"</note> is of the tree kind, I have seen a herb—or rather a shrub—similar to Libanotis in the Apennine Mountains; indeed, it was of that genus but with narrower leaves and a sharp flavor. It so closely resembles the smell and taste of frankincense that there is no doubt that frankincense flows from a plant of the same kind. Therefore, the frankincense tree, the fir, and Libanotis are of the same genus, but they differ by the quality of their regions and their natural strength. In the fertility of the soil of Arabia, frankincense comes forth from the plant; in a colder climate, the fir grows into a tree and emits a less potent but more abundant tear. Libanotis, which resembles frankincense in name, is drier than the fir and does not grow into a tree; being colder than frankincense, it is unable to emit a tear. However, one may infer their medicinal powers and transfer their uses from these observations, and marvel at the works of nature in them, for almost the same principle applies to all kinds of trees and herbs.

<margin>Why scented Sandalwood is mostly "hot."</margin>
Among the scents is also included the wood of **Aspalathus** <note>A fragrant, thorny shrub, sometimes associated with rosewood.</note>, which is sweet; it is sharp and **cooling** <term>refrigerant</term>, not unlike the rose or the **bilberry** <note>original: "vacinia"; likely the blueberry or bilberry, which were considered "cold" in the Galenic medical system.</note>, and for that reason, it is among the rare things. The reason is that a pleasant scent is rarely "cold" <note>In ancient and Renaissance medicine, scents were usually considered "hot" because they were thought to be composed of subtle, airy particles.</note>, because scent is perfected by heat; therefore, it is necessary for heat to prevail. Because of this, most scented things, which the Greeks call **aromatics**, are "hot." In **Sandalwood** and bilberries—which we call blue violets—the "heat" is only in the thinner part, while all the rest is "cold," being thick and greater in mass. But in these, the coldness is not hidden as it is in roses; for while roses may provoke a headache in some by their scent, in others they even draw blood from the nostrils. But Aspalathus is a tree, which in India is the tall **Sandalwood**, but in a colder climate, it is the thorny **strawberry tree**.

<margin>Differences in trees based on region.</margin>
For in hot and humid regions, everything is taller, juicier, and more vigorous, unless the specific nature of the plant prevents it—so much so that even groves of Aspalathus are found in the West Indies. But in hot and dry regions, the plants are smaller and drier, yet strong; in humid and cold regions, they are weak...

# Book Eight

...full of sap; but those which are hot by nature are tall and large, while the cold ones are small. Although some plants are cold by nature, such as **hemlock** <note>original: "cicuta"</note>, they grow better in damp and shaded places, where their powers become even more effective. For the people of **Chios** <note>An island in the Aegean Sea.</note> used to choose such plants—

<margin>Death without pain.</margin>
according to the testimony of **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the successor to Aristotle, often called the "Father of Botany."</note>, they would strip away the bark, mix the sap with water, and give it to condemned prisoners to drink so they might meet death without any pain. Indeed, they were imitating the death that occurs in extreme old age. For the pain felt in death happens either because of a difficulty in breathing or because of the breaking down of the vital spirit. But when the spirits dissolve of their own accord, they bring no pain, just as happens during exhaustion from labor. However, the cause that dissolves the spirit—such as a fever or a wound—usually brings the pain itself. Therefore, the juice of the hemlock, by inducing a heavy sleep, extinguishes the spirits themselves through its excessive coldness without pain. It causes no greater difficulty in breathing than what is required to satisfy the few remaining spirits. Thus it happens that death is not bitter, unlike those who are suffocated by water, and much less so than those who are strangled. Therefore, this death prepared from hemlock juice—and that which comes from the bite of a specific kind of viper, which **Plutarch** <note>A Greek-Roman historian and biographer.</note> mentions in his *Life of Mark Antony*—occurs with a heavy sleep and is very similar to the death that happens in the final stages of old age, which is why it is also without pain. Thus, it is no wonder if the Chians and the Athenians killed distinguished men whom they had condemned to death with hemlock juice, so that the loss of their life and dignity might be compensated by the gentleness of their passing.

<margin>Apples of death.</margin>
There are also **apples of death** <note>Likely the Manchineel tree (*Hippomane mancinella*), one of the most poisonous trees in the world, found in the Caribbean and tropical Americas.</note> recently discovered in the province of Peru in the West Indies; they are like sorb-apples and are fragrant, which is surprising. The tree itself is shrub-like with dense, frequent, and greener leaves like those of a pear tree; nor is it a wonder

<margin>Early-ripening fruits in Persia endowed with poison.</margin>
that in such a variety of regions this plant turns out so destructive. For **peaches** <note>original: "præcoqua," referring to *Malum persicum* or early-ripening fruit.</note> in Persia, where they first arose and from which they took their name, were destructive there, yet when they were transplanted and brought here to Italy, they became harmless and even pleasing in scent and taste. Whence **Martial** <note>A Roman poet famous for his *Epigrams*.</note> says in his *Apophoreta*:

> *Once cheap were the early-ripening fruits on their native branches;*
> *Now as grafted Persians we are held dear.*
> <note>original: "Vilia quæ fuerant natiuis præcoqua ramis: / Nunc in adoptiuis Persica cara sumus."</note>

Many things grow mild when transplanted, while others even turn out worse. Thus, while the "apple of death" bears a fatal juice—with which arrows are smeared to bring death instantly and without any hope of help—the tree also provides a shade that causes the entire face and eyelids to swell and hide the eyes. If the dew falling from the tree drops into an eye, it produces blindness by eating away the cornea. When the wood is burned, it triggers a headache and a most foul odor; all this occurs because a thin and moderate moisture, well-cooked and fragrant, is mixed with much that is thick and destructive. In our region, sorb-apples are rendered unpleasant only in taste, because the destructive matter of the moisture cannot be putrefied by the heat of the surrounding air.

<margin>Hallucinogenic plants.</margin>
Next to poisons are the **hallucinogenic plants** <term>lymphaticæ plantæ</term> <note>Plants that cause "lymphatic" or "frenzied" states, often used for ritual intoxication.</note>, such as **Cohobba** <note>A hallucinogenic snuff used by the Taíno people of the Caribbean, derived from the seeds of the *Anadenanthera* tree.</note> on the island of Hispaniola in the West Indies, which intoxicates by its scent alone and [makes people] phanati...

...makes them [intoxicated], this herb is, I believe, of the genus of stramonium <note>original: "estrimoniæ"; likely Jimsonweed or Thorn-apple, known for causing hallucinations</note>: which, if drunk, turns one to madness. It is in no way dissimilar in its powers to that which the Turks call *Asseral* <note>original: "Asseral," likely referring to *esrar*, a Turkish term for preparations of cannabis or opium</note>, the use of which is very common among them; for it not only makes them joyful and lively, but also drives away all care and fear, so that they are more ready for the duties of war. Saffron <note>original: "crocus"</note> is of this kind among us: for like *Asseral*, if it is eaten too abundantly, it no longer makes one just lively, but intoxicated, and if taken in even greater amounts, it kills. Such things are wine, and the "burning water" <note>original: "aqua ardens"; distilled spirits or alcohol</note> and dregs made from wine, and—as it is said—the *oenopia* root, which long ago took its name from a certain resemblance to wine.

<margin>**Spikenard. Why leaves fall from trees.**</margin>
But to return to fragrant things: Lilies, Spikenard, and Saffron are of that kind. Every Spikenard is a small shrub with leaves longer than rosemary, narrower, somewhat thick, softer, and fragrant; the flower is very small, between blue and purple. The trunk and branches are woody, and it stays green in winter; though if the winter becomes too severe, it dies. The cause for all plants losing their leaves is cold itself; for this reason, in cold regions, when the branches and trunk are covered with straw, the roots with horse manure, and the whole tree is placed in a <term>hypocaust<gloss>a room heated from below by a furnace, common in Roman and Renaissance buildings</gloss></term>, it is no wonder that not only are their leaves kept from falling, but the trees even produce fruit. Even in our lands, leaves are preserved naturally on hotter and drier plants, as I mentioned: Spikenard, Rosemary, Sage, Juniper, Laurel, and Cypress. As for the Box tree <note>original: "Busso," likely *Buxus*</note>, it stays green solely due to its intense dryness and moderate heat, for it is bitter. But in India, because it is a very hot region, no tree loses its leaves except for the pod-bearing tree we call Cassia. It is agreed that this tree is cold and damp by nature for three reasons: it exhausts moisture copiously, its root is far removed from the sun's heat, and it is cooled by the chill of the water it touches.

<margin>**Saffron.**</margin>
But to return to fragrant things: Saffron has a bulbous root, abundant and long-lived; the leaves are like leeks, but so narrow they could be called hair-like. The stem is spotted; the flowers are the color of wine, similar to meadow saffron <note>original: "colchicis"</note>, in the center of which the flame-colored stamens of the saffron rise. Balsam was also once highly valued, but now it is not found; it is established that it was a shrub
<margin>**Jasmine.**</margin>
not very different from our Jasmine. Furthermore, the flower of Jasmine is pure white and fragrant. The tree creeps like ivy and clings to another; it is more like a garden vine, since it sends out nothing of its own to cling with—it does not climb walls or trees on its own like ivy, but must be tied and guided. With a leaf that is green, soft, thin, and darkish, almost like an olive; the flower grows in clusters <note>original: "umbellis"</note>. It is certainly worthy of wonder that this plant has no fruit, or none that is useful, as is also the case with
<margin>**Why no noble fruits follow fragrant flowers.**</margin>
other more noble flowers: not the lily, nor saffron, the rose, hyacinths, or the clove-pink <note>original: "gariophylo"</note>. They believe the cause is that the entire vital power is consumed in the flower; or, since the seasons for flowers and fruits are different, and fruits consist of a moist and thick substance to be excellent, while flowers are hot and dry, it is very difficult to find a tree with such a diverse temperament that it can satisfy both in their own times.

# Book Eight

So it is rare that a famous son follows an excellent father, or that a graceful old age follows a youth noble beyond its years; Philostratus <note>Flavius Philostratus, a 3rd-century Greek scholar who wrote 'Lives of the Sophists'</note> even observed this in the case of Hermogenes of Tarsus <note>original: "Hermogene Tharſenſi"; a famous 2nd-century orator who allegedly lost his memory and talent in his early twenties, living a long but unproductive life thereafter</note>.

<margin>Powers of Balsam.</margin>
<margin>Indian Balsam and its powers.</margin>
<margin>Codrus the physician.</margin>
Therefore, to return to the matter at hand, some in our age think that Balsam <note>original: "Balſamum"; specifically referring to the rare and highly prized 'Balm of Gilead' used in antiquity</note> has perished. That juice was of a golden color; it healed wounds, removed wrinkles, and protected the faces of the dead from corruption [decay]; it also ground down stones of the kidneys, wiped away spots from the eyes, and resisted poisons—especially aconite <note>original: "aconito"; a highly toxic flowering plant known as monkshood or wolfsbane</note>—and even the chills of fevers. In all these things, the powers of Balsam were excellent. But now, another kind of Balsam is brought from Hispaniola <note>original: "Hiſpaniola"; the Caribbean island comprising modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic</note>, red in color tending toward black, heavy, and smelling of something burnt. It immediately strikes the head, and it stings the tongue more sharply but later, like pepper. It heals fresh wounds very quickly—as fast as any other remedy—and removes wrinkles. I would believe that this kind of oil is effective, if not for everything, then at least for most things for which true Balsam is used. The Italian physician Codrus is said to have discovered it; he was so eager to seek out new things that, although he was very wealthy, he nevertheless died an old man in the southern part of the New World near the Port of Pumida and the islands of Zorobari <note>likely referring to the Bastimentos or Chiriquí islands in modern Panama, which Columbus called 'Zorobaro'</note>.

<margin>Three ways how scented oils are made.</margin>
<margin>How the oil of Nutmeg or smooth Myrica is made.</margin>
Therefore, to return to the history, the tree which produces that oil is the Goacomax <note>likely *Guaiacum officinale*, the 'Lignum Vitae' tree, famous for its medicinal resin</note>, which is almost similar to the pomegranate in form and size: but yet with a leaf a little larger and thinner, the bark as if dry, wood which burns like a torch, and fruit like clusters of grapes, though with sparser and slightly larger berries of a wine-like color. These, when boiled for a long time in water with the twigs, yield that kind of oil. In this way, oil reflecting the scent and powers of the plant is easily expressed in those things which contain oil in abundance. But in those things where oil is not abundant, we are accustomed to extract the scent and powers into oil in three ways. The more common and older method of Dioscorides <note>Pedanius Dioscorides, a 1st-century Greek physician whose 'De Materia Medica' was the standard botanical manual for centuries</note> is this: flowers were infused in pure oil for four days and exposed to the Sun; then, after the oil was very carefully pressed out, an equal amount of fresh flowers was added, and again exposed under the burning Sun. It was permitted to do this as many times as necessary until the oil drank up the scent; thickeners <note>original: "ſpiſſamenta"</note> were also added for ointments, such as from honey and other fragrant things. The second method consists of expression; in some cases without the help of art, as in the Myrobalan <term>Myrobalan: a dried fruit resembling a plum, used in tanning and traditional medicine</term>, and in others which are dry and naturally fragrant, such as the smooth Nutmeg or Myrica <note>original: "Myrica nuce leui"</note>. Divide them into small pieces, and having infused them in Cretan wine for three days, dry them in the shade for two days; thereafter, heat them moderately in a pan, and meanwhile sprinkle them with rose water, and express them under a press. In this way, one may extract oil from aromatics. But for those things which are fragrant but lack an oily substance, like flowers, they yield it by this example: sprinkle flowers over almonds, and arrange alternating layers of flowers and almond leaves <note>referring to the flesh of the almond used to absorb volatile oils</note>; keep them compressed for as long as it takes for the scent of the flowers to vanish. When these are discarded, substitute other flowers for them in the same way, and repeat this as many times as needed, for there is not just one method for all, [I will show/teach]...

...and once the almonds have contracted the greatest scent, then submit them to the press. However, it is necessary first to strip them of their skin and roast them a little. In this way, the oil gains more strength and becomes less liable to spoilage, because no moisture remains in it.

But the third method is not suitable for flowers, but for woods and things similar to them, such as **Cloves** <note>original: "Gariophylis"</note>. They are placed crushed in a glass vessel **A**, and distilled with as gentle a fire as possible. If it is permitted, it will be much better to extract the oil by placing the vessel in boiling water <note>This refers to a 'bain-marie' or water bath, which provides a steady, indirect heat to prevent burning the delicate oils.</note>. A glass cap **B** is placed on the top of the vessel and sealed with clay <note>original: "luto"; a paste used by early chemists to make apparatus joints airtight</note> so it does not "breathe" [leak]. To this, a tube **c** is attached in the usual way, to which another tube **D** is joined, so sealed with clay that nothing can escape. This tube passes through a wooden vessel **E**, which must be kept filled with very cold water. Through a small pipe **H**, you draw off whatever water has already become warm, adding fresh water recently drawn; for **D** is thus cooled, and the vapors are not burnt but pass into water or oil. Turned through the slanted part of the tube **F**, which extends beyond the vessel full of water, they fall drop by drop into vessel **G**. As I have seen, at first a certain cloudy liquid flows out, carrying the thinner substance of the matter; afterwards clearer water comes out, and finally the oil, which carries the smell of something burnt rather than the scent of the thing from which it flowed.

<margin>Scented waters.</margin>
The distillation of waters is done in the same way, but it retains the scent far better if you use this art, for fragrant rose water turns out wonderfully. Take an earthenware vessel **A**; stretch a thin linen cloth **B** over it, and sprinkle roses or bilberries <note>original: "uacinia"; likely referring to whortleberries or a similar dark berry used for color or scent</note>, or other flowers or herbs upon it. Then have a pan **C** that covers the vessel, and place fire upon the bottom **D** <note>This describes "distillation by descent" or a specific arrangement where the heat is applied from above</note>. Thus is distilled not only the most fragrant but also the most effective water. Rose water is usually placed sealed in the Sun so that it may be deprived of the "smoky" smell while still retaining the scent of the rose. Water is also made quickly when a glass cup is placed under heated or boiling juice, in which the vapor turns into drops; the drops collected there are gathered into water. In this way, vinegar is easily turned into "water" [distilled vinegar], which is useful for clearing spots and cataracts <note>original: "suffusiones"</note> of the eyes, especially if rue <note>original: "rutha"; a bitter medicinal herb</note> is boiled in white vinegar. And there are those who, in the first method, place musk and other more precious perfumes near **F**; the water then retains not only its own scents, but also those of the musk and other things that are added.

# Book Eight

<margin>
Why in distillation not all odors are retained.
</margin>
But why is the scent of certain flowers not retained in the distilled waters? Why, for instance, does the water from **Jasmine**, the **Carnation** <note>original: "Gariophylo flore"; specifically the Clove Pink, known for its spicy, clove-like scent</note>, and the **Lily** turn out devoid of fragrance? It has been said elsewhere that this is because no thicker part is joined to such a delicate substance. Therefore, in these cases, it will help if the fragrance is joined to a thicker material—one that will not burn—by placing it alternately with the leaves of plants that lack a scent of their own, and then distilling it. This is the only hope for drawing out the scent, since when these flowers are infused in water, they do not release their aroma but instead rot. Furthermore, if the fire is not applied moderately, it burns away
<margin>
Water from oats that intoxicates.
</margin>
those things which are of an earthy nature. If, however, the fire is moderate, it merely sharpens the substance. This is why the **Muscovites** <note>The people of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, often used as a general term for Russians in this period.</note> use water distilled from **oats** because they lack wine; it warms and intoxicates no less than wine does. For since oats are of a thicker substance, it is necessary that through distillation they become heated, thinned, and sharpened, approaching the nature of **"burning water"** <note>original: "aquæ ardentis"; an early term for high-proof distilled spirits or alcohol</note>. Hemp leaves turned into a powder
<margin>
The powers of hemp leaf flour.
</margin>
strike the head and produce a pleasantly intoxicating drink. But it is also a marvel what they report even among the **Tartars** <note>A general term for the nomadic peoples of the North and Central Asian steppes.</note>: that water distilled from **milk** can intoxicate.
<margin>
Water obtained by the distillation of milk can intoxicate.
</margin>
It must be, then, that the milk was quite thick and spent a long time over the fire. Thus, this perhaps occurs with the milk of horses. Furthermore, what more is there to doubt? Any water, when it is distilled many times, can achieve this effect; for it becomes heated, thinned, and receives more of the power of the fire. This is why "burning water," when distilled repeatedly, is brought to such a point of sharpness that it cannot be drunk. It is clear, therefore, from these facts, both that wine has a fiery power, and that from almost any thing—especially dense things—a drink can be made through repeated distillation which will warm and intoxicate more than wine.

<margin>
Mead, an intoxicating drink.
</margin>
Truly, even without distillation, drinks are made that intoxicate: such as **Mead** <note>original: "Medo"</note> among the Muscovites, which consists of honey and hop seeds, and is kept in pitch-covered vessels. Yet almost none of these ingredients alone would be enough to cause intoxication. **Hop** seeds with barley, rye, or wheat make *Zethum* or *Zithum* <note>Ancient names for beer or ale.</note>, which 
<margin>
The method of preparing Zethum.
</margin>
is called **Beer** <note>original: "Birra"</note> among the Germans. The method is this, as **Nicolaus Poll** <note>A famous physician to the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I.</note>, the Emperor’s physician, left in writing: soak the barley in water until it bursts; then it is dried, ground finely, or rather submitted to the mill. Take two parts of this and seven parts of water; they are boiled together until the water is reduced by a third. Then they take half of that water, to which they add a 40th part of hop seeds and as much barley as before. These are all boiled for about three or four hours. Then they mix the remaining half of the strained water with the first portion and boil it again until it is reduced to half. Finally, having poured it into a wooden vessel, they distribute it after adding a little yeast.

<margin>
Zethum made from rice.
</margin>
Indeed, just as those who inhabit the North by necessity make *Zethum* from barley, rye, and wheat, so those in the South—since they are not permitted to use wine due to religious laws—prepare *Zethum* from **rice** according to their superstitious law. All these drinks intoxicate, but the one made from rice is milder—not because rice is colder than barley, but because that kind of *Zethum* lacks hops, for hops are considerably hot and dry.

<header>On Plants.</header>

# On Plants.

<margin>Ancient oxymel</margin>
Ancient **oxymel** <note>A medicinal syrup made from honey and vinegar, highly regarded in classical medicine.</note> would be healthier than any **beer** <note>original: "zetho"; derived from the Greek *zythos*, a type of fermented barley drink.</note>, and even slightly more expensive. For since it consists of thirty pounds of honey, twenty-five of vinegar, nineteen of water, and three of salt—and there are those who would increase the water or add **savory** <note>original: "thymbram"; summer savory, an aromatic herb often used in cooking and medicine.</note>—let all these boil together ten times, then be strained and aged in a vessel. Although it admits so much water for the sake of sweetness, it is made nearly as cheap as beer, yet far healthier.

<margin>Mignol drink.</margin>
There are also other pleasant and intoxicating drinks, such as **Mignol** among the **Senega** <note>The people or region of the Senegal River in West Africa.</note>, which extends slightly south beyond the Fortunate Isles <note>The Canary Islands.</note>. This juice has the substance and color of whey, except that it verges more toward gray, <margin>The coconut, a type of palm.</margin> not unlike the *faucia* tree. Another drink is drawn from the **coconut** (which is a type of palm) that is more excellent than the former. This tree grows abundantly in the province of **Chiman** on the **Sureni** coast <note>Likely referring to regions described in early Spanish or Portuguese voyages to the Americas or the East Indies.</note>; it is as tall as a palm with palm-like leaves, and its fruit is larger than a human head. From the outer surface to the middle, it is covered with membranes and oakum <note>Fibers used for caulking ships.</note>; from the thicker part they weave ropes, and from the thinner part, clothes. Near the middle is a shell like that of a walnut, beneath which is a thin and white marrow <note>The coconut meat.</note>, similar in taste, substance, and nature to fresh almonds. Furthermore, when this fresh marrow is ground, it emits a milk no less sweet than the milk of animals. In the very middle of this marrow, a juice is contained that can be compared to no other drink for its sweetness. Moreover, from the shell that surrounds the marrow—since it is shining, black, and hard—cups are made for a most pleasing use.

<margin>Ten uses of the palm.</margin>
But since we have happened upon the mention of palms, and because no tree provides so many uses, it will be timely to report on it. India produces this tree, which they prune in the month of August; meanwhile, a white "tear" <note>sap</note> flows out, just as usually happens from pruned vines, which for three whole days resembles wine. But if you boil this down to a third of its volume, it becomes a most sweet honey. If it is neither boiled nor drunk, it turns into vinegar. Conversely, if the honey itself is purified with water, it turns into wine within twenty days. They express oil from the kernels of the fruit; from the inner bark of the tree they make ropes; from the wood, charcoal; and the fruits themselves are eaten in place of walnuts or almonds. Charcoal is also made from the outer shell, while from the innermost fibers, clothes are spun that are more delicate even than cotton and almost equal to silk. The leaves are used in place of tiles for covering houses, so that this tree—the coconut—may be fully utilized. Thus, while all types of palms have many uses, <margin>The form of the palm.</margin> the coconut is the most excellent. It is a palm with very long, prickly green leaves, curved because of their length; the bark is soft and entirely uneven due to very large, overlapping scales, not unlike the back of a fish covered in scales. I saw such a tree in the Temple of Peace in **Genoa**, <margin>Four differences in transplanted trees.</margin> though it was not fruit-bearing. For among trees that are transplanted, some do not live at all, such as **Aloe wood** <note>original: "lignu Aloes"; agarwood, prized for its scent, not the succulent aloe plant.</note> from India when brought to Italy. Others live but do not produce fruit, such as the palms at Genoa. Others produce fruit, but it is blighted or stunted, such as **pepper** in our lands; and some yield perfect fruit because they are tolerant of both climates, such as vines.

# Book Eight

<margin>Palm hearts which are eaten.</margin>
These were transplanted from Spain to the **Indies** <note>The author likely refers to the West Indies (the Americas), as evidenced by the mention of "Hispaniola" later in the text.</note>. The highest part of the palm trunk, where the leaves join the stem, is soft; when cut away, it is not only eaten but even considered a delicacy. Its flavor is somewhat bland but slightly bitter. The entire wood has a fleshy substance, but only in this specific part is it so soft that it can be eaten, especially in very young trees. A palm remains "young" for a long time, because the person who strikes a palm tree rarely sees its fruit, so late does it bear. The **palm heart** <note>original: "Palmites"; referring to the edible inner bud of certain palm species.</note> provides the same taste; it has the same fleshy, white, and solid substance. However, only its lowest part, which joins the root, is eaten; the shoots that resemble palm leaves are also white, but they are woody and not fit for food. The flavor is the same as the top of the palm trunk, and therefore it is usually eaten with salt, pepper, and oil. Yet the "palm heart" shrub differs greatly from the palm tree; for while the palm is a tall tree bearing **dates** <note>original: "dactilos".</note>, the "palm heart" shrub produces clusters like grapes, though it is similar to the palm in other respects.

<margin>Why hepatic aloe has thick leaves.</margin>
Furthermore, just as the "palm hearts" have dry shoots, other herbs have very thick, fleshy leaves, such as **Aloe** and **Houseleek** <note>original: "Semperuiuum"; literally "always living," a name for succulents like Sempervivum tectorum.</note>, and an Indian tree with very large leaves. This tree is not as fleshy as Aloe but is thorny, which is remarkable, though the thorns on its back are small. Therefore, just as fleshy plants contain much moisture, so do prickly vegetables—such as all kinds of **thistles**—provoke urine, because a "fiery moisture" must necessarily abound in them <note>In the medical theory of the time, plants with "fiery" qualities were thought to stimulate the kidneys.</note>. There are many types of thistles, but we shall teach the principal ones further below.

But why does Aloe have such thick leaves when it is so very bitter? It is very similar to Houseleek, but blackish and about a **cubit** <note>Roughly 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> in size, as I have often seen. The reason is that since it is also prickly at the edges of the leaves, there must be an abundance of heat and dryness in such a copious moisture to be able to produce thorns. For this reason, since the thorns are small compared to the size of the leaves, the moisture within must be "burnt," making the juice extremely bitter.

<margin>Description of the Holy Wood.</margin>
But I return to rare trees, foremost among which is the one called **Holy Wood** <note>original: "lignum sanctum"; also known as **Guaiacum**, a dense wood used in the Renaissance as a primary treatment for syphilis.</note>, which is brought from the islands of the West Indies, from whence the **disease** <note>Refers to syphilis, which was widely believed at the time to have been brought back from the Americas by Columbus's crew.</note> also crept in. And although we have published eight books on the nature of that disease, I have proposed to describe the form of the tree here. It grows in **Hispaniola** <note>The island comprising modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic.</note> and the surrounding islands of the New World. It is slightly smaller than a walnut tree, with spotted bark that alternates between green and ash-gray. The leaf is smaller and greener than that of the strawberry tree or the hazel. The flower is white, the fruit is saffron-colored, and its shape and size are like two **lupins** joined together. The tree is so common that groves of them are seen everywhere, just as oak forests are seen among us.

<margin>Method of extracting the "tear" from any wood.</margin>
From this wood—and indeed from any other wood—we extract a **tear** <note>original: "lachrymam"; a term for the gummy resin or sap that "weeps" from a tree.</note>, which is more precious than the wood itself, in this manner: the wood is cut into pieces the thickness of a finger and exposed to fire; then, whatever "tear" is in the wood is collected.

<margin>Why Cassia fistula does not grow in our regions.</margin>
There is also a fruit which they call **Cassia fistula** <note>The "Golden Shower" tree, prized for the laxative properties of its pod pulp.</note> in those regions; it is a smooth, rusty or black pod the size of a thumb, and sometimes longer than a cubit,

## On Plants.

...slanted, with a very sweet but unpleasant juice, and small seeds similar to <term>lupins</term><note>A type of legume; here used to describe the shape of the seeds.</note> but far harder. It is a tall tree with leaves almost like a nut tree but narrower and thinner. The flower is saffron-colored and, like <term>gorse</term><note>original: "genistae"; a yellow-flowering shrub.</note>, it cannot endure the cold. It does not grow in our regions because the harshness of the climate prevents it from the start, and as it grows, it lacks moisture, for in our lands the groundwater lies much deeper.

<margin>Which shadows are healthy and which are deadly.</margin>
The powers of trees, even from their shadows, are remarkable. For as we have said, some are deadly: such as the <term>Yew</term><note>original: "Toxico"; often referring to the poisonous Taxus baccata.</note>, the **Walnut**, **Spurge**, the mature **Fig**, and the **Indian Service-tree**. Others are healthy, such as the **Lotus**, the **Beech**, and the Indian **Hobio** <note>Likely the Jobo tree (*Spondias mombin*), common in the Caribbean and South America.</note>. To these, some are useful because of their scent, such as the **Rose**, **Myrtle**, **Spikenard**, the **Citron** <note>original: "Malo medico"; the 'Median Apple' or Citron, prized for its scent and medicinal properties.</note>, and **Juniper**, just as the **Boxwood** is considered harmful. Among these, the most celebrated for its variety of colors is **Brazilwood**; others call it *Verzinum*. The province of **Brazil** is named after the forests that consist of this timber. The tree is not large, similar to the <term>Holm Oak</term><note>original: "enzinae".</note> but thinner and more crooked; the leaf is like an oak's but not as rough. The bark falls off the tree on its own due to its strength or, rather, its dryness.

<margin>The Holm Oak tree.</margin>
Since we mentioned it is like the *enzina*: the **Holm Oak** is a type of oak in **Spain**, smaller and not so straight, whose acorns are eaten because of their sweetness.

<margin>A description of red ink.</margin>
With age, **Brazilwood** becomes better and turns more red, which distinguishes it from counterfeit versions; it is light, slightly sweet, and has an astringent taste. It has an excellent power for dyeing and for writing, and this red ink is prepared in many ways. Some put its sawdust into a powerful and still boiling <term>lye</term><note>A liquid made from wood ashes used for cleaning or as a chemical base.</note>; an eighth part of the wood scraped with glass is sufficient. With a small amount of **alum** added among hot ashes, it is boiled for an hour and immediately put to use; <term>gum arabic</term><note>original: "lachryma Arabica"; literally "Arabic tears," the hardened sap of the acacia tree used as a binder.</note> is not required. I have also been accustomed to prepare it another way: I cut the wood, drawn into very thin threads, into small pieces, which I put into ten times their weight of water. Leaving it to soak for at least six hours, the water is then boiled with the wood until three out of four parts have evaporated. This produces a red, splendid color; if you boil it a little more, it becomes blood-red; if even longer, it becomes blue. However, in neither way can it be kept for long unless it is used immediately. For it is characteristic of all colors derived from plant parts to change over time and not to be entirely pure, because the substance of plants is weak and full of moisture. This is why the **Indians** extract all colors from the same plant by boiling it for a longer or shorter time. A more reliable and vibrant red color is made from <term>cinnabar</term><note>A bright red mineral consisting of mercury sulfide.</note>; it is dissolved in water already infused with gum arabic, or in egg white brought to the appearance of water by long stirring. But even this has its fault, for if you mix in too much liquid, the cinnabar settles and the color is rendered too thin; if too little, the moisture is consumed very quickly because cinnabar is excessively drying.

Among the types of trees that excel in the variety of their colors, the root of the **Elm** is next after the **Olive**. For this reason, vessels and tablets made from these are of very pleasing use, not only because of the color,

<header>Book Eight</header>

# Book Eight

...color, but also because of its splendor. The cause of the variety of colors is the variety of heat and the oily part. For just as in clothing, so too in these things: when oil is spoiled, it changes the original colors. But while in clothing it is called a stain, in these things the variety is pleasing because it is joined with brightness. Thus, the juice of the **lemon** <note>original: "limunij"</note>, by changing the color in hides with an alternating variety, makes them commendable; for while it alters the previous state, it retains the luster and is said to render the hide variegated rather than stained.
<margin>How hides may receive various colors.</margin>
The roots of **Indian canes** <note>Likely referring to bamboo or similar tropical reeds.</note> are also pleasing for their variety of color and luster. And in all these things, the trees that grow in the mountains are superior to those in lower-lying places. But while plants take on all
<margin>All types of flavors in plants except saltiness.</margin>
colors, they do not do so with flavors; for they seem to lack a **salty** <term>salty flavor</term><note>original: "falsum"; likely an OCR error for "salsum" (salty), as the text proceeds to discuss saltiness ("salfugo") and the theories of Theophrastus regarding the absence of saltiness in land plants.</note> taste, though they possess the rest: bitter, sweet, sharp, and acidic. **Bitter** plants include gentian, aloes, and *santonicum* <note>A type of wormwood.</note>, a kind of absinthe. **Sweet** ones include licorice, sugar, and <term>polypody</term><note>A type of fern whose rhizomes have a bittersweet flavor.</note>. **Sharp** ones include pepperwort, pepper, watercress, garlic, and onion. **Acidic** ones include wood sorrel and sharp-dock. **Tasteless** ones include turnips, mallows, and beets. However, **Theophrastus** <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany" (c. 371–287 BC).</note> believes that no plants have a salty taste—although **musk** may be somewhat salty—and he says the cause of this is that the nourishment of the plant itself cannot be salty in any way. Yet, since there are many salty lands, and the herbs that grow on the seashore are nonetheless not salty, one should not think the cause is a lack of salty nourishment. Therefore, we say that many plants are salty, yet not as many as are bitter or sweet, nor so evidently so. Since a salty flavor alone is erosive, and plants are slow to expel waste, it is for this reason hardly possible for a plant to be exceptionally salty. For a plant is moist, and saltiness erodes moist things, as we see even in animals, which are worn away and eaten into by the mere humor that carries this flavor. Indeed, certain plants, when they do not strongly endure salty soil—such as citrons, lemons, and <term>Median apples</term><note>The Citron (*Citrus medica*).</note>—wither immediately if they are not frequently drenched with water, because the unsoftened brine kills the plant on the spot. Furthermore, since all flavors can exist in a thin substance except saltiness, and the plant draws only thin nourishment, it will be able to draw all flavors except saltiness. Brine is also the weakest of flavors, for a great quantity of salt is necessary for water to be rendered salty; since, therefore, that which is salty provides little nourishment, is drawn up with difficulty because it is thick, causes much offense, and affects the taste very little, it is necessary that few plants appear salty, and those that are, only thinly so.
<margin>Sargassum, a herb of the sea.</margin>
However, the Indian Sea nourishes a salty herb which they call **drifting sargassum** <note>original: "salgazum mobilem"; likely *Sargassum*, the floating seaweed.</note>, which stays on the surface of the sea and is so abundant that it resembles flowering meadows; for it is partly green and partly saffron-colored. It is nourished, however, not by salt, but, as I said, by a fatty moisture that is joined to the salt. 
<margin>Seaweed, a herb of the sea.</margin>
Our sea <note>The Mediterranean.</note> also nourishes a very soft kind of herb called **seaweed** <note>original: "alga".</note>. By a similar reasoning, leaving behind the brine, it is nourished by the fatness of the water; wherefore it sprouts in the spring, is green in the summer, and dies off in the winter. Because it is nourished by this fatness, it is well-suited for carrying jars; for this reason, the **Venetians** <note>The glassmakers of Venice, famous for their fragile Murano glass.</note> send glass vessels to us buried within it. Moreover, those that are salty and for that reason...

## On Plants.

<margin>The incredible size of trees called Ceibas, and called *Gordas* <note>Spanish: "Fat ones."</note> by the Spaniards.</margin>
<margin>Soil that does not allow the roots of trees to sink deep into the depths produces untrustworthy and fickle men.</margin>
<margin>The lifespans of trees.</margin>
...[morta]ls and will be as if dry; for trees grow with rich nourishment, and not falsely so. For this reason, the soil of India must be considered the richest and least salty, because trees there grow to an immense size. Indeed, they report that a certain tree was found there of the **Ceiba** <note>The Kapok or Silk Cotton tree (*Ceiba pentandra*), famous for its massive buttress roots.</note> genus (for this is the largest genus of all trees) which was split into three parts among the others, of which each individual trunk was encircled by a circumference of twenty feet. The spaces between the trunks near the ground were separated by the same number of feet; indeed, through these very spaces, a fully loaded wagon could be easily driven. But where the trunks joined into one—which happened at a distance of about fifteen feet from the ground—the thickness of the tree was forty-five feet. From the lowest part of the thicker trunk up to the place where the branches first came forth was eighty feet; the upper part from which the branches hung was beyond measure. The cause of such great height is the fertile soil, the strength of the sky, and the nature of the tree: for its wood is very light, having a small amount of earth and a great deal of thinner moisture. Large trees usually rely on deeper roots, which is why in dry regions the root only proceeds three or four cubits into the depths, nor can trees of more solid material grow to such an immense size, as seen on the **Spanish island of the New World** <note>Hispaniola, modern-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic.</note>. And there, in the mountains where trees do not send their roots deep into the earth, the men are untrustworthy and fickle; perhaps because the excessive dryness, or the frequent change of winds, renders the minds of mortals mobile and light, and therefore untrustworthy and inconstant. For men generally follow the nature of their climate. Furthermore, the trees themselves, which do not send deep roots due to the dryness of the soil, cannot live long. Indeed, the nature of trees is naturally extended into an immense age. For **Josephus** <note>Titus Flavius Josephus, a 1st-century Romano-Jewish historian.</note> relates that the **oak of Abraham** <note>The Oak of Mamre, where tradition says Abraham pitched his tent.</note> still remained in his own time. Between the destruction of Jerusalem and Abraham's dream, there are exactly two thousand years.

<margin>Oak wood is least susceptible to water damage.</margin>
<margin>Apples of Paradise <note>Early modern name for bananas or plantains.</note>.</margin>
<margin>Why trees do not have leaves as wide as garden vegetables.</margin>
After the oak come the palm, the plane tree, the beech, the olive, the pine, and the elm; **Theophrastus** <note>Ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> thinks otherwise, but one should believe the facts more than the trifles of the Greeks. Generally, the great size of trees and the breadth of their roots indicate a long old age. The cause of a longer life is the smallness of the fruit and, so to speak, sterility, as well as the solid substance of the wood. This is also why oak wood remains unharmed forever under water; it only turns black, remaining solid, and is neither destroyed by the water nor easily consumed while it lives. By a contrary reasoning, the tree that bears the **apples of paradise** <note>original: "poma paradyse"</note> has a very short life; for in the second year the trunk withers. It bears fruit in clusters, like grapes or berries, but the size of an apple, and sometimes a hundred in one cluster; thus the cluster reflects the size of a chest. It is veiled in a saffron-colored <note>yellow</note> covering, which, when removed, reveals a very sweet and pleasant fruit beneath. It bears a leaf so long that it equals a standing man, and it is quite wide. Thus, the tree is exhausted by the multitude and size of the fruits and the leaves. For this reason, almost no long-lived tree has large leaves; rather, these belong to herbs, cabbage, **sorrel** <term>sorrel</term> <note>original: "lapatho"; a genus of herbs in the buckwheat family.</note>, and the **gourd** <note>original: "cucurbitae"</note>, nor is this beneficial to the tree...

<page-num>232</page-num>
<header>Book Eight</header>

## Book Eight

...its height <note>The sentence likely begins on the previous page, describing a plant like a reed or a fast-growing herb.</note> perishes in the same year it is born. For large leaves require abundant moisture; however, when this is plentiful but not "fatty" <note>meaning nutrient-rich or oily</note>, it brings about death quickly. For this reason, wild plants have a longer life than cultivated ones, and those that are born on land live longer than those in the water. For these reasons, trees with spongy wood have short lives, such as the laurel, the pomegranate, and then the fig, as well as those that bear fruit; for they all luxuriate too much in their fruit relative to the size of the tree.

<margin>The greatest fruit-bearing trees.</margin>
Among the fruit-bearers, let me not pass over the vine in silence, which sometimes bears fruit three times in a year, which is why it is called "thrice-bearing" <note>original: *trifera*</note>, though the last grape does not ripen. It is common for the fig to bear fruit twice in the same year—the first being rarer and larger, the second being as much more frequent as it is smaller. It is clear, therefore, that both trees bloom as many times as they are about to produce fruit.

<margin>Why mistletoe grows on other trees.</margin>
There are also trees that cling to other trees, such as ivy, and others that even grow inside them, such as mistletoe. When its seed is eaten by a magpie or a thrush, it is not digested, but being mixed with dung, it produces roots through heat and moisture when it falls upon a tree. It gains three benefits from the tree: first, it has more "dung" <note>The author suggests the bird droppings provide a concentrated source of nutrients on the branch that soil cannot offer</note>, for not as much can be gathered on the ground; second, because it is covered by the branches, it is not easily harmed by rain or sun; and third, because it is not washed away by the moisture of the soil. It is therefore very dense, because it is not "cooked" in the bellies of birds, and it requires little moisture but much heat. It grows best on the fir, the oak, and the pine.

<margin>Why wheat is turned into darnel.</margin>
Other trees also change, but herbs do so more frequently: darnel <note>original: *lolium*; a weed often found among grain</note> into wheat, and wheat back into darnel. This happens by a logic almost similar to how blind and lame people do not necessarily produce blind and lame children, but healthy ones; and yet from the healthy, the blind and lame are born again. By the strength of the soil and the sun, darnel passes into wheat, and imperfect things into those that are perfect; by the weakness of both, perfect things pass into the damaged. Your "Prince of Poets" <note>A reference to the Roman poet Virgil</note>, O Prince, expressed this change beautifully when he said:
> Unlucky darnel and sterile oats dominate. <note>original: "Infælix lolium, & steriles dominantur auenæ" from Virgil's *Georgics*.</note>

<margin>The method of grafting.</margin>
Grafted trees change more evidently when shoots are inserted into the "tunics" <note>the layers of bark and cambium</note> of others, as when a peach is grafted onto a walnut; the tree then bears small, green, somewhat bitter, and hard peaches. The natures of both plants are mixed no differently than in mules produced from a donkey and a mare. However, it is necessary for the times of bearing fruit to match, just as in animals. For if an early cherry is grafted onto a late-fruiting medlar, when the shoot draws nourishment, the trunk does not supply it; and when the trunk supplies it, the shoot—because its own time has passed—does not draw it, since it has already cooled and lost its leaves. They say, however, that a vine grafted onto a cherry bears early grapes, though this happens neither always nor everywhere. But there is a superior method for these: pierce the trunk of a three-year-old or slightly older cherry with a drill. Through that hole, lead a branch of a two-year-old vine that has grown nearby, carefully filling the space with dung, then closing it with wax and oakum <note>original: *stupa*; fiber used for sealing</note>. In this way, the shoot that sticks out draws nourishment from both plants. Then, after two years in a warm region, or after three in a cold one, cut the branch away from the vine next to the cherry.

# On Plants.

...so that the vine draws nourishment from the cherry tree alone, and this vine produces early grapes; in the same way, a rose grafted onto an apple tree produces flowers in the middle of winter.

The same principle applies when linseed is placed within an onion; it produces a flax plant with the leaves of flax, but with a sharp, pungent taste. It is necessary, however, for the nourishment to be compatible.

<margin>The annual and daily turning of leaves in plants.</margin>
Certain trees also turn their leaves at the summer solstice, such as the olive, the lime <note>original: *tilia*</note>, and the elm. Others, however, follow the course of the Sun through a full semi-circle every single day, such as the lupine and the heliotrope <note>meaning "sun-turner"</note>; hence the name given to the latter. The cause of this last movement is a thin moisture that reacts to the heat of the Sun much like leather <note>original: *corij*</note> reacts to fire; for leather, when placed near a fire, curls toward it.

<margin>Why flowers open in the morning.</margin>
By almost the same reasoning, flowers—since they are thin and spongy—are dried by the heat of the Sun and then constricted by the onset of cold at sunset. But after they have "drunk in" the moisture of the night, becoming filled with sap and swollen, they are necessarily forced open by the morning heat of the Sun. However, the plants whose leaves turn at the solstice have a different explanation for their miracle. For when the leaves of other plants have already begun to fall, in these trees the moisture is more tenacious and they turn; because of this, the change in the leaves becomes conspicuous. Thus, this happens to all trees that retain their leaves at that time. We only notice it, however, in the leaves of those trees where the "domesticated" side differs greatly in color from the "wild" side. But you should not believe that this entire turning happens exactly on the day of the solstice; that would border on a miracle. Rather, what has happened gradually is attributed by mortals to the specific moment when the process is completed. <margin>On nuts blooming on the feast of Blessed John the Baptist.</margin> This is like the belief regarding a certain kind of dwarf walnut, which is thought to put forth leaves, flowers, and fruit all at once on the night preceding the feast of Blessed John the Baptist <note>Midsummer Eve, June 23rd</note>. If this were truly the case, what other more illustrious argument for our religion could we desire against the stubborn Jews, or the proud followers of Muhammad, or the talkative philosophers? But as I said, because the nature of the tree reaches that state near that time, the whole event is turned into a religious tribute to that most famous saint.

<margin>Trees that are of the herb kind.</margin>
There are also certain plants that fall between the categories of trees and herbs, as we have already said of rue, and likewise sage, and then also the cabbage. The kidney bean <note>original: *phasellus*</note> even becomes tree-like in the Kingdom of Senegal, of which we have already spoken; it grows most abundantly from a tree, and the beans are small, red, and have a black "eye." But in our regions, these seeds belong to herbs. The cause, therefore, is that a plant which is an herb due to more abundant moisture turns into a tree in a hotter and drier climate and soil. For we have already shown that the genus of herbs is generally more moist than the genus of trees. Nothing prevents small and short-lived <note>original: *morticinas*</note> herbs from sharing a common species with long-lived and great trees, just as occurs among dogs.

<margin>Oil of a wonderful nature.</margin>
The memory of these things reminds me to report on the nature of the oil produced in that same place <note>referring to Senegal</note>: in color it imitates saffron, and it stains food more than saffron does; it has the scent of violets, but the taste of our olive oil. There also grows a tree on the island of Porto Santo <note>An island in the Madeira archipelago</note>, which...

<margin>The dragon's blood tree.</margin>
The first <note>original: *herba*, referring to the catchword from the previous page</note> is found by those traveling from Spain toward India; it bears a fruit very similar to a cherry, but of a blue color. I believe it to be a type of cherry, but the variety of the regions causes its "tear" <note>the resin or sap</note> to be used as **Dragon's Blood** <note>original: *sanguinis Draconis*; a bright red resin used for medicine and dye</note>, for it is remarkably red and shining. It is processed into lozenges, and it is believed to be especially effective at strengthening the teeth, as the ancients did. And certainly, just as it surpasses true dragon's blood in color—which, according to Dioscorides <note>a famous Greek physician and botanist</note>, was obtained from the *sideritis* herb—so too is its use almost unknown. However, Brasavolus <note>a Renaissance physician</note> thinks that *sideritis* is a species of yarrow <note>original: *millefolij*</note>. Therefore, this "tear" flows either spontaneously or when the tree is wounded, and it is inferior to the first kind.

<margin>The incredible trade of woad.</margin>
Next in honor among plants for its color is **woad** <note>original: *glastum*</note>, which is used to dye cloth a blue color; the common people call it *Guadum*. No other herb requires so much silver to be spent on it, for from such a lowly commodity, the tax revenue rises to many thousands of gold coins. 
<margin>The beauty of Lithospermon.</margin>
But while this herb is more profitable, the most beautiful of all is **Lithospermon** <note>literally "stone-seed," likely Gromwell</note>; between its leaves, seeds shine with the hardness of stone and the whiteness of pearls. I speak of the Cretan variety, for the Italian kind degenerates quite a bit from this one.

<margin>Why the palm tree curves into an arch.</margin>
But someone will perhaps ask about the wood of palm trees: why does it curve into an arch <note>original: *fornicem*</note> when other woods, when pressed by a weight, bend into a bow? This is a common report, and I find Theophrastus <note>an ancient Greek philosopher and the "father of botany"</note> to be a witness to such a great miracle. Xenophon <note>a Greek historian</note> is the authority that this also happens with the pack-saddles of donkeys. I believe the cause is that it bends before it is even pressed; once it is already curved, it flexes upward, for it has fibers <note>original: *neruos*</note> that incline toward one side. Or, if it can bend toward either side, this happens because of dryness, just as in leather, for weight can dry things out by pressing them. But in donkeys, nature devised this so they would feel the harm of the weight less.

<margin>Sweating wooden statues.</margin>
It is worthy of less wonder that statues "sweat," for the reason is obvious: when an oily moisture is forced out by the power of heat, it presents the appearance of sweat. Because of this, woods consisting of cedar, olive, vine, and cypress sweat the most. This happens more when the south winds blow, because the moisture is then 
<margin>Woods that emit fiery sparks when broken.</margin>
more abundant and thinner. But those plants which grow in sulfurous and bituminous soil, if they are of an airy and fiery substance and contain little earth and water—such as the Alder, Fir, Pine, and Pitch-pine—tend to emit fiery sparks when they are broken, especially if they have already begun to rot. By a similar reasoning, the bark of certain trees becomes so white and shining with age that they glow at night like a burning coal <note>original: *prunæ*</note>.

<margin>A herb that excites sexual intercourse up to 70 times a day.</margin>
I shall not fear to place among the miracles of plants what Theophrastus relates in his fourth book regarding shrubs: an herb brought from India which, when chewed, allows a man to fulfill the act of intercourse seventy times in a day. Whether this be true or not, I would not wish to affirm; I will only add what pertains to our present purpose: namely, that in the act of Venus <note>sexual intercourse</note> two things are necessary: "wind" <note>original: *flatum*; referring to the vital spirits or gasses</note> and seed. Therefore, just as in <term>satyriasis</term> <note>a condition of uncontrollable sexual desire or persistent erection</note> the <term>ueretrum</term> <note>the male reproductive organ</note> is immoderately extended without the desire for coitus, so nothing prevents...

<meta>Continuing from the discussion of the Lithospermon and other specific herbs, the text now transitions into a broader physiological study of plant life, comparing the "humors" and structures of plants to those of animals.</meta>

# On Plants.
<page-num>215</page-num>

...that there is a herb which, when tasted, has the same effect, and if eaten gradually, it will likewise gradually promote the production of seed <note>Referring to human fertility or semen</note>. We have shown, therefore, that there are certain plants that stir up excessive sexual desire <note>original: *Venerem immodicam*; literally "immoderate Venus"</note>; which specific ones those are, however, we shall explain in our complete history of plants. 

Now it is useful to teach why flowers do not have a single color like leaves. This happens because their moisture dries up and no more is supplied. 

<margin>Why flowers have various colors.</margin>
For leaves, since a constant supply of moisture is provided by the action of heat, all are necessarily green. 

<margin>Why all plant leaves are green.</margin>
For this same reason, the upper surface of stagnant waters appears green, as do damp places on the ground situated under the eaves of roofs where the rays of the Sun do not reach. 

<margin>The elemental balance of plant parts.</margin>
Therefore, the leaf is always the moistest part of the entire plant and usually the coldest. The seed is the hottest and driest, while the flower is to be placed in the middle of these. Again, the root is the coldest and driest, while the fruit is the hottest and moistest; the trunk is in the middle of these, though it leans closer to the nature of the root. Furthermore, the hottest and driest part of the trunk is the wood; the bark is the moistest and coldest; and the <term>matrix</term> <note>The pith or "heart" of the plant</note> is placed, as it were, in the middle of these. Nevertheless, as I have said, the whole trunk is clearly cold and dry. 

<margin>The use of parts in trees.</margin>
Leaves cover the stalk, flowers, fruit, and seed. The wood sustains everything, much like bones do in animals; it is covered by the bark for the sake of protection. Yet, in some plants, the bark is also that through which nourishment is carried. The matrix itself, in some cases, serves the purpose of nutrition, and in all plants, it provides moisture to the wood. For this reason, those plants that lack a matrix are all abundant in "tears" <note>resins or saps</note>, such as the <term>Holy Wood</term> <note>original: *lignum sanctum*; usually referring to Guaiacum, a dense medicinal wood from the Americas</note>. Those that have a plentiful substance in the matrix lack tears, such as the Elder tree <note>original: *Sabucus*</note>. 

The root exists for the sake of drawing nourishment from the earth; flowers exist for the sake of the fruit or seed, for they always turn into those. The fruit, indeed, exists for the sake of the seed, for in every fruit the seed is contained beneath the <term>pericarp</term> <note>The part of a fruit that encloses the seeds</note>. Thus, the fruit is seen as the perfection of the plant, but the seed exists to propagate the species. In plants where there is no fruit, the seed provides the utility and use. 

In this matter, nature seems to have been more unkind to plants than to animals: for plants, their "clothing" <note>leaves</note> falls away in winter, while for animals, it grows—namely, their hair.

<margin>The weapons of plants.</margin>
Nature has also armed plants just as she has animals, with thorns, hardness, size, and ease of bending. But there are also "errors" <note>birth defects or abnormalities</note> as in animals, and they are more frequent the more lowly the creature is. Hence it happens that they abound in small animals, in those born from rotting matter, in fish, and in minerals, just as they do in plants.

<margin>Monsters of plants.</margin>
In the case of animals, "monsters" <note>original: *monstra*; refers to omens or biological wonders</note> are properly named from "showing" <note>original: *monstrando*; the Latin root of monster means "to show" or "point out"</note> because of their rarity. However, one may also transfer this name to plants. 

<margin>That all plants consist of a certain number of leaves, and how.</margin>
For if plants maintain their order, they consist not only of specific parts but also of a certain number of leaves. Nature was so skillful even in the smallest things; understand the reason for this: since plants lacked movement for the purpose of reproduction, it was necessary for her to force both sexes together, which is why several often combine into one. Since, therefore, in animals a single spine was necessary (like a keel in ships) into which all bones would be implanted, and in plants the "thorns" or veins <note>original: *spinæ*</note> perform the role of a nerve, it was necessary that if there were one nerve in plants, or if there were several...

### Book Eight

...several leaves on both sides, right and left, in equal measure, and then the branches will emerge. For even in animals, all parts appear to be doubled, as **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle discussed bilateral symmetry in his works on the parts of animals, noting that nature tends to create pairs.</note> rightly says. Therefore, since a leaf was necessary at the very tip of the summit, and yet a pair was necessary on either side at the nodes for any plant having a single thorn, the logic of this order required that there be two leaves at each node, but three at the summit. Accordingly, when the plant is dry and cannot put forth many leaves, the *Enophyllum* <note>original: "Enophyllum"; from the Greek for "one-leaf," likely referring to a species like *Maianthemum bifolium* or similar single-leafed plants</note> is produced near the nodes, the form of which is as follows:

<margin>The remarkable form of the Enophyllum.</margin>
A single leaf grows upon a short stalk without veins or <term>nerves</term> <note>The "nerves" of a plant refer to the vascular bundles or veins within the leaf structure.</note>; it is softer than ivy, yet very similar to it. Where the leaf joins the stalk, a thin, green, and curled sheath emerges at the same time, taller than the leaf, in which small seeds are contained. The entire herb is quite green; it has a single root in the shape of a serpent's head. Since it rises in the meadows in the month of April, it withers near **Pavia** <note>original: "Papiam"; the Latin name for the city of Pavia in Italy.</note> in May. It has no smell or taste and is believed to be beneficial for wounds. Therefore, since there was not enough material here, the leaf had to grow from the "nerve" and at the summit, for otherwise the whole plant could not be covered. By this reasoning, the material is "fat" and scarce in the *Enophyllum*; in the *trifolium* <note>Clover</note> it is moderate and scarce, but "fatter" in the *Elleboro* <note>Hellebore</note>; for if the material had been thin, it would not have been necessary to make so many leaves. In the *pentaphyllo* <note>Cinquefoil; "five-leaf"</note> it is very thin, as it is in the *eptaphyllo* <note>Septfoil; "seven-leaf"</note>; for the material would have been reduced to fewer parts if it had been thick. For the more leaves there are, if the stalk is not thick, the thinner they must necessarily be—whereas when the material is dry and scarce, there are few nerves or none at all, as in the *enophyllum*, *trifolium*, and *pentaphyllo*. Where there is a great abundance of material, there are more nerves, as in trees. Each nerve, however, keeps its own order; when there are many, they seem to confuse the order and number of the leaves. In the same way, although the movements of the stars consist of several equal motions, they appear confused and unequal.

Therefore, it is now manifest that the leaves at the summit of plants must be an odd number. For they either emerge from the nerves alone and become an *enophyllum*, or they grow on both sides and become a *trifolium*, *pentaphyllo*, or *eptaphyllo*. The *elleborus* has nine leaves; for if there are more, it is better that they be arranged two by two along the whole plant near the nodes, so that the summit does not undergo too much of a burden. But by the opposite reasoning, if there are few leaves, it was better for the whole mass to be brought to the top of the plant, for there the leaves better cover the whole plant, and therefore they also cover the flowers and fruit.

<margin>It is shown that leaves were made for the sake of the flowers and fruit.</margin>
The evidence that leaves were made for the purpose of covering the flowers and fruits is that leaves are born before flowers and much earlier than fruits. In those plants where leaves are perpetual <note>Evergreens</note>, they also have fruit or flowers throughout the whole time of the year. If the leaves were to be born later than the flowers, the greatest part of the fruit would perish in these plants. In winter, when the leaves fall, no flowers or fruits are born; they seem to be born for that reason alone, for when the tree does not bear in winter, the leaves fall. Therefore, the leaves of plants that have them only at the summit are odd in number because it is first necessary to cover the "back" of the plant, and then others emerge from there equally to the right and left.

# On Plants.

First, it is an indication [of this order] that no plant with a naked trunk has pairs at its summit; furthermore, the middle leaf is always larger, thicker, and more robust than the others, and those closest to it are larger than those further away. Additionally, a cavity in the stalk always lies opposite a <term>nerve</term> <note>The author uses "nerve" (Latin: nervus) to refer to the veins or vascular bundles of a plant.</note>, and the trunk itself is more easily bent toward that cavity than toward the nerve.

<margin>Why the nerves of leaves are odd in number.</margin>
By the same reasoning, the nerves of leaves are also odd in number, as in the plantain; for there are either five, seven, or even more, because besides those that stand in pairs on the sides, a middle one is added. But if the plant’s material is abundant enough for leaves while only a single nerve exists, for the same reason they will be odd at the summit, yet grow in pairs at every node throughout the rest of the plant. If there are more nerves in the trunk, such as two, then there will be four leaves at the nodes, or two and two, but not directly opposite at the summit; indeed, there may be six or ten. The same logic applies to the branches, so that—unless something has been damaged or is a <term>monstrosity</term> <note>In early modern science, "monstrificum" referred to a biological fluke or a "wonder" that deviated from the natural law.</note>, which as I said frequently happens in plants—one may calculate the number of leaves in all cases by a certain logic.

<margin>All pomegranates consist of a fixed number of seeds.</margin>
In a similar way, this holds for fruits: and to take an example from the more difficult cases, <term>pomegranates</term> <note>original: "mala punica"</note>, according to their kind and those born from the same tree, maintain a fixed number of seeds; some have nine hundred and forty-four, others one hundred and twenty-eight, and others another number, with all of them tending in a certain order from the wider circumference of the rind toward the narrow center. So it is with the "female" of pears, and so with apples or medlars. Some fruits dry out and are preserved, such as walnuts and hazelnuts; others are preserved but do not dry out, like pomegranates; some are not preserved at all, like cherries. <margin>How hard-skinned fruits may be revived.</margin> Those that are kept dry can be revived to look as if they were recently plucked from the plant if, after the rind is perforated, they are lowered into a well in a small bag for eight days, or buried under moist earth for fifteen days.

There are many things pertaining to these matters, yet they are not among those that must be discussed now for the discourse to be complete. <margin>How plants are transported to distant regions.</margin> Such matters include how plants may be transported from region to region, as from India to Italy: some indeed by transporting the seed; others whole in vessels, covered in earth; the shoots of others buried in honey. Since the moisture of honey is thin, sweet, and tempered—neither fatty nor prone to rot—it is most suitable for nourishing tender buds. For this reason, even walnuts are kept green in it for a whole year, and indeed fruit and flesh for many days without rotting. <margin>How juices are preserved.</margin> But juices, after they have fermented <note>original: "efferbuerint"; literally "boiled over," referring here to the fermentation process where gases are released.</note>—for thus the watery moisture, which is the principle of rot, is released—are preserved by pouring oil over the top. The juice of <term>Fumitory</term> <note>original: "Fumiterrae"; a medicinal herb (Fumaria officinalis) used since antiquity for skin and liver ailments.</note>, however, even when treated this way, passes from bitter to harsh and sour, because the earthy part (which is the cause of bitterness) sinks down, leaving the juice tasteless; when this is spoiled by the air, it turns sour, as do all sweet and tasteless things. It is better, therefore, both to have cooked it for a long time and to keep it in a very cold place...

<header>Book Eight</header>

# Book Eight

<margin>Where truffles are found, they melt the snow.</margin>
...[to] have hidden. For, as I have said, all decay is hot; because of this, truffles <note>Latin: *tubera*. In this context, the author refers to underground fungi, likely truffles or similar subterranean growths that appear to generate from the earth's "putrefaction."</note> grow, and they melt the snow standing directly above them. For the heat of decay, while it separates the earthy moisture, creates roots without a sprout, which are called truffles. Conversely, when it cooks cold, moist, and thin matter, it sends out sprouts without roots, which we call mushrooms <note>Latin: *fungi*.</note>. Therefore, mushrooms are moister, while truffles are more substantial. But as I said, decay is the path toward fire when it remains, yet such things do not burn because the decay has already ceased. 

<margin>Why the leaves of Laurel and Juniper crackle when they catch fire.</margin>
However, laurel <note>Latin: *laurus*; likely Sweet Bay (*Laurus nobilis*).</note> leaves burn very quickly because they contain something decayed and dry; juniper <note>Latin: *iuniperus*.</note> leaves do as well, but only due to their intense dryness. But those things which catch fire quickly before their watery moisture is either expelled or dried out necessarily emit a crackling sound; for this reason, laurel and juniper leaves crackle loudly while burning. There are some who believe that divination <note>The ancient practice of *daphnomancy* involved listening to the crackle of burning laurel leaves to discern the will of the gods.</note> is possible from burning laurel leaves, whether because the tree itself is sacred to Apollo, or because this flame is divided into various shapes, or because nature contains something that moves the mind.

<margin>The method for making gold and blue writing ink.</margin>
I know that I have now completed the history of plants, but since I have taught the composition of red and purple ink, I will also add the others. Blue <note>Latin: *cœruleum*.</note> is made from blue earth or lapis lazuli <note>Latin: *lapide cyaneo*.</note>; then gold is made from <term>purpurina</term> <note>A metallic powder used to imitate gold, often made from ground brass or bronze.</note> or real gold, and all the remaining colors are perfected from metallic substances, following to the letter both methods by which we previously taught how to mix red from cinnabar.

<margin>The method for preparing black writing ink.</margin>
As for the common black ink, it is made thus: take one pound of fresh crushed <term>oak gall</term> <note>Galls are growths on oak trees caused by wasps; they are high in tannin and were a primary ingredient in ink for centuries.</note>, half a pound each of gum arabic <note>Latin: *lachrymæ Arabicæ* ("Arabic tears").</note> and pomegranate flowers with their rinds; let them soak for eight days in six pounds of water. Afterward, let them be boiled until a third of the water remains; then, once the boiling pot is removed from the fire, add one pound of very finely ground <term>copperas</term> <note>Latin: *calchantum*, likely ferrous sulfate (green vitriol), which reacts with the tannins in galls to create black pigment.</note>. Let everything be mixed until it cools. After ten days, let it be strained through a thick linen cloth and stored. I know someone who made an excellent batch, which nevertheless, after six months, completely vanished from the pages—a great deception! But now, let us move on to the history of insects <note>In the early modern period, "insects" was a broad category often including any small invertebrates or "creeping things."</note>.
