# BOOK NINE
## On Animals that are
## generated from decay.

<margin>On the difference of insects.</margin>
There are two primary kinds of animals: the first is that which retains life in a part that has been cut off, and it is called an insect <note>Latin: *infectum*. Renaissance naturalists used this term for "segmented" creatures (from *in-secare*, to cut into) including worms, spiders, and centipedes, noting that they could often survive dismemberment like plants.</note>; this pertains to their imperfection, as the same thing occurs in plants. The others are perfect animals, to whom this ability does not apply at all. Among the insects, some fly, such as flies and bees; others live on the ground, such as worms and lizards; others are of an ambiguous kind, such as ants; others live in the waters, such as scolopendras <note>Latin: *Scolopendræ*; here referring to centipedes or marine polychaete worms.</note>; others fly and yet live in the waters, such as water spiders; others in both water and land, such as crocodiles. <margin>The marvelous size of serpents.</margin> Most noble of all are three kinds: Serpents for their size, and Bees and Silkworms <note>Latin: *Bombyces*.</note> for their work. History testifies that serpents grow to an immense size: for Marcus Attilius Regulus <note>A Roman general during the First Punic War.</note> at the Bagradas river in Africa killed one of 120 feet using siege engines and ballistae. And in the belly of a "Boa" <note>A legendary giant snake described by Pliny the Elder.</note> killed during the time of Claudius Caesar, an entire infant was found. This kind is nourished by milk and pursues lactating cows. They also report that there are Dragons <note>Latin: *Dracones*; in this context, usually referring to giant pythons or legendary large snakes.</note> that can suck an entire Elephant dry and kill it. <margin>Four-footed serpents.</margin> There are also in Calicut <note>A city in Kerala, India.</note> of East India animals similar to serpents—namely in the mouth, eyes, and very long tail, without hair, and the size of wild boars—with a somewhat larger head, but they have four feet and lack venom. Others similar to these, which they eat on the island of Hispaniola <note>The Caribbean island containing modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic.</note> in West India, are called Iguanas <note>Latin: *Hyuana*.</note>; they are spiny on the back, voiceless or without a voice, with four feet, the tail of a lizard, very sharp teeth, and are larger than rabbits or the size of hares. They live indiscriminately in trees, on land, and in the water, enduring hunger for many days, with skin marked by various colors and smooth like other serpents; the upper belly is like that of birds, but very wide from the chin to the chest. There are also those they call *Bardatos* <note>Likely referring to "bearded" or "armored" lizards, perhaps the Tegu or a similar reptile; the name suggests a resemblance to horses wearing decorative trappings (*phaleræ*).</note> from their resemblance to caparisoned horses; they are pleasant to the taste, the size of a rabbit, marked with white and ash-gray colors, and usually live in pits in the ground which they dig with their feet. These also have four feet, snake-like skin, and a tail: West India produces these near the same island. In Golden Castille <note>Spanish: *Castilla del Oro*, a 16th-century province in Central America.</note> vipers are frequent which reach 20 feet in length, and whose heads are no smaller than a young goat's. In the kingdom of Senegal, serpents of marvelous size without feet or wings are found, of the kind we called Boas. Taprobana <note>Ancient name for Sri Lanka.</note> sends even larger ones. <margin>The cause why serpents grow to an immense size.</margin> The cause of the serpents' size is the heat of the region, for serpents have hard flesh, making them suited to grow to an immense size, just as trees...

<header>Book Nine</header>

# ## Book Nine

Trees grow most when they are of a denser substance; likewise, so do Elephants. But cold hindered serpents; for this reason, they cannot reach such great size except in the hottest regions.
<margin>Why small serpents are all most deadly</margin>
Yet those that are unable to grow even with the help of heat are necessarily of a very dry nature, and for that reason, they are the most deadly. They say that the Kinglet or Basilisk <note>original: *Regulum seu basilicum*. The name 'basilisk' is derived from the Greek word for 'little king'.</note> kills men either by its voice alone or by its gaze. If this is so, it is necessary that the air is infected by both its breath and its sight; for that image which it sends out with the help of light must necessarily be full of poison. Therefore, just as women tarnish mirrors while they are detained by their monthly periods <note>This refers to a common ancient and medieval belief, cited by Aristotle and Pliny, that a menstruating woman's gaze could physically dull or stain a polished metal mirror.</note>, men and animals can be affected by the voice or the gaze of serpents.

<margin>Serpents are not found in clover.</margin>
It has been observed that serpents and snakes, and those creatures in which poison is present, do not live or hide in clover <note>original: *trifolio*</note>, because that herb is fatal to them, just as they are to others; for this reason, it is conveniently sown in hotter places. Even the vipers that inhabit the waters retain little or no poison, for they cannot be dry. Yet poison is either an immoderate dryness or is joined with immoderate dryness. And so, just as not all serpents are poisonous, neither do all animals endowed with poison creep. For scorpions, and toads <note>original: *buffones*</note>, and spiders, and certain kinds of crabs in the West Indies <note>original: *India occidentali*</note>, and some ants, although they have feet, are nevertheless not without poison, just as wasps and many other things are not.

<margin>The Tarantula.</margin>
But nothing is more marvelous than that kind of spider they call the Tarantula, which seizes those it has bitten with death through lethargy. The remedy is plainly found in music: either because they are prevented from sleeping, such as by the din of trumpets, or (which is best) because they are incited to dance. For by dancing, the sluggishness is shaken off, and with it the poison, which is by nature very cold. For also in Plato’s *Phaedo* <note>A dialogue concerning the death of Socrates.</note>, the silence and stillness of Socrates is commanded by the executioner so that the hemlock <note>original: *cicuta*</note> might be able to kill him. Therefore, it is not the music itself, but the exertion that shakes off the poison; yet they are incited to exertion by various kinds of music, just like children and the mindless.

<margin>Why poisonous animals lack wings and feet.</margin>
Why then did nature give poison to so few animals with feet, and even then in such a small amount? Because if they were strong in their feet, they would be too destructive; for this reason, nature also created them slow and tiny. The spider in the West Indies grows to the size of a sparrow, because this animal is by nature cold, as I have said, which we have also shown from the aid of its poison. But there, as it is larger, it is less poisonous. For that reason, nature made no bird poisonous; or if she did, its poison will be weak, like a wasp’s, or it will not be large, or not long-lived, or not common and tiny, or it will live in deserted places. It is manifest, therefore, from the purpose itself why serpents are without wings and feet.

But this pertains to the purpose; the specific reason is sought: we have said that those things endowed with poison are immoderately dry. Because of this, nature mixed horns, and claws, and bones into their flesh, and did not adorn them with feathers, for in this way she fashioned a drier body. And therefore...

<header>On Animals Born from Putrefaction.</header>

# On Animals Born from Putrefaction.

<margin>The dung of serpents smells pleasant.</margin>
The dung of serpents often has a pleasant scent, much like that of the largest lizards which they call crocodiles. These are similar to crocodiles in size and shape and are born in the West Indies and elsewhere, though far more rarely. Indeed, for snakes that have a pattern like a painted cup on their forehead, their dung smells best; for as I have said, a good scent arises from dryness. Since serpents are dry by nature, their waste is perfectly "concocted" <note>In ancient medicine, "concoction" refers to the process of digestion or ripening driven by internal heat.</note> and thus smells pleasant. For this same reason—their dryness—their parched skin is cast off by them in the spring, which they call their "old age" <note>original: *senectam*. The Romans referred to the sloughed skin of a snake as its "old age," implying the animal renewed its youth by shedding it.</note>.

<margin>Why snakes shed their "old age."</margin>
They say that if one's eyes are rubbed every morning with the discarded skin of a snake, they will never be seized by dimness of vision or cataracts. But just as that is less than true, it is more a matter of wonder that if this skin is burned while the Full Moon is in the first part of Aries, and the collected ash is sprinkled on the head, it induces terrifying dreams. If the face is washed with it diluted in water, one appears terrifying; if held under the tongue, it makes one wise and eloquent; if held under the sole of the foot, it makes one favored in the presence of princes and magistrates.

<margin>The "old age" (skin) of serpents.</margin>
Truly, whichever serpents have either a spur on the tail or a horn on the forehead are immoderately dry, and for that reason, they are the most deadly. Therefore, for serpents to be endowed with poison, they had to lack hair, feathers, legs, and wings; it was also necessary for them to drink very little, and for their eyes to be red.

<margin>Why there are few poisonous animals in the water.</margin>
For this reason, almost no fish are poisonous; if they are, they are so in their driest part, such as the "sea hares" <note>original: *lepores marini*. A type of toxic sea slug (Aplysia) well known in ancient toxicology.</note> in their gall, and "spider fish" <note>original: *aranei pisces*. Likely the weaver fish, known for its venomous spines.</note> in their spines. Furthermore, wasps are poisonous in their stinger because that is their driest part. Again, it is an indication of how much destruction they could bring to other living things if serpents were capable of running or flying, for almost no predatory animal has been swift except for the tiger; and in regions where "dart-snakes" <note>original: *iaculi*. A legendary snake said to perch in trees and launch itself like a javelin.</note> climb trees, men can hardly live.

<margin>Animals from rotting matter are almost as numerous as the things that rot.</margin>
But leaving these aside, let us return to the gentler race of bees. They are produced through breeding and also from the putrefaction <term>putredine<gloss>The process of decay which, according to the theory of spontaneous generation, could spontaneously produce new life.</gloss></term> not of all things, but of oxen—just as wasps come from horses, drones from asses, and hornets from mules. Thus, it seems that individual types of animals, when they rot, generate a specific kind of creature. From the leaves of the Nightshade comes a worm distinguished by green and saffron colors, bearing a saffron horn on its forehead the length of a finger, which I have often seen. The willow has its own bugs, and the rue has its destructive little worms; the poplar has some, the fir has others. Therefore, Virgil seems to have sung correctly concerning the origin of bees:

# Book Nine

->It seethes, and animals wonderful to behold appear,<-
->Lacking limbs at first, but soon buzzing with wings<-
->They mingle together; more and more they snatch the thin air:<-
->Until, like a rain shower poured from summer clouds,<-
->They burst forth: or like arrows from a pulsing bowstring,<-
->Whenever the light-armored Parthians first enter into battle.<-
<note>original: "Aestuat, & uisenda modis animalia miris..." This poetry, echoing Virgil’s Georgics, describes the "Bugonia," an ancient belief that bees were spontaneously generated from the decaying carcass of an ox.</note>

Indeed, while Aristotle remains quite uncertain regarding the generation of these creatures, it is nevertheless established that neither honey nor wax could have been produced from any other animal. For honey must necessarily be born from a mixture of thin moisture, fat, and dew. It was therefore necessary for the animals to be small so they could settle upon flowers, flying so they could return quickly, numerous so they could gather the smallest amounts, and industrious so they could fill their hives rapidly. Yet such tiny creatures were thought unable to incubate an egg; therefore, bees are generated from the honey itself. This species even thrives in the coldest regions by a clever invention of nature: for they lie hidden during the winter. Thus, in Muscovy <note>Historical name for the region of Russia around Moscow.</note>, there is such an abundance of honey and wax that it is almost held in contempt. The length of the summer day there, lasting nearly eighteen hours, mitigates the climate.

<margin>
Silkworms were known to Aristotle.
Book 5 of the *History of Animals*,
chapter 19.
</margin>
In the same way, silkworms are born from the leaves of the mulberry tree in warmer climates, just as bees are produced from oxen. It is clear that Aristotle knew of these, for he says that Pamphyla, daughter of Plateis, on the island of Cos, was the first who taught how to weave silken garments from the thread produced by the silkworm. This animal is born first as a worm of its own kind that has horns, then from that a caterpillar, afterward the silkworm, and finally the <term>necydallus</term> <note>original: *necyda-lus*. Aristotle's term for the pupa or the moth stage of the silkworm.</note>, with this entire transformation being completed in the space of six months. It resembles a butterfly, but it produces eggs through the union of male and female; meanwhile, it eats nothing, but wastes away once the eggs are laid. It does not fly, except in a way that seems to imitate a hop. However, it is a wonder how, if the creature was known then, silk clothing was once held in such high price? It is true that Procopius <note>A 6th-century Byzantine historian.</note> recounts that certain monks from the Indian city of Serinda brought the eggs of these little worms to the Emperor Justinian, and he says this occurred nearly 840 years after Aristotle; and Virgil says:

<margin>Then elsewhere.</margin>
->The Seres, unknown by face but known by their fleece.<-
<note>original: "Ignoti facie sed noti uellere Seres." The "Seres" was the Roman name for the people of East Asia, particularly the Chinese, whom they identified primarily by their silk.</note>
<margin>And Pliny: The Seres</margin>
->*The Seres comb the fleeces from the leaves.*<-

I believe that those famous for the wool-work of the forests, who comb the white down from the leaves after soaking them in water, were indeed using our modern silk, which was celebrated by the ancients and, as I said, known to Aristotle. However, the knowledge died out because the method of nurturing them was uncertain—or perhaps because Pamphyla taught how to weave using threads brought from India (already known by the victory of Alexander the Great) without the worms themselves having been transported. From there, it was first under Justinian that both the eggs and the art of rearing them reached us through the monks. In the meantime, while the truth lay hidden, the ancients were persuaded that silk was combed from the fuzz of leaves—either because this seemed more likely, or because silkworms occurred there spontaneously in the woods, or because the inhabitants hoped they could better hide the origin of silk in this way. But as the whole world has become known through the favor of this Caesar and my maternal grandfather, it has become clearly open that there is no other kind of silk besides this. Therefore, silkworms are the most useful creatures after bees. Toward...
<meta>catchword: "uehuntur" (they are carried)</meta>

<header>On Animals born from putrefaction.</header>

# On Animals born from putrefaction.

<margin>A new purple dye</margin>
There are brought to us now certain "seeds" for the preparation of a purple color for silk, which are similar to **bugs** from which the heads have been removed; because of these, the price for red silk has been reduced by nearly half. In former times, this dye was made from the tubers of the **burnet** <note>original: "bibinellæ," likely referring to Pimpinella or a similar herb whose roots provided dye.</note> herb that grow near the roots.

<margin>Locusts and the damage they cause.</margin>
Locusts seem to be prepared by nature as an enemy to the human race. They are not abundant everywhere, but Africa alone is almost constantly burdened by this plague—and what is more marvelous—it suffers this nearly every other year. We have seen them in Italy, as a portent in the sky a few years ago, covering the light no differently than a dense cloud. The provinces upon which this calamity falls are stripped of their crops and every sprout in a single night; you would say that **snow** had fallen throughout the entire night, if only they were as white as they are black. Their form is like that of Italian locusts, but of a dark red color, slightly larger, and endowed with the power of flight. There are those who believe they are carried to us over the sea by the winds, not of their own will, because of their great multitude and the distance of the region. They are born near marshes, and when they fly into the cultivated land of Africa, they do not reproduce, or do so very little. Those left in the marshes cannot multiply so much that it becomes necessary to fly out for food; they are content with the brush and marsh-weeds. For this reason, they most frequently raid the province only every other year, and often even more rarely. Truly, those that do go out, having consumed the crops and being forced to fly on in search of food, are eventually cast into the sea by the winds. Sometimes, however, by the persistence of the winds and their own strength, they are carried all the way to the opposite regions of Africa; of which evil Sicily was first to partake, and later Italy was not exempt. It has been found by experience that the care taken to destroy their eggs with **fire** has been beneficial, for it deprives them of offspring. If, however, this care is not applied, it has been seen that this evil sprouts again the following year, causing no small inconvenience; for besides certain sterility of the land, they also bring the danger of **pestilence** and serve as an omen of future war.

<margin>Why locusts, ants, and butterflies produce eggs, but bees do not.</margin>
But why is it that these creatures, though they are smaller than bees—namely ants, butterflies, and locusts—lay eggs, while bees cannot? The cause is that when they give birth, they do not fly, but retain the form of a caterpillar or a chrysalis, or they remain with them, such as silkworms and locusts. For eggs in such small animals would be a hindrance to flight. Therefore, since it was better for bees to be long-lived because of their extraordinary usefulness—for their life is extended into the seventh or even eighth year—it was impossible for them to lay eggs. We must believe that not only such tiny creatures, but even larger animals, take their origin from **putrefaction** <note>The process of decay or rotting.</note>; indeed, all of them, since it is already established regarding mice, and fish are generated spontaneously in fresh waters. For when, as I have said, putrefaction has preceded, the fat is separated from the ash, and the **Sun** immediately infuses a "soul" <note>original: "animam," the vital life force or breath.</note> suitable to that matter. Whence it happens that 
<margin>Why all animals born from putrid matter end pains.</margin>
all animals which are generated from putrid matter, such as cockroaches, worms, and **scorpions** <note>original: σκόρπιοι (skorpioi)</note>, will end pains wherever they arise, if anything can. For they are made of the hottest and most moist matter. For this reason, it is no wonder if <term>Cantharides</term> <note>Spanish flies, often used in historical medicine for blistering or as an aphrodisiac.</note> do not do this, as they come from...
<margin>The various power of Cantharides.</margin>

<page-num>224</page-num>
<header>Book Nine</header>

<meta>The catchword "Notissi" from the previous page likely refers to the "notorious" nature of the insects discussed at the break.</meta>

...for they are generated from eggs. However, they also possess other powers instead of these. For in a moderate dose, they cause a very great tension and erection of the penis <note>The author is likely describing Cantharides, or "Spanish Fly," which was used historically as a dangerous aphrodisiac and medicine</note>. In a larger dose, they flay the bladder and cause the passing of blood in the urine. In an even larger dose, they drive people insane.

<margin>Glow-worms.</margin>
By the same logic, there are the **Glow-worms** <note>original: *Cicendulæ*</note>, which Italy produces. These are smaller than flies in size, but as much thinner as they are longer. They fly and sparkle on summer nights, having six feet and wings harder than those of flies—for they are of the hornet kind <note>The author classifies them with "hornets" likely due to their hard wing-cases, or elytra</note>. Their internal organs are very white, and the outer skin is polished—so much so that while it is alive, it shines so brightly that I have sometimes read letters in the dark as if helped by a burning candle. They transform from caterpillars into hornets, or what is more likely, from hornets into caterpillars. Since the caterpillar is larger than the winged insect and shines less, it is as if it were then worn out by old age; and then it is likely that it lays its eggs, and not while it is flying.

<margin>Water which brings brightness in the dark.</margin>
This kind of living creature teaches us that a liquid can be made which shines in the dark. This occurs in the decaying parts of those things that possess the highest whiteness, light, and transparency. I do not doubt that it can be done; but from what materials and in what manner is still uncertain to me.

<margin>The Cocoyum.</margin>
The **Cocoyum** <note>The West Indian click beetle or fire beetle, known today as the *Pyrophorus*</note> presents an even greater miracle than the glow-worm. This animal is sent from the Spanish island of the New World <note>Hispaniola or Cuba</note>; it is clearly of the beetle kind, with a size like our beetles which we call "stag beetles" <note>original: *cervinos*</note> because of the length of their horns. It flies no less than the glow-worm and shines from its body, but much more from its eyes—so much so that it resembles a candle. For the eyes are very large in proportion to the body and protruding. One can read and write by its light; the Indians <note>Indigenous peoples of the Caribbean</note> were also accustomed to hold banquets using only that light. They contain such a great and clear light within themselves that a greater miracle can neither be found nor desired. Their light is gradually extinguished as their life fades, so that the light perishes entirely along with the life; so closely is this power joined to the vital soul. However, that liquid which was shining in the eyes and belly remains; when rubbed on, whether because it still retains some light or because it ignites the skin with its heat, it makes the skin itself as red and shining as a glowing coal.

<margin>The Pyrausta living in fire.</margin>
<margin>Hairy worms in the snow.</margin>
The generation of the **Pyrausta** <note>A legendary fire-dwelling insect, often called a "firefly" in a literal sense in ancient texts</note> is as marvelous as the light of the glow-worm. For **Aristotle** reported that the Pyrausta lives among the fires of Cyprus that are found in copper-smelting furnaces. He also wrote about red, hairy worms found in the snow. One must believe that the Pyrausta is either generated in fire, or (which is more likely) that creatures born elsewhere lead their lives in these places, since fire and extreme cold can generate nothing on their own. Therefore, they are generated from the residues at the bottom of fire and snow. And just as the worms are very hot and thus able to endure such cold, so the Pyrausta is very cold. The Pyrausta is therefore generated from the decay of the very solid moisture of metals, in the vicinity of the fire, so that the moisture is not destroyed by the fire; nor, having been born nearby, does it become unable to endure the fire once it has matured.

## On Animals from Putrefaction.

<margin>The Ephemeron.</margin>
The history of the **Ephemeron** <note>original: *Ephemeri*; referring to the Mayfly</note> is also very well known, according to the same author [Aristotle] and Cicero: it is a creature born with four feet and as many wings near the Hypanis, a river of the Bosporus. It leads a life lasting from morning until evening, which is how it earned its name <note>The name "Ephemeron" comes from the Greek meaning "lasting only a day"</note>. In the morning it is a child, at noon a youth, and in the evening it is old; it dies as the sun sets. It seems that Nature has expended much more labor and time on its generation than on the use of its life. One may marvel at such great care from the Creatress, providing so many instruments and faculties in an animal of such short life. It sees, it hears, it flies, and it walks.

<margin>The Gnat.</margin>
<margin>All flies sting; gnats do not.</margin>
<margin>How we may keep gnats and flies away.</margin>
Nature armed the **Gnat** <note>original: *Culicem*; referring to mosquitoes or midges</note> to do us harm—a tiny and common creature, so much so that it is scarcely possible to live comfortably near water. With its robust proboscis—so that Nature seems to have been contemplating the Elephant while creating this animal—it bores through not only human flesh but also the hides of horses, drawing blood with sharp pain. Finally, with its remarkable buzzing <note>original: *bombo*</note>, it disturbs sleep on summer nights, such that nothing is more hateful. Nor does it strike incidentally like the flies that attack everyone everywhere; rather, it chooses whom it strikes, for it delights only in sweet blood. The fly is hated, but it is kept away by fine-threaded netting: for it fears entangling its wings, as is well established by experience. This same method should also be observed for keeping gnats away.

<margin>Wonderful kinds of ants.</margin>
The genus of **Ants** <note>original: *Formicarum*</note> also becomes winged when it grows old. Truly, just as bees maintain a kingdom, so ants maintain a popular state <note>Meaning a republic or communal society</note>. Some grow quite large in hot regions, so much so that Rhazes <note>original: *Rasis*; a celebrated Persian physician and scholar</note> records that in the famous city of Susa in the region of Persia, an ant was raised publicly in the Bird Market <note>original: *foro Auiano*</note> which ate a pound of meat every day. Others, truly, on the Isthmus of Sur and in Northwestern India, build little huts so hard, in the likeness of honeycombs, that they can scarcely be broken even with axes; in this way, they bring ruin to the trees.

<margin>Cockroaches or Beetles.</margin>
Among the kinds of **cockroaches** <note>original: *blattarum*; here likely referring to grain beetles or weevils given the context of flour</note> which lack wings, the grain-dwelling ones are prominent. If these are nourished among bran, it is marvelous to say in what a great multitude they grow: from ten to three hundred in the interval of a few days. They are raised to feed black-capped warblers and nightingales; there is no healthier food for them in winter. Many barbers maintain this care, for these insects are active and warm these birds, who are endowed with only a thin spark of life.

<margin>The Acaris, the smallest of animals.</margin>
<margin>The Garapate.</margin>
<margin>The Nigua.</margin>
Even the smallest of animals are of this kind, such as the **Acaris** known to Aristotle, which is born in wax. Now the West Indies sends another new kind, the **Garapate** <note>A type of tick or mite</note>, which is thinner than crushed salt. But there is also a certain atrocious pest of the flea kind called the **Nigua** <note>The Chigoe flea or jigger</note>. This animal is much smaller than a flea; adhering to a person, it lacerates them so much—while being unable to be seen or caught—that the feet, and sometimes even the hands, of some people fall off. A remedy has been found if the area is smeared with oil and scraped with a razor.

It seems to be a property of animals generated from putrefaction that they are insects...

<header>Book Ten</header>

<margin>Why certain animals regenerate cut-off limbs.</margin>
...so that cut-off limbs are reborn in them: such as the tails of serpents and lizards, the claws of crabs, and certainly the eyes of swallows, and as many think, even those of serpents. The cause of this is that they are <term>imperfect animals<note>In Renaissance biology, "imperfect" animals were those thought to lack certain complex systems or those born from "putrefaction" (spontaneous generation) rather than seed.</note></term>: hence the eyes are not reborn in adult swallows, but in swallow chicks, and in fetuses also, very often while they are in the womb, damaged limbs are restored. Physicians would say this is because they are more moist. But while these things are marvelous, a future age will show other far more marvelous things in such matters. But leaving these things aside, let us pass to perfect animals.

# BOOK TEN
## On Perfect Animals.

<margin>Perfect animals, being nobler, are categorized by nine distinctions.</margin>
**O**F the perfect animals, some live only in the air and lack feet—although Aristotle did not know these—such as the **Bird of Paradise** <note>original: *Manucodiata*; early European explorers believed these birds spent their entire lives flying because the trade specimens from Southeast Asia often had their feet removed.</note>. Others live in the air and on land, such as the **Eagle**, and most other birds. Others are terrestrial but similar to birds, like the **Ostrich** <note>original: *Struthio camelus*</note>. Others are common to both water and land, like the **Beaver** <note>original: *fiber*</note>. Others are swimming birds like **Swans** <note>original: *olores*</note>. Others are flying fish. Others are purely terrestrial, like the **Dog**. Others live under the earth, like the **Mole** <note>original: *talpa*</note>. Others spend their lives only in the waters, like the **Dolphin** <note>original: *Delphin*</note>. It is not our purpose to touch upon every species, but only these nine genera and the more noble species contained within them.

<margin>An animal of uncertain genus and form.</margin>
There was an animal of varied genus and uncertain nature which we saw in **Pavia** <note>original: *Papia*; a city in Northern Italy</note> on the 19th of January of the present year. It was the size of a fox, but somewhat longer, with the mouth and gape of a hare, with long hair and two very long teeth: indeed, they protruded by the length of a human finger, much like a squirrel’s. It had serpent-like eyes, for they lacked corners and were black. On its head was a cap, very similar to a goat’s beard, but acting as a crest like that of a peacock. Its fur was beautiful and like a **Marten’s** <note>original: *mustellinus*</note>, except that over the neck it looked like white wool. Its front feet were like a **Badger’s** <note>original: *taxi*</note>, and its ears and back feet differed not at all from human ones—except that on the feet was a bear’s claw instead of a human nail. On its back and hind part were about a hundred spines, like a **Porcupine** <note>original: *histricis*</note>, some of which were curved at the tip; otherwise they protruded immovably. Unlike what is told of the porcupine, they were not "shot out" <note>A common medieval and Renaissance myth suggested porcupines could fire their quills like arrows.</note>; however, when it moved, they made a clattering noise as they struck together. Its tail was like a **Goose's** <note>original: *anserina*</note>, but the feathers ended in spines. If you did not see the rest of it, you would call it a goose: with white and ashen areas of feathers, and a broadness emulating a goose.

<margin>The Hedgehog</margin>

But, by Hercules, it was born for the health of man; for by its dryness and its temperate nature, it aids the liver, kidneys, bladder, stomach, and lungs. Opposed to this animal, as if from a different region, is the sheep with its softest fleece. Sterile pastures increase the fineness of the wool. Whence Virgil says:

<margin>The utility of sheep, Book 3 of the *Georgics*</margin>
> If the care of wool is your concern, first let the prickly woods,
> The burrs, and the caltrops be absent; avoid lush pastures. <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 3.384-385. The author suggests that poor soil makes for thinner, finer wool fibers.</note>

> Around her, the nymphs were carding Miletian fleeces. <note>Virgil, *Georgics* 4.334-335. Miletus was an ancient Greek city famous for its luxury wool.</note>

<margin>Praise and wonders of Britain</margin>
Therefore, Britain is now renowned for its fleece. And it is no wonder, since it produces no venomous animal—indeed, none even hostile except for the fox and, formerly, the wolf. But now, with the wolves also exterminated, the flock wanders safely. The flocks quench their thirst with the dew of heaven and are kept away from all other drink, because the waters there are fatal to sheep.

<margin>Why there is a multitude of crows in Britain</margin>
However, because worms abound in the damp pasture, the multitude of **Crows** <note>original: *cornicum*</note> has grown so great that, on account of the damage to crops, rewards have recently been proposed by public decree for those who destroy them. For where there is food, there are the animals that feed upon it; and they multiply immoderately when it abounds everywhere.

<margin>Why Britain lacks serpents</margin>
Yet, as I said, it lacks serpents for three reasons: first, few can be generated because of the immense cold; second, because the land is excellently cultivated, those that are born are exterminated. Furthermore, once the land was free of them, they could not arrive from elsewhere, as the sea prevents it, since it is an island.

<margin>The wonder of the Pike fish</margin>
The same logic almost applies to wolves. But there is a marvelous thing which I have heard from so many men that it would be more impudent to disbelieve a lie from so many witnesses than to defend the truth against their authority: that the **Pike** <note>original: *lucius*</note>, a river fish which the Italians call the *luccio*, if its belly is cut open for the sake of showing its milt, and then it is sewn up and placed back in the ponds among **Tench** <note>original: *tinchas*</note>, it is healed by their slime while the pike rubs its belly against them. This, however, has an obvious cause: the internal organs were not wounded, the slime itself is glue-like, and the air is not inclined toward corruption. I do not know if this would succeed for someone trying it in Italy. What else? To return to the history of sheep, does it not happen even more wonderfully on account of the regions, that in hot regions the tails of rams sometimes weigh fourteen

<margin>The tails of rams of immense weight</margin>
pounds, and twenty, and thirty, and sometimes even forty.

## Book Ten

...there may be forty, so that no **ram** <term>wether; original: *vervex*</term> here is as large as a tail is in those regions. This happens because this animal is very moist and, among quadrupeds, cold. Since the other bones cannot be extended, lest the whole animal be overwhelmed by its own fat, it sends all the moisture into the tail. It becomes immense with flesh and fat, and even the bones and sinews are extended not a little; for things of a moist nature, like fish, are always suited for growth. But

<margin>Rams with four horns.</margin>
is it not also worthy of wonder that some rams have four horns, some of which I happened to see? However, this is a lesser miracle than what **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher and naturalist (384–322 BCE), whose *History of Animals* was a primary source for Renaissance science</note> reports: that he saw a goat having a horn on its leg. This happened, without doubt, by an error of nature and an abundance of material suited for generating horns; but since in these cases the head would be weak, nature preferred to divide the burden rather than trouble the ram with a heavy weight.

<margin>Dogs into wolves, and wolves into dogs. The Lycisca. Silent dogs.</margin>
Dogs guard sheep, and over many generations, they may pass into a wild state: first as dogs, then into wolves, just as tame wolves after many generations pass into dogs. From this comes the **lycisca** <term>a hybrid offspring of a wolf and a dog</term>. Nor does the variety of their voice stand in the way, since in the West Indies, on the **Spanish Island** <note>Hispaniola, modern-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic</note>, the dogs are entirely silent. How much more are they able to howl, since even some domestic dogs howl, although this is regarded as an omen. A dog may also be bred with a fox or a **tiger** <note>In early modern natural history, "tiger" was often used broadly for various large felines</note>, producing common offspring that reflect the form of both. For when the times of gestation in the womb coincide, they can be mixed—as was said regarding trees—provided there is common food. An **alopece** <term>a dog-fox hybrid</term> from a dog and a fox, which I saw, was male and silent; I do not know if all such animals are so. Nature seems to have deliberately joined this most ingenious animal to man: for nature always strives to link like with like, and a similarity of character produces and maintains friendship. Indeed, the dog would be a burden to man if its nature were not so skillful; it is loved for the diligence and wit by which it pleases.

<margin>The fiercest dogs.</margin>
The fiercest, strongest, and largest dogs are on the island of **Corsica**, both because of the air—for things that are naturally dry grow in a humid environment—and because of their exercise and upbringing. They have a very large head in comparison to the body, which is also large. Food, fighting, the air, upbringing, and nature change them so much that they seem to differ in species. They are taught to hate certain races of men, as once

<margin>A dog of wonderful sense.</margin>
at Rhodes they were taught to hate the Turks, and **Bezerillo** <note>a famous and brutal attack dog used by Spanish conquistadors against Indigenous populations</note> was taught to hate the Indians. This was a dog that distinguished Indian men from Spaniards, according to the author **Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo** <note>Spanish historian and colonial administrator (1478–1557) who wrote a famous history of the West Indies</note>. They are especially maddened by human flesh, which sharpens their senses beyond nature. Thus he was trained to lead those who were willing, to tear apart those who were unwilling, and to spare those who were prostrate. While some attribute this to the will and indulgence of God, I attribute it either to the food of human flesh, or to habit, or rather to the **help of demons**. For I cannot be persuaded that such great cruelty would please God. This dog understood the voices of those fighting and those pulling back, having been taught to attack, tear, and drag those pointed out by finger or by name.

# Concerning Complete Animals
<note>In the Aristotelian tradition, "complete" or "perfect" animals generally refer to those that are red-blooded, breathe air, and produce live young, as opposed to "imperfect" creatures like insects or shellfish.</note>

ff iij

<margin>The Wolverine.</margin>
That animals are born with habits similar to those of humans in almost every region is shown in Lithuania by the **Wolverine** <term>original: *Rosomacha*; also known as the Glutton</term>, an animal the size of a dog, with the face of a cat, and the back and tail of a fox. For this creature is so voracious that when it gorges itself on carcasses and its whole belly is full, it squeezes its abdomen between two trees that stand close together to expel what it has eaten, and then returns to its feasting. Thus, the Lithuanians are said to be the most voracious of men. <note>This colorful description reflects a common Renaissance myth about the wolverine's eating habits, often used as a moral allegory for greed.</note>

But to return to dogs: no animal is so docile. They are taught to hunt, to scout, and to retrieve. For a dog to be so clever, it was necessary for its constitution to be of a **dry nature** <note>In ancient medicine, a "dry" temperament was associated with keen intelligence and memory, while "moist" was associated with dullness</note>; however, because of this, they are prone to **rabies** <term>original: *rabies*</term>, which is the greatest of evils and incurable for bitten men once they begin to hate water. As **Ovid** <note>Publius Ovidius Naso (43 BCE – 17 CE), a Roman poet</note> says:

> *And no medicine heals the dreaded waters.*
<note>original: *Et formidatis nulla medetur aquis*; a reference to hydrophobia, a symptom of rabies where the victim is unable to drink.</note>

<margin>How dogs are taught to retrieve.</margin>
They hunt almost by instinct, but they are taught to scout. Some search for birds by scent—these they call "keen-scented" <term>original: *sagaces*</term>, and the common people call them **Braques** <term>original: *brachos*; a type of pointing dog</term>. Others hunt hares and deer, which keep their original name. There are also "net-dogs" <term>original: *retiarij*; ancestors of setters</term>, who terrify partridges and quails with their gaze until they are caught in a net. It is common to all dogs to guard the home, to bark at strangers, and to chase the poor and those in ragged clothes. They are gradually trained to retrieve: first with a piece of bread thrown, but in such a way that the dog is forced to obey the one commanding and calling him back. Later, the bread is enclosed in a box with a nail, so that when the hungry dog goes for the bread, he carries the box when called, so as not to leave the bread behind. Gradually, the bread is removed from the nail, so that finally, by habit, he brings back the box by biting the nail. In this way, he eventually learns to bring back iron, and by the same method stones, and whatever is most difficult. Finally, a small board with bread is thrown into the water; then a nail with bread is attached to a wall with the same industry, so that the dog does not stop until he has pulled out the nail. In all these things, **hunger** must be the teacher, according to that line of **Persius** <note>Aulus Persius Flaccus (34–62 CE), a Roman satirist</note>:

> *The belly is a master-craftsman that draws out voices denied it.*
<note>original: *Venter negatas artifex edi uoces*; from the prologue of Persius’s Satires, meaning that necessity or hunger drives one to learn difficult skills.</note>

In the space of six months, I trained a dog in this way: no child could seem more teachable or more prompt at commands, as he understood even my nods. And although everything depends on the diligence of the teacher, those that are shaggy are chosen, especially those with hair that is not straight, but thin, soft, and leaning forward; these seem more clever, more patient of labor, and more obedient. These also bark little, like the **Maltese dogs** <term>original: *melitei*</term> which are quite pleasing, though of no use due to their small size. There is no fixed size for dogs, nor a single temperament, nor one color, nor one voice. Some almost equal oxen in size, others are no larger than mice; some are mute, others noisy, and others even howl. They are red, white, tawny, black, or variegated; some are fat, others runners, others lean; some are coarse and almost rustic, others gentle, cruel, or fierce; some are timid, and some are fit for everything, whether they excel in their senses or their wits. In short, nothing so closely rivals the differences in the habits and variety of men as the dog.

Indeed, some prefer elephants, and others prefer **long-tailed monkeys** <term>original: *Cercopithecos*</term> to dogs, in...

# Book Ten

...by industry and sagacity. **Arrian** <note>Arrian of Nicomedia (c. 86 – 160 CE), a Greek historian and philosopher who described Indian elephants in his *Indica*.</note> reports that he saw an elephant which had two cymbals on its ears, and with its **trunk** <term>original: *promuscis*</term> it would touch them alternately in rhythm; it danced according to the beat while the other elephants imitated him and led the dance. These same creatures are moved by mercy; they adore the king, they understand and demand an oath, they venerate the stars, and they feel pity for themselves. They recognize their rider and seek revenge against those by whom they are unjustly troubled. Indeed, nothing seems to be missing from their humanity except speech, while many men appear even more like brutes in their discipline and manners than the elephants themselves.

Their height is so great that a man standing upright with his hands extended might only equal it. In thickness, they sometimes exceed three buffalos, and their hair is similar to the hair of those animals. Their eyes are like those of boars, and their upper teeth—the tusks—protrude by two cubits <note>A cubit is approximately 18 inches or 45 centimeters.</note> or even more, with the point turned upward. The tail is like a buffalo’s; the feet are round like circles down to the nail, in which there are five nails the size of an oyster shell. On the tail, the hairs are very sparse; the tail itself is about three spans long, while the ears are two. 

On the upper jaw, the long trunk itself grows as if from the nostril, made of a hard and sinewy material covered with a strong hide. At its end, a certain attachment protrudes, circular like the tip of a pig’s snout. The mouth of the elephant is hidden underneath, much like a pig’s, and they use their trunk to bring food to the mouth. That part has incredible strength; for with one blow, it easily topples trees that twenty men would attempt to fell in vain. 

The females are more robust, more hot-tempered, and more cruel, but nevertheless smaller than the males. They walk so softly that, much like the sea, they cause nausea in those who are not accustomed to sitting on them; the young ones, however, walk with a steady gait, no differently than **ambling nags** <term>original: *asturcones*; a breed of small, easy-paced horses from Spain</term> or well-trained mules. With the trunk, they collect small coins <note>original: *stipes*; small offerings or money</note>, which is why the trunk is also called a "hand." They receive their rider with bent knees and, as I said, adore the king. With the same trunk, they pluck branches from trees to feed upon, and sometimes graze on grass. They love and inhabit muddy and marshy places like pigs; if you consider it rightly, they have no closer kinship with any other animal. 

They are spurred on by glory, and understand the voice of their driver so well that they will strike some and spare others. It is customary to tie a strong sword of two cubits to the trunk, with which they strike down both men and horses. They are feared by horses, just as they themselves dread fire; thus, the Indians protect themselves against them with torches, so that the elephants, struck with fear, may cause more damage to their own side than to the enemy. They are also said by a certain natural instinct to dread the squeal of a pig. 

The teeth [tusks] I mentioned are of such great size that, when protruding, they exceed the height of a man standing upright with outstretched arms, even if they are curved. Their thickness is like that of a human head, and their beauty is marvelous; for the teeth of the elephant are properly
<margin>Ivory.</margin>
**ivory**, though all its bones are sometimes called by the same name. Nothing is better for making combs, and they are of no small use in other works,

-># On Perfect Animals<-

...since it even sits among gems and competes with marble. Because of its solidity and the refined nature of its constitution, it is rendered a most long-lived animal. This is one privilege of elephants: for though they are surpassed in size and strength by whales and certain serpents, and in sagacity by man—and equaled by dogs—yet in the length of their lives, as far as I know, none is more outstanding. It is well known that they live for two hundred years, though many authors affirm they reach three hundred. Indeed, neither animals living in the water (on account of the more liquid moisture) can live so long, nor birds (because of their smallness), nor is a better temperament granted to any other quadruped. 

Although it may seem to move slowly, it nonetheless overtakes running men because of the vastness of its body. Two pack-saddles are placed on its back with two chains positioned under the belly; upon these, a wooden castle is fixed, in which at least six men, and sometimes as many as fourteen, fight armed with every kind of weapon. But this type of warfare, once celebrated, has become worthless because of the violence of <term>firearms</term> <note>original: *tormentorum igneorum*, literally "fiery engines," referring to the cannons and musketry that made the wooden towers on elephants easy targets.</note>. Thus far nature seems to have progressed in brute animals, that she might create the most gentle, longest-lived, robust, and rarest in size. And this is the ultimate state for this mortal matter, except for man, for whom she thought to bestow something better. 

For the elephant's blood is even quite sweet, and thin despite such a great mass. The elephant senses smells with its <term>trunk</term> <note>original: *promuscis*</note>, and it has two breasts under its forelegs, so small they cannot be seen from the side; nor do they correspond in any part to the great size of the body. The male begins to mate in the fifth or sixth year, and it truly copulates, nor does it return to its passion except every third year. The female begins to carry young at age twelve at the earliest, and fifteen at the latest; she carries the fetus for two whole years, and once she is pregnant, the male does not endure to mount her further. The calf, when born, equals a three-month-old calf in size. It consumes an incredible amount of drink and is of the greatest appetite. It flourishes around the sixtieth year of its age. It also breathes through its trunk; one member provides it with so many benefits. It is impatient of the cold, and for that reason, it is chiefly born in India.

<margin>Rhinoceros.</margin>
Where also is the **Rhinoceros**, a rare animal, the size of a horse, with hair very similar to a weasel's; it has the head of a deer, in which a single horn grows three cubits in length, in the middle of the forehead and straight, but broad at the base and tapering to a point. The neck is short, with a very sparse mane tending to only one side; the legs are thin like a <term>chamois</term> <note>original: *capreolo*, meaning a small goat or roe deer.</note>, the back part of the hind legs is very shaggy with hair, and the hooves are cloven. In general, if one pays attention, its nature is not unlike a deer's except for that horn; it is extremely wild. It is also born in Ethiopia among solitudes and squalid earth, and among serpents; it is believed in a marvelous way that its horn opposes poisons.

<margin>Elk.</margin>
But with the opposite quality of air, the <term>Elk</term> <note>original: *Alces*</note> is born deep under the Northern Pole; it is similar to a deer, with longer front legs, having a fleshy but short trunk. If its hoof is hung from the neck, it is said to <note>The text likely implies "to heal" or "to prevent."</note> <term>epilepsy</term> <note>original: *comitiales*, referring to the "falling sickness" or "comitial disease."</note>...

# Book Ten

...is believed to be able to heal [with its hoof] if anything else can, and is falsely said to lack knees. <note>This refers to the Elk (*Alces*), which medieval and Renaissance writers often claimed had no joints in its legs, forcing it to sleep leaning against trees.</note>

<margin>A monstrous animal.</margin>
<margin>The Chiurca.</margin>
Ethiopia sends another animal, very similar to a fox in its front part, but with the tail and hindquarters of a long-tailed monkey; it has human-like front feet and the ears of a bat. It possesses a pouch under its belly, in which it carries its young everywhere, and does not let them out except when it wishes to nurse them. The West Indies also sends the **Chiurca** <note>This is a description of the Opossum, which was a marvel to European naturalists due to its marsupial pouch.</note>, of the weasel family, which carries its children with it in the same manner.

<margin>Unicorn cows.</margin>
<margin>Deer-like cows.</margin>
In the same Ethiopia, there are cows bearing a single horn in the middle of the forehead, a little longer than a palm’s breadth, which curves back toward the spine; their hair is blue. Others have horns like a deer and blackish hair, which the same region produces.

<margin>The Lion.</margin>
The **Lion** is also born in these same places, arguably the boldest of all four-footed animals. It is believed that its bones, when struck together, strike out fire <note>original: *ignem collisa*, a common early modern belief that lion bones were as hard as flint</note>. It has a long body, a tawny color, a piercing gaze, and a long tail which it shakes frequently. Its fur is not straight in the front but soft and curly, and shorter on the hind parts. It is armed with a large head, a wide gaping mouth, and very large, very hard claws. Its roar is harsh. Nature made it prone to anger because it is very strong; and on account of its "hot" temperament, it suffers from a fever every other day, during which it lies prostrate and roars, not all day long, but at fixed hours.

<margin>Kinds of weasels.</margin>
There are also animals noble for their skins, such as the lynx, and many of the weasel kind: **Martens**, **Squirrels** <note>original: *Varij*, referring to the 'vaire' or grey squirrel, highly prized in furriery</note>, **Lardironi** <note>likely a regional name for a type of stoat or weasel</note>, **Ferrets**, and **Genets**. Spain sends these last ones; they are similar in form and habits to the domestic weasels which we call **Beech Martens**, though their skin is variegated and distinguished by alternating black and ash-colored spots.

<margin>Sable skins.</margin>
But of all, the **Sables** <note>original: *Zebellinae*</note> are by far the most precious for their beauty and rarity. The Lapps send these from the furthest reaches of the North.

<margin>Neck skin is more durable.</margin>
The skins from the neck are generally more durable, as seen in the fox, the ferret, and the *lardirollo*; for nature has fortified that part with a thicker hide because of the danger [of predators], and thus it happens that the hairs are held in longer.

<margin>The Suac, an animal of very sweet flesh.</margin>
In **Sarmatia** <note>A historical region encompassing parts of present-day Poland, Ukraine, and Russia.</note> there is seen an animal similar to a sheep in size, very swift, whose wool is ash-colored. It has very small horns and its flesh is so sweet that the Emperors of the **Tartars**—for so the **Scythians** and **Parthians** are now called—do not disdain to hunt its herds. <note>This likely describes the Saiga antelope, known for its speed and its presence on the Eurasian Steppe.</note>

<margin>Why certain animals have a very pleasant scent.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle, Problem 13; Theophrastus, On the Causes of Plants, Book 6, Chapter 26.</margin>
Aristotle had denied that pleasant odors exist in animals—and so consistently that he affirmed the **Panther** smells good only to certain animals, but not truly so. Nor does Theophrastus disagree with this. But since the excrement of animals is abundant and moist, it can hinder the sweetness of the scent. In plants it is not so: since their "waste" is small, dry, and well-concocted. Therefore, for animals whose waste smells good, it must be small and dry, as in the large lizards—which we spoke of above and called "crocodiles"—and in snakes. Thus, so that nature would leave nothing untouched, she diligently strove to create a scented animal, and not just one, but by various means.

<header>On perfect animals.</header>

# On perfect animals.

<margin>The Civet.</margin>
Nature therefore fashioned the **Civet**, an animal very similar to a cat but larger, which Spain exports. It is armed with teeth and is so wild that it does not grow tame over any length of time. Its hair is quite rough, and its snout is elongated, like that of a badger. In the genitalia of both the male and female of this species, Nature created a small pouch from which a fluid—falsely called "semen"—is collected with a silver spoon <note>original: *semen argenteo cocleari excipitur*. Renaissance naturalists often used the word "semen" for any potent glandular secretion.</note>. It has such a fragrant odor that just three grains of it surpass the weight of many pounds of the most aromatic wood. Indeed, it was necessary for Nature to achieve something great in such a difficult undertaking. For humans also tend to strive when they approach a difficult task, so that they might produce something worthy of admiration; and when a goal must be surpassed, we strive to achieve it by no small margin. 

<margin>The Musk deer.</margin>
Nature observed this same rule in the **Musk deer**. I have seen this animal only when dead, in the Street of the Standard-bearers in Milan <note>Milan was a major hub for the trade of exotic medicinal and aromatic goods.</note>, whereas I have seen living Civets, both male and female. The Musk deer is similar to a roe deer in size, shape, and hair, except that its color is more of a bluish-gray. Its hair is also thicker than that of a roe deer. It has two teeth above and two below, and it differs from the roe deer only in this and in its scent; for the variation in hair might arise from its native region, just as animals moved to other lands produce offspring far more different from themselves than this slight variation in hair caused by a change in climate. 

Therefore, a bladder <note>This refers to the musk pod, a scent gland found in the male musk deer.</note> collects below the navel of this animal and is filled with a blood-like substance, which in the strength and sweetness of its scent surpasses and excels every other substance known to this day. It is clear that animals of this kind were known neither to Aristotle nor to Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC) was a successor to Aristotle and is often called the "father of botany" for his work on plants and scents.</note>. This is not surprising, since even Galen—to whose work these animals were more relevant, as no modern ointment is now without them—did not know them at all, though he lived more than four hundred years after those earlier authors. Because of this scent-bladder, I can hardly say how much pleasant odor the whole animal gives off, even though, as I said, the one I saw was not only dead but had been so for a long time. Furthermore, if that pouch is placed in a chest for many years, all the clothes kept inside will be fragrant with a wonderful scent.

<margin>The Beaver and Castoreum.</margin>
The same strength exists in the scent-glands of the **Beaver**. It is abundant in Persia, but it is imported from the city of Badakhshan <note>original: *Balaschcham*, a region in modern-day Afghanistan and Tajikistan famous in the Middle Ages for rubies and musk.</note>. There is such power in it when it is not yet old or adulterated that **Varthema** <note>Ludovico di Varthema was a 16th-century Italian explorer whose travel logs provided Europeans with some of their first eyewitness accounts of the East.</note> reports that four men, who one after another moved it to their nostrils, immediately suffered nosebleeds. But out of greed, the Persians allow no pure **Castoreum** <note>A yellowish secretion from the castor sacs of the beaver, highly prized in medicine and perfumery.</note> to reach us. I have never seen the beaver itself. They say it is an animal the size of a dog but elongated, gentle, with black and shiny hair. It has a very long tail which, from the middle downward, is very similar to the tail of a fish. With its webbed hind feet—like those of a goose—it swims in the water with the double help of its back feet and its tail. It builds houses out of wood with marvelous skill; for it uses the sharpness of its teeth, which are very strong, just like a saw for cutting wood.

<header>Book Ten</header>

-># Book Ten<-

<margin>How wild animals may be tamed.</margin> All wild animals can be tamed if they are fed human milk by a woman immediately after they are born, or, what is easier, if they are fed dog's milk. In this way, even cats learn to love their master and to fawn upon him and accompany him no differently than dogs do.

<margin>The Cercopithecus</margin> There is also the **Cercopithecus** <note>original: *Cercopithecus*. While this term usually referred to long-tailed monkeys in antiquity, the description here of a man-sized creature with human-like legs and genitals likely refers to a Great Ape, such as a chimpanzee or orangutan, which were often called "Wild Men" by early modern travelers.</note>, an animal of rare form, the size of a man and with the shape of a man. Indeed, by its legs, its male organs, and its face, you would call it a wild man of the fields, though it is entirely covered in hair. No animal persists in standing longer than it, with the sole exception of man. It loves children and women just as the men of its own region do, and when it escapes its chains, it attempts to lie with them openly, which we ourselves have witnessed. Nevertheless, it is still a wild animal, but of such industry that you might say some men possess less natural wit—not our own people, of course, but the barbarians who inhabit the harsh regions of the sky, such as the Ethiopians, certain Numidians, and the Lapps.

<margin>The light dog.</margin> But let us pass on to other things, among which is the **light dog** <note>original: *canis leuis*. This is the Three-toed Sloth, which early explorers like Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo described. The name is ironic, as the animal is famously slow.</note>. This animal is sent only from the West Indies; it is the size of a hare, but nearly as thick as it is long. It grows so fat and has such very thin legs that while it walks, it drags its belly along the ground because of its weight, for its heaviest body cannot be supported by such weak legs. It has four claws on each foot, but the digits are not divided—rather they are joined together—and they are sharp and hooked like those of birds, which it uses to climb trees. And although it can scarcely walk on the ground—covering only fifty paces in a single day—it nevertheless dares to climb trees. Its eyes and mouth are small, and for that reason, it does not bite. Its face is round like an owl's, with a smooth neck on all sides which it moves in different directions as if in a daze. A crown of hair surrounds its face, which seems to draw it out in length. It lacks a tail, and its hair is between white and ash-colored. All these things, though wonderful, do not seem entirely inconsistent with nature. But that it appears to feed on air and dew, and that it sings almost the entire night with six notes perpetually descending, so that a musical proportion of a <term>sesquioctave</term> <note>A sesquioctave is a musical ratio of 9:8, representing a whole tone interval.</note> is preserved with a semitone in the middle—that is truly not unlike a miracle. By day it is silent and sees little, which is why this alone among the four-footed animals can truly be called nocturnal.

<margin>Why there are more nocturnal birds than animals.</margin> There may be others, but nocturnal birds are more frequent: the eagle-owl, the bat, the little owl, and many others. The reason is that there are not as many obstacles in the air for flying birds as there are on the earth for walking quadrupeds. And since seeking food is a matter of greater difficulty by night than by day—especially for those animals that live by prey, since others lie hidden and safe, whether by their own strength like boars, or by the suitability of their location like nightingales among thickets and brambles, or by the height of their location like ravens and crows in towers, or by extreme narrowness like small birds, or by fortifications like the fox—it was necessary that an animal intended to wander only at night should be endowed with wings; otherwise, it would be consumed by hunger. For cats, wolves, and foxes, as well as roe deer, do seek food at night, but the day is as common to them as the night. And so, nocturnal birds...

<margin>The Cat.</margin>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "perfect animals" (complex quadrupeds), shifting from the primates and sloths mentioned previously to the specialized anatomy of cats and the ecological balance of the New World, specifically mentioning the anteater.</meta>

<page-num>235</page-num>
<header>On perfect animals.</header>

# On perfect animals.

We cannot say that quadrupeds are nocturnal, except for this animal described above.

Nature gave the **cat** <note>original: *Murilegus*, literally "mouse-gatherer," an older Latin term for the domestic cat.</note> a greyish-blue and shining eye so that it could see at night. Horses and wolves also see better at night than humans do; however, human reason showed us how to create lights, and for this reason, nature neglected to provide us such great care for seeing in the night. Wherefore it is also believed that the cat's pupil grows according to the cycle of the Moon. It has also been observed—so that it might seem less a marvel—that the pupils of men change not only on different days but even within the same day, so that at one moment they appear large, and a few hours later, they are seen to be diminished. <margin>Visible parts of the eye.</margin> I call the "pupil" the black part in the middle; however, that which lies around it and varies according to the difference of men and animals is called the **Iris** <term>Iris: named after the Greek goddess of the rainbow because of its varied colors.</term>. The *pessi* <note>original: *pessi*. In Renaissance anatomy, this likely refers to the ciliary region or the colored ring of the eye.</note> are located around the iris, and the white of the eye is around the *pessi*; the interior corners are called "fountains" <note>the tear ducts or medial canthi</note>, the exterior ones are called "bucks" <note>original: *hirci*</note> or *paropiae*, and the circumference of the eye is called the *Eon*.

But to return to cats: there are various kinds of them, perhaps because almost all savage animals are similar to them in appearance—panthers, lynxes, leopards, and perhaps even tigers. For they share the size of their claws, the strength of their hides—which are patterned, multicolored, and beautiful—a round head, a short face, a long tail, agility of body, ferocity, and a diet acquired through hunting.

<margin>Every animal feeds on those things from which it is generated.</margin>
It is common to every living thing to feed on the materials from which it is born. Since it is weak from the beginning, from where else would it get its food than from where it was born? But in those creatures that are born from putrid matter, this habit almost always remains, since they never reach great strength: thus **gnats** <note>original: *musciliones*</note> feed on wine, worms on mud, and caterpillars and others on the same leaves where they were born. Birds and quadrupeds, however, seek another kind of more solid food with a harder beak or with teeth that have already grown.

<margin>When any animal becomes abundant, another is born that feeds upon it.</margin>
<margin>The ant-bear.</margin>
When some animal becomes overly abundant, nature usually brings forth another to feed upon it. This serves a double benefit: so that the multitude of the first does not bring great ruin to a place, and so that a convenient food supply is provided for the others who eat them. Thus, since ants are excessively abundant in some parts of the West Indies, an animal was born there which they call the **ant-bear** <note>original: *ursus formicarius*. This refers to the Giant Anteater (*Myrmecophaga tridactyla*), which early explorers described as a type of bear due to its size and claws.</note>, because it snatches them up and devours them with its tongue. In this way, the region's losses are provided for, since this animal seems prepared for no other use. For it is neither wild nor prone to biting, and is called a "bear" more for its bodily resemblance than for its strength or ferocity. It breaks apart the very solid homes of the ants with the moisture of its tongue; then, once these are scattered, it draws those sticking to its tongue into itself and devours them.

For animals that could not easily become the prey of others, nature has provided other checks: either by the fewness of their offspring, the brevity of their life, the necessity of a harsher climate, or some difficulty in giving birth or rearing, so that they do not grow into an immeasurable multitude.

<margin>Crocodiles.</margin>
If **crocodiles** produced many eggs, and if "crocodile-lizards" <note>likely referring to smaller monitor lizards or similar reptiles</note> multiplied too much, they would become far too numerous; but they cannot live except near water, for they are amphibious...

<page-num>236</page-num>
<header>Book Ten</header>

# Book Ten

...and besides that, they are vulnerable to the injuries of the waters, nor if they pursue anyone can they turn themselves, but they are only able to proceed straight ahead. From this, there is a certain opportunity for flight. Some who are aware of this nature, trusting more in reason than in the terror of the monstrous beast, turn about with many strikes; since the beast cannot at all bend itself to the side, they finish it off—even though it has the hardest and impenetrable skin—wherefore it is better dealt with by the blow of a club than by a thrust, or a spear, or a sword.

<margin>Fish in hot and sulfurous waters.</margin>
But let us now come to the fish: which are sometimes found in hot sulfurous waters, as at Buda <note>Modern Budapest, Hungary.</note> in Pannonia <note>An ancient Roman province in Central Europe.</note>; sometimes indeed in alum-bearing waters, as at Julium Carnicum <note>Modern Zuglio, in the Friuli region of Italy.</note>. There are immense living creatures in the waters, especially in the sea and even more so in the ocean, particularly under the **Torrid Zone** <term>Torrid Zone: The tropical region of the Earth near the equator, which ancient geographers believed was too hot to support life, though here the author notes it produces giants.</term>, because there heat and moisture contribute to growth, and saltiness to preservation. The vastness of some, such as the **Whale** <note>original: *Cete*</note>, is incredible. 
<margin>The Orca.</margin> 
<margin>The Turtle.</margin> 
<margin>The Whale.</margin> 
The **Orca** <note>original: *Orcas*</note> is seen, which as if it were skirmishing above the waters, has two huge wings. The **Turtle** <note>original: *Tartaruca*</note>, whose shell Ludovico Varthema <note>original: *Ludouicus Vertomanus*, an Italian explorer who traveled to India and South Asia in the early 1500s.</note> reports to have seen weighing one hundred and three pounds. Thus, some fish exceed the size of small houses and huts, and others, like the Whale, even exceed palatial homes.

<margin>The Octopus.</margin>
<margin>A monstrous fish.</margin>
There are also fish with feet, such as the **Octopuses** <note>original: *polypi*</note>, so named from the multitude of their feet; its head induces bad dreams because, being hard for digestion, it sends out dark vapors no differently than an onion, but far more powerfully. Others are shapeless, such as one that has skin like a pig's, almost the size of an elephant, with a pig-like head, leathery feet, without teeth, and with small eyes; it has two holes under the belly near the tail. Its tail is very long, an arm's length in width, which length each ear-fin fills; the skin is thicker than a finger is wide. Perhaps it is of the octopus kind. It happens that many fish lack teeth, but few take no food. 
<margin>The Sturgeon.</margin> 
Yet the **Sturgeon** <note>original: *Sturio*</note> does not feed; some have called this the *silurus* <note>A large species of catfish.</note>, for it has no mouth, but only a small round hole through which it avoids the mud; and yet it grows to the size of a young ox. Indeed, I have seen those that exceeded one hundred and eighty pounds; its flesh is most sweet and it lacks bones.

<margin>The Walrus.</margin>
On the other hand, the **Walrus** <note>original: *Morss*</note> is a fish near Muscovy <note>The Grand Duchy of Moscow, or Russia.</note> in the lakes from the northern ocean, having very large teeth, from which they are accustomed to make the hilts of swords. For the teeth of fish are not only of this kind but also of other large ones, white as ivory, but far more firm in workmanship.

<margin>Animals that smell good but are of little use.</margin>
There are also scented fish, such as a certain very small kind of octopus, and a certain species of flying beetles among the insects; then among birds, the hens of the West Indies—or rather a kind of vulture—for it follows corpses and corrupt things, yet it smells good on account of the intensity of its heat and the dryness of its temperament.

<margin>The Torpedo.</margin>
There are also fish famous for their powers, like the **Torpedo** <term>Torpedo: An electric ray. Ancient and Renaissance writers were fascinated by its ability to deliver a numbing shock that could travel through a fisherman's spear.</term>, which the Genoese call the **Tremoriza** <note>original: *Tremorizam*, likely named for the "trembling" or shaking caused by its electric shock.</note>.
