# On complete animals.

<margin>The Sea Urchin.</margin>
...root. <note>This fragment "rizam" (root) likely completes a word from the previous page, perhaps describing the attachment of a sea creature.</note> A very common type is the **sea urchin** <note>original: *echinus*</note>, which is covered in spines; the hands of fishermen who catch them grow numb and sluggish due to a certain innate power, which however only exists while the creature is alive. But there is another "echinus," not of the spiny torpedo-fish type, but of the shell-fish kind, which the Latins call the **Remora** <note>The suckerfish, famous in antiquity for supposedly being able to stop ships by clinging to their hulls.</note>. It is named *Echeneis* <note>The original Latin text here uses "Echinus" again, but provides the Greek etymology for "Echeneis."</note> from the Greek phrase *to hold the ship* <note>original: ἀπὸ ἔχειν τὴν ναῦν (*apo echein ten naun*)</note>, because it stays ships by clinging to their hulls. This is why it delayed the trireme of **Gaius Caligula Caesar**, which was a bad omen for him. It is very similar to a large slug and is rare, so much so that it has not been seen since those times. From this, it is clear that the remora is different from the torpedo-fish, although **Aristotle** thought they were of one kind due to the similarity of their names and effects. <margin>Book 2 on the nature of animals, chapter 14.</margin>

<margin>The cause of the variety of color in shells.</margin>
There are also animals in the sea that do not move, such as shellfish and oysters, in which nature is seen to have played in a marvelous way with a variety of colors. The reason is that, just like trees and herbs, they take on forms and colors according to their species, but they do not retain those colors later due to an abundance of moisture; in shellfish, however, because of their earthy substance, the color remains and is fixed. This variety occurs through the specific order of their ridges, because even a small thing that is varied and mixed in passing appears to be crafted in a certain fixed order as the spaces grow equally. However, it is common to almost all other animals that their hooves, claws, hair, horns, and beaks follow the color of their skin; yet this is not always necessary. <margin>Hooves, claws, hair, horns, and beaks follow the color of the skin.</margin>

<margin>Why the sea makes shells hard, but not seaweed.</margin>
But I shall return to the sea: for it is the father of monsters. By its saltiness, those things that remain fixed grow hard; thus it is for oysters, shellfish, and **coral**, although the latter is soft while it hides under the water. But why do the shells harden and not the seaweed <note>original: *alga*</note>, which also grows in the sea? The reason is that seaweed grows, and for that reason, it cannot resist the waves of the sea; therefore, it was created thin by nature so that, by being compliant, it might escape and avoid the sea's force. Shellfish and oysters stay at the bottom and are created thick from the beginning. We have said above why seaweed is soft, and it follows by the opposite reasoning that shells are hard. <margin>Turtles.</margin> **Turtles** <note>original: *Testudines*</note> seem to be of an ambiguous nature; the ocean of the **West Indies** <note>referring to the Americas</note> sends forth the largest ones, whose shells can serve as shields. Six men can sometimes hardly carry one. <margin>The Manatee.</margin> The best fish there is the **Manatee**, which can scarcely be carried on a wagon by two yoked oxen; its flesh so closely imitates the meat of a calf <note>veal</note> that if someone did not tell you it was a fish, you would swear it was meat. This happens because great heat "cooks" the moisture; for the flesh of a land animal differs from the substance of a fish in that a fish’s moisture is processed by very little heat. They report that a stone is found in the head of this fish that is most healthy for treating kidney stones. It has breasts, with which—by a rare example—it suckles its young; it gives birth to twins, matching the number of its breasts. There are those who call it the **Boa**, because its head is exactly like that of an ox, it has two arm-like appendages, a flat back, and a skin of scales and very hard hide. It is as teachable as a dog, becoming quite tame, and it remembers injuries. There is also the **Shark** <note>original: *Tiburo*</note> there, easy to catch and useful because of its voracity, and notable for its size... <margin>The Shark.</margin>

...strength, as well as the healthfulness and sweetness of the flesh.

Among the greatest wonders of the sea is the **shark** <note>original: *Tiburo*. From the Spanish *tiburón*, likely referring to a shark species, possibly the Tiger Shark.</note>, in which the male has a double reproductive organ and the female a single womb. It has a double row of teeth and gives birth to live fish of its own kind rather than laying eggs. The **sea seal** <note>original: *uituli marini*, literally "sea calves."</note> is an even greater object of wonder: it has breasts and hair, and it snores in a marvelous way while sleeping on the shores. Even **Pliny** <note>The Roman author of *Natural History*, the standard reference for nature in the Renaissance.</note> was hardly believed when he said its hair, when made into a belt or other ornament, stands up when the tide rises and lies flat when it ebbs. Now that this animal has become known in the **West Indies** <note>original: *Indo mari*</note>, and the inhabitants of the island of **Hispaniola** <note>The island comprising modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic.</note> call it the **Sea Wolf** <note>original: *Lobum*, from the Spanish *lobo marino*.</note>, this no longer seems like a tall tale. They claim that placing its right fin under one's head induces and strengthens sleep. And this is the same fish whose skin we mentioned earlier is never struck by lightning. Indeed, if everything reported about it is true, I do not know if nature has created anything more miraculous, since the wearing of that same skin is believed to heal certain diseases. They even say it can be trained and is capable of learning; it recognizes its masters and, according to legend, once greeted the Roman people with a lowing sound and gestures. It seems that nature, much like fortune, has denied everything to some and granted everything to others.

<margin>The Sawfish.</margin>
On the other hand, there is a useless fish called the **Viuella** <note>likely the Sawfish.</note>. Although it is large, its meat is not pleasant to eat. However, the form of this fish is marvelous: it bears a sort of cartilaginous "sword" on its forehead about four palms long <note>roughly 32 inches or 80 cm</note>, or even more from the base to the tip, which is serrated with sharp and powerful teeth.

<margin>Flying fish.</margin>
**Flying fish** are also born there, which I myself have seen. They are small and winged, having long wings next to their gills, about a palm's length or more. While these are wet, they support the fish in the air, but when they dry out, the fish falls back. They travel in schools and are at constant enmity with the **dorados** <note>The Mahi-mahi or Dolphinfish.</note>. Many are found near **Bermuda**, also known as **Garza Island** <note>original: *Garzam insulam*, likely named for the herons (*garzas*) found there.</note>.

<margin>Why fish are hardly ever tamed.</margin>
<margin>Dolphins.</margin>
Fish are rarely tamed because they possess little and dull intelligence. For this reason, **Dolphins** are the most easily tamed, as they are the swiftest of fish, the most intelligent, and not at all lacking in human-like emotions—especially mercy. They have a hooked snout and a mouth positioned somewhat awkwardly under the head; this is so that, being so fast and strong, they are not permitted to do whatever they please to everyone. For the same reason, almost all birds are easily domesticated, while quadrupeds, having an intelligence midway between birds and fish, are sometimes 

<margin>Why hares and mice are not tamed.</margin>
tameable and sometimes not. Some animals cannot be tamed because of fear, such as mice and hares; for how can you love someone you are convinced is plotting against your life? This is what those who live in fear convince themselves of. For this reason, even if **tyrants** bestow favors on many, they are loved by no one because of constant fear. This happened to **Nero** <note>The Roman Emperor famous for his cruelty.</note>, yet you should not think that Nero was not generous to many people. Thus, fish, because of their intellectual dullness and the difficulty of handling them, are hardly ever tamed. Furthermore, as I said, fear is usually a factor.

<margin>Why dolphins are the most tameable of fish.</margin>
Since the dolphin is strong in intellect, very bold, and the only one among the fish that breathes air, and for that reason can be handled easily, it must be that either it alone, or at least...

# On Complete Animals <note>original: *De perfectis animalibus*. In Renaissance biology, "perfect" animals were those considered fully developed or complex, such as mammals and birds, as opposed to "imperfect" insects or spontaneous generation.</note>

...and it becomes the most tame among all fish. If it could be moved into shallow water, it would differ very little from a **dog** in its tameness.

<margin>Why the sea is sterile in some places.</margin>
It must also be considered that it happens in the sea just as it does on land: there are certain regions in it that are sterile, while others are very abundant with fish. For in some places, food is plentiful, while in others it is absent; moreover, the diverse odors and varied tastes of the lands <note>Likely referring to runoff or the composition of the seabed.</note> taint the waters, which the fish either seek out or flee from. Nevertheless, the shores usually abound with fish because of the food found there, and the deep pools <note>original: *gurgites*</note> because of the safety they provide.

<margin>The abundance of birds of every kind is the greatest proof of the air's healthfulness.</margin>
By the same logic, the air also abounds with birds, while other air—so to speak—becomes sterile. The abundance of every kind of bird serves as an indicator of the air's health in two ways: both because the birds themselves are highly sensitive to the qualities of the air, and because food is also available to them. Truly, this sign should be applied to entire regions, not just parts of them; for it is possible for birds to be abundant even in a valley where the air is heavy compared to the plains and hills. Truly, the hills and plains possess the best healthfulness of air. This is why in the **Moluccas** <note>The "Spice Islands" in modern-day Indonesia.</note> islands under the equator, a dead bird is gathered from the ground or the sea which is never seen while living: because it lacks feet. 
<margin>Bird of Paradise.</margin>
Although **Aristotle** <note>The Greek philosopher whose biological works were the primary authority at this time.</note> denies that any bird lacks feet, this one—which I have now happened to see three times—lacks feet solely, so to speak, because it lives in the high air and far from all human sight. Its body and beak are similar in size and shape to a **swallow**, but the feathers of its wings and tail, when it spreads its wings, exceed a **hawk** in size and almost equal an **eagle**. You can imagine the thickness of the feathers; for it is as great as reason teaches is appropriate for the smallness of a little bird. They are, therefore, very thin, and except for their thinness, are entirely similar to the feathers of female **peacocks**; they do not resemble the feathers of male peacocks, as they are not "eyed" <note>The "oculi" or eye-spots found on a peacock's tail.</note> like those seen on a male peacock's tail. The back of the male of this little bird is curved inward, and reason itself teaches that the female lays her eggs in that cavity, since the female also has a hollow belly, so that they can incubate the eggs using both cavities. A thread hangs from the male's tail, longer than three palms <note>A "palm" was a measurement based on the width of a hand, roughly 3-4 inches.</note>, black in color, somewhere between square and round, neither thick nor very thin, but not unlike the thread with which cobblers are accustomed to sew boots. We believe that while the female incubates the eggs, she is tied more firmly to the male by this; nor is it a wonder that they live perpetually in the air, for there is no doubt that the bird is naturally supported with its tail and wings spread in a circle. Even a change in movement can shake off any weariness it feels. I believe its only food is **heavenly dew**, which serves as both food and drink. They claim this is also the case for the **swift dog** <note>original: *cani leui*. Possibly referring to a greyhound or a legendary lean dog believed to live on air.</note>, and also for the **Chameleon**. 
<margin>Why the Chameleon changes color.</margin>
It is reported that the **Chameleon** changes color from the things adjacent to it; it is an animal not unlike a lizard, but not a little larger, slow in motion, and with a wide, gaping mouth. Nevertheless, it does not turn white; its skin has the color...

<page-num>240</page-num>
# Book Ten

...of a watery color spontaneously, and as if shining. It has been shown that colors are transferred into the underlying material; from there, when they are transferred—both because it shines and because it has almost no color of its own—it receives and reflects a foreign color. No one should wonder at this, since a hare hides among clods of earth because its color is very close to a dark gray, and it easily changes into the likeness of the earth itself, remaining hidden by that similarity. Moreover, that color of the Chameleon is a certain potential for all colors except white, because white is too intense. It could also be that the Chameleon, by looking at a color, changes its **spirits** <note>original: *spiritus*. In Renaissance biology, "spirits" were subtle fluids or vapors that carried life and emotion through the body.</note> and the **humor** <note>original: *humorem*. Vital fluids like blood or bile that determined health and temperament.</note> in which those spirits are contained, expressing it through the skin. For when a great deal of blood arrives, the cheeks of children redden out of shame; others turn pale with fear; others turn dark with anger, because the blood, already "toasted" by heat, is poured out to the face. The very sight of a color can also change the blood: from red, an image of red is born, and red blood is spread about. What wonder is it, then, if the imagination is affected, that the thin humor of the Chameleon—which is congealed by air alone, not unlike the air itself—simultaneously receives and reflects every color?

<margin>The Ostrich <note>original: *Struthiocamelus*</note></margin>
And so, to return to the bird <note>Referring to the *Manucodiata* or Bird of Paradise mentioned on the previous page.</note> which is itself of a very thin substance, nature seems to have carefully provided such a miracle so that it could live in the air. However, it is not likely that it feeds on pure air, because air is too thin. Nor does it feed on tiny insects, for no gathering occurs there for their generation—which is undoubtedly necessary—nor are such insects seen in the bellies of these birds as they are in swallows. Yet this is not a definitive proof, since it must be believed that the Birds of Paradise <note>original: *manucodiatas*</note> are consumed only by old age. But neither do they feed on vapor, since vapor is more abundant lower down, from where they would be seen descending; vapor is also sometimes destructive. Therefore, it is likely they feed on dew throughout the night.

Just as the Bird of Paradise is a bird in such a way that it never inhabits the earth, so by a contrary logic the **Ostrich** never departs from the earth, so much so that you could not call it a bird unless you looked at its form. It took its name, I believe, because it imitates the **camel** in the length of its neck and legs. It is, in fact, a little taller in stature than a man. *Struthio*, moreover, is the Greek word for a "little sparrow"; the compound name <note>original: *Struthiocamelus*, or "Sparrow-Camel."</note> is used as if by irony, just as if one were to call someone a "Pygmy Giant" or a "Gigantic Little Man."

The Ostrich is of the sparrow kind, but with the size of a camel; the neck, beak, eyes, and head correspond to a goose, but in proportion to its own size. The wings and tail have feathers of many colors—blue, white, red, black, green—and no other bird has such delight or beauty in its feathers. For this reason, soldiers decorate their helmets with no others. Although there are some who, because of their rarity, now fix both the wings and the tail of the Bird of Paradise into crests, adding the superstition that whoever carries them into war will not be wounded. The ostrich's body is covered with thin feathers, and the legs with even thinner ones, so much so that they look like human legs rather than a bird's; for in their size and roundness, and because they taper narrowly and gradually toward the knee, they resemble a human thigh, especially since they lack feathers...

<page-num>241</page-num>
<header>On Perfect Animals <note>original: *De perfectis animalibus*. In Renaissance biology, "perfect" animals referred to complex creatures with red blood and specialized organs, as opposed to "imperfect" insects or mollusks.</note></header>

# On Perfect Animals.

They lack white flesh <note>The author likely refers to the dark, beef-like meat of the ostrich compared to poultry.</note> yet imitate it; their feet are split like those of oxen, with hooves; the leg is like a goose’s, but in proportion to its great size. Its gait is slow. The one I saw was gentle, though I do not know the temperaments of the rest. Their eggs resemble the size of an infant's head and are round; when they grow old, they take on the appearance of ivory. They are often hung in temples, for they last a long time because they are very hard, and once the moisture is removed, they become almost like bone. It has lashes on its upper eyelid and runs as fast as a horse—so swiftly, in fact, they say a horse will flee from it and not dare to look at it. It runs with its wings held upright, yet it does not fly. They say it can hurl stones with its feet and even **digest iron**, which happens because of its intense heat and the thickness of its stomach. They also say it hatches its eggs with its eyes <note>A common medieval and Renaissance myth: that the ostrich hatches eggs simply by staring at them intensely.</note>; however, it does not actually hatch them this way but merely watches over them, for the chicks are brought forth by the heat of the Sun. I have never heard its voice. It is certain that this is the largest of birds—if indeed it ought to be called a bird at all.

<margin>The Eagle.</margin>
Truly, the largest of the flying birds among us, and the one which all others fear, is the **Eagle**, known to everyone. It is of a most noble sort, much larger even than a goose, though more so in its wings and tail than in its body or weight. However, in <margin>Bialozor <note>The "Bialozor" is a Slavic name for the Gyrfalcon.</note></margin> Jurra in Scythia <note>A historical region covering parts of modern Russia, Ukraine, and Central Asia.</note>, there is a bird called the **Bialozor**. It is white under its belly with a certain brilliance, and its wings and tail are larger even than the Eagle’s. Other birds dread it so much that the Eagle itself is terrified when it is seen, even though it does not exceed the Eagle in body size.

<margin>The Greatest Bird.</margin>
In India, they also report a predatory bird that is far larger than an eagle. It is black and purple with white feathers running through it. Its beak is yellow, marked with blue and crimson <note>original: *phoeniceo*</note> colors, so beautiful that nothing could be more pleasant to see. Because of this beauty and its great size, the handles of daggers <note>original: *capuli*</note> are often made from the beak of this bird; it is well known that this beak must be exceptionally hard. This is established as the largest of the flying birds. <margin>The Swan.</margin> Hence it is necessary for birds to have huge wings, as is the case with **Swans**, which are distinguished from geese almost entirely by their size. Although they are entirely white and are said to sing most sweetly among all birds, their voice—as I have observed while listening frequently—is like that of a goose. Yet this highly praised kind of bird tears apart its own and devours them; however, at the moment of death, it sings sweetly. Hence Ovid says:

->So, when the fates call, cast down in the wet grass,<-
->The white swan sings by the waters of the Maeander.<-
<note>original: *Sic ubi fata vocant udis abiectus in herbis, / Ad vada Meandri concinit albus olor.* From Ovid's *Heroides*.</note>

<margin>Alcatraz <note>likely referring to the Brown Pelican.</note></margin>
There is a genus of fish-eating birds, famous for the size of their beak and body, called the **Alcatraz** in the West Indies. It is marked with ash-colored and saffron feathers, with a beak two spans long ending in a point—though the beak of both the stork and the crane is not far from this size. <margin>Picutus <note>The Toucan.</note></margin> But the **Picutus** has a beak larger than its entire body, though the body itself is only slightly larger than a quail. The beak is therefore quite long, three fingers wide where it joins the head, and hooked. It uses this to drill into trees, where it is often harassed by long-tailed monkeys <note>original: *caudatis simijs*</note>, despite its skill and its beak...

<header>Book Ten</header>

...it defends itself beautifully despite being tiny. What is marvelous about it is that it has a feather in place of a tongue, which makes it very different from the nature of other birds; it hisses loudly, and the same land nourishes it as the **Alcatraz** <note>original: *Alcatraz*. In this period, the term was used for various large seabirds like the pelican or gannet found in the New World.</note>.

<margin>The Kinglet. The Hummingbird, the smallest of birds.</margin>
But regions differ in smallness just as they do in greatness: among us, surely the smallest of birds is the **Kinglet** <note>original: *Regulus*, likely the Goldcrest or Firecrest.</note>, which flits through the thickets, half the size of a sparrow. But the same India <note>The "Indies" often referred to the Americas in Renaissance natural history.</note> sends the **Hummingbird** <note>original: *passer muscatus*, literally "musky sparrow," an early name for the hummingbird.</note>, which someone might rightly judge to be a flying hornet or wasp because of both its speed and its smallness. It is adorned with feathers of gold and green and other shimmering colors; its size is a little larger than a bee, its beak is like the thinnest needle, and together with its nest, it barely equals the weight of twenty-four grains of wheat. It builds this nest from cotton. It is bold, and it attacks the eyes of those seeking its nest, being safer due to its speed and smallness. It is established, therefore, that this bird is of the thinnest substance, and for that reason warm and bold; for since it has a beak, feet, a tongue, wings, organs, feathers, claws, and a brain, then many other things in it must be of a subtle and well-crafted substance. And as I believe, this is the smallest of all birds. Just as the most skillful bird lives in that same

<margin>The Foolish Sparrow.</margin>
India, which they call the **Foolish Sparrow** <note>original: *passer stultus*. This refers to the Weaver bird or Oropendola, named "foolish" ironically because of its incredibly clever nest-building skills.</note> by the opposite sense of the word: it is a black bird with shimmering white feathers on its neck, the size of a thrush. It protects itself against long-tailed monkeys—of which there is an incredible number there—in such a way that even a human could not find so many advantages against danger. First, it chooses a tall tree covered in thorns, so that the predator is terrified by the height and kept away by the discomfort of the thorns. From the most prickly branches of this tree, it hangs a very tough nest so that it cannot be broken by an enemy. It constructs a narrow entrance so the enemy is kept out and only the bird itself can enter; it is wide at the bottom so it can live comfortably with its chicks, especially because it is forced to collect their waste in the same place, with no other exit open than the one through which it entered at the top. But because it knows the enemy uses its hands just like a human, it extends the length of the nest to four palms <note>A "palm" was a unit of measure roughly 3 to 4 inches.</note>, so that even if a hand is inserted, it is still far from the bottom, and in this way, it protects the eggs or chicks hiding inside.

<margin>The Parrot.</margin>
A most talkative and beautiful bird, as well as very teachable, is the **Parrot**, which both Indias <note>Referring to the East and West Indies.</note> send. It speaks very easily because it has a broad tongue and excels in memory and talent. We have reported the causes of these things above. Next in speaking is the magpie, then the crow, then blackbirds, thrushes, and even starlings. Birds meditate when they are learning words.

<margin>Our Peacock.</margin>
I would believe that nature could fashion no bird more beautiful than our **Peacock**, unless I were to see it: with so many eyes in its tail, with feathers so long and thick, with such a variety of colors, such brilliance, and such selected kinds of colors. Even white and black—the former of which is somber on its own and obscures the others—are avoided <note>The author suggests the peacock's natural colors are superior to simple black and white.</note>. He himself senses his own beauty and cries out...

<header>On perfect animals.</header>
<sig>hh ij</sig>

# On perfect animals.

...while it looks at its feet, it despises their deformity <note>A common medieval and Renaissance belief that the peacock, though proud of its feathers, is ashamed of its "ugly" black feet.</note>, and raises its tail into a wheel, exposing it to the Sun so that it may appear more beautiful; it rejoices in the admiration of the men who gaze upon it, and for that reason, it holds it up until it is exhausted.
<margin>The Indian Peacock.</margin>
Thus it happens that there is an **Indian Peacock** <note>original: *Pauo Indus*. Based on the description of the fleshy, color-changing skin on the head, the author is describing the North American Turkey (*Meleagris gallopavo*), which reached Europe in the early 16th century.</note>, which some consider to be a rooster. For it too admires its own tail when turned into a circle, moving exultantly. However, it falls far short of our peacock in beauty. On the other hand, the **Indian hens** I have seen are more beautiful than ours, adorned with peacock feathers, but they lack a full tail, nor do they raise it into a circle. Therefore, the species of animals are to be distinguished not by their colors, but by their very behaviors. The Indian peacock is also adorned with skin around the head, the color of which it changes at its own will. For while it is of varied color, distinct with white and ash-grey, when the blood flows into it, it becomes now blue, now red. And since it is a wrathful creature, it offers the appearance and effect of an angry man, having that skin instead of a face. But another thing is even greater: that it sometimes gathers this skin so that it can hardly be seen, and then it is pale; but at other times it extends it, so much so that it covers the entire beak, and then it usually appears purple. This is proof, therefore, that it is extended together with the blood. However, I have also seen it pale and extended at the same time. It is gathered and contracted because it is thin and loose, like the skin of the **scrotum** <term>scrotum: the pouch of skin containing the testicles</term>, which sometimes appears entirely contracted and sometimes greatly extended. Therefore, looseness and thinness are the causes of both the extension and contraction, as well as the change of colors.

<margin>The Rooster.</margin>
But our **Rooster** <note>original: *Gallus*</note> always has an upright and red crest, unless it is unwell; and if this animal were rare, it would be most worthy of admiration not only for its form but for its song. It exults in its voice, and it is heard from afar, even at night at a distance of a thousand paces or more. It sings when it wakes from food; 
<margin>Why the rooster sings.</margin>
yet usually it sings when the Sun is at its meridian, at midnight, and when the rays first begin to shape the dawn. It follows, therefore, the strength of the Sun, and divides the whole natural day into eight parts; yet not only at sunrise, but when it approaches the boundaries of the dawn, and likewise before noon. It is sewn into the **parricide’s sack** <term>culeus: a leather sack used in Roman law for the execution of those who killed their parents</term> along with a serpent, a dog, and a monkey, 
<margin>Why are the rooster, monkey, serpent, and dog sewn into the parricide's sack?</margin>
though it is innocent of this crime, and is cast headlong into the sea. For just as the monkey is not a man yet appears to be one, so is he who has killed his own father. The **Serpent** excels in treachery and is most hostile to the human race, no different than a parricide. **Dogs** seem to hate everyone, and this animal alone spares absolutely no one, not even its own kind. The Rooster, though innocent of this fault, is perhaps added because of its similarity to the **Gauls** <note>A pun on the Latin *Gallus*, which means both "rooster" and "a person from Gaul" (modern France). The author suggests Roman historical animosity influenced the choice of animal.</note>, whom the Romans especially hated, or because it is most proud. It is cast into the sea as if unworthy of any element, and as one whose company would infect the air, earth, and water; for this reason, it is sewn into the sack after being first beaten with blood-red rods.

But leaving these superstitions aside, let us return to the most holy and wise laws of nature. It had been decreed to make birds that would fly, and the air...

<page-num>244</page-num>
<header>Book Ten</header>

<margin>Why birds have small heads.</margin>
...might adorn it (for let this example of birds be taken as a principle for other animals as well), and for that reason it was necessary for them to have the lightest possible head. Consequently, among all living creatures, birds have the smallest heads; those birds that do possess a large head are endowed with thin bone, a hollow space for the brain, and large wings. From this smallness of the head, two disadvantages followed: the first

<margin>Why birds lack teeth.</margin>
was that they were dull-witted <note>In ancient and Renaissance physiology, a small head was often equated with a lack of "room" for complex reasoning or memory.</note>, and the second was that they lacked teeth. For a small beak was necessary for a small head, and thus teeth would have been of no use—partly because they could have no strength, and partly because the smallness of the beak and mouth would have hindered chewing. Nature removed the first inconvenience through the heat and dryness of their temperament. This also benefited the generation of feathers and the lightness of the entire body. Furthermore, so that the whole body might remain dry, Nature willed that they be satisfied with very little drink; and

<margin>Why birds lack a bladder.</margin>
for that same reason, they also lack a bladder <note>Birds do not have a urinary bladder; they excrete nitrogenous waste as uric acid along with their feces to conserve water and reduce weight for flight.</note>. But to compensate for the lack of teeth, Nature substituted a second stomach, so that hard things might be gradually digested within it. Since hard foods

<margin>Why birds have two stomachs.</margin>
could not be crushed by teeth, they required a longer time and a more solid, narrower stomach <note>The author is likely distinguishing between the crop or proventriculus and the muscular gizzard (ventriculus).</note> in which a small amount of food could be contained, which otherwise would not have sufficed for the body. Therefore, it was necessary for a second one to be substituted, in which the food could be halfway digested and where enough food could be held. Nature also made their feet small, because such weight would be useless for flight, and gave them a sharp sense of sight, because they have a need to see from a distance and look down from on high. If some birds deviate from this norm, they do not achieve perfect utility; for some claim that **Diomedean birds** <note>original: *Diomedeas*. In classical mythology, these were the companions of Diomedes turned into birds, often identified by later naturalists as shearwaters or albatrosses.</note> have teeth, but such things are necessary for variety rather than for practical use. The **bat** <note>original: *Vespertilio*</note> has teeth but lacks feathers, and its wings and body are entirely cartilaginous. Indeed, when it falls to the ground, it can hardly rise again to fly.

<margin>Tame birds.</margin>
Almost all birds are tame by nature, especially those that do not feed on flesh. For in the **New World** <note>original: *orbe nouo*. A reference to the Americas, reflecting the era of exploration during which this was written.</note>, when ships first arrived at uninhabited islands, many birds—especially those of the dove kind—allowed themselves to be caught by hand. Nor do birds fear the company of men unless taught by experience. Hence, not a few hermits have kept tame birds from among those that are usually wild, such as sparrows and crows.

<margin>The Mole.</margin>
But leaving the birds, let us pass to an animal of another kind that lives underground, which they call the **Mole** <note>original: *Talpam*</note>. It is ash-colored, similar to a mouse in shape and size, except that it lacks eyes. For of what use would eyes be to one living perpetually underground? Indeed, it hates the air so much that if it is forced to come out into the light, it dies in a very short space of time. It also differs in its tail; for why should one living underground be fashioned with such a long tail? For the same reason, it has very short legs and very sharp claws. The shortness of the legs is necessary for one pushing through narrow passages, and the sharpness of the claws allows it to dig through the earth with ease. Moreover, it performs this work so quickly and extensively that those who first see the earth dug up by a mole are greatly amazed.

# On Perfect Animals.

<margin>Humans are participants in the divine counsel.</margin>
It is clear, therefore, that Nature has been wonderfully diligent in all things, and has provided for everything not just incidentally but by design. Humans—to whom God has granted this benefit so that they might find the first cause of things—are participants in that primary Nature; nor is the Nature which established these things of a different kind from the minds of those who have been able to fully understand the reason why they were made so. Therefore, no animal living permanently underground and endowed with blood has been found except for the mole. For certain kinds of serpents and harmful frogs have been found not only under the earth and in very old tombs, but—what is more wonderful to say—even inside solid rocks. But these properly lack blood, and do not give birth to offspring of their own kind, but rather eggs or nothing <note>The author is reflecting the Renaissance belief in spontaneous generation, where certain "lesser" creatures were thought to arise from inanimate matter or rot rather than from parents.</note>.
<margin>Animals found within solid rocks</margin>

<margin>Crabs.</margin>
There is also another genus of ambiguous life and discordant form, which is signified by the name of "crab." There are many types of it: the marine, the river-dwelling, and the terrestrial type is also found, which hides in the earth, especially in the West Indies. The one that lacks a tail is called <term>Gammarus <note>Original: "Gammarus." While this often refers to a lobster or crayfish, the author distinguishes it here as a tail-less variety of crab.</note></term>. It produces white stones in its eyes; when a crab has shed its harder shell, it puts on a soft one, and then the stones become very large as the material of the shell is consumed into the stones <note>These "stones" are gastroliths, calcium deposits stored in the stomachs of crustaceans to help harden their new exoskeleton after molting.</note>. The *Gammarus*, however, moves from its side crosswise.

<margin>Pulses unique to each animal.</margin>
And let these things suffice concerning the more portentous animals. Now it must be known that for individual animals, the pulses and breaths are different and unique: for instance, in dogs and goats, which you would never dare to claim are similar to humans, nor to each other. But certain limbs retain this ratio of the pulse even after being torn from the whole—though Aristotle and Galen might disagree—so that the tongue of an ox might throb for a whole day; for that implanted power still remains. Or perhaps that heat, while it is dissolving like air in water, moves the bubbles; for even dry stones, burnt horns, and <term>agalochum <note>Aloeswood or agarwood, a fragrant wood used in incense and medicine.</note></term> move bubbles in water while the water enters to take the place of the air. This, then, which we have said about the ox’s tongue is quite remarkable—they claim that if it is younger, it even moves when thrown into water, though I myself have not yet experienced this.
<margin>Book 6, Concerning the Opinions, Chapter 10. <note>A reference to Galen's work *De placitis Hippocratis et Galeni*.</note></margin>
<margin>An ox's tongue, once removed, throbs even for an entire day.</margin>

<margin>Neither fly nor dog entered the Temple of Hercules.</margin>
More wonderful still is what Solinus <note>Gaius Julius Solinus, a 3rd-century Roman geographer whose work was popular in the Renaissance.</note> reports as still enduring in his own times: that neither dog nor fly enters the Temple of Hercules in Rome. I heard a few years ago that in Venice there was a house of exchange into which flies would not enter, which was later consumed in a public fire. Perhaps because it was situated on high and was very drafty, and being stiff with iron and marble, it was avoided by the flies? For flies hate all metals because of their coldness and because they have difficulty sticking to them. But for the dogs, another reason must be sought, unless perhaps something is buried or hung in the temple's vestibule that dogs flee from. I have often heard from Carthusian monks that they are not infested with bedbugs <term>cimicibus <note>Bedbugs</note></term>; this is supported by the testimony of so many that it would be shameful to deny what is light-minded to believe. Nevertheless, they offer the reason that they do not eat meat <note>Carthusian monks followed a strict vegetarian diet, leading to the folk belief that their blood or environment was unappealing to parasites.</note>. Or so it is claimed.
<margin>Carthusian monks are not infested with bedbugs.</margin>

<page-num>246</page-num>
<header>Book Ten</header>

# Book Ten

...whether it occurs because of cleanliness, or some other art, I have not yet been able to determine. However, I labor less to seek the cause of *why* it is so, when it has not yet been sufficiently explored by me *if* it is so.

<margin>Nature has armed all animals against six types of disadvantages.</margin>
Therefore, let these many great things said about animals suffice. Nature has armed each of them against the scarcity of food and drink, for the preservation of offspring and the young, against diseases, against the injury of the seasons, against other animals, and finally—with a certain peculiar diligence—against man, because he is the most clever <note>Original: *sagacissimus*. This implies not just intelligence, but a keen, hunting-like shrewdness or "scent" for things.</note>. In the first place, she armed them against the lack of food by means of speed, sagacity, and by ensuring they were born in places where there would be plenty. She provided the pleasure of Love <note>Original: *Veneris*, referring to Venus/sexual reproduction.</note> and affection for their offspring for the preservation of the species. Swamps, thickets, hiding places, caves, thin branches, waters, and mountain peaks—all these she gave for the protection of the young. She also taught them herbs for health, as well as abstinence and rest; these are greater aids than those provided to man through the help of the medical art, which often suffers from the ignorance of physicians. Against the calamities of the seasons, she provided trees, mountains, burrows, hides, wool, hair, and feathers. Against other animals, she provided spines, teeth, speed, jumping, wings, claws, hiding places, poison, water, sagacity, and horns. Against man, however, she armed the fish with the element [water], which is the safest protection; indeed, if they were not deceived by their own greed, they could hide safely in the depths. Snakes are protected by the lowliness of their bodies, which is why they hide in burrows during the winter, and when they emerge, they are concealed by the grass.

<margin>Why man alone, almost among terrestrial animals, does not see at night.</margin>
Birds she protected by day with wings; quadrupeds with swiftness. At night, she made it so that man could not see without light, whereas almost all quadrupeds see—dogs, wolves, hares, horses, donkeys, oxen—and thus they can wander safely and enjoy food and drink, while by day man possesses all the glades. But for birds, because light was denied to them even at night, the tops of trees and towers and then the evening gave them a bed, so that they might be safe from the snares of man by both the difficulty of the location and the darkness. This arrangement for all animals also resulted in a benefit for man: since he was to be the wisest of all, a very moist and very cold brain was necessary. He had to have a very hot heart so that his very soft body could endure labors; yet a very soft body was necessary so that it might consist of the finest matter, fit for a spirit capable of such great things. Therefore, in a very moist and very cold brain—to trace the matter from first to last—it was entirely impossible to place shining and dry eyes, such as those found in the cat <note>Original: *murilego*, literally "mouse-gatherer."</note> and nocturnal birds, which possess a very dry brain. 

->Wherefore, I shall now first begin to speak<-
->of the necessity and form<-
->of man.<-

# BOOK ELEVEN
## On the Necessity and Form of Man.

<margin>Why man was created.</margin>
**W**e must therefore first determine for what purpose all things were created, and whether all things were defined primarily for the contemplation of man alone. Thus, the beginning of this discussion must establish whether animals are understood by nature only by their genus <note>A "genus" is a broad category or "kind" of living thing.</note>, or also by their parts, or even as individuals—a question that carries even greater uncertainty regarding man. Next, we must ask whether animals, plants, and other things exist for their own sake, or for the sake of man; and if they exist for man, do they do so directly, or through a certain order where some exist for others? For example, are grasses for the sake of the hare, hares for the fox, and foxes for the convenience of man? Indeed, no more beautiful or difficult a debate than this has ever been found in ancient times. For there is a great doubt as to why there are not more genera of animals than these, if nature attempted to fill whatever she was capable of producing, or why she was content with these alone. 

This doubt is usually answered in many ways. Epicurus <note>While the author attributes these ideas to Epicurus, the verses that follow are actually from the Roman poet Lucretius’s *De Rerum Natura*, which explains Epicurean philosophy.</note> spoke beautifully on this, saying that nature made everything she could, but only those things remained which possessed some excellent power by which they could protect themselves. For he says:

> And the earth attempted to create many monsters 
> Of wondrous appearance, arising with strange limbs,
<margin>Then he also adds:</margin>
> The androgynous <note>original: *androgynum*; an individual possessing both male and female characteristics.</note>, between both sexes. 
> For whatever you see breathing the vital air, 
> Either cunning, or courage, or finally mobility 
> Has protected and preserved that species from its earliest age, 
> And there are many things which, because of their utility to us, 
<margin>Then a little later:</margin>
> Remain entrusted and handed over to our protection. 
> But those to whom nature granted none of these things, 
<margin>These things themselves lay helpless.</margin>
<margin>Finally he adds:</margin>
> Could not live by their own accord, 
> All entangled in their own fatal shackles, 
> Until nature reduced that species to extinction.

But Epicurus errs in two ways: first, because the doubt still remains since other forms of animals could have been created which might have survived, such as wolves with horns, or dogs with sharp claws. Secondly, because he suggests, quite impiously, that nature established all things by chance. Therefore, one of two other things seems necessary to me: either that the forms of living things are established by the number and powers of certain stars <note>The author is referencing the common Renaissance belief in "astrological biology," where the heavens influence the shapes and types of life on earth.</note>, or that they are perpetually varied by the succession of time. Evidence for this is their diversity in various regions, as was demonstrated above, and also in different eras. It is clear that not all of these, when considered as individuals, were made for the sake of man or for other animals, since many moles live and die for themselves. Nor [is it the case] of the greater part...

To say that so many kinds of serpents which are deadly to man were made for the sake of man is the mark of a completely insane person, as are the lethal poisons. What then? Were there many artisans <note>The author uses "artifices" (craftsmen) to suggest various creative forces or divine powers responsible for different aspects of the natural world.</note>, and did each one look out for the benefit of his own work? He who made man fashioned him so that he would be most wise, so that he could use all other things conveniently, or at least avoid those which could not be of use. Thus, he who created eagles was wiser than he who created the cuckoo, and yet each one looked after the permanence of his own structure. Since he had created man so that he might use all things conveniently, it seems to have happened that all created things appeared to be for his sake. But it is not so; for each thing was created for its own sake, nor was the quail made for the hawk any less than animals were made for the sake of man. Therefore, those things which seem to have been born in a worse condition are seen—falsely—to have been made for the sake of the better.

And so, from this arises the solution to another doubt: why certain animals are unhappy, and appear so, such as hares, frogs, and does. Whence that poet said:

They would be happy enough by their own nature, but the wisdom of other craftsmen <note>the creators of their predators</note> stands in their way. I speak of excellent individuals whose power dominates many, such as kings especially, and sages. Truly, the supreme wisdom of such a great craftsman <term>opifex</term> <note>A term for the divine Creator or Architect of the universe.</note> seems to me to consist in two things: that nothing was left useless in such a great mass, but all things either lived or were food for the living; and that from this so foul dross <note>The "feces" or "dross" refers to the heavy, physical matter of the earthly realm.</note>, he might fashion something that would rule over all these lower things and be similar to those supreme separate substances <note>The "separate substances" are the celestial intelligences or angels, who exist apart from physical matter.</note>. It appeared necessary that he [man] should have knowledge of all things; for which reason he imparted as much of sense, memory, and prudence as was possible to place in such crude matter. And since the higher beings excelled mortals in five things—wisdom, happiness, integrity, length of life, and security—he was unable to grant security to a mortal, but the others he bestowed as much as he could. 

Since the matter was fragile and crude, it required many aids, and was made thin. Heat indeed was necessary so that it might be thin and suffice for movements; thinness was needed for the wit <note>The "ingenium" or natural capacity for intelligence.</note>, solidity for length of life, and temperament for the sweetness and moderation of character. Who does not see that these almost conflict in two ways? But nevertheless, the most perfect composition provided all things; yet, lest it turn out entirely perfect, many and almost infinite things stood in the way. ### On the Necessity of Man
<margin>ii</margin>

...sane but out of their minds <note>original: "sani uecordes." The author is likely referring to people who are physically healthy but mentally unsound or morally bankrupt.</note>, and in a word, many would turn out wicked. Just as it happens with the gifts of the mind, so too it occurs with the body: for many are born maimed, weak, sickly, ugly, foul, cowardly, or short-lived. Yet man was not created for the sake of these specific individuals, but for the most perfect ones and for the entire species of the human race, which contains all those good things granted to it. Therefore, just as we do not judge the trees themselves by fruit that is eaten away, rotten, unripe, or falling off by some natural flaw, so too we are not the concern of nature because of the wicked; rather, just as fruit is grown for the sake of the perfect specimens, so the tree is grown for its best. He [the Creator] therefore left certain traces of their former celestial matter in these lower things, when in the beginning he separated this mortal part from that [divine] part. Nor should he be accused for not leaving the best things behind because of the bad, or for not granting us things that would be contrary to mortal nature. He fortified everything with a kind of soul, and as best as he could, he created living things with feeling and, finally, even intelligence. 

He thus endowed man with everything. From there, in a certain order, he passed from the most imperfect things—as the available matter supplied them—to the most perfect. The beginning, therefore, was from metallic things, which are like premature <note>original: "abortiuis," here meaning underdeveloped or incomplete parts of the earth's creation.</note> parts; then metals, stones, plants, sea creatures—sponges, sea anemones <note>original: "urticis," literally "nettles," but used here to describe stinging sea life.</note>, and shellfish—worms, ants, gnats, fish, birds, hares, dogs, elephants, long-tailed monkeys <term>cercopytheci</term>, and finally man was created.

For what use, after all, is a fly? To speak of one of the most vile and insolent of animals. I answer: the animal itself, as it remains in its own species and for its own sake, exists for the adornment of the world. It has been granted everything necessary for its life, and not just for life, but for a blessed life. It was made for itself, not to be a nuisance to man. For not every fly is a nuisance to humans; some remain forever in the woods, and in certain regions they do not exist at all, such as among the Lapps <note>original: "Lapones," referring to the Sámi people of northern Scandinavia.</note>, and even in the West Indies <note>original: "India occidentali"</note> there are few. Therefore, the general good ought to be preferred over the inconvenience of a few. 

Divine wisdom, therefore, made the best in each thing that could be devised from such matter. Many hares are unfortunate, but not all; for some have never seen a man or a dog, nor have they suffered persecution. It is the same regarding the species and its individuals, just as it is with a man and his own parts: who is so mad <note>original: "amens"</note> that he would not rather lose some limbs than perish entirely? So too, individuals are like the limbs of the species; it is far better for them to perish while the species remains unharmed, than for the species itself to be either destroyed or never to have been established at all. Yet it is also far better within a species that something is preserved as well in a few individuals as in many, and no function <note>original: "operatio," referring to the vital activities or "work" of a living being.</note> is completely lost. In an animal, if a limb perishes, the function also perishes, and the animal is rendered lame or blind; and yet it is better to live, even though one will eventually die. How much more is this true for the species, which is not lacking in any functions, nor is it deformed, and has achieved eternity, even if in a very few individuals...

# Book Eleven

<margin>Why all carnivores are more sagacious than the rest.</margin>
<margin>Why no flesh is as "hot" as plants.</margin>
<margin>How man could be both the hottest and the most temperate.</margin>
...is situated. Therefore, man was created from the most refined elements <note>original: "refractis elementis." This refers to the idea that elements become more "distilled" or potent as they move up the food chain.</note> so that he might attain every advantage. For first, plants are nourished by the elements; then, animals by plants; and finally, man by animals. For this reason, all carnivores—whether among fish, quadrupeds, or birds—are more sagacious than those that do not eat meat. This is due to two causes: first, because their food is elusive, for it must be found and then pursued, whereas for the others, merely finding it is enough. The second reason is that the food itself, namely flesh, is already made of refined elements. Because of this, no flesh is "very hot" in the way that is frequently seen in the seeds and parts of plants. Thus man, who also feeds on meat (and especially that of birds), was able to possess a nature that is simultaneously very delicate and very dense, very hot and very temperate. Insofar as he possesses a great deal of air and heat, and the cold elements within him—earth and water—have receded furthest from their own [heavy] nature, he is "hottest." Yet, because nothing in him is more "cooked" than it ought to be, and he consists of very little and very pure earthly matter, he is the most temperate <note>The author uses "temperate" here in the sense of a "perfectly balanced temperament" of the four humors.</note>. Because of this, when a man’s body is consumed [by fire], he leaves behind scarcely five or six ounces of pure earth.

<margin>Man was made for four reasons.</margin>
<margin>The threefold race of men.</margin>
Man himself was created for four reasons: first, that he might know divine things; second, that he might connect mortal things to those divine things, existing as a middle point; third, that he might rule over mortals. For it was necessary that in this [terrestrial] genus, just as in the celestial one, there should be something best and most noble to command the rest—here by force, but there [in heaven] by free will. The fourth reason was so that every function of thinking might be fulfilled, and there would be a "deceptive animal." For the beasts could not be deceptive due to their stupidity, while the higher beings <note>The "superi," referring to angels or celestial spirits.</note> could not be so because of their uprightness. Therefore, through his understanding, man is made similar to the gods, but through his depravity, he is similar to the beasts. Thus, there is a threefold race of men: the **Divine**, which neither deceives nor is deceived; the **Human**, which deceives but is not deceived; and the **Beastly**, which does not deceive but is deceived. As for that which both deceives and is deceived—the category that occupies the largest part of the human race—this is not a simple type, but a mixture of the beastly and human races.

<margin>How kings, sages, and peoples are known to the "Intelligences" in themselves.</margin>
But now I shall explain how nations and provinces, as well as kings and sages, are known to the Intelligences <term>Intelligences: immaterial celestial beings or angels believed to oversee the world</term> who guard them. First, I will pass over what we demonstrated in the book *On the Immortality of Souls*, namely that all individual things are known through conditions contracted through many generalities; for that is not the primary way of knowing them, but involves a different sort of reasoning. Instead, I now proceed to teach that kingdoms and peoples, as well as kings and sages, are known in themselves and far better than the wicked, the private citizens, or the ignoble. The whole human race is known, as is the entire habitable earth; and just as any province is a certain part of the whole (such as a hundredth or thousandth part), so too the mortals who live in it are known as a certain part of the whole human race. Indeed, kings themselves, and armies, and sages are the causes of these things, determining whether provinces perish or flourish in long-lasting happiness.
Therefore... <note>original catchword: "itaq;" (itaque)</note>

<margin>The three principal gifts of man.</margin>
Nature armed him with three protections: **intellect** for the invention of necessities; **speech** for mutual assistance; and **hands** for the perfection of all those things which he had either devised through his intellect or learned from others through speech. For no other animal truly speaks, since their "word" does not proceed from the mind, nor does any possess hands, but rather something merely resembling hands. Thus, through reason, he first discovered necessities: houses, clothing, weapons, and food. Later, he began to measure the earth and the seas. Not content with these, he used <term>planispheres</term> <note>flat maps representing the celestial or terrestrial spheres</note>, <term>scioterics</term> <note>original: "sciotericis"; instruments like sundials that use shadows to measure time or position</note>, and <term>armillary spheres</term> <note>models of the heavens made of overlapping metal rings</note> to call down the vast mass of the heavens—hardly even conceivable by the mind—to the earth; by reducing it to a narrow scale, he placed it before our senses and eyes. From this, he established natural philosophy and the other sciences. Finally, he applied his mind to laws, by which a multitude might live in peace.

<margin>Four areas in which men disagree.</margin>
For men used to disagree among themselves—and even now no less than wild beasts—concerning **law**, **language**, **territory**, and **customs**. For a Christian is worth no more to the followers of Muhammad, nor a Jew to either of them, than a wicked and most vile dog. He is mocked, oppressed, beaten, plundered, and finally killed or driven into slavery; he is harassed with violent rapes and foul treatments, such that a man would suffer less from a tigress whose cubs he had stolen. Moreover, there are four "laws" <note>here meaning religious systems or codes of living</note>: that of the **Idols** <note>referring to ancient Polytheism/Paganism</note>, the **Jews**, the **Christians**, and the **Muhammadians**.

<margin>The argument of the Idol-worshiper against the other laws.</margin>
The worshiper of Idols prefers his own law based on four arguments. First, that his side emerged superior in battle against the Jews so many times that he eventually wiped out that law; therefore, the worship of one God was no more pleasing to the supreme Maker and Ruler than the worship of many. Second, that when a people has a supreme King, it is proper for each person to flee to his officials and courtiers in private matters—especially the smallest ones—rather than bothering the King himself for every minor cause. In the same way, since that supreme God has the least concern for these lower matters, and the business of private individuals makes up the smallest part even of these lower things, they think it more appropriate to seek refuge with the gods who are the ministers of that highest one for every unworthy business, rather than bothering Him—whom it is a sin even to attempt to grasp in thought—with such lowly causes and prayers. Finally, they hope that through this law and these examples, they may pass from mortality to divine worship, just as many renowned for virtue have done, such as **Hercules**, **Apollo**, **Jupiter**, **Mercury**, and **Ceres**. As for miracles, they argue that manifest help from their gods and oracles were no fewer than in all other religions; nor is their opinion about God and the origin of the world less absurd—indeed, it is far more...

<margin>Six months of darkness and light in certain regions.</margin>
Therefore, leaving these matters to the judgment of victory, let us pass on to the differences between provinces. The variety of locations is so great that under either pole there is one continuous night of six months, with a day of the same length following it; yet in nearby places, the night lasts four months, and in more remote ones, two or one. These regions are inhabited under the Northern <note>original: "Boreali"</note> pole by the Lapps <note>original: "Lapones"</note>, Norwegians, and Swedes; under the Southern pole, however, dwell the Brazilians <note>original: "Basilij"</note> and the inhabitants opposite Japan <note>original: "Antijapones"</note>. It is well established that Novgorod <note>original: "Nouogrodiam"</note> is a large city and the capital of the province of the Muscovites, where in summer the light remains for several days at a time and where honey is produced in the forests without any cultivation. The city itself is made famous by a very large and beautiful temple.

<margin>Perpetual darkness in the Georgian kingdom.</margin>
But all these things are shown and permitted by the logic of the sphere itself. What is more difficult is what is reported by Hayton <note>Hayton of Corycus, a medieval historian and monk from Cilician Armenia</note>: that in the kingdom of the Georgians there is a province called Hamshen <note>original: "Hansem"</note>, about one hundred thousand paces in circumference. He asserts that he saw it himself, and it is so dark that it resembles night, and for that reason no one dares to enter it; yet the crowing of roosters, the neighing of horses, and the shouts of men can be heard from within. This region is located on the third map of Asia between the Anti-Taurus and the Moschic mountains, not far from the city of Zoriga. But since this has happened, it must suffice to have told the fable or history of such a great miracle.

<margin>A threefold reasoning for the size of cities.</margin>
There is another distinction in regions based on heat and cold. For whichever are near the poles are stiff with frost; those under the zone which the Sun presses upon are boiling with heat; those in the middle are closest to being temperate. It is impossible for cities to be populated under the poles because the land is sterile and the transport of crops is inconvenient; for this reason, people must either live as wanderers or in small villages. But those who inhabit a temperate region have moderately sized cities, for they can bring crops into them more conveniently, and they live better and more safely in these than in villages. Indeed, they are stronger because of the multitude of men and walls, and the various arts can better assist one another. It happened in Rome, however, because it held the empire of the world, that it reached an incredible size—not of its walls, but of its people. Yet in the burning regions, it is necessary for cities to be very large: first, because the soil is either sterile if it lacks water, or extremely fertile if it has plenty. Because of this inequality, when a place suitable for nourishing a multitude is found, it is natural for a very large city to be built and for a very numerous population to flock to it. Another more powerful cause is that since merchandise comes from far away and through deserted and dangerous places, it is necessary for many to travel together...

->On the Human Condition.<-

# On the Human Condition.

<margin>The four greatest cities of the world.</margin>
...merchants travel in the manner of a military column for security; therefore, once they have established a base in some city, it would be too inconvenient for that company to wander, not only for the merchants but for the cities themselves. Thus, it is better and far easier for all neighbors to flock to that single place. When this persists for many years, it happens that even from a small village, a most populous city is born. Such cities are Quinsay <note>original: "Quinsai"; modern-day Hangzhou, China</note>, Singui <note>likely Suzhou</note>, Memphis—which they call Cairo—and Khanbaliq <note>original: "Cambalu"; the Mongol capital, modern-day Beijing</note>. If anyone should raise an objection regarding Byzantium or Constantinople—although it ought by no means to be compared with these others, which have a circumference of sixty miles or more—the cause of its size is nevertheless the presence of the imperial seat.

<margin>The 62 distinctions of languages.</margin>
The third reason for distinction between peoples is language: there is nothing else in which man differs more from man, since other animals signify the same emotions with the same voices. One man is no more understood by another man than a swallow is by a lion. Truly, I could hardly explain the number of linguistic differences. There are, however, six simple types: from the mouth—and these almost hiss; from the tongue against the teeth; from the protruding tongue—and this is twofold, such as at the lips and at the palate; from the throat; and from the chest. In general, the tongue produces speech in four simple ways: sharp, reflex, upper, lower, and free. The Roman <note>Latin</note> language is "free." Furthermore, fifty-six composite modes are formed, which, when added to the six simple ones, make sixty-two types of languages based on the difference in pronunciation. But these vary individually according to the logic of names, such as "man" in Latin <note>original: "homo"</note>, "man" in Greek <note>original: "ἄνθρωπος"</note>, and "man" in Spanish <note>original: "umbì," likely a corruption of "hombre"</note>, even if there were no variety in pronunciation. There is also some difference in pronunciations, for either the same word is subjected to many types of pronunciation, or some words to some types and others to others; who, then, does not know that the types of languages are infinite? There are, 
<margin>The German language, like the Greek, successfully joins names.</margin>
however, among these some that do not easily join names together <note>forming compound words</note>, such as the Roman and Spanish languages. Others use composite names with wonderful success, such as Greek and German.

<margin>Humans who eat human flesh.</margin>
The final distinction was by customs, such as those who eat human flesh, whose kind still persists in the New World on the island of Hispaniola <note>original: "Hispanam insulam"</note>. It is necessary that these men be wild, and they have the same relationship to others as wolves do to cattle. This began from hatred; then, they were enticed by the taste, and since all wicked things increase among men by their own growth, it passed into a customary act of vengeance.

<margin>Giants.</margin>
Besides these, there are natural distinctions of sex, age, and temperament—so much so that a man differs more from another man than a goat does from a wolf. They differ, therefore, first in size: those who are immense are called giants, and those who are small are called pygmies or dwarfs. Although many monuments testify that giants existed, this especially ought to serve as proof: that in the times of Claudius Caesar, there was an Arabian named Gabbara, nine feet and nine inches in height. If this were reduced to our measurement, it would fill seven cubits <note>original: "brachia"</note> and a quarter...

## Book Eleven

...with the sixteenth. It may seem less wonderful in our age, since an island of giants has been found in the New World. I do not know, however, if that man whom the Emperor <note>likely referring to Charles V</note> presented to Italy with no small admiration was born from that island.

<margin>A large man in our age does not reach the length of three arms.</margin>
One thing is sufficient: that the size of Gabbara <note>original: "Gabbara"; a famous giant mentioned by Pliny the Elder, reportedly brought to Rome from Arabia during the reign of Claudius</note> was marvelous, since a large man today does not fill the length of three arms <note>original: "brachiorum"; a unit of measurement, often a cubit or a "braccio," roughly 2 feet</note>. I am moved, however, by the authority of those who once wrote on military matters, who established the average height of recruits as five feet; as the ancient foot measure is a fourth part smaller than our own foot measure, so Gabbara was five arms and three-quarters in length—or nine inches <note>the author is calculating Roman vs. 16th-century units</note>—which measure is double the common height of men in this age. So it was not said without reason by those authors that a man of such size was seen neither after the time of Claudius nor for a thousand years before Augustus.

<margin>The wonderful smallness of a dwarf.</margin>
Regarding dwarfs <term>pumiliones</term>, in the past year a man of full age was carried about, the length of a cubit <note>about 18 inches</note>, in a parrot's cage. But the great height of giants is no less useless for experiments of the mind than the bodies of dwarfs.

<margin>Colanus the diver.</margin>
Others are rare by nature rather than size, like Colanus the diver <term>urinator</term> <note>from the Latin 'urinari', to dive or plunge under water</note> of Catania, which is a city in Sicily; it is well known that he flourished just before our time, or rather in our own age. He used to hide under the water for three or four hours at a time, just like a fish. Nor is this very surprising, since now in the West Indies pearl divers, intent on hunting oysters, hide under the water for a whole hour everywhere.

<margin>The greatest displays of strength.</margin>
What shall I say about strength? A certain dancer used to dance before us carrying twins on his shoulders, just as many on his arms, and one on his neck. Another performer <term>circulator</term> lifted a stone, which four men could not carry, by his hair—having first taken another man onto his shoulders, which he did to help balance the weight. The same man, incredible to say, first held the mast of a ship with his teeth; then he moved it to one shoulder, and from there to the other with no help from his hands, while the mast stood upright the whole time.

<margin>The method of producing men wonderful in size or nature.</margin>
Though these things seem wonderful, they consist of four factors: the nature of the climate, breeding, diet, and art. As I said, some regions produce larger men, others smaller. It is possible to produce dwarfs just like Maltese dogs: for they are born from a small father and mother, they are bound tightly with bandages <note>referring to the practice of tight swaddling to restrict growth</note>, and they are not fed abundantly but sparingly. And would that this invention were as useful as it is easy. By the same reasoning, large men are procreated from large parents; they are exercised and fed abundantly, and they are not restricted by bandages. But nature is deceptive in size, not in smallness, regarding strength and character. For from divers, divers are born naturally; from there, art and endurance assist nature. It is possible in all these things to proceed by always increasing until human nature can bear no more, and then a return occurs.

<margin>The wonder of the Senegal River.</margin>
The Senegal River shows how much a region can influence this; that province is in the farthest part of Africa on the western side, where those who are on this side of the river toward the North... <note>original: "Boream"; the north wind or the North</note>

<header>On the Necessities of Man.</header>

# On the Necessities of Man.

Those who inhabit the North <note>original: "Boream"; the North Wind, referring to the northern regions</note> are ashy in color and small of body, but those who live beyond are black, tall in stature, and robust. This is because in that area the whole region is lush, while the other is squalid.

<margin>Three reasons why illegitimate children are of bad character.</margin>
Now, to speak of upbringing, we must see why illegitimate children <term>spurij</term> <note>strictly, children born of an unknown father or a promiscuous union</note> are mostly of bad character and rarely bear good fruit. First, they are born from low-born women without character, such as servants. Then, others are born from immodest, lying, gluttonous, and stubborn harlots; and since they take after the mother, they become like her themselves. Furthermore, their education is neglected. Also, the father is usually possessed by a shameful and immoderate lust when he begets them. Thus, the mother's nature has more power, then the education, and thirdly the father's affection. 

<margin>The method of procreating illegitimate children of noble character.</margin> 
Therefore, so that illegitimate children may be considered of noble modesty, choose not a servant or a harlot, but a virgin—poor but of noble birth—whom you shall instruct in good principles and moderation. If you have sons by her and educate them liberally, they will be similar to legitimate children. 

<margin>Vices of wet-nurses, which most harm boys.</margin> 
Therefore, choose a wet-nurse who is neither one-eyed <note>original: "luscam"; can also mean squint-eyed or having poor vision</note>, nor a drunkard, nor sickly, nor of bad character. A one-eyed nurse will make the infant one-eyed—not through her milk, but by the habit of his gaze. A drunkard prepares him for and weakens him toward convulsions, and will make him a drunkard and intemperate. A sick nurse makes a sick child; an insane one, an insane child. 

<margin>A nurse with black eyes makes the infant's eyes black.</margin> 
A wet-nurse has the greatest power to mold the character and the body, so much so that one who has black eyes may darken the infant's eyes, even if they were light by nature. Furthermore, those who spend time with the infant contribute greatly to the training of his character and even to the position of his eyes; therefore, do not pair him with a cross-eyed <term>strabum</term> servant or maid. Whatever kind of eyes you wish the boy to have, choose such a nurse. 

<margin>Four useful things for a boy that are obtained at no expense.</margin> 
Once the infant is weaned, you shall see that he has these four things, which are obtained at absolutely no expense and are therefore common even to any poor man: you should ensure he has a beautiful name, graceful manners, physical agility, and that he becomes ambidextrous <term>ambidexter</term>, which is also a precept of Plato. There are other more useful things that require a small expenditure, but are nonetheless not so easy for the very poor. 

<margin>Four other things very useful for a boy, but not so common.</margin> 
These are also four: a noble craft, living in the city, knowing how to write, and knowing how to calculate. 

<margin>How we can prevent a boy from stealing.</margin> 
Above all, you must take care that he is not a thief. This is achieved by this trick: send him to different places before you assign him the duty of buying things. Watch him when he does wrong and beat him without stating the cause <note>original: "indicta causa"; a legal term meaning without a formal trial or explanation</note>. For when he thinks to himself that you know what he did not think you knew, he will believe that nothing is hidden from you, and in that way, he will take care not to deceive. Also, buy him necessities so that he has no need to have money—I mean all the necessities you wish to allow him. In this way, through the practice of a craft, you will lead him to youth. Then, when the man is of a perfect age in both sense and body, he is to be left to his own character.

<margin>Proportions of the human face.</margin>
The form of a perfect human body is this: the face is a tenth part of the total length from the start of the hair to the tip of the big toe. A space divides this into three equal parts: that which is from the top of the nose to the hair...
