# Book Eleven

...origin <note>continuing from the previous page: "the origin [of the nose]"</note>, and from its base to the chin, so that the nose is the third part of the whole face and the thirtieth part of the total length of the body; the opening of the mouth, or its length itself, is equal to the length of the eyes, which extends from the outer corner <note>original: "hyrci"; literally "the goat," a term used for the corner of the eye or the tragus of the ear</note> to the tear duct. But this space is equal to the gap between the eyes, so that the distance from outer corner to outer corner is divided into three parts: namely, the two eyes and the middle space between them. This total width is double the length of the nose, so that the length of the eye or the opening of the mouth is double one-ninth part of the length of the face; for this reason also, the length of the nose is one and a half times <term>sesquialtera</term> the length of the eye and the opening of the mouth. Since the nose is triple the space that lies from the bottom of the nose to the mouth, this space will be half the opening of the mouth or the length of the eye. The circumference of the mouth is double the length of the nose and triple its opening. Therefore, the length of the entire face is one and a half times the circumference of the mouth, or the space contained between the outer corners of the eyes. For this space is equal to the circumference of the mouth. The circumference of the nose at its base is as great as its length; the length of the ear is truly equal to the length [of the nose], and the circumference of the ear to the circumference of the mouth itself. The opening of the nostril is a fourth part of the length of the eye. Thus, let them be arranged:

Nature uses such exact diligence in measurements, but no less so in temperament and mixture; therefore, it is now time to speak of this, beginning from generation itself.

# BOOK TWELVE
## On the nature and temperament of man.

<margin>The cause of the resemblance of children to parents.</margin>
WHEN the paternal seed dominates the maternal, the children are like the father in mind; if the opposite, like the mother. If, however, the paternal seed commands the menstrual blood, they are made like the father in body; if it is overcome, like the mother. Because of these factors, children are indeed like their fathers in mind, but like their mothers in body. For the menstrual blood is often more powerful due to its quantity compared to the paternal seed, just as the paternal seed [is more powerful] than the maternal, which is less and thinner. For the same reason, in tender age they resemble the mother, but as they grow up, they are made more like the fathers. And indeed, males come from heat, and females from cold; it is therefore fitting that males—being warmer—will be more like their fathers (who are themselves warm), just as females, who are generated from cold, will be like their mothers.

<margin>The method for procreating male children.</margin>
From this, a threefold method for procreating male sons has arisen. First, that the man should exercise, use more solid food, and have intercourse more rarely; for thus the seed becomes warmer. Second, that the mother should lie down on her right side, and rest upon it immediately after intercourse. For Hippocrates <note>The ancient Greek physician often called the "Father of Medicine."</note> said: males are generated on the right, females on the left. The herb called "male" Mercury <term>mercurialis</term> <note>likely *Mercurialis annua* or *perennis*; in early botany, plants with paired seed-pods were often labeled "male" due to their resemblance to testicles.</note> also contributes to this, as it has two things like testicles for seeds, whereas the female has clusters, according to Dioscorides <note>A Greek physician and botanist; his *De Materia Medica* was the primary pharmacopeia for 1,500 years.</note> from whom Pliny <margin>Book 4, chapter 183. Book 25, chapter 5.</margin> took it. I was examining both of these in our garden with Thomas Isaeus, the physician, while I was writing these things. From the second observation, many in our [neighborhood...]

<page-num>200</page-num>
<header>Book Twelve</header>

...they obtained their wish for a son; this third thing they have not yet happened to experience.

<margin>All children retain some trait from their father or grandfather with exact precision <note>original: "ad unguem"; literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for reaching a state of perfect completion or precision.</note></margin>
<margin>Why illegitimate children are more robust.</margin>
But to return to the matter, I know I showed in the second book, in the section on the disagreements of doctors, that all children retain something of the father or grandfather with exact precision: I speak of a wart, a scar, a likeness, or habits, or the lines of the hands. Thus, if these seeds are well mixed and joined down to the smallest parts, robust offspring result. For this reason, illegitimate children <note>original: "spurij"; those born out of wedlock.</note> are more robust, since because of the intensity of love, the seeds are greatly mixed. By a similar reasoning, those who produce few offspring—for the seeds do not always match—beget healthier and stronger ones: because those which did not match, when they are mixed, have obtained a strong cause for their mixture.

<margin>Why mules are long-lived.</margin>
For the same reason, mules are longer-lived than the horses and donkeys from which they are procreated. This is not because they abstain from sexual intercourse, for even those among them who mate live a long time, and horses that abstain from intercourse live but a short while. It remains, therefore, that this happens because of a strong mixture; for where there is a strong mixture, there is a thinness of substance, and where there is thin substance, there is also solid substance. For when those things which ought to be mixed are at odds, they require the greatest motion to be thinned out, from which they emerge thin and solid.

<margin>Why two men of the same temperament and using the same diet obtain different spans of life.</margin>
Hence it happens that two men endowed with the same temperament reach different spans of life, even though they use the same regimen; for one will die in youth, the other as a very old man. For one will be of the longest life if he consists of a dense and subtle <note>In this context, "subtle" refers to a refined, thin, or purified quality of matter.</note> substance; of a short life if subtle and rare <note>The author uses "rare" in the classical sense, meaning porous or less dense.</note>; of a moderate life if thick and rare: for it cannot consist of both dense and thick, as I have said.

<margin>The appearance of Augustus</margin>
There are those who guess the length of life from the shape of the teeth. Nevertheless, Augustus—who lived seventy-six years—had teeth that were sparse, small, and rough; yet he had eyes that were bright and vibrant, such as Alexander the Great had, as Adamantius the Sophist <note>Adamantius was a 4th-century physician and "sophist" known for his work on physiognomy, the practice of judging character from physical appearance.</note> records.

<margin>The harms of Venus <note>In medical texts of this period, "Venus" is a common euphemism for sexual activity or intercourse.</note>.</margin>
A small use of sex also contributes to length of life and strength, for in it a great deal is poured out from that arterial blood and purest spirit. Generation requires these things, for the sake of which sex itself was established. It also melts the bodies, and harms the brain and nerves, and makes them tremulous; it accelerates old age and gray hairs, and especially weakens the eyes.

<margin>Two kinds of veins and blood in us.</margin>
But since mention has been made of arterial blood, one should not be ignorant of the fact that there are two kinds of veins in us: some indeed are thin and immobile, existing on the very surface of the body, in which the blood is lukewarm and red; others truly are thick and pulsing beneath these, in which is contained yellow and very hot blood, which comes from the heart, just as the origin of the first kind is the liver.

<margin>The utility of the pulse and motion of the heart.</margin>
These thicker veins pulse together with the heart and at equal times. By this motion, the natural heat itself is preserved, and whatever sooty waste <note>original: "fuliginosum"; according to the medical theories of the time, the "natural heat" of the heart produced a smoke-like byproduct called "soot" that had to be expelled through the pulse and breath.</note> has been collected is cast out. For while they are dilated they are cooled, and while they are constricted the soot is cast out.

<margin>Why those who run have a pulsing of the veins.</margin>
That the heat is kindled from the motion itself is indicated by a violent pulse, the desire for breathing, the burning of the body, and the sweat flowing after a run.

<page-num>261</page-num>
<header>On the Nature of Man</header>

<margin>The best method for extending life.</margin>
We shall provide for the length of life by the best method if it were permitted to turn gold into a certain "water" <note>original: "aquam quandam"; refers to "potable gold," a legendary alchemical elixir believed to grant immortality or extreme longevity.</note> without any corrosive agent. I have spoken above of another kind of water, but this one is better because it is more solid. Because of its thinness, it can penetrate solid things, and because of its purity, it can perfect and cleanse the <term>vital moisture</term> <note>original: "humidum uitale"; in medieval medicine, this was the essential fluid within the body that sustained life and heat.</note>; furthermore, because of its density, it can make that moisture more solid and better. Many things have been written on this subject regarding how we might be able to liquify gold by Philipp Ulstad <note>Philipp Ulstad (c. 1473–1543) was a Nuremberg physician and alchemist famous for his work *Coelum Philosophorum*.</note>, a patrician of Nuremberg. Other things are written under the name of Ramon Llull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a Majorcan philosopher; many alchemical texts were falsely attributed to him in this period.</note>, which are not at all true. However, he added the "noble water" of the Emperor Frederick III, by which certain people reached their hundredth year, if indeed that which he describes is truly the same one.

<margin>The variety of respiration.</margin>
<margin>Why among fishes only the Dolphin emits a voice, while others are mute.</margin>
<margin>The greatest sign of a long life.</margin>
But to return to the benefits of respiration: all animals breathe, either obviously or hiddenly. In the air, birds, serpents, and quadrupeds breathe; in the water, however, fish regulate their heat with gills. The proof of this is that when they are moved into the air they are suffocated, just as quadrupeds are in the water. In the Achelous River, fish seem to emit a voice by shaking their gills. But they do not truly do so, because they do not breathe air. The Dolphin emits a voice because it breathes air; fish that do not use air are entirely mute. Crabs, however, use both water and air for respiration, and both in moderation. Flies, gnats, and silkworms breathe obviously. You might hardly see slow-moving creatures <note>original: "Tardigrada"; used here in the general sense of "slow walkers" like tortoises, not the modern microscopic organisms.</note> breathe, such as the crab, the tortoise, the snail, hornets, chameleons, the salamander, and the gecko. The cause in these cases is that where movement is frequent, frequent and large respiration is necessary; where movement is small, respiration is neither fast nor large. Because of this, large animals that breathe little and slowly are short-lived, such as oxen. For small respiration is an indication of small heat, which cannot govern a large mass for a long time. Nevertheless, the greatest sign of a long-lived life is to grow much and slowly. The next best sign is to grow little and slowly. But if one grows much and quickly, this is an indication of a short life. To grow little and quickly is proof of a very short life; for moisture that is very easily extended is also quickly consumed. That which is consumed slowly is fatty and dense and not at all watery, and for that reason, it is not easily extended. For this reason, the elephant, then man, and after that the camel (which sometimes reaches its hundredth year), are considered to have the longest lives.

<margin>The long lives of the author's ancestors.</margin>
<margin>Why man is of bad character.</margin>
I have learned from the genealogical records that from the birth of my great-great-grandfather to this day, 266 years have already passed, so that it is believed no family in Italy has a longer lifespan. A nearly similar thing happened in my maternal line: from my great-grandfather Alvysius <note>Luigi.</note> to this day, 167 years have passed. The cause of long life in man is maximum heat, an abundance of fatty moisture, and a solid thinness; the cause of brevity, however, is much dissolution. Man, therefore, is by nature very hot and very moist; because of this, he is also of bad character. For because of heat, he turns out cruel, deceitful, inconstant, and angry; but because of moisture...

# Book Twelve

<margin>Why wise men are the worst men.</margin>
...flux, weak, unable to endure labor, and a lover of luxuries: at once gluttonous and lustful. For this reason, since wise men are by nature very hot and humid, they are the worst of all unless they are perfected by philosophy. <margin>Why wise men are Melancholic.</margin> The industry they have acquired from their studies helps them to perpetrate these things; as does <term>melancholy</term> <note>original: "melancholia"; in the medical theory of the four humors, this was the "black bile" associated with deep thought, but also with physical and mental imbalance.</note>, which is produced from the thicker humor that dissolves due to excessive study and staying awake at night. Hence, to say that wise men have suffered and committed shameful acts is nothing other than saying they followed their nature, and that the study of philosophy did not benefit them. Others, mindful of slanders, have ruined their own people. Thus, the dissolution of moisture is the cause of a short life, just as abundance is the cause of long life. <margin>Why plants are more long-lived than animals.</margin> For that reason, animals live less long than plants. For it was necessary for animals to move, and therefore to have heat to consume fuel; but with heat consuming the moisture, as I said, life becomes shorter. <margin>Subtlety is useful in all things, but necessary in small ones.</margin> Furthermore, thinness <note>original: "tenuitas"; here meaning the "subtlety" or fineness of a substance that allows it to permeate others.</note> in all things is useful, pleasant, and welcome if joined with solidity: in small things, it is even necessary. Because bees are of a thin substance, they are therefore very sagacious and live for a long time, even to their seventh year. Hence Virgil:

> For no more than a seventh summer is passed. <note>original: "Neq; enim plus septima ducitur estas"; a quote from Virgil's Georgics (4.207) regarding the lifespan of bees.</note>

<margin>The long-lived life of certain animals.</margin>
The ant also lives a long time, as much as the bee. There are those who extend the life of the turtle to sixty years and more, argued by the fact that they grow much and slowly; as I said, this argument holds true not only in humans, but in all animals and plants. <margin>An account of the thinness of corpses.</margin> That man is therefore of the thinnest substance among all things, as is his fat, is shown by the tomb of Duke Alexander of Florence <note>Alessandro de' Medici (1510–1537), the first Duke of Florence. The author is suggesting his body oils were so "subtle" they seeped through solid stone.</note>. Although it consists of the whitest and thickest marble, it was nonetheless defiled by a stain as the fat of the corpse passed through it, as well as by the droplets from the columns falling onto its base. Regarding Alfonso d'Avalos <note>Alfonso d'Avalos (1502–1546), the Marquis of Vasto and a famous military commander.</note>, although his corpse had been dried with many medicines as well as salt and sand, the fat passing through the lead fell from the casket onto the stones placed beneath and defiled them; and yet, the bodies of the dead are not of such thinness as those of the living. <margin>Longevity and nobility, two chief gifts of mortals.</margin> Therefore, two chief gifts of mortals—longevity and nobility—flow from thinness itself, as if from a parent. <margin>Why man is the most lustful of animals.</margin> Among all land animals, man is most prepared for <term>Venus</term> <note>original: "ueneri"; a common Renaissance euphemism for sexual activity.</note> because he is the hottest and most humid; however, he is surpassed by birds, since they emit very little seed relative to their body size. <margin>Why wise men are weak toward sex.</margin> But wise men are less prompt toward sex because of contemplation, since their spirits are dissolved by study and are carried from the heart toward the part opposite the genitals—namely, toward the brain. Because of this, they generate sons who are weak and most unlike themselves. <margin>What might excite a dying lust.</margin> Therefore, it helps most to spend time with beautiful girls and to read erotic stories. Furthermore, it is beneficial to have paintings of beautiful virgins in one's bedchambers and never to cease sex entirely, especially since nothing is better for alleviating rare cares; baths are also useful for those who are too much dissolved by the looseness of their texture. Indeed, the very erection of the member is caused by breath <note>original: "flatu"; the catchword for the next page. In early medicine, "flatus" or "pneuma" was believed to be the airy spirit that inflated the body during arousal.</note>

...is produced by a thicker vapor, and sometimes while it is pushed down due to excitement or compassion, the member is uprighted. I have seen the member of certain men become tense while they were being hanged, and this is a type of convulsion; even the imagination of another's pain arouses sexual desire in some. So much so that, as **John of Mirandola** <note>original: "Ioannes Mirandula"; likely referring to the philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494).</note> relates, a certain man could not achieve an erection unless he was beaten; many others could not unless they were whipped. For this state follows the imagination: hence some, while they blush or feel fear, are prevented from the practice of Venus <note>original: "ueneris uſu"; a common euphemism for sexual intercourse.</note>, and they believe themselves to have been targeted by sorcery. Furthermore, the removal of the testicles, besides taking away sexual desire, prevents baldness and the growth of a beard, by producing nearly opposite effects: it also protects a man from <term>gout</term> <note>original: "podagra"; a painful form of arthritis traditionally associated with rich living and sexual excess.</note>. <margin>On hair loss.</margin> If, however, baldness or the falling out of hair or fur happens for another reason, **oil of tartar** <note>original: "oleum tartari"; a solution of potassium carbonate used in early medicine and alchemy.</note> is the best remedy; it restores falling hair and makes that which has not grown appear. Thus, nothing was made by nature without a reason, since it is heat that draws out the hair, and this oil is extremely thin and quite hot.

<margin>Why man has the largest feet.</margin> But because of heat and moisture, the human body was destined to be heavy, and for that reason it was necessary to lack wings, since it would not have been able to fly; therefore four feet were needed. But then the man would have been prone with his head down; so that he might stand on only two feet, both upright and without help, the largest and longest feet were necessary. Therefore, no animal has larger feet than man; the same logic applies to the other parts. But since **Galen** <note>Claudius Galenus (130–210 AD), the most influential physician of antiquity.</note> wrote abundantly on these matters in his books *On the Use of the Parts*, there is no reason for me to repeat what was well said by him. <margin>The reason for teeth.</margin> It is only fitting to notice this: that the parts of man are so delicately crafted that if the upper teeth are bent slightly inward, they fall out very quickly; if outward, quickly but not as much, for in speaking and eating, when they do not meet each other correctly, they weaken one another and fall out. <margin>The case of M. Antonius Maioragius.</margin> This happened to our friend **M. Antonius Maioragius** <note>Marcantonio Maioragio (1514–1555), an Italian scholar and philosopher.</note>, a man who was certainly most learned and eloquent. Teeth also grow in old age, even later than one might think; but such things should be regarded as miracles, not as the rule. For I saw in Genoa **Antonius Benzus** from the town of Porto Maurizio, in his thirty-fourth year. He was pale with a sparse beard and a stout habit, from whose breasts so much milk flowed that he could almost have nursed an infant; and it did not just drip, but was <margin>A man producing copious milk.</margin> driven out with force. This man was a soldier, and had suffered no small hardships his entire life.

<margin>Why the skull is made of several pieces.</margin> But to return to the composition of man: it was necessary for the skull to consist of several pieces so that it would be safer, for if one part is broken, it is not necessary for the whole to be ruined, and so that veins and arteries could enter more easily, and smoky wastes could exit. <margin>Skull sutures are very thin for four reasons.</margin> Nature joined its parts with very thin sutures so that they might be held together more firmly, so that the heat of the brain would not vanish, so that the approach of cold would be less open, and so that membranes would adhere to them more firmly. And although the sutures were thin, the bones <margin>What thick and hard skull bones signify.</margin> are nevertheless quite thick. However, if the bones of the head are thick beyond measure, they reveal people who are slow to learn, hardly different from wild beasts, and forgetful.

<header>Book Twelve</header>

# Book Twelve

<margin>The Indians have very hard heads and very thick bones.</margin>
The Indians of Hispaniola <note>The island comprising modern-day Haiti and the Dominican Republic.</note> possess such traits, as Gonzalo Fernández de Oviedo <note>original: "Gonzalus Fernandus Ouiedus"; a 16th-century Spanish chronicler of the Americas.</note> relates; they are so hard, in fact, that it was agreed among the Spaniards that the Indians' heads—even when bare—should not be struck, because it would break their swords. For this reason, I do not think it a mere fable what Herodotus <note>The ancient Greek "Father of History."</note> left in his writings: that the skulls of the Ethiopians are thick and extremely hard. Since there is no lack of bony matter for the brain, an abundance of heat renders the bones very thick and hard. Because 
<margin>Why the membrane of the brain is very thin and very hard.</margin>
such bones join themselves to similar membranes and to the brain, it is necessary that those people be dull, forgetful, and difficult to teach. For the membrane of the head which surrounds the brain <note>The <term>meninges</term>, specifically the dura mater and pia mater.</note> must necessarily be very thin in those of moderate temperament, so as not to harm the brain with its weight, yet hard enough so that it does not allow the substance of the brain to slip or shift during concussions. It cannot be thick without loss to the brain, unless the brain itself is thicker than is right. And another membrane is placed around it which, because it is suspended from the bone and does not touch the brain itself, could not weigh the brain down; this one is made not only hard but also thick.

Similar care even extends to the hair; for since it was necessary for the 
<margin>Why hair is thin.</margin>
head to be covered, and because it lacked flesh, nature devised hair as the lightest and safest covering. She made it grow most abundantly there, whereas in other parts of the body it cannot grow long without help; in this part, she also consulted beauty, so much so that not only for women but even for the boys whom the ancients kept for pleasure, they placed the greater part of their beauty in their hair. The most excellent hair is golden and shining, which is known to be the thinnest and most lovely; for as black hair falls away from the grace of that color, it is also correspondingly thicker.

But although nature has shown many proofs of thinness in man, nothing approaches that degree of refinement seen in the face. From 
<margin>The three greatest wonders of the human face.</margin>
this, two miracles depend: first, that although there are almost infinite numbers of men, they are all so distinguished by such a small space of the human face that not only can no two be identical, but they are immediately distinguished from those they know. The second is that she has attached such great beauty to the human body in such a small part, that for its sake we are willing to die, and we are driven even to madness by the stings of a beauty no longer seen. Sometimes she adds such great ugliness that the mere memory of it excites nausea and loathing. Nevertheless, in both structures—of the eyes, nose, mouth, teeth, forehead, and cheeks—she has not been forgotten. There is a third argument of skillful nature in this part, and a great one: that by such small changes in it, the distinctions and appearances of the joyful and the sad, the daring and the fearful, the angry and the pitying, the loving and the hating, the hopeful, the despairing, the healthy, the sick, the dying, and infinite other affections of both the soul and the body appear.

<margin>What is more wonderful inside the human body.</margin>
Indeed, inside there is another proof of nature’s wonderful refinement and industry: namely, the <term>septum of the lung</term> <note>Likely referring to the mediastinum or the membranes dividing the thoracic cavity.</note>, by which the <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: "aspera [arteria]"; literally "the rough artery," the classical term for the trachea.</note> is separated from the pulmonary vein.

# On the nature of man.

<margin>Book 3 of *On Natural Faculties*, chapter 14, at the beginning.</margin>
For air freely and perpetually passes through by breathing in and out, but for the very thin blood enclosed in the venous artery <note>original: "venali arteria"; an archaic term for the pulmonary vein, which early anatomists believed carried air or "spirit" to the heart.</note>, no exit lies open. Whence it is a wonder how Galen <note>A Greek physician whose theories dominated Western medicine for over a millennium.</note> dared to say that spirits are thinner than vapors, since vapors are carried freely outward while the spirits remain within.

<margin>The order of the parts of the human body in density.</margin>
Therefore, the order of the parts of the human body will be this: The thinnest part of all is the spirit <note>original: "spiritus"; the "pneuma" or vital life-force believed to circulate in the vessels.</note>, then bile, after that fat, then marrow, then the blood of the arteries, then milk, after that the blood of the veins, then black bile, then phlegm <note>original: "pituita".</note>, melancholy, the brain, lung, flesh, spleen, liver, veins, arteries, nerves, membranes, ligaments, cartilages; bones, however, are the thickest.

<margin>The thinnest passages.</margin>
Among the passages, however, the thinnest are those which, as was said, stretch from the rough artery <note>original: "arteria aspera"; the trachea or windpipe.</note> into the venous one; next, those which pass from the right into the left ventricle of the heart through the septum. Then where the branches of the portal vein are joined to the branches of the vena cava in the vicinity of the liver. None of these are open to the eyes, but were found by reason alone. After these are the passages that proceed from the veins into the arteries, then those of the bones, and then those of the skin, which are manifest to the sight and through which the hairs come forth: which we also usually call by the Greek name <term>pores</term> <note>original: "poros".</note>. Yet the necessity of these is so great that if they are constricted or obstructed, a fever attacks. Vapors <note>original: "halitus".</note> pass through these perpetually, and often sweat as well.

<margin>The cause of bloody sweat.</margin>
Sometimes even blood passes through, whence comes bloody sweat, when thin blood, thinned by fiery heat, is squeezed out due to distress of the mind. Although Aristotle, in the third book of *On the Parts of Animals*, refers this to indigestion <note>original: "cruditatem"; literally "rawness" or a failure of the body to "cook" or process food into healthy blood.</note>. And in the seventh place are the ends of the veins and arteries, through which the blood itself passes into the solid substance of the limbs. Common to those five transformations, however, is the process through which blood is drawn into "dew," <note>original: "rorem"; referring to the "ros," a stage in medieval nutrition where fluid settles on tissues like dew.</note> then into the hollows of the limbs, and is afterward applied, joined, and assimilated, so that the more impure part is separated, while the rest is rendered thinner and denser until it reaches the substance of the limbs. But just as a scarcity of blood does not properly nourish the strengths and the body, so too an excess is burdensome—both in itself, and because it indicates the body is not being nourished, and because it is necessary that most of that blood also be waste-filled.

<margin>Why strength does not increase as blood increases.</margin>
But when blood nourishes the body, the veins are thinned and the body is increased; in old age at least the flesh can be restored, but in youth even the solid parts themselves are restored. Therefore, the animal and the plant increase, for the logic of growth is the same in both, since it is a work of nature while that which is being increased can still be stretched.

<margin>At the end of the booklet *On Mixture*. The manner in which things increase.</margin>
The manner in which each thing increases, as Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous commentator on Aristotle's works.</note> rightly explained, is such: Imagine the shell of an egg made thinner by that which is contained within it; the form will indeed remain, but the matter will be changed. So every cavity which is in the body, when it is full of juice <note>original: "succo"; nutritive fluid or humors.</note>, is extended while the form remains; therefore, growth is according to form—for that remains—not according to the matter which is perpetually added to it. For that which is increased or nourished must remain, and in this they differ from "generation" <note>In the Aristotelian sense, "generation" is the creation of a new thing, whereas growth is the expansion of an existing thing.</note>. In every addition, therefore, which is made to the body, some part is separated, the rest is thinned and thick— <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword is "satur," likely completing the word "densatur," meaning "is thickened."</note>

<page-num>266</page-num>
<header>Book Twelve</header>

...is saturated. This also occurs in the generation of seed and milk.

<margin>The use of milk is beneficial for the length of life.</margin>
Furthermore, milk is both thick and thin; for this reason, since it is also sweet, it nourishes like nothing else. Thus, it contributes greatly to the longevity of life, second only to oil and honey. It is no less useful than those, but more dangerous in that it may curdle; therefore, it should be taken only when fresh, from young goats grazing on thin herbs, and drunk immediately after milking in the morning, followed by rest.

<margin>Why dense things are called thin.</margin>
<margin>What concoction does.</margin>
Now, someone might wonder why denser things are called thinner. The reason is not obscure: thin things cohere properly and do not admit cracks or channels, and for this reason, they are rendered dense. Therefore, concoction <term>concoction</term> <note>original: "concoctio"; in pre-modern medicine, this refers to the "cooking" or refining of food and humors by the body's internal heat.</note>, which separates the excrement <note>original: "excrementa"; here meaning waste products or unneeded matter.</note>, thins and condenses the substance. It makes it sometimes heavier, sometimes lighter: where it separates little or nothing, it makes it heavier, as in fruits which become heavier when ripe.

<margin>Which regions produce a long-lived life.</margin>
To return to the matter we were first discussing, the cause of the length of life is, as I said, the density of the matter. Closest to that cause are the aids to life, and then the regimen <note>original: "regimine"; the prescribed lifestyle, including diet and exercise.</note>. The fourth place belongs to the abundance of fatty moisture, and the last is left to the air. Britain extends the life of men to a hundred or a hundred and twenty years. Other regions are believed to extend life to a hundred and fifty, which they locate in the East of India. There is a long-standing reputation that the Indians and Ethiopians enjoy a long and healthy life. Lippus Brandolinus <note>Aurelio Lippo Brandolini (c. 1454–1497), a celebrated Italian humanist and author.</note> reports in his book *On the Condition of Human Life* that certain people are led to the very end of life without any discomfort. <margin>Laurentius Bonincontrius the astrologer.</margin> He likewise mentions Laurentius Bonincontrius <note>Lorenzo Bonincontri (1410–1491), an Italian astrologer, historian, and poet.</note>, whose handwritten astronomical book I have in my possession; at eighty years old, he enjoyed such a complete memory that whatever had happened to him as a boy, or what he had read in his youth, he held so well in his memory that you would believe they had been seen or read that very day. Therefore, the greatest aids not only to length of life but also to avoiding the discomforts of old age are a moderate diet, free from gluttony, from too much strong wine, and from exhausting lust <note>original: "venerisq; effoetæ"; literally "exhausted Venus," referring to depleting sexual activity.</note>. A joyful mind and long sleep, combined with exercise—not using medicines or bloodletting—are key. Indeed, air that is pure, bright, well-ventilated, and humid, and which is moved by winds from the east, is best. Britain has humid and warm air, and it is very little subject to decay because of its saltiness. Indeed, the dietary regimen, since it consists of meat and milk, is most conducive to the longevity of life; for Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek "Father of Medicine."</note> wrote that "weaker foods make a short life." Whoever, therefore, is denser lives longer; yet to this density, it is not softness but looseness that is opposed. Therefore, even soft people can be long-lived, but the "loose" <note>Referring to people with porous or "slack" physical constitutions.</note> can hardly be so, or at least not without great discomfort. <margin>Why man is soft.</margin> Indeed, it was not permitted for man to escape softness, but he could escape looseness. For besides the fact that man was destined to be very moist and lacking in "earthy" parts—and therefore soft—because the elements themselves were tempered, there was the added benefit that he might feel very easily and exquisitely. For this reason, children are vigorous in their senses, and among men, those endowed with softer flesh are more sensitive, and among the limbs, the brain is soft, since it is the basis of every sense.

<header>On the nature of man.</header>
<sig>II ij</sig>

# On the nature of man.

<margin>Four efforts of nature.</margin>
It seems to me that nature has shaped four things with the greatest diligence. The first of these is **man**, due to a certain divinity <note>original: "diuinitate quadam"; Cardano often refers to the human intellect as a spark of the divine.</note>, to say nothing of his other qualities. I place the **Elephant** in the second position because of its longevity and docility, and because its skin is as thick as a man's is soft. The **Diamond** holds the third place among gems for its brilliance, its hardness, and because it is not destroyed by fires. The fourth place is left to **gold**, because it consists of the thinnest <note>original: "tenuiſſimæ"; here meaning the most refined or purest.</note> and purest substance; it is touched by no rust, yielding neither to water, nor fire, nor time, and it is as much heavier as the diamond is lighter.

<margin>How animals are generated in the mother’s womb.</margin>
These, then, are the rewards of subtlety <term>subtlety</term> <note>original: "subtilitas"; the central theme of this work, referring to the intricate, hidden, or refined workings of nature.</note>. But see how much assistance this subtlety provides even in generation itself, taking the example of the egg as a starting point. First, therefore, while the heat provides nourishment, the seed of the hen gradually turns the white of the egg into tubes <note>original: "fiſtulas"; referring to the early formation of blood vessels or channels.</note>, and then indeed into something of the yolk; for the wings and legs are formed from the yolk. Evidence of this is found in those chicks born from an egg with two yolks without a separating membrane, which are born with four wings and as many feet; this is considered a prodigy <note>original: "prodigium"; in the 16th century, a "prodigy" or "monster" was a biological anomaly seen as a sign or omen.</note>, such as once occurred in Milan.

<margin>How a chick is born with four feet and wings.</margin>
Thus, whatever is empty is agitated and dried, and passes into membranes, nerves, and harder parts. Therefore, that which is formed first is the artery and the vein, and the site of the heart is established where the seed itself is located. Consequently, since the seed is in the middle of the animal, that which is produced first ought to reside in the middle. This is the heart and the liver. However, that which lies around the membranes is less dry; for this reason, one membrane encircles everything on the inside, and it is necessary that the bones be covered on all sides by a membrane. Thus, the same reasoning applied to necessity in generation as to utility in the things generated: namely, that there should be a transition from the hardest extremes to the softest parts through a middle ground. When the heat is further increased, the spirit <note>original: "ſpiritus"; the vital force or "pneuma" believed to drive physiological processes.</note> bores through the matter—supplied either by the egg or by the mother—until it reaches the membrane of the egg; or, in a viviparous quadruped giving birth, until it reaches the womb. Therefore, heat and motion, then the formation of tubes, drying, and shaping follow one another in turn until the animal is perfected. Nor is the animal's own heat always necessary; in some, it is preserved in the eggs, as with fish. In others, it is necessary that the offspring be nourished in the belly, as in vipers. In some, the laid eggs remain joined to the body until the offspring are born, as in crabs. In others, something similar to maternal heat suffices; this is how they raise chicks from eggs without a hen.

<margin>Method of brooding eggs without a hen.</margin>
Fill two pillows with chicken manure that has been very finely ground, then sew onto both of them soft, thick chicken feathers. Place the eggs with the thinner end pointing upward upon one pillow, then place the other pillow on top in a warm place. Leave them unmoved for two days, but after that, until the twentieth day, turn them so that they are warmed equally on all sides. Then, on the appointed day—which is around the twenty-first—gently lead out the chicks, which will already be chirping from the egg. This is not surprising, since Aristotle relates that in Syracuse they are brooded underground, and in Egypt with no help at all.

<margin>The bodies of animals are potential for the soul.</margin>
Indeed, the bodies of animals, before they are perfected, are in a state of potentiality toward the soul, and are ready to receive it; but when they have received...

<page-num>268</page-num>
<header>Book Twelve</header>

...they arrive at the actions themselves. They rest, however, of their own accord, and this period of rest is called **sleep**. But when they rest because the object of their perception is absent, they are not truly at rest but are merely having a respite. While the forms of things are being completed and while things are being generated, nature undergoes infinite <note>original: "absq; numero"; literally "without number."</note> imperfect forms. But because these are not recognized except by their own specific accidental qualities, the senses do not grasp their number. Therefore, while imperfect forms are infinite in number, the perfect ones can be understood within a finite number in any given age. For since matter is finite, and because it possesses a perfect soul, it demands a certain quantity; thus, the species of things cannot be infinite in number. However, whether one soul is "more" of a soul than another is a question that belongs to the investigations in the books on the *Secrets of Eternity*.

<margin>The subjects treated in this book. See Aristotle, *On the Generation of Animals*, Book 3, Chapter 10.</margin>
In this book, I have proposed to treat only those things which are subject to true demonstration. Now, a true demonstration is one in which, as <term>Aristotle</term> <note>The Greek philosopher (384–322 BCE) whose works on biology and logic formed the foundation of medieval and Renaissance science.</note> says, the senses agree with those things which have been proven through logical proof. For this reason, I have abstained in this book from all the most lofty questions as well as from uncertain matters.

<margin>The life of man is one hundred and twenty years.</margin>
<margin>Praise of Moses.</margin>
But I return to where I digressed: A very long life was necessary for man to achieve the contemplation and knowledge of all things. This life generally ends, if not sooner, around the hundred-and-twentieth year. Yet it is rare that one happens to reach that age without great infirmity. They report, however, that <term>Moses</term> reached that age without any loss of faculty. Indeed, his eye was not dimmed nor did a tooth fall out—the two specific discomforts that most often plague the elderly. It is much more a cause for wonder because many of the <term>Jews</term> after him reached that age, though perhaps not in such a state of integrity. For we must consider <term>Moses</term> to have been an outstanding man, even setting aside his divinity, for having ruled such a stubborn and unrefined people for so many years and for delivering such a useful law to them. Truly, this longevity occurred for the <term>Jews</term> because of their dietary habits—as they avoided "unclean" foods—and because of the temperate climate in which they once lived.

<margin>Why teeth fall out in humans due to age.</margin>
But why do teeth fall out in old men, while in other animals they merely become unsightly? In the first place, it was necessary for there to be many teeth, so that if one was injured or worn down, they would not all suffer. Secondly, it was necessary for the front teeth to be thinner and faster-growing, because they are used for cutting. But since they would not have lasted easily, nature willed that they fall out and be reborn <note>Referring to the transition from primary "baby" teeth to permanent teeth.</note>; the back teeth, however, never regrow, for they were sufficient for the longevity of the front ones even so. Without the front teeth—once they have fallen out—the back teeth have no use. Therefore, as the bones dry out, the roots of the teeth necessarily become thin, and they cannot stand firm when they are no longer gripped on all sides by the bone. For this reason, it is no more possible for a man to avoid the loss of teeth than it is to avoid old age or death. Furthermore, the constant labor of the brain brings about this dryness of the bone, leading to poor <term>concoction</term> <note>original: "coctio"; the physiological process, similar to digestion, by which the body "cooks" or matures nutrients into blood and tissue.</note> and the premature aging of the adjacent parts. Thus, it is inevitable that teeth become jagged and eventually fall out. However, they seem to be longer-lasting and firmer in dogs and other animals...

...and stronger because of the brevity of their lives. Dimness of the eyes occurs because the eyes require much subtle <term>spirit</term> <note>In Renaissance physiology, "spirit" referred to a refined fluid or vapor that moved through the nerves to facilitate sensation and movement.</note>, both of which are lacking in old age; however, a man can, through certain arts, protect and guard himself against this inconvenience better than he can against the decay of his teeth. Teeth also become worse or better because of the food we eat; in some people, the teeth are weakened because the gums are eroded and fail. I saw, by a contrary logic, a man whose gums had grown so much from the long-term <margin>A marvel concerning the growth of the gums.</margin> vomiting of <term>acid humor</term> <note>Likely referring to stomach acid or bile.</note> that they covered his teeth entirely. By this experiment I am led to believe—since nothing is so similar to this humor as vinegar with its dregs—that if someone were to rinse their mouth with vinegar and black dregs, the gums would receive no small increase. For since it is astringent, it even erodes the stony matter <note>original: "lapideum"; referring to dental tartar or plaque.</note> that grows around the teeth, by which the gums are pushed away. However, the drink of <term>Zethus</term> <note>An ancient or poetic term for beer or ale.</note> spoils the teeth, as is manifest in those who use it.

Having spoken of the variety of drinks, it would be shameful if we did not also speak of breads. I will omit how a few nations use bread made from dried fish ground in a mill and then kneaded with water, as is their custom. There are four types of grain from which bread is <margin>Four kinds of bread.</margin> usually made: in the North <note>original: "iuxta Baoream"; literally "near Boreas," the North Wind.</note>, it is made from **rye**; in temperate and warm regions, from **wheat**. But wheat is twofold: **Asian wheat**, which is darker, lighter, and sweeter than ours; it does not grow in spikes, but like **millet** in a plume, yet not so soft, since many spikes fill it out. In the West Indies, however, they make bread from the seed of **Maize**, from which they also make wine. It is the fruit or seed of a plant that, in its stalk, stem, and leaves, resembles our **Sorghum**—also called *Milica* or red grain—yet the seed itself is a little larger, and the stalk itself is surrounded by leaves, which does not happen in Italian Sorghum; but I believe this happens because of the difference of the province. It is sweeter, and truly, like Sorghum, it is crumbly, and neither fatty nor sticky. It yields an annual harvest with the same fecundity, and all the more where the sky and earth are in greater agreement there. I would even dare to rightly call the despised Sorghum here by the name of Maize, or Maize a type of Sorghum.

The fourth kind of bread is made from the **Yucca** root <note>This refers to Cassava or Manioc (*Manihot esculenta*), which was frequently called "Yucca" by early Spanish explorers.</note>. The plant is similar to our broom, which we call hemp, yet the root itself is very much like a carrot, but larger; it is white inside, but rough on the outside and nearly the color of wine. There is something truly marvelous in this species: it reflects the human condition, for the bread itself is life-saving to man and can be kept for a year (which is made from the root once the juice has been pressed out), yet the juice itself, if swallowed, kills instantly, <margin>Yucca: a bearer of deathly poison and of health.</margin> and can hardly be cured by any aid. Thus, as I said, death itself is joined with health and lies perpetually beside it. For that reason, while they are preparing the bread, they diligently squeeze out all the juice, which is known to be of the same genus as the juice of **hemlock** but stronger; for those who wish to meet a voluntary death there kill themselves by a drink of it, as if it brings a gentle end. In places where we use wheat, rye is common...

<page-num>270</page-num>
<header>Book Twelve</header>

# Book Twelve

<margin>Mamey.</margin>
In the place of delicacies among the West Indians, besides the other plants described above, there are the fruits of the **Mamey** tree. These are the size of a huge peach, or a pomegranate, or a quince, with a rusty-colored rind and flesh like a pear. It contains a triangular pit, within which is a rusty-colored marrow with the flavor of a peach; inside that pit is yet another marrow, or rather a kernel, which is extremely bitter.

<margin>Guanabana.</margin>
There is also the **Guanabana** <note>Also known as Soursop.</note>, the fruit of a tree shaped like a pine cone and the size of a melon. Its rind is the thickness of a finger, and inside, instead of pulp, is a liquid of a pleasant and agreeable flavor. It contains seeds that are not unlike pods in size, shape, and color. The tree itself is large with long, great leaves. This fruit is most healthy, as it is very easily digested and never rots.

Now indeed, while certain things are individual and specific to each nation, they agree in a common logic, not only in those things pertaining to nature, but also in customs. Almost all use bread, though the material from which bread is made varies; all use a certain healthy, pleasant, and
<margin>Variety of mourning displayed among nations.</margin>
agreeable drink, though this differs from region to region. Thus, almost everyone shows grief when relatives or close friends die, and they change their accustomed way of living and dress. As a result, some grow a beard who were not used to doing so; others grow out their hair after being shorn; others shave their hair who used to grow it long, like women; and others remove a beard they were accustomed to wearing. For those who usually wear dark clothes, funeral dress is white; for those who wear bright clothes, it is black. Thus we see that the logic of mourning is the same for all, yet the customs of mourning are diverse.

<margin>Why tears and sighs soothe grief.</margin>
Tears and sighs soothe mourning. Sighs draw out the "soot" <note>original: "fuliginem"; in Renaissance medicine, this referred to the smoky waste products or "exhaust" produced by the heat of the heart, which needed to be expelled to prevent suffocation of the vital spirits.</note> held in the heart from grief so that the heart may be cooled. Tears, however, press out the watery part of the blood that has been overheated, after which the <term>spirit</term> <note>The subtle fluid believed to flow through the nerves, carrying life and sensation.</note> can pass through freely.

Therefore, since pain and sleeplessness usually attack as a result of mourning—as happened to me in the year following the death of my wife, Lucia Bandarena—although I was 
<margin>Three things which deliver a man in mourning from danger.</margin>
fortified by the teachings of philosophy, nature nonetheless resisted. Mindful of the marriage bond, I rescued myself from danger through sighs, tears, and a five-day fast. For I am by nature more loving of my kin than is fitting. 
<margin>Sudden death due to "dry" mourning.</margin>
Whence my mother's sister, Tomaxina, when she had lost her husband, two sons, and as many daughters to the plague, and had refused to weep or lament according to custom out of modesty toward my father <note>original: "sororij patris mei"; her brother-in-law, whom she viewed as a stern and serious figure.</note>, who was a grave and harsh man, she suddenly fell dead, having burst inside with a great loud noise. 
<margin>The harms of suppressed mourning.</margin>
I know others who, seized by a destructive fever because of the concealed mourning for a brother, died in a short time. And even if things go as well as possible and death does not follow, the certain reward of suppressed grief is gray hair. There are, therefore, three common aids against the dangers and damages of mourning: tears, sighs, and fasting. When the force of the grief has subsided a little, you should fortify yourself with philosophy and harden yourself against those pains with its precepts. But to meditate on these things immediately after the onset of grief is neither easy nor safe.

# On the nature of man.

<margin>Why there are different kinds of languages.</margin>
But you will ask: if the general institutions of men are common to all, why are languages so diverse and the types of speaking so varied? This happens because of the nature of different places. For instance, Italians can scarcely emit a voice from the chest, while the Hebrews do so most easily, and can hardly speak except with a certain resonance. <note>The author is likely referring to the guttural sounds characteristic of Semitic languages compared to Romance languages.</note> Consequently, when words are transferred and cannot achieve their proper pronunciation, they degenerate. Furthermore, the common people, while speaking without care, corrupt and adulterate words; thus, the variety of languages always takes its origin from the common folk, as the sheer number of speakers prevails. From there, in marketplaces with a mixed dregs of nations and various tongues, other names for things are constantly arising; and as these new names are born, just like men, it is necessary for those that stood in their place to perish. The utility, however, that is gained from the variety of languages is that all the affections of the mind can be explained. An indication of this is that you cannot express the sentiment of Homer <note>original: "Homeri"</note> in Latin or in our mother tongue, nor that of Virgil in Greek or the mother tongue—much less the meaning of Francesco Petrarch’s <note>original: "Francisci Petrarchę"</note> senses, published in his mother tongue in his poems, in Latin or Greek. But just as there is utility in the variety of languages, so there is commerce in their similarity.

<margin>Why the deformed are wicked.</margin>
Therefore, we have given the cause for the human form, nature, and purpose. It remains for us to contemplate those who fall short of it. We are accustomed to call these people "deformed" <term>mutilos</term> <note>While "mutili" often means maimed, in this context it refers to anyone with a congenital physical disability or "defect."</note>: the blind, the deaf, the cross-eyed, the lame, the six-fingered, and such "monsters of nature" <term>monstra naturæ</term> <note>In the 16th century, "monsters" referred to biological anomalies or birth defects, not necessarily something frightening.</note> who are endowed with depraved morals. Astronomers settle this matter very easily, saying that the "unfortunate stars" rule them, from which a collection of outrages takes its origin. We, however, shall say that nature erred in easier things, and for that reason, she failed more truly in the most difficult things. Thus, while all deformed people are wicked, not everyone who is physically unblemished possesses upright morals; for more is required to form a soul without fault than a body. Therefore, the worst of all are the hunchbacks, since the error lies near the heart, which is the principle of the whole body. Next are the blind and the cross-eyed, because nature failed near the brain. Then come the mute and the deaf, for nature failed in a less noble part of the brain. Then the lame; these are followed by those who are blemished in a major limb; after whom come the six-fingered, and those who have joined fingers, for nature erred in less necessary parts. The last place is for warts and marks that mimic scars. But one may root out warts with oil of vitriol <note>Sulfuric acid.</note>, even those that are natural. <margin>How a place may be depilated.</margin> Likewise, a place is made hairless if you first smear it with oil, then apply a cloth soaked in lye, in which lime and orpiment <note>original: "auripigmentum" – a yellow arsenic sulfide mineral used historically in depilatories and pigments.</note> have been boiled and dissolved. For this medicine can pull out hairs by the roots; and unless you first apply oil as I said, or if the medicine stays on too long, it flays the skin. The first water from the distillation of gypsum and rock salt <note>original: "salis gemmæ"</note> does the same; the second distillation is sharper. <margin>On erasing marks of the skin.</margin> In the same way, the marks of smallpox and those that look like lentils <note>Freckles.</note> are removed by very sharp distilled vinegar; however, on the following day, one must wash the place with water in which bran and mallow have been boiled.

<margin>On the motion of the heart.</margin>
Now at last it remains, since we have spoken about all things, that we also deal with the "principle" itself: I mean the heart. For how it is moved and in...

<header>Book Twelve</header>

# Book Twelve

...whether it leaps and palpitates from **affections of love**, has been sufficiently debated. Truly, this motion is natural: for if it does not obey the will, it is not voluntary; if it is the source of functions and not disruptive, it is not "violent" <note>In the Aristotelian physics used by the author, a "violent" motion is one forced upon an object from the outside, whereas a "natural" motion comes from its own internal essence.</note>. Therefore, it is natural. 

But one type of natural motion is simple, and another is composite. The heart is expanded by a specific faculty and is also constricted by it; it does not collapse on its own. For the constriction happens slowly in those who are weak, and the constriction follows an abundance of "sooty air" <term>fuliginous air: waste vapors produced by the body's internal "heat" or metabolism, believed to be expelled through the heart's motion and breathing</term>; therefore, the motion is composite.

Is it then heat or the soul that causes this? It is better to describe heat as the instrument, but the soul as the **prime mover** <term>prime mover: the primary source of motion that initiates all other actions in a system</term>; for heat cannot pull something in opposite directions, but the soul can. 

The motion of the heart is therefore similar to the motion of the heavens, both because it proceeds from the soul, and because it has a cycle of return, and because it never ceases and is steady. Yet, this motion of the heart is composed of drawing in and pushing out, while the celestial motion is simple. This heart motion is not circular, but moves from the center and toward the center, while the celestial motion is circular. This heart motion changes according to the **affections** <note>original: "affectibus"; here meaning emotions or psychological states like fear or joy</note>, while the celestial motion is without change. This one occurs by means of heat, while that one occurs by the soul itself. The remaining differences between the heart and the heavens are the disadvantages of mortality. 

Furthermore, the affections of the mind move the heat; consequently, once the heart—which is the instrument—is moved, the body must necessarily move. Thus, from the affections of the mind alone, the entire body is clearly transformed.

# BOOK THIRTEEN
## On the senses, sensible objects, and pleasure.

<margin>A demonstration that there are only five senses.</margin>
**F**OR the senses exist for the sake of our safety. Truly, those things that encounter us are either nearby or remote. Of those that are nearby and occur externally, the sense of **touch** was established for their sake. Of those things taken inside—and since these are only taken in if we are willing—it is enough to explore them by **smell**. However, for those things that are not touched but still encounter us, **sight** is provided so we can see ahead to flee when they approach directly; when they approach from the side, they are forced to move the air and make a noise, over which **hearing** is set in charge. It is manifest, therefore, that we and the more perfect animals had need of five senses; if nature had established a sixth, it would be of no use. Thus, there shall be only five senses. **Aristotle** also attempted to demonstrate this, but he used common assumptions.

<margin>The common sensibles are also five in number.</margin>
But the things common to all sensible objects are also five: **magnitude, number, motion, rest, and form** <note>These are known as the "common sensibles" in Aristotelian philosophy—qualities like size or movement that can be perceived by more than one sense, such as seeing a rolling ball and feeling it move.</note>. Sight alone attains all of these perfectly because it requires them in the light; touch does so less perfectly because its task is only to distinguish these in the dark when we cannot use our eyes; for while we can use our eyes, it is enough for touch to recognize its own proper sensibles.

<margin>The objects of the sense of touch.</margin>
These are: **hot, cold, moist, dry, heavy, light, soft, hard, sticky, brittle, smooth, and rough.**

<margin>The eye is superior to the other senses for six reasons.</margin>
**Sight** is the most noble among all the senses that perceive externally: because it reaches further, perceives more, is more refined, is faster, recognizes more differences, and is more divine. Who doubts it perceives from afar, since it reaches the stars? It perceives more because nothing lacks a certain light or color, both of which are the primary objects of the eyes. It is also most refined, for no sense perceives such minute differences in things as it does. It is fastest, as it alone acts instantly; for the ear must wait for the arrival of sound, and smell requires respiration <note>The author refers to the fact that we must inhale to smell, whereas sight was believed to happen instantaneously.</note>. It recognizes more differences in colors and all the common sensibles, as I said, either alone or most effectively when compared to touch. It is more divine as it alone is not changed by the act of sensing nor does it grow weary; among the senses, it alone exists as the most similar to the **intellect**.

<margin>Why we fear in the dark.</margin>
Thus, it is no wonder if nature has compelled us to fear in the darkness, as if we were abandoned by our best leader. Therefore, it is not blackness or the obscurity of the shadows that drives us to fear, but because we seem weak and exposed to every injury when deprived of the help of our eyes.

<page-num>274</page-num>
<header>Book Thirteen</header>

# Book Thirteen

<margin>Why we have eyelids</margin>
...Indeed, that this is so is shown by companionship, which alleviates fear even though darkness and obscurity remain. There is hardly anyone who fears even in the thickest darkness when among many companions; furthermore, we fear more in unknown and unusual places than in familiar ones. Therefore, the eyes themselves serve as a protection, acting as so many friends and guards. For this reason, nature fortified the eye alone with **eyelids**, so that it alone, like a king, would not be forced to work against its will, nor be forced to rest when it did not wish to. Rather, at its own discretion, it might see what it wants and turn away from what it hates.

<margin>The sense of the eye is the most delicate</margin>
In contrast, even the ear is forced to hear what it does not wish to, and the sense of touch is forced to feel. That the eye is of the most delicate substance and power of sight is indicated by three things: first, that it judges most exquisitely; second, that the image of the thing seen does not consist in any physical subject—for if it did consist in the air, it would primarily have its seat there and would consequently be torn away by blasts of wind, which does not happen; and finally, that it is greatly harmed by sex <note>original: "venere". The author follows ancient medical tradition, such as that of Galen, which suggested that sexual excess depleted the "vital spirits" and weakened the eyes.</note>, by the loss of blood, and by those substances which constrict the blood. Therefore, the best part within us is also that which is the most subtle. 

<margin>Sight is located in the aqueous humor</margin>
This sense is located in the **aqueous humor** <note>The "aqueo," or the clear, watery fluid in the front of the eye. Ancient and Renaissance science believed this was the primary seat of vision.</note>, both because it was necessary for light and brightness to be placed in a transparent thing, and because we have said that air does not enter into the mixture of the eye; thus, it could only be established in water. Furthermore, the spirits, if they were in a hot or dry environment, would have been consumed by their own thinness. Nor was dryness necessary to hold the "species" <note>The "species" were the visual forms or images emitted by objects that the eye perceives.</note> so that judgment might follow, since light and brightness persist on their own. Sound, however, since it does not persist, had to be preserved within the sense organ so that judgment could follow; for this reason, the sense of sound was placed in a dry environment.

<margin>Why those who see well at a distance have a poor sense of smell, and vice versa.</margin>
Therefore, because the eye is established in the cold and the moist, while the faculty of smell is established in the hot and the dry—and both are in neighboring locations—those who see well and far off have a weak sense of smell, and those who have a good sense of smell generally do not see far. The eye, then, makes use of light and color.

<margin>The seven kinds of colors and flavors.</margin>
But there are several kinds of color. **Aristotle** divides them into seven, and he matches just as many flavors to them, so that the most pleasant flavors correspond to the most pleasant colors, the saddest to the saddest, and the middle to the middle. After we observed that he reduced them to seven, although he assigns no special honor to the numbers, we—thinking he took the number from the **wandering stars** <note>The seven "planets" of the pre-Copernican solar system: the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>—have dedicated these colors and flavors to the planets.

| Color | Flavor | Planet |
|---|---|---|
| White or Yellow | Sweet and Oily | Venus |
| Saffron-colored | Austere | Jupiter |
| Crimson | Sour | Moon |
| Purple | Acidic | Mercury |
| Green | Sharp | Sun |
| Blue | Salty | Mars |
| Black or Dark | Bitter and Rough | Saturn |

<margin>Why there are not seven kinds of smells, sounds, and sensible qualities. The fourfold sense of touch.</margin>
But why are there not just as many kinds of smells, sounds, and sensible qualities? Among the sensible qualities, there were indeed more, and the sense of **touch** is not just one. For the sense of touch seems to be fourfold: the first is that which distinguishes hot, cold, moist, and dry. The second is that which recognizes pain and pleasure. The third is that which specifically perceives the joys of sex, since we feel no such affection or anything similar in any other part of the body. The fourth is that which distinguishes heavy and light. It perceives "rough" and "smooth" by means of pain and pleasure; for that which is rough is that which inflicts distress...

### On the Senses and Sensible Things

<sig>mm ij</sig>

...[produ]ces, the smooth which is pleasant; the friable and the tough are perceived by reason. Thus there are four modes of touch. However, it is not fitting to assign only seven differences to so many modes. In the sense of smell, the specific qualities and their distinctions were hidden because this sense is very weak in us. In sounds, however, since they proceed from only one principle rather than from the first four qualities, it was impossible to find so many types. Therefore, why this occurs only in taste and sight is sufficiently clear.

<margin>The method for calculating distance, and from there the height of a tower using a mirror.</margin>
Indeed, you may grasp the power of the eye from these two experiments. First, with a mirror, you will be able to measure the height and distance of a tower, and thereafter even the depth of the sea. Once the mirror is set down, look at the summit of the tower within it, and measure the distance from your feet in ells <note>original: "ulnas". An ell is a traditional unit of length, usually representing the length of a man's arm.</note>. Then, having carefully marked the spot of the mirror, move back a little from the previous spot with the mirror by a known number of ells, and move yourself back just enough so that you see the summit of the tower again. Therefore, multiply the distance between the mirror's locations by the distance of the mirror from your feet in the second position, and divide the result by the difference of the distance between the feet and the mirror in the first and second positions. The result is the number of ells of the mirror's distance in the second position from the base of the tower. Once this is found, multiply the height of your eye by the distance now found from the mirror to the base of the tower, and divide this by the distance between the mirror and your feet in the second position; the result is the number of ells of the tower's height.

For example: let the distance of the feet and the mirror be twelve ells; then let the second position of the mirror from the first be four ells, and at that time let the feet be fourteen ells from the mirror, and my height be six ells. Multiply the distance of four between the mirror's locations by the fourteen-ell distance of the mirror and feet in the second position; this makes 56 ells. Divide these by two (the difference between the fourteen and twelve-ell distances of the feet and the mirror), which results in 28 ells for the distance of the mirror in its second position from the base of the tower. Multiply this by six (your height), which makes 168. Divide by the distance of the mirror and your feet in the second position, which was 14; the result will be 12 ells for the height of the tower.

<margin>How the depth of the sea may be known by seeing a stone at the bottom.</margin>
In the same way, we shall measure the depth of the sea. For if a mirror is placed above the eyes so that we see a stone from the stern—which we judge to be directly beneath the prow—we shall subtract double the distance of the feet from the mirror's vertical line from the space between the spot directly above the stone and your feet. We shall multiply the remainder by the height of the mirror above your eyes, and divide the product by the distance of your feet and the mirror; the depth of the sea will result.

<margin>What beauty is.</margin>
Therefore, such are the powers of the eye that we might select these two easier examples from infinite possibilities. In truth, every sense rejoices most in things it has come to know; things known in hearing are called **consonances**, and in sight, they are called **beautiful**. What then is beauty? It is that which is perfectly known to the sight, for we cannot love things which are unknown. Indeed, those things...

# Book Thirteen

<margin>Why we are delighted by beautiful things.</margin>
...the sight recognizes those things which consist of simple proportions: double, triple, quadruple, one-and-a-half <note>original: "sesquialtera," a 3:2 ratio</note>, and one-and-a-third <note>original: "sesquitertia," a 4:3 ratio</note>, as we have said regarding the human face. Thus, when columns or trees or the parts of a face are arranged according to that ratio, the sight immediately understands the equality and symmetry within them, and for that reason, it is delighted. For delight is found in knowing, just as sadness is found in not knowing. Furthermore, obscure and imperfect things are not known for the reason that they are infinite, confused, and indeterminate; since such things are infinite, they cannot be known. Therefore, imperfect things cannot delight, nor can they be beautiful. Whatever is commensurate <note>proportionally measurable</note>, therefore, is also accustomed to delight.

For this reason, the various styles of placing columns were born: the <term>pycnostyle (columns set close together)</term>, the <term>systyle (columns slightly wider apart)</term>, the <term>diastyle (wide-spaced columns)</term>, the <term>eustyle (the "ideal" spacing)</term>, and the <term>araeostyle (very thinly-spaced columns)</term>, in the comparison of length and thickness with the spaces and the <term>epistyles (the stone beams resting on the columns)</term>. Whatever the eye does not recognize, it judges to be lacking in the proportion of small numbers, and deems the whole thing to be inept, ugly, and crude.

<margin>Vitruvius’s most subtle reasoning is explained.</margin>
<margin>Three things sought for the pleasure of love.</margin>
This was the intention of <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, the Roman architect whose works defined classical proportions</note> Vitruvius: to translate the principles of harmony from the ears to the eyes in buildings and their parts. In matters of love <note>original: "venereis," things pertaining to Venus</note>, therefore, we seek beauty, nobility, and variety. Beauty delights by itself, as I said; and in colors, we seek purple and rosy hues, which are the colors most distant from the extremes. Nobility is joined with rarity; we love rare things more because it is not so easy to possess them. We always "strive for the forbidden and desire what is denied." Variety, change, and things untouched also belong to the category of rarity. So we are sometimes more distressed by illicit things because such things are harder to attain. 

All our pleasure, therefore, is either in those things which are lovable in themselves—that is, beautiful or recognized by the eye—or in those things where we seem superior to ourselves. We seem superior when attaining those things denied to others, whether because they are noble, or rare, or untouched, or guarded by a watchman, or endowed with virtue, or illicit. In all these things, or in part of them, the soul is delighted and rejoices, and seeks them even at the loss of reputation, fortune, and life. This is that "cruel love" about which I shall speak below.

<margin>Those who see sharply love less.</margin>
Therefore, those who see sharply love less, and not only less but more rarely, because to one who considers carefully, a perfect face is rare and lacks flaws—especially since smooth, hairless skin and a rosy color are required for beauty. Thus, most people love because they are blinded by a quick glance <note>original: "acie praevertantur"</note>, or they love before they truly inspect what they wish to love.

<margin>Why some love even against their will.</margin>
For this reason, very many love even if they do not wish to; they are compelled to love when the image of beauty is present, no different than those who are burned by pain. For the power of imagining does not obey the will in its entirety; nor, if you imagine something beautiful, is it within your freedom not to love. Therefore, once a beautiful form is conceived within the imagining power, we are snatched away toward love even against our will. Because of this, scholars <note>original: "studiosi"</note> love more vehemently due to the strength of their imaginative faculty. This happens through practice. And so it happens for the same reason concerning...
