### On the Senses and Sensible Things

<margin>Why lovers are sometimes prevented from being able to practice love with their beloved.</margin>
...regarding the act of love <note>original: "veneris actum"</note>, they are hindered by excessive love. For the will contracts the <term>spirits (subtle fluids believed to carry life and sensation through the body)</term>, and recalls them to the higher parts of the body; love thus hinders the imaginative faculty, by which they are most helped. For it is characteristic of man not to be able to attend well to two things at the same time. But compassion assists love—which is why love is ready for those who use force, for it dilates and moves the spirit and kindles resistance—because the power of imagination is excited. Tears, however, flow from those <margin>The cause of tears.</margin> suffering force because, in pain combined with hope, the heart and brain are contracted; then, by the heat, whatever moisture is found not only in the brain but also in the entire blood is squeezed out through the fountains of the eyes. Even horses and pheasants weep when they perceive imminent danger. But where hope is missing, there is no movement and no tears. For this reason, in extreme fears or sadness, they do not weep. Therefore, the poets rightly depicted **Niobe** <note>In Greek mythology, Niobe wept for her slain children until she turned into a stone that continued to weep.</note> as having turned to stone upon the death of her sons, not weeping. Tears flow also from joy, because in that state too, the blood is carried outward with an impulse. For this reason, some have even died of joy. The eyes show all the affections of the soul, and indeed even its character; but especially joy and sadness. <margin>The double privilege of the ears.</margin> Just as ears are far inferior to eyes in these respects, so they excel in these two: in the transmission of instruction and in exciting the affections of the soul.

There are three kinds of differences in sounds: high, low, and middle. These proceed from fast or slow motion. Great, small, and middle sounds proceed from the magnitude of the impulse. But soft and harsh sounds come from the nature of the instrument. There are also rare <note>widely spaced</note>, frequent <note>closely spaced</note>, and middle sounds, as well as dissonant, consonant, and middle. Therefore, <margin>Why sound alone moves the affections of the soul.</margin> sound alone among all things that can move the senses moves the emotions most of all, because it alone exists with manifest motion. A great, harsh, and hurried sound that is not very harmonious moves one to anger and battle, so much so that it makes a man forget himself. For this reason, in battles, especially at the start, soldiers clash with trumpets and drums and raise a shout; for it is a great thing to offer oneself to death. Unless they were nobles seeking glory, or those whose minds are disturbed—which happens most of all with discordant sounds and shouts—they would not do it willingly. Therefore, **Caesar** rightly rebuked **Pompey** <note>A reference to the Battle of Pharsalus, where Caesar criticized Pompey's tactic of ordering his men to stand still to receive the charge.</note>, who at the start of a battle restrained his soldiers from their charge as if they were going to a wrestling match or were about to debate the trifles of philosophers. Soft, rare, small, and harmonious sounds lead a man to compassion. Soft, fast, small, and harmonious sounds lead to alacrity. Low sounds at the end, moderate and mixed from harsh and moderate, slow and small, lead to chastity and prudence.

<margin>The experiment of the lance.</margin>
This is truly marvelous, which anyone can nonetheless test: if a lance is placed against a **lyre** <note>a stringed musical instrument</note> so that it touches it, or against a person’s mouth—if someone holds the rest of the lance's head in their teeth—they will hear sounds, voices, and words from afar as if the hearing were in the teeth, which they could not otherwise hear. Finally, see what kind of movements the emotions create in the spirits, and choose such sounds for the... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

# Book Thirteen

...to move the affections <note>original: "affectus movendos"</note>. Indeed, men agree more regarding sounds than other sensible things because sound is a most simple thing and varies only by general differences. Tastes, smells, and colors, however, also arise from a mixture of the <term>primary qualities (the elemental building blocks of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness)</term>.

<margin>Why almost all men agree on sounds, but not on tastes, smells, or colors.</margin>

<margin>Three things common to all sensible objects.</margin> Furthermore, there are three conditions common to all sensible objects. The first is that, as I have said, they are known through proportions, and for this reason they give delight. Thus it happens that since the <term>diapason (octave)</term> <note>original: "diapason"</note> consists of a double ratio <note>2:1</note>, it delights the ears most of all. Next is the double octave <note>4:1</note>, then the <term>diapente (fifth)</term> plus an octave <note>3:1</note>, then the fifth <note>3:2 ratio</note>, and after that the <term>diatessaron (fourth)</term> <note>4:3 ratio</note>. The <term>ditone (major third)</term> approaches the ratio of 5:4 <note>original: "sesquiquartam"</note> and the <term>trishemitone (minor third)</term> approaches 6:5 <note>original: "sesquiquintam"</note>, once the "eightieth" <note>likely referring to the Syntonic Comma, a tiny interval of 81:80 used in tuning</note> has been subtracted, as I taught in my writings on arithmetic. The intervals of the six voices also consist almost entirely of whole proportions: one having a ratio of 6:5 <note>original: "superpartiens quintas"</note>; the other having a 5:3 ratio <note>original: "superbipartiens tertias"</note>.

The second reason is that all moderate things please: not that sound so great and heavy in the mountains of **Hispaniola** <note>original: "Hispanæ insulæ" (the island containing modern Haiti and the Dominican Republic)</note> that it deafens men, nor a sound so small that it fatigues the listener by the very effort of hearing. The same applies to fast and slow, high and low pitch, and soft and—what is more significant—harsh sounds.

<margin>Why the fourth sounds dissonant below a fifth.</margin> The third reason is that in all things, better things delight when they follow worse things; but conversely, they cause offense. Thus light after darkness, sweet after bitter, roses after dill, and consonant voices after dissonant ones. For this reason, it happens that the <term>fifth</term> in high pitches and the <term>fourth</term> in low pitches offends the ear, whereas in the reverse order they delight. For a low voice following a high one strikes the ear and remains; therefore, since a low sound is simpler than a high one, it will delight. If done in the opposite way, it offends the ear. But as we have already shown above, the harmony of the fifth is simpler than the fourth. By the same reasoning, a fourth above a major third soothes the ear, but below it, it causes pain; for a 5:4 ratio is more easily perceived than a 4:3 ratio, because the 5:4 ratio depends on the 3:2 ratio <note>the major third was often derived from the fifth in Renaissance music theory</note>. Therefore, both in sounds and in paintings, things that offend must be mixed with those that delight, but with a double law observed:

<margin>A precept for pleasure in sensible things.</margin> First, that the things which offend should leave a smaller impression on the sense than those which delight. Second, that they should not be divided into such tiny parts that the sense cannot perceive them. For we have said that <term>consonance (or harmony)</term> is the ratio of several voices perceived by the ear. If, therefore, they are cut into such minute pieces that they are not perceived by the sense, they will not only fail to delight but will even offend. This is why the painting of very tiny flowers is neither pleasing nor delightful; the same applies to very small letters. But in these, as in the carving of gemstones, even the smallest error or crookedness renders them ugly. For the sense judges individual things by comparison: thus in large things it perceives large errors, and in small things, small errors. Truly, hearing recognizes even smaller differences than sight, and therefore more than any other sense. Indeed, in high pitches, it beautifully detects one part out of thirty-three, or even out of eighty. For it judges the major third to be harsh without that small reduction, but sweet once it is removed. In rhythm <note>original: "temporibus"</note>, it divides one beat into sixteen...

<margin>In letters and the carving of gems, even the smallest errors produce great deformity.</margin>

<header>Of the Senses and Sensible Things.</header>

# Of the Senses and Sensible Things.

<margin>A way of increasing delight in music.</margin>
...divides parts. Hearing is therefore more subtle than sight, either because—as I have said—it is the only sense that exists entirely in motion, or because the objects of sight, namely colors, spoil one another through their intense proximity, or because sight is concerned with many things while hearing deals with a most simple and unique object. Thus, increasing the time of the beats and extending them contributes not a little to pleasure, so that in place of the <term>hemiola (a musical ratio of 3:2)</term>, which is the only one the musicians of our time know, the division of time might be extended into five or seven parts. Having heard this only once, I rightly put forward that proverb: <note>original: "omne rarum pretiosum"</note> "everything rare is precious." For since sound moves the emotions <note>original: "affectus"</note>, the power within it is most manifest.

<margin>Remarkable examples of moving the emotions through sound.</margin>
Among many examples from the ancients, I find two that are excellent regarding the power of sound to stir the emotions of the soul. One is of Timotheus <note>a famous Greek musician and poet</note>, who, by changing the <term>musical mode</term>, compelled Alexander the Great to leap up from a banquet, driven by a sudden surge of excitement. The other is that when Agamemnon was about to depart from his fatherland to set out for Troy, doubting the chastity of his wife Clytemnestra—for that was her name—he left behind a <term>citharist (a player of the cithara, a professional lyre)</term> who, by the sound of that instrument, so incited her toward chastity and restraint that Aegisthus <note>the lover of Clytemnestra</note> was unable to possess her until after the musician had been killed.

<margin>Hydraulic organs.</margin>
But those sounds which delight the most also lead toward a lack of restraint, especially when they make students too devoted to music. Such is the case with <term>hydraulic organs (water-powered pipe organs)</term>. Nero, being charmed by their wonderful sweetness even amidst the dangers to his life and empire, the desertion of his armies and generals, and the manifest threat of his own death, did not neglect his care for them. These instruments contain water, and air mixed with the water in several pipes emits a melody blended with a whisper. Vitruvius <note>a Roman architect and engineer</note> hands down the theory of these; but since it is established that the books of Vitruvius were common knowledge by the age of Nero, it does not seem likely to me that those things which were constructed by such common methods would have been so dear to Nero. Therefore, I judge that Vitruvius’s standard should be considered a basic model rather than an exquisite theory.

<margin>The nature of the psalter.</margin>
But musical instruments did not only please the "Nephew Caesar" <note>referring to Nero, a descendant of the Caesars</note>; the sweetness of the <term>psalter (a stringed instrument similar to a harp or lyre)</term> also captivated King David, a most brave and stern man, and it even used to soothe the Raging Saul. Nor should it be believed that the harmony of this instrument—which the Sacred Page mentions so often and which alone among others was judged fit for celebrating divine praises—is a common thing. It is established that it has seventy-two strings and is shaped exactly like a triangle; its harmony <note>original: "symphonia"</note> is incomparable.

<margin>A musical instrument that might express the sound of twelve instruments at once.</margin>
<margin>The imitation of musical instruments.</margin>
We have also seen other instruments of singular pleasure and craftsmanship, such as those which express the voice of trumpets, drums, pipes, flutes, lyres, horns, lutes <note>original: "testudinis," literally "tortoise shell," referring to the body of a lute or lyre</note>, the <term>phorminx</term>, the <term>syrinx</term>, the heptachord, organs properly so called, and the <term>sambuca</term>. Hydraulic organs counterfeit the songs of birds (so well that unless you saw it, you would not believe it), so that you would say it was a bird. Horns are very close to human voices once holes are added; whereas formerly, without them, soldiers were incited to battle. Whence Virgil says: <note>original: "Crepuerunt cornua cantu"</note> "The horns blared with a song"—surely a disordered music without melodies.

# Book Thirteen

<margin>The cause of thunder.</margin>
...dull and more like thunder. The cause of thunder is that a cloud is suddenly torn apart by lightning. Therefore, being suddenly shredded, it gives off a heavy, violent, and disordered sound, so much so that it sometimes kills chicks in the egg and fetuses in the womb. Thus, this sound is the most removed from music. Yet it is not impossible for a harmony <note>original: "concentum"</note> to arise from many such thunders occurring at a distance, which, when heard, is considered a miracle.

<margin>The privilege of smell.</margin>
Next to sound in nobility is smell, whose unique property is either to restore or to cast down our strength, because it seeks out the brain itself on its own. For neither sound, color, flavor, nor heat or cold are carried directly to the brain. Therefore, of all the things that are sensed, only smell can either kill or restore a person. For a good smell nourishes the spirit—in which the work of the soul shines forth—while a bad one destroys it. For that reason, incense is burned for the gods, because the divine part within us rejoices in smells. <margin>The omen of smell.</margin> And for this reason also, it is considered the best omen, and a sign of some present divinity, when a good smell is sensed without a cause. And while the bodies of others may stink, it is believed that the bodies of saints smell sweet for this reason: the power of divinity fighting against the laws of nature. Yet it is not impossible according to nature for a fresh human corpse not to smell bad—as is reported of Alexander <note>Alexander the Great; historical sources like Plutarch claimed his skin breathed a natural perfume</note>—or for an old and dried one to smell good. For since the bodies of certain dead animals smell good, and the human temperament is extended into a similarity with every animal, it is clear that some human corpses can smell good; for a good smell is found either in a very dry animal or in its driest part. This sense alone, therefore, seems to be common to the soul and the body, and it is for this reason that it is transferred with vapors, like things that are touched and tasted; yet without these vapors it lacks all matter, like things that are seen or heard. Because of this, we do not call those who excel in other senses "sagacious" <note>original: "sagaces," a term the author notes is derived from the keen tracking sense of animals</note>, but only those who excel in smell, like dogs and vultures.

<margin>Why people with a keen sense of smell rarely see far and are more ingenious.</margin>
Truly, people who excel in the sense of smell rarely see far, and they are more ingenious. This is because a warm and dry temperament of the brain excels in smell, but such a state is unfit for sight. This is because the instrument of smell is located in the brain near the root of the eyes; however, the brain is quick to imagine because of the heat, and it is tenacious of images <note>meaning it possesses a strong memory</note> because of the dryness.

<margin>No animal could or should take pleasure in any sense other than taste and touch.</margin>
No other animal is delighted by smell itself, but man alone. For even if dogs sense the odors of flowers, they are not delighted by them. For it was not possible, nor was it advantageous, for beasts to be delighted except in taste or touch. These were indeed necessary for them, so that they would not perish from hunger, neglect reproduction, or fail to avoid harmful things, as they would if they did not feel pleasure and pain through taste and touch. But in other sensible things, as I have said, there could be no delight or pain; because delight is situated in the recognition of the <term>proportion</term> <note>the mathematical or aesthetic balance</note> of the things being sensed, such as <term>double</term> <note>a 2:1 musical ratio</note> and <term>hemiola</term> <note>a 3:2 musical ratio</note>. But to recognize these belongs to a higher power than that which exists in beasts; therefore, they could neither be saddened, nor feel pain, nor be delighted by them. Much less was it advantageous for them; for they would be very easily lured away by pictures or sounds...

## On the senses and sensible things.

...lest they fall into snares through smells. The evidence for this is that stags, who are only stunned and do not take pleasure in the sound of the lyre, are thus exposed to the traps of men; so too are quails by a simulated female voice, and wild birds by those trapped in a cage. What a loss wolves and fish suffer from scent, and how miserably they are subjected to the deceits of men! But to lack a sense of smell would have been more miserable, because it was necessary: nature would have added pleasure to the other senses of beasts in vain if it were for no use other than their destruction.

<margin>Why smells are joined to flavors.</margin>
<margin>The marvelous power of garlic.</margin>
Smells are rightly added to flavors by cooks, because there is nothing particularly special in the flavors themselves. Yet, while certain things added to flavors are pleasing, they might be displeasing on their own, such as garlic. For garlic added to savory dishes <term>obsonia</term> <note>original: "obsonijs"; refers to seasoned dishes or side-dishes eaten with bread</note> is delightful, though its smell by itself is bad, and after you eat it, it infects the breath with a most foul odor. In some cases, this is even worse after a day, because its thick substance generates a vast multitude of thinner vapors over a long period. Even the blood carried to the lungs retains the smell, and the excrement itself smells of corrupted garlic; something also sweats out from the stomach through the throat into the lungs. For this reason, a method was devised so that the scent is perceived only while tasting and not returned <note>That is, without causing the eater to have bad breath</note>, nor causing offense; this will happen if you leave the garlic in vinegar, or rub it on the serving dishes, but discard the substance itself.

<margin>How scent without the substance is left in side dishes.</margin>
<margin>How a half-ounce of cinnamon suffices for a whole year.</margin>
<margin>So that all things are cooked quickly and well.</margin>
The same reasoning should be observed with pepper, ginger, and cinnamon, where their flavor and scent might delight you, yet you fear their heat. There is another method for these from Apicius <note>Marcus Gavius Apicius, a legendary Roman gourmet and supposed author of the famous Roman cookbook "De Re Coquinaria"</note> for the benefit of the household budget, by which the scent and flavor remain, and a half-ounce <term>semuncia</term> <note>Approximately 14 grams</note> of cinnamon or garlic suffices for an entire year. Take thin, fragrant cinnamon, divided into small pieces to the weight of a half-ounce, and place it among twelve or sixteen blanched almonds and tie them up tightly. When these are removed for use, put others in their place. In this way, with little expense, you will eat everything fragrant with the scent of musk. But if you wish to add flavor, boil it in, as you would for the sharpness of mustard. This also causes legumes and meats to be cooked very quickly, even to the point of dissolving, for by the heat and thinness in which it excels, it penetrates and liquefies them.

<margin>Description of Garum.</margin>
<margin>Against all insects.</margin>
Indeed, there are those who are delighted by a sharp flavor, others by a salty one, which is why Garum <term>Garum</term> <note>A fermented fish sauce ubiquitous in ancient Roman cuisine</note> was used by the ancients if anything was. Here is its description: the intestines, blood, and gills of tuna are enclosed in a vessel, sprinkled with much salt, and after two months the liquid is drawn from the bottom. Another kind is made from the intestines of large fish, and even from very small fish, especially Picarels <term>Maenis</term> <note>A small Mediterranean fish often used for salting</note>, preserved with salt. Its use, as I said, was pleasant to the ancients, and also healthy, though among us it has now fallen out of fashion. They report that because of garum placed in a pit, locusts gather and are lulled to sleep, just as fleas are drawn to goat’s blood. This is more certain and in accordance with the decrees of nature against mosquitoes, bedbugs, ants, fleas, locusts, lice, cockroaches, and caterpillars: that they are expelled by the smoke of a fire made from burning those of their own kind. Anything sharp, such as vinegar and squill <note>A medicinal Mediterranean plant, *Drimia maritima*</note>, but especially Wild Larkspur which they call *staphisagria* <note>Stavesacre, a plant used historically to kill lice and other parasites</note>—all these things ward off, put to flight, and kill, to such an extent that...

# Book Thirteen

...a thread wrapped around the head, provided it has been moistened with its seed dissolved in oil, either drives away or kills all lice: as I said, no small amount of vinegar also helps. Thus they report that gnats <note>original: "culices"; mosquitoes or small flies</note> are kept away if a sponge soaked in vinegar is suspended in the middle of a room: for they dread the smell. They are also repelled by flowering hemp placed on the bed, as they say; likewise by a horsehair suspended before the bedroom, which, if it is true, can be considered a kind of magic trick <note>original: "præstigij loco"; implies a folk superstition or "old wives' tale"</note>.

<margin>For moths in clothes.</margin>
This much is certain: wormwood <note>original: "absinthium"</note> does much to protect garments from moths: so does cedar oil <note>original: "cedriæ lachryma"; literally 'tears of cedar'</note>, and the leaf of the citron or "medicinal apple" <note>the citron tree, *Citrus medica*, was prized for its scent and perceived medicinal properties</note>, and savin, and nard, and whatever things have a strong smell accompanied by bitterness.

<margin>How vinegar is made.</margin>
Vinegar is made by adding salt and any sharp substance that does not rot: I have tried pepper, with great profit if <term>siliquastrum</term> <note>likely referring to wild pepper or the pods of the Judas tree</note> is kept. It is also made by fire; for when it boils, it is then exposed to the sun, and once vinegar has already been mixed in, the whole easily turns sour. Another excellent method: take cornelian cherries when they begin to redden, and blackberries, and "hundred-berries" <note>original: "centimora"; likely a regional name for a prolific field berry like the mock strawberry</note> which grow in the fields; while they are unripe, dry and grind them, and having taken them up with sharp vinegar, shape them into small discs. These, when they have been dried, immediately turn wine into vinegar. The cause of these things is that fire and the sun cause the oily moisture to vanish, whence it sours, since the substance is thin; but if it is thick, they turn into saltiness, and then into bitterness. Indeed, this composition is acidic in power, in which heat is enclosed, which causes whatever is oily to exhale.

<margin>To prevent wine from souring.</margin>
But if you wish to prevent wine from souring by the opposite method, hang bacon <note>original: "lardum"; salt pork or fatback</note> from the lid of the vessels; by its fatness and saltiness, it prevents the separation and thinning, which are the causes from which vinegar is generated.

<margin>To remove a musty smell from wine and the vessel.</margin>
By the same art, but not for the same reason, they remove a musty smell from both the wine and the vessel at the same time by suspending medlars <note>original: "meſpilis"; a fruit that looks like a small brown apple</note> from the lid of the skins; these, cut into four and sewn with a thread, are lowered into the wine for a month. And although he firmly asserts that what I have said follows, nevertheless this has not been as clearly observed by me as I would wish.

<margin>To keep must sweet for the whole year.</margin>
A safer method and one found through certain reasoning is this: if must <note>unfermented grape juice</note> is placed in a vessel pitched inside and out and sealed, and the vessel itself is submerged in a river for a month, it will remain sweet for the whole year if it was such from the beginning; for the wine is preserved for the future by the warmth of the pitch, while the coldness of the water prevents it from fermenting. For this reason, lest the sweet parts exhale—for must passes into wine because of heat—it remains, therefore, both must, sweet, and turbid.

<margin>How wine vessels are pitched.</margin>
But it is necessary to teach how vessels are usually pitched <note>lined with pitch or resin to seal and flavor the container</note>: melted pitch <note>original: "pix"</note> is poured into the skins, and they are shaken so that it sticks everywhere: then add one pound of Illyrian iris, and an ounce and a half each of saffron and aloe wood, and two "pondo" or pounds each of hyssop and nard:

<margin>A 'pondo' and a 'libra' are the same.</margin>
for <term>pondo</term> and <term>libra</term> <note>the standard Roman pound</note> are the same. Therefore, before the pitch cools and congeals, these should be added so that they stick to the pitch, yet not while it is still boiling, for they would be burned. This quantity of aromatics ought to be placed in a vessel of ten amphorae; moreover,

...are matched exactly to our *brentae* <note>original: "brentis"; a regional liquid measure often used in Northern Italy and Germany</note>. For an amphora contains eighty-four pounds of wine by weight. Pitching <note>the process of coating the inside of a wine vessel with resin or pitch to seal it</note> is done every year, or at least every other year. However, wines placed in a pitched vessel, unless they are very potent, turn into flat, spoiled wine <note>original: "vappam"</note>; for this reason, vessels are not pitched in our regions. When wines become <margin>To restore spoiled wines.</margin> cloudy or disturbed before they perish entirely, you should use this remedy—even though I remember having said much on this above. Take two eggs, or even more; use the yolks if the wine is red, but only the whites if it is white. Mix these with three parts of powdered river stones and two parts of very finely ground salt. Stir this for three days, five times a day or even more frequently, but it is necessary to have first transferred the wine into a clean vessel. This will cure it if any hope of recovery remains. It works even better if as much honey is added as there is salt; for these three—honey, eggs, and salt—purify all liquids, while the stone is very helpful in drawing the sediment downward. Also, sour cherries, when added, have been shown by certain experiment to clarify the wine as they force it to ferment. 

You can also keep fresh figs in wine for the whole year in this <margin>How to keep fresh figs all year.</margin> manner: Pick them without any water or dew and place them in a new, square earthenware vessel so that they do not touch one another. The vessel itself should be carefully closed with a lid on top and placed so that it floats in the wine—which will happen because of the air inside. The figs will be preserved for as long as the wine remains uncorrupted. It is clear, however, that the vessel must be thin so that the subtle essence of the wine can preserve the figs; for the moisture of the wine prevents them from drying out, while that same moisture, being resistant to decay, prevents them from rotting—provided, as I said, that the wine remains sound. 

Pomegranates and quinces, <margin>How pomegranates are preserved.</margin> and many other fruits of that kind, are preserved by being coated in gypsum or chalk; for when they are kept in a cold place, they remain uncorrupted by the cold and dryness. Others place them, before they reach full maturity, into earthenware vessels while they are still attached to the tree, so that the vessels hang from the tree. They carefully tie the mouth of the vessel to the branch so that no air can enter, and leave them thus. 

If, however, pomegranates tend to split open on their own, a squill <note>a bulbous flowering plant, *Drimia maritima*, often used in ancient agriculture for pest control</note> planted nearby will prevent it. This same plant protects <margin>So pomegranates do not split open.</margin> all seeds from gnawing animals, for they flee from its pungent <margin>Lest seeds be harmed by animals.</margin> odor. The juice of houseleek <note>original: "semperuiuui"; literally 'ever-living', likely *Sempervivum tectorum*</note>, if the seeds you wish to sow are soaked in it, also keeps them uncorrupted; for small animals and birds flee from its smell as if it were harmful, because it is an extremely "cold" herb. 

To have early-ripening fruits, water them often with warm water, <margin>How to have early fruits.</margin> expose them to the sun, nourish them with pigeon and horse manure, and gradually prune away useless branches and anything unnecessary. But if you wish for late-ripening fruits, you should act by the <margin>How to have late fruits.</margin> opposite method: leave them in the shade and covered with many leaves. Cut the already formed fruits along with their branches before they ripen; they will bloom again and send out other fruits. To bring these to maturity in winter, enclose them in earthenware vessels hanging from the tree. But if the fruit rots on the tree or animals are born within it, <margin>Lest fruit rot on the tree.</margin> this happens from an abundance of moisture; therefore, bore a hole through the tree from the bottom, so that...

...serves as a substitute for bloodletting <note>original: "venae sectionis"; an ancient medical practice of bleeding a patient to balance the "humors," here applied to trees to release excess sap</note>. For whatever excess moisture there is will burst out. Alternatively, you may drive a glowing iron nail into that same spot; this remedy <margin>To change the color of fruits.</margin> acts as a cautery <note>the burning of tissue to stop bleeding or prevent infection</note>. 

If your goal is to change the colors of the fruit, graft it onto a tree that bears fruit of the desired color. For example, if a citron is grafted onto a mulberry, red citrons will grow if the mulberries were red. Some believe that peaches become red if red roses are planted beneath them, as if the trees were moved by a kind of imagination <note>a Renaissance-era belief that plants could be influenced by the visual presence or "spirit" of nearby organisms</note>—a phenomenon that is certainly seen in the palm tree, where the female tree pines away and wastes away for love of the male. Two trees <margin>Trees that accept another tree through grafting.</margin> will receive any kind of grafted tree: the quince and the wild fig, so generous is their nature. Even the olive is sometimes grafted to the vine; this was seen long ago by Varro at the house of Macius Maximus and is called an *Eleostaphylon* <term>Eleostaphylon: literally "oil-grape," a rare hybrid believed to produce fruit with the combined flavor of olives and grapes</term>. It bears fruit that carries the flavor of an olive mixed with a grape berry. However, it is grafted by the method I mentioned above for grafting a vine onto a cherry, for this method is safer.

<margin>So that fruits grow without a stone.</margin>
Regarding how trees like the peach, pine, and others with stones or pits are said to produce fruit without a stone when grafted to a willow: this has not yet been proven to me to this day. Others affirm that a grape grows without a stone if the branches—such as the vine—are split through the middle, the pith is carefully extracted, and they are then planted joined back together. The same is said for other trees propagated by planting cuttings. There are those who strip the stone itself of its shell after it has opened naturally, then wrap it in wool and bury it again. 

But the most useful graftings <margin>The most useful graftings.</margin> are performed on the almond and the grape on the myrtle. From the former, a peach is produced with a stone of pleasant flavor; from the latter, the delightful scent of myrtle is added to the flavor of the grape. <margin>How to have fruits of different colors from the same branch.</margin> If, however, shoots of different grapes are cut through the middle (with the pith preserved) and then joined and planted, fruits of various colors will come forth from the same tree and those same branches. This is most successful with grapes, which is why there are white, black, and even green grapes on one vine. 

<margin>Plants are changed by their own grafting.</margin>
Not only are the fruits of plants changed by grafting from another species, but if the trunk itself is cut back and branches of that same tree are re-inserted into it, fruits far different from the first will arise. In this way, so many kinds of apples and pears have been created. For any tree becomes soft and domesticated through grafting; <margin>The difference between wild and domestic plants.</margin> indeed, wild plants are drier than domestic ones. Therefore, they have rougher bark, more frequent leaves and fruit (though smaller and less sweet), and even smaller, thinner flowers—though these are more fragrant. The whole plant itself is smaller and more prone to thorns, if it is of that kind.

<margin>Why the rose is thorny.</margin>
One might ask, why are there thorns on a rose? The reason is that it was necessary for it to be fragrant, and for that scent to be firm yet minimally heating, so that it might be more pleasant. For cool scents refresh the soul more, because the brain is troubled by constant heat due to its movements. Since, therefore, the flower was of a delicate substance and was a smoky vapor <note>original: "fumerus"; referring to the aromatic "exhalations" or "vapors" believed to carry a plant's scent</note>, it needed to be joined to something earthy. Thus, the rose flower has an earthy substance that is also warm and delicate; otherwise, it would not be fragrant. But if it was such a vapor, it was necessary for the whole plant to be of that kind and of thicker parts, so that the delicate part...

# On the Senses and Sensible Things

...the flower would be formed from a separate part. When, however, the whole plant was earthy and dry, it was necessary for that earthiness either to be retained (in which case it would have dried out quickly) or, if it were advantageous to expel it, it could have been mixed with the leaves. This, however, would have made the leaves stubborn and prone to falling off quickly due to excessive dryness. It remains, therefore, that the best outcome occurred: this dry material—which is like the dregs <note>original: "sex," likely a typo for "faex," meaning dregs or sediment</note> of the flower and is burnt up—is expelled separately. Since it could not have emerged through the tougher bark unless it were pointed, the thorn <note>original: "spina"</note> emerged. Where these thorns are more frequent and smaller, they indicate a rose that is more fragrant, more delicate, and hotter, and thus more suitable for purging <note>the use of rose preparations as a mild laxative in early medicine</note>, though not at all tenacious in its scent. Such is the wild rose, whose flower is often completed with five petals, but whose thorns are sharp, tiny, and frequent, even covering the leaves themselves, so that one cannot safely touch them because everything is so crowded with thorns. Domestic roses, however, have a flower with dense and fleshy petals; because of this multitude of petals, they seem more fragrant. Their thorns are thicker, fewer, and less sharp. The domestic flower itself is better for making sugar preserves <note>original: "saccarum condendum"</note> and rose water because of its fleshier substance.

<margin>An oak, when cut down, sometimes turns into broom.</margin>
<margin>The transformation of plants through weakening.</margin>
Furthermore, the cutting of a trunk matters so much that an oak, when cut from the bottom, sometimes withers, and sometimes—though rarely—transforms into broom <note>original: "genistam"</note>. Most frequently, however, the oak degenerates into another kind of oak called the "trembling" oak <note>likely the aspen, *Populus tremula*, which ancient observers sometimes associated with degenerated oaks</note>. Certain garden plants are also said to degenerate with age, such as cabbage <note>original: "brassica"</note> turning into radish. That they do sometimes degenerate is certain: for instance, wheat turns into rye <note>original: "siliginem"</note> if it is sown in a damp and cold place for three years. We spoke of darnel <note>original: "lolio"; a weed often found in grain fields</note> above. Plants that degenerate rarely return to their original state, whereas those that merely change do return.
<margin>How to grow the largest celery or leeks.</margin>
To obtain large specimens, such as leeks or celery—according to a certain experiment and many similar ones—take several seeds of the same kind, hide them in hollowed-out goat dung, and plant them. You will marvel at the effect, for the tender sprouts, compressed together, grow in such a way that they take the place of a single, massive plant.

<margin>How to grow a plant with multiple flavors and scents.</margin>
By the same reasoning, if you plant the seeds of lettuce, rocket, celery, basil, and leek together in the same dung, a herb will grow that carries the flavor and scent of leek, lettuce, rocket, celery, and basil all at once. If you wish to add color, scent, flavor, or a <term>theriacal</term> <note>pertaining to "theriac," a famous ancient universal antidote against poison</note> or purging power to the fruits of plants, soak the seed for three days before sowing in such a substance. For example:
<margin>How fruits or vegetables may acquire a particular power.</margin>
use concentrated must <note>original: "sapa"</note> for sweetness, perfume for a pleasant scent, wild cucumber juice for a purging power, or theriac against poisons. Once the plant is nourished by such things from the beginning, the effect will be stronger and more perfect if, when planting cuttings, you remove the pith and place such substances in its stead, having also left the cuttings in those liquids for three days before planting.
<margin>How mushrooms arise.</margin>
You will have mushrooms <note>original: "fungos"</note> when rain falls upon burnt vine-clippings, or if, in the absence of rain, you sprinkle water over the remains of burnt clippings.
<margin>How to distinguish deadly mushrooms.</margin>
Otherwise, cut a black poplar tree and pour water mixed with leaven <note>original: "fermento"; yeast or sourdough starter</note> over its fragments and near the trunk. For mushrooms born in this way are hardly ever bad...

...they can [be identified]. Those that are broad and have blisters are truly dangerous, as are those that crumble easily when touched by fingers. These are reddish with a sticky moisture; if placed in milk, flies will die. Thus, practical experience is joined with utility.

<margin>Kinds of Thistles. Chards.</margin>
Thistles are eaten more safely—the summer fruit of a prickly herb well known even to the ancients. To this noble genus, several others succeed, so that the whole year seems distributed among them. For at the end of summer and in autumn, there are wild thistles—or rather Spanish ones—smaller but more pleasant in taste. Then, at the beginning of winter and throughout the winter, there is the Chard plant <note>original: "Cardi"; likely *Cynara cardunculus*, the cardoon, a relative of the artichoke</note>, which is white, bushy, somewhat bitter, and covered in thorns; not only its leaves are eaten, but also the lowest part of the stem and the uppermost part of the root, which is almost bulbous. In early spring and through the summer, wild thistles are eaten again; however, the leaves are avoided because of their fuzz, and the root because of its hardness, so instead the woody lower part of the stem and the top of the root are consumed. In almost all bitter plants, the woody part—where it sprouts into leaves—is abundant in juice, soft, and less bitter, retaining a pleasing flavor while losing what is unpleasant to the palate. All such things are eaten with salt, vinegar, oil, and pepper, not only pleasantly but also healthfully. For salt aids digestion and provides a pleasing flavor; pepper, besides this, adds a fine aroma; vinegar tempers the heat of all the other ingredients, just as oil tempers their dryness, while also contributing no small amount to the pleasure of the taste. The fifth kind of prickly plant is the <term>Scolymos<gloss>the Golden Thistle, *Scolymos hispanicus*, used both as a vegetable and for its medicinal root</gloss></term>, useful for medicine rather than food. While almost all kinds of prickly plants benefit the stomach, purge the kidneys, and resist poisons, this kind of thistle—which naturally has a divided root—cures pestilential diseases in a wonderful way. A sixth kind is preferred from India, called the *cerium*, which resembles wax candles with its straight, white stalks. But it is so large that it equals a spear; its fruit is no larger than a nut but quite pleasant, red and full of seeds. There is also the *Pithaia* <note>The Dragon Fruit or Pitaya</note> there, with fruit like an eggplant but of remarkable size, surpassing what are called watermelons or *anguria*; it provides good nourishment and a sweet taste. Again, the eighth kind is the Pineapple <note>original: "Pinea"; early European explorers often called the pineapple a "pine" because of its resemblance to a pine cone</note>, because the fruit is very similar to the fruit of the pine tree; it has a most pleasant scent and flesh better than quinces. The last of the most noble kinds of prickly herbs, which India <note>In this period, "India" often referred generally to the East or West Indies (the Americas)</note> also possesses, is called the *Tuna* <note>The Prickly Pear cactus, *Opuntia*</note>; its fruit, without any danger, causes much blood to be passed with urine <note>The red pigment of the prickly pear fruit can color urine, a harmless condition called beeturia/pseudohematuria</note>, yet it nonetheless brings no small benefit to the stomach.

<margin>How olives are freed from their pits.</margin>
Olives differ little from all these in taste, but art has found something to add: they crush them with wooden mallets in a hollowed-out board to remove the pits; they are eaten in no other way in Genoa <note>original: "Ianue"</note>. It is wonderful that olives become much better when kept in olive oil—a clear proof of their excellent dryness. <margin>Colymbades olives.</margin> The best among all, and especially the Spanish ones, are the *Colymbades* <term>Colymbades<gloss>from the Greek 'kolumbao' (to swim), referring to olives pickled in brine</gloss></term> variety. These are harvested with their small branches, washed in water, dried for a day, and then preserved with salt spread beneath them and brine poured over, as we taught above.

## On the Senses and Sensible Things

<margin>How all fruits may be preserved.</margin>
Moister fruits, such as pomegranates, pears, and grapes, are best preserved if they are collected after a long period of dry weather and cleaned of any spoiled berries (if they are grapes). The stem should then be dipped in boiling pitch or, if that is unavailable, in wine. Afterward, let them dry for two days in the Sun and arrange them among chaff so that they do not touch one another. Since all rot originates from watery moisture, as has been shown elsewhere, it is necessary that once this moisture is removed, the fruit will not spoil; it is removed most effectively from the part where it is introduced—namely, the stem.

<margin>How cucumbers may be preserved.</margin>
<margin>How all roots and herbs may be preserved.</margin>
<margin>How preserves are made.</margin>
<margin>How sugar and honey are purified.</margin>
<margin>How meats may be preserved in the summer time.</margin>
Cucumbers, however, are preserved by a different art: if placed in the dregs of sweet wine with the jar sealed, they remain unspoiled for as long as the dregs themselves last. The rest of the multitude of things that take their origin from garden vegetables—such as turnips, samphire <note>original: "cretanus"; likely *Crithmum maritimum*, or rock samphire</note>, and watercress—are preserved in vinegar alone, as I have experienced, though fennel is conveniently added to all of them. Other things are better preserved as sweets, such as gourds, melon rinds, and citrus peels, the flesh of the citron <note>original: "mali medicæ"; literally "Median apple," a large citrus fruit with a thick rind</note>, whole walnuts, and lemons. Those things which are preserved whole are usually picked before they are fully ripe, such as turnips, nuts, and lemons. They are soaked for a long time in water, which must be constantly changed, then boiled until they become soft and dried in the shade; then, pour over them honey or sugar that has been purified by fire. After seven days, draw off the liquid, boil it again, and pour it back over, repeating this three or four times. In this way, they will be rendered very sweet and clear. I have already mentioned that they become moldy if any watery moisture remains. Honey, sugar, and other juices are purified with egg white and water by skimming the foam and boiling. It is said to be "cooked"—and indeed it is—when a drop of it congeals. Even cooked meats in the summer may be dried for an hour in a windy place in the shade, after the water has been carefully (though not perfectly) squeezed out. Then, sprinkled with white vinegar and salt, you shall place them in a jar in a cool spot, turning them over every day. This pickling will suffice for ten days. Alternatively, sprinkle the meat thus cooked and dried with salt and crushed juniper seeds, and submerge it in a jar full of white vinegar placed in a cold spot, turning it daily: you will marvel at the grace of the flavor and scent.

<margin>How fish may be preserved.</margin>
<margin>Things that correct spoiled water.</margin>
<margin>By what things water is corrupted.</margin>
<margin>How water and wine may be cooled.</margin>
Things that are soft are not boiled when you wish to preserve them, except for fish; for these are fried moderately in oil and stored among bay or myrtle leaves sprinkled with salt. Bay leaves preserve not only fish, but they also improve water that has already spoiled, rendering it harmless and sweet-smelling; they are also a ready aid against poisons. Lime also improves water, as does boiling, but nothing is better than bay leaves. Water is corrupted chiefly by those things which are themselves corrupted by water; such things are wheat and, especially, human corpses, for if they are increasingly corrupted by water day by day, it is necessary that they should violently corrupt the water in turn. But if water or wine in vessels is warm, submerge those vessels in other water in which a pound of saltpeter <note>original: "halinitri"; potassium nitrate, used here for an endothermic cooling reaction</note> has been dissolved, moving them constantly. For the outer water is cooled because vapors exhale from it as if by a certain fire, yet they are not produced in the same way as by fire. But better still, waters are cooled by ice and snow. These are preserved until the end of summer in large

<header>Book Thirteen</header>

# Book Thirteen

<margin>How ice and snow may be kept in summer.</margin>
...of fire, pure, hardened by the cold, and stored for a long time among straw and marble stones <note>original: "saxaq; marmorea"; possibly referring to marble-lined pits or heavy stones used for insulation</note> and crystals in a wine larder open to the North wind. They are also preserved very easily in the caves of certain mountains.

But I come now to the roots which were proposed to be preserved, and the other harder parts, which must first be moderately boiled, then dried before they are submerged in vinegar. For they take in the vinegar better and are rendered softer, which is why we choose the more tender ones, such as in the case of turnips and the roots of lettuce and bugloss <note>original: "buglossi"; the plant *Anchusa officinalis*, often used in salads or medicine</note>. With similar ingenuity, human industry even attempts arts for the delight of the eyes. Hence our friend the bookseller Nicolaus Landrianus <note>Niccolò Landriani was a prominent Milanese bookseller and publisher in the 16th century</note> has embossed images upon leather in such a way

<margin>How carved leather may express lifelike figures in relief-molds.</margin>
that they appeared to be made of Cyprian bronze. For the leather, when it has been slightly moistened, is carefully pressed into warm wooden relief-molds <note>original: "proplasmatibus"; models or molds used for casting or embossing</note>, or those made of other material; wax is added so that the empty space is filled exactly, and with paper laid over it, it is tightened between the boards of a press. That which has been carved is then painted in its own proper colors.

<margin>The marvelous apparatus of stage sets. Praise and inventions of Nicolaus Siccus, Captain of Justice.</margin>
From there come the magnificent ornaments of stage sets: thunder, rain, and snow—these consist of bits of wool <note>original: "pappis"; likely seed-down or cotton used to simulate falling snow</note> moved by alternating bellows. From there come Suns, stars, and the Moon in a counterfeit sky, which Nicolaus Siccus <note>Niccolò Secco (1513–1560), an Italian adventurer, playwright, and official</note>—a man as excellent as he was most splendid, and most learned in every kind of science and the nobler arts—represented in that comedy which, at your command, he composed, produced, and decorated in the presence of Philip, Prince of Spain, the son of our Emperor <note>Referring to Philip II of Spain and his father, Holy Roman Emperor Charles V</note>. Who would not marvel there at the Sun and the stars shining in a clear sky, then hiding behind dark clouds, or dimmed by white ones, the motion of the heavenly body matching the time of the play’s performance? There, sapphires, chrysolites, and real pyropes <note>a type of red garnet</note> were imitated by lights hidden behind glass dodecahedrons and icosahedrons <note>twelve-sided and twenty-sided geometric shapes</note> of the natural color of glass. Only diamonds and emeralds were missing, so that in his faking, he might not seem to have faked at all. He produced stage thunder—what more can Jupiter or Neptune himself do?—while you could even see ships being carried and tossed as if on the sea.

<margin>How wild beasts may be killed.</margin>
This diligence has left nothing unattempted. From this also come snares, hooks, nets, bows, dogs, and hawks. Nor are these enough; deceits must be added. Aconite <note>monkshood</note>, spurge <note>original: "Thitymali"</note>, and all kinds of buttercups <note>original: "ranunculi"</note> are mixed with food; they indiscriminately kill birds, wild beasts, and all fish. Nux vomica <note>the seeds of the Strychnine tree</note>, as I have experienced, kills dogs instantly; the same makes birds dazed if it is mixed into their food.

<margin>How birds may be captured.</margin>
I remember that I once caught crows by hand when I had mixed that crushed nut into meat. Small birds are rendered dazed if they eat grains that have been soaked either in wine dregs with hemlock juice, or in "burning water" <note>original: "aqua ardente"; distilled alcohol or brandy</note>, or even in the dregs of a stronger wine alone, or in a decoction of white hellebore with the gall of an old ox. Those that walk in flocks are also captured in flocks: such as partridges, even more so geese, and most of all ducks. For it is necessary to feed tame ones of their own kind, with clipped wings, near waters surrounded by a rampart, with a plentiful and very pleasant food there. For ducks, among other things, this is sorghum boiled in water.

<header>On the Senses and Sensible Things</header>

# On the Senses and Sensible Things

...of the water; at night, while the tame ones <note>original: "cicures"; domesticated decoys</note> call out, the wild ones descend for food. For all animals share a common understanding of four calls: food, sex <note>original: "uenereorum"; literally "of things pertaining to Venus"</note>, fighting, and fear, and they understand one another. Therefore, when the nets which they call "coverings" are drawn—for they hang entwined upon stakes—they are closed, so that sometimes they bring back a thousand ducks captured in a single rush. And although it may seem marvelous, it is nevertheless certain that no fowling is more successful. Tame birds are chosen, however, which are most similar in color to the wild ones.

<margin>How fish may be caught.</margin>
Fish are also caught with food: the bait, therefore, ought to have four qualities. It should be fragrant, for this lures them from a distance; such things are anise, the juice of all-heal <note>original: "panacis succus"; likely referring to *Opopanax* or a similar medicinal plant</note>, and better than all of them, cumin. It should be of a pleasant flavor, so that it invites and deceives those eating; such things are blood, especially from a pig, cheese, particularly from a goat, bread made mostly of wheat, and butterflies, the yellow ones being the best among them. It should be "head-striking" <note>original: "caput feriens"; referring to substances that act quickly on the brain or nervous system, like an intoxicant</note>, so that it swiftly carries the force of the poison to the head: such as "burning water" <term>burning water (aqua ardens): a period term for distilled alcohol or spirits</term> and the dregs of wine. Finally, it should be a poisonous substance that renders them dazed: of which kind is the flower of the marigold, which they call *calendula* because it blooms every single month. For this herb, whose flowers are yellow, when cut into pieces, renders even very large fish dazed within the space of an hour. There is a type of flax which, when it had once soaked in a branch of a river, brought forth two hundred large dead fish to the surface of the water, besides the small ones, to my amazement in just a few days. There is lime which, even if tempered by water, still kills fish. There is the juice of any kind of spurge <note>original: "tithymali"; plants of the genus *Euphorbia*, known for their toxic, milky sap</note>; there is either kind of nut, the "vomiting nut" <note>original: "uomica"; *Strychnos nux-vomica*, containing strychnine</note>, and that which is called *methel* or the "sleep-bringer" <note>original: "somnifera"; likely referring to *Datura metel*, a powerful hallucinogen and sedative</note>. But nothing is more excellent than that fruit which is carried from the East; they call it *cogolum* <note>original: "cogolum"; likely *Anamirta cocculus*, also known as Cocculus Indicus or "fishberry," used for centuries to stun fish</note>; it is a black berry very similar to the laurel berry, but smaller and rounder. Our own composition for catching fish, which has been tested, is: a quarter-ounce of Oriental berries, a sixth-part <note>original: "sextans"; a Roman measure, one-sixth of a unit</note> each of cumin and "burning water," an ounce of cheese, and three ounces of flour; let these be crushed and worked into small pellets.

<margin>Horses and mules, so that they are not harmed by flies.</margin>
Other things not only lure, but some even turn things away, such as the juice of gourd leaves <note>original: "cucurbitae"; pumpkins or squashes</note>; if someone rubs this onto the hair of mules or horses in midsummer, by no small miracle of nature they are free from the annoyance of flies. This has very often been useful to me, but it is now far more useful to approach the inner chambers of the mind <note>original: "animi penetralia"; suggesting a transition from physical or natural history to psychology or the philosophy of the soul</note>.

# BOOK 14.
## On the soul and the intellect.

<margin>The knowing parts of the soul.</margin>
For one wishing to approach the powers of the soul, especially the human soul, which is our present subject, a new kind of discourse is necessary. As the philosopher <note>original: "philosophus"; likely referring to Aristotle, who wrote that "the soul is in a way all existing things"</note> rightly said, the soul seems to be all things: sensible things because of the senses, and things that are understood because of the intellect. I remember, however, that more was said on this in the book titled *On Immortality*, as well as in other books written by us. There are, therefore, two parts of the mind: the connected part, which is divided into three—reason, memory, and imagination—and the separable part, which is twofold—intellect and will. Besides these, there is a certain sixth kind of power by which the soul knows sensible things, not only according to their own specific nature, but also by comparing them with one another. And since appetite is twofold—one without sense and the other with sense—the affections themselves reside in the will and the sensible part of the soul: such as mercy, cruelty, anger, gentleness, boldness, fear, faith, treachery, shame, impudence, hatred, love, joy, sadness, lust, self-control, sluggishness, readiness, and moderation. Therefore, we must first speak of the intellect and the will.

<margin>What the intellect and will are.</margin>
The intellect is the very thing which is understood; for example, when I understand a horse, my intellect is the form <term>form (forma): the essential nature or mental blueprint of a thing, rather than its physical matter</term> of the horse. Therefore, it is a general form and like primary matter <note>original: "prima materia"; here used as a metaphor for the mind's capacity to be "shaped" by any thought</note>. But the will is active when it is carried outward; therefore, it is subsequent to the object of its desire, and it is not identical to the object then, but rather similar to it. They differ, therefore, in two main ways: First, the intellect is the thing itself that is understood, while the will is only similar to it. Second, because the intellect exists at the same moment the thing is understood, but the will comes after. Just as light and darkness are to the eye, so are hatred and love to the will, and falsehood and truth to the intellect.

<margin>Why truth sometimes follows from falsehood, but falsehood never from truth.</margin>
But why does truth follow from both false and true premises, while falsehood never follows from true ones? This happens because something of truth can be contained within the false; for example, in the false statement "a man is a donkey," there is contained the truth that "he perceives" <note>Since both humans and donkeys are sentient animals, the specific falsehood contains a general truth</note>. But in the truth, since it is pure, nothing of the false can be contained. Since, therefore, deduction from the whole to the part is the best method, truth can follow from falsehood, but falsehood can never follow from truth. Truth, then, does not follow from the falsehood itself, but from that part of the truth which is contained within the falsehood.

<margin>Why we delight in understanding.</margin>
Moreover, the intellect is affected by the understanding of truth with no small pleasure for three reasons: First, because this work alone is uniquely our own, and shared only with the gods <note>original: "diuis"; in this period, often referring to God, angels, or divine beings</note>; all other things are shared with some kind of beast, or even with all or most of them.

<meta>catchword: Second,</meta>

The author argues that the intellect is unique to humans and the divine, providing a source of profound pleasure.</summary>

<header>On the soul and the intellect.</header>

# On the soul and the intellect.

Second, because this task belongs to a more noble power: for the work itself is the perfection of that power. Third, on account of the utility which follows from the intellect and the knowledge of truth. Falsehood, however, is always hateful for its own sake; yet, because it sometimes serves to satisfy a desire, it is found pleasing. <margin>Why the telling of fables delights.</margin> Nevertheless, we are delighted by aptly composed fables <note>original: "fabulis"; refers here to myths, stories, or fictional narratives</note>, because they seem lifelike and contain wonders. For this reason, children are more delighted by them than old men, and the foolish more than the wise, because children and the foolish believe there is more truth within them. <margin>Why things heard delight more than things read.</margin> Furthermore, things heard are more pleasant than things read: and among those things which are read, those written in a foreign language are more pleasing, and rare books delight more. The cause in all these is one and the same: namely, rarity. For rare things are contained in rare books, known to fewer people; things which are difficult are rarer because fewer people know them; things which are heard are very rare; and rarest of all are those things told to us alone. Hence, nothing is more delightful to a person than conversations about great and secret matters. For those things known to everyone become cheap, even if they are precious; for this reason, the priests wished their ceremonies to be handed down obscurely: and these things would be nothing if they were not shaded by certain shadows of obscurity. Yet, an obscurity that does not allow writings to be understood is an argument for ignorance, just as moderate obscurity is an argument for wisdom. <margin>The three duties of a wise man.</margin> It is, moreover, the duty of a wise man: first, to have brought forth beautiful doubts; second, if it can be done, to have brought forth useful ones; then, to have taught the solution and the cause; and finally, to have said nothing absurd regarding the rendering of that cause—in which category the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato's philosophy</note> err the most. Contemplation itself cheers the soul and prolongs youth. For we truly live only while we contemplate. That life alone is truly the one that befits the gods in eternal age; and among us, this is the only such life.

<margin>How the affections of the soul change the body.</margin> Indeed, all the remaining affections <term>affections (affectus): the movements of the soul or emotions that impact the physical state</term> besides joy change the body itself, and with it the state of life, as will be manifest from these points. All the senses are delighted and saddened by different things. But even for the sake of delight itself, the spirits <term>spirits (spiritus): subtle, vaporous substances believed to carry life, heat, and sensation through the arteries and nerves</term> are carried outward; out of sadness, they flee inward. In vehement affections they do so quickly; in small ones, slowly and gradually. It is clear that the blood itself is carried along with the spirit. When it is carried outward, it is dilated, cooled, and strengthened, provided the forces are robust. When it is contracted, it is crushed and consumed. If the heat is strengthened, digestion <note>original: "concoctio"; the internal "cooking" of food into nutrients</note> flourishes, sleep is brought on, waste is digested, and diseases are cured—which we shall also teach further below. But when the heat is contracted, sleep is prevented, digestion is corrupted, waste is retained, and diseases are created.

We must speak now, therefore, of a few affections of the soul, so that by the same reasoning we may understand the others. <margin>The effects of fear.</margin> Therefore, in fear, the blood is immediately and in a mass driven into the interior parts. Whence men tremble, the voice is lost or wavers, and the body turns pale. If this persists and is intense, it induces gray hair; and with the blood contracted within, the man either wastes away or, with an inflammation <note>original: "phlegmone"; a term for heat-based swelling or inflammation</note> excited, suffers death.

In sadness, however, heat returns not all at once but gradually; therefore, the legs do not tremble, nor do they die suddenly, but they remain awake; the internal organs <note>original: "præcordia"; refers to the area around the heart and diaphragm, considered the seat of emotions</note> do not digest well, young people are suffocated, and those of advanced age waste away, suffering from <term>bad humors</term> <note>original: "cachomia," likely cacochymia, an imbalance of the bodily fluids</note>, poor complexion, and various diseases. Anger pours heat outward suddenly, yet it first seethes so much within that in those of hotter and drier <term>temperaments</term> <note>The four temperaments (sanguine, choleric, melancholic, phlegmatic) were thought to determine health and personality</note> a fever may be triggered. Certainly, the whole body grows warm in all people, which makes anger useful for those who either have an abundance of <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: "pituita"; one of the four bodily humors, considered cold and moist</note>, or whose physical condition is wasting away due to sadness or fear. Vehement joy carries the pure blood outward, such that in those with strong constitutions it usually cures diseases, but in the weak, it can kill; it is a remedy for anger, but even more so for fear.

<margin>Of Hope.</margin>
<margin>Of Shame.</margin>

<margin>Of Love.</margin>

<margin>The true substance of the intellect.</margin>
But hope is the opposite of sadness, and if it is without fear, it gradually spreads the natural heat. For this reason, among all the passions of the soul, hope alone is useful to everyone: it brings about digestion and sweet sleep; hence it also renders the body well-colored and plump. However, immoderate hope is almost similar to joy and does not allow for sleep. For every violent movement of the blood takes away sleep, since sleep is the rest of the spirits and the blood. Shame, truly, consists of hope and fear; therefore, the blood fluctuates in it with a double motion. It is familiar to children and young women; it bathes the face in a pleasing redness, and unlike fear, it does not bring harm when disturbed, but rather hatred. Hatred itself is also composed of hope, but also of sadness rather than fear. Envy, moreover, is a "thin" or slight hatred. It is clear, therefore, what bodily conditions arise from hatred and envy. But since love is the opposite of hatred, it will be a kind of "suspected joy," for suspicion is the opposite of firm hope—I mean firm hope, just as fear is the opposite of inconstant hope. Suspicion is a small fear, just as boldness is the greatest hope. It differs from joy because in both there is firm hope, but in boldness the goal is modest, while in joy it is pleasant. It is necessary to remember these things carefully in the following sections so that the <term>phenomena</term> <note>observable physical effects or symptoms</note> may be understood. Indeed, all these things change the body so much that if they are joined with a <term>melancholic humor</term> <note>Black bile, associated with depression and introspection</note>, they induce <term>ecstasy</term> <note>original: "ectasin"; a state of being "outside oneself," often a trance or loss of sensation</term> and stupor. If you were to burn these people or cut them with a razor, you would find they feel nothing at all: some lie there voluntarily as if dead; others even divine the future, and these things are regarded as great miracles among the unlearned. Yet, as Hippocrates says: *If the tongue suddenly becomes uncontrollable, or some part of the body grows faint with stupor, such is the nature of the melancholic.* But Galen <note>A famous Greek physician whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> by no means grasped the meaning of this. For this reason, he marvels at the sayings of the ancient master. It is necessary, however, that the body suffers during the passions of the soul, because these do not occur without the body. The intellect, however, does not change the body, except either because it must operate alongside reason and imagination, or because the whole human being is delighted while the intellect understands. For the intellect itself is entirely separated from the body by its nature. For now, while I write these things, my intellect is those very things which you understand through these writings; and while I deal with medical matters, it was medicine; and while I was writing about numbers, it was then number. So much so that to others...

<header>Of the soul and the intellect.</header>

# Of the soul and the intellect.

It happens to all those who have written on various subjects that, when I reread my own writings, I seem to myself to be a different person from the one I am now. Truly, in the intervening time, the human being understands principles but does not perceive that understanding, just as one does not always perceive oneself sensing when the mind is withdrawn. Therefore, when a person sleeps, or is still an infant, or is drunk, although they may seem to be idle, they still understand; however, the operation is not shared with the conscious self. For when the person recovers their senses, they understand again without difficulty. Thus, the form of the intellect is eternal, since our intellect remains and exists even while you read and contemplate these words, and the forms—that is, the essences of universal things—remain the same forever. It seems, then, that the souls of the wise are especially immortal; but in the senses, there is no such permanence, and for that reason sensory perception perishes, and even that which is sensed does not remain the same.

<margin>The two types of artificial memory</margin>
Therefore, we do not imagine things or use reason in the same way: memory is, as it were, more similar to the intellect. It is aided by order, because things that consist of a clear order are so easily held that they reflect as if they were a single thing. This is twofold—concerning things and concerning words—and each serves as a support for the other. Hence, <term>artificial memory</term> <note>The "Art of Memory" (ars memoriae) was a classical technique using mental "places" and "images" to remember vast amounts of information</note> is also twofold: the memory of things, which consists of images, was discovered and handed down long ago by <term>Cicero</term> <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), the Roman statesman and orator</note> and <term>Quintilian</term> <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35–100 CE), a Roman educator and rhetorician</note>, by which words are held; and the memory of words, by which both things and then words are held. This latter type consists of the first syllables of names or beginnings, from which words and then poems are made. Of the same kind is that which consists of the conjunction of numbers. It is remarkable how much both methods benefit extemporaneous actions and games; from this, we have received the reward of our beautiful invention: namely, the reputation of memory, which has helped us greatly.

<margin>Passive memory.</margin>
Nevertheless, everything that exists depends on writing <note>original: "lapidi," literally "on stone," likely referring to the permanence of written records</note> and on this invention, aside from the passive memory that flourishes within us. Active memory, however, and especially both types of the artificial kind, are greatly aided by the imagination. Indeed, artificial memory is hardly anything other than the translation of things and words into the order and power of the imagination. This brings such a great advantage—specifically regarding words and numbers—that you can more easily recite a hundred items with it than ten without it. Yet reason is the leader of all mortal virtues and is unique to man as a mortal being. But truly, as he possesses intellect, he cultivates arts and sciences, as well as certain artificial inventions that do not belong to the arts because they lack utility or are of an uncertain category; every art, however, is of a certain and useful category.

# BOOK XV.
## Concerning Subtleties of an Uncertain Kind or Useless Nature.

<margin>Why boards are least broken when struck through the middle of another</margin>
**O**f this sort are matters such as why, if a blow falls upon a board, a board placed underneath is not broken as much as when wedges are driven in. Certainly, it is because the force of the blow is distributed throughout the whole of the supporting board, and thus becomes weaker in each individual part. Nor is one part of the wood forced to descend while another part is left behind—which is the very beginning of a fracture. Furthermore, the blow is tempered by that intervening layer. Since air also lacks its own driving force, it cannot violently enter the second board placed below, and therefore cannot split it.

<margin>Why glass vessels exposed to fire do not break when a small fork is placed underneath.</margin>
A similar case is why glass vessels exposed to fire do not break when a small fork <note>The author likely refers to a "furcula" or small metal support used to lift the glass slightly off the direct heat source.</note> is placed beneath them: because the wood <note>The author may be implying the fork is wooden or that the interaction between the materials prevents direct thermal shock.</note> does not grow hot in the same way, and it compels the parts of the glass to expand or mix evenly. Otherwise, glass breaks because the watery moisture within is converted into vapor before the rest of the material can adapt.

<margin>A playful instrument.</margin>
Truly, there is an instrument made of seven rings that is of no practical use. It consists of a thin iron plate <term>bractea</term> <note>a thin strip or laminate of metal</note> a finger's width wide and a palm's length, in which seven round, narrow holes are arranged at equal spaces along its length. These holes receive seven thin rods, about an inch in height, which are movable at the bottom and bent at the top so that they hold rings the size of a finger enclosed within them. These rods are themselves held by the following ring below the bend. Because of this, all the rings except for the first are prevented by the one preceding them from jumping freely outside the forward rod. Everything is made of iron, including the little "boat" <term>nauicula</term> <note>a shuttle-like piece, often called the "slider" in modern versions of this puzzle</note>, the appearance of which we have rendered exactly in the margin, long and wide according to the size of the underlying plate. With this instrument, a game of marvelous subtlety <note>This is a classic description of the Baguenaudier, also known as the "Chinese Rings" puzzle.</note> has been devised. 

The first and second rings are sent through the empty space A; then the "boat" is passed through those same rings. After that, the first of them is lowered through the empty space A, after which the third ring is pulled upward through the empty middle part of the boat, just as the first two were; and there the boat is pushed in. Then, with the first also brought upward, three rings now surround the boat itself. You will then lower the first two, having first removed the boat, so that the boat remains enclosed by the third ring alone; from there, it will be possible to bring the fourth over it. Thus, this entire industrious task is contained within three rules:

First, that a ring to be pulled up or let down must have only one ring before it into which the boat is enclosed. Second, that while you let them down, you should always let down the first two together, and pull up one; or by letting down one, you pull up the first two. Third, that whichever ring is pulled up or let down, it is necessary to pull up all those that come before it...
