### Concerning Useless Subtleties.

...is to remove them and again to lower them. Therefore, the first two are not hindered by any other from intervening: I call the first a ring, which is free in sixty-four turns <note>The author is describing the "Chinese Rings" or "Baguenaudier" puzzle. The number of moves required to solve it follows a binary sequence; for $n$ rings, it takes roughly $2^n$ moves.</note>, if the little boat <term>navicula</term> <note>This refers to the sliding bar or shuttle used to manipulate the rings in the puzzle.</note> is moved without error. It is included in all the rings and contains all the rods included in thirty-one moves; in others, the little boat is brought back to the last rod. Indeed, it returns in the same number of turns, so that there are eighty-five from the release to the transition of the first or the last, and let it return by the same number. Therefore, the whole circle will be completed in one hundred and ninety turns. This is useless in itself, but it can nevertheless be transferred to the ingenious locks of chests. <margin>The most subtle game of Latrunculi.</margin> There is a similar subtlety in the game of *latrunculi* <term>latrunculi</term> <note>An ancient Roman strategy board game, often compared to chess, involving the capture of pieces by surrounding them.</note>, but it is more delightful because of its variety and competition: for just as the "little boat" is of a most subtle invention in that genre, so is *latrunculi* among all games. We have, moreover, written four books on games in the past.

<margin>The ridiculous subtlety of Ramon Llull.</margin> A third kind of useless subtlety may be seen in the books of Ramon Llull <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1315) was a Majorcan philosopher who developed a "logical machine" of rotating discs to combine concepts and "prove" truths.</note>. It is a matter altogether worthy of laughter: to wish to hand down all learning while knowing none of it. <margin>The diligent subtlety of Plautus.</margin> The diligence of Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a Roman playwright. The "names" mentioned refer to acrostic summaries of his plays often found in manuscripts.</note> is less to be detested in this regard, because he spent less labor in composing the titles of his plays through letters which form the beginning of each verse of the plot summary. But that man [Llull], through combinations, promised to hand down all learning, as I said. Since there was no art beneath those commonplaces, while some people thought an art lay underneath, he found not only those who would admire it, but also those who would look up to it and interpret it. And while these interpreters offer themselves, they do not explain a difficulty—of which there is none—but rather try to introduce one.

<margin>The marvelous subtlety of Rhabanus.</margin> But the subtlety of Rhabanus <note>Rhabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), a Carolingian scholar famous for his "pattern poems" where text is arranged into visual shapes.</note> is placed in the fifth kind, a work of immense labor and quite curious. He observes the law of poetry and numbers at the same time: first, he explains the image of figures by the placement of letters; then, with the letters included in the figure, he again contains the meaning and history of the figure; and with these, he even constructs poems. Indeed, in the whole series of poems, he explains everything, again containing the meaning of the figure. Thus he depicts crosses, trees, birds, and countless other things by this art, of which this may be one example:

# Book Fifteen

If you observe, this poem is read by descending vertically:

->The hallowed form of the cross shines in venerable attire.<-
<note>original: "Forma sacrata crucis uenerando fulget amictu." This is likely an example of a "grid poem" or carmen figuratum where words are hidden in a block of text.</note>

And again, while you move from right to left, this other one is found in the enclosure:

->Great honor clothes it: I speak this more lightly to the nation.<-
<note>original: "Magnus uestit honor: leuius loquor hoc nationi."</note>

If these things had some practical utility joined to them, I would judge the man worthy of the highest praise; but as it is, one may laugh at the effort just as much as one admires the ingenuity. An individual example may be pleasing, but a great number of them certainly produces boredom. And this is almost the one thing common to all such pursuits for which there is no use among men.

<margin>Proclus's books do not pertain to the art.</margin>
Of the same theme, but of somewhat more useful argument, are those four books of Geometry by Proclus on the *Elements* of Euclid <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose commentary on the first book of Euclid's Elements is a major source for the history of Greek geometry.</note>; for they teach nothing new, and for that reason, they do not pertain to the "art" <term>ars</term> <note>In this context, "art" refers to a practical, productive branch of knowledge or technical skill.</note>. However, because that subtlety is varied and not entirely of one single type—as is the case with Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), a Carolingian scholar famous for his "In honorem sanctae crucis," a collection of highly complex visual poems.</note> and Llull—they ought not to be cast aside and scorned as altogether useless. For when there are many examples of even subtlety itself, it becomes a kind of art.

<margin>How whatever things are demonstrated in the elements of Euclid can be shown without any change to the single proposed circle.</margin>
Therefore, by a similar argument to that of Proclus—more for youthful display than for manifest utility—both I and Ludovico Ferrari <note>Ludovico Ferrari (1522–1565) was Cardano's brilliant student, famous for solving the quartic equation.</note> discovered within a few days a method by which whatever is demonstrated by Euclid could be perfectly shown by us with a fixed compass width. This was done according to whatever invariable width might be proposed by an opponent, excluding only the inscription and circumscription of circles. And although while we were writing these things, Ludovico himself had published this entire demonstration excellently in print, nevertheless, because that work was written for the sake of a competition, I do not think it will survive, since it contains almost nothing else of excellence. Even if some parts are excellent, they are placed separately and are not of one kind, as the subject matter required. Thus, I have considered it worth the effort to add it here again, lest such a rare example of subtlety should ever perish. But how? With brief demonstrations, so that those who shrink from geometry may not be seized by boredom. Therefore, first, the fourth proposition of the first book of the *Elements* <note>Euclid's Proposition I.4 is the "Side-Angle-Side" (SAS) theorem for triangle congruence.</note> must be demonstrated, just as it is by Euclid, since it requires the help of no preceding construction. Then the fifth; for as far as the demonstration is concerned, it needs only the fourth (which we shall call the first), just as the fifth needs the second. As for drawing the lines, the width of the circle proposed to us will suffice, since it is permitted to produce lines to any length in a straight direction. Then our third will be that which is written as the eighth by Euclid in the first book of the *Elements* <note>Euclid's Proposition I.8 is the "Side-Side-Side" (SSS) theorem for triangle congruence.</note>. Another triangle having been placed on the opposite side upon the base, and a straight line drawn from vertex to vertex: for it is established (as is also shown by Proclus in the third book from the second proposition and by common sense) that the triangles are equiangular; and since they are also equilateral, they will be equal by the first proposition. Furthermore, one may transfer triangles, since Euclid in his fourth proposition...

In this context, the author is describing a geometric challenge where the compass is "fixed" or "rusty," meaning it cannot be opened or closed to different widths.</note>, I will describe two circles according to the given width, with their centers made at the ends of the lines. These circles intersect each other at the proposed angle and on the opposite side; by drawing lines from the centers of the circles to that intersection, and then from intersection to intersection, the goal is immediately clear from our third proposition and the definition of a circle. 

But if anyone is so perverse as to not even admit that circles intersect anywhere except at the angle, we shall repeat the circles on both sides as many times as necessary until they finally either intersect or touch. Through our second and first propositions, we will achieve this, and finally, through the third, the proposed angle will be cut in two <note>Bisected.</note> by a straight line drawn from the angle to the opposite intersection of the circles. 

We will establish our fifth as the tenth of **Euclid** <note>Euclid 1.10: How to bisect a given finite straight line.</note>, its force and figure being demonstrated by the method of the preceding one. The sixth will be his eleventh <note>Euclid 1.11: How to draw a straight line at right angles to a given straight line from a given point on it.</note>; here, from the given point on both sides, we will take a distance equal to the width of the circle. When both are divided in half by the fifth, the parts joined at the point will be half the width of the compass, and both joined together will be the width itself. Then, with the ends of that line placed as centers where the circles intersect, a line drawn to the given point will be perpendicular according to our third. 

Then we shall establish **Euclid’s** thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth as our seventh, eighth, and ninth, since they require nothing other than what has already been demonstrated. The tenth proposition will be this: *Given two unequal lines touching each other, to cut off from the greater a part equal to the smaller*; this is **Euclid’s** third. Yet **Euclid** demonstrates this even for lines that are not joined. To demonstrate this, therefore, let the angle they contain be divided by an indefinite line. Afterwards, with the center made at the end of the shorter line, I will describe a circle that intersects the middle line; and where it intersects, having again made a center, I will describe a circle that falls upon the end of the smaller line, but will cut the larger to the equality of the smaller. For when the triangles are transposed—whose vertices are at the point of junction of the proposed lines, and whose ends are the intersections of the circles with the lines—the dividing middle line is the common base of both, according to the method allowed by **Euclid** in his fourth proposition of the first book of the *Elements* <note>The SAS (Side-Angle-Side) theorem.</note>. Unless the given lines were equal, a part would be equal to the whole, which cannot be. 

But if you say that the circle having its center at the end of the smaller line does not reach the middle line, let those angles be bisected by the fourth as many times as necessary until they reach it. Then, with the demonstration repeated, the goal will be achieved as before. The eleventh will be: *Construct a triangle of two equal sides upon a given line.* We shall divide it in half and erect a perpendicular from the point of intersection by the sixth; once the triangle is completed, the goal is clear by the first. From this, without circles and by the preceding [proposition], according to the method of **Euclid**...

<header>BOOK XVI On the Sciences.</header>
<meta>catchword: -tem (continuation of "partem")</meta>

# BOOK XVI
## On the Sciences.

<margin>12 properties of the circle.</margin>
**B**ut those sixty properties of figures, which I intend to set down here, are not without great utility. Twelve of these are attributed to the circle. First, in a circle, lines that intersect one another create parts that are proportional. The angle formed by their intersection is equal to the angles at the circumference standing upon both arcs <note>This refers to the theorem that an interior angle is half the sum of the intercepted arcs.</note> taken together. A quadrilateral <term>quadrilaterum</term> <note>A four-sided figure.</note> inscribed within a circle always has its two opposite angles equal to two right angles. Furthermore, the two rectangles <note>In this context, "rectangle" refers to the area produced by multiplying two lengths—the product of the sides.</note> formed by its opposite sides, when added together, are equal to the rectangle formed by the diagonals of the quadrilateral <note>This is known as Ptolemy’s Theorem.</note>. However, for a quadrilateral that is circumscribed around a circle, the sum of two opposite sides is equal to the sum of the remaining two opposite sides. Indeed, the circle is the most capacious of shapes in proportion to its perimeter <note>The isoperimetric property: for a given boundary length, the circle encloses the most area.</note>, and all regular shapes contained within it are more capacious than any others that can be contained by the same number of sides. Moreover, figures within a circle that are equilateral (having equal sides) are also equiangular. It has a point in the middle—the center—from which all lines drawn to the circumference are equal. If a point is fixed outside the circle, any lines drawn to the far side of the circumference, when multiplied by the part outside the circle, will produce a rectangle <note>a product of lengths</note> equal to the square of the tangent line <term>contingens</term> drawn from that same point. If the diameter is extended outside the circle as far as one likes, and another diameter is cut at right angles in the center, and the fourth part of the circumference starting from the end of this diameter is divided into any number of equal parts, and a straight line is drawn through the last of these to the line lying outside in a straight line with the diameter—then that line adjacent to the diameter will be equal to all the straight lines drawn as perpendiculars from the points of the circumference divisions to the diameter below, extending to the opposite part of the circumference; all these lines, as is clear, are parallel to the diameter that was produced externally. But if from the same extremity of the diameter any number of lines are drawn, either inside or outside—to the part adjacent outside, and to the other part of the circumference inside—there will always be rectangles formed from the whole line times the part included by the circumference (for the external ones), and from the whole line times the part of the diameter included by the inscribed square (for the internal ones), which are always equal.

<margin>5 properties common to the circle, the hyperbola, and the ellipse.</margin>
Those properties which are common to the circle, the hyperbolas, and the defect <note>original: *defectio*. This is a literal translation of the Greek *ellipsis*, the term for an ellipse.</note>, are as follows. A perpendicular line drawn from a tangent to the diameter (aligned with the point from which the tangent was drawn) divides the segments of the diameter in the same proportion as the whole line—extending from the point where the tangent originates to the center of the circle and through to the other part of the circumference—relates to the part...

<header>Book Sixteen</header>

# Book Sixteen

the outer part. The radius <term>semidimetiens</term> <note>literally "half-measurer"</note> is also a mean proportional between the line extending from the center to an external point, and the line from the center to the point where a perpendicular falls from the point of tangency upon that same diameter. Moreover, when two tangents are drawn from the ends of a diameter, and from those same points two lines are drawn through the same point on the circumference to the opposite tangent, the rectangle formed by the parts of the tangents bounded by these last lines will be equal to the square of the diameter.

<margin>2 properties of the Ellipse.</margin>
There are two properties of the **Ellipse** <note>original: *defectio*, a term referring to how the figure "falls short" of a circle</note>: the first is that its ratio to the surface of a circle is as the rectangle of the diameters of the ellipse to the rectangle of the diameters of the circle (which is a square). The second arises from this: that the ratio of one ellipse to another is as the ratio of the rectangles contained by their own respective diameters.

<margin>3 properties of the Hyperbola.</margin>
Again, there are two <note>The text says "two," but lists three distinct points</note> unique properties of the **Hyperbola**: the first is that two lines can be found which, starting from a center placed outside the hyperbola, will always become closer to the sides of the hyperbola, and yet will never touch them <note>These are the asymptotes</note>. It is therefore evident from this that it is possible to take an infinite number of other straight lines, parallel to the first ones and joined at a single point, toward which the sides of the hyperbola will approach closer and closer forever unto infinity; yet they will always remain separated by some certain distance, however small I might wish. The third property is that if two points are marked on any part of the circumference of the hyperbola, and two pairs of lines are drawn parallel to each other toward the asymptotes <note>original: *non tangentes*, the "non-touching" lines</note>, the rectangles formed by those lines originating from the lower point and the other point will be equal to each other.

<margin>6 properties of the Parabola.</margin>
There are six unique properties of the **Parabola**. First, the ratio of the parts of the axis is as the square <note>original: *duplicata*, the duplicate ratio or square</note> of the perpendiculars drawn from those points to the circumference of the parabola. Second, when the perpendicular itself is equal to the part of the axis that terminates at the vertex from the end of that same perpendicular, that perpendicular shall be called the **upright side** <term>latus rectum</term> of the parabola; and this will always have the same proportion to any perpendicular from the axis to the circumference as that same perpendicular has to the part of the axis lying between the perpendicular and the vertex of the section. These perpendicular lines are called **ordinates** <term>ordinatæ</term>. It is evident, therefore, that for any part of the axis of a parabola and its perpendicular, the same line is always subtended in continuous proportion. Third, if a point is marked on it away from the axis and a tangent is drawn from it, and many lines parallel to this tangent are drawn from one side of the circumference to the other, then a line drawn from that same point of tangency parallel to the axis will bisect all those lines drawn parallel to the tangent. Furthermore, any segments taken in any way that have equal diameters are themselves equal. Finally, the surface area itself is equal to the rectangle formed by the entire base multiplied by two-thirds of the axis <note>This is the famous theorem of Archimedes on the quadrature of the parabola</note>.

Sixth, when three lines tangent to the periphery of a **parabola** intersect, the two outermost ones are cut by the middle one; the ratio of the three parts of the lines will be uniform. Specifically, the ratio of the lower part to the upper, and the ratio of the other upper part to the lower, and the middle part of those lines which terminate at the periphery of the parabola.

<margin>A property common to all conic sections, the circle, and opposite hyperbolas.</margin>
It is common to all conic sections and the circle, as well as to opposite hyperbolas, that when two tangents meet at a single point, and a straight line is drawn from that point of intersection through to the opposite part of the circumference—or, in the case of opposite hyperbolas, to the straight line drawn through the points of contact—the ratio of the whole line to the part that lies outside the oblique lines <note>The "oblique lines" here refer to the tangents forming the angle</note> is the same as the ratio of the parts contained within the oblique lines of that same line.

<margin>A property of opposite hyperbolas.</margin>
When the remaining side of a triangle (whose base cuts the base of the hyperbola at right angles) is drawn, the midpoint of the exterior part of the axis of the hyperbola is called the **center**. The exterior part turned toward the point of contact is called the <term>latus rectum</term> <note>original: *recta*; literally the "upright" or "straight" line. This is a fundamental parameter that determines the curvature of the conic section</note>, defined by the ratio of the square of the perpendicular from the vertex of the cone (parallel to the axis) to the base of the triangle, and the rectangle of the parts of its base. Therefore, when a flat surface simultaneously cuts two cones with equal angles placed opposite one another at their vertices so that their sides lie on the same straight line, both sections of the cones will necessarily be **hyperbolas**. Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Perga, the 3rd-century BC Greek mathematician known as "The Great Geometer" for his work on conics</note> usually refers to these two sections as "opposite" hyperbolas <note>These are the two symmetrical branches of a single hyperbolic curve</note>.

<margin>6 properties of the spiral line.</margin>
There are also six properties of the **spiral line** <note>This refers to the "Spiral of Archimedes," which is generated by a point moving along a line at a constant speed while the line rotates at a constant speed</note>. First, a tangent line drawn from the end of the spiral meets a perpendicular line drawn from the start; it always cuts off a portion of the tangent such that it holds a ratio to the circumference of the circle (of the same order) according to the numerical sequence. From this it is clear that the portion of the first spiral from the perpendicular will be equal to the circumference of the first circle, and the portion of the perpendicular from the second spiral will be double the circumference of the second circle, and the portion from the third spiral will be triple the circumference of the third circle, and so on. Second, a tangent drawn from any point of the first spiral meets the perpendicular drawn from the start of the same diameter, cutting off a part equal to the portion of the circumference of a circle whose radius <term>semidiameter</term> is the line from the start of the spiral to the point of tangency, enclosed between the first straight line of the spiral (which is understood to be in motion) and the position the spiral reaches after moving directly from the point of tangency. The third property is that the areas <term>spacia</term> of the spirals are related as follows: the first is a unit of one, the second six, the third twelve, the fourth eighteen, and so on, increasing perpetually by six. Fourth, the ratio of any circle to the area of its spiral contained within the same straight line is as the square of the circle's radius to the rectangle formed by the radius and the line of the preceding spiral, plus one-third of the square of the radius of the circle surrounding the first spiral. <margin>The special property of all straight-lined figures.</margin>
One thing is common to all straight-lined <note>original: *rectilineis*; figures made of straight lines</note> figures: if each side is extended, all the exterior angles taken together—even if there are a thousand of them—are equal to four right angles <note>360 degrees</note>. This depends on the fact that all the internal angles are equal to as many right angles as double the number of sides or angles, minus four; this is derived from the logic of the triangles into which the figure is divided.

<margin>Three special properties of triangles.</margin>
For in any triangle, the three angles taken together are equal to two right angles, while an exterior angle is equal to the two opposite interior angles taken together. Furthermore, the area is equal to the product of half the sum of all sides <note>the semi-perimeter</note> multiplied by the difference of each side from that same half-sum, multiplying all together rather than adding, so that three multiplications are performed <note>This is a verbal description of Heron's Formula for the area of a triangle</note>.

<margin>A property of the square.</margin>
It is a specific property of the square that its side is the <term>mean proportion</term> <note>A value $x$ such that $a:x = x:b$</note> between the sum of the side and the diagonal and the difference between them. This happens because the square of the diagonal of a square is double the square of the side itself.

<margin>A property of the equilateral and equiangular pentagon.</margin>
In an equilateral and equiangular pentagon <note>a regular five-sided shape</note>, the side is the greater part of a line divided according to the <term>mean and extreme ratio</term> <note>the Golden Ratio</note>, in comparison to the line which <term>subtends</term> <note>a chord connecting two non-adjacent vertices</note> two sides of that same pentagon.

<margin>A property of a similar hexagon.</margin>
The side of a hexagon—provided it is, as I said, equilateral and equiangular—is equal to the radius of the circle circumscribing that same hexagon.

<margin>A property of a similar heptagon.</margin>
In a heptagon <note>a seven-sided figure</note>, the side, the line subtending two of its sides, and the line subtending three sides together form a triangle (if it is, as I said, equilateral and equiangular). The ratio of the sum of the side and the three-side chord to the two-side chord is the same as the ratio of the two-side chord to the side; and again, the ratio of the side and the two-side chord to the three-side chord is the same as the ratio of the three-side chord to the two-side chord of that same heptagon.

# On the Sciences.

<margin>2 Special properties of the sphere.</margin>
<margin>The property of the five solids contained within a sphere.</margin>
<margin>1 Special property of the parts of a sphere.</margin>
The surface area surrounding a sphere is four times that of its greatest circle <note>This refers to the "equator" or any circle passing through the center of the sphere</note>. Furthermore, the sphere itself is the most capacious of all solid bodies in proportion to its perimeter <note>Meaning it contains the most volume for a given surface area</note>. It contains—and can be contained by—the five [Platonic] solids, which are the only shapes that can have all surfaces equal, all solid angles equal, and all sides mutually equal to one another. Regarding the parts of a sphere that are divided by a plane perpendicular to the axis, there are three special properties. First, the surface area of any portion of a sphere is equal to a circle whose radius <note>original: *semidimetiens*</note> is the straight line drawn from the vertex of that portion to the edge of the circle that forms its base. From this it is clear that the ratio between the surface areas of two parts of a sphere separated by a plane is the same as the ratio between the segments of the diameter divided by that same plane (provided the diameter is perpendicular to the plane). Furthermore, the ratio of the solid volumes of the sphere's parts, when a single plane divides the diameter perpendicularly, is equal to the ratio of a body formed from the square of the larger portion’s axis multiplied by a line consisting of the smaller portion plus half the axis, to a body formed from the square of the smaller portion multiplied by a line consisting of the half-axis plus the larger portion.

<margin>Three special properties of the right cone.</margin>
This, however, depends on the following: a cone having the same base as a portion of the sphere—if its height has the same ratio to the height of that portion as the sum of the remaining portion's height and half the axis has to the height of that same remaining portion—will be equal to the axis <note>This is a complex Archimedean ratio describing the volume of a spherical segment</note>. From this it is clear that any sphere is four times the size of a cone whose base is the sphere's greatest circle and whose height is half the diameter of the sphere. Also, any cone is equal to a "spherical sector" <note>A pie-shaped wedge reaching the center</note> that terminates at the center from the outer surface, when the cone's height is the radius of the sphere and the base is equal to the surface area of that sector; thus the bases and heights will then be equal.

<margin>2 Special properties of rectangular conoids.</margin>
<margin>A special property of obtuse-angled conoids.</margin>
In a rectangular conoidal body <term>paraboloid | a 3D shape formed by rotating a parabola</term>, a portion cut by a plane and ending at the apex is one-and-a-half times <note>original: *sesquialtera*</note> the size of a cone sharing the same base and axis. Again, portions of rectangular conoids maintain the same ratio to one another as the squares of their respective axes. However, when an obtuse-angled conoid <term>hyperboloid | a 3D shape formed by rotating a hyperbola</term> is cut by a plane, the ratio of the part at the vertex to a cone with the same base and axis-portion is equal to the ratio of a line made of the conoid’s axis-portion plus three times the line from the center of the hyperbola <note>the "oblique side"</note> to that same axis-portion plus twice the line from the center of the hyperbola.

<margin>4 Special properties of the spheroid.</margin>
There are four special properties of spheroids <term>ellipsoids | egg-like shapes</term>: when one is divided by a plane through its center, it is divided into two equal halves. Any such portion will be double the size of a cone having a base and axis equal to that portion of the spheroid. If a spheroid is cut anywhere other than through the center, the ratio of that part to a cone with the same height and base is as half the axis plus the axis of the remaining portion is to that same remaining axis-portion of the other side.

<summary>This page outlines the geometric properties and volume ratios of spheres, cones, and "conoids" (paraboloids and hyperboloids), drawing heavily from Archimedean solid geometry. It explains how these curved shapes relate to one another and to the five Platonic solids.</summary>
<keywords>sphere, cone, conoid, paraboloid, hyperboloid, spheroid, Platonic solids, Archimedes, solid geometry, ratios</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the mathematical discourse from page 307, moving from the properties of spheres to those of spheroids and cylinders, before transitioning into a broader discussion on the methodology of geometry and the introduction of algebra, which the author calls the "Great Art."</meta>

<page-num>508</page-num>
<header>Book Sixteen</header>

...of the <term>spheroid</term><note>A solid figure resembling a sphere but not perfectly round, such as an ellipsoid.</note>. From this the fourth point is clear: that when a spheroid and a portion of a sphere maintain the same or equal height and base, they will be equal to each other in volume.

<margin>2 Special properties of the cylinder.</margin>
From this, there are two special properties of the cylinder. First, a cylinder is three times the volume of a cone that has the same height and base. Second, regarding a sphere whose diameter is equal to its own height, and whose greatest circle is equal to the base of the cylinder, the cylinder itself will be <term>one and a half times</term><note>original: *sesquialter*; this refers to the 3:2 ratio discovered by Archimedes between the volume of a cylinder and its inscribed sphere.</note> the volume of that sphere. These, therefore, are sixty properties of geometric figures—both of surfaces and of solid bodies—that are most outstanding in their nobility, beauty, and the wonder they provoke. For it does not escape me that such properties are nearly infinite, but others cannot be compared with these in elegance: either because a demonstration of them has not yet been found; or because they cannot be understood by the simple definition of their names; or because they do not relate to <term>equality</term><note>The concept of two different shapes having exactly the same area or volume.</note>, but rather seem to wander. For equality is the specific goal of the geometer.

<margin>Three ways of finding geometric theorems.</margin>
But if a figure differs in some other way, such as being "greater than" or "known," the "greater" is sought for the sake of finding equality, and the "known" is sought for the sake of something equal to what is already understood. One may achieve this in three ways, and it is called a "demonstrative proof" if it proceeds directly, or "by negation" when it is deduced by responding to an impossibility <note>Also known as *reductio ad absurdum*, proving a point by showing its opposite is impossible.</note>. The third way is through "continued power," as when the magnitude of a parabola or the surface of a sphere is demonstrated by **Archimedes**; this is the method we most often use in the most subtle discoveries. This method is two-fold: the simple type, which consists of a comparison of the greater and the lesser (as in determining the magnitude of the surface of a sphere);

<margin>Geometry: the most subtle of sciences.</margin>
The other type arises from proportions which lack a limit <note>Likely referring to infinite series or the method of exhaustion.</note>, as in the area of a parabola. It is no wonder, then, that geometry is the most subtle of all sciences. Yet, because it takes its beginning from the most obvious things, it rightly offered the opportunity for it to be the first of all subjects taught even to boys. It is marvelous how briefly it drags you from a few very clear <term>axioms</term><note>Self-evident truths that require no proof.</note> to the most obscure matters. Thus, it also rises immediately from the lowest things to the most sublime.

<margin>The five-fold use of the Great Art.</margin>
Arithmetic follows closest upon this, whose most subtle discovery is the art which we have called the **Great Art** <note>original: *Ars Magna*; Cardano’s foundational work on Algebra published in 1545.</note>, discovered and published by us—though others have called it the **Algebraic Art**. Its utility is manifold: to sharpen the intellect; to find and explain the unknown sides <note>roots or variables</note> of quantities; to describe those same quantities with lines according to geometric principles, whether as planes or solids; to solve proposed problems and riddles; and to be able to refute poorly solved ones. For example, the size of the side of a heptagon <note>a seven-sided polygon</note> was wrongly sought by **Charles de Bovelles** <note>original: *Bouillus*</note>, and the equality of a circle's circumference was falsely claimed to be found through a balance <note>original: *libramento*; a reference to using physical weights to "prove" math.</note> by **Nicholas of Cusa**, which was then rightly exploded by **Johannes Regiomontanus** <note>original: *Ioanne Monteregio*</note>. All these things consist of the simplest figure, which shows lines, areas, and even bodies;

<margin>The discovery of Michael Stifel in arithmetic.</margin>
but also following the fourth [proposition] of the second book of **Euclid’s** *Elements*, and the six propositions immediately following it. We shall also praise certain individual discoveries, such as **Michael Stifel's** discovery regarding sides <note>referring to roots of numbers</note>, which was translated by us into the first book of our *Perfect Work* <note>original: *operis perfecti*</note>.

# Concerning the Sciences

However, in the Diatonic system, we have added two <term>strings</term><note>Meaning notes or pitches, following the ancient Greek practice of naming notes after the strings of the lyre.</note>: one below the lowest and the other above the highest, so that the proportion of the semitones remains consistent. 

While there are two extremes and a middle—which they call the **Tenor**—across different voices (for what was said regarding the diatessaron refers only to one), a fourth voice, the **Altus** <note>The alto voice.</note>, has been added. Because it fills the empty spaces, it excels the others in sweetness. For when something is skillfully added to a thing that is already perfect, it usually contributes greatly to its ornament. For this reason, it fits all the voices with wonderful art. It uniquely observes the <term>deep-toned voice</term><note>The bass voice.</note>, against which it often raises itself to the highest pitch. At times, as if changed into the deep-toned voice itself, it plunges into the depths, observing the higher voice of the whole harmony through contrary motion. For the most part, it plays around the middle by filling in the spaces. Because it is so noble, it requires a singer of excellent nature and talent; if these are lacking, the voice amounts to nothing at all.

<margin>
Rules of singing.
</margin>

Furthermore, the singing of notes is easy: we call these notes **Ut, Re, Mi, Fa, Sol, La**. However, to utter the words is more difficult. Therefore, since boys learn the notes first, they are often transferred to the words with no small difficulty. This transition is made in three ways: The first is that one learns by ear the <term>diapente</term><note>The interval of a fifth.</note>, the <term>diapason</term><note>The interval of an octave.</note>, the diatessaron, and the other middle consonances, as well as the seventh, ninth, and second; and then, having learned to produce them with the voice, one utters words and syllables according to those magnitudes of pitch. This is truly difficult, since the sixth and the third are <term>double</term><note>Meaning they can be either major or minor.</note>, and it is not permitted to produce them without imagining the notes, and...

# Book Sixteen

Thus, if you substitute one for another, you will disagree by a <term>semitone</term><note>The smallest interval in traditional Western music, a half-step.</note> with the remaining voices. The second method is to conceive in your mind, on whatever space or line, which pitch and of what magnitude it ought to be, and so utter the syllables <note>the lyrics or text</note> under the pitch of that location. This method is better than the first, but when <term>dieses</term><note>Quarter-tones or small melodic intervals.</note> and semitones or "feigned tones" <note>original: "toni ficti"; referring to *musica ficta*, or notes outside the standard scale like sharps and flats</note> occur, it will not suffice, and they will be uttered with difficulty. The third method is the best of all: that you retain the notes and the magnitude of the pitches in your imagination and voice, while with your tongue you utter the underlying syllable; and this, as it is the best, is also the most difficult. Therefore, we shall achieve this in three ways: first, through long practice, so that having gradually set aside the musical note, you may utter the syllable upon the notes—first with those of longer duration and in unison, then gradually with those ascending and descending, and soon with the <term>diapason</term><note>An octave.</note>, the <term>diapente</term><note>A perfect fifth.</note>, and the <term>diatessaron</term><note>A perfect fourth.</note>. Likewise in those consonances which they call cadences, and finally in other pitches; after this, you may transfer yourself to notes of short duration. The second way is that you learn to keep the tongue immobile, and thus utter the pitch without notes or syllables. Afterward, practice under only one syllable always, such as under E or I. Finally, proceed to uttering the actual syllables. This method takes its variety from the manner of delivery, just as the first does from the music itself. The third, which in my judgment is better, is done with the help of another person who utters the notes while you sing the syllables; in this way, both the duration and the magnitude of the pitch will be preserved, and you will gradually transfer yourself through habit to that which is most difficult. There was also another shortcut in learning, so that one might learn best without the "hand" <note>The Guidonian Hand, a mnemonic tool used by singers to find pitches.</note>; this will happen if you teach the student all the pitches of a single octave, for all the rest recur in the same orders, and thus the mutations according to the called keys, which are always held in three places because of the semitones. For the changed keys are compared to one another by a reasoning such that, because of their similarity, they are all reduced to two, though they seem to be six. Three are indeed called <gloss>soft **b** <note>original: "b mollis"; the origin of the flat symbol (♭), specifically B-flat.</note></gloss>, and as many without it; if you observe these diligently, you will reduce them to only two, not only by a wonderful and concise reasoning, but also an exceedingly easy one.

<margin>How the meridian line may be found at any hour without the Herculean stone <note>The "Herculean stone" is the magnet or lodestone used in a compass.</note>.</margin>
After these comes the discipline of **Optics**, whose most subtle discovery is the invention of clocks <note>Specifically, sundials or gnomons.</note> which teach the hours by shadows; **Vitruvius**, like many other things, translated this into his own work. Lately, it has been discovered how, upon a multi-faceted block of wood with many planes described on the right and left, shadows show both the same hour and the parts of the hour with exquisite precision; then the instrument will be placed exactly <note>original: "ad unguem"; literally "to the fingernail," meaning perfectly.</note> according to the position of the meridian line, from which we shall have it.

Truly, this science of optics seems to be a middle ground between mathematics and that most beautiful science of natural things, which we call **Philosophy**. Its scope lies open most widely. We have written concerning its worthier parts in our books *On the Secrets of Eternity*, *On the Higher Realms*, *On the Immortality of the Soul*, and *On the Variety of Things*. But the noblest part of it is that which [treats] the nature of times—

# On the Sciences.

...teaches how to know the weather in advance and the temperament of the air. It is **useful** indeed for Farmers, Sailors, Merchants, and Generals, and finally for the whole human race; it is both pleasant and healthful. The states of the atmosphere consist of two different sets of qualities: one involves the cold and the hot, while the other concerns the moist and the dry. In this category, there are five types: Fair weather, which is also calm; Windy; Clouds; Rain; and Hail, or a rough storm. Snow is considered in place of rain when it is winter.

<margin>Signs of Winds.</margin>
The signs of winds are held to be as follows, according to natural laws: a certain swelling <note>original: "tuber"; likely referring to a "bulge" or distortion of the Moon's shape due to atmospheric conditions</note> joined to the Moon, which I have seen immediately followed by a very strong wind; a small cloud around either of the "asses" <note>original: "asinorum"; referring to the *Aselli*, two stars in the constellation of Cancer (the Crab) used by ancient observers to predict weather</note> foretells winds coming from that same direction. Red clouds scattered across the whole sky, or a red Moon, likewise the setting of the Sun among red clouds, or flying clouds; the sound of bells, which at one moment is heard perfectly and at another is scarcely perceived; banners placed on the tops of towers when they move; and halos around the Moon which suddenly dissolve—all these show the winds and the direction from which they will arise. <margin>Signs of Fair Weather.</margin> But truly, a clear Moon as it sets or rises, and the stars, as well as a bright and clear Sun at its setting, or if the Sun sets with only a few clouds, and crows croaking together in flocks as if with joy, and the owl hooting constantly at night—these all announce fair weather.

I do not trust that I can explain the signs of storms better than your poet <note>The author refers to the Roman poet Virgil</note>; although my speech is free, Virgil's is contained by poetic meters as if by shackles. Thus, in the first book of the *Georgics* <note>Virgil's famous poem on agriculture</note>, he says:

<margin>Presages of Storms.</margin>
> But when it thunders from the region of the fierce North Wind <note>original: "Boreas"</note>, and when
> the home of the East and West winds <note>original: "Euriq; Zephyriq;"</note> thunders, all
> the fields swim with full ditches, and every sailor on the sea
> furls his damp sails. Never has rain harmed the unwary:
> for as it rises, the cranes of the air flee it in the deep valleys, 
> or the heifer, looking up at the sky,
> catches the breezes with wide-open nostrils;
> or the shrill swallow flies around the lakes;
> and the frogs sing their old complaint in the mud.
> Often too the ant, wearing a narrow path,
> has carried her eggs out from her inner chambers, and the great
> rainbow <note>original: "arcus"</note> drinks; and as it leaves its pasture in a great column,
> the army of crows has clattered with crowded wings.
> Now you may see various birds of the sea, and those which around the Asian
> meadows search the sweet pools of the Cayster <note>A river in ancient Lydia, known for its waterfowl</note>,
> vying to pour much dew over their shoulders:
> now they thrust their heads into the waves, now run into the water,
> and you may see them delighting in the desire to wash in vain.
> Then the wicked crow calls for rain with a full voice,
> and stalks alone by herself upon the dry sand.
> Not even the girls carding their nighttime tasks
> are unaware of the winter storm, when they see the oil 
> sparkling in the burning lamp, and the crumbling "mushrooms" <note>original: "putres fungos"; referring to the carbon buildup or "snuff" on a lamp wick, which ancient people believed predicted rain</note> forming on the wick.

# Book Sixteen

He also added this as a certain sign, which is worthy of observation.

->Then those signs from the Sun:<-

> *If the Moon should grasp the dark air with a blackened horn.* <note>These lines are adapted from Virgil’s *Georgics*, a famous Roman poem about farming and nature.</note>
> *When the Sun has dappled his rising birth with spots,*

<margin>
Signs of cloudy weather.
Signs of hail.
Signs of frost.
</margin>
There are also several halos <note>original: "Areæ"</note>, or those with strong colors. Bellowing oxen lick their hooves and return to their stalls; hens covering themselves in dust; shrieking mice; and even cats washing their heads with their paws all predict rain. There are also smaller signs, which show clouds and a misty day even when winds are absent. Strong winds with rain, or when hail is absent, are signs of the winds themselves, and you should expect rain alone. Frost will harm the vines and trees and indicates a shortage of wine whenever a full moon occurs during a cold and clear time while the trees are already putting out buds (this happens in our regions in March, April, and the beginning of May), or at least if the Moon is full of light.

<margin>
The power of the winds.
</margin>
All these things happen through the wrath of the winds, which produce wonders. For these winds rage on the ridges of mountains, so much so that while I was crossing the Apennines, the wind carried off my hat and drove it with such force—like an arrow shot from a crossbow <note>original: "scorpione"</note>—that it almost fell as a portent <note>A "portent" is a sign or omen, usually of something extraordinary or supernatural.</note> with the rain into the nearby villas. It even moved the horse I was sitting on for two paces, so that I was nearly thrown headlong. For this reason, I am led to believe that the story told by Poggio <note>Poggio Bracciolini (1380–1459), a famous Italian scholar and traveler.</note> was not a fable. He recounts that when winds arose, a town called Borghetto—six miles distant from Rome—was destroyed, the church of Saint Rufina was moved, and an entire inn was carried off intact.

<margin>
Concerning the rain of frogs, stones, and fish.
</margin>
Therefore it is not surprising that it rains frogs, small fish, or stones; for the force of the wind carries frogs and fish from the ridges of mountains, and it also carries dust which is compressed into stones by the power of the winds. The evidence is that they fall not far from mountains, as once occurred on the Alban Mount, and in the valleys from the nearby higher peaks of the mountains. Georgius Agricola <note>A German scholar known as the "Father of Mineralogy."</note> reports that at Chemnitz, muddy earth rained down with water. And among the Swabians, in the year <term>1534</term>, the air stained clothes with a red cross; this happens due to dust carried down with the rain, but the form of the cross appeared because of the threads, which resemble the shape of a cross when they are woven.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of natural phenomena from page 312, moving from weather signs to the physical transportation of animals and plants by wind, and then transitioning into the history of science and medicine.</meta>

<page-num>313</page-num>
<header>On the Sciences</header>

It has been observed. The eggs of small animals are also transported, such as those of frogs and fish, which are released during whirlwinds and rainstorms; these are the creatures that seem to fall as "rain." Therefore, it is not at all surprising if you look at the causes, for these things do not happen except during great movements of the winds. For this reason, such events were frequent during the time of the Roman Republic, because very powerful winds occurred even more often then. Indeed, the force of the winds seemed greater in ancient times: because of this, not only these monstrous events occurred, but also floods and inundations.

<margin>Why floods occurred in the past.</margin>
<margin>Why wonders falling from the rain, or excessive winds, portend evils.</margin>
These dire portents occur, then, because of immoderate winds. Moreover, immoderate winds arise from heavy heat and dryness. From this, they reveal coming treachery. As it says in the proverb: *an immoderate wind, and treachery flourishes.* For either the cause of these winds is taken from the stars—the victory of Mercury and Mars, or of more powerful constellations like the Dog Star <note>original: "Caniculæ", referring to Sirius</note>, Arcturus, and Orion—or, to bring it closer to our own experience, it is a hot and dry constitution of the air. This afflicts those with "weak heads," driving them toward treachery, sedition, and slaughter. The common people often have such "heads" due to their little experience in affairs and their lack of self-control. It happens that they, or the worst among them, are driven toward crimes. But it also happens that they are deceived, and in such cases, it was believed that supplications made to the gods had prevailed.

<margin>From where new plants and fish appear in waters where they were not previously found.</margin>
Fish are also moved into ponds and new waters, and new seeds into foreign lands; for instance, Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and the "father of botany."</note> reports this regarding Silphium <note>original: "Lasere", a prized medicinal plant of the ancient world that eventually went extinct.</note>. Because of this, it was mistakenly believed that the origin of fish and new plants began from rot or putrefaction. The greatest evidence against this is that these things are seen mostly after storms, and never after a long period of calm weather.

By the same logic, though more rarely, a new and unknown genus of birds is sometimes transported from distant regions into our own by the force of the winds that carry them.

<margin>On Medicine.</margin>
It is much the same, though almost more divine, that medicine considers through these seasonal patterns of the air how to predict the health of bodies and the types of diseases. Hippocrates <note>The famous Greek physician.</note> treated these matters especially in the third part of his *Aphorisms*, and Aristotle in the first part of his *Problems*, and it is marvelous with what subtlety they did so. But if I wished to touch upon everything, I would never reach the end; that famous painter <note>Referring to Protogenes.</note>, though excellent, was criticized by Apelles because he never knew when to take his hands off the tablet. Why should I recount the signs of a hotter or colder year, or a sterile versus a fertile one? These would demand entire books, especially since nothing is more difficult for a human than the knowledge of future things. Indeed, this is so obscure that unless it is aided by some divine inspiration, it hardly brings any praise. Because of this, those who have been distinguished in it—and they have been very few—have deservedly been called "divine." It is easier to find men who excel in the sciences; from their number I have selected twelve, leaving the judgment of each to the reader.

<margin>Nothing is more difficult for man than the knowledge of future things.</margin>
<margin>Men outstanding in brilliance, of whom the first is Archimedes, and his praise.</margin>
Let Archimedes be the first, not only because of his monuments which are now commonly known, but because of his mechanical inventions, by which (as Plutarch <note>A Greek historian and biographer.</note> records) the strength of the Romans...

# Book Sixteen

...he often broke; [Plutarch] reports his marvelous inventions in the *Life of Marcus Marcellus*, and we find others no less significant from Galen’s testimony. In both fields <note>Referring to theoretical and practical mechanics</note> he was not so much the first author as he was inimitable. Nor did Cicero (who was accustomed to calling that whole class of men "Greeklings" <note>original: "Graeculos", a diminutive often used dismissively by Romans for Greeks</note>) disdain to praise his genius and to seek out his tomb among the thorns and briers amid the ruins of Syracuse.

<margin>Praise for Ptolemy</margin> Next is the glory of Ptolemy of Alexandria, who devised such clear explanations of the stars that they might suffice for all eternity. He alone dared to express the measure and subtlety of the divine craftsmanship, if I may not say he actually discovered it. Indeed, in his other inventions, which are numerous, he is by no means unlike himself.

<margin>Praise for Aristotle</margin> I am rightly uncertain who should obtain the third place, as many compete equally for it; but let it be granted to Aristotle of Stagira, the Macedonian teacher of Alexander the Great, who refined natural and divine matters and logic in a marvelous way. He pursued the life, habits, and structure of animals with incredible sagacity. Although he wrote what was esteemed in every discipline, no conspicuous error could be detected in his writings over so many centuries.

<margin>Praise for Euclid</margin> The fourth place is occupied with equal arguments by Euclid, Scotus, and John Swineshead <note>original: "Suiffer", referring to the English mathematician Richard or John Swineshead</note>, whom the common people call the Calculator, with equal hope; but Euclid is preferred for his antiquity and utility. Indeed, his praises are twofold: the unshakable firmness of his teachings in the *Books of Elements*, and a perfection so absolute that you would not dare to compare any other work to this one by right. Because of this, the light of truth shines so brightly in him that only those who are familiar with Euclid seem able to discern the true from the false in difficult questions. He was a native of Megara; he wrote many other things which are still extant with equal subtlety, but they are far less useful.

<margin>Praise for Scotus</margin> Next to him follows John Scotus <note>Duns Scotus, the "Subtle Doctor"</note>, this being his fatherland: he worthily earned the title of "Subtle Doctor" because of his learning and his consistently sharp insight.

<margin>Praise for the Calculator</margin> An inhabitant of that same island <note>Great Britain</note> was John, as I said, Swineshead, nicknamed the Calculator. In the solution of just one of his arguments—which concerns "mutual action" and goes against experiment—all posterity has labored. They report that when he was an old man, he wept because he could no longer understand his own inventions while reading them. From this I believe it is beyond doubt (as I also wrote in my book *On the Immortality of the Soul*) that the barbarians <note>The author uses "barbarians" to refer to those outside the traditional Mediterranean center, specifically the British</note> are not inferior to us in talent, since Britain, divided from the whole world under a wintry sky, has produced two men of such illustrious genius.

<margin>Praise for Apollonius</margin> The seventh place is owed to Apollonius of Perga, who was almost a contemporary of Archimedes. He wrote eight excellent books on the elements of conics, of which only the first four have been published to this day—so foully defiled by the translator that you could not even rightly say they have been "published."

<margin>Praise for Archytas</margin> Next to him, but far more ancient, let Archytas of Tarentum be placed, so that an Italian man may also hold some seat among such distinguished men. Beyond the flying wooden dove which he is said to have constructed, he provided a true demonstration for placing two lines in continuous proportion between two other proposed lines...

# On the Sciences

...discovered. Eutocius <note>Eutocius of Ascalon, a 6th-century mathematician who wrote commentaries on Archimedes</note> transmitted this discovery among ten other false ones. <margin>Praise of Algebra.</margin> To him succeeds Muhammad, son of Moses, the Arab <note>Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi, the 9th-century polymath</note>, the inventor, so to speak, of the Algebraic art. Because of this invention, he acquired his surname from the name of the art itself <note>Cardano erroneously suggests "Algebra" comes from the name Al-Khwarizmi, though the term "Algorithm" does</note>. <margin>Praise of Al-Kindi.</margin> The tenth is Al-Kindi, also an Arab. He is a prime example of the authors of books mentioned by Averroes; his surviving little book *On the Ratio of Six Quantities*, which we will submit for printing, demonstrates his skill, for nothing is more ingenious. Next follows <margin>Praise of Geber.</margin> Geber the Spaniard <note>Jabir ibn Aflah, a 12th-century astronomer from Seville</note> with a most famous invention: while Ptolemy seeks the sixth quantity from five with the greatest labor, Geber seeks the fourth from only three. He also improved many things pertaining to the state of the heavens. From this, you may easily understand that intense heat hinders great genius far less than icy cold does. <margin>Praise of Galen.</margin> Last in subtlety but most famous in his art is Galen, renowned for his methods, his work on pulses, and his dissections. But he is so wordy and so fond of contradicting others that he becomes tedious to his readers; you can hardly endure the one trait, while in the other resides a grave loss to the arts, which the men of our own age have attempted to restore.

<margin>Praise of Vitruvius.</margin> Now indeed, the craftsman Vitruvius should be numbered among these famous men; if he had written of his own inventions rather than those of others, he could have been ranked among the very first. <margin>What is greatest in each author.</margin> Certain qualities stand out in each: in Archimedes, the equality of the sphere with the cylinder <note>The discovery that a sphere has two-thirds the volume and surface area of its circumscribing cylinder</note>, which was inscribed upon his tomb. In Euclid, order; in Aristotle, the connection of ideas; in Galen, the method of division. Others also possess certain illustrious gifts, even if they do not excel in subtlety. Who would not admire the passions in Homer, the gravity in Virgil, the pathos and richness in Cicero, or the quality of speech and the figures of style adapted to the meaning of the words in Quintilian? <margin>Seven types of subtlety in authors.</margin> Nor is there only one kind of subtlety for which authors are celebrated, but several. Aristotle's comes from natural talent, whose rivals are Theophrastus and Duns Scotus. From talent and imagination comes Archimedes. From imagination alone, like that of the Calculator <note>Richard Swineshead</note>. From the senses combined with imagination, like Euclid’s. From reason, like Ptolemy’s. From judgment, like that of Algebra <note>Referring here to its inventor, Al-Khwarizmi</note>. From the senses and experience, like Vitruvius, whose rival was Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria</note>, most famous for his inventions, though they were of little practical use. The most excellent thing in Vitruvius is his method of making clocks: whether by drums and water, or in anaphoric clocks <term>anaphoric clocks: water clocks that show the movement of the stars</term> based on the zodiac, or by the analemma <term>analemma: a geometric construction used to describe the sun's position on a dial</term>, which is common to concave, flat, and spherical dials.

But since we have come to the craftsman, let us also pursue the arts, which have become so famous in our age that what I write here may find little belief among posterity. But if anyone considers that every age has had its miracles—the most ancient had so many floods and fires; the Romans had their wonders and oracles; the following age also had its miracles—there is no reason for posterity to doubt the inventions of the arts of our time, nor for us to doubt those things worthy of admiration passed down by others who lived in previous centuries. New inventions of the arts appear every day, and they are contained by no limit; in some cases, it is enough merely to know what you want. <margin>The spear-sword.</margin> Recently, someone discovered the design for a spear-sword; for when the sword is directed...

# BOOK XVII
## On the Arts and Artificial Things.

<margin>Recently invented arts.</margin>
Among the other inventions of things, is not the design of the **Nautical Compass** <note>original: "Nauticæ pixidis"; literally "nautical box," referring to the magnetic mariner's compass</note> first worthy of admiration? By it, so many seas are furrowed; the safety of so many men, such vast sums of money, and the lives of Princes themselves are entrusted to the deep sea, the vastness of the waters, and the whirlwind of the winds—all by a vessel so small and a mere rod, indeed, a modest needle. Nor is it enough merely to have trusted these things to it, unless it also directs and teaches us, and that a stone devoid of senses <note>The lodestone or magnet</note> should excel so many wise men who possess eyes and ears.

The next praise could be granted to the invention of **war engines** <note>original: "tormentorum bellicorum"; here referring to gunpowder artillery and firearms</note>, were it not that they seem invented for the destruction of the human race rather than for utility; hence even the name of the inventor is cursed.

To this succeeds that wonderful art of **printing books with types**, which is second to none after the first invention <note>likely referring to the compass or perhaps speech/writing</note> in utility, dignity, or subtlety; even if it were placed in the first rank, we would believe it rightly done. To these three, all of antiquity has nothing equal. I pass over the remaining wonderful inventions of this age, which are additions to the ancient arts rather than surpassing the genius of our ancestors. If I wished to enumerate these, a whole book would not suffice, but I will submit a few as examples.

Vaults in houses; bells in temples; stirrups in saddles; gears in clocks; the distinction of clear lines in glass; the form and speed in minting gold coins; the wheel by which many threads are spun at once—which was deliberately suppressed in Venice so that the livelihoods of poor common women and their children might be protected. Certain things have also fallen out of use after a long interval of time, such as the construction of **Quinqueremes** <note>Ancient warships with five banks of oars</note> and the composition of **Gold-solder** <note>original: "Chryfocollæ"; a substance used by ancient goldsmiths to join pieces of gold</note>.

<margin>Three arts illustrated by their subtlety.</margin>
Truly, the arts which are most distinguished by their subtlety are **Painting, Sculpture, and Modeling** <note>original: "Plastices"; the art of working with clay, wax, or plaster</note>. For if the eye is even a little too raised, or the nose too narrow, or...

# On the Arts and Artificial Things.

<margin>Exquisitely carved gems.</margin>
...a lip [of a vessel] that is slightly crooked; however much effort you expend, you will have utterly wasted it. In sculpture, the ancients excelled to such a degree (this is attributed to the Indians) that the hand then knew more than the eye can now recognize.

<margin>Precision is the mother of beauty. Walls built exactly upright last forever.</margin>
I have seen two carnelian stones of such a miraculous sort, featuring figures of unknown animals. Indeed, precision <term>subtilitas</term> <note>original: "subtilitas"; here referring to extreme delicacy or exactness in workmanship</note> itself is absolutely the mother of all beauty. And not only of beauty, but also very often of durability: just as in walls, an exact structure built to a plumb line <note>original: "ad perpendiculum"</note> makes for a most firm and eternal work; whereas if it deviates but a little from it, it is amazing how quickly it collapses.

<margin>Arts aided by precision. Painting is the most precise of all mechanical arts. Vesalius.</margin>
Those arts which are merely aided by precision, even if they are not glorified by it, are the military art, magic, chemistry <note>original: "Chymistica"</note>, and mechanics—which is contained under architecture. Painting is not only aided by precision but also glorified by it. For painting is the most precise of all the mechanical arts, and truly the most noble. For whatever modeling <term>plastices</term> <note>original: "plastices"; the art of modeling in clay or wax</note> or sculpture attempts, painting fashions even more wonderfully; it adds shadows and colors, and joins optics to itself, even adding certain new inventions. For it is necessary for a painter to know everything, since he imitates everything. The painter is a philosopher, an architect, and a master of dissection. Proof of this is that famous imitation of the whole human body, begun many years ago by Leonardo da Vinci the Florentine, and nearly finished; but the work lacked such a great artist and investigator of nature's secrets as is **Vesalius** <note>Andreas Vesalius (1514–1564), whose work revolutionized the study of human anatomy</note>.

<margin>Snow-white color. Bright-white. Milky. Black. White. Red. Green. Sky-blue. Wax-blue. Water-colored. Purple.</margin>
But since we have mentioned the colors necessary for the art, I think it right to weave in an account of them. If this is taken from the things themselves and by example, it will not produce that confusion of the ancients. I believe I shall perform a worthwhile task if I touch upon, if not all, at least the more noble distinctions between them. I am well aware that through the fault of writers and the similarity of words, those who have written about these things have confused everything. Therefore, it is necessary for me to deviate from their opinions with a useful but unusual example. I am not teaching how you might understand the names of colors as written by the ancients—for that is a task of immense labor—but how you might be able to name and teach them correctly and clearly. I shall take my beginning, therefore, from the most obvious ones, as is the custom in teaching. **Snow-white** <term>niveus</term> color is like freshly piled snow; it differs from **bright-white** <term>candidus</term>, such as is found in the brilliance of lime; thus, we shall call fresh lime "candid" rather than "niveous." Nearest to these is **milky** <term>lacteus</term>, with less brilliance and no luster. **Black** <term>niger</term>, like that in extinguished coals, is directly opposed to white. Under **white** <term>albus</term>, we include snow-white, bright-white, and milky. **Red** <term>rubeus</term> is like flowing blood. **Green** <term>viridis</term> is like meadows before they flower; the emerald among gems expresses this most beautifully if it is of noble quality. Like **sky-blue** <term>caeruleus</term> (named from the sky <note>original: "coelo"</note>, not from wax), which we shall also call celestial; the sapphire is more elegant. But **wax-blue** <term>ceruleus</term> <note>The author distinguishes between "caeruleus" (sky) and "ceruleus" (wax) to clarify color naming</note> is like bee-glue <note>original: "propolidi"; a resinous mixture honeybees collect from tree buds</note> or new wax, a color a little darker than a calm sea. **Water-colored** <term>aqueus</term> is very similar to water and clear. **Purple** <term>purpureus</term> is named from our purple [murex dye], which is a little brighter than red...

<summary>This page discusses the necessity of precision (subtilitas) in the arts, championing painting as the most noble mechanical art due to its mastery of anatomy and optics. It also introduces a systematic classification of colors based on natural observations to resolve long-standing terminological confusion.</summary>

# Book Seventeen

<margin>
Fiery.
Yolk-colored.
Saffron.
Golden.
Straw-colored.
Leaden.
Livid.
Ash-gray.
Silvery.
Rusty.
Blonde.
Rosy.
Pomegranate-red.
Citron-yellow.
Dusky.
Pale greenish-yellow.
Wine-colored.
Reddish.
Prannian black.
</margin>
...to be white; hence **fiery** comes from flame. This is more splendid and clearer than purple, just as purple is more so than red. **Yolk-colored** <note>original: "Luteus"</note> comes from the yolks of eggs: the more vivid this is, the more it becomes **saffron**, more splendid and a little more reddish. **Golden** is like polished gold; it differs from **straw-colored** because it shines, while straw-colored does not. Straw-colored <note>original: "Palearis"</note> comes from straw, like the husks of wheat; but this term is also more specific to the appearance of healthy urine. **Leaden** is named from its similarity to lead; it is very much like **livid**, yet livid shines not at all. This latter color reflects the appearance seen when children are struck with leather straps, the blood rushing to the spot but not flowing out. **Ash-gray** is named from ash. **Silvery** is like silver: it differs from leaden because silver is whiter and more splendid. **Rusty** <note>original: "Ferrugineus"</note> is the color of iron that has contracted rust. **Blonde** <note>original: "Flavus"</note> is like the color of premature ears of grain. But **rosy** is white mixed with redness, like roses. A slightly more reddish version blooms in virgins, boys, and girls, yet even this will be called rosy. **Pomegranate-red** is like the blooming flowers of the pomegranate tree, though it is somewhat paler. **Citron-yellow** is like the rind of a medicinal apple <note>The "medica mala" or citron</note> when not yet ripe, a mixture of green and straw-color. **Dusky** <note>original: "Pullus"</note> is, as it were, of an uncertain kind, darker than rust; this color belongs to the earth which the farmer has recently turned with a plow. **Pale greenish-yellow** <note>original: "Luridus"</note> is a mixture of straw-color and green with a shine, such as is found on the backs of certain serpents. **Wine-colored** is that which belongs to noble amethyst and the seeds of grapes. For the color of wine itself is fiery or **reddish**; therefore, we shall properly call the color of the grape-seeds by this name. **Prannian black** <note>original: "Prannius"</note> is a shiny black color, named after a gemstone of that color. I am not unaware that I previously divided these into seven categories, which I have here expanded into thirty species.

<margin>The nobler arts lie hidden, and what they may be.</margin>
But I return to the arts: almost all of the nobler ones lie hidden, partly because the properties of things are still unknown, and partly because they require a more subtle invention. Those which are hidden include: the method of making flexible glass <note>A legendary lost invention often attributed to the era of Tiberius</note>; the discovery of treasures; the method of giving a ringing sound to bronze and removing it from tin <note>original: "albo plumbo"; literally "white lead," a common term for tin in this period</note>; the mining of useful things from every quarter; the transmutation of colors; a perfect method for changing spoiled wine into vinegar—which was discovered in my lifetime and also perished in my lifetime, even though we have handed down many useful things on the subject above; the discerning of the specific powers of things; the art of prolonging life, of which we spoke above; the making of material that can resist the force of fiery engines <note>likely referring to cannons or siege engines</note>; and the invention of flying, which was recently attempted by those two and turned out most poorly. **Vincius** <note>Leonardo da Vinci (1452–1519)</note>, of whom we spoke above, also attempted it but in vain; he was an outstanding painter. Above all is the magic of **Tiridates**, for which he was gifted a huge sum of money and the kingdom of Armenia by Nero, while he was teaching him to do things that cannot be done.

<margin>Clocks without a cord.</margin>
Nevertheless, some of those things which lay hidden for a long time have been discovered, such as **clocks without a cord** <note>This refers to the invention of the mainspring, allowing for portable watches as opposed to weight-driven clocks requiring ropes</note>. In place of a cord, wheels stand with a "snail" <note>original: "limacis figura"; likely a worm gear or a spiral fusee</note> placed above them with twenty-six teeth, and in some even more; by these, a toothed axis is turned, which drives the whole machine. In another, there is a wheel with forty-eight teeth arranged at the bottom, and intertwined with another wheel, so that when it is turned by the pressure of the "mill" <note>the driving gear</note> which is at the bottom, the other wheel, also intertwined with the same number of teeth, turns...
