# On Arts and Ingenious Things

<margin>A marvelous seat.</margin>
...let it carry the whole machine with it as it revolves. By a similar reasoning, a seat for the Emperor was invented, arranged so that in whatever position it might be placed, he sits unmoved and comfortably while being carried. This is derived from the principle of gimbals <note>original: "armillarum ratione," literally the "reasoning of armillary rings." This refers to a series of concentric rings that allow an object to remain level despite the motion of its support.</note>, for when three steel circles are set up, moving on poles—up and down, forward and back, right and left—since there can be no more positions, it is necessary for the occupant to remain at rest perpetually, however the carriage <note>original: "essedo"</note> is driven. This has some similarity, however, to gimbaled lamps, from whose example the reasoning was drawn. For even if they are turned around, being wide open, they do not spill the oil at all. Janellus Turrianus of Cremona <note>Juanelo Turriano (c. 1500–1585), a renowned clockmaker, mathematician, and engineer for Emperor Charles V.</note>, whom we also mentioned above, is the inventor of these things.

<margin>Marvelous examples of the craftsman’s subtlety.</margin>
<margin>The statue of Memnon.</margin>
<margin>Small, subtle, fragile works.</margin>
There are also examples of subtlety belonging to the craftsman rather than the art itself, such as Homer’s *Iliad* written on parchment which was contained within the shell of a nut; or an ivory ship that a little bee could hide with its wings. Close to a miracle comes the statue of Memnon, which gave forth a great sound whenever it was illuminated by the rising Sun. This is no fabled story, as the grave author Cornelius Tacitus mentions it, and Strabo records that he heard it himself. There was once a four-horse chariot, the work of Myrmecides <note>A famous ancient Greek sculptor known for his microscopic miniatures.</note>, which a fly could cover; or Callicrates' ants made from ivory itself, whose parts others could not perceive with their eyes. In our own age, cages are fabricated from boxwood the size of a hazelnut, with a perfect bird inside; and what is more wonderful, made in the space of seven hours. To the Prince of Urbino <note>Likely Guidobaldo II della Rovere (1514–1574).</note>, and this also happened in our age, a ring was given as a gift to be worn on the index finger, which had a gemstone in which was a perfect clock; besides the line distinguishing the hours, it would warn the wearer with a single strike for each hourly interval. These works of admirable subtlety, however, can neither be long-lasting nor useful, as they are hindered by every single moment; instead, they produce only admiration, and thus benefit the craftsman more than the buyer. For true fineness <note>original: "tenuitas"</note>, just as it is properly an argument for a certain celestial nature and shows a mixture through every single part, even the smallest, so that which depends on art, when joined with frailty, is entirely useless. Truly, to be able and to know how to separate what is most fine in everything is the work of a certain divine art.

<margin>Four arts outstanding in subtlety.</margin>
However, arts outstanding in subtlety are found, even if they are not divine. Among these, four are more famous in their whole kind: Magic, the Art of Hiding Signs <note>This refers to both cryptography and the semiotics of observing human behavior.</note>, and Chemistry; let us add some examples of these. The reading of signs occurs, for example, when someone enters your presence. Now, signs are the words of the innermost affections of the soul: the movements of the eyes, the cause, the place, the time, the habits of the mind, the posture of the body, the appearance, the company, your own conscience, power, and the opportunity which he seizes. If you consider these things correctly, you will easily understand what he who comes to you has in his mind. Sometimes it will be permitted to divine from only three. An enemy comes to you with a quick step and intent eyes: if he is an unarmed old man, prepare your tongue; if an armed youth, prepare your hands; by this little bit, however, one may save life and honor. There is no reason now for me to discuss every single detail.

It concludes by defining "subtlety" in craftsmanship and listing the four most subtle arts: Magic, Cryptography/Observation, and Chemistry.</summary>

# Book Seventeen

<margin>Three ways of hiding letters: the first by transmutation, writing everything with only three letters.</margin>
But I come now to the method of hiding messages, which is three-fold. The first is by transmutation <note>original: "transmutandi," referring to what we now call a substitution cipher</note>, which is commonly used—as Suetonius <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (c. 69–122 AD), Roman historian who described the private communications of the emperors</note> once wrote concerning Caesar—such as if one writes **d** for **a**, or **n** for **b**. This method, however, can be of infinite varieties. The second method is done by translation <note>original: "translatione," here referring to a system of encoding or transposition</note>, and this is of two types. The first is when we write everything using only three letters for example’s sake; this is done more easily by adding an aspiration <note>original: "aspiratione," likely referring to an 'h' or a breath mark to increase the possible combinations</note>, so that there is no variation in these letters except for that. **Cb'abb'aacb acaccab'bb ababbbaa cabbca'ab b'abcbacab bbb'aca bbcbbabbabb'ab'b cba abbaac b'b'aac ababb bab cabcbbbaac bbb'a a'ac aaabaa bbb'ca cbabb'aba cababbaa'ca 'abbc a'cbabab.** <note>This block is a demonstration of a cipher using only three characters ('a', 'b', and 'c') to represent the entire alphabet, a precursor to the Baconian cipher.</note>

<margin>A second mode of writing secretly without suspicion.</margin>
The other mode of translation is so that the letters lie hidden. In some cases, there is a certain mark of suspicion, as in the Laconian Scytale <note>original: "Laconica Scytala," an ancient Greek tool used by the Spartans for cryptography, involving a strip of parchment wrapped around a staff</note>; in others, no suspicion at all is left behind, which is the most elegant method. For you shall take two equal parchments marked out for writing, and on those same lines, you shall make small holes scattered across from each other on both sheets, yet made according to the size or height of the letters. Some holes will contain seven letters, some three, some eight, or ten. Let all the holes together contain 120 letters, counting all the characters that can be written within them. You will give one of these parchments to the person you wish to write to. When there is a need, first write your message as briefly as you can, so that the message contains a smaller number of letters than the gaps can hold. Then, on the parchment placed over the holes, you shall write that message. Likewise, in one space and another, finally fill the remaining spaces of the first parchment by completing, erasing, and filling in sentences until a coherent sense is established. You will complete this second sentence on the second parchment, so that the words and sentences seem to hang together; in the third parchment, you will also fit it so that, with the first letters left unharmed, the whole message, number of words, and size remain consistent and retain a pleasant harmony. Once these tasks are finished, place the template <note>original: "exemplar," the parchment with the holes</note> you have cut out over an identical sheet of parchment, and at the edges of the holes, you shall mark very faint points as far as the letters you wish to write reach. Then take a third parchment and write the letter in continuous words with a decent order of spaces and size, and also of the letters themselves, so that the primary message and its words are contained within the boundaries of those points. Therefore, no suspicion of deceit remains; when the other person receives it and places the template over it, they immediately understand your mind's message. Even though the labor involved is not light, nothing equal to this can be found for communicating a message to one’s friends in dangerous times. <note>This technique is known as the "Cardan Grille," a landmark in the history of steganography where a secret message is hidden within a seemingly mundane letter.</note>

<margin>A third mode of writing letters which are read only when immersed in water or exposed to fire.</margin>
The third method of hiding is done when letters are written with <term>alum</term> <note>a naturally occurring mineral salt (potassium alum) used here as an invisible ink</note>. For they lie hidden, but once immersed in water they are read, because the water makes the parchment darker, upon which the alum shows white. Those written with <term>sal ammoniac</term> <note>ammonium chloride</note> appear while they are exposed to fire. Likewise, others are written with lemon juice, and others with the juice of onions; all of these, once applied, can be read when exposed to fire; otherwise, they remain hidden. But there is need for no small amount of careful diligence. With <term>calchanthum</term> <note>original: "calchantho," usually referring to blue vitriol or copper sulfate</note> and the "tears" of the larch <note>original: "laricis lachrima," larch resin or turpentine</note>, and with the salt which [is called] nitre... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; "nitrum" at this time could refer to natron or saltpeter.</note>

<summary>Girolamo Cardano explains three primary methods of secret communication: substitution ciphers, steganographic grilles (the "Cardan Grille"), and the use of invisible inks made from chemicals and organic juices.</summary>
<keywords>cryptography, steganography, Caesar cipher, Cardan Grille, Scytale, invisible ink, alum, sal ammoniac, Girolamo Cardano</keywords>

## On the Arts and Craftsmanship

<margin>For erasing letters.</margin>
What we call soda <note>original: "nitrum"; in this period, this term often referred to various salts like saltpeter or sodium carbonate used as cleaning agents</note> is extracted with water and fire, and with it we can now erase written letters. But take care that you do not handle this delicate work in a passing or careless manner. They are also abolished by that "secondary water" <note>original: "aqua secunda"; likely nitric acid or another corrosive "strong water" used in alchemy</note>, the method for which we described earlier while dealing with the removal of hair.

<margin>Notable chemical inventions.</margin>
The chemical art <note>original: "Chymistica ars"; referring to the broad field of alchemy and early chemistry</note> possesses many wonders, many vanities, far more doubts, not a few beauties, some healing powers, certain effective things, others almost divine, many of no importance, others of great hope, and finally some which, out-numbering all the rest, result in the greatest losses. Indeed, chemical inventions include drawing glass into very long threads and the ability to make it tough or extremely hard; it is certainly established that I once saw a small sphere made of glass which, when struck against a stone floor with all one's might, did not shatter but bounced back to the ceiling beams. To this same art belongs, as I said, marking glass with white lines, or carving images into it, fabricating false gemstones, purifying camphor <note>original: "Caphuram"</note>, mixing and changing metals, or imitating more noble ones.

<margin>How silk is whitened.</margin>
<margin>Method for making varied roses.</margin>
Silk is also whitened in this way by the smoke of sulfur: for it dries excessively and even stains flowers, especially roses for the same reason, for when a part is turned white, the color becomes variegated.

<margin>Vessels for melting metals.</margin>
This art has also taught how to make vessels for melting metals: for they are made from ram horns, especially the tips, and from bones reduced to ash and worked with a pestle. If indeed you add emery <note>original: "Smirin," an abrasive powder</note>, or the tips of deer horn, or the jawbones of a pike <note>original: "mandibularum lucij"</note> that have been fired and quenched two or three times in vinegar, the vessels will not break, nor will the metal escape. These are added inside and everywhere so that the vessel does not soak up the metal, but especially at the bottom.

<margin>Charcoal from valley wood is superior.</margin>
<margin>Method of making the best charcoal.</margin>
<margin>Many ways of applying fire.</margin>
<margin>Why things that melt easily, when joined with stones, cause an easy melting of metals.</margin>
Such is the skill of the art that it even adds distinctions in charcoal beyond those we reported above: for the author thinks those from valley wood are superior to those from mountains, for the wood of the valleys is less dense <note>original: "rariora"</note>, and therefore so is the charcoal, and fire easily consumes all less-dense things. But he also labors greatly in the making of it, so that it is made above ground rather than underground as is the custom, because it burns better and is more useful. For it is a wonder how much difference it makes how fire is applied in the treatment of metals and other things perfected by fire; the variety of fire is especially clear in the making of purple pigment <note>original: "purpurina"</note>. Therefore, it matters greatly whether you apply a perpetual or an interrupted fire: fierce or soft, large or small, gradually or suddenly, all around or from one side, agitated by bellows or still: long-lasting or brief, touching the vessel or outside of it, with a flame or with coals alone, enclosed or free, direct or reflected, from charcoal or wood, or—what is more important—with other burning material added which retains its own power even in the fire. It also matters much with what each thing to be melted is associated. For marble, galena, lead, and iron dross <note>original: "ferri spuma," literally "iron foam" or slag</note>, when joined with the stones in which metals are contained, help their melting in a wondrous way, and...

# Book Seventeen

...they preserve their substance: for while they are being liquefied, they prevent the thin moisture contained in the stones from being consumed, by a reasoning contrary to what was said above regarding poisons. Therefore, when the stone is heated but not dried out, because of the contained moisture, the metal itself which adheres to the stone must necessarily be liquefied as the fire is finally increased.

<margin>
Why a crust prevents the liquefaction of metals.
</margin>
But why is metal not more easily liquefied by adding water or some other moisture? On the contrary, it is more difficult: is it because water is cold and thin? It can neither liquefy the metal due to its thinness, nor can it be truly heated before it is consumed due to its coldness. Thus also the crust <note>original: "crusta"; the slag or oxidized layer that forms on top of molten metal</note>, which floats upon the metal, prevents it from being liquefied; for being so compressed, it cools all the internal parts and so prevents them from melting, or the crust consumes the entire thinner part of the metal, and once that is removed, the metal does not dissolve. Similarly, when metals stick to the bottom, they do not melt, even with fierce fires, since heat seeks the upper parts; the small amount of heat that remains at the bottom soon consumes the moisture and prevents liquefaction. For these two reasons, metal cannot be liquefied at the bottom of vessels.

<margin>
Chemical inventions, either not yet known or obsolete.
</margin>
But the inventions of this art <note>the "chemical art" or alchemy</note> are the smallest part of those which could be discovered: such as the composition of electrum <note>original: "electri"; here referring to a specific alloy of gold and silver or a legendary alchemical metal</note>, the softening of glass without fire, and true purple—for what is now in use is such in name alone. These things, once discovered, have now perished and are no longer known. Likewise, the composition of the most beautiful and hardest stones, and of the thinnest waters; with the former, one may fashion vessels, and with the latter, extract gold and silver from the dregs. There are far more than one could write down, but I have set these down as examples. Indeed, the use of a thing often lies hidden along with the thing itself; for neither the utility nor the necessity of war machines <note>original: "bellicorum tormentorum"; referring to siege engines or early artillery</note> nor of the types with which books are printed <note>movable type printing was still a relatively recent and revolutionary "subtlety" for the author</note> was known before the invention of the art.

<margin>
How horns may be softened.
</margin>
It is also a work of the chemical art to soften horns, which is done by long boiling; especially by adding a small amount of ash <note>original: "cineris"; wood ash or potash acting as an alkali to break down the keratin</note> into the water. This does not happen before the eighth hour. From these are made hilts and handles of swords, inkwells, cases, and other vessels, as well as rods, combs, and game pieces <note>original: "latrunculi"; pieces for a popular strategy board game</note>.

<margin>
How bones may be softened.
</margin>
They report that by a similar method, bones themselves are softened with the juices of celery, yarrow, radish, and horehound mixed with vinegar, if the bones are immersed in these and buried in horse dung <note>a common historical method for maintaining a steady, low fermentation heat</note>.

<margin>
The method of fortifying cities.
</margin>
But let us set these aside; we must move on to the arguments for the subtlety of various other arts. I wish to take five examples from architecture for myself: First, indeed, the fortification of cities. This consists of a threefold art: by prevention, by repulse, and by the safety of the defenders; nor is anything else to be found besides this. We prevent by three means: namely, water, a ditch, and a wall. A ditch makes access difficult; it helps for defense not a little because of the descent, but far more because of the ascent; for this reason, both banks should be steep, but especially the one next to the city or town. The width should be forty paces, and the depth multiple...

<page-num>323</page-num>

# On the Arts and Artificial Things

...if you have made a moat, it is not only impregnable but brings despair to those who strive to attack. Let this moat have seven paces of springing water, since water that is born there <note>original: "scaturientis aquæ"; referring to a natural spring source within the moat</note> cannot be intercepted or removed by any art. While the water remains, it drowns those who enter; those it does not drown, it prevents from ascending because their footing is made slippery and they are weighed down by the water. It also prevents <term>tunnels</term> <note>original: "cuniculos"; horizontal mine shafts dug by besiegers to collapse a wall from underneath</note> so that they can hardly be dug out, for it is by these that walls are undermined. Added to this is the fact that the water dissipates and dissolves things thrown into it, and prevents fire from being used to spread destruction against the walls.

The walls should be thirty paces in thickness, made of thin cement and brick-stone, with the exterior made of "living" <note>natural, unquarried, or very hard</note> hard stone, protruding slightly in a rounded shape. Its height should be one hundred paces: ten below the ditch, sixty to the top of the ditch, and thirty above; let it be supported on the inside by a very thick earthen rampart. These specifications are for towns; smaller ones suffice for cities where the protection lies in the soldiers. If, however, these defenses are present, the city itself will be rendered entirely impregnable. 

The defense consists of ramparts and towers every two hundred feet, with the wall straight in the middle but inclined toward the city at the top. For in this way, it does not block the shots from the towers, and the enemy's fireballs are rendered useless. The highest part of the wall should be round, so that fragments shattered by siege engines do not kill the defenders. In the inner part, there should be a channel through which the guards can travel safely. The earth at the bottom should also be hollowed out so that the blows of those digging <term>tunnels</term> will resonate, allowing the soldiers to walk about securely. 

Every hundred paces there should be a sewer and a well; for the necessity of water compels soldiers to depart, and its utility is great against fires, and so that it may be thrown boiling onto the heads of the enemies, along with a thousand other advantages it provides. Waste corrupts the air <note>this reflects the "miasma theory" that bad smells caused disease</note>. 

Furthermore, several secret ways leading from the walls to the heart of the city prevent many inconveniences and bring great advantage to the defending soldiers, leaving them no reason for retreat. Four or five other secret ways, known to no one except the Prince himself, should extend for five miles or even further into dense groves, which long custom forbids cutting down. This is beautifully effective for sending out messengers, importing provisions, and bringing in reinforcements. 

The walls of the city houses themselves should be surrounded and fortified by another wall, as I have said, and no house should protrude. Recently, when **Bura** <note>likely referring to a contemporary siege in the Italian Wars or a classical reference to the city in Achaea</note> was captured, a shack of a house collapsed from the impact of a [cannon] shot because it protruded, and the leaders of the city, who had gathered in it to consult, were killed. And while the French were besieging our city <note>Milan</note>, **Marcantonio Colonna** and **Camillo Trivulzio** perished in a similar accident; because of this, their forces were first cut down, then broken, and finally their power was utterly torn out of **Insubria** <note>The region of Lombardy, northern Italy</note>. The use of those very roads which lead secretly outside the city is almost necessary for sending out scouts. One should not flee to this aid immediately, nor wait so long until the situation is hopeless, but use them while the siege is raging and unexpected.

<margin>
How it is possible to converse from a distance via torches when a city is besieged.
</margin>

There is also another remedy for communicating plans to besieged cities, which is safe and always ready, nor is it any less possible to understand what they want...

...they may wish, those who come or are about to come to provide aid, rather to reveal the state of the city; this differs little from a letter. Therefore, if the city itself desires to signal what it wants to a scout, or to the commander of an army coming to its aid, five towers should be placed far apart from each other so that they are clearly seen as distinct from a distance. On each, burning torches should be placed, and the individuals holding them should have the words they intend to signal written before them. As each letter occurs that pertains to their specific torch, they should signal by raising or lowering it, or by moving it to the right or left. By a similar method, the plans of the commander coming to provide aid can be understood from the highest tower, with the enemy army standing in between, by anyone joining the letters together—entirely without the enemy noticing, let alone knowing—because the torches of the auxiliaries will be kept low.

->On Tuesday night at the sixth hour <note>Midnight in Roman timekeeping</note>, we shall attack the enemy: you must sally forth with all your soldiers and fight bravely: for our entire safety depends upon this.<-

But I return to the fortification of the city: if it consists of high walls, besides the massive expense in building them, it has this disadvantage: when the walls fall by the force of <term>siege engines</term> <note>original: "tormentorum"; referring to heavy weapons like catapults or early cannons</note>, they provide a most convenient and safe bridge for the enemy. Lower walls, however, while safer against the <term>ramparts</term> <note>original: "aggeres"; mounds of earth or timber built by attackers to scale a wall</note> constructed by the besiegers, keep neither the houses nor the soldiers safe.

<margin>Gaius Caesar's Bridge.</margin>
But let us now move to another more ingenious example, and no less useful. Its author was Gaius Caesar, as he records in the fourth book of the *Gallic War*. He completed a bridge over the Rhine in ten days by this method, which we have set out to teach as it is well understood by only a few. Join two <term>timbers</term> <note>original: "tigna"</note>, indicated by the letter **c**, a foot and a half thick and of such length that, when fixed at the bottom of the river, they reach the surface of the water, with a two-foot interval between them. Then, having sharpened them at the bottom, driven them in with machines, and secured them with <term>pile drivers</term> <note>original: "fistucis"</note>, you will fix them leaning according to the nature of the river on one side, so that one of the timbers is closer to the bank. Fix an equal number of similar timbers joined in the same way, forty feet apart in the lower part of the river, leaning against its force; let these be called **f**. You will join the top joints of **c** and **f** with a beam two feet wide—that is, according to the size of the joint—with two <term>braces</term> <note>original: "fibulis"</note> on each side, from the inner part of the timber to the outer, so that each brace grips each timber and binds them. You shall construct similar ones directly opposite on the other side of the river so that beam **e** is equidistant from the other beam, and in the same way...

...and joined three-fold. Join these beams, positioned along the river’s course, with many other transverse beams placed on top and likewise connected to each other. Once <term>poles</term> <note>original: longuriis</note> and <term>wattles</term> <note>original: craticulis; woven branch-work used to create a flat surface</note> are spread over these, the bridge is completed. For its security, many timbers should be firmly driven in the upper part of the river, slanted against the force of the current and separated from the main structure; in the lower part, <term>piles</term> <note>original: sublicae; heavy stakes driven into the earth</note> are also driven against the force of the river, but slanted much further and joined to the whole structure. In this way, the upper timbers will catch the force of the river and any beams thrown into it <note>referring to debris or floating logs sent by enemies to destroy the bridge</note>. And as the mass itself is pressed more by the waves, it is rendered stronger by its mutual grip. This bridge is stable, sufficient for any load, and not easily torn apart. However, a swift construction can be achieved using only ropes and <term>capstans</term> <note>original: ergatae; winches for hauling</note>, or inflated skins, or joined logs.

<margin>Two theaters with a stage forming an amphitheater.</margin>
A more ingenious but less practical design for an amphitheater, which Pliny mentions, is as follows. When the son of Marcus Scaurus <note>Marcus Aemilius Scaurus the Younger, known for his extravagant architectural projects in the 1st century BC</note> was about to host funeral games for his father, he could not equal the pomp of Curtius <note>Likely a reference to Gaius Scribonius Curio, though the author may be conflating names from Pliny’s accounts</note>, because the latter had hosted them at the greatest expense, being far superior in wealth; thus, he attempted to surpass him through ingenuity. Therefore, he built two theaters in the shape of a semicircle with a stage. These, once the spectacle on the stage had been presented, would be revolved on hinges to form an amphitheater. While he presented the games in its <term>orchestra</term> <note>the semi-circular space between the stage and the seats</note>—and while the spectacle had previously been on the stages—the Roman people, the conquerors of nations, hung suspended and were even spun around by the bold mockery of two hinges and a hanging machine. It is rightly asked, since the Latin stage is 90 parts distant from the highest peak of the theater (of which the whole diameter is 120, as Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer whose work "De Architectura" is the foundation of classical building</note> teaches), by what art it could happen that, with the stage remaining unmoved, both theaters could come together into one amphitheater. Therefore, let two semicircles A B C and A D C be set, with the midpoints being B and D. And let the arcs A E and C F be, the larger 93, the smaller 96. Wherefore, rightly, A E and C F, the larger will be 87, and the smaller...

# Book Seventeen

Section 89. Therefore, with the <term>hinges</term> <note>original: cardinibus; the pivot points for the rotating structures</note> placed at E and F, the distances AE and CF will be greater than 59 3/4 and less than 59 1/2. Thus, AE and CF will project beyond the straight line AC (that is, beyond the semi-diameter) by more than 27 1/2 parts and less than 29 1/4. However, the <term>stage</term> <note>original: scena</note> projects 30 parts beyond that same semi-diameter, because it stands 90 parts away from points B and D. Therefore, when points A and C are rotated, they will not touch the stage. Nor will they obstruct one another, because AE and AF are less than 169 1/3 by 1/10th of a part, while AB and AD are greater than 169 1/3 by 1/10th. Thus, a position can be found in which the theaters, when revolved, do not hinder each other. Nevertheless, one must rotate them slowly and alternately, since, as I have said, the gap by which they can be separated barely exceeds 1/10th of a single part.

There are also two other methods, though less elegant, by which theaters can be constructed according to this logic: in one, the theaters resemble the shape of an egg rather than being perfectly round; in the other, although the amphitheater is divided in the middle, it is not done correctly nor according to the diameter.

<margin>A method for easily lifting weights.</margin>
The fourth example of <term>subtlety</term> <note>original: subtilitatis; here meaning technical ingenuity or mechanical complexity</note> is found in <term>pulleys</term> <note>original: trochleis</note>. It works on this principle: A weight, A, is attached to the lower pulley, which contains two <term>sheaves</term> <note>original: orbiculi; the small rotating wheels within a pulley block</note>, B and C, which turn around. In the upper pulley are two others, D and E. The rope is passed around D, descends through F to C, ascends through G and passes over E, descends through H, passes around B, and ascending, is fastened to the pulley at K. Therefore, the weight is pulled from L; and because it is supported by the segments AB, FG, HK, <note>the text describes the various lengths of rope supporting the load</note> only a fourth part of the weight A is sustained by each individual rope. For this reason, it can be pulled upward by a fourth part of the required strength. If there were three sheaves in each pulley, it could be lifted by a sixth part of the strength; in this way, a boy would be able to pull an immense weight upward, except for the resistance offered by the heaviness of the ropes, the roughness of the sheaves, and the difficulty of the movement itself. But because the proportion of time is the same as the proportion of power, it will be pulled four times more slowly with two sheaves, and six times more slowly with three, than if a single person standing above were to pull it with a single rope using the same strength—or even slightly more. Indeed, it is far slower than sixfold or fourfold because the length of the rope adds further to the weight. Thus it happens that the boy, using these pulleys, will scarcely pull the same weight in the space of one hour that a man six times stronger, standing above, can lift instantly with a single rope. Therefore, it is a matter of art and ingenuity that any person can lift any weight whatsoever. However, so that the rope may be pulled by many people, it is drawn beneath a sheave parallel to the ground. If one wishes to pull even more easily, we use a <term>capstan</term> <note>original: ergata; a vertical-axle windlass used for heavy hauling</note>, a machine used by everyone. For this device, by means of rotated axles, pulls any weights as the rope winds around. In this case, too, one may lighten the labor as much as one likes by the length of the axles; for the longer they are, the more easily they pull.

<header>On Arts and Mechanical Matters.</header>

# On Arts and Mechanical Matters.

<margin>The method of pulling or pushing very great weights with small forces.</margin>
By a similar logic, we have <term>screws</term> <note>original: cochleæ; literally "snails," referring to the spiral shape</note>, which we also call <term>vines</term> <note>original: uites; named for the twisting growth of a grapevine</note>. There is the screw-housing A B, and within it the "male" or threaded vine C D, which is turned as usual. The handle E F, joined to this inner screw, is turned by the axle G H; this is done easily for the reasons already mentioned. At the bottom, K L, a weight of many pounds—let us say M—is attached perpendicularly to the screw. When G H is turned, K L will be pulled upward, and the weight M will rise. Conversely, if G H is turned the other way, K L will be pushed down, and by this same logic, it will bend an opposing piece of iron of incredible thickness. Let us demonstrate, therefore, how the weight M can be moved and by what reasoning. If there is a weight of 100 at M, and there are ten spirals in the screw to support it, each individual spiral bears only ten units of that weight. Furthermore, each spiral holds only as much weight as the proportion of its circumference to the rope by which M is suspended. Therefore, the more numerous and "lower" the spirals are in C D—that is, the closer they are to a flat circle—and the larger they are, the lighter the weight M becomes, and the easier the motion. However, the easier it is, the slower it moves. Thus, in a space of two <term>cubits</term> <note>An ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger (approx. 18 inches)</note>, a screw can be made with such wide and low spirals that a weight M could easily be pulled upward by a ten-year-old boy. But as I said, the easier it is to move, the more slowly it will progress. Therefore, when the weight has been pulled the length of K L, it must be suspended by the supports of the machine at points N and O. Then, having released the screw by turning it the opposite way, we reattach the weight at the bottom of K L. We pull again and lift it by the length of K L, repeating this connection until we have pulled a ship or some other immense weight out of the sea or a river. This, we must believe, was the instrument of <term>Archimedes</term> <note>The famous Greek mathematician of Syracuse (c. 287–212 BC), credited with inventing the screw pump and various compound machines</note>, though the accounts have been amplified by Greek vanity and antiquity, which drew the admiration of the ancients toward him. For in this way, a boy can easily pull a loaded ship that twenty teams of oxen could not move from its place. The device should be made of the hardest <term>steel</term> <note>original: chalybs</note> so that it does not bend, yet very light so as not to hinder the work; it should be solid and smeared with oil. For the application of oil assists through its slipperiness, and since it is not prone to rot, it prevents rust. <margin>Oil smeared on iron or steel provides a double benefit.</margin> Furthermore, the smaller the instrument is, even if it pulls with more difficulty, the more admiration it will generate.

<margin>The logic of carriages.</margin>
Leaving this machine behind, we must move on to wagons and carriages. Anything that rests on larger wheels moves most easily and quickly over soft ground, because the clinging mud occupies only a very small part of the wheel and thus causes little hindrance. A larger wheel always covers a distance more quickly, provided it is strong enough to carry the load. Also, the fewer the wheels, the more quickly the journey is finished. If there are many wheels and they are small, they cover less distance because of their smaller circumference; if they are large, they add weight by their mass without covering more ground than a single pair would, and therefore move more sluggishly. For this reason, the Roman Emperors were carried in an <term>essedum</term> <note>A prestigious two-wheeled chariot used for fast travel</note>, which is a carriage with two large wheels. For when the weight...

<page-num>328</page-num>
<header>Book Seventeen</header>

If the load is not particularly heavy, or if it is drawn by many horses, the journey is completed very quickly. For this reason, massive <term>war machines</term> <note>original: tormenta; in this context, heavy artillery or siege engines</note> are carried on <term>chariots</term> <note>original: essedis; specifically two-wheeled carriages or war-chariots</note>. On the other hand, the principle of ease is exactly the opposite of this. For on solid ground, many small wheels are better for ease than a few large ones. This is because the weight is distributed, as it were, through the wheels; thus, the calculation is an addition of those proportions rather than a multiplication. For example: six "doubles" multiplied by each other result in a ratio of sixty-four to one. But those same six added together make only a twelve-fold ratio. There is a great difference between addition and multiplication. Therefore, the weight that one wheel bears as sixty-four pounds is equivalent to only twelve when spread across six wheels. In this way, help is gained from smallness, for the slower a thing moves, the easier it is: and it has been said that weights are carried and moved more slowly on small wheels than on large ones; therefore, they move more easily. A third reason for ease is added when the axle is not pressed down: for a free axle is turned more easily. For this reason, the greatest weights are entrusted to firm ground on small and low wagons which do not sit upon the axles of multiple wheels. But in wet and muddy ground, not only do a few large wheels move much faster, but they also carry weights more easily. And since spokes fixed directly from the axle turn the wheel more quickly and easily, those projecting slightly further outward support the weight better and are more suited for recovering momentum.

<margin>The logic of capstans.</margin>
We have said regarding the axles of <term>capstans</term> <note>original: ergatarum; a vertical-axle rotating machine used for pulling heavy weights or anchors</note> that they ought to be longer: for in proportion to their length, each end reduces the weight. Doubling the length, therefore, reduces the weight by half. Likewise, four times the length reduces it to a fourth part. This is so much the case that if four men pull or drag one hundred pounds with a single axle one <term>cubit</term> <note>A unit of length approximately 18 inches</note> long, those same men will move two thousand four hundred pounds using four axles of six cubits each—once the added weight of the axles themselves (which is minimal) is subtracted. This principle was demonstrated above when we were discussing the <term>steelyard</term> <note>original: statera; a type of balance scale using a lever and a sliding weight</note>. Thus it happens that in the largest wheels, by men stepping along the rungs, the greatest weights are pulled as the rope is wound around the axle. For as the diameter of the wheel is to the diameter of the axle, so is the weight lifted by the rope to the weight and strength of the men who turn it from inside the wheel.

<margin>Why a blow strikes, but a static weight does not.</margin>
There is a similar consideration regarding impacts: for an ax strikes with a blow, but things are not split when pressed by even the greatest weight; and yet, the weight would seem to have more force than the blow. The cause is that the air cannot escape during the blow. Although it cannot escape in such a tiny moment of time even with a sharp point, it is forced—lest it become too dense—to enter the pores of the underlying wood and, acting like a wedge, to divide it. This is evidenced by the fact that a slightly slower blow makes a very great difference in dividing, as the air slips away. But if the blow of a broad object is swift, as the air enters, whatever is beneath it is shattered everywhere as if into nothing—such as those who are struck by the ball of the machine they call a <term>bombard</term> <note>original: bombardam; an early type of cannon or mortar</note>. But a man can hardly move anything large very quickly, even if it is very light, for this reason:

# On the Arts and Artificial Things

<margin>How and where a blow occurs.</margin>
Whatever is struck must be resolved into air and spirit. <note>The author refers to the physical dissipation of energy upon impact, often described in early physics as a release of "spirits" or compressed air.</note> But why does a sword strike most forcefully at its tip? Because the hand itself is the center of movement, while the periphery is at its most powerful at the point; thus, by that distance and leverage, even armor and helmets are split. In the same way, we are safer when very close to kicking horses than when we are a little further away. <note>This describes the arc of a swing: the further from the pivot (the hand or the horse's hip), the greater the velocity and force.</note> <margin>Why pulling the sword during a forceful blow contributes most to cutting.</margin> Pulling adds not a little to the force, because if that which is being divided is not also pulled, the blade is hindered from cutting; but when it is pulled rapidly, that which hinders is stripped away, and the object being divided grows hot. For this threefold reason, blows delivered with a pulling motion at the upper part of the sword cut much better. <margin>Why longer spears pierce more than short ones.</margin> Longer spears also shake more and pierce more than short ones because they possess greater weight and are driven with greater force—even if our initial intuition might deceive us into thinking otherwise.

<margin>How locks are made safe from pick-hooks.</margin>
The logic of keys is more subtle, but of the same kind. When a lock is divided according to its width, only a short hook can be inserted; since it is so close to the axis, the bolt cannot be driven back. Even a long hook, if it is cramped, lacks the necessary strength and power. Furthermore, bolts that are harder and distinguished by multiple <term>wards</term> <note>original: septis; the internal plates in a lock that require a specifically shaped key to pass</note> are safer against pick-hooks. The most secure lock is one that has a barrier that must be lifted by one part of the key while the other part moves the bolt, with a partition intervening between the barrier and the bolt.

<margin>Demonstration of the wonderful strength of the axle in wheels where gems are carved.</margin>
But let us return to the account of wheels. Gems are carved and bored with wondrous art, which is as follows: A large wooden wheel is wrapped with a small cord, and that same cord is wrapped again around a small wheel which stands above the large one, in the manner you see illustrated in the diagram. When a large portion <term>A B C</term> (let it be <term>A B</term>) is turned in a full circle, the small wheel <term>G</term> is rotated. Therefore, however many times the length <term>A B</term> is contained within the total circumference <term>A B C</term>, that is how many times the small wheel <term>D E F</term> will revolve during a single rotation of the larger wheel, which we shall call <term>H</term>. Thus, the ratio of the circumference of <term>H</term> (or its axle) to the circumference of <term>G</term> (or its axle) will be the same as the ratio of the number of revolutions of <term>G</term> to the revolutions of <term>H</term>. Consequently, <term>G</term> will be driven with the greatest momentum because it covers its distance in the shortest space of time; for this reason, the axle <term>G K</term> will be able to bore through and grind down gemstones. <margin>How the fastest and most violent motion is created.</margin> By this same logic, if small teeth are made on <term>G</term> to drive the axle of another wheel, the larger that wheel is, the faster it would revolve when its teeth are engaged. Therefore, by repeating this ratio of the larger wheel several times, the motion of the final axle will become extremely fast and violent. However, this requires that the primary moving force be very strong and the wheels themselves very light. From this principle was born the measurement of <term>clocks</term> <note>original: horologiorum; literally "hour-tellers," referring here to mechanical gear-driven clocks</note>, where the primary movement is divided by the subsequent wheels.

<margin>The structure of scorpions and ballistae.</margin>
The ancients used this same mechanical subtlety in the construction of <term>ballistae</term> <note>large engines for throwing stones</note> and <term>scorpions</term> <note>engines for shooting arrows</note>. For if they are wound too tightly, they break; if too little, they produce weak shots. Therefore, the matter must be brought to a precise measure. Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer whose works were rediscovered in the Renaissance.</note> believes that this "target" of tension ought to be derived from sound. <note>Ancient engineers tuned the tension of the twisted sinew bundles in siege engines by striking them and listening to the pitch, much like tuning a musical instrument.</note>

# Book Seventeen

<margin>A question regarding joined planes, solved in four ways.</margin>
If two surfaces are joined, should they not be impossible to separate? Since no air is trapped between them, and since no part of a straight line can be partly in the plane and partly in the air, it is necessary that once separation begins at one end, it must also happen at the other. Therefore, the movement would occur without time, or a vacuum would be created. <note>The author is wrestling with the physics of cohesion. If two perfectly flat surfaces touch, separating them "instantly" would create a vacuum, which many Renaissance thinkers believed nature would not allow.</note> It is more likely, then, either that perfectly flat surfaces do not exist; or that air is always trapped within the pores; or that air remains between the surfaces themselves because they do not truly touch; or that the surfaces themselves bend rather than being pulled apart all at once; or finally, that they simply cannot be torn apart at all.

<margin>A way of distinguishing the weave.</margin>
But now I return to the arts. If fineness in woven fabrics is joined with density, it results in a better and more durable item relative to its weight. Thus, in serge <note>original: "sarza", a durable twilled woolen fabric</note> there are 2000 threads in the width—the width being the size of a cubit <note>original: "brachij", a traditional unit of measure based on the length of the arm</note>, the measurement of which was demonstrated above. It is woven obliquely, not transversely. Therefore, thinness in all the works of nature is a companion not only to elegance, but also to strength and solidity, because the parts cling to one another best, just as in fine sand. It costs so little, yet I have made much profit in my purchases. But as in natural things, so too in those made by art: the things that are woven, and the materials admitted into the texture, undergo their own limits of fineness.

<margin>Both mixed and simple things, as well as woven ones, undergo a certain limit of fineness.</margin>
Thus, even in those things considered the thinnest by nature, another calculation of fineness is found—for instance, when garments or threads are defiled by a stain. They may be cleansed with lime, or oak ash, or with tartar, or lemon, or the juice of soapwort. <note>Soapwort is a plant whose roots and leaves produce a soapy lather when agitated in water.</note> These things can work joined together or even individually. And why should we wonder at this, when sharp white vinegar can achieve the same?

<margin>How stains may be removed.</margin>
But in all things, beyond the materials themselves, skill is required. For instance, in removing stains, one must wash the spot, then squeeze it firmly (not lightly), and wet it again and squeeze it once more. When you have done this four or five times, you will see the garment immediately cleansed of oil or grease. Take care, however, lest the color be destroyed by cat urine; for then a "stain" will appear which is not actually a stain, but a loss of pigment. Therefore, in such cases, the color must be restored, not the spot cleansed.

<margin>With what materials colors may be restored.</margin>
Purple is restored with cochineal; red with brazilwood; blue with indigo and woad <note>Woad is a plant (*Isatis tinctoria*) used since antiquity to produce blue dye.</note>—but with violet added, without which there is no place for green. For instance, rusty-colored fustic wood <note>original: "shuodenum lignum", likely referring to a species of yellowwood or fustic used in dyeing</note> combined with brazilwood produces green; yellow is produced with indigo and woad <note>Note: Combining blue dyes like woad/indigo with yellow components (like the fustic mentioned) produces greens; the author's specific color mixing terminology here reflects historical dyeing recipes.</note>; and black with ink. Truly heavy grease stains are said to be abolished by the finest ash of the bones of castrated animals, which is sprinkled over the stain and compressed between boards and linens for twenty-four hours.

But you may ask: why can they not cleanse stains in white or yellow cloth, when they work for all other colors? Is it because the cleansers are so strong that they create another stain, or that in white and yellow they strip away the proper color? There are, however, things that can wash out stains in all colors. But 

<margin>For whitening the teeth.</margin>
the method and the material differ for cleansing linen, wool, and silk. Teeth are cleansed with "oil of tartar"—tartar changed into liquid while buried in a marble vessel. The same result is achieved by the water that first falls from the distillation of saltpeter and alum, and also, gradually and beautifully, by the root of the mallow plant.

# On the Arts and Artificial Things

<margin>How you may quickly put a book into order.</margin>
There are some things, however, that are not restricted to a single kind of art, even if they consist of a marvelous ingenuity. For example, if you were to attempt to put a book in order quickly, you should construct another book made of thinner paper that has been hardened with a light hammer. Then, using a double thread that is not fragile—or even a fourfold thread—drawn from the top to the bottom and fastened here and there, take two identical copies of the text <note>original: "exemplaria", referring to printed or manuscript copies of a draft</note> produced from the same type or template. You shall cut out the sentences—from the front of one copy and from the back of the other—and insert whichever ones you wish between the threads and the paper. You may change, transpose, add, or remove them as many times as necessary until the order of not only the sentences but even the words is suitable in every part. Then, using some glue, you shall attach the removed pieces of the small books to clean sheets of paper. In this way, with three days of labor, you will bring the whole book into order better and more easily than if you had labored for an entire year in transcribing it. For often, an earlier change will be displeasing when a better one is offered; in this method, a place for rearranging always remains. <note>This is a remarkably modern description of a "cut and paste" editorial process, using threads as a temporary holding system before final gluing.</note>

<margin>How a blind person can be taught to write.</margin>
Since nothing is difficult for one who treats matters with subtlety—for this also lies outside the standard rules of art—there was a plan to teach a blind person how to write. A brass tablet is engraved with hollow letters in alphabetical order; the blind person leads a stylus through each individual letter <note>original: "elementa", here meaning the individual letters of the alphabet</note>, holding their order in his memory until, having been taught by long habit, he learns to trace the same with a pen. This is a truly wonderful thing, though perhaps of less practical use.

<margin>A man lacking hands and arms performed all tasks.</margin>
Following this example, I remember seeing a certain man who, although he completely lacked arms, could vibrate and aim a spear with his right foot, sew a garment, eat, write, and even thread a needle. I hope there will be no lack of witnesses to such a great miracle, as the matter was performed in public.

<margin>An instrument by which the puller is pulled.</margin>
There is also a work of art (though not of a single craft) which is an instrument: if you hang from it with your hands, while you pull, you are pulled more vehemently. It is constructed in this manner: **a b** is the upper floor; the beginning of the pulling rope is **c**; **d e** is a piece of wood or iron inclined at the top, to which the rope **c d** is fastened; **d f** is a piece of wood which lies beneath the ceiling panels and prevents **e d** from returning. To this **f d**, a weight **g, f** is hung, so that **f d** can be moved around whenever **f d** is not pressed upon by **e d**. For **f d** is fixed to a small wheel; therefore, when **c d** is pulled, **f d** slides back toward **e**, but stays to the side because of the weight **g**. Therefore, the iron **e d** which was held back by **f d** will slide back to the ceiling **h e**, pulling **d c** upward. <note>This describes a complex counterweight mechanism where the act of pulling triggers a weight-driven return or assistance.</note>

<margin>An instrument by which anyone pulls himself upward.</margin>
An instrument that easily pulls a man upward consists of a pulley <term>trochlea<gloss>a wheel with a grooved rim for a rope, used to lift weights</gloss></term> with an iron hook. In it is a small wheel of the usual sort, around which is a rope; on the rope is a weight **a** slightly less than the weight of your own body, and on the other side is a transverse bar **b**. Therefore, once the hook is attached, you pull **b** downward so that the weight **a** rises upward and **b** reaches the bottom. Then, sitting upon **b** and grasping **a c** with your hands—because the weight **a**...

the weight is a little less than the weight of your body, <term>A</term> <note>A counterweight or pulley component mentioned on the previous page</note> will descend again as you ascend quite easily. When you wish to descend, you will do so of your own accord; since your body is heavier than <term>A</term>, you will descend rapidly once the rope is released.

<margin>*Another instrument of Agrippa for the same purpose.*</margin>
Another device by Agrippa: He constructed two pairs of pincers, entirely similar to one another; you see an image of one described in the margin. <term>KMO</term> and <term>LMN</term> are pieces of steel joined at <term>M</term> with a motion that revolves around a pin, and together they form one complete pincer. The uppermost parts, <term>KM</term> and <term>LM</term>, come together in such a way that while they are being tightened, one goes under the other, resembling the shape of a <term>screw</term> <note>original: "cochleæ," referring here to a spiral or snail-shell shape that grips the rope</note>. The rope lies between these when in use. Furthermore, the straight sections <term>NM</term> and <term>OM</term> have a ring at the bottom into which a strong cord <term>NO</term> is inserted. The use is as follows: the rope is gripped, as I said, by tightening <term>KM</term> and <term>LM</term> through the tension on <term>NO</term>. It is tightened by placing a foot upon <term>NO</term>; for the heavier the body is, the more <term>NO</term> will be pulled down, and the more tightly the rope will be gripped by the pincer. Therefore, the ascent is safer the heavier the climber is. Then, you join another pincer to the rope a cubit <note>A unit of length, roughly 18 inches or the length of a forearm</note> higher than the first; while you lift the rest of your body by standing on the foot placed there, you remove the lower foot and the pincer itself, and place it just as far above the second one. In this way, you can ascend safely as if by a ladder to the very top, using a single rope with a hook and two pincers. The screw-like shape prevents the pincer from accidentally slipping down the rope.

This is the method for ascending, but it is quite unsuitable for descending if compared to other instruments. Therefore, he devised a very easy method for descent. A <term>screw</term> <note>cochlea</note> made of steel, a palm's length and hollow inside so that it can receive the rope <term>HG</term>, shall be called <term>AB</term>. Around it is a smooth small casing made of <term>brass</term> <note>original: "aurichalco," a gold-colored copper alloy similar to brass</note>, perforated above and below. At its bottom are two attachments in which the cords <term>C</term> and <term>D</term> support an iron bar <term>EF</term>. When the person about to descend sits upon this, he will descend very swiftly and without any discomfort. But if he pulls the rope <term>G</term> below him, or pulls <term>ABC</term> toward himself, the screw-mechanism will not descend because the rope <term>GH</term>, made straight by the tension, does not permit the screw to slide. Similarly, when he pulls <term>G</term> toward himself and it is turned upward, it will in no way descend but will remain still. Therefore, he can descend both very swiftly and rest very easily with no labor. Even sailors know this; sitting on a simple small stick, they descend by wrapping the rope three or four times around it while holding rope <term>G</term>; if they let it out gradually, they descend, but if they pull more vehemently, they remain still while sitting. But the difference is this: those who sit on a stick fall easily because they are tilted by the slant of the rope, unless they are experienced and bold. But this instrument, which I have seen and handled often, is without fear because it always keeps <term>EF</term> in equilibrium, and anyone, no matter how inexperienced, may safely sit upon it.

<margin>*An account of medical subtlety. The utility of mixing.*</margin>
There are also uses of the medical art derived from subtlety that are of no small importance. The first arises from the <term>mixing of medicines</term>, through which harmful powers are hidden and the remaining powers are directed toward their proper ends.

<header>On Arts and Ingenious Things</header>

# On Arts and Ingenious Things

<margin>The four primary qualities.</margin>
The parts of the body are distributed in a specific order. For physicians are convinced that hot medicines are drawn to cold limbs, and cold medicines to hot ones. In the same way, dry substances are drawn to moist parts, and moist to dry; by the same logic, our body utilizes secondary and tertiary qualities beyond these primary ones. For it is well established that there are four primary qualities: **hot**, **cold**, **moist**, and **dry**. They are named thus either because all other qualities flow from them, or as <term>Galen</term> <note>Galen of Pergamum (129–216 AD) was the most influential physician of antiquity; his theories of humors and qualities dominated Western medicine for 1,500 years.</note> prefers, because these alone penetrate to the innermost parts and make that which they act upon similar to themselves. For a thing does not become soft simply by the touch of something soft in the same way that something becomes hot by the touch of something hot.

<margin>Why living bodies consist of the hot and the moist.</margin>
The power of heat is more manifest among the primary qualities, and then that of cold. In terms of being acted upon, the moist is more receptive than the dry; for this reason, all living things consist of the hot and the moist, because their actions are more powerful for a two-fold reason: heat is more suited for acting than cold, and moisture is more suited for being acted upon than dryness.

<margin>The works of heat.</margin>
Furthermore, the works of heat are: to warm, to thin, to scatter, to <term>concoct</term> <note>original: "concoquere"; in Galenic medicine, this refers to the "cooking" or digestion of humors to make them useful to the body</note>, to soften, to make porous, to digest, to dry, and finally to burn away.

<margin>The works of cold.</margin>
<margin>The works of the dry and the moist.</margin>
The works of cold are: to chill, to constrict, to retain, to make hard and raw, to dampen (through condensation), and to freeze. The works of the dry: to dry, and to make rough and hard. The works of the moist: to dampen, and to make smooth and soft. Cold condenses in one way (through its own nature), but heat condenses in another way (by accident), for as it perpetually digests whatever is thinnest, it leaves behind that which is thicker.

<margin>Why heat performs greater works than cold.</margin>
While heat warms, it dissolves and increases its work; cold, by making things dense, hinders them. For this reason, as shown above, the works of heat are greater, more evident, and swifter than those of cold.

<margin>Secondary qualities.</margin>
<margin>Tertiary qualities.</margin>
Therefore, those qualities which arise from these four are called **secondary qualities**: to thin, to burn, to draw, and to make soft, rough, or porous. The **tertiary qualities** include: purging the blood, generating seed or milk, and benefiting the eyes, or sexuality, or sterility.

<margin>How all qualities differ and agree.</margin>
The primary qualities are the very substance of the <term>elements</term> <note>The four Aristotelian elements: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.</note>; in mixed bodies, they are partly substance and partly impressions, while the others are called "accidents." All qualities agree on four degrees or orders of intensity: The **first**, when the quality itself is perceived obscurely. The **second**, when it is manifest, but without causing harm. The **third**, when it causes pain, but can still be endured. The **fourth**, when it can by no means be sustained. Among qualities, let **opium** be an example of this; among flavors, let it be <term>siliquastrum</term> <note>A term often used for "wild pepper" or pungent pods like capsicum, known for intense heat.</note>, which is far sharper than pepper. Pepper itself is placed in the third order of those things that bite and warm.

<margin>How medicines are best mixed.</margin>
Therefore, when these are mixed, one must maintain the measurement so precisely <note>original: "ad unguem" (to the fingernail), an idiom meaning "perfectly."</note> that what is superfluous is cast out, what is harmful is hidden, and what is useful remains.

For in this way a medicine will be best constructed: when it is most powerful in helping, and those parts which might harm are entirely put to sleep. This is known through experience; hence, in my judgment, Galen dared to add things to the <term>Theriac of Andromachus</term> <note>A famous ancient "cure-all" or universal antidote consisting of dozens of ingredients, originally formulated by Nero's physician.</note> (which had been proven by such long use) wrongly and only for the sake of his own ambition.

But also in the selection of simple medicines, one must use no small amount of care...

<margin>Why the top of oil, the middle of wine, and the bottom of honey are the best.</margin>
I pass over what is eroded, spoiled, or aged; for now, I speak of the substance itself. Just as in oil and every other fatty substance, the uppermost part is to be chosen. For everything fatty is light and pure by nature; therefore, that which is at the top is lighter and purer, and consequently also richer. The best wine, however, is proven by its strength, and that which is in the middle is stronger; for that which is at the top is spoiled by the air and the vessel, and that which is at the bottom is spoiled by the vessel and the dregs. Therefore, the best is in the middle. The bottom of honey is approved because it deserves praise for its sweetness. Furthermore, the sweetest is that which is most dense; the most dense is the heaviest; and the heaviest among liquids always settles at the bottom. Therefore, pure honey, which is also the best, lies at the bottom of the vessel. This was an ancient discovery recounted by <term>Macrobius</term> <note>Macrobius (c. 400 AD) was a Roman writer whose works preserved much ancient scientific and philosophical lore for the Middle Ages.</note>, but physicians also possess an abundance of such observations to the point of satiety.

<margin>All human events hang by the thinnest thread and are divided by a fine line.</margin>
Among the actions of physicians, the most delicate is the depressing of a cataract <note>original: "nebulæ in oculo depressio." This refers to "couching," an ancient surgical technique where a needle was used to push a clouded lens out of the field of vision.</note> and the extraction of a stone from the bladder. For if you stray but a little, blindness is prepared instead of light, and death instead of health; so thin is the thread upon which all the goods and evils of mortals hang. But this is the way, this is the rule of all human affairs: if anyone reflects rightly on these things, he will be less anxious about death as a thing necessary for all, and will apply more diligent care to life. But I have spoken of these things at length in the book on <term>Fate</term>. Yet since the ends and beginnings of all things are hidden, no true happiness should be seen among mortals, and nothing in such a great mass should seem worthy of wonder to a wise man; rather, all things are like a single dream—either many things that delight us, or brief but empty sorrows that affect us. This is how things are, even according to the <term>oracle</term> <note>Likely referring to a classical source or a proverbial truth about the vanity of human life.</note>, but let us leave each to their own opinion and allow them to be happy in their vain persuasion.

<margin>The greatest things consist of the smallest beginnings.</margin>
Truly, they will at least not deny that these "great things" of theirs—these immense happinesses—arise from the smallest beginnings. For that reason, it is not just fitting but necessary for whoever desires to appear happy among mortals to observe even the smallest details.

<margin>The shape of the clouds.</margin>
Among the works of art, the most subtle is the method of cauterization <note>original: "ratio urendi," the medical use of heat to treat wounds.</note>, and among theoretical studies, the science of pulses. But there are also other things in other fields that are pleasing and worthy of admiration, such as the nature and position of clouds. For there is no doubt that all clouds are flat; first, because they appear so when viewed from mountains, and second, because they are carried in straight lines by the winds. Indeed, if something were shaped like an orb and carried straight, it would be bent inward and broken apart; furthermore, there is no cause that could produce this roundness. Let the cloud then be represented by **gd**, the eye by **h**, and the point above the eye by **a**. Since the distance **dk** will be very small because of the angle **dhk**, and because of the small proportion it holds compared to **hd** and **hk**, it will follow that **ad** appears to touch the earth at **k**. By the same logic, **bl** and **cm** will appear smaller than **ah**. Therefore, **abcd** and **aefg** will appear as segments of circular lines touching the earth at **g** and **d**. Yet the cloud itself at point **a** is higher than in any other part, gradually opening up and appearing as the interior of a sphere or orb...

# On Arts and Ingenious Things

...the third surface and part, such that point **A** will seem to be the greatest distance from the earth. And so a cloud above one's head appears higher, and from there it seems to gradually incline down toward the earth, which is always apparent to those watching. Indeed, since this happens everywhere at the same time, it is manifest that the cloud is not round, but flat. Thus when the line **DK** is not seen, then the cloud appears to touch the earth at that point. <margin>Clouds and rain are not seen farther than 100,000 paces.</margin> This happens, however, when **HD** and **HK** contain **DK** sixty times; but **DK**, since it is equal to **AH**, never reaches 1,000,000 paces. Therefore, neither a path that is not very long, nor rain, is seen further than **120,000** paces away; more truly and precisely, however, it is no more than **100,000** paces <note>A Roman pace (passus) is approximately five feet. 100,000 paces is roughly 95 miles, which the author proposes as the limit of the horizon for atmospheric phenomena.</note> distant. For this reason, no one will say it has rained in Gaul <note>modern-day France</note> while they are in Milan, since usually—and especially while it is raining—clouds do not rise even to five hundred paces, and we can rarely see rain further than **30,000** paces away.

<margin>Why fires carried through the air seem to rise and set.</margin> For the same reason, the fires <note>original: "ignes," referring to meteors or "falling stars"</note> that are carried through the sky seem highest when they are directly above us; but when they rise or set, they seem to cling to the earth. This is not because they are actually descending or ascending; rather, they are carried in a straight line parallel to the plane of the earth and the horizon. It happens because of the variation in perspective, so that they appear lower the more remote they are.

<margin>Zephyrus, the sweetest word.</margin> <margin>The power of accents.</margin> <margin>Concerning "yes" and "no."</margin> <margin>Concerning the Duel.</margin> <margin>Concerning embassies.</margin> There are also works of subtlety in words, in accent, and in speech. Among words, *Zephyrus* <note>The West Wind; original: "Zephyrus"</note> sounds sweet for three reasons: first, because it has the letter **z**; second, the letter **y**, which the Latins do not have <note>These letters were borrowed from Greek and retained an exotic, sophisticated sound to Latin speakers.</note>. Nor do the Latins have anything so soft, nor do the Greeks have anything else like it. The third reason is its meaning, by which it is understood as the softest wind among us, the *Favonius* <note>The Roman name for the West Wind, associated with spring and gentle breezes.</note>, which is also the most pleasant. Accents are also a proof of the greatest subtlety, since first one nation is distinguished from another by them, then within the same nation one city from another, and village from village; and in the same city—incredible to say—individual districts are distinguished by them. You see how great the power of words is: by two syllables, kingdoms fall or are preserved; the innocent are killed, the guilty escape; all human calamity and happiness depends on them. In a single combat <note>A judicial duel or private duel of honor.</note>, a little word imprudently blurted out grants the choice of weapons and the victory to the enemy, bringing death and dishonor to the one who spoke it. In an embassy, insolence, rashness, or a word uttered inconsiderately causes so many wars, so many slaughters, and so much upheaval; it overthrows kingdoms and lays waste to entire regions. Therefore, subtlety rules in all things. Its power is felt by Kings, provinces, cities, villages, and individual homes. Consequently, there is a greater necessity for wisdom in ambassadors than in the commanders of armies. For the latter usually teach how to choose the lesser of two evils, while the former can prevent evils from happening at all. Yet the rashness of a commander seems greater, because its outcome is more immediate.

<margin>Subtlety in speech.</margin> <margin>Seven modes of subtlety in speech.</margin> In speech, however, that which is affected is annoying, while that which flows spontaneously is most pleasant. For in these matters, when art imitates nature, it moves away from the suspicion of being "artificial" and flows more clearly. But there are seven modes of subtlety in speech, each of which renders it more obscure. The first is grammatical, by division: *I fear* <note>The Latin text ends with "metuo" (I fear), which is the catchword for the next page's first sentence.</note>...

# Book Seventeen

...mine or yours, the second is **Sophistical**, and the third is **Mathematical**. This third type is threefold: either connected, such as which point on a circle is closer to the circumference; or derived from assumptions, such as whether those things assumed by Archimedes in his demonstration on spirals concerning a straight line equal to the circumference of a circle can be proven; or derived from things already demonstrated, such as whether there can be one general rule for a cube equal to "things" and a number. <note>original: "regula cubi æqualis rebus & numero". This refers to Cardano’s own groundbreaking work in algebra solving cubic equations, where "things" (res) represented the unknown variable $x$.</note> The fourth is **Physical**, and this is twofold: concerning the object, or concerning the cause. Concerning the object: are new species of things produced in every age? Concerning the cause: does the motion of the heavens consist of eccentric circles? The fifth consists in the **continuity of a discourse**, as in a booklet on the immortality of the soul, when we gradually lead a person from one point to another. The sixth is the **transition from one genus to another**, as when we teach how to draw up water with a screw <note>original: "cochlea", referring to the Archimedean screw</note>, because while it is turned, the empty lower part is made full. The seventh is **acquittal by law**: [for example] let it be that he who does not obtain half the votes is not condemned, and he who has not obtained two-thirds of the votes is not condemned. However, since many others might remain unjudged, they are deemed acquitted or condemned by another law, according to whoever was closer to the required number of votes. There are twelve judges; a certain man is condemned by seven and acquitted by five. If eight had condemned him, he would be punished; if six had acquitted him, he would be freed. With five acquitting and seven condemning: **Geometrically** he is condemned, yet according to the privilege that favors those being acquitted, he is freed; **Arithmetically**, he would remain unjudged. There are many other modes in this category, which I intend to pass over for the sake of brevity, since they may be discerned from the preceding examples.

<margin>Why urine alone among all liquids appears more brilliant from a distance than from nearby.</margin>
Let us return to natural questions: why is urine alone among all liquids more brilliant from a distance than from nearby? Other liquids are the opposite way, and for that reason, it is easily distinguished. Urine alone contains sediment, and only in the lowest part; from nearby, this sediment casts a shadow over it, but from a distance, the part containing the sediment is illuminated by the pure part, because it possesses a fiery light. Other liquids do not have this shadow because they are pure; or if they are impure, the impurity casts a shadow over the whole; hence, as they are further away, they appear darker, as I have said elsewhere. Moreover, urine is of a very thin substance due to heat—so much so that although it is salty, it nevertheless exists as lighter than water, though not all urine is so.

<margin>Urine is lighter than water.</margin>
<margin>Why and how urine is beneficial for inflation of the belly.</margin>
For this reason, urine is beneficial for inflation of the belly <note>bloating or flatulence</note>, and far more so than salt water. For by its thinness, it penetrates to the innermost parts and carries with it the power of salt, by which the wind is dissipated and the internal organs are strengthened. This thinning is caused by heat, and for this reason, urine that is fresh, warm, and from unpolluted boys (for this is the hottest age and sex) is chosen.

<margin>Whether hot springs can be produced by art.</margin>
Naturally warm waters are more similar to urine. But in those which contain sulfur and alum, or salt, or asphalt, they are more turbulent because they are mixed by external heat. Those, however, which contain iron, or silver, or copper, are clear, for they are made so by nature mixing the "excrements" of metals; therefore, art cannot imitate these, though it can imitate the former.

For it is that celestial heat which truly mixes them, as has been said quite often, and...
