# On Arts and Artifacts

<margin>The difference between celestial and mortal bodies in production.</margin>
Here, it produces something similar to itself, which it possesses in potentiality. For the heat of the heavens is such that it contains man in potentiality, yet produces man in actuality; however, this natural heat of ours produces something in potentiality that is like the thing in which it is contained. For example, a man does not generate a man suddenly and without a medium; rather, he produces seed—which is a man in potentiality—since it is shed by the man himself, who exists in actuality. <note>Cardano is discussing the Aristotelian concept of "act and potency" (actus et potentia), explaining how celestial influence and biological heat work together to create life.</note>

<margin>The similarity between celestial and mortal things.</margin>
<margin>Why broth from beef is more succulent than from veal.</margin>
But just as there is a difference, so too is there a similarity, the observation of which requires no small amount of consideration. There are stars there [in the heavens], and here there are gems; there are intellects and moving substances there, and here are animals of diverse kinds. There is a variety of substance and thickness of bodies there, and here there is the greatest variety of earth, water, and air. There are many miracles and portents there, such as "battle lines" and "swords" <note>This refers to celestial phenomena like comets or auroras that were often interpreted as weapons in the sky.</note>, and here there are two-headed births, and infants born hairy or with teeth. There are certain substances joined to bodies there, just as here there are plants and minerals. There are perennial motions there, and here the circulation of waters. There is light and radiance there, but also here. In general, this nature—the rival of the higher realms—has fashioned as many things here through genera, species, and accidents as existed there. Certain properties are scarcely seen in those [higher] things, but are more manifest in mortal ones. Yet, while some things seem to proceed by a hidden reason, they nevertheless have a very manifest cause. For instance: why is it that although the flesh of a calf is moister, the flesh of a cow is more succulent and fatty (as Galen <note>Galen of Pergamum (129–210 AD) was the most influential physician and medical researcher in the Roman Empire, whose works dominated European medicine for over a thousand years.</note> also testifies), and yet the broth made from beef is succulent and fatty, while that from veal is thin and tasteless? The cause is that in beef, that fat is denser than in veal; therefore, it evaporates very little because of the fire, and renders the water fatty.

<margin>Why butter prevents water from boiling over.</margin>
<margin>Why clay draws out impurities.</margin>
<margin>Why a nut helps with cooking.</margin>
Why does butter sometimes prevent water from boiling over? Is it because, being dense, airy, and fatty, it draws to itself the vapors that cause the water to boil? Why does clay draw out impurities? Because it is tenacious and is not dissolved by heat, but rather becomes dense. Thus, when things boil, straws, sawdust, earth, and anything of that sort are mixed in and stick to it. Why, then, does a nut <note>original: "Nux", likely referring to a walnut.</note> cause chickens to cook faster? Is it because it possesses a sharp power and causes heat to penetrate, in the same way as was said earlier regarding mustard?

<margin>Why balsam could only be irrigated from one specific well.</margin>
<margin>Why the gaze of cannibals is so terrifying.</margin>
By the same reasoning, why could balsam only be irrigated from a certain well that was near the Nile? Is it because everything that is nourished is of the same nature as its nourishment? Thus, the water of the Nile is very thin and of an airy substance; when imbued with a certain kind of bitumen, it can nourish balsam shrubs, but no other water can, unless it is similar to it. By the same reasoning, they report that the "eaters of men" <note>original: "anthropophagi"</note>—called "Caribes" by some and "Caribales" <note>original: "Caribes... Caribales", referring to the indigenous people of the Caribbean, from whose name the word "cannibal" is derived.</note> by others—have a look so fierce, grim, and terrifying that other men who are captured or dead can scarcely bear their gaze. Trustworthy authors report this even of Marius <note>Gaius Marius (157–86 BC), the Roman general and seven-time consul.</note> when he was a captive, and of Nero when he was dead. Therefore, food changes one's appearance and nature; this was clearly demonstrated in the second book of *Contradicting Physicians*. <note>This refers to Cardano's own medical work, "De venenis" or "Contradicentium medicorum."</note> It is easy, therefore, through habit and diet...

<header>Book Seventeen</header>

# Book Seventeen

...to change the character and form of living beings in kind, and then even to add marvelous properties to them.

<margin>Why those who see poorly with one eye become cross-eyed.</margin>
Some things also have an obvious cause, such as why those who see poorly or see nothing at all with one eye from childhood become cross-eyed. The reason is most manifest: for since the eye does not see from the opposite side, it is forced to bend and distort, and from habit they become cross-eyed. These people, moreover, have eyes turned obliquely toward the nose and looking backward. But if blindness happens after infancy, they do not become so cross-eyed, for two reasons: first, because the eye is already accustomed to staying in its proper position and not being distorted; and then, because the nerves are already stiff and do not easily serve new movements. The remaining reason is that adults deliberately turn their necks instead of the eye.

<margin>How the muscles are moved.</margin>
But from this again arises a most subtle contemplation, which Galen <note>Galen of Pergamon (129–c. 216 AD) was the most influential physician and medical researcher of the Roman Empire.</note> admits he does not know how to solve: in what way the muscles are moved. For the unrefined, children, and beasts move them aptly toward the actions they desire, even though they do not know their function, nor do they even know they possess them. Therefore, it must be thought that since two things are necessary for appropriate movement—the selection of the limb and the selection of the muscles in the limb—the first proceeds from the soul and the spirit, while the remainder comes from habit. For if you watch infants when they try to walk, they pull all their muscles, now this one, now that one, and thus finally they grow accustomed to contracting the specific muscle serving each movement. This is clearly observed in those playing the lute <note>original: "testudine", literally "tortoise shell," referring to the ancient lyre or the Renaissance lute often fashioned from such shapes.</note>; for they touch those strings on both sides which it is appropriate to touch, led by habit alone. 

But a greater difficulty seems to me to be concerning the limbs: why beasts move the tongue and not the hands for the sake of speaking, or the feet and not the head for the sake of walking. But it seems that this also happens from the same cause. For when you throw a newborn puppy into the water, it moves all its limbs; but when it perceives that it is less suffocated with its head extended, and better supported when its front feet are moved—by that power which the Greeks call <term>phantasia</term> <note>original: "φυνταλίαν" (phyntalian). This appears to be a printer's error for "φαντασίαν" (phantasian), meaning imagination or instinctive perception.</note>—it keeps its head as motionless as possible above the water, then moves its tail, then its hind feet more, and especially the front ones. However, it stops moving those from which it does not feel it receives help, until finally it becomes accustomed to the appropriate movements. Evidence of this is that one animal swims better than another as they are more naturally teachable, and an adult better than a newborn, and one accustomed better than one that has never swum; and it happens thus in other movements too. 

Therefore, all these movements consist of two principles: one, that every animal, even an imperfect one, has a power by which it follows what delights it and flees what harms it; the remainder is a kind of memory, or a certain habit, by which it has learned to move the limbs and muscles which it has already experienced elsewhere as suited to that movement. And for that reason, we see some who, after a long illness...

<header>On Arts and Artificial Things</header>
<sig>uu ij</sig>

# On Arts and Artificial Things

...we are forced again, no differently than infants, to learn how to walk: thus the muscles and limbs have learned through habit to be applied to the appropriate occasion.

<margin>The nobler arts of predicting the future.</margin>
Of all the arts, those which teach how to divine are more subtle, because, as I have said, to know future things is almost a divine quality. The nobler arts in this genre—besides those which consider the nature of the times <note>original: "temporum natura"; likely referring to meteorology or seasonal cycles</note> as we mentioned above—are Astrology and the <term>method of pulses</term> <note>original: "pulsuum ratio"; the medical practice of diagnosing and predicting the course of a disease by feeling the patient's pulse</note>. For these alone nearly attain their intended end. Indeed, a physician sees death, even while it is still standing far off, with the help of the pulse in a sick man. Therefore, the truly wise man is far happier than a King: <margin>The wise man is far happier than a king.</margin> for when the wise man reflects within himself on those things he knows, and understands how far he is removed from the common crowd, he lives content, secure and certain. But a King, when he recognizes his hardships, his servitude to duty, his dangers, and the fact that he is soon to lose everything, lives uncertain and anxious, then fearful and trembling at every turn of fate. This, therefore, is the highest happiness which God could or would grant to man. Moreover, He willed whatever He was able to grant among good things. For since all other things are placed in uncertainty, the soul itself—being of the thinnest substance—is an abundant participant in immortality, and in a better life of whatever kind than it could possess among the filth of the world.

<margin>The system of studies</margin>
To obtain this wisdom, a careful selection in one's studies is necessary. We shall approach <term>Euclid</term> <note>The Greek mathematician, father of geometry</note> first, then <term>Al-Kindi</term> <note>Al-Kindi (c. 801–873 AD) was an Arab philosopher and scientist known for his work on optics and mathematics</note> to strengthen the imagination. Afterwards, we shall take up the <term>Calculator</term> <note>Richard Swineshead (14th century), known as "The Calculator," a mathematician and logician at Oxford</note>, for through him the imagination is strengthened and freed from all sensory distraction. After this, one must learn Arithmetic, and specifically those things written by us in the books of the *Great Art* <note>Cardano's own "Ars Magna" (1545), a foundational text in algebra</note> and the *Gardens of Numbers*. From there, we shall pass to Archimedes, Apollonius, and Eutocius. Then to <term>Scotus</term> <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major medieval scholastic theologian</note> along with Aristotle and his interpreters: Theophrastus, Alexander, Themistius, Simplicius, Philoponus, Averroes, and "classic" men of this sort. In the sixth place, we shall set Ptolemy, and in the seventh, Vitruvius. From here, we may pass to whatever art we wish to profess—whether medicine, jurisprudence, or theology. This is the proper order of the sciences.

<margin>Those who have written little should have no authority, except in poetry and mathematics.</margin>
Furthermore, in each individual science, one ought to read all the best authors, especially since, by the consensus of all wise men, our life is short. Who these authors are has already been partially stated. Generally, however, a man should not be held in high value in any art if he has not written much, except in the cases of Poetry and Mathematics. For while the other arts depend on judgment in addition to invention, judgment proceeds from the knowledge of many things. If the love of glory spurs them and they have a ready style, it is necessary for those who know many things—and know them in the best way—to write extensively. For glory is the sweetest pleasure, <margin>Why glory is sought.</margin> as is the eternity of one's own name and the image of one's own intellect. This is far to be preferred to the statues and images by which Kings strive to preserve their memory. For how does this current writing differ from my own intellect? Indeed, my intellect is whatever good is within me. Thus, he who reads these words two thousand years from now will see and attain my intellect. And this is the perpetuity of each individual's intellect.

<summary>Cardano argues that wisdom and the "divine" arts of prediction (like astrology and medicine) bring greater happiness than royal power, and he outlines a rigorous seven-step curriculum for achieving this intellectual immortality.</summary>
<keywords>divination, astrology, pulse, wisdom vs. kingship, curriculum, Euclid, Al-Kindi, Calculator, Ars Magna, intellectual immortality, glory</keywords>

<header>Book Seventeen</header>
<meta>catchword: Are (original: Sunt)</meta>

...but not eternity. Therefore, that which is best in us remains after death, even beyond our writings; and since the ages hear me speaking, from a mortal man something is made that remains forever: for the intellect and that which is understood are one, and the substance is eternal. This has been discussed elsewhere.

In poetry, however, he who writes little—provided he is driven by a divine fury—can possess judgment. And in mathematics, because only those things which have a limit are proved, and those which are necessary for demonstrating that limit. Although Euclid and Archimedes knew much more—indeed, far more for that very reason—than they wrote: nevertheless, those who wrote more are more praised and approved in these matters, such as Homer, Virgil, Ovid <note>original: "Naso"; referring to Publius Ovidius Naso</note>, Archimedes, Euclid, and Ptolemy, rather than those who wrote little, such as Theocritus, Persius, Catullus, or Nicomachus, Diocles, and Archytas.

<margin>Praise of Theon.</margin>
Now, let Theon also be placed among the celebrated authors, who explained Euclid’s *Elements* and Ptolemy’s *Great Composition* <note>original: "magnam compositionem"; likely referring to the Almagest</note>. He demonstrated, among other discoveries, that the sphere is the most capacious <note>meaning it holds the greatest volume for its surface area</note> of all bodies.

<margin>The proportion of the sphere's capacity relative to other bodies.</margin>
As that ratio demonstrates, so too do we find this to be true through art—even if not perfectly precisely—what the ratio of the sphere’s capacity is compared to other bodies. If, therefore, the side of a cube is four, the body itself will be 64, and the perimeter <note>the total surface area</note> of all its surfaces will be 96. But a sphere whose perimeter is 96 has, according to Archimedes, a great circle of 24 exactly; therefore, according to Archimedes, since the area <note>the surface area of the circular cross-section</note> is 24, the diameter will be nearly five and a half. Therefore, a cylinder built upon that great circle will be about 132, for it results from the diameter multiplied by the base; but a cylinder [enclosing] the greatest circle of a sphere is, according to Archimedes, <term>one and a half times</term> <note>original: "sesquialter"; a ratio of 3:2, a fundamental discovery Archimedes requested for his tombstone</note> larger than it. Thus, since the cylinder is about 132, the sphere will be about 88. Therefore, when the cube’s boundary is 96, the solid cube itself is 64; but when the sphere’s boundary is 96, its solid volume is 88. Therefore, the proportion of the sphere to the cube, when their boundaries are equal, will be nearly the same and very close to the ratio of 11 to 8. For this reason, as stated above, since the spherical shape is light and contains more, all things possess a certain kind of sense <note>original: "sensum"; here meaning a natural inclination or "logic" in physical behavior</note>, for the more it contains, the stronger it is rendered for resisting; and so the liquid elements, especially air, water, fire, and more obscurely earth, turn themselves spontaneously into a round shape, as it is the safest from external injury.

<margin>The three principal faculties of living things, and the four serving ones.</margin>
Truly, living things themselves, besides this latent sense, have other faculties: three principal ones—generation, nutrition, and growth. Serving these are four others: attraction, which is caused by great heat and much moisture; retention, which is a kind of light attraction, for that which attracts also retains; therefore, it is drawn by a lesser heat, and that heat does not require moisture. If, however, the heat is small and moisture abounds, it is expelled; but when heat and moisture are at their greatest, it is <term>concocted</term> <note>original: "concoquitur"; the physiological process of "ripening" or digesting nutrients into the body’s own substance</note>. Therefore, the greatest heat either exists with the greatest moisture and is concocted, or with a moderate amount and attracts; moderate heat with much moisture expels, and without moisture, it retains.

<summary>Cardano argues for the immortality of the intellect and the superiority of prolific authors before providing a geometric proof that spheres are more efficient and resilient than cubes. He concludes by detailing the biological "faculties" of life, such as nutrition and concoction, based on the balance of heat and moisture.</summary>
<keywords>immortality, intellect, Euclid, Archimedes, Theon, sphere vs cube, geometry, biology, four faculties, concoction, Aristotlean elements</keywords>

# On Arts and Artificial Things

There are also three kinds of causes for the three faculties in animals besides these: for the **retentive**, **attractive**, and **expulsive** <term>expultrix: in Renaissance physiology, the natural power of an organ to drive out what is useless or harmful</term>—though not the **concoctive** <term>concoctrix: the faculty responsible for "digesting" or transforming nutrients</term>—can be produced by fibers or filaments. Likewise, they can be produced by muscles obeying the will, and thirdly by a vacuum, as occurs in the heart. But these matters have been discussed elsewhere. Regarding the expulsive faculty in plants, evidence and an example should be taken from their "tears" <note>original: "lachrymis"; referring to the sap or resin that exudes from a cut plant</note>, for they seem to hate what they expel and flee from it as much as possible. But since they lack organs suitable for flight, they expel it instead. In contrast, many <margin>Where swallows hide in winter.</margin> kinds of animals, such as cranes and swallows, come to us in the springtime to flee the hot regions; in Autumn, fearing the winter, they migrate in flocks to warm regions, which is why they are seen in Alexandria.

It would be an endless task if I wished to explain the wonderful inventions of all the arts, but these serve as examples. I have noticed that those jumping <margin>The logic of jumps</margin> further jump from a higher place; I wanted to investigate the reason for <margin>D A C E B</margin> this. Therefore, let the ground be **A B**. On the ground, let a jump be made from **A** to **C**. Let there be a wall erected above the ground, **A D**. I say that from the height **D**, one will jump beyond the distance **A C**, but by less than double the distance of **A C**. I say the same regarding the throwing of a stone, because it is first carried through the circumference of a circle as if parallel to the ground **A C**. Since the impulse <note>original: "impetus"; the force or momentum imparted to a projectile</note> cannot act beyond double its own strength, it is carried through a circumference equal to the first; however, this subtends a smaller chord than **A C**. Therefore, it cannot be moved beyond point **C** by a space as great as **A C**, which was to be demonstrated. If, therefore, the height **A D** is much greater than the distance **A C**, the landing point **E** will be at a distance almost double that of **C A** from point **A**. But when the height **A D** is smaller than the distance **A C**, the landing point **E** will be at a distance from point **A** less than double **A C**—indeed, less than the sum of lines **A D** and **A C**, but more than the line **D C**. These and such things concerning the arts consist of wonderful subtlety, but no art can be compared in subtlety to the jocular arts <note>original: "ioculariae"; refers to stage magic, prestidigation, or "juggling" in the sense of deceptive tricks</note>, much less to magic. Therefore, it is now time for me to discuss the causes of wonders.

<summary>Cardano discusses biological faculties like the expulsive power in plants and animals (migration), followed by a geometric analysis of how height increases the distance of a jump or projectile.</summary>
<keywords>physiology, expulsive faculty, bird migration, Alexandria, physics of motion, geometry, jumping, impetus, jocular arts, magic</keywords>

<page-num>342</page-num>

# BOOK XVIII
## On Marvels, and the method of representing 
## various things beyond belief.

---

<margin>
The story of a Spanish prestidigitator.
</margin>
**I** REMEMBER when Charles V <note>Charles V (1500–1558), Holy Roman Emperor and King of Spain, who dominated European politics in the 16th century.</note>, the most fortunate Caesar, had come to Milan, while Duke Francesco Sforza <note>Francesco II Sforza (1495–1535), the last Duke of Milan from the Sforza dynasty.</note>, the second of that name, was in power, there was a Spaniard in the Emperor's retinue who performed such wonders and dazzled the eyes of the onlookers so skillfully that those who were ignorant of philosophy <note>In this era, "philosophy" often meant natural science; Cardano implies that a scientific understanding of physics and optics would explain the tricks.</note> considered him a magician. Nor have our ages, nor those much older as I understand it, seen his like, for he did things unheard of and incredible. I recall reading that this art and these tricks were brought from the New World <note>original: "è nouo orbe"; a reference to the Americas, suggesting a colonial exchange of entertainment styles.</note>, where there are wonderful practitioners of them. It is certain that the ancients either did not know these people or worshipped them, as is read concerning Pharaoh <note>A reference to the biblical magicians who competed with Moses.</note> and Simon Magus <note>A figure mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles who practiced sorcery.</note>. And although this art is so wonderful, it is nevertheless held in no esteem, whereas even a common cook maintains some reputation.

<margin>
Why those skilled in the jocular art are held in no esteem.
</margin>
The cause is manifold, I believe: first, because it deals with useless things; second, because it is practiced by low-born men; third, because it once relied on the protection of divinity but is now destitute of it; furthermore, it is condemned by laws; and because Princes, having been deceived in the past while hoping in vain, exposed it to contempt.

<margin>
The works of the jocular art.
</margin>
For what does it profit to either swallow or blow out fire? For those who swallow it first extinguish it with saliva collected under the tongue; those who blow it out wrap it in cooked tow <note>original: "cotto & stupę"; coarse fibers of flax or hemp used for lighting fires.</note>. These are portents of audacity rather than of talent. The inventions of this art are infinite: to transfer, hide, and swallow objects; to draw forth a copious fluid from the eyes or the forehead; to pull nails and thread from the mouth; to chew glass; to pierce the arms or hands with a stylus; to join iron chains while the rings remain whole—indeed, what is greater, I have seen three rings thrown upward descend entangled with each other, though they were whole and separate before and while they were being thrown. They show various shapes in one and the same little book, with the previous ones always disappearing; they bend a sword from the edge against their bare belly all the way to the hilt by pressing it, while others seem to hide and conceal it as it penetrates. They show a boy without a head, and a head without a boy, yet they all live, and the boy suffers no harm meanwhile. Now, if I were to enumerate how many and how great things they do with small wooden statues, which the common people call <term>magatellos: an Italian term for puppets or marionettes</term>, the day would fail me. For they play, fight, hunt, dance, blow the trumpet, and practice the art of cooking; and all these things, as wonderful as they are, are of no utility, as I said. And once you have learned the reason by which they deceive the eyes—for it consists of two things: various instruments prepared for this purpose, and agility of the hands...

<summary>Jerome Cardano introduces Book XVIII by discussing the art of illusion and prestidigitation, recounting a Spanish performer at the court of Charles V. He describes various feats of sleight-of-hand and mechanical puppets, while dismissing the art as a useless but technically impressive deception.</summary>
<keywords>prestidigitation, Charles V, Milan, magic vs. science, puppets, New World influences, sleight of hand, mechanical wonders</keywords>

<header>On Marvels.</header>

# On Marvels.

<margin>How they hide things in the mouth.</margin>
...skill, nor should you deign to learn it as a favor, even if they wish to teach you. Only those things they hide in the mouth consist of natural principles; for they lie hidden behind the uvula <note>original: "columellam"; literally "little column," referring to the uvula or the soft palate</note> in a certain ample space that lies between the windpipe <note>original: "asperam arteriam"; the trachea</note>, the gullet, and the roof of the mouth. Others, however, actually swallow things and vomit them up when they wish, aided by long practice. Some eat poisons after first ingesting a large amount of butter; others handle serpents—but these are either harmless, or have had their teeth pulled out first, or have been weakened by hunger, or are sluggish from the cold, or have been tamed through long association. From this, they merely add boldness to others without providing the means of safety, and by these examples they greatly harm both simple men and children, exposing them to dangers; for which reason they are rightly called itinerant charlatans <note>original: "circulatores"</note>, deceivers, and impostors, and are held in ill repute. Even now, in some cities, they are punished as people who bring about evil without any accompanying good. There are those who pretend to tremble, as if struck by a divine inspiration—a truly wonderful thing because of the perseverance they have acquired through habit. Others are of the class of mimes and dancers; these, besides being harmless, also provide much delight, and are not prohibited by laws anywhere.

<margin>The principle of tightrope walkers.</margin>
Bolder than these are those we call tightrope walkers <term>funambulos; from the Latin funis (rope) and ambulare (to walk)</term>. Now, in these arts there is something more of natural reason; therefore, I shall begin to treat them as if tracing the origin of natural magic from its beginning. For **magic** occurs when something marvelous is perfected through natural, yet hidden, reasons. Therefore, the principle of tightrope walkers is this: A bold and practiced man walks with bare feet upon a very tightly stretched rope; in his right and left hands, he holds a lead weight of ten, fifteen, or even twenty pounds. When he leans to the right, intent on his work—for this reason, he must be extremely daring—he stretches and extends his left arm, while relaxing and pulling in his right. Thus, before the weight of the right side can overpower the left, he balances the weights and brings the body back to equilibrium; then, gradually, he restores both the weights and his arms to their original position. This is necessary, for before he can fall, one side must become heavier than the other by a certain proportion. Since this proportion is acquired gradually, before it is fully reached, he leans to the other side by extending and tensing his arm; therefore, he does not fall.

<margin>The dangers of tightrope walkers.</margin>
He can fall, therefore, if the rope is not exactly taut; if his limbs are gripped by a sudden numbness; if he does not hold his body firmly and intently; if he panics; if he grows exhausted; or if he lacks the art or experience, such that he extends his arm too slowly while leaning, or extends it too much, so that he falls toward the opposite side of what he feared. I set aside the fact that the weights must maintain a certain ratio, or something close to it, regarding each person's weight, size, and even strength. Therefore, if these six conditions are met, there is no danger.

<margin>Various feats of tightrope walkers.</margin>
And so, I saw a certain boy who, with wooden spheres placed under his feet and sometimes even entirely enclosed in a sack except for his arms, walked upon a rope stretched between the tops of towers, while we were in the greatest fear for his life. Another even climbed from the ground up to a tower, which is more difficult; since...

<summary>Cardano distinguishes between deceptive street performers and skilled acrobats, defining "natural magic" as the use of hidden physical principles to create wonder. He provides a detailed mechanical analysis of how tightrope walkers use lead weights and arm movements to maintain equilibrium.</summary>

<keywords>natural magic, tightrope walking, physics of balance, equilibrium, sleight of hand, charlatans, lead weights, circus arts</keywords>

<page-num>344</page-num>
<header>Book Eighteen</header>

## Book Eighteen

...so that people struggle greatly in this exercise. This same man would lower himself head-first from a tower without using counterweights, sliding down a rope to the ground with his hands outstretched; for the strength in his hands and arms was so consistent and firm that he used them in place of weights. The same man—which is a most wretched sight—would hang himself by his foot from a thin cord attached to the main rope where it was closest to the tower, a shameful and horrific spectacle. Then, by the strength of his loins and back, he would grasp the rope with his hands and thus restore himself to the rope again. Both performers would pretend to fall headlong, but the very tip of the foot would cling to the rope with the head hanging down. You can understand how much strength must have been necessary in the tip of that foot, for they were supported only by the curvature of the toes, and that on the rougher <note>original: "syluestrem"; literally "wooded" or "wild," likely referring to the calloused or outer part of the foot</note> part.

<margin>Tightrope-walking elephants.</margin>
A boy also threw himself headlong while holding spheres, one of which stayed between the sole of his foot and the rope; I simply do not know by what logic he remained hanging without slipping off due to the roundness of the object. But why is this a wonder, when I have read in Suetonius that the Emperor Claudius Caesar exhibited tightrope-walking elephants during the games? This is more miraculous in them than in the boy because they lack reason, are so much heavier, and because they stood upon two ropes rather than one. But such is the power of habit, man’s relentless greed, and the remarkable docility of that beast, which is closest of all to human intelligence.

<margin>How one may safely swim across rivers.</margin>
Rivers are crossed more usefully by using a thick leather intestine: when needed, it is inflated vigorously, the ends are tied shut, and it is bound under the armpits. In this way, horsemen and infantry commit themselves safely to rivers in great emergencies; sometimes they have even dared to swim across with this aid alone. We have reported many things above regarding the category of magic when we spoke of mirrors and the "flesh-magnet" <note>original: "carneo’q; magnete"; likely a reference to a specific talisman or a biological "attractor" discussed in earlier books</note>, as well as elsewhere in these preceding books, and in the books on medicine and the ninth book of arithmetic. Nevertheless, we shall now touch upon the main points only of those things which were left untouched by us, so that we may show through a few examples how much the subtlety of the human mind can achieve.

<margin>On a rod which is carried tilted on the tip of a finger.</margin>
To return to the matter at hand, the example of the tightrope walkers is similar to those who carry a rod or a spear upright on a finger. Others carry a small rod on the tip of the finger, tilted because of swords fixed opposite it at the bottom.

<margin>How a stone may be broken with a fist.</margin>
What of the fact that anyone may try this: we can break a stone the thickness of a palm—which one might otherwise try to break into pieces with a hammer—using only a fist. The matter works like this: the stone is stretched out over a wooden surface (or better yet, a stone one). It is raised at one end so that it is barely supported, with no force yet applied. Then, the raised part is struck with the fist; by this blow, it is dashed against the flat surface and shattered into many pieces. But if the fist strikes faster or slower than the moment it reaches the far edge of the stone slab, the blow becomes useless and it does not break. We have also broken bricks in this way with a light blow. For when the edge of the stone is dashed against the slab at the same moment as the force of the blow, the weight is joined with the momentum <note>original: "impetu"; the physical force of motion</note>, and the result is no different than if it were struck by a heavy blow from a hammer.

<summary>Cardano describes various physical "marvels," including acrobatic feats, tightrope-walking elephants mentioned by Suetonius, and the physics of breaking stones with a fist using leverage and momentum.</summary>
<keywords>acrobatics, tightrope walking, elephants, Claudius Caesar, Suetonius, buoyancy, physics of impact, Girolamo Cardano</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Cardano’s exploration of "mirabilia" or wonders, transitioning from the physical feats of acrobats to the physics of leverage and the folkloric "sympathies" and "antipathies" associated with animals like wolves.</meta>

<page-num>345</page-num>

# On Marvels.

<margin>How a rope may be broken with the hands alone.</margin>
Earlier, we mentioned the "trembling strike" <note>This likely refers to a specific physical technique for breaking objects through vibration mentioned in a previous chapter</note>. A new and thick rope can also be broken by skill: its end is tied to a fixed nail or hook, wrapped four times or even more around the hand, then the remaining end of the rope overlaps near the top of the palm, in the part between the index finger and thumb, tending toward the nail; and the head is bent back again toward the bottom of the palm from where it came, and is led around once or twice more. Thus, with a vibrating force, it is snapped in that part where it is overlapped by the rope; for the rope itself which lies underneath prevents the hand from suffering, and the final wrapping prevents it from slipping. Indeed, the rope cuts the rope because of the force, especially when the part lying between the hand and the nail is soft, the hand is strong, and the force is straight and swift. Thus we have often seen these things, which are devoid of any miracle, though they seem marvelous. There are those who maintain the same method for the binding of both hands and break ropes with their hands alone—men of the sort who can easily support oxen.

<margin>How we pull more easily when a person is taken onto our shoulders.</margin>
Now truly, I have also experienced this: when another man is taken onto one's shoulders, two others of nearly the same strength who are resisting can be pulled along against their will, whereas without the extra weight, one man would scarcely suffice. Thus certain things occur through sympathy <note>In Renaissance science, "sympathy" referred to a natural attraction or shared influence between objects that wasn't immediately visible</note>: it is believed a man falls silent if a wolf sees him first, whence that line from Virgil:

->The wolves saw Moeris first.<-
<note>original: "Lupi Moerim uidere priores." From Virgil's Eclogues, 9.54. It reflects a common Roman superstition that seeing a wolf could cause a person to lose their voice.</note>

<margin>A man falls silent upon seeing a wolf, and why.</margin>
This happens not out of terror, for it does not happen when more dangerous lions or bears are seen; nor would it be equal for it to happen when the wolf sees the man first, rather than the man seeing the wolf. Furthermore, we have sometimes experienced this to be true: they do not fall entirely silent, but become hoarse. Since it does not always happen, they said this was the cause when it fails: that the man saw the wolf first. The cause, therefore, is in the eyes of the wolf. For it possesses something hostile to man, by which the breath is restrained; nor can that violent exhalation of breath, which is necessary for the voice, occur. <margin>The feet of horses following the tracks of a wolf grow numb.</margin> For a similar reason, they say the feet of a horse become numb if they follow the tracks of a wolf for a long time; for if the tracks are fresh, the horse is troubled by the smell. Because of this, sometimes neither does the man fall silent, nor the horse become numb, because any impression—even a celestial one—is weakened and rendered void by time, smallness, the nature of the subject, and the opposition of that which ought to be affected. <margin>A wolf's tail hung in mangers prevents beasts of burden from eating.</margin> By the same logic, they say that a wolf's tail hung in a manger for oxen or horses prevents them from eating. If this is not true, it can nevertheless be possible, since those struck by fear because of the scent will forget their food despite being hungry, just as happens to men in times of great fear.

<margin>Strings and drums of a lamb make a discordant noise and resonate poorly when wolf-parts are struck.</margin>
It is more wonderful, and yet true, that strings made from a wolf clash poorly with those made from a lamb <note>This refers to the "wolf-string" myth: the belief that if a musical instrument is strung with both sheep-gut and wolf-gut, it will produce a discordant sound or the wolf-gut will "eat" the sheep-gut</note>, although this same thing happens with the strings of almost all different animals, such as a dog and a lamb. This happens even more clearly in drums, for

<header>Book Eighteen</header>

# Book Eighteen

<margin>Sheep skin torn by a wolf causes itching.</margin>
For sheep skins almost fall silent and creak when in the presence of wolf skins. It should not seem strange that a sheep's skin, torn by a wolf, causes itching; for due to a vehement fear, and also because of their contrary natures, the hide is badly affected. Even if death is the ultimate punishment, the body is nevertheless affected differently by one kind of death than another. A man fears more when tossed in the sea than when facing enemies. <margin>A wolf’s head hung in a dovecote keeps away animals harmful to pigeons.</margin> It is also believed that a wolf’s head, hung in a dovecote—whether by its scent or its appearance—keeps away ferrets and weasels. And why is this strange? For even we, unless we used our reason beforehand, would not approach a lion's head. Who would assure those small animals that the rest of the body does not lie hidden behind the protruding head? <margin>It is doubtful whether a buried wolf’s tail wards off flies.</margin> This would be nearly a miracle, if it were true, that a buried wolf’s tail wards off flies. <margin>Why the intestines, dung, and hide of a wolf are vehemently beneficial for the pains of colic.</margin> This much is certain: wolf dung, intestines, and skin, when consumed or even merely carried, take away the colic <note>Colic refers to severe, fluctuating pain in the abdomen, historically attributed to blockages or "wind" in the intestines.</note>. For these things strengthen the human intestine; since strong limbs (unless they languish from an ulcer) repel disease from themselves. These parts of the wolf strengthen the intestines by drying them, both by their own nature and because they are exceptionally strong; for the wolf even digests earth, and never suffers from indigestion, even if it stuffs itself after a long hunger and devours meat that is almost always rotten. <margin>It is doubtful whether a dried and chewed wolf’s penis immediately excites lust.</margin> Whether a wolf’s penis <note>original: "virga"</note> dried in an oven, if chewed, can immediately cause a desire for lust and excite the power of sexual union, is as yet unproven to me. Indeed, this is not without some logic, yet it is utterly absurd to think it could always do so; for it has been shown that the greatest and most prompt cause of lust is the imagination of the thing we love, so that we may possess it.

<margin>To strengthen the memory</margin>
It is even more marvelous what they report: that a badger's tooth or its left foot, tied to a man’s right arm, strengthens the memory. Perhaps more plausible is what *Symeon Sethi* <note>A 11th-century Byzantine physician known for his work on the medicinal properties of foods.</note> relates: namely, that the gall of a partridge smeared on the arteries of the temples so that it penetrates once a month, is of great benefit for strengthening the memory. <margin>For sharpening the wit.</margin> But melissa <note>Lemon balm (*Melissa officinalis*), traditionally used to reduce anxiety and improve cognitive function.</note> also strengthens it and sharpens the wit, and when eaten makes a man industrious, which watercress can also achieve. Likewise, the brain of a hen aids the wit and memory, so much so that it causes some who have begun to rave to return to their senses. <margin>For cheerfulness. Which dreams are happy, sad, or turbulent. The great power of garlic, and why.</margin> But beyond these things, melissa provides tranquility of mind, and makes one not a little cheerful by driving away cares. Thus, when eaten after dinner, it makes for pleasant sleep, just as cabbage makes for sad dreams, beans <note>original: "phaseli"</note> for turbulent ones, and garlic and onions for terrifying ones. From these foods arose the opinion concerning "hags" <note>original: "lamiae"; folklore entities often associated with witchcraft and night terrors.</note>, who, living on parsley, chestnuts, beans, onions, cabbage, and legumes, seem through sleep to be carried into various regions and there to be affected in diverse ways, according to the temperament of each individual—aided also by the ointment of which we shall speak below. <margin>How those who rise in sleep may be restrained.</margin> By a contrary logic, the teeth of a male horse, tied to the left arm or hung from the neck, drive away bad images in dreams. And thus they restrain those who rise up because of turbulent dreams <note>A reference to sleepwalking or night terrors.</note>. As for the idea that a face smeared with bear fat should increase the intellect—if it be true—there seems to be no rational cause for it.

## On Wonders.

<margin>To prevent a woman from conceiving.</margin>
<margin>So that dogs do not bark.</margin>
That the marrow of a mule, when drunk, makes one stupid—while this could be possible, it is not certain to me. But that a mule's sweat applied to the womb prevents a woman from conceiving is likely enough. Moreover, that the eye of a black dog held in the hand prevents dogs from barking—favoring thieves and adulterers in no small measure—this could be due to the scent. For as everyone knows, dogs perceive scents in a wondrous way, even very faint ones. Therefore, if this is true, it can be tested with a fresh eye, not one removed long ago.

Therefore all such things sometimes work, and sometimes they do not. Not all rhubarb <term>rhubarb: a root used as a powerful purgative in early modern medicine</term> always purges bile—for instance, if it is old, hollow, light, or decayed, or used in a phlegmatic person, or in a very cold winter, or in a more robust body. Why then do you wish that what is said here never fails, when all mortal things are subject to error? Yet these things I have said are generally true, and I have tested them. They say that a stone bitten by a dog, taken in a drink, makes a man shout. Therefore if he shouts, he is either forced or does it willingly. If he is forced, it must necessarily cause great harm, but they do not say it harms. If he shouts of his own accord, then he is either playing—and thus the experiment is mocked—or he lacks his senses. Therefore one should add that it must be "given to the drunk," though I do not know if even so it is true. Nevertheless, a stone bitten by a dog does cause harm and provokes anger if taken in a drink.

<margin>So that a drunk person appears possessed.</margin>
<margin>For curing diseases of sheep.</margin>
<margin>A ram's horn into asparagus.</margin>
Thus they perhaps say correctly that camel froth given to a drunkard in a drink makes him appear possessed by a demon; for since it is excessively dry, it sharply agitates a brain already weakened by drink. It is reported with good reason that a ram’s stomach cooked in water and wine and given in a drink heals most diseases of sheep, for there is a <term>sympathy: the occult principle that things with similar natures can naturally influence or heal each other</term>. Likewise, I will believe on the testimony of many that a ram's horn turns into asparagus if it is buried and rots, though I have not tested it myself. This is not far from a metamorphosis; but decay, as I have said elsewhere, is the mother of many things.

<margin>The right testicle of a leopard is most effective in provoking menstruation.</margin>
<margin>Its bile is an immediate poison.</margin>
<margin>For strangury.</margin>
<margin>For the begetting of children.</margin>
<margin>So that the newborn may be raised.</margin>
<margin>So that clever children are produced.</margin>
The same horn <note>original: "Idem cornu", referring back to the ram's horn</note> buried near a fig tree helps it to ripen its fruit quickly, as they say. The right testicle of a leopard provokes menstruation as much as anything else. But its bile is an immediate poison that kills in a single day. Likewise, a goose's tongue drunk [as a powder] is wonderful for <term>strangury: a painful condition where urine is passed drop by drop</term>. And its testicles, as well as a hare's uterus, are wonderfully effective for procreation, as is the fish called a <term>squilla: likely a shrimp or prawn, though here used as a medicinal ingredient</term>, which has sometimes worked for me. However, impediments must be removed, and both the body and the womb must be purged first. Truly, if those born die immediately and cannot be raised, let the pregnant woman frequently eat turtle eggs. But if a pregnant woman eats <term>quinces: (cotonea) a fruit similar to a pear, believed in this period to "bind" the stomach and strengthen the brain</term> more often, a boy or girl of clever industry will be born. Why is this a wonder? For those conceived by the drunk, or those who eat onions, or those who fast frequently, or those who are too studious, are often rendered insane. For the nourishment of the brain and the "spirits" <note>Early modern medicine believed "spirits" were subtle vapors that carried out the functions of the soul and mind</note> within it, if they are poorly affected, produce such offspring as their own condition was; and so, from the sad, sad children are born, or from the envious, envious ones. Quinces, therefore, ward off vapors from the brain, with the result that the substance of the infant's brain—

...to be held, and especially since I was eating, I had applied salt and pressed the wound, but nothing helped. Blood, stay fixed, as Christ when he was crucified." <note>original: "Sanguis mane in te, sicut fecit Christus in se. Sanguis mane in tua uena, sicut Christus in sua pœna. Sanguis mane fixus, sicut Christus quādo fuit crucifixus." A rhythmic Latin charm common in medieval and early modern folk medicine.</note> Repeat this three times. You might ask, by what precedent? Even more wonderful is what was written by Aetius <note>Aetius of Amida, a 6th-century Byzantine physician</note> regarding the removal of a thorn or a bone from the throat. But since we recounted that in the second book of *Controversies*, I will instead relate another example from Constantine <note>Constantine the African, an 11th-century monk and translator of medical texts</note>. He says: If you take three tiles or dishes from which you have scraped the meat and inscribe them with a stylus with these words: *Iao Sabaoth* <note>original: "Iao Sabaoth," a Greek transliteration of Hebrew names for God (Yahweh of Hosts), frequently used in magical papyri and amulets</note>, fish will gather around them in wonder. Likewise from Africanus: If these words are inscribed on a vessel: "Taste and see that the Lord is good" <note>Psalm 34:8</note>, the wine placed within will never spoil that year. What should I say of these things? Nevertheless, it is well enough established among everyone that, however the matter itself may stand, words have the power to stop blood even to the point of a miracle. We have stated the cause of these things in the second book of *Controversies*.

The same occurs in extracting arrows. It is believed that a squill-fish <note>a type of crustacean or fish mentioned in classical natural histories</note> applied to the wound is very effective for this. Likewise, it is a wonder that those anointed with the fat of a lion are safe from wild beasts, since the animals dread that odor, whether from a living or a dead lion. This is most effective when you approach them fearlessly, for if you take to flight, they will hardly perceive the scent. By similar reasoning, it is handed down that the juice of a small radish or horse-radish, if the hands are diligently smeared with it, allows you to handle snakes safely; for they either fear to bite because they sense the sharpness of the smell, or they are actually stunned by it. As for weasels and squirrels, once they have tasted garlic with their teeth, they hardly dare to bite afterward; and in this way they are made tame. That thing is incredible: that the spur of a rooster's right foot makes one a victor; or that human blood in eighty days congeals into a human form. Far more incredible is that this figure, buried in barley flour for nine days and then having its throat cut, produces blood which, when smeared on the face, makes a person pleasing in the presence of Kings and lovable to all.

<header>Book Eighteen</header>

# Book Eighteen

<margin>Three types of sorcery.</margin>
...[men]strual blood of a prostitute, a spotted lizard—to which the name "skink" is given—and Hippomanes <term>Hippomanes: a legendary substance in antiquity, often described as a growth on a newborn foal's forehead or a discharge from a mare, believed to be a powerful ingredient in love potions.</term>. All these things change the mind rather than compel a person to love the one from whom they were taken. Moreover, they are mostly composed of excrement, or of animals born from rot, or of human seed. An example is that which is made from seed and the womb of a female puppy burning with desire, when a male puppy is present and held before her for a long time but not allowed to reach her; for then she rages as if rabid. There are also other love potions <term>philtra: from the Greek word for love, these charms or potions were intended to excite passion or devotion.</term> which are not consumed, but are mostly taken from the clothes of the dead, candles, measuring tapes, needles, and generally those things prepared for funerals. Sorceries <term>veneficia: This Latin term encompasses both the act of poisoning and the use of harmful magic, reflecting the historical belief that chemical toxins and supernatural spells were closely linked.</term> truly differ little from poisons, and are taken either from those things which are eaten, such as corrupt excrement (like blood or the urine of lepers) in which grain has been soaked and then fed to chickens. Other sorceries occur through contact, which I discussed above. All such things are little different from poisons.

The third type is that which occurs without contact, taken from the excrement of the person whom the sorcery is intended to harm, or from a part of them, such as urine, dung, blood, or hair clippings. These are generally enclosed in the body parts of a dog that correspond to the parts or excrement of the human, and they are sealed in the bone of a dead man and buried in the victim's name: some in a doorway, others in roads that have the shape of a cross, and others in torrents. Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous German polymath and occultist. The author here takes a critical view of his work.</note> filled a huge book with such things—a man born for all evils and ruinous to the human race. If these things were true, I would not have included them in this book, but I have added them to refute the vanity of that man who wrote *On the Vanity of the Sciences* <note>The author is referencing Agrippa's skeptical work *De Incertitudine et Vanitate Scientiarum* (1530), contrasting it with Agrippa's own writings on magic.</note>. These things, therefore, are empty, except for those given in a drink, of which he wrote a great number in his book on sorceries and poisons. Nor is there any safe protection against them except caution.

The rest do not cause harm except through the specific character of the person chanting and the weakness of the souls of those against whom these machines are built. For this reason, such things harm neither Princes, nor brave men, nor the wise; they harm only women and children, and not even all of them, but only the lowliest. Truly, it is not the mark of an honest or noble man to know or seek such things, unless he already preserves such a sound mind that he can despise money. Indeed, to teach such things is the work of assassins <note>original: "siccarij", literally "dagger-men" or hired killers.</note>. Nor could anything of this sort ever be gathered from our books if they had not first been made public by others, though we have passed over them very briefly and obscurely.

<margin>A dispute against certain absurd tenets of magic.</margin>
Therefore, having left behind this part of harmful magic (however "natural" it may be claimed to be), let us pass to that which is useful. First, however, let us refute its vanity in certain matters; for while this book contains general precepts, I have described specific ones in my books *On the Variety of Things*. They say that if a womb or a male member is measured with a wax candle that was used at a funeral, that man or woman is prohibited from the act of love. This would mean either that a male is kept from intercourse with any woman, or only from that woman in whose name the act is done. If only with her—since nothing is made specific to him except the words—then words would have a power independent of human consent. If he is kept from any woman, then it must...

<page-num>351</page-num>
<header>Concerning Wonders.</header>

...[it is] necessary that what does not agree with experience [happens] perpetually, or for a certain time in some individuals; for while there is truly nothing that prohibits generation or imagination in women, nor the breath from which it is extended, it is manifest that this occurs only in some, and not always nor in all.

<margin>The power of seals</margin>
Therefore, to return to the matter at hand, they attribute no small power to seals <note>sigilla: in this context, astrological or magical talismans engraved with specific symbols under specific planetary alignments</note>: those of Jupiter for riches and friends; those of Venus for pleasures; those of Mars for boldness; those of Mercury for cleverness; those of Saturn for the endurance of labor; and those of the Moon for the favor of the people. And I truly wish I could know what would benefit each person; for I am not unaware that both the stones and the timing of the engraving are advantageous, but the figure <note>original: "figuram"; the specific image or shape carved into the stone</note> itself provides nothing. They believe that "star-foam" <note>original: "Astrum famium"; likely a reference to a mineral or alchemical substance, perhaps *spuma maris* (meerschaum) or a poetic term for a white mineral</note> and slaked lime in mallow juice, or the mercury-plant, can make it so that—if the hands are smeared—fire does not harm them. 
<margin>Against fire</margin>
<margin>The power of the toad.</margin>
But they claim that a large toad killed with salt, if that salt is dissolved in water and an undergarment or shirt is washed in that water, will cause the one who wears it to be seized with a most severe scabies <note>A skin condition characterized by intense itching and sores.</note>. These things are either entirely true, or true in part, or at least plausible. Indeed, some things seem truer than they are, while others are truer than they seem.

<margin>Why the strings of a lyre, when tuned equally, skip if one is struck, with the other emitting a sound.</margin>
Of this last kind is that experiment handed down by Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a philosopher whose works on music theory were standard texts in the Renaissance.</note>, which is well enough known and which we have often observed at our leisure. Taking two lyres or lutes, you will place one face up, having first adjusted the strings to a harmony by tightening or loosening them. Afterward, place a small piece of straw across the first and second strings of the lyre that is lying face up. Then, pluck the first string of the instrument you are holding in your hands; when it yields a sound equal to that of the string on the resting instrument, the straw will immediately jump and dance as if shaken by someone. By moving the piece of straw across each string in this way, you will bring the instruments to an equal voice—indeed, the very same voice—with wonderful skill. The cause of such a great effect seems to have been unknown. Is it because it only jumps when it is able to produce an equal sound? Or because the air itself, possessing an equal force, is able to move it, whereas it cannot when it is more relaxed or more agitated? But even this is not true, since a more relaxed tension in a thinner string moves it if it is suited to produce an equal sound. Indeed, equal tension with an unequal sound does not move it. It seems to me, truly, that this happens because the air set in motion always excites sound in the strings, even if it is not heard. However, when the movement is equal, the air agrees in a single motion: because it is moved by the same ratio, it resists it in no way. Thus, it is carried in its entirety to the resting string by the same force by which it is moved, and it moves it with almost as much force as it is moved. In my judgment, no truer or more subtle reason for this can be devised.

<margin>A stone which is ignited by saliva.</margin>
Things which are less true than they seem include such things as a stone that is spontaneously ignited by saliva. It consists of three pounds of quicklime, three ounces of Greek pitch <note>original: "picis Graecae"; a type of resin used in ancient and medieval incendiary mixtures</note>, and an ounce of Herculean stone <term>Herculean stone: usually refers to a magnet (lodestone), but in alchemical recipes, it may refer to a mineral believed to have strong attractive or transformative properties.</term>. These are ground together and cooked in an earthenware pot sealed with bricks; afterward, it is buried in laurel oil for fifteen days, then kept in a dry place.

<header>Book Eighteen</header>

# Book Eighteen

This contains less truth, because it is not always ignited, yet the strings of a lyre, when drawn to equality <note>meaning properly tuned to the same tension</note>, always move straw; nonetheless, this regarding the stone has a more evident cause for its effect.

<margin>A candle that is inextinguishable.</margin>
<margin>A candle burning from ice.</margin>
Many things are wonderful, yet once you know the cause, all wonder ceases: for example, sulfur dissolved equally with wax makes it inextinguishable; however, it is necessary that the sulfur be very pure. Similarly, if a candle coated in sulfur powder and then charcoal is dipped in water during winter time, covered on its upper part with paper, and hung where a drop of ice falls, it will be surrounded by thicker ice. When lit, it will then burn, and to the great miracle of the bystanders, the ice will seem to be burning.

<margin>Meat appearing to crawl with little worms.</margin>
Likewise, the strings of a lyre <note>typically made of animal gut</note> thrown onto hot meat, as they twist and distort, resemble the appearance of little worms.

<margin>So that everything appears partly black and partly green.</margin>
<margin>So that fur and hair appear green.</margin>
Simeon Seth <note>original: "Symeon Sethi"; an 11th-century Byzantine Jewish physician and polymath</note> reports that if the wick of a lamp is placed in cuttlefish ink mixed with verdigris <note>original: "ærugine"; the green pigment or rust that forms on copper</note>, and it is lit without any other light being present, whatever things are there are shown to be partly black and partly green. Earlier, while I was discussing light and luminosity, I taught such things. But distilled water of capers truly makes fur and hair green.

<margin>How a fruit may take whatever shape you wish.</margin>
Among true and natural experiments, it is not absurd to mention that all fruits can be transferred into any form, especially the larger ones that lack a pit, such as apples, pears, quinces, pomegranates, cucumbers, gourds, and eggplants <note>original: "melongenæ"</note>. The art is this: carve the shape you desire into wood at the size of a fully grown fruit. Around this, place plaster dissolved in water to the thickness of your little finger, divided into two parts. Once this mold is dry—for it dries quickly—remove it from the wood; this will be easy if you smeared the wood with oil beforehand. Take this hollow plaster mold, divided in two, and tie it very tightly around a growing fruit that has reached a little more than half its size. Leave it until the fruit reaches its proper magnitude. You will have a fruit with the shape that had been carved into the wood. One may even inscribe whatever you wish, so that you may truly say: *Grow, and rise up duly into my titles* <note>original: "Crescite, & in titulos surgite rite meos"; a poetic allusion to carving names into trees so they grow along with the plant</note>.

<margin>The method of constructing the "fire-loving" stone from human blood.</margin>
This is a true metamorphosis of shapes; another is that of substances, such as when we wish to make the **Pyrophilus** stone <note>literally "fire-loving" stone; a legendary alchemical gem described as containing a self-sustaining light or heat</note>. We allow two pounds of human blood to putrefy for fifteen days under horse dung. Then, after distillation is performed through glass, we save the water that was drawn off. We take the dregs into a vessel called a **crucible** <note>original: "crucibulum"</note>, in which metals are usually melted, and dry them over hot coals until they turn into a kind of lime. Again, we place that lime in a glass vessel and mix it with the saved water, and by a slow fire, we turn it into a stone; or we allow it to be hardened by sharp heat like bricks, or by being buried.

<margin>Books by Agrippa not yet published.</margin>
Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a famous 16th-century German polymath and occultist</note> reports in his work *On Sorcery and Experiments* that this stone is reddish and brilliant. I have seen these books joined to the fourth book of *Occult Philosophy*; that one, however, is titled *The Practice of those things taught in the prior three*, and none of these have been published.

# On Wonders.

<margin>From specific types of plants, while they rot in horse manure, specific types of worms and sometimes species of serpents are generated.</margin>
The same transformation seen in plants and animal parts turning into stone <note>referring to petrification, which was often viewed as a form of natural alchemy</note> can be achieved by the same art: almost every kind of herb can pass into different species of worms or serpents, endowed with various forms and powers of their own. We call this the "Great Metamorphosis." For as we taught above, when the "fatty moisture" <note>original: "pingue humidum"; an alchemical term for the life-giving oily principle in substances</note> is separated from the earthy part during putrefaction—and all things that are able to rot do so, such as herbs, leaves, flesh, eggs, or milk, when placed in a glass vessel and buried in steaming horse manure <note>horse manure was used as a consistent, natural heat source for incubation in early science</note>—it is necessary that such buried things excrete that fatty moisture. Once this is separated, a living animal is generated by the heat of the stars. This generation cannot be prevented except by burning away the waste while the mixture of fatty moisture remains. Indeed, the variety of the material is the reason why different forms of animals are generated. For this reason, we see different animals—varying in form, behavior, and nature—on the leaves of trees according to their variety; this could not happen except due to the variety of the material. Therefore, if things that differ in form differ in species, and those that differ in species differ in powers and behaviors, and those generated from different materials differ in form: it is necessary that those things born from different materials possess different powers, just as was said above regarding wasps, bees, and hornets.

<margin>Water drops in corrupt air turn into toads.</margin>
Sometimes, however, different types of animals are made from the same material but by a different "efficient cause" <note>the agent that brings something into being</note>; for example, water drops in summer generate fleas in our lands, yet in Darien <note>the Darien Gap in modern-day Panama/Colombia</note>, a province of the New World, the same drops immediately turn into toads. Thus, it does not seem absurd to me that a certain man, having spat, showed tiny frogs emerging from his spit within the space of half an hour. In this way, it can be believed with less of a miracle—if I may say so—that the magicians before Pharaoh turned rods into serpents.

<margin>Crete does not nourish venomous animals.</margin>
<margin>For foul breath.</margin>
<margin>For strengthening the stomach and intestines.</margin>
<margin>For drainage from the head.</margin>
<margin>Beans corrupt the air.</margin>
<margin>Citrons rot if hot bread is placed on top.</margin>
<margin>Madder held in the hands dyes the urine.</margin>
<margin>Against caterpillars.</margin>
<margin>The prodigious cure of the King's brother.</margin>
Therefore, things are endowed with wonderful properties, as are regions. Crete does not nourish any venomous animal, even though it is warm. The cause, therefore, is either a lack of food or the air itself prevents them due to its changes; for good odors block them and are fatal to them. Celery <note>original: "Apium"; may refer to wild celery or parsley</note>, though many things are more fragrant, corrects foulness of the breath better than anything else. Is it because, besides its odor, it greatly aids digestion and thins out and clings to things because it is a fatty moisture? Rue <note>original: "Rutha"</note>, though many other things are more astringent and warming, strengthens the stomach and all the intestines with singular excellence. Beans corrupt the air around them, yet they are harmless if eaten; indeed, by a certain property, they stop "fluxions" <note>drainage or runny discharge</note> from the head. Citrons, or Median apples, rot very quickly from the heat of bread, even though they are less harmed by many things that are far hotter. Madder <note>original: "Rubea tinctorum"; a plant used for red dye</note> held in the hands dyes the urine red. And animals harmful to garden vegetables are kept away by water in which crabs or crawfish have been soaked in the sun for ten days. The younger brother of the King of the French was suffering from a most terrible ulcer of prodigious foulness; he was cured by the constant breath of a boy in his twelfth year. This is not without reason: for the spirit <note>the vital breath or life force</note> from the heart of a youth, being of a firm yet pure age, is sincere and can correct corrupted humors <note>the bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were believed to govern health</note>.

<margin>To fatten people.</margin>

<margin>So a woman might not taste from the dishes.</margin>
<margin>Against difficulty breathing.</margin>
...it is possible. If you mix wheat flour with lizard fat, nitre <note>original: "halinitro"; likely potassium nitrate or native soda</note>, and cumin, hens fattened on this food will make the people who eat them so fat that they might literally burst. From the direction of the oncoming wind, the burnt horn and dung of a water buffalo protects plants and crops from blight <term>rubigine: a fungal disease, often called "rust," that was a major threat to grain harvests</term>, as they say. ## Book Eighteen

<margin>Why sciatic pain is sometimes healed by music.</margin>
<margin>How pigeons are drawn to dovecotes.</margin>
I could report countless things of this kind, whose unknown origin produces wonder—and not only in plants, animals, and men, but as I said, in regions, soil, waters, and even in actions. Sciatic pain <term>Ischiæ dolor: sciatica, or severe pain radiating along the sciatic nerve in the hip and leg</term>, when it is most severe, is very often cured by music. Is it because this pain, since it does not affect a primary organ, is soothed when the spirits are drawn elsewhere for the sake of delight, and thus by habit the mind is turned away from the established heat that causes the pain? Pigeons are attracted by this cake: 60 pounds of maize or sorghum, 6 pounds of cumin, 10 pounds of honey, 1 pound of costus <note>an aromatic plant root used in ancient perfumes and medicines</note>, and 5 pounds of chaste-tree seeds. All are cooked in water until the liquid is gone; then enough of the best fragrant wine is added along with 15 pounds of old mortar <note>original: "cementi uetusti"; aged lime or plaster was often fed to birds to provide grit and minerals</note>. A mound of this is made in the middle of the dovecote; when other pigeons catch the scent, they come to the place, and as they mingle with the local pigeons, once they have visited the place, they are unable to leave, lured by the sweetness of the food.

<margin>The witches’ ointment.</margin>
<margin>The causes of true dreams.</margin>
<margin>What terror in sleep signifies.</margin>
The ointment of the witches <term>lamiarum: "lamia" refers to witches or female night-spirits in folklore</term>, which makes one see wonders—for we are now speaking of those things which are not, but appear to be—consists of the fat of boys (as they say), and the juices of wild celery, aconite <note>wolfsbane, a highly toxic plant</note>, cinquefoil, nightshade, and soot. But nevertheless, they are believed to be sleeping while they see these things; they see theaters, gardens, feasts, decorations, clothes, handsome youths, Kings, magistrates, and likewise demons, ravens, prisons, solitude, and torments. These, therefore, are the causes of violent hallucinations. But true dreams occur when the soul elicits what is useful to it from the forms already stored in the spirits, with the help of a heavenly image. This is directed by the intellect, and thus many things are foreseen by those who are of a clean mind and pure from bodily impediments. These [impediments] include food, drink, humors, and the agitation of body and mind, from which violent and therefore mostly false dreams usually arise. But to be violently terrified in sleep and to wake up frightened undoubtedly signifies death, or a serious disease, exile, or torments, or the loss of a dear person. If, however, the fear ceases before one wakes, or just as one is waking, it may be that the person is only in danger of these things.

<margin>Whether there is power in sorcery.</margin>
There is a greater doubt regarding sorceries which are performed, so to speak, without "bait" <note>referring to magic that works at a distance without physical consumption or contact</note>. There was among certain peoples a sacrifice to the demon Moloch, by which, when a King had sacrificed his own son on the city walls, he prevented the Jews from taking the city. Among the Romans, there were the *Hysteropotmoi* <term>Hysteropotmoi: Greek for "those for whom a funeral was held while they were still alive"; literally "those later-born"</term>, that is, those undergoing the fate of those being born from the womb...

<margin>The diamond-hard collar.</margin>
...since sacred rites were performed for them as if they were dead, to the ancestral spirits <note>original: "dijs manibus"; the Manes were the spirits of the deceased in Roman religion</note> while they were away. Unless they entered the house through the roof tiles, they were believed to be finished with life; Plutarch is a witness to this matter in his *Roman Questions*. The same author reports that Ateius, a tribune of the plebs, poured out devotions and dire prayers to the spirits of the underworld against Marcus Crassus <note>Crassus was a Roman general whose disastrous defeat by the Parthians was famously attributed to these curses</note>. Among Christians, in place of those things which are believed to have destroyed Crassus, there are the "Commandments of the Valley of Josaphat," <note>referring to a medieval legal or religious custom involving public bans or excommunications</note> by which people are publicly interdicted, and those who are guilty are thought to be driven to death within a year—specifically those who deny debts or cannot be compelled by the power of the law. These things happen in the territory of Bergamo, as I understand it. Others have sought help not from the gods above, but from artifice; for example, one who fastens a collar made of diamond-hard steel around a debtor's neck, which can be removed by no one except the person who put it on. Two years ago, Zaffarono died by that fraud, having been outwitted by a creditor from Vicenza, when he had fastened it more tightly than he had intended.

<margin>Excellent examples of prophecies from entrails.</margin>
<margin>Artephius’s book on the types of divination.</margin>
But I return to sorcery. Some, after lighting a wax candle in the house of an enemy and moving it into the nearest temple, use dire imprecations; it was believed that our nobleman Gaspare Vimercati <note>a prominent 15th-century Milanese condottiero and statesman</note> once perished by this art. I will say what I think about these things. Fear or hope in the person toward whom it is directed contributes much to the power of sorcery, as does the constancy of faith in the one who performs or carries it out, and then if anything at all besides words is added: chance and fortune. Finally, there is a certain hidden quality which is proper to each individual, not only to the species, but even to this or that specific man. Indeed, I find in Arrian, a trustworthy historian, in the seventh book of the *Campaigns of Alexander*, that before Alexander departed this life, Pythagoras (the brother of Apollodorus) had sacrificed a liver and found it was without a "head" <term>sine capite: in hepatoscopy (divination by liver), the "head" or *caput extorum* was a specific lobe; its absence was considered a fatal omen</term>. The same thing had happened to him while sacrificing for Hephaestion, and later for Perdiccas and Antigonus; and to others for Cimon—the deaths of all of whom followed immediately. Even more marvelous is what they say about the heart at the death of Caesar the Dictator <note>referring to the legend that Julius Caesar sacrificed an animal that was found to have no heart</note>. Arrian also reports that the Chaldeans warned Alexander not to enter Babylon, because it would be fatal to him. When he had entered, he immediately left and inspected the Pallacopas canal of the Euphrates. There are those, however, who say that they fabricated this prophecy by fraud because they were guilty of embezzling a non-negligible amount of money. I find that Artephius wrote much about the types of divination, all of which I have transferred to my books *On the Variety of Things*.

<margin>A method for writing whatever you wish inside an egg.</margin>
Tricks that are not trivial are also performed in this category: such as those who write whatever they wish inside an egg, because the shell is porous and admits colors. Grind oak galls with alum and mix them with vinegar; then write what you wish on the shell with this liquid. Once dried, place it in brine; or, smear the egg with wax and write the letters with a stylus so that the wax is opened and the markings remain. Apply the liquid into these marks, and cook the dry egg until it hardens. Then soak it in sharp vinegar, for in this way the letters become penetrable, and you will see them on the egg when the shell is removed. For the vinegar softens the shell...
