These are of three kinds: some are seen in sleep, some in ecstasy <note>a state of trance or heightened spiritual awareness</note>, and some in pure wakefulness. I will provide examples of these. I was advised more than once in sleep to write this book, which appeared to me to be divided into twenty-one parts. The treatises were varied, and near the middle were a few geometric matters. Perhaps these things will eventually change for the better, or they appear the same as if in mirrors,

The cause is that operations are completed without the labor of the body, and therefore most promptly; however, the judgment of time is taken from the estimation of bodily labor by the reason, which is hindered during sleep. ## On Wonders.

...those who are awake do not extend the time, since they recognize they have not truly passed through these things, but have only conceived them in the mind, which can quickly accomplish all such things.

<margin>What time is, and five most beautiful inquiries about it.</margin>
Conversely, time is contracted in sleep when we either do not dream or dream of few things without motion; for motion is the measure of time. But what is time? Although nothing of it ever "is" <note>a philosophical point that the past is gone and the future is not yet, so time never truly exists in the present moment</note>, yet all things are within it, and it always assists all things. It generates all things and kills them—the author of life and death. And just as the expectation of it is longest, so the memory of it is always shortest. Even though it always accompanies us, we never recognize it. Nor, though there is such a great abundance of it, is any restoration granted: whence it happens that there is no greater or more worthless loss than that of time. It benefited me not a little to have known these things, but some of these apply to time itself, while others apply to those things most closely joined to it. For to proceed so far with something that never "is" is a thing truly worthy of wonder. Therefore, we do not grasp time itself, but that which happens in it, has been done, and remains. Time truly by itself is unknown to the senses, for it consists of the imagination which is known by us. Therefore, wonders are related not only in dreams but also in wakefulness. And this indeed is of three types: the other is intermediate, such as in ecstasy <note>a state of trance or being "outside oneself"</note>.

<margin>A wonderful story of Andreas Osiander.</margin>
It once happened to Andreas Osiander <note>1498–1552, a prominent German Protestant theologian and mathematician</note>—a man most learned in every kind of language, a theologian of Nuremberg, and our friend, as he once indicated to us via a letter—that when he was a youth and suffering from a quartan fever <note>a form of malaria where the fever returns every four days</note>, at the time of the fever's onset, he seemed to be in a forest and pursued by wild beasts and serpents of various kinds. This was most bitter for him, and he could not be persuaded by anyone that he was either in his house or that he was imagining these things falsely. But when his father approached, he was immediately restored to his former state of mind and recognized his house, his bedroom, and the friends assisting him without any fear. But when his father left, that vision was observed again before his eyes, and all the images returned; and this evil persevered as long as the fever, which afflicted him for a long time.

<margin>From where the illusions of hermits come.</margin>
I consider these things entirely similar to those that were seen by those inhabiting the desert <note>referring to the "Desert Fathers," early Christian monks known for their visions</note> in the past for the most part; for I do not deny that certain things are sent to holy men by God or demons, all of which they then attributed to demons or God. For as these things happen to many others, it is not permitted to transfer them solely to God or demons—especially since they say they <note>demons or spiritual forces</note> can represent through imagination all the things they wish even against our will—nor would I believe that so many honest men, who devoted their whole lives to such harsh labors and solitude, lied for such a small reason. But solitude itself and a mind sick from labors and fasting, and a physical temperament changed by rustic foods, could represent what the melancholic humor <note>in ancient medicine, "black bile," believed to cause depression and hallucinations when in excess</note> was capable of in that state.

<margin>The author's wonderful story.</margin>
The second kind of wakefulness is that in which only the mental operation is harmed, yet the power of the soul remains; of which sort I think was what I remember happened to me for a continuous three-year period. It was from the fourth to the seventh year [of my life], for from the hour of...

# Eighteenth Book

<page-num>358</page-num>

...at the time from the second to the fourth hour <note>Cardano is likely referring to the hours after sunrise</note>, or if I happened to wake up later, I saw images at the foot of my bed. They seemed to be composed of small rings of brass, appearing as trees, wild beasts, men, cities, battle lines drawn up for war, military and musical instruments, and other things of this kind, all ascending and descending in turns, one after another. Since I was a small boy and found great delight in these things, I watched them intently. Eventually, my mother Clara and my aunt Margaret asked me quite seriously if I saw anything. But even though I was a small child, I was not unaware that this was a kind of omen <note>original: "ostentum"</note>. For that reason, I constantly denied seeing anything, fearing that if I revealed the secret, the vision would abandon me, or some evil would happen to me for disclosing a mystery. I believe that what Aristotle recounts should be placed in this same category: that some people, because they had seen others hanged, fainted in their own minds. <margin>Aristotle, Problems, Book 7, Problem 5.</margin>

Therefore, to return to the matter: when these visions ceased after seven years had passed and we had moved to a different house, I believe the cause was that which Averroes <note>a famous 12th-century Andalusian philosopher and commentator on Aristotle</note> very beautifully explained in his *Collectanea*. When the "spirit" <note>technical term for a subtle fluid then believed to travel through nerves to convey sensation</note> serving the imagination has received forms while imagining—whether of a sound, or some quality recognized by smell or touch, or even of a dead person or a demon—and, imbued with these forms, that spirit is transferred to the sense that corresponds to that action... <margin>The dead and demons can be seen naturally, and in what manner.</margin> ...in the case of smells, it goes to the organ of smell; in hearing, to the ears; in visions, to the eyes. The person will necessarily smell, hear, or see, even with no physical object present. For if vision is nothing other than the perception of a "species" <note>technical term: the "sensible form" or mental image of an object</note> existing from the spirit within the crystalline lens of the eye, it follows that whether that species is cast off by a physical object or not, whenever this occurs, the person truly sees. And so, while awake, it happens that one hears the voices of demons and the dead, or even of people they know, and feels smells or touches, as occurs with succubi and incubi. However, these things are seen more rarely than they are heard or touched, because for the other senses it is enough to observe a single quality; a single spirit transferred to the sense with that image can report it. In the eyes, however, many qualities are necessary—size, shape, color—and thus it is necessary for more spirits to be transferred. For this reason, nature made the nerves that lead to the eye hollow, and they are the only ones of this kind, because they require far more spirits for their operations. This is also why we are much more fatigued by looking intently than by exercising any of the other senses.

<margin>To see the dead during delirium in the sick signifies imminent death.</margin> From these things, therefore, it is apparent why it is a fatal sign for the sick if they see the dead while they are delirious. For it indicates that the imagination is so powerful that the spirit retains the species it conceived from the imagination even when transferred to the eye. But this cannot happen except during sleep when the senses are quiet, or because of a disease when the senses are too weakened, or because of a very robust thought and power of imagining. Since, therefore, these sick people are neither sleeping nor able to imagine intently due to their weakness, we must conclude the only remaining possibility: that the entire sensing faculty now lies idle because of their extreme feebleness; this, however...

...source, that same man taught elsewhere that a present death is signified by this judgment, saying: when a sick person neither sees nor hears because their strength is failing, death is already near. There is also another argument for the present narrative: that brave men rarely or never see specters <term>spectra; ghosts or apparitions</term>, because they, out of fear, are the least likely to imagine such trembling things. For fear is accustomed, above all other emotions, to produce firm images within us; love follows next. Thus, these "privileges" belong first to those who are afraid, and afterwards to those who are in love. Yet, cannibals <note>original: "anthropophagi"</note>, who are the bravest of men, see nocturnal monsters. This is a fault of the regions and of empty credulity, since others there who abstain from harming men also see such things. Truly the Scythians <note>an ancient nomadic people of central Eurasia</note>, among whom killing men is a sacrifice, although they are brave by nature and by their customs, see neither the dead nor spirits of the dead <term>lemures; malevolent spirits of those who died prematurely or violently</term>. Likewise, neither do thieves. For these evils do not seem to be such by nature—since some fish eat others of their own kind, as do mice and other animals—but rather by the law of nations. For even if these evils were established by nature—that is, against the laws of nature—since nothing remains after death except the intellect, and the intellect cannot initiate physical motion, the dead would not be able to show any images, nor strike terror into the living.

<margin>What an echo is.</margin>
The third kind of waking state is pure and sincere, in which, however, it happens that one sees wonders in many ways: such as when an echo resounds. When it is particularly manifold, it sometimes happens that it returns voices seven times. At night this is marvelous in a wonderful way, and unless it were a common thing, it could terrify anyone, so clearly and slowly does it sometimes return the voices. The cause is the air which is struck back from flat and hollow places; for it does not resound unless there are caves or walls. It resounds from ancient places, and more from a distance than from nearby. It is necessary for the voice to be struck out in an echo and reflected by an intermediate plane. It is very often manifold; we ourselves have heard a triple one.

The ancients did not only know examples of a manifold voice or one returned seven times; indeed in Pavia <note>original: "Papia," the city in Italy</note>, once called Ticinum, there is a great basilica—the Italians call it the "Sala" <note>the Great Hall</note>—which, near the city's citadel, returns voices from its entrance so many times that you cannot count them. Sometimes a thirteenth voice is heard. Many witnesses were present, and among others, an excellent professor of the medical art, Melchior Malheuser, a German and our pupil. You would have believed someone was answering or mocking you. The voices die away gradually and cease; from this, it is wonderfully reflected as "Alas" <note>original: "Ahime," which sounds like the Latin "heu"</note>, like the voice of one dying and failing. This building is square, and is illuminated from the sides in the upper part by many open windows. Furthermore, the front and the wall positioned opposite are solid, except that the door is in the front; the length is about one hundred feet, the width nearly twenty-five. The voice also resounds manifold if you stand near the other wall opposite the door. It seems then to be returned from the high part of the door. And so from each side...

# Book Eighteen

...to the side, and especially for those standing outside the door itself, the voice resonates; in the middle, it does not resonate at all. Hence, no one can doubt that it is either a Demon or some trickery <note>original: "sycophantiam"</note>. For it can hardly be believed to be a mere echo, so clearly, so easily, so often, and in such a certain order are all the voices heard. The height, I believe, is greater than the width by half; for this basilica is very high. I chose to describe it in this way so that people might know where it is appropriate to experience such things, or if they wish to build another example. I learned from those standing by that formerly, in front of the door, an arched porch <note>likely a portico or narthex</note> was positioned opposite, a large part of which still remains. And the usual voices were returned much better to those standing outside the door under the arch—much more richly and with a "greater interest" <note>the author uses the financial metaphor "foenore" to describe the increased return of sound</note>, so that they sometimes resonated thirty times. It is certain that the faster the voice is brought forth, and with greater agitation, the more clearly and frequently it is returned.

<margin>The pupils of cats are not exactly round.</margin>
In this way, other things also deceive us, such as the pupil of a cat, which is seen sometimes in the shape of a boat <term>nauicularis; boat-shaped</term>, sometimes in the shape of a half-moon, and at other times in an even narrower form. This happens because this animal contracts and extends its uvea <term>uueam; the pigmented layer of the eye</term> at will, and the corneal tunic in the cat is very thick. For this reason, especially if you look at it from the side, it appears multiform; but straight on and from the front, it is rounder as it is in us—although there are those who dare to assert (as I have testified elsewhere) that not only in these animals, but also in humans, the pupils grow or shrink according to the light of the Moon. But this has very little to do with actual roundness. Therefore, since many things deceive our senses, they seem "wonderful" or miraculous to us. Thus, they say that the Blessed Anthony <note>referring to St. Anthony the Great, the desert hermit</note> rightly said that those who possess sound senses do not need the type of erudition that comes from books.

<margin>Those with sound senses do not need letters.</margin>
By "senses," he meant not only these internal ones, but the mind itself, memory, and reason. Therefore, it should not seem surprising if fear and circumstance show many things to those walking at night: namely, fires in the sky, falling stars, chasms, dancing flames, shadows, specters <term>spectra; ghostly apparitions</term>, disordered noises, wailings, wild beasts, serpents, robbers, thieves, corpses, spirits <term>lemures; restless ghosts of the dead</term>, masks <term>laruas; malevolent spirits or ghouls</term>, murmurs, the groans of the tormented, rabid dogs, and—as I said—terrors without a manifest cause. Yet these things by no means demonstrate that these experiences are actually Demons themselves.

<summary>The author explains how natural phenomena, such as the complex acoustics of a high basilica and the shifting shape of a cat's pupil, can be mistaken for the supernatural. He concludes that many "ghostly" sightings are actually the result of sensory deception combined with nighttime fear.</summary>

# BOOK XIX
## On Demons.

<margin>The distinction between divine inspiration and the arrival of Demons.</margin>
**T**HEREFORE, there has always been no small debate concerning Demons: and as it seems to me, those who believe they exist and interact with us distinguish their arrival from divine inspiration and angelic encounters in this way. For since the human soul naturally recoils from Demons, the mind itself is disturbed by their presence; it shudders and fears something, though it does not yet know what it is. Evil thoughts and a tendency toward wicked actions usually creep in, or the very snares we are preparing. They also produce or leave behind foul odors and discordant sounds; a sense of suspicion or despair remains after their departure, as is read concerning the guardian spirit <note>original: "genio"</note> of Brutus. But divine inspiration—or should some angel encounter a person—offers itself only to those of a good mind, and approaches gradually without any noise, gladdens the soul, and provides confidence and the best hope. The mind, then peaceful, is carried toward the highest thoughts and is even compelled to love heavenly things. It delights in celestial matters and approaches one who is already meditating on good and soul-saving things. If the soul should be startled by a sudden arrival, it immediately finds rest. These things, indeed, **Saint Anthony** <note>Blessed Anthony the Great (c. 251–356), a Desert Father famous for his discernment of spirits and battles with demons</note>—who was marvelous in this regard—has taught us. For us, this same distinction between deadly and life-giving premonitions of the soul will remain unshaken, even if we were to contend that these things happen solely by the force of nature. For if beneficial and hostile stars are substituted for angels and demons, the same reasoning and the same signs will apply to both. Therefore, many attempt to show that Demons exist by the evidence of incantations. They say that a silver ring—one of which I have seen—if you fashion it <margin>An incantation for the falling sickness</margin> with the following inscribed inside: **+ Dabi + Habi + Haber + Hebr +**, will, when placed on the finger, prevent those suffering from the falling sickness <term>comitiali morbo; epilepsy</term> from collapsing. I have seen a written charm <term>chirographum; a hand-written amulet</term> hung to relieve a headache, as you see to the side, when the patient, who felt no protection from medicine, had thrice recited the "Lord’s Prayer" as they call it.

<margin>An incantation for a headache.</margin>
( Milat ) ( $\ddagger$ ) ( Vitalot )
( Vah )

But let us set these things aside and recount a miracle we saw last year. A woman of patrician birth was suffering from a burning of the urine and a perpetual desire to void it. When all the most distinguished physicians of our city—no fewer than seven—as well as outsiders and several surgeons had been called, I too was present. We could not sufficiently agree among ourselves on the cause of the disease; one thought it a stone, another an erysipelas <note>a bacterial skin infection, often called "St. Anthony's Fire"</note>, others an ulcer, a scirrhus <term>scirrhum; a hard, cancerous tumor</term>, a cancer, a phlegmon <term>phlegmonem; a localized area of acute inflammation</term>, or a bladder condition.

# Book Nineteen

...nothing of these things was effective, nor when remedies were attempted for each symptom individually did anything help. And when the vesicles <note>referring here to anatomical structures or possibly blisters raised by treatment</note> were incised after being stimulated by hot poultices, in addition to the usual sleeplessness and torture, an involuntary leakage of urine occurred because of the incision. From there, she suffered two convulsions, accompanied by a collapse of her pulse and her vital strength. Thus, having been tortured <note>original: "excarnificata," literally meaning to have the flesh stripped away or to be tormented as if by an executioner</note> for seven continuous months by both the disease and the remedies, and with her health completely despaired of, she was abandoned by everyone. 

For there was no danger that she was faking the illness, she who had swallowed so many bitter medicines, endured so many poultices and fumigations, and who allowed that place to be inspected by so many doctors with a speculum <note>a medical instrument for dilating and inspecting bodily orifices</note>, and who tolerated starvation for so long. Finally, she had even submitted to bloodletting, the cutting of the vesicles, caustic medicines, the blade, and fires <note>referring to cauterization, the burning of tissue with hot irons</note>. 

Therefore, when we were weary and uncertain, we finally came to our own opinion, which—as it later seemed—was the most absurd of all. This was based chiefly on the argument that the disease grew worse regardless of what remedies were applied. By now, the pain in the place where the neck of the bladder joins the neck of the uterus was constant; now there was extreme wasting of the whole body; and the **Hippocratic face** <note>a pinched, hollow facial expression traditionally seen as a sign of approaching death, first described by Hippocrates</note> and involuntary flow of urine, along with perpetual sleeplessness, had set in. Ulcers were now everywhere around that area, caused partly by the heat and sharpness of the medicines, and partly by the rough handling of the surgical instruments. Nevertheless, the burning of the urine not only remained but increased, along with such a constant urge to urinate that some believed there was a stone in the bladder. But an examination with a catheter <note>a thin tube inserted into the bladder to check for obstructions like stones</note> rejected that opinion.

Therefore, when the woman's case was completely despaired of, there arrived **Joseph Niger** <note>Giuseppe Nero, a contemporary scholar</note>, an excellent professor of Greek literature who taught publicly, but who was nevertheless entirely ignorant of medicine. They considered this man to be a sorcerer <note>original: "praecantator," one who uses incantations</note> and highly skilled in the arts of witches. This woman had a ten-year-old son, whom Joseph instructed to say that he saw three foul Demons standing before his mother in a **triangular crystal** which he had brought with him. Then, after whispering other words into the boy’s ear, the boy affirmed that he saw another Demon, a horseman much taller than the first ones, carrying a trident; this one bound those three foot-soldiers one by one and, having tied them with chains to his saddle-cloths, led them all away. Then he ordered the crystal to be put away. 

Why should I delay? The woman, persuaded by this trick, slept. The pain ceased, as did the burning and the urge to urinate; her vivid color returned, her flesh returned, and after this she even conceived a child and was perfectly restored to health. I have as many witnesses to this matter as there were friends of the man or the woman, and all the doctors who were summoned; and the fact itself can be seen by everyone, since she was then at death's door but is now healthy.

Therefore, the woman was healed either by a Demon, or by **imagination and faith**—since it is by no means possible to find a third cause besides these. For if the boy was reporting the truth, while Joseph concealed the reality for fear of the law, then she was healed by a Demon. But if the boy was persuaded by Joseph with a single word to affirm that he saw whatever Joseph asked him, and he devised this trick for the sake of the mother's health, then it is manifest that she recovered through imagination and faith. It is a wonder...

He concludes the recovery was likely driven by the psychological power of faith and imagination rather than actual supernatural intervention.</summary>

confirm this opinion by Plutarch <note>A Greek-Roman philosopher and biographer (c. 46 – 120 AD)</note> at the beginning of the *Life of Cimon*, concerning Damon; likewise concerning Pausanias and Cleonice, the Byzantine maiden whom he had accidentally killed after loving her; then by Pliny in the seventh book of his *Epistles*, concerning the phantom that was seen perpetually in a house at Athens <note>This refers to Pliny the Younger's famous story of a haunted house and the philosopher Athenodorus</note>; also concerning boys whose hair was cut off without any visible perpetrator. <margin>The marvelous story of the seven demons.</margin>
But I will here set down a story more admirable than all these histories, which I have heard not once nor a few times from my father, Facio Cardano, who used to confess that he had a familiar Demon <note>In this context, a "familiar" is a spirit companion or guiding intellect, similar to the "Daimon" of Socrates</note> for nearly thirty years. Finally, when I searched his writings—as I had often heard the story—I found it committed to writing and memory in this way: "On the Ides of August, 1491 <note>August 13, 1491</note>, when I had finished my sacred rites, at the 20th hour of the day <note>Using the Italian system of the time, this would be late afternoon, approximately four hours before sunset</note>, seven men appeared in the usual manner. They were dressed in silk garments, with cloaks in the Greek style, and what appeared to be purple boots. Beneath their cloaks were shining red tunics, which seemed to be made of crimson cloth. Their stature was more majestic than is common, and quite conspicuous. Yet not all were dressed the same way, but two of them were clearly of higher rank than the others; for one of those, who was taller and of a ruddy complexion, was followed by two companions; the other, who was paler and smaller of body, was followed by three others. Thus there were seven in total. He did not record whether they had anything upon their heads or if they were bare. Their age was near the fortieth year, yet they appeared no older than thirty. When they were asked who they were, they responded that they were men, as if made of air, who themselves were born and died; yet their life was much longer than ours, as it extended to 300 years. When my father asked about the immortality of our soul, they affirmed that nothing survived that was unique to the individual. They said they themselves were much more closely joined to the gods <note>original: "diuis," referring to divine beings or lesser deities</note> than the human race, but nevertheless were distant from them by an almost infinite interval. They claimed they are no more blessed or miserable than we are, just as we are compared to beasts. Nothing of hidden things remains secret to them, such as books or money, and the lowest dregs <note>The Latin text here breaks off at 'colluuiem', continuing on the next page</note> of them are the guardian spirits of the most noble men, just as the most lowly men..."

# Book Nineteen

...like the trainers of noble dogs or horses. And since they themselves possessed very thin bodies, they could bring us no benefit or harm except for apparitions and terrors, or perhaps knowledge. There were others who had smaller bodies: three hundred disciples in one group and two hundred in another in a public academy. For both of these groups taught publicly. When my father asked why, if they knew of treasures, they did not reveal them to others, they replied that it was decreed by a private law under the greatest penalties that no one should communicate this to men. They remained with him for more than three hours; meanwhile, at his request, they debated the cause of the world. The one who was taller denied that God had produced the world from eternity; the other, on the contrary, asserted that God creates the world through every individual moment in such a way that if He should cease even for a moment, the world itself would immediately perish. To this, my father himself brought forward certain arguments from the disputations of Averroes <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd, 1126–1198) was a medieval Andalusian polymath whose commentaries on Aristotle were highly influential and controversial in the Renaissance</note>, even though that book had not yet been discovered. He [the spirit] also mentioned the names of certain books, part of which have been found and part of which are still hidden. And yet all of these belonged to Averroes; indeed, that spirit openly professed himself to be an Averroist <note>original: "Auerroistam," a follower of Averroes' philosophy, which often emphasized the eternity of the world and a single universal intellect</note>. Whether this be history or a fable, so it happened. That it might seem a fable should be argued well enough by the fact that these decrees do not sufficiently agree with religion, and that my father, with his demons, was in no way happier, richer, or better known to men than I, who have never seen demons. To this, however, he would reply that he had predicted many things which could not have been known so long in advance without the help of demons—such as that Caesar would eventually be superior in Italy, which scarcely happened until thirty years later. He said that demons are liars, according to the word of truth: "he is the father of lies" <note>original: "pater mendacij," a reference to John 8:44</note>. He claimed he cared very little for riches or honors, things for which I am more eager; that he was born to a humble fortune and his early beginnings had hindered him. Finally, he suggested that perhaps my genius <note>original: "genium," referring to a personal protective spirit or guiding force</note> was greater than others, even though they do not show themselves to those people nor to me; nevertheless, a personal spirit is not lacking to anyone for help according to their opportunity. His own spirit had manifested to him and not others to others, either because it was expedient that way, or because he was better and of a purer mind—for he was indeed very good and most religious—or perhaps because he used a conjuration which it is well known he obtained from a dying Spaniard.

There are, again, other arguments for demons: the responses of oracles, such as that of Theophrastus <note>A Greek philosopher and successor to Aristotle</note> concerning the wild olive tree of Megara. These things have been mentioned elsewhere, regarding which Aristotle and Plutarch labored not a little to provide a cause.

<margin>The Telchines demons.</margin>
The Telchines <term>Telchines: In classical mythology, these were original inhabitants of Rhodes known as skilled metalworkers and sorcerers; Cardano here classifies them as dangerous subterranean spirits.</term> also seem to be subterranean demons who crush those digging in ruins or strangle them with a certain fiery spirit <note>This likely refers to "firedamp" or "chokedamp," the toxic or explosive gases encountered by miners, which Cardano interprets as the work of spirits</note>. But many have doubted whether oracles were produced through the fraud of priests; others wish there to be a certain property of that particular earth by which a disease, as it were, is contracted. Indeed, ecstasy <note>original: "ecstasis," a state of being "outside oneself" or in a trance</note> is a kind of disease, and an oracle does not occur without ecstasy, though not every ecstasy produces an oracle. Therefore, there is great doubt concerning these things. Truly, as for the Telchines, we can also blame the nature of the stones, which are either too fragile or abound with a corrupt spirit...

# On Daemons.

...we can say [of places] burning with an abundance of sulfur and bitumen. What moves us more is that since the air and ether are of such great magnitude, and that region is so pleasant, and we see that the earth has its own living creatures, metals, stones, plants, and the water has its fish, it then seems likely that this lowest air, which animals breathe, would not be entirely devoid of such a vast mass of life. Rather, it should be believed that animals <note>Cardano uses 'animalia' here in the broad sense of 'living beings' or 'animated creatures'</note> are there, which are as much more excellent than these lower ones as that region is clearer and purer than this lower one. For since we see this observed by nature in the other elements, as I have said—and not only in the elements but also in the heavens—we must believe that this entire machinery of the higher air is full of these beings, whom we call **Daemons** <note>original: 'Dæmonas'; the term here refers to spirits that occupy the space between gods and humans, often associated with secret knowledge</note> as if they were "wise ones."

<margin>Authors who have written about Daemons.</margin>
<margin>Arguments suggesting that Daemons do not exist.</margin>
I would not wish to follow these matters to the point of absolute precision, as did **Porphyry**, **Psellus**, **Plotinus**, **Proclus**, and **Iamblichus** <note>These were influential Neoplatonic and Byzantine philosophers who developed complex hierarchies of spirits and demons</note>, who wrote copiously about things they did not see, as if they were writing a natural history. I am a philosopher, adhering as much as possible to the teachings of the **Peripatetics** <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle; they generally preferred physical and logical explanations over supernatural ones</note>. These, however, do not admit the existence of Daemons; nor is the opinion probable that grants them a place in such a vast mass. For if they were here, they would be seen like birds, and far more frequently; yet in an entire province, a trace of them hardly appears once in many years. Even **Princes**, whose fortune suggests they should be the wisest of mortals, despise these and similar things. Another point moves many: if they recognize these beings as "intelligences," they would be both mortal and immortal at the same time, which is impossible. If they are not: what prevents them from destroying the human race, since they are invisible and subject to no one's command?

<margin>Whether the dead or the living are happier.</margin>
<margin>All those who die are alone.</margin>
<margin>A virtuous man is most like the gods.</margin>
The same question applies to dead men: are they happier than the living? It has been wisely answered that neither is superior to the other; for while the dead cannot be unhappy, the living can be happy. The condition of the dying is worse: for they are all alone, even if they are Kings and fall alongside many others. For each person dies for himself alone, and seems to die alone. Truly, solitude joined with sharp pain is the heaviest and most intolerable thing. For *it is a comfort to the wretched to have companions in their suffering* <note>original: 'solatiũ est miseris socios habere poenarũ'; a common Latin sentiment expressing that shared misery is easier to bear</note>. But he who dies, even if he dies with a thousand others, cannot have a companion. Therefore, there is then a most wretched emptiness and solitude. Thus, for the living, the greatest pleasure is found in society. Those are said to live who live according to virtue, and they live forever. A wicked man lives in no kind of life; the gods <note>original: 'Diui'; can refer to divine beings or the departed spirits of the virtuous</note> live in both; the virtuous man in one. Because of this, the virtuous man—if such a thing exists—is the only one who can be happy, and he is the closest to the gods themselves among all mortals, and most like them. In this, a virtuous **Prince** is even more blessed, for he is compared to God.

<summary>Cardano debates whether the upper atmosphere is populated by "wise" daemons, contrasting the mystical views of Neoplatonists with Aristotelian skepticism, before reflecting on the existential solitude of death and the divine nature of human virtue.</summary>

# BOOK XX
## On Angels or Intelligences.

<margin>As blows are swifter, they wear things down more.</margin>
**T**HEREFORE, the life of the Divine Beings is happy, secure, and eternal; for men, life is short, unhappy, and full of suspicion and fear, which causes them to be held back from many noble works. Time, however, grinds down what it moves, and the more tightly it grips, the more it wears it away. Whence blows <note>The author uses 'ictus' (blows/strikes) as a metaphor for the rapid passage of time or sudden events that damage mortal things</note>, as they are swifter, so they bring greater harm. Nor does anything seem sadder to mortals than the narrowness of time: it urges, hinders, terrifies, drives one headlong, and makes works incomplete. In the Divine Beings themselves, however, there is nothing to cause them anguish; rather, they pass through all things in a certain equal happiness.

<margin>What the life of the intelligences is like.</margin>
Moreover, an intellect is more long-lasting the more refined <note>original: 'tenuior', meaning subtle or non-material</note> it is: for it is closer to the First Cause the more it is endowed with a refined substance. Every intellect—even if it enjoys eternal rest, happy security, complete beatitude, immense and eternal light, and a clarity so great that a human could not imagine even a thousandth part of it (or if he could comprehend it, he could not sustain it for a moment)—[is vital to the cosmos]. And since the Sun shines by an intellect, which is to it like a soul, if that intellect could depart from it, the Sun would shine no differently than the earth.

<margin>A demonstration showing the clarity of the intelligences.</margin>
Since, therefore, our own eye shines so little with the light of our soul, what shall we say of the splendor of those intelligences, by whose clarity the Moon shines, and from there the other stars, and much more so the Sun? On this account, some think that Michael <note>The Archangel Michael</note> was called the "Intelligence of the Sun," derived from *mico* <note>Latin: "to sparkle" or "to shine forth"</note>, which means "to shine through." But "Michael" is not a Latin word, nor is it composed from *mico*, as they [the words] admit a middle aspiration <note>The author is pointing out that the Hebrew 'ch' sound in Michael (Mikha'el) does not fit the Latin etymology of 'mico'</note>.

<margin>The orders of the intelligences.</margin>
These beings, therefore, Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A late-antique theologian whose 'Celestial Hierarchy' defined the nine ranks of angels for the medieval world</note> arranged into nine Hierarchies: **Angels, Archangels, Thrones, Dominions, Virtues, Principalities, Powers, Cherubim,** and **Seraphim**. These names the Church celebrates in the solemnities of the Mass. Each of these is further distant from the next than the human intellect is from the last of them; yet none of them lacks anything in perfection, because they are placed in different categories. Even the greatest of those beings can comprehend the clarity of God much less than our intellect can comprehend theirs. For Divinity itself recedes by an infinite interval (even from the first intellect itself). This alone is the difference: our intellect is only an indistinct image of the true intellects, but not a true intellect. For as there is a greater difference between the strongest and the weakest horse than between the weakest and a painted one—because the strongest surpasses the weakest by far more than double, and yet each is a true horse, while the painted one is not one at all—so if a painted horse were compared to our intellect, the weakest horse to the lowest intelligence, and the strongest horse to that which is next in order...

<margin>Our intellect is shadowy.</margin>
...you will clearly understand that our intellect is only a certain shadow of the true intellect. For our intellect here, since it receives [knowledge] from the image of things themselves...

It introduces the traditional nine-fold angelic hierarchy of Dionysius the Areopagite and uses the analogy of a painted horse to explain the vast ontological gap between human and angelic intellects.</summary>

# BOOK XX
## On Angels or Intelligences.

...[knowledge] of a certain kind, it remains full of obscurity, error, and doubt. Nor does it always—indeed, not even for long—persist in its work. But those supreme beings, clear, certain, pure <note>original: 'sinceri'</note>, and perpetual, remain assidiously in their blessed work.

Perhaps someone will doubt how, among them, one can be more perfect than another? It should be said no differently than regarding one who knows that the number six <term>senarius; a perfect number whose divisors 1, 2, and 3 sum to 6</term> is perfect without needing a demonstration. This indeed reflects our intellect, for it knows obscurely and doubts, and holds only a shadow of things. Therefore, just as the senses of beasts—which perceive only the outer bark—are to human senses, which reach the marrow, so is our intellect compared to true intellects. Again, imagine one who understands through demonstration that six is a perfect number; since nothing is lacking for his exquisite knowledge, the name "perfect" fits him. Yet, more perfect still is he who has attained it by demonstration, and being led into himself, completes it within himself above the tens <note>This refers to a higher level of mathematical or mystical comprehension beyond basic decimal counting</note>. But he who, beyond these things, having divided the cubes, leaves through them the numbers of their sides, this man is even more excellent than the second. He is also better who knows by demonstration that if the multiples of six are arranged from unity and joined in order, the numbers which are produced, if joined again in the same order, always produce cubic numbers. Therefore, it is manifest enough that our intellect is weak; however, we have not yet said why. But God could not have made it better—not because he lacked the power, but because he judged it better for it to be such as it is.

<margin>The gifts and names of the Intelligence.</margin>
Therefore, so that we may know the nature of these intellects, it will be necessary to know the powers of the bodies which are governed by them. The **Moon**, therefore, governs the elements and the bodies of living things. Over this, the **Angels**—that is, the messengers—preside. **Gabriel** is their prince, that is, the "Strength of God." For by the light of the Moon, all things are brought down to us from heaven, and she is most robust in life. **Mercury** presides over the intellect and all senses; the **Virtues** are over Mercury; over the Virtues is **Raphael**, that is, the "Medicine of God." For the medicine of mortals is sense combined with intellect, through which the virtues in us are acquired. **Venus** is the mother of pleasure and delight, and joins us for the procreation of offspring. The **Dominations** are placed over her, for they have the power of guarding the species of individual things. But guardianship is perfected by generation, generation by coitus, and coitus by love. The highest among the Dominations who presides over Venus is called **Anael**, that is, the "Grace of God." For it is the grace of God to love and be loved, to be joined to the fruitful, and to procreate offspring, as well as beauty itself and pleasantness. Order, the life of all things, is given to the **Sun**; the order of **Archangels**—that is, the "Prince-Messengers"—presides over it; for every power is sent down from the Sun through the Moon. **Michael** is their Prince, that is, "Who is like God?" <note>Michael is the Hebrew name meaning 'Who is like God?'</note> Nor is anything similar to the Sun, whence the Sun [Sol] is also called "Sol" as if it were "alone" [solus]. **Mars** provides boldness; otherwise, we would be in perpetual fear. The **Powers** preside over its orb; for power is joined in fortitude, and fortitude with power. The Prince of the Powers is **Samael**, that is, the "Hearing of God," for power and fortitude are placed in the hearing of God. **Jupiter** is he who mixes and tempers all things, from which come faculties and strengths; his order, the **Principalities**, is established in moderation and temperance...

<header>Book Twenty-One</header>
<meta>catchword: im</meta>

The prince of those <note>referring to the intelligences of the sphere of Jupiter discussed on the previous page</note> is Sachiel, which means the "Rest of God." For it is through temperance and moderation that we attain rest. He is also the author of the tranquility of seasons, of peace, and of happiness. 

But Saturn bestows firmness. He is almost the only one who tempers the moisture and heat of the others, and because of his coldness and dryness, he is believed to be the lord of death and of the dead. The **Thrones** <term>Throni; the third highest order of angels, associated with divine justice and stability</term> guard him, for by him kingdoms are made firm, as are all things that possess longevity. A "Throne" is, after all, a seat; the lord of this order is called Cassiel, which means the "Hope of God," for longevity brings hope and security.

The **Seraphim**—that is, the "burning ones"—rule the eighth sphere <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note>, for those many lights of that orb seem to burn. But the **Cherubim**, meaning the "knowing ones," preside over the first heaven. For who truly knows, if not those who are closest to God and gaze upon Him? 

Truly, it is not easy to grasp the exact number of these intelligences. Since the whole heaven possesses intellect, a vast multitude might not seem necessary. Yet, if there were only a few, it would not seem consistent to have assigned hardships to so many mortals in such a small space, while granting happiness to so few in such a vast expanse. Therefore, we should judge them to be an infinite multitude, not contained under a single order, and certainly not numbering only forty-four. Furthermore, regarding these matters, one should trust only those to whom God has revealed the truth, rather than

# BOOK XXI
## On God and the Universe.

<margin>What an "Aeon" is.</margin>
These beings are not subject to time; nevertheless, one can imagine a space in which they remain, which they call an **Aeon** <term>Aevum; a state of duration between time and eternity, specifically the "time" of angels</term>. This lacks extension and does not flow. Imagine that time is like a circle and the Aeon is its center. Though the circle moves, every part of it is always present to the unmoved center. Thus, time is to the Aeon as an instant is to itself. When compared to time, the Aeon is rightly said to be devoid of division in either direction. I am aware that the word "Aeon" <note>original: 'aeuum'</note> can signify other things in Latin. But this entire realm in which the intelligences exist is necessarily either created 
<margin>In eternal things, "to be" and "to be able" are the same.</margin>
or eternal. In eternal things, that which *is* must necessarily *be*, and that which *is not* cannot *be*. For a mortal nature is no more capable of immortality than an immortal nature is of mortality. 

There is a triple action in the universe: **Change** <note>original: 'Mutatio'</note>, which is from one body to another; 
<margin>What "Influx" is.</margin>
<margin>What "Inspiration" is.</margin>
**Influx**, which proceeds into a body not from another body, but by a hidden reason; and **Inspiration** <note>original: 'Afflatus'</note>, which occurs in the soul and not from the body. In change, that which acts can be corrupted; Influx comes from an immortal body; Inspiration comes from...

# On God and the Universe.

<margin>
God knows all things.
Lots: in what things and by whom.
</margin>
...immortal, nor with a body; and by these three things they differ among themselves. Divine inspiration also teaches, and celestial influence impels; but whether the center of the heavens be the same, or that of an infinite world, belongs to the book on the *Secrets of Eternity* to teach. In this one world, however, if God does not care for each individual thing—since things do not exist except as individuals—then when the individuals perish, the species will also perish. Either, therefore, individuals are sustained by a certain order of the universe, which we call **fate**, or else species could not be restored from **decay** <term>putredine; the process of decomposition from which, in ancient thought, some believed new life could spontaneously generate</term>. Of these views, it is more likely that, because God knows individual things, all things remain within a certain order of the universe, since it is considered absurd among philosophers for a species to perish. Therefore, God knows all things. But where do **lots** <note>original: "sortes"; referring to divination by drawing lots or random chance</note> come from? Are they from Him? Not at all, but sometimes from inspiration; yet our Law <note>likely referring to Christian doctrine or Canon Law</note> affirms that lots are sent and governed by God. This is permitted to them so that, when a dispute arises among equals, they may avoid slander or offense. Of the most noble kind is **geomancy** <term>geomantica; a method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand</term>, constructed certainly with a wonderful logic: concerning which, the celebrated books under the name of **Peter of Abano** <note>original: "Petri Apponensis"; a famous 13th-century physician and astrologer who was later associated with the occult</note> are in circulation. And although certain friends of ours have used these things—not a little in jest—whether through confidence, or their own guiding star for divining, or aided by the protection of demons; nevertheless, we have declared the inconsistency of all these in the fourth book of *On Wisdom*. And **Diogenes** <note>Diogenes the Cynic, a Greek philosopher known for his skepticism</note> used to say: when I look upon this kind of men—the soothsayers or those predicting the future by lots—I think men are little different from beasts; yet when I look at doctors or painters, I think they are little different from gods. These things, therefore, have been said concerning the universal nature of things, not so that we might pursue every detail, or even a large part of them, but so that we might teach the examples, seeds, and principles of all. For indeed, if anyone understands how easily—and, so to speak, with no artifice—things are made by nature which he cannot grasp with his mind, and which he thinks consist of miraculous art, he will not only cease to marvel and will know many things by the example of one, but also, by translating from nature’s works to art, he himself will manufacture things admirable to others with no great labor. Let there be one such example instead of countless ones.

<margin>
Whence the variety of colors in flowers and skins.
</margin>
You see how beautifully and exactly the wings of **butterflies** are distinguished by colors; then the skins of leopards, panthers, cats, and so many other animals. And so many species of flowers are so elaborate that even a distinguished painter, with the greatest diligence, could not represent them to perfection. What then? Will these things—which seem to pertain specifically to the senses, and indeed to a very pure sense—be made (or could they be made) by nature as a craftsman devoid of intellect and sense? Or will the care of the **Supreme Craftsman** <note>God as the "Artifex" or divine architect</note> be distracted by such small and numerous things? Will He Himself distinguish for us the flowers of the cyclamen, the triple-born cotton-plants of Jupiter, the iris, the meadow saffron, the heather, the henbane, and so many other herbs? Will He distinguish the stalks of white hellebore, or finally the whole peony? Far from it! But understand how such great craftsmanship is made without any art. Whatever things are mixed by fortune, however they are distinguished by colors, and without any reasoning—whether they grow, or are divided equally, or are inflated—they display a form distinguished by colors, adorned exactly, and very beautifully depicted. Therefore, the wings of butterflies and the leaves of flowers are divided, and they grow and swell like glass vessels; for when the mass is distinguished, as if in passing, with white, once it is inflated, those colors...

It also discusses the validity of divination, like geomancy, and marvels at how nature produces complex beauty—such as butterfly wings and flowers—through simple physical processes rather than laborious "art."</summary>

<page-num>370</page-num>
<header>Book Twenty-One</header>

# Book Twenty-One

...renders those things distinct by equal intervals. Now you see: if someone wished to have a painted panel, or rather a work variegated with **mosaic-like labor**, with colors mixed into a mass by chance; if that mass were then cut across at equal depths, the hardened pieces would reflect the form of a most beautiful tablet and produce an eternal work, since the colors cannot be washed away. Therefore, you see how the image of the universe shines back in these things: for many things come forth from one, and the unequal from the equal, the artistic from the fortuitous, and the ordered from the disordered. In the same way, from the one God, the supreme and constant craftsman of all, so many things proceed with a certain easy equality.

<margin>In how many ways evils excel over goods.</margin>
But you will say: if God is the author of all, why do evils excel over goods in speed, ease, frequency, and magnitude? In an hour, or rather in a moment, we fall into ruin and become weak; but to be enriched or healed, a long time is needed. A massive evil arrives by chance or by a single word; yet we are scarcely saved by many friends and aids. Finally, in fortune, there are so many griefs, pains, diseases, infamy, unrequited love, fear, and poverty; while there is only one good: not to be in want.

<margin>The end of goods is freedom from pain.</margin>
For this reason, the **Epicureans** <note>Followers of the Greek philosopher Epicurus (341–270 BCE), who taught that the greatest good was the absence of pain and fear.</note> seem to have rightly determined that **freedom from pain** <term>indolentia; a translation of the Greek term 'ataraxia,' meaning a state of serene calmness and lack of physical suffering</term> is the goal of all goods. But in terms of magnitude, what pleasure can be compared to torture? What hope to fear? What happiness to bereavement? What delight to imprisonment? What health to disease? Or what riches can equal the inconveniences of poverty? Finally, there is that end of all things, **death**, the mere thought of which cannot be outweighed by the joys of a thousand lives; yet it has this much good: that it puts an end to all other sorrows.

<margin>Why we love our sons more than harlots.</margin>
Just as we hate death, so we love our sons as if they were ourselves made anew: they are our only aid against that inevitable end. For they are of us, they preserve our appearance, and they reflect our very selves. Therefore, we love them more than **harlots** <note>original: "scorta"; the author is contrasting deep familial love with fleeting carnal desire</note>, even if more is wasted on women for their own sake.

<margin>Why sexual love delights more than scratching an itch.</margin>
For the sake of sons, **Venus** <note>original: "venus"; here used as a metonym for sexual intercourse or the drive to procreate</note> was also made more pleasant by the Creator. For when bodies are joined, because that which provokes it is internal and involves the least amount of pain, therefore—although the tickling sensation is of the same genus as **an itch** <term>scabiei; literally "scabies" or mange, used here to describe the physical sensation of an itch that demands scratching</term>—that sense is far more pleasant. Thus, by this invention, the First Cause provided for the perpetuity of living things.

<margin>How cause, principle, and occasion differ.</margin>
Furthermore, **cause**, **principle**, and **occasion** <note>The author is making a Scholastic distinction between the underlying reason (cause), the starting point or pretext (principle), and the favorable timing (occasion).</note> differ in the conduct of affairs, not only in nature. For we say the **cause** for Alexander crossing into Asia was the easy victory of the Athenians over **Artaxerxes and Xerxes** <note>Persian Kings; the author suggests Greek military history proved the Persians could be defeated</note>, as well as the expedition of **Agesilaus** <note>A King of Sparta who campaigned in Asia Minor</note>, who occupied part of Asia in a very short time; from these, hope was born in Alexander. The **principle** is what Kings use to veil the suspicion of greed and ambition—such as the Persians' crossing into Greece, or the slaughter of Persian ambassadors perpetrated by the Macedonians. The **occasion** was the death of **Philip** <note>Philip II of Macedon, Alexander's father</note>, who left behind battle-hardened armies and a Greece exhausted by disasters, so that all those people sided with Alexander either out of favor or fear.

<margin>What God is.</margin>
But God is not like this; rather, He is the cause, origin, fountain, and principle of all these things that are in the universe. He is the immense whole and the highest perfection, and He contemplates nothing other than Himself. He exists in such light that He alone can contain it, and with such clarity He illuminates both this world and that one, and whatever exists at the furthest edge of the spheres. He is immovable, without variation, and no mortal can sustain His splendor for even a moment, or look upon His brilliance...

<meta>This page concludes the twenty-one books of Jerome Cardano’s "On Subtlety." The previous page discussed the nature of providence and why evil exists in a world created by a good God, using the metaphor of a mosaic or a painted panel to show how divine order emerges from complexity.</meta>

<header>On God and the Universe.</header>
<page-num>371</page-num>

# On God and the Universe.

...can perceive. You could more easily endure the midsummer sun at noon with your eyes for a whole year than you could contemplate the light of God with your intellect for the smallest part of time. To which, however, when one is carried, he is most blessed in that single moment. For this is that **ecstasy** <note>In the Neoplatonic sense, a state of being "outside oneself" to achieve union with the divine.</note>, granted only to the best and wisest, which is better than all human happiness. It is the most subtle substance, and therefore it always rests; for those things which are most subtle are either always moved, like the heavens, or always rest, like the intellect. God, however, is not the intellect, but something far better, more blessed, more powerful, and more worthy than the intellect. You ask then what He is: if I knew, I would be God; for no one has known God, nor does anyone know what He is, except God alone. Since we do not know what He is, much less is it granted to us to know His proper name.

<margin>God and the intelligences lack a name.</margin>
But neither is there a name for the intelligences <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "intelligences" refers to the celestial spirits or angels that move the heavenly spheres.</note>: for there is no name for God, nor for the intelligences. Rather, we use names imposed on them by the imagination we have conceived of them, speaking of their power, or clarity, or dignity. Many things have also been fabricated by wicked men, with which they have dared to babble about God as if He were one of us. But names are taken from the nature of things, and the powers and properties known to us; yet we have taught that the nature of the intelligences—and much more the nature of the sublime God—is unknown to our intellect in every respect. Therefore, in what way will there be any name for the intelligences or for God, or how will it be permissible to impose one?

<margin>Epilogue.</margin>
Here then is the end of the books *On Subtlety*, the material of which does not admit a more elegant style; the multitude of things does not allow it to be shorter; the difficulty does not allow it to be clearer; and the variety does not allow it to be more ordered.

<margin>Thanksgiving.</margin>
> You, therefore, most high God, from whom all good things flow forth, by whose nod all things are moved, whose empire is bounded by no limits, infinite clarity, who alone offers the true light, alone truly eternal, whole within yourself, known only to yourself, whose wisdom exceeds all thought, one and incomparable, outside of whom there is nothing, who directed me—like a worm of the earth—in the shadow of knowledge, to whom I owe whatever of truth is written here; my ambition, rashness, and haste gave birth to the errors: forgive me, and by your unwearied liberality, direct my mind to better things by illuminating it. Since you indeed need nothing, nor can I add anything, I offer perpetual thanks for the innumerable benefits toward me, as do the heavens and the powers of the heavens, the seas and lands, and all the parts of the world itself.

## by Johann Petreius, in the year
## of salvation 1550.

The beauty of this little book <note>The Latin term *libellus* (little book) was often used by Renaissance authors as a modest way to refer to their scholarly treatises.</note>, which you recently published, drew me to add this ornament. My intention was to better acknowledge you and your literary virtues, through which I wished to repay this labor as if it were a deserved favor of gratitude. However, since I knew you were not at all desirous of such things, and because I could provide nothing else that would make this little book more elegant, nothing has compelled me to speak at such length about so great a matter except for the desire that you should know this writing is to be accepted from me as a pledge of my perpetual goodwill toward you. Certainly, nothing in this attempt could delight me more than to indicate to you that I am not unworthy of myself; and though I wish I could add something of a better kind of gift to send to you, I hope at least that, in keeping with the perpetual goodwill of my heart toward you, this little book will be accepted by you as a kind of pledge.
</unclear>
